Update - 21/11/15 Unfinished base game with poor review score has returned to store after new rereleased  "base game plus extra units - Titans" has moved past its initial launch period...
Ok, there is a lot of anger over this release and to be honest it is understandable. This game is a re-release of the original Planetary annihilation with a few extras thrown in and then sold for £29.99! (This has become quite common during these hard times just rereleasing what should have been dlc packaged with the base game and then sold for a premium price).
I was torn about purchasing (supporting this practise,see end opinion) this. I was given a 66% discount as I had already purchased the base game but even then it rankled me knowing it was basically dlc. In the end I treated it as such and got it.  Having spent a few hours trying out all the additions I can say its fairly disappointing. Everything added is what the base game needs to reach a decent state.
I feel sorry for anyone who has the base game alone as its basically unfinished. This full priced "dlc" brings the base game to a finished state and as such should have been patched in arguably for free.
Now that is out of the way... I enjoy the presentation and mechanics of the game itself. I play primarily in single player and skirmishes. Altho the Galactic war single player non campaign (just a series of skirmish matches) has been rather boring so far as in 15 odd matches the ai has not moved, at all... It builds a few buildings then... nothing... This is on normal difficulty. It will happily stay there for hours as I build up all around it. Unfortunately my ai companion is on steroids and obliterates the non-ai every match in minutes making the whole campaign pointless so far...
It is a real shame that no effort was put into making the single player campaign more immersive. I understand that is not the intended goal but to tack on a non campaign is pitiful. I can just hit a skirmish match and get a better experience every time. Wasted opportunity. I suppose it ticks the boxes as it is present but in a most lacklustre fashion.
What this dlc brings to the base game is a lot of needed variety to the units. A handful of titan units, tutorial, bounty mode (more fluff) and slightly altered terrain (also in base game), altho in a very artificial tacked on manner. Dont expect mountains, valleys or anything of the kind. Just a slightly elevated series of platforms that look like they have been pasted on. So basically a lot of extra units.
What should have happened :
Base game remains. Dlc called "Titans" added for £6.99 max. Optionally add more actual content and call it an expansion £12.99. Result - happy customers and reviews resulting in more happy customers, hence more money.
Release future series of dlc/expansions. Happy customers purchase them. Look at crusader kings 2. I have spent a fortune on dlc/expansions which bring meaningful changes to the game and also by the way put 80% of the features of the dlc into the base game for free.
What happened:
Update - 21/11/15 Unfinished base game with poor review score has returned to store after new rereleased  "base game plus extra units - Titans" has moved past its initial launch period...
Base game effectively abandoned and removed from store. (cynical customers might wonder if it was to hide the poor review score. I personally recommended it. ) Dlc called "Titans" branded as standalone added for £29.99. Result - unhappy customers and negative reviews resulting in less customers. Hence less money.
Yes the money men will say if 100k buy it at £29.99 its better than 300k buying it at £6.99 in the shortterm. At the expense of reputation and goodwill. Your reaping the costs now. No amount of countering reviews will change that or removing base games or arguing adding 6 big units and 20 small ones and rebranding the game and selling it twice is a good thing.
This really grates me. This game should be massive. Instead it stalled not due to the gameplay so much as the business model and direction surrounding it which is a real real shame.
So overall:
If you own the original and dont intend to purchase this premium dlc I offer my condolences. You have effectively been abandoned. You have an unfinished game that I doubt will ever reach a finished state.
If you have not purchased the original or are contemplating doing so due to the low price, dont. Wait for this one to go on sale a few months down the line.
I will not recommend it based on the price and the effective abandonment of the original, removing it from steam. I can not support this style of selling games.

The first Tales game, what I actually like.
- The story and the characters are finaly interesting, and I care for them, not like Zestiria, where I was so bored after hours of playing. No matter how sympathetic Sorey and his friends tried to be, I cared too little for them to continue. This is not the case with Velvet, Laphicet, Rokurou and the others. You can realy like them.
- The combat is fast, and easy to use. It has a lot of details, which can later make it more difficult. But if you are just here for the story, there is easy walking mode too.
- The graphics are beautiful, colorful, and detailed. The best of the anime style.
- Only con, that can make you feel the game slow is the narrative and the dialogs, but give it the time it needs to tell the tale. It is not boring.
I can only recommend it to anyone, who loves JRPG, and story-based games.

What an awesome game!
I read about this game before it launched and the idea was intriguing so I added it to my wishlist. A few months later I noticed it was part of Groupies Be Mine 14 Bundle so I paid $5 and picked it up.
For the next few months CONSORTIUM languished in my game queue until last week when I finally decided to dive in--and dive into another reality I did!
CONSORTIUM's story kept me guessing until the end. In fact, I need to replay the game or parts of it to unlock sections of the story I didn't find during my first play-through.
And the ending... Holy crap! When is CONSORTIUM 2 coming out? I want to play it right now!
Before I started my play-through I read about CONSORTIUM's rough launch and all the bugs people encountered but, after 12+ hours of playtime I have yet to encounter a single problem; it looks like just about everything was fixed.
Even though CONSORTIUM doesn't have state-of-the-art graphics I can't help but think the game is beautiful. The character models' cartoony style is perfect and they don't detract from the story, voice acting or gameplay.
I appreciate that Interdimensional Games Inc. focused on the more meaningful parts of the game, e.g: story, mechanics, and UI, rather than trying to (as an indie studio with a small budget) create a game with out-of-this-world graphics.
CONSORTIUM is one of the best games I've played in the last year.
Thank you Interdimensional Games Inc. for providing the experience. I'm looking forward to CONSORTIUM 2--don't disappoint me!

RPG MO truely is a kickback to old-school online RPGs.  The graphics and gameplay are very nostalgic and addictive, and I can honestly say that it wasn't hard to put a couple hundred hours into this game.  With that being said,  I can't recommend it -- why, you might ask?  It may sound cliche, but, that's right, you got it, the management. :/
(*As an initial note, I have never been muted or banned in the entirety of my gameplay.*)
I'm not going to generalize, because the majority of the mods (who simply love and play the game enough to volunteer their time to help keep the peace) are nice folks, and very level-headed.  However, it's impossible to play the game for a decent amount of time without witnessing at least couple of them (who shall remain unnamed), show an insane amount of bias towards certain players they like (who shall also remained unnamed), or act out in entirely immature ways that just cannot be respected.
This wouldn't be such a problem, except they are immune to criticism.  Openly voicing your concern will get you muted/banned (as I've witnessed happen on many occasions), and reporting said behavior to the developers is useless, because they also show favoritism and immaturity.  If you take a gander through posts and replies that the developer had made to reviews, you can view this child-like temperament in action.
It's a damn shame, because the game has promise, but I can't see suitable growth or longetivity in the future, simply because of the lack of professionalism.
Long story short:
Pros -
*Old-school flavor
*Interesting maps to explore
*Addictive gameplay
*Consistent updates
*Helpful and friendly player-base
*Balanced cash shop
Cons -
*No animations (as of yet)
*Clunky movement
*Little variation between different skills
*Repetitive, mindless quests
*Unprofessional and power abusive mods
*Immature management
Playing RPG MO is like grinding away on one of your old nostalgic MMO's, all the while a rag-tag crew of fragile-egoed toddlers are in control of your account's fate.

Starting off by saying this is the best cast of playables since Abyss. Everyone plays off one another, have a backstory thats not too out of the way to explore, and everyone has some sort of painless development (okay maybe Velvet has a segment where she is just intolerable...but so was Luke fon Fabre in Abyss and we forgave him by the end of that game).
Coherent story, with plausible motivations for the characters. While darker than most Tales games, its still an easy to digest game (no pun intended).
Played through with English dub, and everyone did a splendid job with some minor annoyance (Kamoana being most annoying voice, one skit where audio for unnamed youth did not play) but being one of the few English localised Tales titles to have dubbed skits is pretty darn good. Will do New Game+ in Japanese audio and really looking forward to it.
Visually there are some jarring low resolution textures, but that is expected of a game built on an old engine. Still overall presentation is quite well done. Since there were four artists who worked on the characters, some of them looks out of place but for those within the playable cast, it just fits. In-engine scenes were also done well, usually transitioning into gameplay very fluidly. While draw distance is not the greatest, it works for the game since enemies have a leash range so its not like they'll chase you across the map or for you to see whats way below the canyon, etc. Dungeons for the most part are bland, just corridors of enemies (feels almost like FFXIII dungeon design) but you can typically tell what leads to the boss and what leads to a corridor for loot. Larger areas are also bit bland, having not much enemies relative to the map size and just feels like a lot of empty space but at least the scenary is nice.
Music: I only have an issue with the short loops (BGM) that sounds like it happens too frequently throughout the game; there just not many memorable tunes. Sound effects are on point. The intro by FLOW is also not a disappointment.
Gameplay wise, as Tales is a action heavy combat system, the SG system makes this game feels much more like Dynasty Warriors like (spammy, arcadey, fast) while the balance against button mashing is from enemy having resistences to damage types. It works but outside of the reflect only enemies, there should be more unique requirement among enemy types to make them stand out, but sadly once you fight a particular archetype of a mob, you pretty much do it against all variations of that said mob. Bosses, especially the antagonist force and Code Red bosses, were actually quite enjoyable to fight against (bump the difficulty up to at least hard, they're a joke on normal and moderate, and no one should be doing boss fights on simple unless you really just want the story or against Phoenix). Note though this might be the first Tales games I've played in awhile where consumable feels useful, partly because healing in this game just sucks (the good one having a rediculous cast time, better off disabiling all healing artes on every character when playing on hard+). Having progression tied to mastering equipment also nice, scratches the completionist itch while actually feel like there is progress on character strength. Randomised abilities also adds to the incentive to grind loot. Unfortunately, unless you're playing on simple and even then the drop rate is tosh, items with no randomised abilities is actually needed (disassembled into Odorless Fluid) to upgrade rare gear and those are not frequent enough to come by to have a steady supply. Geoboard is an alright subsitude for mount system for a game without a proper overworld, wish there was a faster option though (not counting teleporting potions). Having bosses (dire foe, code red, etc) drop items that actually expands gameplay is nice especially those that drop specific possible randomised skills on weapons since you can control the RNG a bit, but also adds to the completionist journey. For the most part, I wished the dungeons had more than just basic switch puzzles (coloured plant, coloured mana field, activating a path switch) and maybe something more complex cause dungeons don't offer much other than mobs on a long hallway with the occasionaly chest (and if they're not the first time gold chest, its generally garbage). Collecting Katz spirits and random sparkling object (honestly why do I even need to press the action button for these...) doesn't feel very rewarding either (partly because I do not care for cosmetics). That said, I have not touched much of the minigames (not feeling like I want to grind for cosmetic items) so I cannot comment on how they would play but historically minigames are just a timesink in past Tales titles).
Other thoughts: surprisingly theres not much fanservice and works quite well for this game, the free DLC help allievate the Odorless Fluid issue a little bit but because everything is in a set together you also get high end enhancing material as well that can potentially make things easier, but this is easily offset by playing on Hard (I honestly feel the game is best balanced around Hard for the first playthrough).
Going to eventually do NG+ and maybe I'll update this afterwards. Still this is probably one of the better JRPG of 2017, definitely the best one on PC at least.

In terms of compelling characters, it's strong, but it also has the downside of typical tropes. It's very easy to see where most of the characters are coming from and how they developed their personalities save for one character. A character that I think saved this game from being a bit bland. Without Magilou, a character you meet at the start of the game, the other characters and the dynamic would be incredibly bland. Take any of the other characters out and replace them for stone walls and it wouldn't truly matter. Before you learn more of these character's stories, initially it's easy to see what motivates each of them besides Magilou. For me it was sort of that curiosity and the way her dialogue works with the group that made me stick to it more than I would have. Magikazam!
The combat hurts in certain areas that I feel they could have let loose on. Attacks are limited in terms of souls that equate to one attack per soul. It also has a semi-limiting factor of stamina within those souls. While you may have enough souls to perform three attacks, the cost of those attacks may exceed the total stamina you have to perform them. When you don't have enough stamina, your character basically gets countered for a minor amount of damage and you can lose souls for it. While it's good to pay attention in combat, I feel that it's a bit too severe of a punishment for it. In terms of making attacks, I do enjoy the fact you can pause the game and change your combo sets to make use of vulnerablilities, but I feel they made too much o a focus on that. Some attacks feel very fluid and work together well, but may not work on an opponent with certain resistances. It almost nullifies the damage and makes you change yoru combat style.
The story is very straight forward and doesn't take many twists or turns along the way. It's written out pretty well from the very very beginning and doesn't deviate much other than adding on more that you have to do than you initially thought. A common thing to prolong game play. It's compelling enough to see how you will get to your goal that it does pull you in along the way, but if you're not one to really grab onto story, it might lose you half way in. The things that I found to help along the story were the side quests as they weren't actually annoying like in other RPGs. They let you have more insight into the characters and helped you form a bond with them that was relevant to their feelings and emotions. The things that didn't really help with the story was the long time it took to run around the map. You get some speed buffs along the way, but it's not nearly enough to make up for the fact you have to obtain them by walking even more.
I took my time with the game and left it running for some time, but it took me less than 45 hours. Even with doing almost 100% of the side quests and monster hunts, it wasn't that much time to finish. If you were to only play the main story, I'd say you'd get 30 hours or less out of this game.

This is not a bad game... but, its not that good either. I didnt beat the game but I did sink around 27 hrs into this game and reached the half way mark (ignore what steam says). This game is a somewhat boring action/adventure game. I wouldnt call it a JRPG or even a RPG (maybe). The reason being that the combat is not turn based and also there isnt much (arguably any) role playing either. This is the fifth "tales of" Ive played and most of the problems it has carry over from the previous titles. Some of the problems include long 10-20 min sessions of empty walking to get to objectives, back tracking after that and endless amounts of (avoidable) trash mobs.
Surprisingly though I think this is the best tales of games so far. It performs faily well on PC, has interesting characters, nice cutscenes, and the combat system feels more fluid and less clunky than the previous tales games. If you are a die-hard fan of this series then I guess you will LOVE Berseria.
But, I dont think I can recommend it in general. The game's pacing is kinda dragy, the combat gets annoying after awhile, the plot does have its holes, the dungeons/levels are pretty drab and empty, and the game is a bit too easy even on the harder difficulties. The gameplay feels pretty "Brain dead" (sorry for using that word), the quests are almost always just go from place A to B and combat really doesn't involve a lot of skill or strategy. Lot of the game mechanics like cooking or gathering the kat souls for cosmetics feel pointless and forcibly stitched into the game as well. There are a lot of weird issues with this game.
On the whole this is an average action/adventure game. There are better and cheaper action games and RPGs/JRPGs on steam especially considering the fact that Berseria is 50 quid. If you are a long time fan or just want a casual psuedo RPG to turn off your brain and kill time then I guess u can buy it, In all other cases this game might not be for you (atleast wait till it goes on sale).

Sadly I have to say NO.
Why? I'm a fan of the game - since SFII - and I've enjoyed every release. But this one in particular is very unstable.
This game is focused to the pro fighting gamers, Not so bad so far, but they forgot the common user. Yes, Ono said "this game is basic to play but hard to master". They put a lame story mode - very different from USF4 that it had animated openings and endings - with bad quality drawings and a lame cpu difficulty in story mode.
Also the gameserver is really unstable: They try to fix every bug they find - the beta was awesome - but right now, even if they say they fixed it, it puts you waiting for a match every 5 or 10 minutes - even 15 - that is a game killer experience.  It this game is thought to be competitive via online, how is it possibe to have a terrible matchmaking service? Sometimes, the servers don't accept the game results, wasting your time in getting PL points.
Unlike its older brother - USF4 - It doesn't have a search for ranked match in order to find opponents. It is awful and nasty. Why waiting for 5 to 15 minutes instead looking for people who want to play ranked? Imagination can help to fix things, but it seems that the programmers doesn't have a brain to solve constant problems in matchmaking.
Lobbies are still primitive. They work from time to time, So far you can invite ONLY ONE FRIEND to play. It is interesting to see FT3, FT5 or FT10. However, it is advised to ADD FRIENDS FIRST before creating the lobbies via CFN, Here is another mistake. In you have steam and you're my friend, I need to add you TWICE: Steam & CFN. Even in your case, to add me as a friend you need to repeat this process TWICE.
Although arcade mode is not a must for me, several, LOTS OF PEOPLE are asking for it. And they're right. How a fighting game doesn't have an arcade mode?
Graphics are not properly optimized for this game. Several slowdowns even offline kills the game.
Even with the promise to include more characters, arcade mode and an almost 2 hours story mode animated via GPU, this game feels incomplete. I love this game, but the online experience kills it almost immediately. I looked this game for online, but it feels crappy. The netcode is perfect, but the frequence of the matchmaking makes you wish to find matches in USF4, where you find ranked matches almost immediately.
Sites like Gameradar, IGN and EGM were paid to do a review 24 HOURS BEFORE THE GAME WAS RELEASED. Now, where it goes those high scores? Really, I don't trust gamimg press anymore.
Final words: Like this game: Yes. Like the online platform: NO. Like the options the game has: NO.
So the qualification is NO. NOT RECOMMENDED UNTIL EVERYTHING IS FIXED.

I very much wanted to like this game. I enjoy the loop of going out into the field fighting aliens, researching what you find to create new equipment and abilities for your soldiers, and then fighting harder and more dense alien groups. I like the ominous nature of how the story is told, and indeed, how cutthroat some of the missions can be. I have played many turn-based strategy games and enjoyed the majority of them, such as XCOM: Enemy Unknown, all the Harebrained Shadowrun titles and Shadowrun Chronicles, The Banner Saga 1 & 2, Divinity: Original Sin 1 & 2, Invisible Inc., Card Hunter, Pit People, etc.
However, XCOM 2 does not feel much like a turn-based strategy game to me. As Sherif Saed mentions in his VG247 article on the game, "you're always reacting." XCOM 2 is a game more about acknowledging that bad things will happen, and that you will constantly be asked to make decisions with entirely incomplete information. This doesn't mean it's necessarily a bad game, but I do feel like it's a bad strategy game. Whereas Dark Souls is considered "hard but fair," XCOM 2 is "hard and unfair."
Whenever things went bad for me in a mission of XCOM 2, I never felt like I could "go back to the drawing board" and come up with a new strategy. This is the aspect I enjoy about strategy games, and it felt entirely absent from this title. I generally felt like I made the best decisions I could with the information I had available. The majority of missions have a turn timer. When this timer hits zero, the mission ends abruptly. This forces the player to often make reckless decisions to reach an objective. When missions went bad, I often just started rooting for the aliens, just resigning myself to watching them blow the heads off of my soldiers.
I felt that the number of enemies was often overwhelming, the power of enemy abilities was always just a bit higher than mine, and that my weapons were never quite good enough. Research that I would start would never finish when it was still relevant, and I could never finish scanning anything without being interrupted by a civilian rescue mission or some other urgent thing I was "strongly advised" not to skip, although all of my most best soldiers were still recuperating. I would come up with a plan to attack an enemy base in a world region I had yet to contact, only to be constantly interrupted at the worst times imaginable. Hours and hours would pass, real-time, and I would not reach the mission to attack the base.
Though I'm not religious, I've heard the phrase "If you want to make God laugh, tell him about your plans." I feel like the same could be said about XCOM 2. If I want to get wrecked by things I couldn't possibly have foreseen, I'll just go live my life. One reason I enjoy video games is the reliable causality - it's probably no surprise that I don't prefer roguelikes.

The X-Com series has always been one of my favorite PC games of all time. I loved the first X-Com and played the Saga through X-Com Apocalypse.
When the modern X-Com came out I had to pre-order. The game was great, it had its faults but overhaul for the old fans and new fans alike. It was a great game that could bridge the experience of the old titles with modern features without alienating anyone. The first game was a win also for PC Gaming showing that titles are not limited to the typical genres like the dominating FPS type.
The second game doesn't stray too much from the formula, but once you got a winning team you really don't want to change it. It has some changes which sprinkle the game with some diversity and new features but overhaul the two games aren't very different. It feels like a progressive evolution rather than a radical change which is good in my opinion.
With the added new expansion, War of the Chosen, which is great on its own and completely worth the price, the game gets a lot of new mechanics which are very welcomed. War of the Chosen resembles a bit of the Nemesis system used in the Shadow of War game but retrofitted for X-Com.
It is a great game with unlimited hours of fun joy and frustration (it wouldn't be an X-Com game if your soldiers wouldn't miss an 80% shot twice in a row would it?).
If I had to recommend a game for fans of turn-based strategy, this would be it. To be honest, if I could only pick a game to take with me to a deserted island this would probably be it because of the replay value.
Would buy again will definitely keep replaying in the foreseeable feature or until we get X-Com 3!

Right away I'll get to my biggest, but by no means only, positive here - character customization. My God, the customization. First names, last names, nicknames/callsigns, armor camouflage and colors, weapon camouflage and colors, accessories, different armor models, a massive array of colors for the aforementioned armor and weapons, ethnicities, nationalities, personal backstories; you can really, REALLY get carried away designing your army of anti-alien commandos and commandoettes. Oh, and then there's the Steam Workshop, so if you want to make an army of Spartans or clone troopers, have at it. Want to outfit 'em with modern/contemporary weapons? Hit subscribe and you're solid.
Now as for the story/plot - the premise here is a rather interesting twist on an alien invasion story: in a nutshell, we lost. The aliens didn't enslave the world - not directly, but they have a puppet army that polices everybody. XCOM began as a multi-national alien fighting force, and now it's a rebel movement. Sounds awesome and really opens a lot of gameplay doors, so to speak, to accomodate a resistance fighter story. You can buy resources from a black market; you have to protect rebel sympathizers from retaliation strikes; you can choose different hit and run operations; you raid enemy transport supply lines; those are just the basics and the "norm".
One final positive (but not the last one overall in this review) is in the game's diversity. I'm not even joking when I say that there are roughly 20 if not slightly more enemy types you'll have to do the tango with. It starts from basic foot soldiers with assault rifles and starts climbing up to things like mind controlling aliens with long range wrist lasers, snakes that can pull your troopers in with its tongue and wrap around them like a boa constrictor (even though the things are based and named after vipers), the aforementioned foot soldiers but with stun swords, shapeshifting pudding monsters, and so on, all the way up to giant 15 foot robots that, as the game states, were used as the equivalent and counter to human tanks, which is what they essentially are. Now mind you - I've just mentioned only six enemy types. There are many, many more that are introduced, though the examples I gave weren't in any particular order, I should mention.
There are only two problems with this game. One's a major issue while the other one's just a hemmorhage.
The issue is that the game's story and gameplay have what's essentially a ticking time bomb called the "Avatar Project" (mentioning it is NOT a spoiler. Explaining what it is would be a spoiler) that forces you to race against time to avoid losing the game, which happens if the Avatar Project initiates and you don't do anything to push it back. Now some players thrive for that challenge; I am not one of them, and I can see a lot of people sort of intrigued by the game's Steam page and videos, but entirely unaware of this twist of sorts. There are mods and game file tweaks that can be performed to stop it, thankfully.
The pain in the♥♥♥♥♥is the combat algorithm, so to speak, of combat, where the game is based solely on hit percentages determined by things such as perks, the distance between targets, and weapon damage and stats (with boosts in the form of attachments). You would not believe how many "Oh my GOD..." moments you'll have when a soldier with a shotgun is standing right next to an alien or ADVENT soldier with a 90 or even 100% chance to hit, and instead of pulling a Corporal Hicks "EAT THIS!" move, the guy aims the shotgun and then just jerks it to the side and misses the shot like a Stormtrooper. This happens a lot, and it insults your logic and patience a bit because there are countless moments beyond the example I gave where your XCOM operatives will have a perfect kill but will almost deliberately miss. Thankfully the aliens have this issue as well sometimes, though it's more annoying on the player's end since you should by all rights have gotten that kill.
Graphics are great, the gameplay is fairly unique for a strategy game since it's a turn-based strategy where each unit has actions, and once those actions have been spent then the unit cannot be used until the next turn.
XCOM 2; I highly, highly, HIGHLY recommend it. It's one of my favorite strategy games, and perhaps my favorite series of customization of your characters, to the point where you will actually grow attached to them and feel literal grief if they should die in the line of duty. Get a towel to cry into before you start playing this game.

The game :
Planetary Annihilation is a RTS of large scale with thousens of units on a planetary scale. For the first time you can *Anihilate* planets in real time to humiliate youre opponent. You can desimate youre enemy in many ways; Nuclear missiles, massive army of bots, build teleports to sneak behind their defence lines, blast a moon into theire home planet or ultimately annihilate the planet with a *death star* Unfortunately most of the time the game end before you can build such super weapons.
Gameplay :
It is classic RTS. You build a base, gather ressources; energy and matter, build an army and fight. You will have land vehicles, Bots, air units, ships, orbital units and Titans. All class with their unique abilities like: anti tank, anti air or both... You will have to make a good balance of all to succeed.
Multiplayer :
Multiplayer in PA is unique. You can make youre own custom planetary system and try endless of possibilities. There is a nice matchmaking for 1vs1 for quick battles. There is no custom setup as of disabling some unit or tech for now.
Singleplayer :
The galactic conquest offer a different gameplay compared to the regular skirmish or multiplayer. You start with basic tech *less unit* and as you conquer more systems you will get more unit/tech. There is no factions or story in the game but there is a background story in the conquest.
Score:
Gameplay: 5/10
+large scale battles
-No factions
Multiplayer: 8/10
+Many choice of strategy
Singleplayer: 1/10
-No story
Overall: 5/10

This game is seriously boss!  I picked it up on a Steam sale after reading how awesome the graphics were and thinking about Grand Theft Auto V.  What is impressive about this game is that the hand-to-hand combat is as deep and fun as the driving and the gunplay.  Plus, this game has a much more interesting and intense story than many other action games, despite being very much an open world RPG!  United Front skillfully blended the action, RPG elements, and open world concept so successfully that as soon as it was over, I wanted more.  The game is not terribly long but not short enough to be insufficient for a great experience.  The story is very linear and there are not a ton of side missions.  Those that are there are pretty repetitive; bust drug dealers, take down rival gangs, steal cars, races, etc.  All fun things, but you don't want to do the same things over and over again.  There are also bugging minigames, karaoke, and some dating involved.  I don't remember any nudity (unfortunately) but plenty of violence and gore.  For the most part, it's not superfluous and contributes to the character aspects and development of the factions involved.  Environment attacks are excepted because it's just plain disgusting to throw someone into a running AC unit and shred their face off.  However, by the end of the game, you REALLY WANT to do this to the antagonist.  The one thing I can say that I wish were possible with this game were multiple endings (just a few ways to go) consider the whole storyline.  Without spoiling it, there is a thread of ambiguity that permeates the events of this game that appears to give you some freedom and choice, but it doesn't appear to affect the outcome, which makes one question why this would be allowed at all?  It is ultimately only the illusion of choice, which could be frustrating to someone if they were not completely turned on by the story.  However, that is very unlikely based on my experience because of the quality writing, superb professional voice-acting, and gripping content.  Despite this moderate flaw, it's an understandable and at the end, whether you wish you could have done things differently and actually made a choice in how the story ends, the ending is still extremely satisfying.  Overall, this game is quite an accomplishment and definitely one I'm glad I've played.  If the rumors of a sequel are true, I would be among the first to buy it just because I enjoyed the Sleeping Dogs so much.  It's totally worth it at the regular price on Steam, and an incredible value if you can get it on sale!  Just buy it now if you like open world action RPGs when an emphasis on the RPG.  Excellent work, developers.  Keep putting out♥♥♥♥♥♥like this and you'll draw a hardcore fanbase of RPG players.

One of the best games from 2012 in my opinion, Sleeping Dogs puts you in the middle of the action during a gang war between the members of the Hong Gong Triad. As an undercover cop who has deep connections to the area and people, the story has a unique perspective of duty and revenge.
Visual and Audio 9.5/10
I cannot say enough about how beautiful Sleeping Dogs makes Hong Kong look. The visuals are crisp and detailed and its stylized use color makes the city around you really pop out. However the most impressive thing about Sleeping Dogs is just how much that it packs into the screen at any given moment. It’s not really that there is that much going on but that there is never an empty space on the screen, there is always either people, cars, rival gangs, cops, buildings, or street vendors in view; and you can see clearly down a city street for a few block without the game having to limit those details. Sleeping Dogs isn’t without its problems however, character models looked a little stiff during some actions and at times and during cut scenes some of the characters movements didn’t really work in the engine. On the audio side I found the voice acting to be good but not great, and the sounds of the city start to repeat and get old towards the end. Sleeping Dogs does also have an in car radio like many of its contemporaries, and while I did find myself going to download a view of the songs after the playing the game it didn’t have the same type of feel that games like Saints Row: The Third gives.
Story 9.0/10
Overall the story in Sleeping Dogs is great, however it suffers from a campaign that in my opinion was a little bit too long, and a few missions that could have been taken out in general. While most of the missions did do a good job of introducing you to new side missions, game mechanics, or other additional content it felt a bit forced at times. The game has a dual level up mechanic, one for doing good or Cop actions, and one for bad or Triad actions. However despite how you want to play the story makes your Character come off a♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes even if you want to play the good guy. However these are minor complaints and the twists and major plot points will definitely keep you playing.
Game Mechanics 8.5/10
I applaud Sleeping Dogs for its use of melee combat instead of the safer bet of fully automatic gun mayhem, however the combat just doesn’t work and flow as well as a game like Batman Arkham City. You get more attacks by finding collectibles in the game but most of these moves are less practical to just left and right clicking. Besides this the driving is good, but unless you playing with a controller you’re still going to suffer from the mouse and keyboards limited car control. And of course for a game that pins itself as “open world” there have to be side missions, which in most cases I didn’t bother to do after trying them once, the exception being drug busts as it let my play around the melee combat.
Overall 9.0/10
While this game might not have scored as high as other games I’ve played I couldn’t recommend it more. While it didn’t do the best job at some of its mechanics and presentation it shouldn’t be punished for trying something new. In wake of the teased new Sleeping Dogs game I would pick this one up and play it, or just download it if you have it and haven’t played it yet.

While the visuals and the cast and story are pretty good, the game is horribly, -horribly- hindered by absolutely abysmal gameplay design.
Those of you familiar with how the Tales series handles its combat, this game, along with Zestiria, handled things differently. And poorly.
If you played Zestiria, here's what you need to know: Issues were alleviated, but nothing was fixed.
I won't go into the story, but let me list the issues I have with the gameplay...
1: Combo-based combat scenarios are tailor-made for only four out of the six main characters. The remaining two were severely snubbed in their performance, and it makes them fail to carry out a proper combat role.
2: Combat roles are extremely diluted as well, and massively lacking in variety. There's essentially three sets of two that each function largely identical. You've got quick melee hitters with no spells, quick melee hitters with some spells, and slow melee hitters with some spells. And before you ask, no, the slow melee hitters do -not- do more damage with their attacks to compensate for how slow they are.
Whereas older style Tales games had distinct classes, such as dedicated healers, dedicated spellcasters, dedicated heavy hitters, dedicated swift attackers, etc., Berseria is content with having three 'middle of the road' classes and distributing those among a cast of six.
3: While status effects were a nuisance in older Tales games, in Berseria, they've been made infinitely worse. Rather than just afflicting you with all kinds of hindrances, status effects in Berseria also block -all- incoming healing, and last inordinately long. Enemies have a very high chance of afflicting targets with status effects if they hit you, so if you get hit once, you're likely to wind up dead.
4: To make matters worse, every status effect has one healing spell that counters it. One spell can clear a burn, one can clear a slow, one can clear paralysis... none can clear poison... The real kicker is that all these healing spells are distributed among the party members, meaning that only one person in your party can clear a burn, a different person can clear paralysis, etc. Is that person not in your party? Too bad, no heals.
5: The band-aid solution to this awful game mechanism is character swapping. By expending a hard to come by resource, you can swap characters mid-fight. This action will cleanse your status effect... But it will also swap you off the character you wanted to play. You can switch back of course, but again, only if you have that resource.
6: This is generally an overarching theme: Character swapping. There are five elements in the game: Fire, Water, Earth, Air and Neutral. Every character is aligned with a couple of them. One has fire, water, neutral, the other has fire, earth and neutral, one has earth and air, one has water and fire, etc. If enemies are resistant to your main element, you're better off swapping out to a character you do not want to play.
7: The equipment is more manageable than it was in Zestiria, but still a complete mess. Each piece of gear has three set skills, and a few slots for random skills, and it carries two different stats. Unlike in previous games, new, higher grade equipment isn't usually an upgrade. In fact, most of the time, it's a downgrade. Those two slow melees, for example, get an awful lot of equipment that boosts their physical attack, when they're clearly better off with magic attack items considering they're extremely likely to get killed if they use their normal attacks.
Equipment is handed out like candy, and it makes it extremely difficult to manage your inventory and keep track of what you want to scrap for upgrade components and what you actually need to upgrade, unless you don't mind playing spreadsheet simulator for 5 minutes after -every- -single- -battle-.
To recap, whereas previous Tales games like Symphonia were all about offering a variety of different playstyles and encouraged you to have fun with whatever character you like best, whether that's the agile swordsman or the cataclysm-calling mage, in Berseria, everything has been thrown out the window to create some sort of challenge-hunting experience. It's no longer about what you -want- to do, but instead entirely about what you -have- to do. You -have- to rearrange your party for that status effect, or that element, you -have- to swap off if you get hit, you -have- to build your characters in just the right way.
I'd be fine if that was just the hardest difficulty, but it's not. It's moderate.
All of these gameplay design blunders make for a very frustrating experience if you stubbornly try to play the game in a way you enjoy. If you don't care about what you personally want from the game and just play the main character and roll your face across the keyboard after pressing R, maybe you can enjoy a nice 'cinematic experience'.
But for me, this is utter, utter garbage.

There's two ways you can look at this game from a recommendation/review standpoint: that of a regular casual gamer, or that of a fairly hardcore, specifically fighting game player. I lean more towards the latter.
From the view of a casual, regular gamer:
This game, and especially its release, is a travesty. A bare bones (arguably unfinished) game, released with nearly no content for a casual, and released with fundamentally broken online. To be perfectly frank, if you do not love fighting games I couldn't possibly recommend the game in it's release-day form to anyone. That being said, however, there are still some redeeming qualities for the casual gamer. A gigantic barrier to entry in the fighting game genre has always been execution. Thankfully with this release in the franchise, that has been somewhat addressed. The very relaxed input execution requirement, along with much much lower reliance on long, complex combos puts this as one of the most accessible Street Fighter games in recent memory to a player new to the genre. A cast of characters that has no real worthless slots, as well as likable new additions, means you won't accidently make the "wrong" choice in picking a character and putting time into them. For a game that tries to be both the premier, top end eSports fighting game, while also tries to be accommodating and welcoming to new players, I think it skirts that line better than most others.
From the perspective of a seasoned fighting game player... with a bit of patience:
This game is dope, and does dope♥♥♥♥♥♥ As of this writing, online has more or less been entirely fixed in under a week. The online netcode itself is rock solid, playing 4-5 connection players is a dream, with 3-5 only having the slightest bit of rollback if you happen to snag a player from across the country (or in another one all together). Lobbies (for me at least) don't have anymore problems, with multiple slots being added in the future. All the characters are not only playable, but have the tools to be incredibly competitive, as well as just fun as hell. The big changes in core gameplay from SF4 are welcomed, enjoyable, and needed. With a constant stream of new characters coming near-monthly from Capcom, the roster looks to swell larger than it's ever been over the life of the game. Some elitist vets think the game is "too easy" now. Well that's great news for them, that means it should be an easy $500k for them this year! Somehow I doubt that's going to be the case, however....
TL;DR - If you love fighting games, this is it. It's absolutely fun and playable right this second and will only get better. You're going to be playing this for the next 4+ years minimum. Get it. Non-negotiable. If you're not a hardcore fighting game fanatic, but want an excellent, accessible intro to the series and fighters in general, I'd recommend it but possibly when it's on sale, or once they add all the casual content to the game.

I have very few insightful things to say about this game. But I'll try.
All my friends tried to get me into this game. I was skeptical.
After meeting the devs at Pax West 2016, I played it and I flippin' loved it. No one told me about the things that actually sold me on the game.
It has a very robust in-game economy. I dig that.
It has developers that care and actively try to improve the game. I really dig that.
It's not one of those theme park WoW type MMOs, and it doesn't try to grab your money at every given opprotunity. I REALLY dig that.
If you really want, since the paid currency is buyable in a tradable form and sellable over the in-game marketplace, nothing is truly 'behind a pay wall'. That's RAD.
The progression system is kind of like a collect-a-thon, y'know, games like Banjo and SM64 that were popular back in the N64 era. Basically, the more stuff you collect, the better.
For emotionally-invested hoarders like me, being able to use my old gear as components to upgrade my other gear is AWESOME.
There's a creative building sort of element, if you dig that. Some people make very elaborate scuptures, music rollercoasters, stuff like that. This happens away from the combat, usually, in a 'club world' with your friends. But... you also get a 'cornerstone', which is a buildable plot which you can plop down in the more combative areas, and move to other areas later. You can make it simple, or elaborate, or anything in between, but it's really cool.
It's just super rad. Give it a shot sometime.

Game's got really good graphics and sounds. Stages seem to be very detailed, even including the occasional destruction of background objects. Fighting seems to have a good flow to it.
Unfortunately, the game, as it is now, is pretty barebones in regards to content in the single player side. Story mode as it is now is comprised of three fights with one round each, which is, in my opinion, too little. There's not even a basic arcade mode with 8 to 10 3-round fights like before.
Capcom also seems to have done away with a lot of supers that were avalable for returning characters. Most characters have only one super in the command list, which may have some slightly different gameplay element if done under V-Trigger. Whereas in USFIV, each character could have 3 or even more supers/ultras.
Not to mention the occasional server trouble this game gets. Why oh why does this game need to log in to a server if we want to play story mode or survival with battle requests on OFF? And why does the game need to knock you out of the fight, into the menu if it loses its connection to servers during a Hard Mode survival run (on stage 34)?
Buy it if you want the multiplayer. Or if you intend to get into eSports.
Forget about this game for now if you want single player. Gamers are better off waiting until the full story mode is released in june.

The fighting system itself is fantastic.  Characters appear balanced so far for a new title, and it is accessible to newer players and deeper for veterans.  I forsee this game being the staple in the FGC for a long time.
HOWEVER, at this time, the game feels like an Early Access title.  The UI is unintuitive and littered with bugs.  The online segment, while fantastic when it works, is plagued with constant disconnects and broken matchmaking.  For a game that relies so heavily on internet connection to reach its potential, releasing a game with so many problems is criminal.
There is almost no single player content to be had, save for the mildy amusing Story mode.  Even then, that mode is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and clearly rushed out the door.  The artwork is fine and the voice acting serviceable, but the matches are over too fast and do not give a challenge.
There is a great game in here somewhere, and once Capcom fixes its issues I will be happy to change my review.  Until then, I cannot recommend this game.
*EDIT* 3/29/16 - With the recent update and the forthcoming Alex DLC, the future of SFV is looking more promising.  Connections appear to be more stable (for myself, at least) and the 8 player battle lobbies are functioning well.  Buy this game when you find it under $50.

Bastion has to be one of the best games I've played in literal years, and that's no hyperbole. The narration and story is what really drew me in, though. The story is well-executed, letting the player put together the subtle elements of the world into place instead of just handing it to them ready-made, and the use of narration is unintrusive to the actual gameplay whilst still adding a personality to the world and its few inhabitants.
Overall, I'd suggest this to any action-RPG fans, or anyone looking for a good balance between gameplay, art and story in a game.

TL;DR: Massive improvement over Sanctum 1. Leveling system doesn't feel grindy, and helps to introduce old and new sanctum players into the new towers and features. Multiplayer can be annoying sometimes with trolls public play, but overall the community is helpful and welcoming. Playing with friends is very rewarding and fun.
Let's start from the top. If it is not obvious already, Sanctum 2 is the sequel to Sanctum, the Unreal Engine-based game that came on the scene slow at first before it made a big breakout on Steam, prompting this sequel.
First impressions from a Sanctum 1 player: WOW, this game has fixed a lot of gameplay annoyances that the first Sanctum had. Sanctum 2 has trashed the high, inaccessible walls of its predecessor with more sensible barriers that the player can actually mantle. Also, towers can now be partially upgraded in between the proper "levels" so no more sitting on 99 credits that can't do anything because you are one short of the upgrade. All of your towers maxed out? You can now OVERCHARGE them with excess money, with diminishing returns of course.
Next up, the UI. Another massive improvement. Sanctum 1 didn't really give great descriptions of each tower, and the stats of towers were not as easy to read, so knowing the proper abilities of a tower (essential for a Tower Defense game) couldn't be done at a glance. Now, a simple mouse over on the tower tells the player everything they need to know, and range is displayed in a helpful holographic overlay.
Now, the new progression system, at first it may trigger the eyeroll of shoving grindy RPG elements where they don't belong, but the implementation is solid. The player isn't hamstrung from completing levels due to being a lower level. Grinding simply doesn't happen, in the since that you don't find yourself needing to repeat levels endlessly. You can however, enable "Feats of Strength" when you replay old levels to substantially increase difficulty (and your XP reward) if you find yourself wanting to level faster. Being low level also doesn't exclude you from playing with higher level players. Because each player is limited to a certain number of tower and perk slots, you can always find a niche to fill in multiplayer (I enjoy playing the rocket launcher character and managing airborne minions).
Overall, I can't see a reason not to get this game if you enjoy Tower Defense or Action Shooters for that matter. Sanctum offers short, replayable fun for a very low price. Buy this game!

This game could be summed up in "GTA with Triads". And that's a great thing.
First because Hong Kong and the Chinese gangster scene isn't a properly explored field in gaming as a whole. So you have a rich universe, deep characters and an immersive, breathing city, all wrapped up in gorgeous art direction and graphics and nice gameplay.
I won't write about the plot, because in my opinion, the impact and involvement is always stronger when you arrive unbiased. But I can say the story develops as a good Chinese cop movie, with nods to 70's grindhouse flicks and even B-movies here and there.
You have a huge city to explore, on foot or using one out of a crapload of vehicles at your disposal (one way or another). You have tons of stuff to do other than the story missions (favors, jobs, collectibles, events, fight clubs, street races, collectibles, challenges among your friends via Social Hub... did I say collectibles?). A very nice experience for the regular OCD gamer.
The game focuses on fighting instead of gun firing, and I also liked this a lot. Dozens of bone-breaking, spine-chilling ultraviolent moves to beat the heck out of bad guys. Then you jump in a car and engage into an action movie chase, driving with one hand and shooting enemies' tires with the other. Explosions and slow motions abound. Situations like this are common.
One thing that caught my attention is the missions never get repetitive. Or at least they don't look as much. Even if you're using the same mechanics, you're always doing different stuff. There's the obligatory fetch quests. You scare people who don't pay your boss. You take your girlfriend for a stroll. You hijack armored trucks. You hack cameras, pick locks, plant bugs. You break into a guy's house to mess with his Feng Shui. There's even a mission where you must sing horribly in karaoke, on purpose, to help a guy convince his girlfriend to leave the place. How 'bout that?
The voice acting is very good, and the vehicles you take give access to several radios of different styles of music, from 80s pop to hard rock, cheesy Asian tunes and even classical. Nothing compares to find yourself running away from the police while listening to Debussy's Clair de Lune.
I played this via Big Picture with a 360 controller and the experience was pretty tight. I had no technical problems.
Had good laughs with this game. And "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; moments, and edge-of-seat moments, and "In yo face punk!" moments. So I highly recommed this game and the extra DLC chapters (Zodiac Tournament, Year of the Snake, Nightmare), which are also tons of fun.

EDIT: While the below review still holds true for the most part, after having played the game more, I've come to the conclusion that Sanctum 2 has much more of a learning curve than Sanctum. Sanctum is pretty easy to just jump into and enjoy, while Sanctum 2 requires you to learn how to really play the game and get some specific upgrades before it starts being really good. However, once you get to that point, it is a great experience possibly even better than the first despite the shortcomings.
I give this a thumbs up overall because it is still a fun game; the blending of FPS and tower defense that is Sanctum is here, the maze-making strategy is here, and the multiplayer is better and more worthwhile than before. There are some good new features, but as a fan who loved and played a lot of the first, I am disappointed with a lot of the things they did here. But I'll start with the good:
Multiple characters to choose from adds a new element of strategy, and equipping appropriate perks adds further. As all bonuses that can theoretically stack together do, equipping each character with appropriate perks for the best results is a welcome addition to the franchise that allows players to experiment for the combos that best suit them.
Maps are much better designed than in the first Sanctum with much more attention to detail and more thought in strategic use of the environment. The campaign and leveling system are also a welcome addition, giving a feeling of progress, though some unlocks may take a bit too long to unlock. Lastly, there's a wider range of guns and towers available to choose from.
It also looks really nice graphically.
But now, the disappointments. I know this is a new game and shouldn't just be compared to the first, but as this is a sequel, things should get better, not worse, and a comparison will be necessary to make my point.
Most of my issues can be summed up as such: the maps may be bigger, but the game feels so much smaller. Customization was supposed to be an important upgrade from Sanctum to Sanctum 2, but I honestly feel like the first had better customization. Number of guns allowed to each player has been reduced from 3 to 2, with 1 of those being locked to the character until capping your level, meaning only one weapon can actually be chosen for any given character, AND they can no longer be upgraded. Yet despite this, the game is actually more FPS-centric due to the limits on blocks and towers, as even without any feats of strength activated one can't really get away with just towers, again unlike the first, making for fewer different ways to actually play the game.
Number of towers brought to a map maxes out at 4 per player, down from the 6 of the original. Additionally, floors are gone completely and Holo tower and Televators have also left the building, leaving basically only the two slowing towers to support the FPS aspect at all, and no guns which do the reverse (Freeze is gone), severing that integration completely aside from a few perks. Also, towers can only be upgraded to level 3 instead of 6, after which they go into "overcharge," which is just throwing as many extra resources as you want at it to make it more continually more powerful, and I guess is basically the same thing.
Blocks - now tower bases - are limited and given out per wave instead of costing a small amount of resources, preventing players from really building a maze until the map is over, seeing as maps are not longer than 10 waves, which was the shortest in the previous game, where it went as high as 30 in standard mode. Additionally, only 15 towers can actually be built per map, and the base cost of them has increased as much as 10x, no exaggeration; base Gatling now costs 100 instead of 10, and resources given hasn't increased to compensate (if anything it's lower). I guess as compensation upgrade costs don't increase as you continue to upgrade, but it doesn't matter much since they only go to level 3 and then overcharge anyway.
What's the point of the maps being so big if I can only realistically use small portions of them?
Good multiplayer is definitely not a bad thing in my book, but the game kind of shafts solo players. Many maps have multiple entry points for the enemies, occasionally in ways that prevent the two sides from ever joining before the core (and some have two cores), requiring a solo player to juggle two sides, a problem compounded further by the limitations to blocks and towers. A few of these maps existing would be fine, but not as many as there are here, especially since televators are no longer around to allow the player to move around quickly.
The game is definitely a better multiplayer experience than single. It can be played single player, but it will be frustrating at times. Best to get a friend or two in on the action. Again, still a good game overall. If you liked Sanctum but thought it needed some improving, this might be for you. If you liked a lot of things in Sanctum, give it a shot, but be careful.

If you haven't picked up Planetary Annhilation yet, then this is a great time to do so. TITANS adds so many new ways to bring about chaotic destruction on your enemies; combined with the newer features such as asteroids, game saving, resume from replay, its far ahead in features of the admittably poorly timed release of Planetary Annihilation (sans TITANS). While there may be some optimization gains yet to be had, the game plays reliably enough to be fun much more than it is frustrating. Lobbying is no longer a waiting game, and for those who prefer to go it alone, the AI gets more devilish with each passing month, and the  dedicated single player mode has received some much needed revamps. I personally am a huge fan of the map editor - this tool alone gives Planetary Annihilation, and TITANS by extension, so much variation and replayability to be worth the asking price alone. The map editor is quite powerful and can create some truly striking maps. The fact that the engine plays along with your monstrous creations without a fuss really shows just what a great job Uber Entertainment has done. Not to mention that mods are all but officially supported, and you have hundreds of hours of entertainment for even tentative RTS fans. The developers are fairly involved; not only can you often post on the forums and get a reply, but they also hang around in the in-game (modded-in) chat (look for PA Stats) and answer questions. As someone who played a lot of Command and Conquer, especially Red Alert, back in my day, I have to say that I really enjoy this take on the RTS genre; and as someone who rarely played online in my Command and Conquer days, I have to say that online mode is a lot more accessible for newbies and hardcore players alike.
TL;DR: Buy this game, it is absolutely better than before. Definitely worth it if you don't own the original Planetary Annihilation, and I personally still think worth it even if you own PA. If you're feeling cheap... well there will probably be sales, given how often the first iteration of PA went on sale.
FYI, I have over 400 hours with the first Planetary Annhilation, in case you are scared off by the much smaller TITANS game time.

Absolutely everything possible if you're willing to devote the time? Your own private island? Farming and fishing? Olden-tymie graphics? Free-fer-realsies? On paper, this is my perfect game.

As for the grind -- hey, they're real up-front about it being grind-tastic, and they sure aren't kidding. A small and tame example: I wanted to build a house on my island because, hello, a house on my island. Each square of floor requires 300 logs. Your maximum capacity, between inventory and pets, is 55. There is a set rate/speed at which chopping can be attempted, and a high chance of failing to score yourself a single log. There is also a hike between where you can chop trees and where you can stash the logs for future building.
This is also one of the lowest tier woods and one that's easily accessible. We're not even talking walls and furniture yet.

Today, I’m talking about a little first-person action-adventure game called CONSORTIUM. Developed and self-published by Interdimensional Games, Inc. The games development had its start in a successful Kickstarter campaign, which leads us to what we have today. CONSORTIUM’s story starts off with you, the player, travelling forward through time, and to a parallel universe, thanks to a satellite that allows us to connect to a sentient A.I. that exists in the other universe. In this future universe, it seems that everything is just about perfect. Global hunger, energy, and poverty problems has been resolved for the most part, and all forms of war have almost completely ceased. We have people living in space, on the moon, on Mars, you name it. But can things ever really be perfect?
Consortium1You take the role of someone named Bishop Six, a field agent and peacekeeper of sorts in the Consortium, a society dedicated to protecting the galaxy or something. But all is not well, as soon after you arrive on your ship, the Zenlil, one of your shipmates is found dead in their bunkroom. Believing them to have been murdered by another shipmate, you are commanded to begin interrogating your shipmates to find out who the traitor is. If that weren’t enough, you also have the problem of a band of outlaws currently looking to take down your ship. It’s up to you to solve the mystery behind the murder, and take down the outlaws, among other things. But you better watch out, nobody can know where you’re really from, otherwise you might end up causing a temporal breakdown and destroy the universe!
So, let me tell you right now: Gameplay is where this game really shines. CONSORTIUM really isn’t an action game, so much as it is an immersive story told through its great character dialogue, its mysteries, and the in-game lore that comes with it. You communicate to the other characters on the ship through simple button presses, similar to a Telltale game. Alternatively, you can choose to say nothing and make everything awkward with your constant silence. Like I said before, one of the major goals is trying to find out who the murderer on your ship is, but naturally, things can never just be that simple. News gets spread fast on Zenlil, and before you know it, everybody on the ship knows what has happened, which naturally freaks them out. As you question and get to know your shipmates, you find that quite a few of them are less trustworthy than they appear, and others seem way too nervous or in some cases, optimistic about the whole situation. But, for those of you out there who decide that there isn’t enough shooting involved, there ARE action segments included with the game. Depending on how you choose to interact with other characters, you will be forced to engage in combat with bloodthirsty mercenaries who invade your ship, or shoot down enemy spaceships. You are also given the choice of capturing, or outright killing their leader. Just remember: Gameplay, as well as the story itself, might turn out differently depending on what you’ve chosen to do or not do.Consortium3
Everything looks decent in terms of graphics, but the game was built on the constantly aging Source Engine, so you probably shouldn’t expect anything too fancy. Because it IS Source though, you can be almost certain that CONSORTIUM will run on even the lowest-end of gaming PCs. The sound effects are pretty good too, really helping encapsulate that claustrophobic feeling of being on a small little spaceship. The music is absolutely fantastic, but what do you expect when it’s composed by none other than Jeremy Soule, the same guy who did the music for such great games as Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, and Knights of the Old Republic? The developers really use the music to their advantage here when it comes to telling the story, and really puts an emphasis on the importance of what’s going on around you.
If there was one major flaw I could point out about this game, it’s that it was too short for my tastes. If you want a short, but good little immersive plot-central game, I recommend you try out CONSORTIUM. It’s currently on sale on Steam for $19.99.

A fantastic breakthrough in the 'horror' genre. I never enjoyed any horror games until I found this one. The main point of this edgy game is the 'AI Director' which generates unique experiences for each playthrough of each of the campaigns. No playthrough is the same twice, and various infected will always pop up in random places. Same goes for pickups like pain pills to give you an edge when you're low on health, or weapons. They all appear in different places, so you never know what to expect. The characters are throughly created, and fully fleshed out, with witty dialog and a system that allows them to respond uniquely to various events and situations, everything from being healed for a second time in 5 minutes, to weathered speech when you're pretty beat up and complaining about it. A fantastic co-op title, that strongly encourages actual cooperative interactions, and has a fun movie theme with a credit rollout at the end, and poster introductions. Buy!

Left 4 Dead is a co-op game where you and three friends will have to survive hordes of infected people. You can be Bill, the old veteran, Francis, the biker, Louis, the IT guy and Zoey, the student girl. You can also play alone while the rest of the teams are bots. You will have to survive infected people but also special ones like the Smoker that can grab you with its tongue, the Hunter, that jumps on you, the Boomer, that vomits on you, making you attract infected, the Tank, the big bad boy that is hard to kill or the Witch, that you shouldn't disturb if you don't want to be on the ground.
Indeed, the game allows you to be incapacited for a few seconds. People have to help you else you're dead. And you'll respawn in a closet further in the game. Also, you can be healed as there are health packs. You can also boost it thanks to the famous pills. You have few weapons (sniper rifle, shotgun, rifle and pistols) but you can also push the enemies back if needed. You have also pipe bombs and molotov cocktails.
The infected are mainly attracted by loud sounds, so you bet that when you have to activate generators or move bridges or anything else, you'll have an horde on you. Generally, this is a moment where you have to battle until you can escape. The end of a campaign is generally the biggest fight. But the best is the AI director that will change the experience each time: if you're doing well, expect more difficulties, if you're not, less enemies will be there for example.
You have initially four campaigns. Since then, there are two campaigns that were added: one called Crash Course, with 2 levels only but they're kinda long and another called the Sacrifice, that was tied to Left 4 Dead 2.
You have also a versus mode where you're against a human team: at each turn, one will be special infected and the others the survivors's team. So you can be a Boomer, Smoker, Hunter or even a Tank! The goal is to prevent the survivors reaching the safehouse while as survivors, well, it's to reach safety.
The graphics are quite good and the soundtrack is excellent.
Left 4 Dead is an excellent FPS, single or co-op game. Humor is there, the adrenaline is there and given the different difficulties, it's for novices like hardcore gamers.

Squad choice/customization is improved, as is the combat in general (particularly overwatch turns), and procedural maps system is better (though still somewhat lacking and 'samey'), but it falls down on the base/resource management side of the game for me.  Watching a counter go down to gain resources in place of a mission is somewhat disappointing, and counters are a feature of XCOM2, for the worse in my opinion.  The clock of doom is also somewhat annoying, as it limits the freedom to plate spin for a while and gain some experience/swag, and turn sensitive missions are too frequent, especially when playing on harder levels.  And the 'tombola' aspect of research is illogical and I'm generally confused as to why they chose that system - is Chen so dumb that she doesn't make notes and thus be able to re-create her findings to manufacture a Blaster Launcher or HazMat Armour at will?  I'd think not, but Firaxis beg to differ.
On it's current comparison to the original UFO: Enemy Unknown, there have been some leanings that way but the freedom of the original is still missing.  Everything is still very 'prescribed' - you must do this research, you must do this mission, etc.  To aside a little, not knowing when you arrived at an Alien Base in the original whether there was even going to be a Commander there was half the fun.  Scanning their minds to work out who might be worth knocking out, or none, when you felt like it, not when the game says you must.  Yea you can ignore the 'advice' in XCOM2 but there's no gain to that but like I say, it's all a bit too prescribed and forced compared to the original.
I did enjoy the game, but as I say, with caveats.  Mods notwithstanding, XCOM2's re-playabiity is limited due to the timer annoyance.

I've only just recently gotten into the XCOM series after my friend gifted me the first game, after putting 41 hours into that I knew I needed the second game so I grabbed the deluxe edition plus War of the Chosen as I wanted to experience everything the game had to offer. I finished the game today after putting 80 hours into it, so it was definitely money well spent.
Overall I much preferred the sequel, it was improved in almost every way, with big additions, features and more subtle changes that made for a very enjoyable experience. It really felt like the devs learned a lot from the first game, and implemented a lot of fixes and changes the community wanted. One big area of improvement are the cut-scenes, they're very high quality this time around, and they run smoothly as they're videos, and not rendered in engine like in XCOM 1 (30fps videos look fine, 30fps in engine does not), they really helped to tell the story which was interesting, the voice work was also fantastic.
There is one area where XCOM 2 sadly falls short and that's performance, the game is not optimised well at all, you will find countless people complaining about this issue so please don't think it's just me. Any form of explosions will cause big drops in frame rate, as will anything that causes debris to spawn. Also certain mission/mob types also tank the frame rate, it's just not good enough. The game also "freezes" quite often while it calculates, something that never happened in the first game, the issue gets worse the further you get into the game as abilities and enemies get more complex. It really did hurt the game for me, so much so it went from a weak 9 into a strong 8. That being said I still obviously enjoyed it a lot and highly recommend it, just be aware it does have technical problems if you're bothered by that sort of thing.

is a visual novel and dating stat simulator that is the sequel to
.  Now, before I go any further, I'll point out that even though I did play
, I wasn't a fan of it, so I never wrote a review of the game.  (Suffice it to say that my reasons for disliking
had mostly to do with the MC Amy.  I didn't like her personality in that game.)  However, I put aside any prejudices going into
and I'll just state it outright.  In my opinion,
is a much better, improved sequel.
At the end of
, Amy ended up with one of four possible guys: Aaron, Eddy, Hugh, or Lawrence.
picks up from that and when you start the game, you can choose which one of the guys you want to continue the story from and then you can choose whether to play purely in visual novel mode or a combination of visual novel mode and a stat simulator.  However, please note that if you choose to play only in visual novel mode, you won't be able to unlock certain stat-based epilogues and if you're an achievement completionist, this might prove to be a tad annoying.  Obviously, I chose to play with both visual novel mode and stat simulator so that I could unlock all of the endings.  Speaking of endings, with each guy, you can have a total of 5 different endings (2 happy, 2 sad, 1 normal) and 2 different stat-based epilogue endings (1 happy, 1 sad).  Assuming that you choose to play with the stat simulator, the objective is to reach certain goals (i.e. getting a certain number of points for a particular stat like romance, diligence, creativity, culture) to get a 100% happy or sad ending and then to max out on the stat related to the guy that you're pursuing (which is stated right at the top of the stat builder screen) to get the special stat-based epilogue ending.  Thus, there is definitely lots of replayability in this game although it is understandable that the stat building could get tedious for those who are not fans of this game's aspect.
Now as to my personal opinion of this game, I liked it a lot.  As I stated earlier, it's definitely better than
.  I like the idea of a game where you can find out if your marriage/relationship will survive after you get your love interest, and I found that there were scenes in
which felt like those that could happen in real life.  Such examples include a workaholic spouse and an overbearing parent entering the picture.  The art is just as beautiful as in its predecessor.  I liked the stat building myself but as I said before, I can understand if there are those who are not fans of this aspect.
Overall, I enjoyed
a lot and if you're looking for a relaxing VN and slightly challenging stat builder to play, then definitely give this one a look.  It was great to see the developer come up with this idea for a game and I only wish that there were more such games that take such initiative and put a fresh spin on dating sims.  ^^
