I enjoyed this game, and since 'Always Remember Me' was one of the first Winter Wolves' games I ever played, it was great to catch up with the characters. I am delighted by the general premise, that the story doesn't stop at the 'happy ending', that married life can be tough and as much of an adventure as dating.
The art style is very familiar for fans of Winter Wolves' games, though they have re-used quite a bit of artwork (mostly background) from other games, which means Amy may be living in the house the characters 'Roommates' inhabited, and the same town as 'Nicole' went to university. However this is a minor detail and can largely be ignored in favour of story and characters.
The game follows on from the special endings of 'Always Remember Me' with the protagonist, Amy, married to whichever boy you picked. (You can set which route you want to play, so no need for save games). Each marriage has it's own set of problems, from jealousy, to recovering from abuse. Amy is just as much a wet blanket as she was in the first game, but this does at least make the few moments when she asserts herself all the more satisfying, even if this does occasionally lead to the sad ending. I'm not sure if the message here is 'Never stand up for yourself or you'll end up alone' or 'Tact and diplomacy are important life skills'. There are a few minor issues, such as a therapist telling her client that (potentially violent) jealousy just means her husband loves her very much, and taking his side about an assault against the protagonist. But mostly the game is enjoyable and reasonably compelling.
At any rate this game is effectively 4 games in one, each route features 5 different endings (two sad, two happy, one neutral) as well as special epilogues (one for happy endings, one for sad endings).
The game can be played as a visual novel (which is useful if you wish to replay a favourite story), or as a visual novel tied to a stat raising system reminiscent of 'Heirs and Graces'.
All in all this game is delightful, though simple. No competition for Winter Wolves' best games, but still pretty solid provided you like the protagonist.

Trove, though it looks like a childish Minecraft style MMO, is actually a hardcore RPG with tons of content with a wide range of difficulty. At first, the game seems easy while you get eased into what is actually a vast game that will take tons of time to beat on just one class... let alone ~15 which can all be accessed and leveled/geared separately on the same character. Appearance customization, though limited to the "pixely" style of the game, is beautiful and flooded with the most options I have ever seen in an RPG. Of course, the coolest costumes and other cosmetics cost real money or are really hard to get, but everything in the real-money store can be purchased with ingame currency, granted it isn't cheap. Also, much of the game's progression can be skipped by paying real money, but since this isn't a PvP oriented game and the PvP actually balances out all the players' gear, the "pay-2win" has absolutely no effect on other players and free-2-play people can still reach endgame, just slower. Once past the tutorial, you will be left with A LOT of questions since the game doesn't teach you much past getting to level 10, doing dungeons, and doing Shadow Towers. Check the forums and feel free to ask questions in the global chat. The playerbase can be quite helpful, everyone who has spent enough time in the game knows that there is a tremendous amount of stuff to do that you don't get taught by the tutorial.
Currently, there are two major cons about Trove.
First is the emphasis on pure luck for much of the progression, especially in gems. Gems, for those who haven't yet played the game, are basically a piece of equipment. You acquire gems by opening gem boxes, which you get 1-4 per boss fight. Bosses can take a few seconds to beat if you're geared and know the shortcuts to reaching them, so getting a large number of gems isn't an issue. The problem with this system is the stat called Health Regeneration. This stat is universally considered useless, yet it is one of the stats that can appear on gems, along with both types of damage (magical and physical). Also, gems have quality ratings in the form of their rarity and the number of stars they have. Higher rarity and higher stars means the stats on the gem are higher and it increases your Power Rank more. So when you open 50 gem boxes, there is the possibility that NONE of the gems you get are a high enough rarity to even be worth equipping and even if you do get a rare gem, the odds of it having enough stars to be stronger than your previous gems are pathetic. So let's pretend you get super lucky, out of those 50 boxes you got a Stellar rarity gem and it has 3 stars (which is the maximum for a new gem)... Guess what, your amazing new gem probably has the wrong damage stat (magic on a physical class or physical on a magic class) and/or Health Regeneration. So after all that effort, your progress is 0 because that gem is trash. Eventually, you will get the right set of gems for your class after tons of grinding. Now you have to upgrade your gems. How do you do that? Well, you sacrifice the trash gems that you've collected to convert them to gem dust and then use that dust and some of the ingame currency to ATTEMPT to upgrade your gem. Now, for the first 5 or so gem levels, this is fairly easy and you will rarely fail an attempt. As you approach 10... then 15... then 20... then 25 levels, the amount of times you fail becomes agonizing. And if you fail an attempt, your gem can crack and you will need to buy an item with a difficult to acquire currency in order to restore it. There are ways to prevent the cracking and to increase your chances of success, but those aren't easily accessible until you are fairly high level.
Fortunately, there is a Karma system in the game so after every 70 boxes (or 35 if you are paying a subscription), you are guaranteed 1 high rarity gem. This still means you have to pray to RNGesus for high stars and the right stats, but it at least helps curb some of the nonsense RNG. The Karma system also applies to loot boxes, so you are always progressing towards rare mounts, wings, pets, etc. whenever you open a box. Karma even applies to upgrading gems, but is based on different critera, rather than having a set number of attempts to successfully upgrade.
The second con with the game is the server. When you are alone in a world, the game runs flawlessly. If, however, you join a world that is packed with players (ie. any time during the day), then you can expect SERIOUS lag. I mean HORRIBLE lag. Rubberbanding, teleporting through the floor, attacks not registering, instadeath, disconnects, etc. I am unable to use ranged classes AT ALL because ranged attacks simply do not register around 1/3rd of the time for me and that becomes NONE of the time during those laggy periods. I do not lag on other MMO's, my download speed is 900 Mb/s on Speedtest and other players complain about the servers all the time, this is DEFINITELY the Trion servers. The best way to avoid this kind of lag is to avoid areas that are packed with players and to play non-ranged classes if your hits aren't registering. I'm very happy solo farming with my Pirate Captain all throughout the week and doing group content (Shadow Tower and Hourly Raids) for the fat loot.
If you are interested in a fun, explorative and creative game with cool combat, amazing classes and character customization, an INSANE amount of stuff to do, a cool playerbase, and you don't mind grinding, then this is the game for you.

In it's current state, it's as good as a free to play game...maybe even worse. There's a disturbing lack of content for a supposed AAA title, that costs 70$.
Gameplay wise, it's fun, and much faster then previous SF's. I didn't really have any issues technically with launching or playing the game. That's about all that's positive. Oh, it also looks pretty.
The story mode is incredibly thin. It doesn't really offer anything in terms of cutscenes or a compelling story. You'll find yourself skipping over all the text just to get to the next match. From there, you'll probably head to training.
Training is also weak on features. The command list is paper thin as well, and only offers the absolute basic inputs for moves. Nothing to be found for possible combos, or links, or how properties change in V-Skill, or what counters do, crush counters etc. etc. So you're left being pretty uneducated after training mode. Which is strange, because Capcom has changed a lot of things in this version of SF, and you're going to want to spend some time in training to learn it all before you go online. Speaking of online....
It doesn't work. I routinely experienced log in errors, which completely handicaps the ENTIRE game. There's almost nothing to do offline, and even when you're offline, you're required to log in to the server. So the server shuts down, and occasionally takes your game with it. Your match is dead, sometimes the game freezes, and you're forced to shut down. It's a complete mess right now and isn't worth your time.
They've "promised" to fix issues, and update content at a later date, but the more people that buy this trash right now, will only push back that deadline. Don't buy this game.

Sleeping Dogs was originally going to be a direct sequel in the True Crime series many years before actually coming out. Thankfully, this never came to fruition. After a few changes, and a few publishers later, Sleeping Dogs came to be. Some will say it is the spiritual successor to the True Crime series. I'd like to think the connection never happened. Mainly because this game is just that good. Too good to be tied to a deservedly so dead series.
Sleeping Dogs takes place in Hong Kong, and has you playing the role of an undercover cop with ties to a small group of triads, as you work your way up through the ranks, and work from both sides, as a straight up police officer, and an undercover officer playing a triad member who gets in too deep. It's a risky business, but for our main protagonist Wei Shen, it's all part of his life now.
Sleeping Dogs is an open world action game modeled after games like Grand Theft Auto. You can run around freely, drive cars and ride motorcycles, and either take on main and side missions, or do other things as you progress through the game. Sadly, there is not much to do in terms of sandbox play. The world is very nicely detailed, and seems to be alive with the amount of people you will see moving about, but there just is not enough freedom to make this a real sandbox open world game. Most of the things you'll find yourself doing will be set up as part of the game instead. And anything you make up along the way will be few and far in between. Unlike open world games like San Andreas or Just Cause 2, where you can spend countless hours outside of any scripted events, making the game seem like your own little playground. This may be partially due to how constrained the world is. You can wander around streets, and inbetween buildings, and even inside of some, but the world is not as open as I would have liked it to be. Just don't be fooled by how big the map is, as lots of areas can not be accessed outside, due to barriers. Regardless, it is still a pretty big world. Just not ripe for exploration. Hopefully this gets remedied in the sequel.
As for action gameplay, its nice. You won't find yourself using guns often, but when you do, the cover system is decent, and aiming is not too bad. You even get a few max payne style moves, like slo-mo diving thrown in the mix. The star of the combat however would be the hand to hand stuff, which is reminiscent of the Batman Arkham games. You will not be one on one most of the time, but rather one on many. Weaving in and out, doing parries, and a number of nicely animated kicks, punches, and grapples with ease. It's almost like poetry to see it in motion. When you are running from cops, or chasing down the enemy, you'll also find that Wei Shen is a good master of parkour. You don't have a jump button sadly to just jump whenever, but instead the parkour is tied to platforms and obstacles. So you run up to a wall, and Wei Shen will run up and grab a ledge when hit the proper button. He can jump over gaps, slide over obstacles like cars and tables, and more. Again, this is quite nice to see in action.
As for the audio, it's fantastic. You have a nice selection of radio stations, featuring both HK Eastern and Western themed stations, full of commercials, and great music. You also have some amazingly done voice acting, helping to bring the story to life, with a cast of seasoned voice actors and tv and movie stars. The voice acting is also a mix of english and cantonese. Mostly english spoken, but a bit of cantonese here and there for authenticity. Some characters will also only speak in cantonese. While pedestrians will almost always speak in english. But the accents are just right even when spoken in english.
Sleeping Dogs may not be the ticket for anyone wanting a true sandbox open world game, but for those starving for a good action game with an open world set piece, and a great story. Sleeping Dogs is the perfect fix.

Consortium nails the communication with NPC part of RPGs.  If you enjoy the conversation part of games like Mass Effect but want it to be more meaningful you will love this game.  Unfortunately the combat is sparse, flat and buggy and the animations cartoonish.  The voice acting is decent which is huge since that’s most of the game.  On my first attempt I ended up in a shootout after a bunch of talking to NPCs, however there was a bug and the NPC bad guy was shooting before I even got close, so I started over.  On my second attempt I noticed that my changes in dialog really affected the direction of the story, unfortunately the story and dialog choices never interested me and I never felt engaged in my role, felt more like I was part of a Saturday morning cartoon world.  In addition the bugs and cartoony graphics really killed the immersion for me, which in a game where you spend most of the time talking to NPCs without immersion there is really no point.  I ended up getting bored and moved on to other games.
Consortium is alright I guess to see how conversation trees leading to different paths should be done, and I hope all the devs and talent involved in that aspect catch on with other studiosn (cough...bioware...cough) and impart some of Consortiums success on to big budget games in RPGs when it comes to dialog.  But as a game in its own right nailing the conversation aspect of RPGs only gets you so far when every other aspect of the game is bland or broken.

Within the first 45 minutes, I ran into 7 game crashing bugs, some of which, it couldn't detect that I was in the right room, or talking to someone stopped the story character from ever talking again, or characters being stuck in inaccesible areas when I needed to interact with them. Unfortunately, while the game has many innovative ideas, they often just don't work well. For example, the ability to fight battles on multiple planets sounds awesome, but does not work in practice. The game would've been far better off having a larger map size on a single map, because as it stands, the map sizes are very small.
Overall, Supreme Commander Forged Alliance remains the better game. Do yourself a favor and get that instead, and download the multiplayer client "forged alliance forever" which has a very active multiplayer community.

Tales of Berseria is, at the moment, the best JRPG I've played. The combat is fluid and while it does seem like a button masher at first it does have some depth to it. You get several moves you can assign to your skillset in order to perform them, each enemy has aweakness so this makes it flexible to always be geared up in order to exploit enemy weaknesses to your hearts content. You can also change how your teammate AI works so they can perform as well as you desire.
On top of that you have Mystic Artes (special moves) which, unlike previous Tales games which required certain conditions to be met, are activated by pressing a button during a combo chain which makes them flow much better. The best part is that you can even chain all the Mystic Artes of your party members in one move. If you have a controller then activate your Mystic Arte by pressing L2 during a combo then hold L2 and press right on your D-Pad, press right again till your fourth character does it then while holding L2 press up on your D-Pad then down. Note that this switches out the last character with whoever you had in reserve.
The characters are one of the main highlights as well. It's refreshing to play as a group of anti-heroes, at best, or villans, at worst, who are all in it for themselves rather than your normal JRPG heroes who do it because they're either chosen or want to save the world. For Velvet, the main protagonist, revenge always comes first before anything else. The rest of the characters are pretty great too, plus the character development really gets you to root for them.
The story is based around revenge, it's not very complicated and doesn't try to derail itself either. My only complaint is that the final dungeon has a bit of needless padding. The design is a bit tricky at first however the main problem is that the dungeon also contains each characters most powerful Mystic Arte as well and to get them you have to find a key for each of them and use them on the correct entrance in the dungeon which leads to a bossfight after which you get a Mystic Arte for one of your characters. That feels like needless padding since it feels like they could have been given any other way as well.
All in all I'd recommend this if you like good characters and good combat and just JRPGs in general.

It's pretty easy to look over a game, for some, like this. Retro, creation/destruction, simple physics and all around mish-mash of interesting ideas. But what sets this apart from other games in the same niche? Pretty simply...
It NEVER ENDS.
Seriously, I've logged my fair share of hours on the stable version (more to follow) and I've yet to actually find the end of any known universe. So if you're looking for replay value, well it's there. All you have to do is start a new character (which you can do at any time at any difficulty level) and BOOM! Universe served to your face on a silver platter with a golden spoon.
There is a drawback though, because they always exist. The game progresses quickly, but unless you want to see what the developers are up to in the stable version, you'll have to play the unstable one (for now). Eventually everything will be worked out, so if you have a little patience, or you're just plain nosy, it's worth the wait.
But wait! What the heck do you mean by stable and unstable, oh mighty reveiwer?! The stable version is bascially what WON'T cause your computer to POSSIBLY (emphasis on possibly) crash the game out. The bugs are worked out, and everything runs smooth. But you don't get the true Starbounder experience, in my honest-to-goodness-grit-loving-opinion (and who doesn't trust a guy who loves his grits?) Pfft, who wants THAT?! We want to see some action! Weird creatures! Shotguns to faces! Play the unstable version and you'll see that, and more. Pay attention to their almost daily updates on the internet or on Steam, and you'll see exactly what I'm talking about. However, that one is usually running ONLY at night, so if you have an early bed time or are old and tired, it may not suit your "gaming" style per se. However, if you'd kindly put your purse back on the floor and pull your man pants back on tight, we'll continue.
So you might ask yourself, "Hey self, doesn't this look a lot like terraria?" And Self might answer, "Why yes it does!" But it isn't Terraria. It's friggin SPACE. Yeah, there are guns, and bows, and armor, weapons of melee origin, and a little bit of magic, and it's pretty much based on energy consumption, but come on. Why wouldn't there be when you can play as a bird/monkey/star/fish flying a space ship? Seriously, get a grip on your briches, hold on tight, and welcome to the open ended universe!
By the way, did I mention bird/monkey/star/fish/man/shotgun/sniperrifle/crossbow/mosterboss/unending space GLORY?! Couldn't forget that now could we?

Another great installment in the XCOM franchise. I loved this game. It has all the elements of an excellent XCOM entry - great tactical depth and grueling difficulty. My only gripe is that it seems like a remix of the last title - there are Retialiation missions instead of Alien Abuductions, and all the same old aliens are here, with a few new modifcations. If you've played XCOM in the past, there's noting really new in terms of alien tactics, or even unit types. Each of the combat roles from previous games is filled in the same way with a differently skinned creature.
They did change a few things up. They tried to add urgency to the strategic layer and provide a forced time limit on the campaign with the Avatar timer. Rather than add a real sense of impending disaster, the Avatar meter just felt like an annoyance, not a source of real dramatic tension. There are also a few new tactical elements, like damage reducing Armor Ratings and status effects like burning and acid. But there is very little new in terms of style or depth.
Overall, if you like XCOM, you'll like this. I would like to see more depth in terms of various status effects and a wider variety of enemies. Where is the alien equivalent of the sniper class? Or the zombie-maker? Some of the most memorably frustrating things in the original XCOM games was getting nailed by an alien blaster launcher while all your soldiers are still debarking from the transport. Or watching your Colonel get stung Tentacault and turning into a zombie that then attacks and turns all your other soldiers into zombies. That kind of mayhem is missing here, and I want it back. Oh well, maybe there's a mod for that.

Burnout Paradise is quite possibly both the best driving game I've ever played and the most FRUSTRATING driving game I've ever played. Rather than a series of isolated race courses separated by menus, Burnout Paradise drops you into Paradise City and says "go nuts". The city's archetecture and layout is fantastic, with hundreds of "secret" pathways marked by large yellow fences and super jump ramps that can lead to fantastic shortcuts, Paradise City is a wonderful place to explore or simply drive around in. There are even a few carefully-hidden open areas like the old quarry or the stock car race track. I found driving around Paradise City to be a pleasant and even soothing experience at times.
The core of the game's progression revolves around completing a series of events to improve your license grade. There are five categories of event, which range from races and time trials to stunt challenges and demolition derbys. Access to these events is spaced out across Paradise City at road intersections, although this creates a slight bias towards events starting in the more densely-built Eastern half of the game world.
The driving mechanics are simple enough for a driving game novice like myself to grasp; there is no manual gear change, although I find that handbrake turns are exceedingly difficult to pull off, as it appears very hard to gauge whether a simple button press will cause you to turn slightly or perform a donut. However, the feeling of speed made available to the player is exhilerating, especailly asthe city's layout is seemingly purpose-built to allow speeding from point A to B.
The DIFFICULTY in this game, however, is a severe black mark against it. Although it is not explicitly mentioned in-game, as  your license ranks up, your car becomes more difficult to drive, and the game's physics become increasingly erratic over what will and will not cause your car to veer wildly out of control and crash. Cars often seem to have MORE momentum after point of impact, rather than less, and I have even noticed a vast increase in speed when grinding against roadside barriers. Paradise City's traffic can leave the outcome of a race hinging on whether or not a car just -happens- to come out onto a crossing as you are passing by. Furthermore, the game has perculiar standards on what objects can be broken and which cannot. Street lights and some metal fences cause no impediment at all, while many other fences, along with trees and concrete bollards joined by chains, are completely immovable.
At the same time, the AI cars are a mixed bag. Although one of the game's selling points is the freedom to travel however you like to reach a race's finish line, the route the AI takes is invariably the most efficient one, barring the use of shortcuts (which the AI almost NEVER uses), which often don't make much of a difference anyway. The AI racers are capable of tremendous acceleration from a standing start, outstripping ANY car you manage to unlock, yet have been known to commit suicide by slamming into walls and other cars. The only instance of the AI cars "cheating" in the player's favour is their tendency to teleport to behind the player in the "Road Rage" events, thereby making sure they are always nearby for you to run them off the road, no matter where you go.
In terms of visuals, Paradise City is beautiful. The game has a customisable day/night cycle, although the only weather effect I've whitnessed is the occasional fog. AI cars and traffic have their head and tail lights on at all times, allowing you to see what else is on the road ahead, and the game treats you to a slow-motion camera when you crash, with a wealth of detail dedicated to cracking of glass and crumpling of metal. There is a large variety of cars for you to unlock, each one with customisable paint jobs, although these are often restricted to a choice of two colours and three finishes per vehicle. Cars' appearances change as they sustain damage, although no car has any set "health" meter, and any impact that does not cause you to crash leaves only cosmetic damage.
The sound design is excellent, with many of the different cars having their own distinct engine sound, pleasantly rising in pitch as they near top speed. The sounds effects for crashing are visceral, with loud, sickening "crunch" sounds as metal crumples under force of impact. The game's music is a varied mix of classic rock tunes, music from past Burnout games and even classical music available on the game's radio, interspered with in-game advice from DJ Atomica, the only speaking, named NPC in the game.
In terms of playstyle, three different car "types" are available; Stunt, Aggression and Speed. However, in my experience, Speed Cars are perhaps the least useful overall, as they tend to sacrifice durability for speed, which doesn't really help in traffic-heavy areas, and can only use their boost when the meter is full. The other two car types, while not necessarily as fast, grant open access to their boost functions, and are often sturdy enough to play rough with other racers, especially so in the case of Aggression cars. I limit my use of Speed cars to their specific time trial events and little else.
In addition to cars, there are also a total of four motorcycles available to drive. These are slower, but offer much greater handling and more responsive steering. They also have their own separate license and events, which are all a series of time trials with actually quite generous time limits. The motorcycles are also, strangely enough, just as sturdy as the cars are, which can make for some rather amusing bike-to-car impacts that barely even slow you down.
The game's user interface is passable, although I am annoyed that it takes cycling through a series of menus before you can exit the game. Furthermore, there is no option to reset an event and start over, short of quitting the event and then manually travelling back to the starting point. The closest the game gets to a quick reset is quitting out to the main menu, then re-entering the game, which returns you to the last junkyard (car selection structure) you visited. And since some of the events have you travelling all the way across Paradise City, this is a feature that is sorely lacking.
Multiplayer still exists, but it is player-hosted, with EA no longer providing dedicated servers. However, this does not stop the game from requiring all players to have a working EA games account, which must be logged into as the game boots up. The game then attempts to connect to the servers that no  longer exist, leading to a blank white screen and a single button in the corner marked "back to game", which lets you continue.
My experience with the online multiplayer is limited, but from what I can gather a hosted server can support up to eight players (possibly more, I cannot say), with the host having the authority to set up a variety of events much like the single-player challenges.
Due to the lack of online support, the game's DLC vehicles are no longer purchaseable, although said DLC actually exists in the game files, and there is apparently a workaround available on the "PC Gaming Wiki" that allows players to access this DLC for free.
Despite my severe frustrations with the game's difficulty, I still find Burnout Paradise to be fun racing sandbox. If you would be content with a limited selection of cars and events, you could avoid ranking up and play around a Paradise City with more forgiving physics, but if you are intent on progression and unlocking everything, then you will have to accept the game's often erratic and unfair difficulty as part and parcel of the experience.
Recommended, if on sale, although it is only £5 GBP at full price.

I would just like to start off by saying that my review is based off the fact that i basically cant play Fallout 4 without mods cause I find it too boring. However i would recommend this game to anyone who plans on playing the whole game without mods because it is still a very good game. I'm just so used to playing with mods that now I kinda can't go without them
But as far as it stands right now, I probably wouldn't recommend this game to many people. The reasons for this being:
1) Creation Club. Seriously, what a load of sh!t. Basically paid mods. Theres a Nexus mod to add the Hellfire power armor that looks to be pretty much the exact same as the Hellfire power armor the creation club offers. That and the whole having to buy points instead of just using money directly to purchase them is similar to xBox's Microsoft Points or whatever. You pay an amount to get an amount of points and then usually have points left over, but its not enough to buy anything else with, so then you have to buy more points. I get it if you're trying to get money to mod develpers for putting time and effort into making something for others, but if a mod developer feels like he/she NEEDS to get paid for creating something to add to the game then thats just greedy.
2) Newest update completely broke F4SE. Without F4SE, majority of the amazing mods available on the Nexus forums no longer work. And im sorry to say Bethesda, but on pc your games mostly survive due to online modding communities. The vanilla Fallout 4 experience can be really boring and dry without mods. The main storyline of the game is often quite short and linear and can usually be completed in a handful of hours. And then you have hundreds of hours of aimless wandering and sidequests afterwards, which is fine but after a long while i feel kinda like I'm playing a game with no goal... I may as well be playing minecraft. There's also only so much that can be found and discovered in the world. Mods can help with that adding more interesting weapons, armors and locations. Alot of mods are used for general gameplay improvement as well as fixes and patches that some game developers just never bother to release themselves.
All i have to say is THANK GOD I made a backup of my entire Fallout 4 install directory before the update so I'm still able to play with all my mods. But other people.. probably not as lucky.
I'll most likely change my review in the event that the F4SE Team is able to release an update, but as it stands right now I'm definitely not updating my game anytime soon

This kind of felt like a High Concept game. Other than a few bugs, I found my first playthrough to be very enjoyable. The story and choices were fun aspects. The universe and technology was really interesting. The theme, while initially was a little challenging to follow, turned out to be very facinating. By the time the game was done, I was begging for more. And that's actually where the problem comes in.
The game invites you to play it over-and-over, but I couldn't. The game length wasn't long enough to justify it another play through, as choices and repurcissions ended quickly. Even despite the different narrative choices and the mechancal aspects that intertwine the changing story and gameplay, the overarching story will be the same. And it just feels too samey with the other playthroughs.
When the game ended, I was disappointed. It felt like I just finished the very entertaining and scene setting prolog, and it was game over.
Other criticisms include the fourth wall being broken; that just never seems to quite work. I want to get immersed in an RPG-like game, I don't want it to point out "Hey. You're playing a video game!" - Let me be a part of this beautiful world. I fullly grasp the attempt at the metaplot. But it just didn't work for me.
There's so much potential in this game.
Ultimately, Consortium creates a beautiful setting, with smart game mechinisms. I would absolutely recommend people play it. But due to short narrative, unsatisifying cliff-hanger, and a few other minor things, I would only suggest picking it up when it is on sale.

It's a fun game that's on sale often. It's totally worth $5 the next time it's on sale if you have a computer that can run it. I have a Lenovo Y510p laptop with an NVidia GeForce GT750M, and it runs the game like butter on maxed settings.
The hand-to-hand combat is fun and relatively simple. It becomes remincient of Assassin's Creed I and II towards the end, where the game relies more on you countering every blow rather than actually going offensive. It reminds me a lot of Arkham Asylum, although switching targets is not as fluid. The driving is good, feels pretty smooth. The gunplay is easy to get into with a decent cover system, which is good because most of the last half of the game is exclusively gunfights.
The designer that decided to make Hijack Car and Hire Taxi the same button needs to be fired for lack of common sense. I have hijacked too many taxis because I wasn't standing behind the trunk of the car. One of the missions in the game allows you to see collectibles on your map and radar. While it is nice for people that want to attempt to 100% the game, some of the collectible rewards break the game's hand-to-hand combat by reducing it to simply holding B+Y. You'll often have more money than you know what to do with, so feel free to spend it whenever you can. The game doesn't have much replay value after you beat it, but it is a fun experience that you can beat in a weekend.

Consortium isn't a terrible game anymore, but it's still a terrible rip-off. When originally released, it was filled with game-breaking bugs. Alright, so I got this game during the beta, and if you're like me, you're wondering "Is it worth the money?"
Well as of August 29th, 2015, you can still get it for 13 bucks if you bought PA prior to the Titans rehash coming out. So with this 13 dollar price point in mind, my answer would be YES.
There are a couple reasons. First, the new content is pretty damn good. It's a pretty solid addition of units to the roster, and the Titans are very fun to use. In addition, this relaunch with a new expansion has yielded significantly more players online, and that is a huge plus in my opinion. The game also has some visual changes to the background and stars that look pretty great in my opinion.
Look, it's Steam. For 13 bucks you could get a whole new game or even slightly old AAA game during a sale. But I think 13 bucks is a good deal for the content you get here.
I'd also like to take this moment to address a common complaint. People often say "Why should I spend more money for an unfinished game?".
Well if you're unhappy with PA, don't bother getting this. Before Titan's launching, PA was considered done by Uber and many like myself. This expansion doesn't change the "done-ness" factor of the game. It adds new units, a new game mode, some really good balancing, etc. This won't make the game feel anymore more or less done for people.
If you feel the game was unfinshed before Titans, I don't think Titans or anything else will satisfy your urge.
At 13 bucks for a buyer of PA, this game is a solid buy. For a completely new player for 40 bucks, you'll find a very interesting RTS with a unique mapping system and all sorts of quirks.
In either of the above cases, I would recommend getting PA. Uber has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off a lot of people in the past, for completely vaild and not so valid reasons, but I think this relaunch of sorts is well executed.

I was very intrigued by the description and trailer for Consortium. While nothing special to look at, the game has a unique visual style (though graphics aren't really my thing, I would say the game 'looks' functional but unfinished - it needs textures).
Uniqueness is really the quality that carries this game. If you fancy trying something very different, give it a try.
The game manages to blend the rich and involving atmosphere of, say, Deus Ex (right down to detailed news feeds and history, excerpts from books) with an original, self contained setting like Portal did (as in, a setting that is already there whether or not you have 'revealed' it through gameplay). The Stanley Parable was billed as a game about choices, if you prefer not to spend your time making banal choices, this might be preferable. Everything in the game guides the player back into its setting, which is something I find very refreshing these days. The plot itself is seamless and although the choices are obvious, the possibilities are not...
However. It is well that the game relies on its atmosphere, mystery and dialogue - these form the meat of the game, with combat being a rushed and simplistic affair that fortunately only arrives in short doses.
I must also gripe about the length. Though the game has great replayability, if I had any idea quite how short it is, I would never have paid £8 for it in the Steam Sales...as it stands the regular price before that was nearer to £15 and that is simply asking too much for a game that took me about two hours to play through. Replayability or not, I was hoping to be told a story and all I got was the first chapter of one.
Which is annoying, since the games credits sequence is basically an advertisement for a second game. I can't help but feel Consortium was a missed opportunity, as I actually feel a little bit conned by the length and this will certainly colour my decision to buy the next installment - that said, I was *very* gripped by the plot.
I think people should experience Consortium, but I couldn't honestly recommend paying the current rates for it. It felt, to be honest, like buying a demo.

Including a TL;DR because i wrote a book; wait until March.
first off, street fighter 5 is actually in early access to push it's e sports scene so if you're the type who likes trials, and other single player content you are best off waiting until March. There's apparently a short cinematic story mode being later in June, so if you want the full experience you can wait until then if you're so inclined. This review is going to be aimed greenhorns of the series or people on the fence seeking additional information. This was written about 2/20/16 when most of these problems were still in circulation.
With that out of the way, this release of Street fighter 5 is more or less in line with the other games of the series. Gameplay is tight, simple but remarkably complex and most of the game information's will be found by trial and error or via word of mouth. Characters are extremely diverse, and delightful to play. Balance is currently quite stable with no real standouts in excellence or mediocrity. If you've never played a fighting game before you'll probably struggle to follow whats happening tthough. If you're the type to get easily frustrated, or not do homework on how to play outside the game, you will more than likely not have a very fun time.
Truthfully it's a game meant to be played with friends, locally or online. Most of the fun comes from it's competitive nature, and in the regard the game delivers very well. The first day or so, the online component was broken but that seems to have sorted itself out so you can enjoy either to your heart's content. There's still some definite server issues but for the most part it functions normally now. At the moment, lobbies, where you fight specific people 1 on 1 over and over again, currently only has slots for 2 people. If you have a big group of friends, the march content update will allow up to 8 players to play and watch, with the winner of every match staying on ala like an arcade system. The actual online service isn't just steam, by the way but rather Capcom's own system because the game supports crossplay. If you were hoping for communication via text or voice, then sadly you'll have none of that outside of lobbies. Lobbies only support pre-made messages via text, and has no support for voice. Online, ranked and casual has neither. I'm unsure if they have any plans to add such support but at the moment the answer is currently no.
Netcode is solid, though it uses a rollback system so when it is bad characters will literally teleport around, and makes for rather comedic matches where you literally cannot follow what is going on. The current problem, which i will touch on later, is frame skipping from people who aren't meeting 60 fps normally. This can create problems where a good connection can still have teleporting because the game is trying to force 60 when one player can't reach it anyway. There is no fix for this, and because this release does not include a benchmark tool, nor a PC rating filter any match can have this teleporting. Crossplay works great though so that's not a problem at all.
following up from the last point, the current release are noticably more gpu intensive than the betas, so if you say tried the cracked beta to get an idea of how the game will run for you, then decide to buy this you might find you will need to lower the settings than you previously did. Also something to note is the game does not appear to run any better if you try to lower settings beyond automatic, so if you cant run it well under automatic, you can't run it period at the moment. If you're a toaster anon, you'd best just save your money for a better computer, or look to less intensive fighting games on steam like Guilty Gear.
A special warning to Nvidia card users, Nvidia new drivers forces the game to run at 30 fps on some cards, like the gx960, and while Nvidia has confirmed this a bug they have not made it unclear when it will be fixed. I don't believe the beta had this particular issue so I don't believe there is anyway for you to actually check to see if you are effected at the moment beyond buying it. It does appear to effect any newer cards so if you have a titan x or the like you should be fine.
That said if you can run it, it runs great and looks nice. The music is nice, and the general presentation is very strong. Characters are all very clearly different and immediately apparent which is which. Even on lower settings it still looks very nice, so you can still enjoy the visuals if you can't run max on everything. The loading times are kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥but not too bad in comparison to ps4.
There's a couple things you should know about controller support. Currently legacy support on a lot of fight sticks is currently spotty, and if you're a keyboard user you have to edit an .ini file to change your keybinding. Capcom has confirmed both these features are going to be improved however, so this could be fixed eventually.
As it stands my advice is to beginners is to wait, unless you're really hungry to play and don't mind/aren't affected by any of this. Everyone else should probably wait until march when presumbably these issues will be ironed out more. My recommendation is largely neutral and I wish I could give this a sideways thumb, but since i can't I have to go with gut and say no.

The more of these games they make, the worse they get. I grew up playing the original XCom games which is where I developed a fond love of Strategy games. Yes, they were hard, but that didn't stop me from playing them for an entire summer in Primary school. Sure, it had its faults (like the enemies camping out on the second floor after all of the stairwells were destroyed in your base) but it was a fact of life. These were genuine bugs, not oversights or bad design.
These modern XCom games suffer from a myriad of problems ranging from clunky UI's (no, not the actual UI's, I'm talking about what replaced the Geoscape and the Base views) to stupendously ridiculous bugs like being crit shot through a roof on a higher elevation behind full cover by an enemy on a lower "level" than you. And don't even get me started on my dire interest to see the maths they used to calculate the shot odds. I cannot fathom how some of my guys can miss completely sometimes total of SIX turns in a row (!!!!!) when being the equivalent of mere meters away with scopes that supposedly enhance the weapon's aim by +15%. But it is a "pretty" game.
I do miss the ability to command sometimes 10-20 soldiers. I also wish we could have more freedom to buy Engineers and Scientists like the original games instead of liberating them like a prize. Maybe this could have been done differently by giving you specialized scientists? To be honest, they're not much different from the original scientists in the old games; they provide no benefit other than to speed up research. Maybe they could have offered different types of equipment bonuses if you rescued them?
The game is fun when you're doing well but expect to lose at least 1 squad member per mission on higher difficulty settings even when being cautious. The "concealment" mechanic is interesting but it only seemly forces you to choose your movements carefully and is generally useless when it comes to "timed" missions because it takes, for example, 3-5 turns to get near your target in some cases. Often times there will be civilians out of view in a city setting so making hasty movements towards your goal is pretty pointless because around any corner, if there isn't an alien force, there most certainly is something that will give away your concealment so it's pretty moot. I genuinely wish they would have done more with this like given you the option to stay in concealment after a shot if all of your squad is in full cover and passes LoS checks.
Let's talk about Central. I've lost count of how many times I've clicked on his portrait during one of his nagging sessions whilst sometimes actually saying "Get f*cked"; it could add a degree of immersion I suppose but after thirty times it gets REALLY annoying. This goes for the rest of your normal cadre staff on the Avenger.
All told, this game is worth it for £11 but don't pay full price for it. There are SEVERAL game-breaking bugs that carried over from the first modern XCom game and I'm seriously disappointed that these weren't fixed. It's a real shame because there aren't many Strategy games I hold so dear as the XCom IP. It won't stop me from playing it, but I'll try to curb my cursing over stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that bears no explanation and yields nothing but silence from Firaxis.

Well, where do I begin? How about the good stuff?
Burnout Paradise is a perfect racing/crash test simulator. It graphics, while outdated in the current time, are consistent under high speed races and give the general 'sullen' look of the city. It doesn't really take much to get anywhere and all you need is a stunt car, which you are given at the beginning of the game, to have fun. The races are logical and the idea that you can travel on any path is uncommon amongst most simulators today. The cars are nice and some are screen accurate, and in my opinion, the dlc cars are the best.
This brings me to the faults, of which, they are prominent. The online mode is completely broken. A few of the subtler plot points could have been made clearer.
This game is a

Even though I called the twist (the first part of it, anyway) within 5 minutes of starting, I still enjoyed the ride and was suitably creeped out when I got there.
This game may have been middling over all, but I look forward to great things from this dev's future games.  He's clearly got the talent.
The voice acting is not fantastic, but it gets the job done.  He emphasizes the right parts of each sentence to get across the intended meaning while hinting at (but not spoiling) any secondary meanings that sentence might have.  That's better than can be said about the majority of indie voice acting.  Although, that said, there are a few cringy moments mixed in there, too.
I said I called the
of the twist early, but the
of it was a bit confusing.  Not because it was a huge stretch, but just because the details that hinted at it throughout the game could have been made a bit more explicit.  I think the dev was worried about making it "too obvious," but in truth it only seemed obvious to him because he wrote it.

Sleeping Dogs is what happens when the player's character is a result of Chow Yun Fat and a Smartass Jackie Chan/Jet Li doing the fusion dance and turning into a roughly 5'10" Chinese badass who is an undercover cop trying to be a Chest Bursting Xenomorph in a Triad Gang's stomach - metaphorically speaking.  You play as Wei Shen, a dude that just moved back to HK after some family problems back in San Fran. He has a Black Diamond Encrusted Golden Dragon belt in putting the hurt down on goons and the innate ability to have every woman he meets want his eggroll. No seriously, they want it.
Let me first clear up an idea or misconception you MAY have about this game. It is not GTA or SR, you will not have many of the crazy GTA/SR style shenanigans that you see in those games here.  It is an open-world were you do have fists, guns, and can kill random any civilians unfortunate enough to stand in your way, but guns are rare to come across unless it's a scenario were the game wants you to shoot someone, and beating up/killing civilians really isn't any fun compared to GTA/SR and if you're in a mission, the game will obviously punish you for doing so (I mean you're still a cop, c'mon.)  Now this does not make this a bad game at all, it's just a little different than what you may be used to.
Playing with a mouse and keyboard is a little weird at first, but after a few fights, drives, and freeruns, it'll grow on you and you'll feel at home with the well worked fighting/driving/movement mechanics.  Interacting with people,  objects, and cars are pretty much all done with the right mouse button, again, it's a little weird, but you'll get used to it in an hour or two.  Combat is done well, looks awesome, and feels responsive.  Gunplay is pretty good, weapons feel nice for the most part but the pistols for some reason feel and sound better and more powerful than the Shotguns, SMGs, and Rifles do. Firefights can sometimes be too easy when you can just bullet-time your way through by vaulting over cover and pulling off special moves to extend your time in slo-mo.
The story itself might actually be a little on the longer side, that pairing with the fact that I wanted to get as buffed up as fast as possible, resulting in my derping in quite a few side missions and collectible. . . collecting, you can spend quite a few hours enjoying what the game has to offer both in and out of the the game's main story.  Some side missions give you more money than others, this is highly obvious when you can grind stealing cars for some guy named Tran and get more HK (money) than you get completing other side missions or random encounters than can be not as fun/more difficult/etc. That being said, there a lot of side missions that are actually fun and that are more worth your time as opposed to just getting HK from them.  My total time spend in-game was 29 hours, from beginning to the end of the main story, and including my time spet in side missions.
If I were to rate this game on a scale from 1 - 5, I'd say it's definitely worth buying if you're a fan of open-world action games, or just action games as a whole, especially if it goes on sale.  (I really hate number scoring.)  It may not be an "exceptional" game, but it is quite entertaining and isn't a title that should be overlooked for because of any misconceptions people may have or a few shortcomings in terms of gameplay (some of course based on personal taste and what I had noticed in my time playing.)
Tips I have: Go on the dates as soon as you're able to, they unlock locations on your minimap for collectibles you can find to earn health cap increases, new fighting moves, and other rewards.  Like I mentioned earlier, call Tran for easy money, if he mentions luxury or sports cars, your probably in luck as some cars you can steal will get you up to a hefty 100k-400k+ HK.

Yea I'm still a little ticked off that I had to pay extra for this, even though I feel like a lot of this should have been in the original game to begin with, but after the complete cluster @#$% that was the original, broken, unoptimized, glitchy, buggy, even long after it got released, you guys really seem to have gotten your act together with this new game.

This part is for old players coming to Titans. Skip this part if you never played the original.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
New units.
Big whoop, right? Well the units actually add a depth and complexity that was horribly lacking in the original. I was skeptical, but after my first online game where my base got SWARMED BY PROBABLY A THOUSAND BOMB-BOTS THROUGH A TELEPORTER, I think it's safe to say that one unit added a lot--and it's not the only new unit. Despite numbering in the thousands, these little buggers didn't feel overpowered. We already countered a wave of them once in this game, and this second wave nearly succeeded only because it was exploiting a major weakness on the planet I was on. I had no ground defenses or even aerial backup! Thirty more seconds and I was screwed. Luckily my team mate had finished the catalyst in the nick of time and just as my planet was being swarmed, my commander and air fabrication units franticly making defenses as a last ditch effort, we BLEW THEIR PLANET TO BITS and won. Was a great game.
The terrain.
No one is even talking about this but I feel like this is horribly overlooked. A few simple changes in terrain elevation makes the map SO MUCH MORE INTERESTING than the boring spheres in the original. Now you can fortify the high ground and build bases in valleys. All in all it's a lot more interesting.
THE GAME ACTUALLY RUNS NOW WITHOUT A SUPERCOMPUTER.
Now I upgraded to a pretty beefy PC, but the original game was still chugging harder than a frat boy crashing an afterparty at the biggest college in the state. The game ran like absolute crap. Now it doesn't! Even with a REDICULOUS number of units in a 3v3 match, the game held up pretty consistently up until the end, when we got hit by the ungodly swarm of bomb bots skittering through a teleporter.

Here's the part for new players!
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
If you ever played Supreme Commander, you're likely to enjoy this.
If you like cartoony RTS games, stuff that's supposed to be gratuitous and explosive and not supposed to be following any real world 'realism' (Men of War, Company of Heroes, Wargame, etc), then you'll enjoy this. Games like Command and Conqure, Starcraft, you get the idea.
And if you still don't know what I'm talking about, let me put it this way. You control a ton of iddy biddy robots and go murder a bunch of other iddy biddy robots and occasionally make really really big robots and best of all BLOW UP ENTIRE PLANETS OR SMASH OTHER PLANETS INTO PLANETS.
The trailer tells most of the story. It's an RTS but instead of a flat map you get globes to play with. The default controls are screwy in my opinion but I changed them so up goes north and down goes south and it's a lot easier to keep your bearings.
What else? You get two tiers of units to play with. So either invest in stronger units that take more time and resources to build, or lots of spammy tier 1 units. You also get five vehicle classes. Air, sea, vehicles (land, so tanks and armored cars), bots (land, but better than vehicle in some situations due to versatility--I don't really know all the tricks yet), and of course SPACE units.
Oh, and I almost forgot. Titans. Basically, superweapons. Giant killer robots and flying units with special attacks. Some are stompy. Some are shooty. One of them is a big orbital teleporter that rains the unholy hell of your army down on hostile worlds from the safety of orbit. Oh, and there's also a gun that shoots units. No, I mean it SHOOTS UNITS. BUILDS ROBOTS AND LAUNCHES THEM ACROSS THE SOLAR SYSTEM. Also nukes. Can't forget nukes. But nukes are boring!
Did I mention you can smash planets into other planets?! Strap some rockets to a small enough moon or dwarf planet and you can smash it into other planets! If it's too small, it won't survive!
Also they have a Death Star. I mean Annihilaser. Whatever. It's a Death Star. Call it what you will, if you capture this planet and build the big catalyst things that make the lasers work, god help whoever it's pointed at, because this bad boy is a game ender. That being said however, your enemy will be trying to capture it too. Not all maps have this however if you don't like it.
Furthermore I'm pretty sure you can configure your own maps, too. Set up the orbits and stuff. I've not messed with this very much. Seems neat.
Galactic mode still sucks. Don't buy this game if you plan on playing it by yourself. You'll get bored. Get some friends and at least skirmish against the AI. Do you all suck at resource management? No worries, you can nerf enemy resource production or beef up your own to handicap or buff players as you see fit. Suck at multitasking? You can share armies.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
So the game isn't completely awful as some folks act like it is--in fact, it's very good, and I'm actually enjoying it now. I think it was worth the upgrade. I'm still annoyed at Uber, but I think I'll actually forgive them if they keep updating this game as they have been. The game is fun. End of story. Is it worth upgrading? I'd say so. Ever wondered what it would be like to play System Shock (1 or 2) while everyone on the ship was still alive? And you could interact with the crew and witness the drama directly and not through audio logs after the fact? I did, and CONSORTIUM plays a lot like what I imagined it to be.
Beginning of this game was some of the most exciting stuff I've played in a long time. You're on a military vessel in a middle of a crisis, helping the ship's survival, building relationships with crew members, trying to outsmart your foes, on the outside and on the inside. The writing and voice acting is good, the conversations are sharp and the game is very good at acknowledging what you do and shifting the events accordingly.
But the murder mystery at the core of this episode proved to be a tough nut to crack. I'm currently beginning my third playthrough (the second one was interrupted by a progress-stopping bug) and I'm still no closer to discovering the real villain. At this point I'm not sure if I must calculate it logically by using what I know, catch the evildoes in the act somewhere or just grill some witness until they reveal something. Making logical conclusions seems unreliable when the world is so full of ~sci-fi magic~ that the rules change all the time.
"We can telepathically see and hear all through your eyes!"
"But no, there's been a hack, and now no-one can see you!"
"No, wait, I did a counter-hack and I still totally can!"
(And I bet Sherlock Holmes never had to deal with bs teleportation before.)
So I'll keep trying until I stumble on a solution. At this point I've done some save reloading and checked the ways the plot forces some events on you no matter what you do. The more freedom a game promises you, the more invested you become in your choices, the more jarring it gets when you finally hit the bars of the cage, the limitations that the videogame has to impose on you. In the same vein as Aplha Protocol and The Walking Dead became disappointing when you realized how little you could actually change, this game promises you so much more, and it's inevitably a bummer when you cannot always do what you believe you should be doing in a given situation. But it's still a big step in a very exciting direction, and I'm eagerly waiting to see where Part 2 will take us.
Now the words of warning.
The game looks an controls like crap. There's no getting around it. Moving around the plane is a chore. You get stuck on ladders, you can pass through closed doors (and sometimes open doors become impassable), lights go out in different sections seemigly at random (why can't a super soldier pick up a flashlight?) You can never reliably interact with anything - only a certain part of any object is clickable, but a similar object can be non-clickable at all, leading to constant pixel hunts. The same goes for people: half of the time you cannot even click on them, which makes them just part of the scenery.
And don't even get me started on combat. I had to go with the non-lethal route during a fight with a certain person, because the rifle that was in my hands refused to acknowledge I had bullets, both in my pockets and in my inventory! And I had no way to test it beforehand, because combat mode was locked until the scoundrel was all up in my grill.
Multiple replays are mandatory to see all that the game has to offer, and this makes you feel almost like the character from Source Code, who is aware of the fact that he relives the same sequence over and over. What's wonderful is that your dialog choices support this mode of behaviour. Too bad you have to sit through several long unskippable holochat conversations throughout the game that get pretty old once you've sat through them once. One excruciatingly long, detailed briefing explains to you a mission THAT WILL NOT BE HAPPENING IN THIS GAME. On the next playthrough you might as well start the sequence and then go drink some tea.
But is it still worth it? Absolutely!
Don't try it if you are easily annoyed by lack of polish and poor production values. Consortium has been made on a shoestring budget by a small team who were too excited to explore new ways a game can interact with the player, and they're not asking too much for their work. It's an interesting experiment that has potential to lead to better things in the future. If you ever found yourself enjoying E.Y.E., Pathologic or Deadly Premonition, you are the kind of person who can appreciate it when a game offers you something new, even if playing it requires an open mind and a bunch of patience.

If you need a review, then this game is very likely not for you and a "Don't Buy". If you're a longtime competitive Street Fighter player, then you probably already bought this and will buy/enjoy it regardless of any reviews.
Be warned:
> The combat is deep, but requires dozens of hours of practice to develop the muscle memory and skill to really even begin the game. Out of game research is almost required. What character buffs and meter abilities do are not explained in-game, along with some other mechanics. There is no tutorial beyond telling you what to press to block, punch, and kick.
> There is no meaningful single player content. There is no Arcade Mode. Survival Mode is 10, 30, 50, or 100 matches in which your health doesn't restore, but after each match you may be able to buy random health or buffs. The AI is very simple until the last couple matches in which it goes from novice to expert, with nothing in between. Difficulty only increases the number of novice matches you do before reaching the 2-3 expert opponents. If you lose once, all progress is lost, no rewards are earned, and you start at the beginning.
> Story Mode consists of 2-3 fights (only 1 round each) against AI which pretty much stands there and doesn't block, in which you're given full meter at the start. Cutscenes and fights included, each story is over in 5 minutes.
> Earning rewards require you to be connected to the online servers, even if doing a solo/offline mode. Rewards are only earned the first time you complete a mode, and then can only be earned very slowly from online versus matches against random opponents. All costumes are bought from the cash shop. The only non-cash shop unlockables are colors.
> Capcom advertises spending currency earned in-game to buy costumes and characters, but its very similar to a free to play game model. You earn a sizeable amount of currency if you complete Story and Survival modes, but then those no longer award currency, and currency earned online is a slow grind even for expert players, meaning you'll have to spend real money to get more than one or two characters or costumes in any reasonable amount of time.
> The game is unfinished. This is a review of what the game is, now, at $60, and not what it maybe could be a year or two down the line. Various modes advertised such as a cinematic story (intended to be just over an hour long) and trial modes are not yet included and planned for later patches. All costumes are bought in the cash shop, which isn't live as of this review either. Capcom says they may consider an Arcade Mode in the future. Gamepad and fightstick support is also not added, and third party programs are required.
> Servers are unstable. While the game isn't necessarily online-only, but it essentially is. Disconnects even in offline modes will boot you out of matches, reseting progress or ruining a local match. Online matchmaking commonly will match newbies with veterans, when the matchmaking is even working at all.

A few months ago, I would have written a negative review.
Back then, I had stopped playing the game because I had hit a wall: I couldn't find the incredibly rare items required for the next two quests.  I had the highest level armor and weapon so powerful it could kill anything with one or two hits.  My rapid-firing high-damage assault rifle could hit birds at any range.  At that point the game had stopped being fun.  Even the extreme planets were too easy; meteor strikes were few and far between.
But now?  You can start a colony.  Weapons are no longer ridiculously powerful, and the accuracy of some guns has been reduced.  Soon there will be hoverbikes.  Hoverbikes?  Hell yeah.  Colonies?  You're kidding me.
Nope, not kidding.  Colonies.  Nothing like settling on a fiery planet, building a beautiful city inhabited by unique and endearing people, and watching it be obliterated by one giant meteor.  That taught me something... build underground.  So now I have my own little ragtag band of survivors, duking it out with nature.
My final rating: 9/10
Great game, but not perfect.  Keep in mind, Starbound is still in Beta.  I'm sure they'll get at least some of these things fixed before the game hits 1.0.
One more thing: I haven't yet explored all the game has to offer.  I'm sure there's tons more to see, and more problems too, but I haven't found any yet.

Story time! The first tower defense game I ever played was probably that desk defender game where you had to stop papercraft enemies from getting across the screen. If it wasn't, that was the first real one that had effort put in. I was instantly charmed, and it was a first step in me developing a healthy interest in PC gaming aside from things I saw on TV or that were recommended by friends. End story time!
Fast forward to the present and I am playing Soul Locus, a game where Magic: The Gathering (or other TCGs[Trading Card Games]) meets Tower Defense(hereby referred to as TD)! I have not yet seen a TD game do this, so I am very excited.
In Soul Locus you are a Luminary protecting Order(your friendly neighborhood god,) from Chaos(your not-so-friendly neighborhood bully.) You do this with the help of your Guardians (your manifested personality.) These guardians can take many shapes, have many abilities, and their own types with strengths and weaknesses. You play them at the cost of focus. Makes sense, right?
The tutorial is pretty okay, it explains what it needs to, and quickly has you running through levels proper, but all the same it seems slightly sparse in it's current state. I actually got confused for a second when it suddenly stopped giving me direction after giving me a very specific instruction to then just try playing the level anyway and realizing that's what you're supposed to do.
So how does it play, you want to know? Well it's pretty simple. You strategically place your guardians, and strategically level them up. You can pick from range, damage, and speed. If you make a mistake, don't worry, they can be refunded back to you. Aside from keeping an eye on things and leveling them up appropriately, it's mostly about watching the beatdown ensue, and that's never a bad thing in this genre!
There are focus crystals you can pick up to speed up the focus gathering process, essentially enemy soul absorption, and in the modern world of idle games, it's a familiar and welcome addition to TD.
This may sound a bit tried and true, maybe even boring to you, but I insist that it is not! You will often have to level up your Guardians very quickly but also carefully. You also have to manage evolution, as well, and getting the hang of placement not only takes a while, but can often change pretty wildly from map to map! Things stay fresh, in other words.
With the recent addition of crafting, you can make your own Guardians, and it's very well done. You can make items that let you single out abilities, or you can pour 3 items in the mix and get a random Guardian. Great for if you're new, feeling lucky, or just aren't quite sure what you want next. It's very exciting, really, finding out just what's out there and then bringing it into battle to be amazed at how good some of these Guardians are!
The graphics are simple, charming, and do their job, and getting around the UI is easy! They can be a bit blurry or pixelated at modern resolutions, though. The plus side to all this is, this is a very very kid friendly game. It isn't overly verbose, but it is a veritable cuteness overload, with big text and friendly colors! So even if you don't like it, consider your children!
The sound is acceptable. The music, good, even, but I had trouble hearing anything else over the fireballs even when turned down. Some of the sound and art assets could use a little polish or a tune up.
I personally had a lot of fun running through the levels, watching my Guardians grow with me, finding new ones, and am excited about the prospect of discovering more (could there even be some rare godly ones that are hard to create or find the recipe for? I can only hope if not currently, then soon there will be!) The devs seem to be working on Soul Locus at a good pace, making healthy additions and adding levels to keep you coming back, too!
This is the kind of game that no matter how much time you get out of it, if you're a fan of TCGs, TD, or both especially, you'll be glad you put that amount of time into it! I can safely recommend it for everyone who likes TD games.

The strength of your personality manifests through special cards, from which you summon magical creatures. These Soul Guardians are ready to fight the Corruptors who aim to destroy the world you hold dear!
Collect and craft cards, train your Guardians, and experience the story of Soul Locus: Cards of Order!
Soul Locus: Cards of Order is a collectible creature tower defense game. Dozens of levels and over 80 Guardians will be available at final release, paired with a rich RPG storyline that takes you through the floating continents of Dalifor. Each Guardian corresponds to one of six types of Soul Locus that define its strategic use in game. Build a team you design, and level up your Guardians how you choose. Each is customizable!
Crafting is a key component in collecting all of the Guardians available in the game. Crafting materials will be obtained through quests, at the end of battles or by breaking down other cards. Combining materials lets you discover new recipes for Guardians! - Highly Recommended!

Soul Locus blends your standard tower defense genre with some light rpg elements and a dusting of Pokemon.
So you've played a tower defense game, so what could this possibly do that's different than those? This was my gut reaction. Because let's be honest, most tower defense games all generally the same, they have different graphics but the same mechanics.
What Soul Locus does though is take those simple mechanics and add a few different ones of their own to make what I think is a nice change of pace for this type of game.
This game is currently in early access so all the bells and whistle aren't there. However, what is there is a lot of fun and you can see what is going to be some more features to be added soon.
Like most tower defense games you have set places to put your "turrets", but, the turrets in this are actually called Guardians. The Guardians level up during game play using focus, which is generated overtime by killing enemies. Attack range, damage and speed are the categories you can upgrade throughout the round.
Instead of just leveling up those abilities, you can evolve your guardians as well, which will increase stats and change or increase their abilities. Your goal as usual is to survive through all the waves. Don't let the enemies kill your goat, or sheep? I don't remember, there's something you are protecting.
Now, the light rpg parts. You'll earn experience and your Guardians will level up and you can use this skill points to increase their individual attack speed, range and damage.
One of the features that is in the works is the disenchant screen. My guess is as you play you get doubles of some Guardians and you may not need them, so you'll be able to destroy their cute asses and make better ones.
With all these mechanics, and a simple but fun twist on tower defense I like where this game is heading. The $14.99 price point may be a bit much for some, however, things go on sale all the time. Pick it up now or wait for a sale week.

RPG MO is an isometric, crafting based MMORPG with retro style graphics and a decent sized world; it's very similar to Runescape but not nearly as large.  Players may move using WASD, the arrow keys, or with the click of their mouse along a diagonal grid; the game's world.  Though the game is in  its infant stage, the crafting system and skills are quite in-depth, however, its combat skills are lukewarm at best, for now.

It is important to know that the doorways on Tutorial Island are a one-way trip, so it would be wise to learn what each room has to teach before advancing; although you can still find the skill trainers in the starting town.  Each trainer teaches you the basics of combat, mining, woodcutting, fishing, forging, jewelry, cooking, and alchemy.

RPG MO's combat system is currently its Achilles heel.  To engage in combat, for a first strike, players must maneuver their characters as though they are trying to move on the exact space their target is positioned on (monsters do not move); however, moving to a space adjacent to an aggressive monster will also initiate combat but with the monster dealing the first strike.  Once combat is initiated, players cannot run until at least three attacks are exchanged.  While there is a plethora of various weapon types, the only difference between them is the amount of accuracy and strength they add, as well as their handedness; there is absolutely no difference in attack speed between any weapon or combat style.

There are 4 gathering skills and 6 crafting skills, most of which can be done while AFK; however, you still need to keep one eye glued to the game screen to prevent the possibility of being AFK jailed via captcha.  Most gathering skills will help for gathering their respective loot faster as they level, so a higher mining level yields quicker mining.  Similarly, crafting skills also yield more loot as they level but instead by reducing the failure chances, at least on most of them.

Loot from monsters is received in a randomly assorted fashion; each monster can drop, into your inventory, its own list of loot at different drop rates; these can be found by right-clicking a monster and left-clicking "(monster name) drops".
All basic controls are performed with WASD or arrow keys for movement, left-click to move or confirm options, and right-click to open additional options for individual objects/characters.  There is an option to re-map controls and menu short-cuts for a more personalized set-up.
Due to the absence of character animations and presence of low graphic images, RPG MO is playable on many of the lower spec. computers.
RPG MO still has some kinks to work out, but it is still a decent game to play to kill some time.
