8/10
+ Similar to RS
+ Simplistic combat
+ Nice community and it feels rewarding to progress in game.
+ Quite a lot of things to do
+ Not very much P2W - Premium currency is awarded in small amounts.
+ PVP that somewhat supports pures
+ Server stability has been good
+ Some of the background songs are decent.
+ Chat customization
- Chat and it's rules/moderators. Sometimes you accidentally type on a wrong chat channel because you are defaulted to it and moderators mute you without warning. There is a rule that says to only discuss other games in Steam and 18+ channels, which is not nice IMO. Some moderators are not very understanding when it comes to "deciding what behaviour is accepted".
- Clunky UI. Also chat gets in the way and windows don't always close. You sometimes accidentally hit the chat and go to typing mode in which you cannot move and this can cause problems. If you are in a dungeon, the world map won't show.
- Lack of location or acquirement information on certain items.
- Market where you sometimes find other players sell listings for much less and buy lists for much more, which you can easily take advantage of and make a LOT of cash if you keep refreshing the items enough. Exchanging goods that fast is not healthy for the economy.
- Economy. Hard to make money early on and when you get to around 30/40 of all combat stats, you notice that most of the good stuff (even at early levels) for your level cost way too much. For example, a strength weapon might cost 500k at the same level as attack weapon at 10k.
- According to community, the game has been running for 3 years - yet doesn't get many balance improvements.
- You can't move to the walkable area you see (for example, on the other side of a river) without loading grids further away.
- Captchas can get in the way and you get quite a lot of them as a legit player. If you fail 5 to 10 of them, you can get banned from the game.
- Chance to hit nothing with low "aim" on high level monsters will make training hard for certain pures especially when high level monsters drop the equipment they need.
- Certain skills are too expensive compared to others and will most likely be extremely grindy later on when there is no one selling the materials.
- Certain skills have very bad XP curves. at level 1-10 fishing you probably get around 8xp per cast (with 50%, 15%, 0.1%, 50% and 35% chances of getting 1 fish per cast), while woodcutting from 1 to 10 you have about 15-25% success rate at getting 5-13 xp per cast. So yeah, woodcutting is very slow.
- Certain skills and items have too big crafting failure rates. The Success rates are usually around 10% to 60%, less on the higher level gear... this can be very annoying!
- The game needs better weapon balance. Strength weapons should hit hard but rarely (never shouldn't be an option) and accuracy should allow you to hit more often and for more damage at later levels, or something... something similar to RS, maybe.
- Could use a little bit more starting bank space seeing as the first bank upgrade costs 500k.
- Having to go through very high level mobs as a low level player to sell items is not nice

Consortium is an interesting mix of SYS Shock and M Effect, among other titles. It's also a murder mystery, a sci fi adventure and more. The choices you make make some difference to the story, but not a whole lot. Still, the chioces you make, and the discussions you have will alter and affect the behaviour of those around you. THe graphics may be simplistic, but that's not why I bought it. The VR missions are tough, and also rather pointless in my opinion. I focused mainly on the story, and it developed gradually and effectively.
However, I have to say it's also cliched and rather unimaginative. An ex-terrorists son taking hostages? Really? Couldn't have come with anything brighter than that? The final sequence, the JUMP, is really interesting, and apparently it will affect the way the sequel plays if there is a sequel and what happens to the Bishop 6 (the char you play).
It hits more than it misses, but it does miss sometimes very badly. For example characters just standing around doing nothing except tapping at an imaignary keyboard in the air. I guess air keyboard woud be the the term.
I like the characters, I liked the story for the most part. What gets me is that at the end, is a real big shock. I won't tell you what it is, but it makes replayability redundant, and that makes me wonder why that is so when it's one its selling points.
I'd give the game 7/10 or a B- or something. It's a solid game that deserves to be played at least once, I pray there is a sequel, but I also hope it's sensibly priced as this first chapter is way too expensive for a 6 hour game. I guess time is not how it shoudl be judged, but if you were paying 30 dollars for 6 hours, wouldn't you ofeel a tad ripped off even if the game was amazing?
Hopefully these short comings can be resolved in a sequel.
Overall I really, truly enjoyed the game, and haven't played anything like it for a long time. A justified purchase, but perhaps at a lower price point

It looked so promising, but I was disappointed. CONSORTIUM is a game that holds itself together with its plot, but that's where it suffered.
To truly appreciate everything the developers are trying to do, you need to read reems and reems of backstory prose, delve into blogs, read "musings", and even play another game by the same developers. The combat is pretty terrible - it could have been removed or simplified without any real impact to the game. You're constantly thrust into weird scenarios in which everyone else seems to know something you don't. There is a *lot* of talking. Yes, the plot is very important, but sometimes you're going to feel more like a passenger than a driver.
The concept of the game itself being a gateway into an alternate reality broke my immersion more than anything else. The fourth wall was broken and never ended up being repaired. I soon stopped caring about the characters, the ship, or the mission. The setting just didn't have a good draw. The technology is advanced, and there are some interesting concepts in there, but the game might have been more interesting with more simplification.
Set it on an orbiting spaceship instead of an aeroplane; provide a concise glossary or encylclopaedia; cut down the number of weapons to just one (you don't need a lethal assault rifle with a stun-grenade launcher attachment *and* a stun gun with a lethal laser mode); and most of all - utilise SHOW instead of TELL as a storytelling/exposition tool.
I read all of the database entries in Mass Effect because they enhanced my experience, but in CONSORTIUM the extra information is pretty much mandatory reading if you want to understand what's going on - and the entries are *really* long. Let me put it this way: I can tell you all about the First Contact War and how the Mass Relays work in Mass Effect, but I'm still not sure I know what the Consortium itself actually is, what its ideals are, or how it does what it's supposed to be doing.
Conversing with the crew and interacting with them is really important, but if you miss one or two key lines, you can miss a heck of a lot of content (and it really hurts your chances of solving the main mystery).
If you get excited over the idea of a computer game pretending to be a door into another dimension where you can tell people "I'm from another world, playing a computer game, and you're all characters in that computer game. If I load a saved game, I'm breaking the timeline and creating another alternate reality..." then maybe you'll enjoy CONSORTIUM, but for me it was laid on a bit too thick.

Consortium tends to play like an adventure/detective title, with branching dialouge options and Alternate Reality Game based lore, and a smattering of FPS elements thrown in.  And by "branching" I mean "be warned, your decisions and actions will *actually matter* in this game!", which already makes it rather unique.
Movement through the certain areas of the ship tends to be a bit awkward, due to the realisticly cramped quarters, but the overall design is very well put together.  You will be challenged with the exploration and usage of the detailed "micro-environment" setting you find youself in, and forced to make quick descions based on instinct and whatever information you can glean from your surroundings or the NPCs.  Combat is not a huge portion of the game, though tends to be intense when it does happen.  As for the storyline... without giving away too much, it's about as twisty and complicated as they come, with a MASSIVE amount of backstory to flesh things out.
Overall it's a good game with a unique design and plot, where one can wind up exploring a small yet incrediably detailed worldsetting.  I'd reccomend it as a purchase for anyone.

The experience I've just had was infinitely better than that which my first review was based on.
Each issue I had before - largely gamplay bugs and annoying crashes - has been fixed and I did notice a few dialogue changes since initial release too.

I'd highly recommend it despite PC Gamer's criticism of the graphics; they are what they are, to be honest.

A few months ago, I would have written a negative review.
Back then, I had stopped playing the game because I had hit a wall: I couldn't find the incredibly rare items required for the next two quests.  I had the highest level armor and weapon so powerful it could kill anything with one or two hits.  My rapid-firing high-damage assault rifle could hit birds at any range.  At that point the game had stopped being fun.  Even the extreme planets were too easy; meteor strikes were few and far between.
But now?  You can start a colony.  Weapons are no longer ridiculously powerful, and the accuracy of some guns has been reduced.  Soon there will be hoverbikes.  Hoverbikes?  Hell yeah.  Colonies?  You're kidding me.
Nope, not kidding.  Colonies.  Nothing like settling on a fiery planet, building a beautiful city inhabited by unique and endearing people, and watching it be obliterated by one giant meteor.  That taught me something... build underground.  So now I have my own little ragtag band of survivors, duking it out with nature.
My final rating: 9/10

Edit: March Update Review Update (UPDATE!)
TLDR (Update): This game has gotten a lot better since launch with online being more stablized and expected modes being added and working as intended. Capcom still needs to work on preventing Rage Quitting and adding Daily Challenges. Story mode is still releasing on June.
ONLINE
(+) Online: Online is working pretty good! Still getting near perfect to good matches overall. Surprised how well the Cross-Play is working in this game. Hopefully more games adopt this.
(+) 8 Player lobbies working as intended, it's painless to make private lobbies just to play with friends. None of us are getting 1 sided rollback and we are a mix group of PC and PS4s. Having so much fun with this one.
MECHANICS
(+) General Mechanics: It feels great! Not gunna write an essay on it. But this is probably a good game to start if you are interested in a fighting game for the first time.
(=) V-Skill: While it's not universally good, it makes some characters like Dhalsim have amazing options. For a lot of characters it doesn't add much utility.
(+) V-Trigger: V-Triggers can really make a character shine! A universal mechanic that is unique to the characters really gives them more flavor (and power).
(+) Combo Leniency: I'm not good at combo execution. (Filthy casual!) This game makes combos easier so I can focus on my other skillset.
CONTENT
(+) Survival Mode : SF4 arcade mode on the hardest difficulty was easy... TOO EASY! I wanted a survival mode that actually challenged me a bit. And I got my wish.
(+) Tutorial/Challenges : This is a basic mode that was missing from release. The demonstrations give a good amout of general mechanics and per character information. It's a great place to start learning about your character. The Challenges also give you ideas on how to expand your combos for the character of choice.
(+) DLC: First DLC character Alex is great! I hope their next character is as good as this guy.
(=) Store is functional. Decent amount of content with story mode costumes being available. Extra colors, banners etc is a nice touch. I'm saving my Fight Money for characters though.
(-) Daily Challenges: Still missing, still no way to make good Fight Money. This needs to be implemented ASAP. I got enough Fight Money to buy all DLC characters via single player, but that's not repeatable.
(-) Arcade Mode: I like to practice combos and hit-confirms on arcade mode. Training Mode dummy can be set up to play against me and survival mode is okay for this but I'd like a simple arcade mode too. This shouldn't be hard to implement I don't think.
(-) Story Mode: I know this isn't the main story mode (Free Update later in June). But man... it's pretty lame. Thank goodness survival mode exists.

One of the hidden gems of 2017.  You're not going to see it win any huge awards but you're probably gonna see it in the talk with Persona 5 for the best JRPG of the year.  I absolutely enjoyed this game from start to finish.  While not perfect, this game is definitely worth any price.
Positives:
+The characters make this game, from the edgy Velvet and Eizen to the relaxed Rokurou to the carefree Magilou, you learn to love these characters throughout your adventure.  Even non-playable characters are a joy.  The villains are made to be evil, but also aren't evil just for the sake of being evil and very few characters overall remain static for the entire game.
+The story is pretty linear, outside of quests before and after the end of the main story, there isn't much to distract you from the main point of the story.  From the start of the game the goal is made apparent: get your revenge and everything you do in this game is for that, getting your revenge.
+The game is beautiful.  From the game's opening sequence to the final boss, each place feels unique and you get multiple moments where you just have to stop and stare at the environment you are in and take a screenshot.
+Each character feels unique.  Even when using two characters primarily used for melee the battle style and artes you can use changes.  You can even equip them differently to change them more, such as making your mage's physical artes do more damage at the cost of less damage from the magic artes, which I really enjoyed.
+Good amount of replayability.  Higher difficulties and self imposed challenges (i.e. low level run, character solo, females only) will probably bring me back to replaying this game.
+Magilou. She's great.
Negatives:
-There can be times when it feels the game slows down.  There were parts where it was an hour of story and just talking to people before you could go out and explore the new area and fight the new enemies, and once you're done you hop into another hour of newly uncovered story.
-Similarly, there are a lot of optional event conversations within the party.  While completely optional, listening to these unlocks certain titles for characters which can change up their battle style and you also miss out of the personalities and relationships the characters develop with each other.  While each of these conversations are 1-2 minutes long, they add up and there was nothing more that I hated than seeing another one pop up after completing a conversation.
-Backtracking.  The game sometimes has issues with this.  While warps usually appear at the end of a dungeon and items exist to warp out of a dungeon or anywhere in the world, for story events they are sometimes disabled due to a story event happening on your way back.  While not awful, it can be frustrating when you complete a dungeon, want to leave, but can't because something is about to happen on your way out and you need to find where.
-A lot DLC, while I never purchased any of it, it does sting to see all of the DLC being more expensive than the main game, and most of the DLC being purely cosmetic.
Overall, this is a 9/10 game.  Not perfect, but does many things to remedy the flaws.  If you are looking for a JRPG or just want to get into the JRPG genre or the Tales series, this is an excellent place to start.  I look forward to eventually replaying this game.

Sleeping Dogs is a hard game to understand. On the surface its a more-than-competent GTA Style Sandbox Crime Game. Taking the slow time shooting system from Max Payne, the arcade crashing shooting from Burnout and the martial arts combat system from the Batman games its a hodgepodge of mechanics that build on the existing GTA IV mechanics and add depth to each one. Instead of shooting out a car Sleeping Dogs allows you to hjack it from another, and instead of clumsy firefights where you scramble for cover Sleeping Dogs has you vaulting over cover to pull off headshots in slow-motion glory. Its a beautiful and tehnically stunning vision of Hong Kong that has as much detail as it does character. Where the game goes deeper is where the mechanics, narrative and presentation intersect. Sleeping Dogs is one of those games made to explore a theme or idea: that of duality and ideniity. In this way the cliched-ridden undercover cop tale is told with a thematic focus on the many sides of protagonist Wei Shen and the work he does. Smart writing and briliant gameplay mechanics that reinforce the idea of duality show that this isnt just a pandering money-grabber but a well-though gaming experience where every mechanic, line of dialogue and even the outfits within the game play a part in creating a unique experience around this theme; different outfits have different bonuses, so you will find yourself dressing to suit the mission you will be doing. The ending seems a tad bit rushed and of a lower quality than the rest of the story, but overall it is still thematically consistent and worth reflecting on. Sleeping Dogs has many personalities. It wants to be an artsy game exploring deep themes while also being a commercially successful mayhem title. I say it comes damn near to succeeding at both, alot like its protagonist Wei Shen.

At times, XCOM 2 is more aptly titled as 'Keyboard Puncher Simulator' because of how unbelievably frustrating it is. Like when your best soldier misses a shot with a 99% hit-chance at point-blank range and then promptly gets murdered by some lowly alien scrub from halfway across the map.
At other times, XCOM 2 is a brilliant tactical strategy game that actually makes you think and rewards you for doing so with some of the most satisfying moments I have ever experienced in a video game. Like when my squad wipes an enemy reinforcement drop in one go or when my sniper bullseyes a sprinting enemy at full-health from a building on the other side of the area and kills it instantly. It's the kind of thing where you say to yourself "That was cool, so I'll just do this one last thing real quick and be done" but then suddenly it's 3 hours later and you're still going.
The game is not without its flaws though. I've seen plenty of people on here complain about stuff like the turn-timers, and I agree with them. Those things are kind of a nuisance, which is why it's so great that the modding community is incredible here, and have created a number of mods that can adjust or outright turn off the timers, along with tons of other really helpful and generally fun stuff that just makes the game so much more enjoyable. I adored XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It's one of my all-time favorite games, and I really love XCOM 2. It's an exceptional game and I recomend it to anyone with a reasonable tolerance for frustration or at the very least, some extra money to buy a new keyboard when they inevitably rage-smash their current one.

Your experience here is short without any completed story arcs, not that the game is long enough to do a good one. The poor writing starts when you are thrown into a world without any boot strapping to tell you anything about what is going on. I only became comfortable with the organisation I was working for and even knew what my character's role on the ship was after doing some reading outside of the game, after my first play through. The dialogue is poor, mainly because the characters lack real depth, the events in the game are pulled right from badly written 90's films (Under Siege 1992). Combat is clunky, when there is combat, and the combat simulator missions are unfinished and not, fun.

CONSORTIUM does not feel like a well tested or polished experience. This really needed more time in development. The component parts are here, but it hasn't been crafter or polished into a fine product.

Is a very interesting game. The combat is secondary and pretty old school, but the dialog parts are very good. The game itself is not huge, but the story is interesting and has allot of lore to it.
While the game is short, the whole point of the game is to play it a few times to actually figure out what is going on. Well, at least figure out whats going on in this episode of the game...
The first play through is like playing a mix between Sherlock Holmes vs Jack the Ripper, Star Trek and Dues Ex.
If you are looking for something that is not like most other games you could give this a try.
The Master Edition v1.2 was stable for me and I had no issues playing through the game. (Win 8.1) Cost wise I think the game is worth around 15 EUR. So waiting for a sale might be the thing to do. That said, if the price is around that for the next episode I might just get it.
A few minor tips when playing [No spoilers]:
*While Primary seems important. The meat of the game are the secondaries so do not make yourself feel rushed by the Captain when she gives you primary stuff to do. Basically the primary is more about "continuing" the plot rather than resolving. So enjoy the game and, mostly, do what you think is most important rather than what other people say.
* The inventory is based on you having energy OR inventory items. So you have to balance the two. Thats why you some times cant pick stuff up. However you can vent energy whenever you want and regain new from terminals all over the plane.
Suit slots do not take up space though. So put the weapons you use in the dual mini slots above and under the backpack.
* I recommend getting to grips with the controls, totally, when you are in the VR section at the start so you are not caught off guard later.
Oh yeah and... wise people are cautious about trust. :P

Almost feels like the Simcity 2013 we've waited for as (many of us have played) SC4 fans.  Much larger maps than SC2013, better gfx than SC4, and plenty of community mods out there (though not anywhere close to what SC4 has).
I really was gung-ho into this game... and then that's where the problems started.  What problems?  I don't know, it wouldn't tell me.  It just told me people were unhappy... so I gave them things to do.  Industry wanted offices, but the offices didn't want to build, citing quality of life.  My quality of Life info-graphic in the information overlay panels, said it should have been fine.  I even had a modern-looking industrial park surrounded with parkland like IRL.  I don't know how I could have improved things at this point, so I opened more roads out of town, where it'd allow me to.  I also started trading, exporting goods, figured as with any REAL city that'd spur industrial development and hence income... nope.  It sure made the city some money, most of which went back into funding infrastructure and city utilities like POWER, WATER, and FUEL.  My cities, every one of them, seemed to start to fail at around 890,000 residents.  I provided bus lines when traffic got too bad, that cost a lot of money for my city (as it doesn't provide any income due to bus fares, I found that quite aggrivating and unrealistic by itself).  So I looked into other options, to build alternate roads... that option was out, even with all the park-space I left (up to 20% per development, and reverse-frontage lots didn't save me even with new-residential-construction work in my IRL past) to save space to add in larger roadways.
So I looked into other options such as trains and high speed rail... OOPS, THERE ARE NONE.  FAILURE... FAILURE FAILURE FAILURE!  Alternative transportation IS OUR FUTURE!  WHERE IS IT?   There's a subway, but it was telling me I had to knock out any building or park land that occupied it's path, so it was next to useless, having to knock down the whole city to build a subway that there'd be no one left to use it!  That was aggrivating to the point where I gave it the alt-F4 salute and haven't played it since.  It was such a nice breath of fresh air to be free of the simcity 4 grid once and for all, but it does not come without it problems.  There are road mods, highway mods, and other cool things available to help you with this game - even a no pollution mod to help fix some of the quirks that break your cities... but they could do nothing to save me from being traffic'ed to death.  I never hit a million people.  Maybe I just stink at this game, but I came away knowing that while this game will be loved by many, it needs work, a lot of it.  For the price they charge, you should opt for the new XXL version if you don't own this game already, as it's pretty much just a re-build of XL (this game) with a few new features.  Could I recommend this game?  No, no I cant, go get XXL if you don't own this game yet, as it supports multicore (which EVERYONE can use by now, it's 2015).  It's a good game don't get me wrong, but my biggest issue with this game is that I couldn't figure out from what it told me beyond who wanted to move into the city that I should be building housing for, is that what problems needed tackling.  Why is my industry vacating and leaving 50% of it's space empty, and not wishing to build, no matter how far I knock down taxes?  Why are the people truly unhappy?  Why are they unhappy with the commute, it's a CITY, it's going to have congestion, no matter how well you do on it.  I can cram over FOUR MILLION people into a large tile on SC4 (and am quite proud of it), but I can't seem to crack a million on this game without pulling my hair out (and getting lagged out once or twice, but that requires only backing out to world-view and going back in, easy enough and seconds on a modern SSD raid setup).  The new game (XXL) is said to improve on these lag-facets and some of the bugs, while some remain, I'd much rather send you along to the newer XXL version than to spend money on last-year's model (XL, this game).  If you already own this game, XXL is not worth the upgrade unless you're a die-hard that wants multiprocessing and a few other options.  Some of the pros if I haven't listed enough of them are decent size maps (XXL has even larger ones, reportedly), and abilities to build off-the-grid if you want, and blueprints to adhere to if you choose to...
My biggest issue with this game is the lack of trains, the lack of high-speed rail, and the difficulty of building a subway system.  I am sure that many people may criticize my feelings about this game... but honestly, while I really want to love this game, the first two dozen hours brought me much pleasure, the last several hours (maybe another dozen), brought me only pain and discomfort I can only liken to a stomach virus.  It takes the fun out of the city-building/management challenge when you're playing blind - not knowing what is killing your city - not knowing what is wrong and how to fix it appropriately before your city vacates.  I want a better excuse than quality of life... that's BS.  Take quality of life out of why my offices won't build where they're needed, and maybe you'll have fixed this game 50%.  I want alternate transportation... THIS ISN'T ROME!  We have trains/bullet trains/monorail/maglev is coming out now... let's look into the future, this is a game, not real life, DEVS - USE YOUR IMAGINATION!
Also, When I start my city, or even before, Why can I not make my own map?  Why is the terraforming so limited... it does not even change the gfx of the map overlay (e.g. if you flatten out part of a ravine, it'll still LOOK like a 2d ravine is there even though it's flat)... we want more terraforming options and better map-feature-change feedback.
This really IS deep down inside a GOOD GAME, unfortunately, the enjoyment of many is cut short by a lack of good positive feedback, as I might as well be having all the read-outs in GREEK, or be playing a racing game with the monitor off until the race is over.  Focus interactive is on the right track on the new game (XXL), honestly, they're getting better, but the mere fact that to fix this game will require re-doing it from scratch pretty much, I'd hold out and see what lies in store for the future.

First off, the core game itself feels like a huge step back from what was established in Street Fighter IV. The roster's much smaller, the three-frame links make combos way too easy to pull off (you can mash everything out; no plinking or double-tapping needed) and the engine is just a touch slower than the already pretty slow SFIV. There are some good things this game brings to the table- The V-system makes the characters much more unique in play style and reminds me a lot of BlazBlue's Drives or Injustice's Traits. Also, attacks do more overall damage, so matches go by faster, and you're forced to really strategize your approach and step up your ground game. It almost feels like a return to form for the series after the more technical, FADC-laden shenanigans of SFIV, but even that game was better, and I'd still rather play 3rd Strike, Alpha 2 or Super Turbo over this any day of the week. Other than the V-system, Street Fighter V is a step down from its predecessors in every regard. Even pro players pointed out prior to the game's release that it was way too slow and easy for them.
Even if you disagree with my thoughts on the fighting system, you cannot deny that the game as a whole is unfinished as of right now. It's not worth the $40 I paid to pre-order it from Green Man Gaming and DEFINITELY not worth the full $60. The game lacks basic modes that have been standard to fighting games for years. There's no arcade mode, and in its stead is a collection of short stories that each last THREE fights. The stories are told through static images and text, and the battles are so mind-numbingly easy that you can mash your way through every fight without even thinking. Mind you, this story mode serves as the appetizer to the full-course story mode that's coming in June, but it's pretty sad that this, Survival and Training make up the whole of the single-player experience. The online was also pretty bad at release, but it seems to be fixed now. We got trials and a lobby system for the online in March, but still no word on DirectInput support or the removal of the obnoxious input lag this game has. All of this stuff should be a standard. We shouldn't have to wait for everything. Street Fighter V is basically an I.O.U. from Capcom; a AAA release that feels like early-access. It's Marvel vs. Capcom 3 all over again.
It seems to me like the only reason why Capcom decided to release this game early in such a barebones state was so that the professional scene would have ample time to practice for EVO 2016. Had they delayed the game until June, people would have had less than a month to practice for the main event of what is set to be the biggest fighting game tournament in years. But Capcom needs to realize that Street Fighter V is a game first, and an eSport later. Not everyone buying this game wants to kick it with Daigo Umehara and Justin Wong in Las Vegas, and I feel like those people are going to be the ones burned the most by this release. Guilty Gear Xrd, King of Fighters XIII and Killer Instinct are all far superior fighting games that shipped with a wealth of great single-player content to supplement their vast online communities, but SFV is becoming more attractive to the mainstream simply because it's Street Fighter. If you're looking for a fun game that offers good content for the price, please don't drink the fighting game community's Kool-Aid. I've seen plenty of fanboys on Shoryuken and other sites defending this game based on Capcom's promises (because we have every right to trust them after all the promises they've broken in the past). If you criticize this game on a fighting game community forum, you're most likely going to be told that you're just butthurt because you suck at the game and you need to "git gud".
Who knows- maybe SFV will improve in the coming months and be worth picking up, but right now, that simply isn't the case. And even then, the neutering of the game's fighting system only served to alienate this long-time fan, and I'm not the only one who feels this way.

This game had its problems. So did its predecessor. As a result, I don't think it got the attention it deserved. The first Sanctum game was fun, as is this game. So I figure it deserves a chance.
First, I'd like to note that this game is radically different from the game that was released at launch. Coffee Stain Studios has been a truly dedicated developer, working on both expansive DLC for the game as well as free patches and updates to give players the best experience they could possibly offer. If I were you, I'd try to ignore initial reviews of the game, as this version is almost entirely different.
This game offers three distinct gamemodes. The first is campaign, which you do to unlock new maps and progress through the very poorly conveyed story. The story of the game is given through comic-book-style panels, and while this does help with budget it feels awful cheap. I'd rather them leave it out entirely to be honest. The goal is simple, build a maze of blocks to slow down enemies, build up to 15 (not 10) towers on top of said blocks to shoot at the enemies, use the guns you got to help your towers. Survive for the set amount of waves by protecting the core to win the map. In the end the game is a Tower Defense, but because of the shooter aspect it also has that element of horde survival gameplay.
The second gamemode is Survival. You play with the same parameters as the campaign, same 15 tower limit, same map, same waves, however after you complete the normal waves, they restart and send buffed enemies at you. The goal of this mode is to survive as long as possible, and is more of a marathon than it is a survival game. This is where the competitive gameplay mostly happens, with players rankings being listed on leaderboards. Maximizing strategy and efficiency is the key to doing well.
The final mode is a mode added post-launch called Sandbox. You get to tweak everything from tower limit to enemy toughness to resources dropped per-wave. If you want the game to be all about those towers, you can do that. If you want the game to rely solely on your shooting prowess, you can do that. It lets you mess around and play the game how you want to play it.
Gameplay works by alternating building phases where you create towers, build walls, and set up defenses, with battle phases where you take on the hordes. For the most part this works fairly well. However, we run into the problem of timed build phases. Every once in a while the game will give you only about a minute or less to build all the defenses you want, then it throws the wave at you whether you like it or not. While this does change the pace of the game, it mostly detracts. This is a strategy game in the end, and the timed waves are the opposite of strategy, relying on panic to change the pace. The game would have benefitted from having these timed waves removed entirely, or at least having an option to turn them off.
Enemies in this game don't always necessarily head right for the goal. Some enemies prioritize killing the players before reaching the goal. By the way, this game has a health system in it ala Call of Duty, a game this one probably takes a few too many cues from. You can be knocked out once your screen becomes a little too "Bloody screen so real", which will remove your from the action for 10 (sometimes vital) seconds and putting you back at the start. Numbers would have been nice.
Guns were buffed in this game in a major way. No longer does the game force you to spend your tower resources on your guns. Now, your guns are at their maximum capability from the get-go, making them extremely powerful. As waves progress, enemies become more resilient, so it turns into a situation where you either specialize your guns to help you as a player crowd control while your turrets take out large targets or vice-versa, or that you buff your towers and they do the major lifting, or that your towers buff you and you kill most of the stuff. The game allows for a lot of versatility of play. Unfortunately this leads to the undesired effect that you may be doing more work than your towers, at least initially. Whether you see this as a problem or not is a matter of perspective. Some people prefer it as mostly tower defense, others enjoy the shooting. I'm personally neutral on the subject.
In place of the gun progression, the game has introduced a perk system. By the time you hit max level you'll be able to equip up to 3 perks, which all affect how you can play the game. Some are just straight up damage boosts while others offer different tactical options. Mixing and matching perks to work with your towers can be a challenge in and of itself, as there's a lot of different perks to choose from, many of which are not the same as they were on launch. They're a nice addition to the game to help you specialize your playstyle and strategy.
Also added in to this game as a new feature are character classes. There are four different characters to choose from (five with the DLC "Road to Elysion"), and each has a sort of "built in perk" to their character. Each class gets a signature gun that is locked to their character, which is annoying because it removes some of the customization you can have. However the classes are built around these weapons so it's understandable, but it's still a nuisance. In addition, your character can have a secondary weapon, which can be any other gun in the game, including the other characters' signiture weapons (give you've progressed far enough). The classes add some good variety and are a nice fit for the multiplayer.
The maps are all fairly varied, ranging from open fields with a lot of mazing capability to prebuilt labarynths and large fields connected by narrow passways. Finding optimal maze routes on all the maps is a good, challenging experience. All the maps also have a lot of secrets to find, including codes that unlock backstory on a website called the Elysian Archive, a real cop-out to providing that same backstory in-game, but it provides a neat little "sidequest" in a way. The game loves to leave easter eggs and references in all the maps, and it's a fun time just exploring between waves to see what you can find. That said, some of the level design on some of the maps is lacking, and sometimes downright cruel to the player. Waves may be too harsh for certain limitations, or sometimes they're not harsh enough for the player capability given in the level. All in all it could use a little more work, but they're generally fun to play on.
That said the game has flaws. First, it is a tower defense game. If you don't like tower defense that's half the game. Secondly, the game is a shooter. If you wanted a tower defense game, you won't be happy. However, if you like both, this game should give you a good time. The control scheme can be kind of weird at times, and you may want to rebind the controls. The game also has insane difficulty spikes. You'll be fine until the forest. Then you'll hit the forest. Then certain maps will make you want to not play the game. The shooting mechanics are also pretty mundane. For all guns you have a primary fire, which does what you expect the gun to do, and a secondary fire, which is usually a niche attack for certain situations your gun can't normally handle well. It works well enough but it's not terribly interesting. Also, the progression system is a little too "Call of Duty", forcing you to level up before getting what you want, which is not welcome in my opinion.
All in all the game is fun. There's a lot of depth to the strategy, the game has vastly improved since its launch, and there's a lot of content to be had for only 15 bucks (USD). In addition there's 3 DLC expansions to get at this point, each adding 4 maps, 2 new guns, and 2 new towers, with one adding a new character. I suggest grabbing it and the DLC on sale at the very least.

A fun game still neck-deep in development. While the gameplay is fun, it lacks in fully utilizing progression and making building more accessible to players. The more variety and involvement in progressively-generated objectives, the better. As for the building, perhaps tools designed to ease the building process for non-builders would benefit. Perhaps players could design their own structure blueprints, such as "This is a castle room," or "This is the furnishing for my castle room," or "This is a different set of furnishing for my castle room." To cut down on lugging massive stockpiles of junk (in an inventory with an admittedly broken pickup-sorting), this should probably be tied in with the 3d printer, costing pixels after an on-hand stock is used up. Really, I feel as if the 3D printer might not get as much love as it should. While the things the staff are doing now certainly look like fun additions, they feel quite small and toying compared to actually pushing for an official release, as opposed to "early access".
Recent updates have stunted some of the minutiae in the game (temperature, hunger), but if minutiae is too tedious, then the idea is to mediate or automate the process so it's less of a burden on experienced players--many games could benefit from the sort of management to automate timed actions as resources warrant. "If I have food, just automatically eat when I'm hungry," or something. It sounds complicated, but it's a consideration point. This trickles into Techs sometimes, where the game essentially nerfs some Techs as not useful, and others monopolize the player character's slots. If they won't allow more tech to be equipped at priority, then perhaps tech should be designed in a way where one player's tech can benefit the entire party somehow. Maybe everyone can board that one player's boat.
Party dynamics could be an interesting investment, perhaps a la Lost Vikings, where each player can specialize in a diversified subset of capability. Perhaps different aspects of gameplay could find intuitive ways to meld together, if we break down the components of resourcing, building, and defending. Shuffling equipment requires too much precision, and the less juggling, the more immersive the gameplay becomes because there's less "I accidentally scrolled to my stairs instead of my crossbow and the enemy killed me." Segwaying from this to multiplayer, perhaps servers should come with certain permissions to allow strangers onto servers but with lesser permissions--no ability to destroy player structures or to procedurally generate new planets on that server unless they're on a whitelist.
Starbound's a good multiplayer game that benefits from cooperation, although there's a high emphasis on virtual creativity, which can be a slippery slope for people who prefer exploring. Exploring can become a bit samey after a while, and there should probably be consequences and challenges involved to deepen this experience, with rewards more fitting than another chest that's missing a new blueprint. Pretty soon you're just blindly hunting down specific rare biomes to catch 'em all. The character design of the alien races is especially good, which each species having their benefits and drawbacks, although at this stage this is purely cosmetic. As long as the lore doesn't try to negate the player's own personal manifestations of their character avatars, the best step is fleshing out in-game what's hinted to come. The progression system, while linear even at the point where it does branch off, does come with its rewards, but these rewards only carry you so far, and there's an interminable amount of resource collection to do by hand. If you just happen to be good at making your own things to do, then this game will net you more mileage. Overall, you have to balance the shopping list of engagement and the rote tedium, but future updates show much promise.

If you like speeding through cities, dodge traffic and ram your opponents into walls (or the aforementioned traffic), then this game is for you.
Featuring an open city, a variety of cars and events, a so-so soundtrack and the never ending joy of bashing opponents to smithereens, Burnout Paradise offers arcade racing fans a treat.
If you want to crash into some human enemies, go online and partake in pretty much everything you did in singleplayer!
What I'm enjoying most online, though, are the co-op events, where the players unite (more or less) to achieve a common goal, like managing to get to a certain place or do barrel rolls over each other.
It's a bit sad that Paradise may be the first and last Burnout making it to PC, as Criterion (and especially EA) seems more focused on Need for Speed.
What's also sad is that one of the bigger DLCs never made it to PC: Big Surf Island, which not only includes a whole new are to explore, but also new game modes and cars.
But rejoice as modders try to bring exactly that to the PC!
It's already playable, although it's still missing a lot of stuff, including singleplayer events, traffic and game modes, but you can explore Big Surf Island, drive a lot of new cars (including whatever cruises through Paradise) and partake in online events!
It's called the "Vanity Pack". Go and get it. Seriously.
And while we're at DLC: The in-game store has been shut down a long time ago, but you can still get the Legendary Cars, Toy Cars and the Boost Specials from retailers like Amazon.
All in all a fantastic game. Get it!
10/10 go play it

When I first fired up The Final Specimen, I had the strangest sensation: an odd itch to check my pocket for the reassuring weight of a pile of quarters. Everything about this game screams old school arcade action - from the cartoon-style graphics to the three-button control scheme - and a reminder of what challenging platform gaming was all about. The story is engaging, the snappy fully-voiced dialogue reminding me of Family Guy/South Park and providing a welcome interlude between levels.
The overall design is exceptionally well built out. You can tell the developers spent a lot of time playing platformers, as even the opening level sends you on a trip through a series of tubes that could have come straight out of an old Sonic game. The enemies are especially well-designed if slightly unforgiving - it takes some trial and error to figure out the best way to approach and defeat bosses and even some regular mobs, but the abundance of health powerups and extra lives ensure that you'll make it through long before you run out of quarters.

Nifty open world crime game, and hence some superficial similarities to GTA. Much more melee/kungfu orientated which works well, though there is some opportunity for some limited gun/weapon stuff. The melee/counter system actually has some similarity to the Batman games (or at least Arkham Asylum & City being the only two I've played), probably due to the Square Enix connection. However, I've found it to be a bit more diverse with the inclusion of grappling moves,  unlockable melee combos, and a wide variety of environmental finishing moves. At one point in the game, I put an opponent through a glass aquarium for it to shatter everywhere, then picked up a fish and proceeded to beat another opponent senseless with said fish! Driving is fine and not overly sensitive (though a lot more responsive than say GTA4 and certainly something I had to adjust for when I played GTA4 after) and they have a reasonable range of vehicles (including bikes and boats). Lots of DLC available too, though I have yet to obtain any and can't comment on whether they're worth the trouble. Fun game in a different, refreshing cultural setting, though it doesn't have the endless social satire like the GTAs or even Saints Row.

Background - Bastion was originally released on the XBOX Live Arcade and eventually made its way to PC. Not much more to say here, except that the game was made by 11 people, I think.


Gameplay - The gameplay of Bastion is super simple. First of all the whole world floats because of something called "The Calamity". You start off unarmed and find a hammer named the "Cael Hammer". In the beginning of the game, you use it to whack things as hard as humanly possible. Not much else, here, really. I'd call it an Action RPG, but others tend to call it an Action Adventure, but I dunno. Maybe it's both. But you will basically be running around here and there whacking things with a giant hammer if you so choose. A little way through the game you get a shield that'll let you counter enemy attacks for massive damage and maybe stun them, and then after that, you find a repeater rifle. This is your basic loadout until you get to the "Bastion" which is where you meet Rucks. Rucks is the narrator of the game and will narrate everything you are doing, and even throw in lines absolutely specific to what you are doing. For instance, there are a lot of smashable things. If you pick up the hammer, and smash ALL of the things, then the narrator will say, "Kid just rages for a while.” in response to you taking your time to stop and smash all of the things. The whole game is made up of this kind of combat, so you either get used to it quick or you end up putting it down fairly quickly.

There are also structures you can build on the Bastion. A few of the notable ones are the Vigil (which makes you money if you do the things listed),  The Shrine where you can invoke "The Wrath of the Gods" by adding idols that make the game even harder, but reward you more money, and The Distillery, which you need to level up. This game encourages childhood drinking, I think. Anyway, you wander off level to level with the lovely narrator guiding you on your journey. It's great.


Visuals - Visuals are REALLY good. I'm not sure if they're hand drawn or what, but they're REALLY pretty. The game is also in a semi-isometric view at all times, which can get kind of weird, but it works for this game. Good enemy and character design, and the environments are all pretty detailed.


Sound - THE SOUNDTRACK IS SO GOOD. LIKE I'M GOING TO BUY IT. REALLY. IT'S GOOD.
GIVE IT A LISTEN.


Story - So you wake up thanks to the narrator, and you take on the role of The Kid. Like I said, you get the hammer, and a shield, and a repeater. You're going to The Bastion because of something called The Calamity to look for survivors. That's it, really. The story unfolds from there, and it's really good.


Multiplayer - There's no multiplayer. Most RPG's don't have them.


Other Information - The only complaint I have is that it's short. I sunk 6 hours into it and beat it while doing about half of the side missions.


Overall - A short, but sweet elegant dessert that requires you to slow down and enjoy it. Sure there are longer games out there, but this one is special. In the words of Egoraptor, "It's kind of like comparing a snack food to a high-class dessert. You can just chomp away mindlessly at snacks because that's how they're made. They're addictive by nature; they just make you reach for more even though you don't really want more. But a high-class dessert takes some slowing down. It demands that you take a moment to really enjoy how complex and satisfying it is. In the end you'll always think more highly of the high-class dessert because it gave you a feeling of TRUE satisfaction. It's not designed to go on forever; it was designed to finish off a meal. And it was so good you wanted more, but what you had was delicious and you're glad you had it. OR YOU CAN JUST BE A PIG AND EAT IT ALL-*gross eating noises. “If this remotely interested you, there's a demo available on Steam and I think on XBOX 360. Hard to know when I don't own a 360.

Bastion exceeds all expectations of a smart action video game.
You play as the Kid, tasked with journeying to various locations (or basically, levels), fighting your way through enemies and reaching the end. And that's really the gist of it.
That may seem like a simple formula, and it is. But everything that comes along with the package: straight forward game play that challenges you with quick reaction times, customizable weapon choices and upgrades which supply strategy, various difficulty settings allowing you make this an extreme walk in the park or a warzone; all of this makes Bastion solid fun. Enemies try to surprise and outthink you with various forms, all of which have different weaknesses and strengths, keeping yourself constantly on your toes. While you fight your way through these places, you'll have to watch out for your health and limited number of special moves per level, which will decline with the various hazards and terrain that you may take for granted. And finally, bonus locations which supply challenges and rewards for your weapons, keeps the entire experience from getting boring.
And while the great game play may be what you go for, the game likewise ties in fantastic personality, art, music and story. The art really is something else and has its own feel to it, while the soundtrack has a rock and blues genre that is amazing and highly recommended to buy with the game. The story is also very well done and heavy, especially if you dig for it. Bastion rewards you with its story if you take the time to unlock certain achievements for back-story and histories concerning the characters. By the time I was done with the game I was blown away by the direction it had taken. This isn't just a story about an apocalypse and trying to fix it; by the time it was over, I knew the characters, what they were trying to do and why they were doing it. The ending is also one of the best I've experienced in a game, especially if the correct steps are taken to receive the best one.
I could continue to go on about this game, but I'll end the review here. In short, Bastion is a terrific action adventure that tells a rich story, shows beautiful art, gives a great soundtrack and leaves you with an unforgettable game. Great job, Supergiant Games, you're one of my indie favorites.

Serena: Sincerely Intriguing
Serena is a point and click adventure PC game found for free on Steam. It is a short and basic indie game that is narrative driven. For those who enjoy reading, mystery, and casual gaming, this game is enjoyable. The game is not very graphically demanding, and is therefore playable on most PC builds. The game is also very small in file size so it is quick to download and start playing playing. My blind playthrough of the game (which I streamed on Twitch) lasted a little under an hour. I most likely would have completed the game faster but there were a few moments I found myself confused by either the controls, or what my next objective really was.
The most immediate thing I noticed when starting the game is that it has no main menu, or pause menu. The game just begins when you load it from Steam, which took me by surprise. I then tried to lower the sensitivity of my mouse looking and found that hitting the escape key simply closed the game. After getting my bearings and realizing this was going to be a point and click narration/reading game, I tried moving away from the table you start the game sitting at. I struggled for a minute or so trying to figure out how to move around and get out of the chair, only to find that the mouse turning into a pointing hand indicated the ability to move. You could only move if you were pointing the mouse in a very particular part of the screen, and this would continue throughout the game. At times I struggled to figure out where I had to point the mouse to move around. I feel like this maybe could have been done better by at least having a mouse button or keyboard key be used to zoom back out when you zoom in for a closer look on specific objects. Even after completing the game however, I still can’t pinpoint exactly what the completion conditions of the game were. At times I was aimlessly wandering the playing space, sure that I had explored and examined everything needed to move on. I would find there was some object I overlooked, thinking it would be unimportant, but was apparently a catalyst to progression.
The story of the game starts slow but later became pretty interesting. You play as a character who seems to be having trouble remembering some major details about his past and especially his lover, Serena, as you begin the game unable to even remember her face. Throughout the course of the game you will wander around your quaint and secluded log cabin home, examining all the objects within it to attempt to jog your memory. Meticulous searching and thorough analysis of every object is key, as you must gather as much information as you possibly can. Players will do well to not focus on completing the game or thinking of necessary goals. Instead, they should try to just sink into the story and atmosphere of the game, letting mystery, intrigue, and curiosity guide them naturally through the playing space and events. The story absolutely heated up near the end of the game and subverted my expectations for what I thought was going to be a routine and predictable outcome. I underestimated the game’s ability to surprise me and change things up, and it surely did in it’s last section, to positive degree. I won’t detail the story and spoil it, as it would make playing the game utterly pointless, since it’s pretty much all the game has to stand on.
At first the game felt cheesy and poorly written, but as the game progressed I realized it was more of a ploy to get the player comfortable and get their guard down. I wasn’t really emotionally grabbed in the early portion of the game, but as the main character went through more emotions and became more complex, I related more and was drawn in. For anyone who has experienced a breakup, there may be parts of the game that really resonate with you, I know it did with me.  There were times that I was genuinely affected on an emotional level as I listened to the main character go through the waves of emotion about his breakup with his wife. The writing becomes a lot more refined and beautiful in the more serious later parts of the game.
Serena was an enjoyable experience and I’m glad I took the time to experience a game that I feel is pretty unique. It’s a casual game that is accessible to anyone, mechanically, technologically, and financially.  I recommend casually sitting down alone or with friends and playing through Serena yourself. Though for gamers looking for something more complex, challenging, visually appealing, or thrilling, this may not be a good use of your time.

The game plays out a lot like a film, but you also get a feeling your not completely in control. Your actions are via dialogue with the AI characters and though you do have choices you don't really feel as if these choices will have much effect and are mostly a choice between your character looking dumb or acting like you know whats happening (when you've not got a clue). At another point I was told to surrender and holster my gun by pressing H key, I did but the AI still told me I'd regret not doing as I was told and a shoot out happening anyway.
The general path of the story is good but some of the actions that occur don't feel very realistic (like simply requesting a priate lets your aircraft pass and all will be forgotten). There are other little things and snap you from being drawn in, the character eyes sometimes turn too far and show all white as well and limbs clipping objects (like gestures from arms slicing through chair arms).
If there was a scale of how much potiental the devs have got with this concept it'll be 11 out of 10 but you get the feeling playing the it just missed the mark. I desperately wanted this game to draw me and at times it did but those little oddities just broke my from the depth of the game and I was just playing an adventure game again. I get the feeling I'm missing lore in the game that would improve my involvemtn but get the feeling that I'd have to invest a whole lot of time reading computer enteries to get to this level and I'd rather be playing than reading to be honest. This said thoughI hope the dev's produce a follow up to this.

I admit that I was skeptical when I bought it, but I figured, "Eh, it's only five bucks."  Now that I've played it, I feel that I more than got my money's worth.  Town of Salem is an excellent game that's almost always tense and entertaining.  You need multiple skills to win, including luck, deception, and deduction, but even when you screw up it's a good time.
I only have two real gripes about the game.  The first is the community; a lot of players are pretty offensive, both in language and behavior, and more than a few will quit at the drop of a hat if things start to go against them.  This doesn't include everyone, mind, but more players than I'd like.  The second is that lag, when it hits, kills the game, more than doubling play time, silencing chat, and preventing players from using their abilities.  It's not a common occurrence, but it's extremely frustrating when it does.
Still, those complaints shouldn't deter one from a game that is, on the whole, a lot of fun.

The good: Great atmosphere, decent voice acting. Genuinely adult writing about a relationship, loss, regret, etc. It's also free.
The mixed: It appears to use the engine from a hidden object game. This lowers system requirements while keeping the level of detail high, but makes moving around more akward than it could be.
The bad: In order to progress the plot, you have to click on just about everything. Sometimes several times in a row. When enough things have been clicked on, the game progresses and you get different responses on the same items (in addition to other changes). This can lead to a lot of frustration when you can't remember what things you've already clicked.
No ability to save your progress. I realize that this is a short-ish game, but having to redo everything after quitting mid-game is a PITA.
Bottom line: If Dear Esther is a walking simulator, this is a clicking simulator. Games like this rely heavily on well-written scripts and atmosphere to succeed. I think that despite its flaws, it does ultimately succeed. If you're expecting revolutionary game design, you'll be disappointed. If you're up for a fairly grim story told through clicking on things in a room, then you might like this game.

Ive been a fan of these RTS titles all my life, from the free copy of Total Annilhilation I got with my Packard Bell PC when I was 5 years old through to the Supreme Commanders up to present (and I wondered why I never had a girlfriend!) so naturally I delved into the first Planetary Annihilation game without question. And for the most part I have no regrets. Its a cracking game. Reminiscant of its  predessecor with some contemporary ideas. Titans improves on this considerably, It takes the best of Supreme Commander like the experimental units and Sub Commanders and adds them to an already sound all round game. Some other noticable improvments are the maps featuring levels, it sounds trivial but being able to have half your base defended by a cliff rather than your own defences is better for gameplay. There has also been some scaling fixes it seems along with some much needed pathing, in the original somtimes I couldnt place metal extractors on metal because they were merging into mountains or somthing of the like. Not a problem in Titans so far.
The new units may seem like not alot, but they make all the difference in the world. It depends on your playstyle what you will use the most but I certainly use the sub commanders they are a really great feature, they can build anything and everything fast and are a powerful combat unit. Theres also a planet destroyer which is highly amusing and also surprisingly practical, and the extra Space ships are a thing of beauty too.
HOWEVER there are still issues from the first one that have not been addressed as of yet. Its still Assassination only on skrimish, which can be frustrating at times if you settle in for a night of waring only to have the enemy commander spawn right next to you and you win or die within minutes. its not just every now and then either atleast 3 out of 5 games i have to restart because the enemy AI has spawned in exactly the same place on the same planet. Sometimes we dont even build units the game starts and the commanders just have it out with each other until one dies and takes the other with it. Thats how close they sometimes spawn! Also still no second Team, which again given the scale of these games doesnt seem like a biggy, but what makes its predecessors great is choosing sides, the Arm or the Core from TA, the Cybran, Aeon or UEF from Sup Com, very different teams with different units, it makes for better war. while playing PA your attacks can always be countered with exactly the same units on the recieving end. It takes a little of the "mu ha ha my army is better than yours" away if you both have the same army. But thats more personal preference than a necessity. Atleast you'll always know what the enemy are capable of.
So over all, while TA is still the best (with its soundtrack still gracing my ever aging Ipod) and SupCom still a little more epic and diverse, this game does not dissapoint or embarrass this sort-of-franchise in anyway. Titans has only made it better and who knows, maybe the next one will give players a little more choice in gameplay options and teams like most other RTS...But for now, im happy to just blow up planets with my new favourite toy.
I'd go for Titans for sure. You wont go back to the original once you have it thats for sure, and you will probably have many late nights with sweaty palms and drinking insane amounts of Tea while playing this game. Well done Uber Entertainment!
PS If your older than maybe 20  you should totally whack on the TA soundtrack while playing, your childhood will come flooding back. Ha!

The first time I played through the game I found a fun, interesting, tightly woven adventure story with humor, action, drama and rising stakes... very enjoyable.
But interestingly, I didn't have to resolve every single thing to get through the game's narrative. Still, I felt a stong desire to resolve a particular situation and uncover this part of the story. So I played through again. And then a third time.
On the third playthrough I resolved the situation and uncovered something that not only fit with things that the game had been hinting at, but also blew my mind because the "narrative device" of exploring this complex alternate universe turned out to be more complex than it appeared on the surface. I finally got a small part of what the game had been trying to tell me all along.
Once you realize what might really be going on -- it is HUGE.
Not not only did I WANT to play the game again and learn as much as I could for my own enjoyment -- and I'll mention here that I've played the game all the way through about a dozen times, finding new and interesting things each time -- but I also felt that from a narrative perspective that I NEEDED to play through and learn as much as I could because of what I realized was going on.

This is my first review I ever written and may ever write, so I don't know how to begin.  I grew up with the half-life series, I remember playing it when it first came out and I was just 7 or 8 years of age. I remember the headcrabs scaring me, the blaring lights warning me of danger, the first time picking up the crowbar and hitting zombies. I remember fearing vents. But those were the best moments of my life that I wish I could do again. Playing Half-Life is like a gateway drug into gaming for me, the movement, the guns, the action and the story I made up for Gordon Freeman kept me coming back for more and more and exploring more games as well as getting into gaming as a whole. I played games beforehand like Doom, Quake, Mega Man and Tie Fighter, but  they never hooked me like Half-Life. And when it was over, I felt like I've finally found a calling and began to play more and more. It was ecstatic. Playing it again, all these years later, yes the graphics have dated but at the same time, I feel like it's still as believable and realistic as when I first played it back in '98. That could just be nostalgia, but I think out of all the games in my library, I'll come back and play and beat Half-Life again and again.

Interactive media and motion picture had a baby.  CONSORTIUM is an outstanding example of how immersive storytelling can be accomplished, with decisions and impacts that really matter.
A quick example: forgetting to charge your energy reserves before meeting with your boss can determine whether or not a crew member dies....  Not because it's scripted that way, but because you have to run to need energy reserves in order to inject a wounded crew member with healing nanites.  And if you aren't prepared, they bleed out before you get back.
There are numerous other instances that truly inspire that this game is indeed another universe, that the characters are living, coping, and otherwise dealing with the stress of being in a tense military situation.
Sadly, the graphics do not live up to this - The game went for a slightly cartoony look instead of a realistic look.  That said, it works well with the chosen art style, and it isn't the visual art that makes the game.  It's the audio, the writing, and the humanoid interactions and reactions.
The game is a little short for what I was hoping (was able to fully complete 1 variant of the story in 2 hours), but it has quite a bit of variation and replayability based on what you do and don't do.
TL;DR - Highly recommended if you want a story-driven adventure game that doesn't rely on logic puzzles or item gimmicks.  Plus, its story is awesomely meta.

I adore this game. It's difficult to find much wrong with it now that they've meticulously patched it, fixing all the performance issues and irritating bugs.
This is possibly the first game I've played where the characters seem like real people with real relationships that really matter. You feel as though you're really leaving an impression on them as you attempt to solve the myriad mysteries of Zenlil, the futuristic plane, while a conspiracy of powers you can't hope to understand weaves its web below the surface. I'm even a big fan of the graphic style, which brings back nostalgic memories of 90s CG television shows like Reboot. Who knew flat-shaded textures could have such a charm to them?
While it wraps itself in the guise of a first-person-shooter, Consortium is a conversational game first and foremost, with almost every encounter with danger solvable without needing to resort to circle-strafing and machine-gunning. As such it can be a more sedate experience than you're comfortable with if you're looking for a more conventional FPS. I'd very much recommend it to people who are more inclined towards adventure games and other more story-based genres.
With how open-ended the game is and how many ways you can alter and affect the timeline, I reckon I'll be giving Consortium a bunch more playthroughs before the next installment.

I just want to say that I have been playing Cities XL Platinum for about a week now and have had no issues running or using it whatsoever.  I have a nice system, but not tricked out or fancy.  Quad core, 660 Nvidia card, 8gb RAM and lots of disk space.
I have had a void in my life for a long time because of the lack of Simcity and Emperor  ROTMK type games. Games that were more about building your city and managing it rather than trying to figure out the interface or why you can't get the water pipes or electrical to match up.  I had tried many others like Anno (althought not the latest one) but they never felt right.  I want to work with the city more than I want to learn how to use the interface.  Of course I want lots to do and stats to pay attention to but the combination of building my city myself and seeing it grow on its own is what I really like.  Cities XL Platinum really does that for me.  I will proabably buy the new one now, especially because of the discount.
What I like so far:
- Many useful tutorials.  However, if you are familiar with this sort of game you will probably only need some of them.
-City building itself and placing of zones, etc is very easy to learn and there are lots of choices.
- Visually awesome looking with multiple zoom levels.  I especailly like being able to zoom down to ground level to see what my city is really like.  You can even click on a person or car and the camera will just follow them.
-Plenty of helpful information about your city in both statistics and graphical overlays so you can make informed choices.  I especially like that the colored, graphical overlays, icons  and so on show up in all the zoom levels so you can check out that information whenever you want.
- Overall, very fun and absorbing.  Its easy to get focused in on my little world and lose all track of time.
- Very large and dedicated fan base with mucho mods and user content available.
What I don't like so far:
-  Occasionally it is hard to manipulate the zones or roads for what I want to do.  But that has been getting easier for me as I learn more about how they work and the choices I have.  So I am not worried about it.
-  I really have nothing bad to say.

Tales of Berseria. What a wonderful game!
A lot of people have already said basically everything that needed to be said about this game, but I guess I'll add my recommendation to the pile. Tales of Berseria (ToB) is a JRPG with a fighting-style combat system and a part of an old and pretty popular franchise. Tales of games have always been about story and characters (and interesting action combat called Linear Motion Battle System), and ToB certainly continues that trend. And, oh boy, does it do it well.
You follow the story of young lady named Velvet Crow. She has a reason to be angry, and so she sets out to kill that reason. Painfully. After she breaks (literally) from prison, sets a couple of cities on fire and kidnaps a child. You know, the usual. Velvet, as you might imagine, is an anti-hero which is a welcome break from typical "insert yourself"-protagonists. She is not evil, but she does some horrible things. Somewhere behind that anger and hatred is a kindhearted person, but you can't call her good either. And her story is an emotional roller coaster that is pretty good at making you care about the events and dialogue. At least it was like that for me. Speaking of dialogue, a rather colourful and entertaining cast of main characters joins Velvet on her journey to liven things up. And I'm happy to say that party dialogue is one of the best parts of the game. The dynamic between characters is on point and listening to their banter (or 'skits' as it's called in Tales of series) is very enjoyable.
The meat of the game in terms of gameplay is, of course, combat. And in ToB combat is something I didn't get tired of at all despite there being, well, a lot of it. You assign various moves that you unlock to several buttons and then chain-combo them together as you please in a fast paced real-time combat system. Interrupting enemies, taking their weaknesses into account, blocking at the right time and executing special moves is also rather important. And the combat animations are of high quality as well.
Unfortunately, not everything is great. The game engine for ToB is pretty old, and due to it being released on PS3 one can definitely see that there isn't much graphical prowess on display. The design for various game areas and dungeons is also pretty uninspired and somewhat dull. You can't really call enemies original either. Character customization is nothing to write home about - it's there and it's lackluster when compared to something like Xenoblade Chronicles or any western CRPG, but that's nothing new for the genre. You have upgradable equipment (only weapons and cosmetic items change the model) and titles with different passive bonuses as well as your active skills loadout. And that's about it. Creating an effective build with focus on something like the amount of action points or critical hits is still possible, so it's serviceable.
Can all of that detract from the experience of enjoying the game? Yes. Is the game still great? Yes again. With a good cast of characters, involving storyline and fun flashy combat Tales of Berseria is a no-brainer purchase for JRPG fans and one of my personal contenders for Game of the Year 2017.
