A trail of different coloured balls are pushed along a track by a beetle, and using a launcher, you must fire a randomly coloured ball into the trail, being careful to place it next to a ball of the same colour. When at least three collide with one another they'll be eliminated. Eliminate all balls (which destroys the beetle) before the trail reaches the end of the track to pass to the next stage.
Everything starts off sedately enough as the convoy makes its way slowly along some fairly straightforward tracks. But as the stages progress, the whole thing moves faster and tracks become ever more elaborate, criss-crossing over itself or being intertwined with a second track with another trail being simultaneously pushed along it, as well as additional colours being added to complicate the assortment and make matches more difficult to obtain.
Thankfully, there are power-ups to aid you as reward for clearing balls, such as wild balls which will match with any colour, fireballs which destroy all balls within a certain radius, lightning strikes that fire a vertical bolt up the screen to clear everything in its path, and upgrades that temporarily slow or even completely halt movement of the trail briefly.
It's a casual time-waster that's fun to dip in and out of every so often, but while early stages are fun enough and easy-going enough to allow you to take your time setting up massive combos and chain reactions, by the back third or quarter of the main adventure mode, I found the pace and number of colours to manage to be too frantic to be all that much fun anymore. Rather than setting up an epic set piece of destruction, it feels more like damage control as you focus on the immediate threat at the front of the trail and are constantly trying to put that fire out. The front end of play is slow and considered and the back end of it is reflexive, and that's actually where I started to get bored as I slipped into autopilot for one stage after another.
Everything has an Egyptian theme to it in both look and sound, along with an overworld map screen that I don't understand the purpose of given that stages themselves repeat and have no shared theme to link them together into a combined "world" on a map that has what seems to be a completely arbitrary stage number attached to it. But there are plenty of stages along the way and many hours to sink into this across three difficulties.
I got the game in a bundle for a few euro and could live with the purchase more easily that way, as I wouldn't be in a hurry to pay the full asking price for it. But I guess what it's worth is up to each person individually, so if this sounds like your kind of thing that you're willing to drop the full amount on, then go for it.

TL:DR of this review is I cannot recommend this game because of some serious bugs, performance issues, and balance issues.
With that out of the way Xcom 2 IS a great game and better than Xcom: Enemy Unknown and Xcom: Enemy Within in most ways. If you liked those games and don't mind issues I'd expect from an early access title then go for it. But sadly at the end of the day the frame rate fluctuates VERY wildly (from 60FPS all the way down to 10 at times) on a high end system (i7-4790k, GTX 1080, 32GB of RAM, and the game on an SSD), it's what can only be described as stupidly buggy (I've gotten half way through the final mission about 4 times now only to have it freeze at the same exact point), and there are some serious balance issues (enemies getting multiple turns to your one turn and enemies being able to move during your turn if you move a unit into eyesight of them). I had hoped that they would fix the game but it seems that instead of that they decided to make a $40 expansion. When I can finish the final mission without it freezing, dropping to 10FPS, or having some borderline cheating AI decide it gets to move 3 times and kill half my squad I'll update this review and consider War of the Chosen. But for now Xcom 2 is a mess. A pretty and kinda fun mess but a mess all the same.
Edit. I finally managed to complete the final mission without it freezing or soft locking on me but sadly it took 7 total tries.

The “Extra-Life” -- the original gaming MacGuffin. As a kid, nothing matched the feeling of excitement when discovering a 1-Up in a secret area -- it was my first brush with an endorphin rush, and it’s where my love for gaming began. Though over time, the extra-life has slowly become somewhat of an antiquated notion; a relic of the gaming past. I never realized the nostalgic weight behind that feeling until I played The Final Specimen: Arrival, and when I found that glowing “T” in the suburban bushes of Doofusville. It’s a feeling I didn’t realize how much I had missed as a gamer, and it also made me convinced as to why TFS is a truly special entry in contemporary gaming.
Modernity never graces itself anywhere throughout TFS in all avenues, allowing the player to resign themselves to an earlier time in gaming, and without compromise. The result: the player sinks into their seat, and a familiar feeling settles in and the player embarks on an uncontaminated, and highly sentimental experience. TFS isolates a core gaming era, where Super Mario Bros. set the table for the side-scroller onslaught and players’ insatiable desire for more challenging gameplay within familiar mechanics. TFS is cemented in that time, consumed by the same preoccupations of those early developers: two games per one of their competitors.
These feelings are seldom found in nostalgia-trip games of the past few years. Many have mistakenly assumed that pixilation and 8-bit soundtracks are sufficient to encapsulate the essence of the floppy-disk game -- but few have matched TFS in its almost stubborn effort to remain true to its comrades. It is a staunch vestige of a lost era; an artifact that increases in value along the way.
The game wants you to fail; you never feel safe. But at the same time, it wants you to learn; to develop a very specific mindset. Your controllers become an extension of your body, and you slowly become a veteran as you play. When the sting of a missed opportunity to an extra life hangs above your character’s head, a motivation burns to never miss a similar opportunity – you begin to think a step ahead each move. It is a sting seemingly forgotten in modern gaming -- possibly for the best -- though TFS does not offer that debate, and frankly it doesn’t have to.
There is a romanticism to The Final Specimen: Arrival; a love letter to the days of the floppy-disked side-scrollers you once incessantly searched your childhood basements to find on a rainy Saturday. It calls to the early 90’s player, and demands your entire return to that time. But what makes TFS so special is its refusal to offer a refined nostalgia, and it instead doubles down on both its imperfections and camp value -- the player could have found this game in a cereal box, and that’s where its genius lies.
I highly recommend The Final Specimen: Arrival -- it is a welcome and enjoyable jaunt down a precious memory, and you will not want to put it down.

This is one of those ambitious, small budget video games that fails to impress. While it starts out as an interesting journey it eventually falls short of its promises.
But what is this about? Cachiche is a town in Peru known for its spirits. Our protagonist arrives there to find out more of the background story of these ghosts. Gameplay consists of walking around and talking to the townsfolk. Additionally, we are required to take photos from time to time and show these to other people who can comment and provide us with more details.
Through our camera we often see things differently. For instance, a dog may appear in skeletal form. In most cases our best bet is to return to the same character called "El Brujo" who knows more about the local witches and can comment on the strange phenomena we see through our device.
The game looks ugly. Character models look soo simplistic that they look more like dolls. There are some areas in the countryside where walking through certain areas activates a filter. I believe the idea here was to indicate that these things affect our journalist and that he may be having an out-of-body experience. On the other hand, this filter looks so ugly that it is easily mistaken for a glitch. Beside walking we can take a taxi to fast-travel between key locations.
The game's ending is unsatisfactory as it hardly provides any explanation. Our hero regularly makes journal entries throughout the story but after a while these become inconsistent - I have to admit these entries have a relatively appropriate command of English compared to most, similarly ambitious titles.
A little more work could have made for an interesting title. In its current state, however, I cannot recommend "1,000 Heads" as its unfinished story and barebone graphics all act as deterrent factors.

What a strange game. In terms of gameplay, it's pretty straightforward - it's a first person walking simulator where you take pictures of interesting people and things.
What makes the game weird, though, is the overall plot. The story somehow has the paradoxical ability to be both subtle and specific at the same time. It also has some oddities scattered throughout the world that serve no other purpose than to make you feel uncomfortable in this dark, mystifying town that you've found yourself in.
My main issue with the game is the random drops in frame rate that often happen. It usually occurs when you walk into an area that is wide open, as opposed to the more "corridor" style paths. Though, this may be because of the Unity engine that it uses, because we all know how
Unity is. One thing that I didn't like about the game was the almost-complete lack of direction it gave you. While you did have "objectives" that you had to accomplish, they were all as vague as they could possibly be. One of them was "Find something from home". Listen ♥♥♥♥♥, I don't live here. I don't even know where I am right now. Also, the game was very obviously scripted by someone for whom English was not their first language. The voice acting (while decent) was all in Spanish, and every translation came off as alien-ish. It was like each character in the game was some kind of extraterrestrial that came to Earth to study our species. We're talking "Hello, fellow hue-mon" caliber weirdness. And for some reason, cars are almost always brought up in conversation. Even when cars have no relevance to the picture that they're trying to describe. You'll have a picture of a tree, and the caption will say something like "that man looks like he's waiting for a car", when there is clearly no man and clearly no car. Honestly though, the translations are so bad that they actually loop around and become amazing. They gave me quite a few laughs.
If you can get past the various flaws that this game has, though, it's really not that bad. Its uniqueness allows it to be interesting enough to make you look past these few problems just so that you can hopefully reach the end and find out what all of this means. Which is great, because if I couldn't have overlooked those problems, I would have missed out on one the strangest and most intriguing games that I've ever played. Also, you can finish it in one or two hours, so you don't have to devote a whole lot of time to it. I'd recommend it for people that are like me; people that enjoy games that bleed atmosphere and make you not only want, but
to solve the mysteries of the world that has been created for you. If you're coming here for the hella-tight gameplay and the MLG 360-noscope "♥♥♥♥ yo momma" action, though, then you've come to the wrong place.

You could be interested in this game if you like short, dense, dialogue driven games in a near future setting - with a focus on replaying different permutations of choices.
You are dumped on a high tech airplane that functions as mobile base as the enforcer of a multinational all-powerful corporation. You get know your 16 fellow corpers then someone dies and suddenly there are fighter airplanes on the horizon and someone in the plane seems to feed them information and sabotage as much as possible. The meat of the game is to talk to your fellow specialists, watch their actions, threaten them (or not), deduct information, cross reference alibis, and find the traitor (if there is one). Dialogue (and background dossiers on the info-terminals) are extensive, well written and well performed.
Solving the mystery around the traitor(?) is the big draw of the game but since it is quite short (about 5-6 hours) and events are dense and develop quite differently depending on how you talk to people replaying the game just for kicks can be very motivating if you are the kind of player this appeals to.

The downside is that it runs very slowly as your city gets larger and larger.  This can become a problem as a population booms.  So many calculations per second that even eight-core AMD processors simply can't straighten it out.  It's a programming flaw that has been in the Cities XL series since the beginning, and the programmers haven't sorted it out. (It has nothing to do with your graphic card, as some mislead people might suggest.)  It is still superior to Sim City (a little bit childish, really) even with this downside, and if you're debating which to get, I'd push this your way.  Get both, they're now in the budget section!

Blackwake is a great game for those who want to try out a co-operative multiplayer game where each team member becomes crew of a 16th-Century military ship, along with one leader - the Captain - who commands the crew and steers the ship.
This game relies on teamwork and there is no single strategy to follow, as there are hundreds of possible outcomes.
Pros:
- Runs very well on Mac OS X and Windows. (However, I had better frame rates on the Mac version using the same hardware.)
- Uses very little data, playable on most Internet connections.
- Multiplayer co-operative team effort.
- Game is very stable and will run very well on older computer hardware using low graphics settings.
- Immersive, integrating crew strategy on board ships along with a First-Person Shooter element of gameplay by allowing your crew to board enemy ships and fight with melee or other hand weapons.
Cons:
- Audio/voice communication is almost required, as the players below deck on Galleons rely on instructions from the Captain for positioning, timing and mutually agreed strategy.
- Key bindings cannot be modified, but this will probably change later in the development cycle.
- Non-ASCI Steam profile names are translated into "x", or if there are more than one on the server, "x<random number>". The game therefore is not compliant with Unicode characters used in profile names.

Sanctum 2 brings back basically everything that made the first game great, and expands upon it. Sanctum 2 is better than the original in almost every way possible, and is definetely worth your money if you're fan of tower defense game and/or first person shooters.
Presentation: 8.0/10 - Although much better looking than the original, the grass and rocks around you are rather low resolution. Nothing feels like hexagons or squares, and the world is just overall much brighter and unique. Unlike the original game, your surroundings well change quite a bit. You'll go from the bright un-natural habitat of a science work place, to the rather dark and dreary, but sometimes bright, forestry areas where enemies roam. Another thing that helps the game are the great looking drawings of the characters telling a mini story during the load screens. Sanctum 2 is a much better looking game than the original.
Gameplay: 9.0/10 - Isn't the gameplay still the most important part of any game? A lot of times it seems like that's not the case with all the games that make empty promises about original gameplay and functions. Luckily Sanctum 2 succeeds in making an original and fun experience. It's the same premise of the first game, but more advanced and built upon. You build your defences before the waves of enemies start and when they do start, it turns into a 6.5/10 FPS. Simple, yes, but definetely fun. The AI is slightly more advanced in this great sequel, but they still feel pretty stupid. Even at the hardest level, I found myself wanting some more challenge when blasting my enemies. This is not to say that Sanctum 2 is easy, however. You'll still have to guide your enemies in a certain direction and play with your mind a little to make sure you make it to the next wave. It may sound like I'm focusing on all the bad things, but that's only because at the time I'm writing this, I'm trying to find things wrong with it.
Plot: 6.0/10 - This is where Sanctum 2 falls. Although the first game didn't have a plot, I think it's better that way. Coffee Stain Studios could've made a truly engaging story, but they ended up just explaining what we already knew. There's a core you have to protect, do it, move to the next level, oh look more enemies. That's basically all the story is. They do introduce characters to the game which is a good touch, but not enough to save the story.
Overall: 7.5/10 - Good.
"Sanctum 2 brings something we haven't truly seen for a while; originality. It expands upon all the great parts about the original and forgets the bad parts. Oh, and did I mention that it's addicting as hell!?"
- Marcus

Burnout Paradise is the racing game for the players that also want turn their oponents into wrecks.
The game starts off with some lady saying: 'welcome to Paradise City'. (It's the hub world) It's awsome! Now do whatever you want and have fun!
After that you are dropped into the garage or rather the wrecking yard and given a blue trashed looking muscle. Turns out your new half broken car works as good as new. While all this is happening you are being told, or rather hinted at, what to do by DJ Atomica. He's the guy who was the radio anouncer in SSX3.
If you have no idea who the guy is, he is basically your average cheesy amrican dj who, unlike in SSX3 (really good snow boarding game), is a jerk to you in this game.
And although I can see where the game designers were coming from, they tried too hard in making him the 'tough love get backup on your feet guy' and made him a jerk instead.
The good news is, he is just there to give you hints and tips that you don't need, so just turn the speech volume to zero as no one else ever talks.
Now back to the game play. (Note, this only covers the single player, as multiplayer needs an EA acount to work and I know what that means to some people, cough cough.) And it's some good game play, allright. For starters every single car in the game has boost (AKA nitros) and even the first one can get some serious speed going.
There are also 3 types of cars: stunt, race and takedown. Stunt, first off, is the basic one. Do crazy stuff like driving on the wrong side of the road, near misses, slamming civilans ect,  to get boost and use boost to go fast... realy fast!
Then there's racers. Racers can't use their boost bar unless it's full. But using the boost until its empty is called a burnout. Burnouts fill at least half (usally more) of the boost bar, meaning that when combined together with reckless driving will let you do burnout after burnout, making you go much faster and further then a stunt car could ever go.
Only downsides are: 1# as explained before, the boost bar MUST be full to be used. #2 racers usally have worse turning than stunt, so you may end up crashing into something ( CURSE YOU BUSSES!) and losing all your boost. And 3# racers are weaker than the  other 2 types of cars, so it's harder to get take-downs with them.(Take-downs will be explained just about now.)
Lastly are take-down cars: they are the slowest but the strongest of the lot. With take-down cars you have a smaller boost bar to start off with than stunt cars, but the bar can be made up to 3 as big by getting take-downs.
Causing your opponent to crash in any way, is called a take down. There are many ways you can take someone down, so heres a sample list: slamming them into a wall, landing on top of the poor fool, ramming into the back of them so the foe crashes into a  bus/other foe/brickwall, scraping the foe against a wall for so long that the in-game physics says "that's it, I'm outa here!" and the foe flips over the side railing and gets turned into scrapyard modern art. And so on...
Then there's  the physics system which decides that you are awsome and that your foes suck. So them grinding you against a wall or ramming your behind will not kill you, but you will kill them when it's the other way around. This makes you feel like an awsome badass that cannot be stopped.
Then there's the game types. 1# races. Races are the most simple. Get from point A to point B, only you can get take-downs the whole way. The early races are easy-ish but get harder and harder as time goes on until they get a tad frustrating. Just make sure you bring the map up(can be found in key bindings) and plot your course before you race.
Also, forget the piece of crud gps that's in the game. But when you start playing you may say or be thinking "Huh? What gps?" That's my point, the stupid thing is too small to see!
Next up are time trials. However, unlike most racing games the time trials in this one give you a set time right from the beginning without any check points. Also, they each can only be done with one car. But winning with the said car gives you a slightly better version of that car with slightly more boost.
But if you're like me, you do it for the fun as well as a new paint job.
After that there's take-down events. This is basically darby racing where all you have to do is take down a certain number of other cars and you win. But one thing I have to point out about this mode was how well it was done. In this mode, if you get too far away from the other drivers they spawn behind you. Allthough you can sort of tell when this happens, it means that there is no going the wrong way.
Up next is 'marked man'. It's like a game of tip, only the other drivers are out to wreck your car and you have to get across the finish line. It's really as simple as that, exept dying too much causes you to lose but you can repair your car along the way  by using the auto repair shops.(More about them later.)
Lastly for the events there's stunt driver or something.(I forget what it's called) where you try and rack up enough points by doing stunts before the time runs out.
Then there's shops. Auto repair makes your car as good as new, as well as giving you lives back in events. Paint stations give your car a random paint job.(Although choosing your own from the junk yard is better.) And finally the junk yard. It lets you change cars and paint jobs as well as use new cars that you unlocked.
As for the soundtrack, it might not be for everyone as the song 'Girlfriend' may be the worst thing ever for you. And the bunch of classical music they put in there is a bit weird at the time when you just rammed some car's wheel off and sent them to their doom.
Also, the songs stop whenever you crash, as a way of punishing you. But you can just avoid all of this by playing your own songs as from what I've experienced. The game alt tabs fine.
I also recommend playing this with a controller as you can fine-tune your stearing more.
Just a tip: If you're sick of the annyoning "tick-tick-tick" noise as well as the timers just press the D pad up until the street signs at the top of the screen turn green. Although I don't know which button to use on the  keyboard to change this, I'm sure it's somewhere in the key-bindings.
So all in all this is simply one of the best racing games I have ever played. So I'm giving it a 9/10 as it's just that good! Also, if you want to check out some of the other' Burnout Games' then avoid 'Burnout 3', but give 'Revenge' a try. As for  'Burnout 1 and 2', no idea as I don't have them.

I admit that I was skeptical when I bought it, but I figured, "Eh, it's only five bucks."  Now that I've played it, I feel that I more than got my money's worth.  Town of Salem is an excellent game that's almost always tense and entertaining.  You need multiple skills to win, including luck, deception, and deduction, but even when you screw up it's a good time.
I only have two real gripes about the game.  The first is the community; a lot of players are pretty offensive, both in language and behavior, and more than a few will quit at the drop of a hat if things start to go against them.  This doesn't include everyone, mind, but more players than I'd like.  The second is that lag, when it hits, kills the game, more than doubling play time, silencing chat, and preventing players from using their abilities.  It's not a common occurrence, but it's extremely frustrating when it does.
Still, those complaints shouldn't deter one from a game that is, on the whole, a lot of fun.

Generally a unsatisfying experience. I'll try cut it short and put down the ways that make the game something I cannot recommend.
The level design is unenjoyable. While it trys to escape from the tropes of regular tower defense ways, the method it does it just doesn't quite work as well as it could. The thing that makes a good tower map layout is loops. Causing the mobs to go round and round hitting the same turrets as many times as you can. But many of the maps don't really allow for this, while there is certainly some room for loops often I found the shapes to have these awkward little spots where you just can't make the loop work and room goes to waste.
There are ways that you can screw yourself over if you build up a maze in a certain way and in the next turn the game changes the flow of monsters in a way that means your high powered turrets aren't being used and you have to panick while enemies bash away at the powercore while you try to pick them off with your weapons. I understand that the game wants you to adjust your maze in major ways between waves, but sometimes I've built it in a certain way that I just can't or I'd rather not.
The special enemy types can be frustrating to take down. There is an armoured one will armour everywhere except a little spot on it's rear, so you'll be running behind it shooting away at it, and when the enemy hits a corner it will suddenly snap to a new angle. There's no smooth rotation, it's just bam, it's now at a new angle and now you have to move to compensate for this. All of which might just be okay, but perhaps you've built a maze with many angled corners. Now the monster will be snapping to new angles every few seconds while you're trying to shoot away at it's rear. The only way to do a significant amount of damage is on straights. Ahh it's just frustating.
The sound design is lacking, especially in the weapons. I can't quite put my finger on what it is exactly, perhaps the lack of punch that makes you feel like you're actually making a dent.
I didn't like having abilities that and towers make you more effective and make the game more fun locked off until you put in the required time to unlock them. Some people like this.. and I know it was designed to keep you engaged and also to make you to try some unlocks that maybe you wouldn't use.. but I just don't like these systems.
It really feels like this genre could be something special, but I can't see that something in this game. Perhaps another studio will be able to fill that hole.

It *does* fix that in Sanctum 1 your hand weapons were completely ineffectual (save the freeze gun) by the late waves, bizzarely *losing* the ability to upgrade them in the process. I can maybe see that the tower base limits were to force you to build incrementally, rather than splurge all your money on building the maze up-front, although for many maps they just don't give you enough of them. The tower limit is at least perhaps an intent to make you form concentrated kill-zones, rather than just carpeting the map with scatter lasers. It's still got rocket-jumping. For one character.
A lot is missing. Holo blocks. Floor tiles. The overview map you could put beacons on. Televators. A final map which isn't one miserable luck-based will-the-boss-be-distracted-or-just-carve-a-beeline-through-my-defenses difficulty spike.
But the real reason for the big, red thumbs-down is persistent unlocks. For a PvE co-op game they are utterly stupid, since if any of your friends don't want to spend the requisite hours grinding missions over and over with difficulty feats enabled, they're going to be less effectual and have fewer choices than you, and thus have a less fun experience. Stupid, stupid, stupid.

A fun game still neck-deep in development. While the gameplay is fun, it lacks in fully utilizing progression and making building more accessible to players. The more variety and involvement in progressively-generated objectives, the better. As for the building, perhaps tools designed to ease the building process for non-builders would benefit. Perhaps players could design their own structure blueprints, such as "This is a castle room," or "This is the furnishing for my castle room," or "This is a different set of furnishing for my castle room." To cut down on lugging massive stockpiles of junk (in an inventory with an admittedly broken pickup-sorting), this should probably be tied in with the 3d printer, costing pixels after an on-hand stock is used up. Really, I feel as if the 3D printer might not get as much love as it should. While the things the staff are doing now certainly look like fun additions, they feel quite small and toying compared to actually pushing for an official release, as opposed to "early access".
Recent updates have stunted some of the minutiae in the game (temperature, hunger), but if minutiae is too tedious, then the idea is to mediate or automate the process so it's less of a burden on experienced players--many games could benefit from the sort of management to automate timed actions as resources warrant. "If I have food, just automatically eat when I'm hungry," or something. It sounds complicated, but it's a consideration point. This trickles into Techs sometimes, where the game essentially nerfs some Techs as not useful, and others monopolize the player character's slots. If they won't allow more tech to be equipped at priority, then perhaps tech should be designed in a way where one player's tech can benefit the entire party somehow. Maybe everyone can board that one player's boat.
Party dynamics could be an interesting investment, perhaps a la Lost Vikings, where each player can specialize in a diversified subset of capability. Perhaps different aspects of gameplay could find intuitive ways to meld together, if we break down the components of resourcing, building, and defending. Shuffling equipment requires too much precision, and the less juggling, the more immersive the gameplay becomes because there's less "I accidentally scrolled to my stairs instead of my crossbow and the enemy killed me." Segwaying from this to multiplayer, perhaps servers should come with certain permissions to allow strangers onto servers but with lesser permissions--no ability to destroy player structures or to procedurally generate new planets on that server unless they're on a whitelist.
Starbound's a good multiplayer game that benefits from cooperation, although there's a high emphasis on virtual creativity, which can be a slippery slope for people who prefer exploring. Exploring can become a bit samey after a while, and there should probably be consequences and challenges involved to deepen this experience, with rewards more fitting than another chest that's missing a new blueprint. Pretty soon you're just blindly hunting down specific rare biomes to catch 'em all. The character design of the alien races is especially good, which each species having their benefits and drawbacks, although at this stage this is purely cosmetic. As long as the lore doesn't try to negate the player's own personal manifestations of their character avatars, the best step is fleshing out in-game what's hinted to come. The progression system, while linear even at the point where it does branch off, does come with its rewards, but these rewards only carry you so far, and there's an interminable amount of resource collection to do by hand. Even playing first mission in Xcom EU, I have noticed what was wrong for me in this, let's say, 3rd trilogy: either "one move one move" or "one move one shot" or just one shot. Is it such a military tactics?: having made a shot and, looming on the line of fire, to perform kind of "head out-in" animation. Missions, that take place on small maps ( you can forget about to explore quite large areas and 9-floor skyscrapers from the XCOM 3 Apocalypse), have always the same: 3*X mobs are popping out from nowhere to sometimes kill a soldier with a single blow. It seems, this game has pretty tough balance as if nobody was care about it and developers have spent all their time for creation of cut-scenes, animation and pathos atmosphere.
You know, there are things "in real life" that always happen. So, I'm not surprised when you missed an alien while shooting in front of it. But wonder: why do you still need rng for it? It's not the task for those walls and blocks to give bonuses (or to be demolished together with a character) but to protect, absorbing damage. You can mention roofs that doesn't cost you anything to climb on (like a King Kong and to jump down in a disgusting buggable manner, breaking a ceiling), to give another bonus until it's destroyed with easy. What material is this wall made of? - Is it made of probability? What size does this stone have? - Probably big?
Whether well enough shot is modelled here? I'd say "pretty bad". Even if the probability theory was born in attempts to analyze games of chance, I'm not sure that it's worth to try card games with only one card in a deck. Wanna to write this review in TWO languages (may be even in one and a half). But it's more than a SINGLE Xcom-base or just ONE shot, though less than the whole THREE bullets for a clip. I loved the XCOM series so much and can't accept this "extremely small numbers law" in it, and never will. Frankly speaking, the chance for this review to be positive was quite high - about 95 percent but... missed
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ещё проходя первую миссию в XCOM EU, я понял что для меня не так в этой, скажем, 3-й трилогии: "1 ход 1 ход" или "1 ход 1 выстрел" или только один выстрел. Где очки действия характерные для пошаговых стратегий? Как сделать выстрел и уйти в укрытие? - Никак? Это такая военная тактика?: выстрелив, маячить на линии огня, исполняя типа "морду высунул-убрал" анимацию. Миссии, которые проходят на маленьких картах ( можно забыть про исследование достаточно больших пространств и 9-ти этажных небоскрёбов из XCOM 3 Apocalypse), всегда имеют одно и тоже: 3*X мобов выскакивают из ниоткуда чтобы иногда убить солдата с одного удара. Похоже в этой игре плохо проработанный баланс, как если бы все силы разработчиков ушли на создание кат-сцен, анимации и атмосферы пафоса.
Некоторые вещи в реальной жизни происходят всегда. Поэтому я не удивляюсь если происходит промах при выстреле в пришельца в упор. Удивляет другое: причём тут вероятность вообще? Вместо того чтобы давать какие-то бонусы, все эти стены и блоки должны элементарно защищать поглощая урон, а не быть снесёнными вместе с персонажем. Можно упомянуть про крыши, забраться на которые ничего не стоит (подобно Кинг-Конгу и спрыгивать вниз в ужасной забагованной манере, пробивая потолки) и дающие очередной бонус, пока не разрушена (с лёгкостью). Из чего сделана эта стена? Из вероятности? Какой размер у этого камня? Вероятно большой?
Достаточно ли хорошо здесь смоделирован выстрел? Я бы сказал "отвратительно". Даже если теория вероятности и была рождена при попытке анализа азартных игр, вряд ли стоит играть в карты с единственной картой в колоде. Пишу этот обзор на ДВУХ языках (или даже полтора). Но это больше чем ЕДИНСТВЕННАЯ база-XCOM или ОДИН выстрел, хотя меньше чем целых ТРИ патрона в магазине. Любил когда-то XCOM-серию игр, но не принимаю этот "закон чрезвычайно малых чисел" в ней. Вообще-то, шанс для этой писанины быть позитивной был высок - почти 95 процентов, но... промах

I'd also go as far as to say that the narration and soundtrack are the best of any game that I've played.

Bastion is one fantastic gaming experience, with a beautiful vibrant world to traverse, an amazing dynamic narrrative, and some great (If a little simplistic) combat that really seems to add up to a tuly one of a kind journey.
I was lucky enough to buy the game for around 3 dollars after it went on sale, Which to me seems a hell of a deal considering the amount of hours it soaked up through two back-to-back playthroughs. While the campaign lasts only a few hours to complete, I found myself instantly wanting to play through it again. Despite these multiple playthroughs, I never found the game to be repetitive in the slightest. Although it's for that reason I feel the game could have benefitted from an extra level or two without seeming too drawn out. There are tons of weapons to unlock and upgrade as you move through the game, each one having it's own unique feel and mechanics. Almost all of the weapons are fun to use, giving the game a little more flavor as you mix and match to find the best tools for the level you're on.
The artwork and story of the game complement eachother perfectly, with the rusty narration of Rucks guiding you, the young hero along through the broken remains of a once great land as you try to undo a horrible calamity. It makes for a beautiful melancholic atmosphere that keeps you engrossed all the way through.
Overall, it's a gem of a game with a visual flare and simplistic gameplay that sets it apart from others in the action RPG genre, and I would highly recommend it to any fans of that type of game.

Consortium is a very interesting experience, one that is very rare to come by when it comes to Indie Games. I'm going to say this flat out, I cannot recommend this game to everyone, and a part of me still regrets spending the $20 I had on it. That being said, this isn't a bad game, but it also is not a very good one. Consortium suffers from a wide array of issues, but even with all of them, I cannot say I did not enjoy my time spent with it, it just honestly feels incomplete. It is a very different RPG experience you will not get from a lot of other games, but it has so many issues its hard to say whether or not they justify it's good points.

Consortium is a FPS and also a Sci-Fi RPG. You play as a person living in the 20th century who uses a device to travel to the future of a parallel universe. You awake onboard a space ship with the task of simply living in this world. The ship is fairly small and leaves little to be explored, but all the characters on this ship are interesting for various reasons. Some people are average workers with a good personality, while some are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and even one is a religious extremist. If you are into games with a heavy focus on dialogue, you might be interested in this title, the problem is that most of the said dialogue includes details of the people onboard, and not on the world you are living in. This can be a huge let down for people, as you spend most of your play time learning about people, with no depth for anything else. However, even with the lacking explanation of the world, the dialogue is pretty damn good, and almost every voice actor plays their character perfectly, it honestly is some of the best voice acting I've seen in a game, which is really impressive for such a low budget title.

When you aren't walking around, talking, and making decisions ( which actually do have a large impact on the gameplay, and really encourages multiple playthroughs ) you are fighting... MAYBE. This I feel is one of the strongest aspects of the game, you are given the decision of lethal or non-lethal combat, or skipping combat entirely. You will be placed in a situation where combat is about to happen, but if you make the correct decisions in the dialogue trees, you can talk your way out of it. This is something rarely even seen in a game, and it really is refreshing to see it here. That being said, violence is definitely an option, and if you don't want to talk your way out of something, opening fire on anything that lies in your way is an option, which really is the best part about this game, options. You are constantly deciding things, how to interact with other people, how you are going to deal with enemies, its all dependent on what YOU want to do, which is something that should be present in other RPGs.

But even with all of these good things the game offers, it has a lot of problems that are persistent throughout your whole play through. The game, while having an interesting and colorful art style, is ugly and outdated. Its not really a problem for me, and may not be for others, but it really is an absolute fact. The game is buggy, you can get stuck in walls, characters will fade through door ways, dialogue choices may disappear which will cause a reload, it really is a mess. Apparently it is not as bad as before, but it still is a huge issue. The inventory management is annoying, it uses an "energy" system. You hold energy to heal and repair armor, and also use the non-lethal weapon. Energy takes up inventory space, which means carrying even 50% energy will really limit your choices of weaponry and items. Everything is just too heavy, and I can see this being an issue in the sequels if more combat takes place. Yes combat doesn't take up that much of the game, but I still feel it is an issue. I think worst of all is how short the game is, I finished it in about 4 hours. Granted, I skipped the like 3 side quests, mainly because I couldn't figure out what to do for some of them. Yes, it has high replayability, and it is a great experience, but the price of $20 honestly leaves a bad taste in my mouth.

If you want to play a game that has a huge focus on dialogue and choices, and don't mind how short it is, this game is something you should look at, even people who are looking this style of gameplay may or may not enjoy this experience, so just be cautious. If you are willing to spend $20 on a risk, or it goes on sale, go for it. Otherwise, you're probably better of skipping it.

Consortium is the big boy alternative to the walking simulator.
The first thing that is apparent once you start this game is the degree of bone-crushing depth to the world the developers have created. There are dozens of pages of lore contextualizing every character in the plot, every event in the meta-narrative, and the vision of the future created for this game. This is exactly what people of a certain old school demographic in gaming claim to want in an RPG, but it is instead built upon a mediocre Half Life-esque shooter's skeleton.
I say that, but there is more than one path to progress through the game in which the player doesn't need to engage in combat at all. In fact, Consortium places gunplay in the back seat, leaving the plot to be the driving force. The more active gameplay is, however, still in the car, unlike other "games" lauded for their plot but devoid of anything but the simplest interactivity. There is challenge to the combat, sometimes born of the situations, sometimes born of the tight spaces of the ship or the sheer number of enemies players are expected to deal with in one fight. There are also minigames, most notably a Missle Command-esque game that, while not difficult, is engaging enough. The point is, Consortium, while focused on story, does not shun gameplay, or even the fact that it is a game. There are even dialogue options for players who wish there to be no 4th Wall at all.
And the subject of dialogue options brings me to the final point in this game's favour: The degree to which the player shapes the story. Consortium is near the level of Obsidian's Alpha Protocol in terms of the permutations each event can have, and each conversation, no matter how trivial, has at least two different potential statements a player can make. This helps immensely in helping the player engage with the rest of the cast, who are all distinct in personality, and for the most part well acted, even if some performances are clearly better than others.
As I said, Consortium is a big boy alternative to the walking simulator; games that use a focus on story as an excuse to be little more than a film with a few QTEs or childishly easy puzzles. It has RPG-level depth at FPS prices and is not ashamed to go into the absolute minutia about the world it seeks to build for future sequels. If those sequels stay true to this game while improving the more combat-oriented approaches, they would deserve consideration alongside the greats in the Science Fiction genre of video games.

I LOVED Sanctum (the first one) I was really REALLY looking forward to the second one. It is fun, and I think it added SOME cool new features, but, I have to say I am disappointed in some major ways, and I'd like to elaborate on them. So let me explain how and why Sanctum 1 is better than Sanctum 2.
In Sanctum one you could spend your resources on building blocks, to put towers on, except in this case I'm specifically talking about using them to shape your enemies path, made it the longest, most efficient path. In Sanctum 2, you and your teammates get a certain amount of blocks, and sometimes one person gets more, or all of them. Sure you can transfer them to eachother, but only if your friends are willing. How does this negatively affect the game? I played the other day, looked at the map, planned out how I wanted to shape it, and spent the entire game, every wave, building blocks, and never getting enough to fully build the path I wanted to. In the first game, that never happened.
Sanctum 2 is also, IMO, dumbed down and made more noob friendly.
In Sanctum 1, you could upgrade your towers AND your gun with your resource points. This made choices more complex, especially with friends, deciding who would do what. In Sanctum 2, you CAN'T spend points on your weapons. You use perks instead for that. To me, the way they changed the perk/level up system, it plays less like an FPS/TD, and more like a TD/RPG, and not in a good way.
In Sanctum one, if you build something and didn't like it, didn't like the placement, wished you had some something else, or wish you had upgraded something else, it's too bad. Live and learn. If you wanted to take it down, you'd get SOME resources back, but not all. In Sanctum 2, you can build something, upgrade it, and then take it down later and get a full refund of your resources. This just makes the game noob friendly, and less challenging.  You know those RPG's where you can't change your stats, so if you want that really badass class, you have to work at it? And then there's the ones where you use the easiest stats to level up, then when you're max level, go change your stats again? Doesn't that kind of take away all the fun and challenge, and prestige of having that class? Well, now you can enjoy that noob strategy in the noobed down sequel to a much better game.
OK, now, having ranted all that, I will still say Sanctum 2 is a good/fun game, but having played the first game, I know what's missing. If Sanctum 2 was actually the first game I'd say "wow, this game is really fun/awesome, I love it!" Then if Sanctum 1 came out next I would say "OMG I can't believe how much better this game is! They took everything bad about the other one and removed it/made everything better."

Sorry, but to me, this game is complete boredom, but hey, maybe you like it this way!
The only way to get your health back is to eat food, which when you start is few and far between. Someone in game said something about sleeping in a bed, which was not helpful at all. Or if you have plenty of time and don't mind just standing on the same tile for ever, your health will very slowly return 1hp a minute.
There is very little animation here, you char is basically a stick figure that never changes. Walking or doing anything else for that matter all uses the exact same unchanging image. You do get a few choices to alter the head, facial hair, chest and lower body, basically just different colours. But so small a choice that it is impossible to differentiate between players. It's like half a dozen choices as to what chars look like and several of each onscreen at the same time. The only way to find who you’re looking for is to hold the mouse over each player until you find the right name. By default, player names are not visible until you mouse over the character. Unknown if you can make this info display all the time.
Magic seems overly complicated. Equip a magic pouch; install temporary spells in to said book.
Using the bank is functional but rather complicated. Find a chest; it has to be a special type of non-reward chest. Once you open it, it displays all items in it as well as what you are holding (weird), Select an item, then decide if you are placing it in the bank or removing it. Drag and drop would be a better system IMO.
Collecting resources is slow and grindy. For example, equip an axe, click on a tree then wait for you inventory to fill up, no stacking at all in the game. Run to the bank (remember it's a chest), store your items, run back to the tree, repeat until you get bored with that, then go mining and do it all over again for rocks. Or, maybe you want to make a potion, go digging up sand, take it to a forge to convert it to a vial, never discovered how to actually get any further than the part. And keep in mind that initially whilst collecting resources there is a very high failure rate. Good thing about the fail rate is you don't need to take any action to try again, it just keeps collect until your inventory is full.
Chatting is almost impossible. At times, depending on how many people are playing, text will scroll too fast to be able to keep track of anything. So if you decide to ask a question in game because you are stuck on something, you may or may not get an answer because other players may not see your question or they may just not reply. Usually they do. It is possible to make a private chat section, but I found no way to add other players. Also by default, all text is displayed until you filter out unwanted sections.
If you like trying to figure out things like this via trial and error, waiting for things to happen, and grinding like there is no tomorrow then go ahead and try the game you might like it.
Yes, it is early access, so hopefully it will improve. But for me, I doubt I will play it much in its current state, but will check on it from time to time as it seems like it has potential!

Starbound is a rather odd creature. It more or less takes the system of something like Terraria and adds an extra level of progression. As you kill bosses and collect better resources, you can go to more planets with more danger, more resources, new bosses, etc. The grind isn't nearly as bad as Minecraft for a sandbox in terms of collecting resources, and there's a lot of content in terms of building, decorating, etc. But there's a few things to note.
-Exploring planets is not as good as you may expect. They all fall into different biome types with certain sub-biomes, for the most part, and going places costs a considerable amount of fuel so you likely won't spend loads of time wandering the galaxy.
-While building is fun, I always felt almost discouraged from doing it. Every time I'd go to add to my house, I'd just say "well, I'll beat the boss here and move on, so what's the point?" and I'd never really progress to building much more than a little hut or shack.
TL;DR So, I think the game is fun, especially if you like sandboxes, but there are some things that I don't necessarily dislike as much as find... weird. I don't really know. If you're thinking you'll like it, buy it. I doubt you'd be dissapointed.

My husband and I both purchased the Collector's Edition for FO4 and, initially, we were both very excited to dive back into the universe of the games we've loved for years, but that love and almost all of our excitement has been completely doused, muted, and we've been left feeling pretty betrayed by the unethical practices Bethesda has employed regarding their latest blunder: the Creation Club.
The modding community for FO4 is filled with hundreds upon hundreds of creative and talented individuals who have spent countless hours/days/months working on modifications to make not only the game more enjoyable by way of adding content, missions, and/or graphical adjustments but by providing a way (through these mods) for players to really customize their experience to the point where it's almost a unique experience. All of that hard work, all those thousands of mods, all the time and effort, and game being played and it was all for free.
And then comes along the Creation Club where all that hard work and effort, all those untold hours of gameplay and enjoyment are basically worthless, broken, and tossed to the wayside in favor of Bethesda deciding that need to milk their customers for even MORE money on top of the money already shelled out for the game itself, the dlc, and/or the season pass. The CC where it makes dozens upon hundreds of free modifications useless and/or broken which, in turn, breaks players' saves and renders them corrupt or just plain unplayable. The CC where Bethesda decided that they wanted to make these mods cost money that they will get the lion's share of cash spent on these "paid mods" which leaves the creators of said mods with a pettance comparatively and the community in an uproar.
Yes, I fully believe that these talented and hardworking mod makers should be getting paid for their work because they do put in the hours, the sweat, the tears, and do their best to deliver a product to the community that benefits them in their games. But I do not support, in any way, what Bethesda is and has done with their Creation Club. It's an absolute affront their community because they're taking something that we (the community) has enjoyed for YEARS free of charge and decided, "No, you gotta pay us again and again for the privilege of playing your game the way you want to near two years after the fact because we're money hungry and thought this tactic that has
elsewhere is going to really take off for us".
This just tells the community and the mod makes that they don't really matter, only their money does.
Shame on you, Bethesda. Absolute shame.

Summary for those who are physically unable to scroll down: XCOM 2 is a good sequel and remains loyal to the series.
This game is great. For one, it changes up some elements of XCOM: EU to make them fresher but still retains the stuff that make the games so enjoyable, like uncovering new gear, enemies, classes, abilities, etc.
Now, however, you're on the run.
After Earth lost the war against the aliens, they took over and began conducting experiments on civillians undercover whilst opting under the guise of a friendly, peacekeeping organisation called ADVENT. Aliens have been modified to reduce the negative impact they would've implied in their original form, particulately the floater species in particular - instead of being half-mechanical, grotesque puppets with jetpacks attached crudely to their backs, they now appear like gleaming, golden and elegant.
Of course, this doesn't make the aliens' forces weaker. After 20 years of improving the various species that make up our new alien overlords, they are stronger than ever, with even greater potential.
So, instead of it being sort of fair, this is an all-out guerilla war. You need to lead a resistance that is mainly made up of scared alcoholics and shady rookies to slowly whittle away at the Elders' grip on our world.
Gameplay-wise, it's as good as ever. Now, in most missions, you start off in concealment, (ignore the gigantic hijacked craft above us, please.) which adds the opportunity to set up ambushes for the pods of ayy lmaos patrolling.
The only downside of this is that more missions are timed now, negating that element of stealth most of the time. You can still set up ambushes, but they won't be the clockwork full-squad ambushes you were probably hoping of.
Classes have been reworked slightly - there are two main branches of abilites to choose from for each class, like the sharpshooter dividing up into 'sniper' and 'gunslinger'. The two branches mainly focus on the two different weapons given to that soldier. Of course, you can still mix 'n' match abilities as you please.
You don't even need to buy the DLC to enjoy the base game, although if I could choose one, I would go with the 'Shen's last gift' DLC. Even without the DLCs, there's a total of 18 enemies (excluding their upgraded versions), 5 classes and countless abilites, weapons and armour to admire in action.
Character customization is more in-depth now - it's much easier to make a character look like a familiar face.
Alongside all of those features, there are a number of QoL changes, including status indicators, warning signs if you will move into an environmental hazard, etc.
So, yes. Buy this game. (Not at full price though, but then again that goes without saying - this IS steam.)

I kickstarted Planetary Annihilation some years ago and until today I was unable to ever play it. The vanilla version had long refused to even launch and this one possessed an incredibly odd bug wherin the camera pannedperfectly smoothly and I experienced no loss of framerate, but everything happening in-game, unit movment and combat and the like, was so stuttered as to appear like a slide show, making the game completely unplayable. I was greatly disheartned, but from the blue an unofficial community moderator named mikeyh_ reached out to me and helped me solve the issue, which turned out of all things to be a networking issue. I still question the wisdom of using online servers to manage in-game activity for single player, however, I was greatly pleased to finally give the game a try. My initial impression is strong. The game feels immediately familiar to me, and will be so for anyone who has played Total Annihilation or the Supreme Commander series. Overall game flow is focused on mass production of units and large-scale battles, with various economic shortcuts designed to get your war machine up and running as fast as possible, such as the ability to place multiple structures with one order and queue continuous production from multiple factories. However, the pace of the game is much faster then its predecessors, taking you fron just your starting commander, a powerful, well-rounded unit capable of basic construction, resource reclaimation and combat, to a fully-fledged, multi-unit army in mere minutes. Adding to the mix of infantry robots, vehicles, air and sea units seen previously, PA adds the extra twist of orbital combat, and potentially multople planets You can build transports to ferry units between worlds, as well as teleport gates to move them directly, anit-orbital defenses to repel enemy fleets, and spy satillites and space-to-ground artillery to support your ground forces. And in addition to the nuclear missile silos, you can now build Death-Star style superlasers, and even engines used to slam moons into planets. This expansion also adds enourmous super units in the vein of Supreme Commander's experimentals, which are built directly by your constructors and provide a grandiose, game-changing centerpiece to your assaults. So far I've played only the tutorial and a single campaign battle and I am already enjoying the game immensely. I look forward to seeing just how large the game's battles can get. I appriciate the gesture of giving away this standalone expansion for free to us kickstarter backers, and it was well worth the unusually long wait for me to play it. I will have more to say in the future.

Bastion is one fantastic gaming experience, with a beautiful vibrant world to traverse, an amazing dynamic narrrative, and some great (If a little simplistic) combat that really seems to add up to a tuly one of a kind journey.
I was lucky enough to buy the game for around 3 dollars after it went on sale, Which to me seems a hell of a deal considering the amount of hours it soaked up through two back-to-back playthroughs. While the campaign lasts only a few hours to complete, I found myself instantly wanting to play through it again. Despite these multiple playthroughs, I never found the game to be repetitive in the slightest. Although it's for that reason I feel the game could have benefitted from an extra level or two without seeming too drawn out. There are tons of weapons to unlock and upgrade as you move through the game, each one having it's own unique feel and mechanics. Almost all of the weapons are fun to use, giving the game a little more flavor as you mix and match to find the best tools for the level you're on.
The artwork and story of the game complement eachother perfectly, with the rusty narration of Rucks guiding you, the young hero along through the broken remains of a once great land as you try to undo a horrible calamity. It makes for a beautiful melancholic atmosphere that keeps you engrossed all the way through.
Overall, it's a gem of a game with a visual flare and simplistic gameplay that sets it apart from others in the action RPG genre, and I would highly recommend it to any fans of that type of game.

Alright, where to begin... Let's start with the pros. (please read the whole review to see why I'm recommending it)
The game engine itself is absolutely FANTASTIC. The fighting mechanics, the graphics... You name it, it's top notch. Absolutely wonderful. That being said, unfortunately at the moment there are MANY flaws, which I will list here:
1) Characters number
If we compare it to Street Fighter IV, the roaster of characters is extremely inferior in number, especially after the whole updates "Super, Ultra and Omega". Hopefully capcom will NOT do the same thing again and release more versions of the same game or it would be pure utter crap (which should not be the case, considering that we have a season pass and characters already confirmed to come out).
2) Online not working properly
I got disconnected once when I was at level 28 of Survival, causing me to lose all my progress. The frustration was... Quite loud, so to speak. As well, for those competitive players, finding a match on your own takes forever. I prefer to just put the passive search on and whoever finds me, I accept.
3) No arcade, no modes
This is quite ridiculous that a game like Street Fighter, the ARCADE GAME for excellence, doesn't have an Arcade mode... Or a Team Battle mode... Or a Tag Mode... Whatever mode you wish to place in here, it's missing. All we have is a shabby story mode made out of still images, single round fights and not much really to offer. The "challenge mode" is locked and will be released for free in March.
Now, why am I recommending the game?
Because it's Street Fighter. It's Capcom's head title and I'm sure they will work hard on it to fix all of these issues, as they are already doing. It's not enough yet, but I'm sure it will get better.
So, be aware that for now you are buying an "Early Access" game. If you don't want to spend 90 dollars for the deluxe edition, go and get a deal this weekend (February 20th-21st) on Greenman Gaming. You can get the full package for 68 dollars, saving you up some money.

As of 2/19/16, Street Fighter V is a fantastic game. Not a perfect game. Not a flawless game. But, the game itself IS fantastic. While it launched with horrendous server issues that plagued almost everyone, 3 days later, the game works fine for me. In fact, it's worked fine since the day after launch, minus Battle Lounges (where you can invite your friends to play with you, regardless of platform). I've spent the past two nights duking it out with friends and randoms. Matchmaking could be faster, but I still get matches in under a minute most of the time. So, I've no complaints there. The roster is as big as SFIV's was at launch. But, unlike SFIV, I legitimately feel that every character is a strong competitor right out of the gate.
Now, I've never given a damn about arcade mode. Frankly, I thought it was rather dated. You have a cutscene at the beginning, a cutscene in the middle, a cutscene at the end. Other than that? Just a series of fights against idiotic AI. Story mode in SFV is essentially arcade mode with the extra fights cut out. You have a cutscene, 2-3 fights, and another cutscene or two. But, Survival mode is where it's at. Survival mode is FANTASTIC. You have a varying number of rounds to survive based on what difficulty you choose (Easy 10, Normal 30, Hard 50, Hell 100), and your meters/gauges carry between rounds. After each round, you're given what I'm fairly certain is a random list of bonuses to choose from that cost Score (your actual score, mind you), or you can choose to forget them and keep on keepin' on. Why do Survival mode? That's how you unlock alternate colors in SFV. There's actually a legitimate reason to do them. And you can get fairly deep in strategy, too. You just want the colors? Maybe you spam the health bonuses, which will mean a low score, but you don't care about that, you want the colors. Or, maybe you're doing a score attack, so you choose to Double Down every round. Or a time attack, so you choose Attack Bonus.
SFV was completely worth the money I paid in my own opinion. I've played quite a bit already, and I know I'll put tons more time into it in the future. The only things missing that I would love right now is Trials mode (coming in March), and Endless Battle (coming in March). I could also go for online training, but that's the least important to me. Ultimately, I think the Steam community might be a bit harsh regarding the game, but, that's what these reviews are for. Don't take my word for it, read more reviews. Watch gameplay online. Maybe ask some streamers on twitch. SFV is a fantastic game for me, but who knows if it will be for you?

Space RPG game with FPS elements. No its not like Mass Effect.
I bought this the minute I saw it on Steam. Why? It looked cool and the story/setting got me intrigued.
The first hour was a bumpy ride because of a wide variety of bugs. The devs were very honest about it, admitted they should have released it as an early access game.
I waited, patiently, a few weeks for the devs to fix their game. I started over because the patch also deleted the savegames (which was announced by the devs as well).
This whole game takes place on a rather small spaceship and you're a Bishop, lead operations if I'm correct.
The ships hierarchy is based on chess. You have your pawns, rook, queen, king, etc.  So you always know the status of a crewmember.

I went to a village and became the Godfather. Then I came home and downloaded Town Of Salem.
The game ranges from 7-15 online players who have each been assigned a role. Each role has special perks and abilties, but not all of them have to play in the town's favour. Town roles are Jailors, Sheriffs, Escorts, Doctors, Investigators, Mediums and other ones, but there's also 3 mafia players - the Godfather, the Mafioso and the Framer, along with a Serial Killer, Jester and Executioner who are neutral. Different game modes change the game by adding new roles like Witches, Werewolves and Arsonists, who generally make the game harder. The hard part of the game is finding out who is good and who is evil before you are murdered brutally. Each player must do an action at night like killing, speaking with the dead and even having sex. In the morning, any dead are mourned and a will that players can use to write down information that they wish others to see after they're gone, and the death note left by the killer are shown. Then there's a 45 second discussion that players can participate in, followed by a town vote on which player should be excecuted. If a player has reached a certain amount of votes ( beginning with 8 and going down to 2 over the time of the game ), he/she must then plead their innocence before the town can vote guilty or innocent. If there are more guilty votes than innocent, the person in question is executed, but if they're voted innocent the person is let off and players can vote another in the hope of making the town vote their suspect until the voting period ends. This was just a simple explaination of the game, so if you're interested there's lots more to find out by playing yourself. You can play for free with ads and a slower rate at
or you can buy on Steam and get super fast, ad free gameplay along with the chance to customize characters! If you like mysterious games, I'd reccomend you at least play a few classic mode rounds on the website version.

First off, as you can tell by the number of hours that I put in the game, Town of Salem is a game that I very much enjoyed playing, although it was mostly first 40 hours. Once past those 40 hours, the scroll update fell upon Town of salem.
I would have recommended the game without a doubt before the update that introduced the scrolls.
Town of Salem is a fun game(similar to the Werewolf game), that requires you to be deceitful and think logically in order to win. You have to think strategically your every move, choose who to trust carefully. You get a role at the start of each game, with its own objectives and skills.
Most roles are fun and require a unique way of playing it. The townies are the most numerous and have to work together, the mafia must also work together, but in secret and most of the neutrals have their own agenda.
The two main game types allow for some very fun games.
The classic game type forces you to play with a given set of roles that make for a balanced game.
The custom game type let the host decide what the roles are going to be, which adds a lot of replayability and diversity to the game.
If you like the Werewolf type of game, I think you'd like town of Salem.
However, I cannot recommend Town of Salem as of right now.
Since the scrolls were introduced, the game is a lot more frustrating.
The scrolls are in-game items that allow you to boost your chances of getting a specific role.
For instance, I can boost my chances of getting the role "Serial killer" from 7%(the default value) to 52%.
This will logically decrease the odds for all the other players, from 7% to 4% if only a single person has a scroll. Once you get the role you wanted, it will burn one scroll of that specific type.
How do you get scrolls? You have to buy them for the most part. They each cost 200gold, and although you can get gold by playing the game, it is far easier and faster to just pay for gold with real money.
I don't have that big of a problem with the cosmetic purchases, like the different skins, houses ,etc, even though they can somewhat affect the balance of the game, as, if you're playing with a friend, you can tell more easily who that friend could be by looking at the different skins.
But the scrolls really messed up Town of Salem.
Since the scroll update, I get a lot more often the boring roles simply because I have a very low percentage of getting them due to other people using those scrolls.
I already bought the game, it is not a free to play on steam, I already for paid, there is no reason why an in-game purchase should affect the balance of the game. I understand that for the browser version they would add it, as it is free-to-play, but there's no reason why it should be there for the steam version. It doesn't make the game pay to win, it makes it pay for fun. Remove the $5 Town Points and let the game be fair again.
While it was more tolerable back before the update to get the boring roles simply because everybody would have to get them at one point, but the chances of getting them were fair, unlike now. You could still expect to get a fun role in the next game. Not anymore. It's rare that I find a game where all the odds are 7% for every single role.
Furthermore, leavers utterly destroy the game. When you start a game and half of the townies are gone, it breaks everything, as the town has no chance of winning right off the bat. There isn't any penalties for people who leave the game. Therefore, you can expect at least 2 people per game who will leave during the first round, and more afterwards.
To make it worse, a role(medium) is all about interacting with the dead townies to get some clues as to who is what, but since most people just leave straight away, it makes it pratically useless in most games.
In conclusion, Town of Salem is a fun game, even considering the very annoying quitting, but I'll only recommend it once the damn scrolls are gone and the devs add some penalties for quitters.
In the present circumstances, it is only a matter of time until another "Werewolf" game comes out on steam, without anything similar to the scrolls, at which point, Town of Salem will likely become deserted.

Long War 2
This is a review of the mod of the base game, which is so extensive that it deserves a review of its own.
XCOM in its many variations is basically the ultimate 'triumph against overwhelming odds' experience. You start off with hopeless rookies and turn then by degrees into an effective war machine, capable of grinding entire armies of fearsome aliens to mincemeat in turn-based combat.
XCOM2 LW2 is the development of this theme to its logical conclusion. It is utterly unforgiving even at the 'veteran' level I am playing. 'If you don't play it just right,' one expert advises, 'you will be crushed, even if you win every encounter.' Never a truer word spoken.
LW2 has a true touch of genius. It modifies the tactical mechanic of the base game so that now several missions are in progress ('being infiltrated') simultaneously - take them if you can, refuse them at your peril, because every mission you decline (particularly the ones with red icons) is another nail in your coffin. You can start individual missions early, and face even better-armed, more rugged opposition; or late, tying up your squads in infiltration; or send a smaller squad, crossing your fingers that they will be able to cope. Do you level up a small number of elite teams, or go broad with a huge roster of half-trained amateurs?
Every decision at the strategic layer matters, too. You will need a laboratory, for example, in a way that wasn't really necessary in the base game. But when, and how do you afford it, with supplies so tight? You will have to contact other regions at breakneck speed to even stand a chance of success; how to balance this against the need to develop the Avenger's facilities at the same time? You will not be able to keep a morgue full of alien corpses as you could in the base game, relying on supply drops for resources. You will need to decide what you can afford to sell at the black market while still pressing forward with research and equipment production.
This against a background of an AI which is considerably improved. More than once I've managed a jail-break, for example, only to get my VIPs slaughtered by an undiscovered pod as they try to scamper to freedom. (And the two concealed Rocketeers on my Liberation mission were catastrophic).
All these modding decisions, and others like them, such as the increased variety of troop types, to my mind make LW2 so much better than vanilla XCOM2 that it's difficult to imagine going back to the base game. It runs fine, too. There can be a drop in frame rate when a new pod of a dozen or so enemies is triggered, but I had no LW2-specific bugs or crashes in over 150 hours of playing the mod.

But. (There is always a 'But').
First, is LW2 actually playable, in accordance with its own internal logic, as described at the outset above?
Some of the 'under the hood' mechanics, though vital to survival, simply cannot be understood except either after many hours of play, or extensive research at places like Reddit, Pavonis, or UFOPaedia. The Commander would not have had these resources available to him. It is at least possible to play vanilla XCOM2 once with every (sensible) decision taken as a matter of first impression, and have some prospect of success. (Some people started on Ironman when the the game first came out, to get just that experience). In this respect LW2 is in a 'Catch-22' situation; you can't play it unless you know how to, and if you know how to, then it is enemy known, rather than enemy unknown.
Second, much of the apparent increased freedom of choice turns out to be illusory, because there is is in reality only one way to beat LW2, namely by the so-called 0% mission, where you simply ignore the infiltration mechanic and go in with all guns blasting against Advent's finest, racking up corpses and experience, and 'breaking the strategic layer'. The odds at the outset may look horrifying, but believe me, they will look a great deal worse a few months down the line when Advent have half-a-dozen buffs to health and armour, besides a raft of high-quality equipment, and are only six pips short of victory on the doom clock. For me, this realisation struck when (in early September) I finally liberated a region, only to find that some of the regular Advent troops had stats almost as good as their 'boss' because of all the buffs they had already received, see
And that was with full infiltration, with the enemy 'vulnerable' - against a fortified or 'impregnable' target, it seems Advent get even better stats, in addition to greatly inflated numbers.
It's clear from reading the posts on the forums that LW2 suffers badly from what I would call 'buff creep' or 'nerf creep'. The developers have very sound ideas about how to better balance the game, improve the perks trees etc. but always, 'very late in development' the 'beta testers complained that the game was getting too easy' so Advent get buffed a bit more, or the player's units get nerfed a bit more.
Some of the same points are mentioned by Marbozir
. As he points out, there are of course mods to 'fix' anything you don't like, or you can tinker with the .ini files yourself, but why go to the trouble of creating such ingenious mechanics, and then buff/nerf everything so much at the last minute that they can never be used as intended?
In conclusion, then, a great mod - an entirely new game, really - But.
