Okay, seriously.  This game is really good and highly addictive, and it can be a real time sink.  This game is not for those who are averse to a good challenge, so many of the negative reviews here are from people who, frankly, just couldn't stand the pressure.  It's pretty hard, it's very unforgiving.  You will have soldiers die.  You might fail missions and yes, there can be consequences for that.  Yes, a lot of missions have timers.  At the end of the day, though, this is an extremely well-made and well-balanced tactical game.  It more or less improves on everything from its predecessor...  Many of the changes in gameplay are balanced to make it more challenging.  And this game is challenging.  It doesn't always allow the same slow, ponderous play style as Enemy Unknown/Enemy Within.  Many, perhaps most missions have a timer of sorts.  Honestly, though, this shouldn't present you with too many problems as long as you keep your head about you.  It's still all about ambushing your enemies however you can, you just don't always have as long to do it is all.
Despite my high praise for this game, I will say that it is definitely rife with its own problems, most of them technical.  Its anti-aliasing support, for example, is absolutely awful.  If you suffer poor framerates, dial down your AA to start with.  In fact, graphical optimization in general is abysmally poor, which makes me very glad that I have such a powerful video card.  In fact, my system overall is greatly in excess of the recommended settings and in 4K I was only pulling about 30FPS, with an absolutely massive disparity between geoscape/overworld and the performance in actual missions.  Still, the game is gorgeous, especially with the settings dialed up. Additionally, some serious frame dropping and lag occurs...  But not during missions!  It seems like the worst of the performance issues are either on loading screens (almost understandable, but still difficult to excuse) or on the Avenger (i.e. in-between missions during the meta/strategic part of the game).  Also, crashes occur pretty frequently; fortunately though, the game does auto-save every turn.  I'm not sure how this works out in Ironman, though, and in fact I fear that it could end up being too frustrating.  Finally, the missions could generate a little bit more intelligently...  I've had a few where 3 high-powered enemies were spawned right next to something I had to defend in a mission, making it ridiculously hard to actually complete the mission.  Granted, I'm all about games that are hard, but even if a game is hard it should at the very least be *fair.*  Fortunately, the procedurally-generated maps should provide quite a lot of replay value.
So overall, while this game isn't without its problems, don't let that deter you from getting it.  It's awesome, and sucked away a lot of my life for a solid month.

It’s been said that the RTS genre is dying.
After a Sunday playing this game with friends, I beg to differ.
Planetary Annihilation: Titans is a massive, brilliant game. The game comfortably supports massive armies, battling across a half-dozen worlds, all in a single session.
Multiplayer games are hosted on dedicated servers, which was a great choice. In our games, there were something like ten thousand units between each of our armies plus our AI opponents, all supported with a minimum of latency. The only lag you’ll likely experience is graphical. One of my friends had issues with framerate, but turning down the settings seemed to solve the problem.
You can read other reviews for a list of features. My personal favorites, however are:
+ Multi-planet combat. I enjoyed figuring out ways to transport my army/navy from one planet to another.
+ Balance between orbital, air, and ground/naval combat. Make sure you have an army that can deal with each of them.
+ Lots of fun ways to deal with an entrenched opponent: Nuclear interplanetary missiles, crashing an asteroid into them, activating a freaking DEATH STAR
+ Titan units: In a game that for the most part emphasizes macro, Titans are super fun to micro. The army-teleporting Helios is my personal favorite
Not everything is rosy. We did have a few problems:
- The multiplayer game arrangement interface isn’t great. We sometimes had problems all connecting to the game, and experienced strange, cryptic error messages. Once we were actually IN the game, we had no problems however.
- There’s no automated matchmaking for anything other than 1v1s. I’d love to see a team game and/or FFA matchmaking.
All in all, though, this is a fantastic game. If you’re at all a fan of strategy, I highly recommend it.

So I've seen a lot of Negativity over Street Fighter V, namely about the woes of online play (how quick we are to forget that MK X didn't work properly for 2 weeks eh?), the short story mode and survival being the only solo modes on offer.
That said however, I think of a lot the hateful reviews are being taken from a Rose-Tinted Glasses perspective.
Firstly, Online modes being the main focus? That's not exactly new and many of those same reviewers that have bemoaned SF V have had nothing but praise for every Call of Duty ever. Not exactly something I'd call Reputable and Trustworthy since Call of Duty has been nothing but a stripped down version of CoD 4: Modern Warfare for the past few years, with the stripped out parts being packaged off and sold to us as DLC.
The solo modes? How often does anyone actually WANT to play a fighting game solo for more than an hour honestly? You play the story, you forget about it, you move on to training mode, lobbies and online matches or offline versus your friends for the rest of it. While SFV has an unforgivably short story mode (it really is a "Is that all?" and can be finished in one 30 minute session) Survival mode is plenty long enough to get your solo fix, Hell Mode boasting 100 consecutive matches.
As for online, the problems are pretty much solved or being solved, DLC will be obtainable with ingame free currency (except premium costumes) lobbies are up and running and any and all content that adds new features or modes will be completely free.
All in all, SFV is actually a pretty solid fighter, with a Back to Basics theme that makes it more "Street Fighter" but with enough depth and new mechanics to keep it interesting at the higher end of gameplay.
Don't let the haters put you off, try it, you might like it.

A quality game that is worth buying despite it's flaws if you are a city building enthusiast.
The MegaStructures are a great feature that encourage you to make numerous cities with varying specialties.
KEEP IN MIND: There is a known issue with this game where it slows down over time as well as when your city gets extremely large. This should not be a surprise, however, as a city wth 250,000 citizens with jobs and traffic requires more caculations then an empty lot. That being said, there is some "work" that needs to be done to work around a few known issues where the game becomes really slow and choppy when left running for extended periods of time. (A quick google search will resolve those issues.)
Also, as with any city game, if you have an older graphics card, a slow processor or a lack of RAM, you will have troubles with a sprawling metropolis of 250,000+ citizens.
Though it does lack the "driving mission" feature of SimCity 4 Rush Hour, this game is a superior rendition in almost every sense of the word to SC4, is highly moddable, gorgeous looking and comes with a solid sound track to boot. Resource management, city-to-city trade, a very diverse and yet easily managed Supply and Demand system, traffic concerns and the need for things like Holidays, Hotels and Food makes this a more detailed and realistic Sim City without the old technology and feel of Sim City 4 nor the various drawbacks of SimCity 5 (or Origins or whatever the hell they called it.)
A great pick up for a city building enthusiast.
Coupled with the fact that I got platinum for dirt cheap because I owned CitiesXL 2011, it was a must buy.
Suggested Purchase Price: $10 or less.

While I'm not recommending this game for casual players at this point in time, the core mechanics of Street Fighter V are fantastic. More experienced players are likely to appreciate what Street Fighter V has to offer at this time. Servers are working well now, despite the hysteria surrounding first day server issues, which are pretty standard for a major release. So while the single player content is lacking, those looking to battle actual people are likely to have a blast with the game, even in its form right now. Many serious players are also going to love that they get the chance to hone their skills in the training room, which leads to why the game was released early. Capcom wanted to get SF V out in time to be accepted at Evo 2016, and if you're a part of the fighting game community in any way, you understand why this is so important. I am dying to see how the pros compete with SF V's mechanics, and the idea of having to wait over a year for SF V at Evo is far more of a negative than a rocky launch.
With that said, the game does have its flaws, mostly the single player aspects. Survivor Mode is currently a let down, seeing as how the first two thirds of the matchs are a push over, with the last third suddenly ramping up in difficulty without warning. Unfortunately, this is currently the only way to get alternate colors unlocked. Survivor mode would be a lot better if it was limited to 10 rounds, with the difficulty settings determining the CPU's level of play. Nobody wants to do 99 matches in a row, only to lose the last match.
It's important to understand that Capcom is planning on doing a lot more with Street Fighter V, and they will be contiously adding content. A lot of people are afraid of the cost of DLC, but it's also important to point out that new characters will be purchasable with in-game currency. Even if it ends up being hard to earn *every* character through the currency, the relative cost of buying individual items is still far superior to having to buy new editions of the game like in the past.
Again, the game in its current state is not for everyone, but for those who enjoy the multiplayer aspect of fighting games, SF V already offers plenty of depth to explore. :jorji:

I have played Starbound for more than 3 hours. I couldn't press the play button at the time because 64-Bit version of starbound for linux was broken. Anyways lets get into the review.
Before you think about buying this game, please read the reviews. Starbound was alright for an early-access game when I first bought it. This was around 2014, and when the winter update just happened. At the time, there were performance issues, missing features or just very narrow features, and "alot to explore". But now, it is just pathetic, and progression is very♥♥♥♥♥♥
To start off, when you first play this game, you are introduced to a tutorial. It might teach you a few things or might teach you nothing; to me there really isn't a point in the tutorial. When you finish the tutorial you are congratulated by your "first mission" which Starbound still calls part of the tutorial. In your "first mission", you will have to dig to the core for 20 core fragments. This has to be so ♥♥♥♥ing boring because you sit there for an hour with a copper pickaxe or two from the crates you looted on the starter planet and your matter manipulator. The copper pickaxes break way too fast, and your matter manipulator is so helpless. It is like punching your way to bedrock in Minecraft. Note that you are forced to the tutorial for every new character you create.  Once you collect these core fragments, you have to find a way to get back to the surface. if you dug a hole straight down with a few turns, I have some bad news for you.You can't beam up to your ship if you aren't directly under the sky.  So you then spend another hour or so diging your way back up, and finally you are done with the mission. Congratulations, you will have to this about 20 more times for missions with pointless lore. You will have to travel planets to get a guy a cup of coffee, a women a bug in a jar, and do this to get upgrades from your ship.
Combat has to be this games biggest failure, and sitting next to combat is exploration. Combat is NOT based on character progression. This means that you will see some lucky people that haven't even played the game for more than 10 minutes carrying around 10K damage weapons they found on some planet. Combat is very plain and basic. If you have a sword, you just swing it until you kill someone. 2 handed swords have parry, where you can block with the sword, and you can use a shield with one handed weapons, including guns. There is no point in dodging because the collision boxes are ♥♥♥♥ed up. Even if the collision boxes are ♥♥♥♥ed up, if you go online and PvP someone, the latency is unbearable no matter how close you guys are. Guns aren't even that special, the bullets are pretty fast you don't really need skill to aim them. Even firing a bow or a javelin/spear feels like firing a bullet. If you prefer bow and arrow, good luck finding some with quality damage in treasure chest. The magical weapons aren't that impressive either.
One issue I am having with this is game is it's main selling point- exploration. This is has to be the lamest feature in the game. Even though the mobs have random limbs and faces, you can still predict their attacks like you are a prophet. But in the end, it doesn't matter what mob you come across, you can blow them up or cut them up in 3 mouse clicks.There are only a distinct number of biomes, barely 10 biomes exist. Also there is no point in building a base on a planet or building period because once you finished the missions and fully upgraded everything, your ship will become the size of a planet itself.
Progression in Starbound sucks. You progress by doing missions, missions that consist of grinding. Every few missions comes a boss mission, which aren't that competitive. You can start "exploring" the universe as soon as you finish the "first mission", as long as you have the fuel, you can just start romaing around.
This game is also terribly optimized too, been like that since I first got it. Even from other reviews, people say this game can't take on the outpost on their rigs.

I want to like this game. I really do. And from a gameplay aspect, I do like it. But holy mother of Gill is this game (and it's netcode) unoptimized. As of this writing, the client is remarkably unstable and suffers from microstutter and unexplained framerate drops. The netcode is an asynchronous mess, with the "host" having an inherent advantage over the connectee. This game uses a type of netcode called "rollback", which attempts to emulate a lag-free experience. Lag-free it is, at the expense of stability. Imagine your opponent teleporting around the screen instantly, hitting you with attacks that you couldn't see coming. That's the type of netcode this is.
Have a dual core? Don't bother. This game chokes on CPU like no tomorrow. Hell, I have to disable cores in affinity settings on my overclocked i5-2500k (4.6ghz) just to help make it stable.
As of this writing, I'm going to recommend NOT purchasing this if you intend to play on a laptop or have even a remotely inconsistent internet connection. All it takes is one hiccup to send the stability spiralling downward.
But hey, the DLC can be gotten for free amirite?
EDIT: They still haven't fixed the netcode.

It has it's own unique charm, the game runs pretty well, looks good, but has this endearing sort of buggyness (being fully aware this is an Alpha build) and doesn't take itself too seriously, while being just serious enough to be challenging.  Sure, some of the mechanics are bugged or straight up broken, like melee combat which brings back memories of being a low-level Morrowind character, but it still manages to be insanely fun.  Most of the people playing the game are pretty chill, there's usually several well-populated servers.  Winning/losing is meaningless at this point, so just try to have a good time.  This game is an absolute joy

This game is like an extremely heavily modded XCom rather than a completely new game. Most of the UI and mechanics from XCom remain intact. The only difference is that you are now the one doing the raiding instead of the aliens.
A lot of people can't stand it because this is a complete switch from the defensive play style of XCom.
XCom one is about you on the defensive and wait for the enemy to attack then you respond. As the enemy increase the pacing, you will also need to follow up. Strategically, the enemy is the one doing the pacing with you holding critical event to slow the game down and hopefully not loose too many support in the process. Tactically, most the game involving you playing the defensive. When you play defensively in XCom, you would move slowly and ground out the enemies one by one. This is the most common and most effective tactics everybody used in XCom.
Xcom 2 forces you to go into offensive mode. Strategically, the enemy still leads the pacing with their doom counter. You have some influence on it but you can't hold them forever. Tactically, it's a whole different game. You have to comand a small team performing surgical strikes against a near unlimited amount of enemies. As they can call in unlimited amount of reinforcement, you will have to make a break for it before they ground you into meat paste with numbers. That means you really have to play aggressively. Taking out targets at speed with flanking manuvers and luck.
Overall, I would say it's a very good change-of-pace compare to XCom. Not everyone cup of tea but it's more exciting to take risks and win.

If you find yourself getting frustrated I recommend just exploring at your own will for awhile then heading back to the quest. Don't get too caught up with it, the game wasnt made to rush. A game with limited potential, RPG MO is ruined by two simple things.
1. Antibotting:  The nature of the captcha system vs. the nature of this game.  It encourages you to go afk by automatically crafting/fishing/cooking/etc. without repeated clicks.  So when you go afk to do something in real life, the captcha system comes up and tells you you'll be banned.  It's one of the worst mistakes such a crappy little game can make, and I cannot support them in making it.
2. Powertrippers:  I'm not sure why, but every chat room is filled with unrealistically pompous moderators.  People with their heads so far up their own asses that they threaten 50% of the playerbase every time I look at the chat.  I chose not to get involved with them, but it was quite enough to watch the way they treated new players.
If they fix these two issues, this grindy little game could take up far more of my time.  These two issues have been so for ***THREE*** years, so don't hold your breath.  That number is not made up... This is an old game that refuses to improve and gets a thumbs down from me.

Very interesting game. Not perfect, but impressive, as in it leaves an impression. The concept puts the recently popularized idea of ludonarrative dissonance in a scewed perspective. In this game, you are placed in a world obeying the rules of a game. Is the protagonist always in the right place at the right time? Does he always know what to say? Does he never miss a shot or make a wrong move? He is "save-scumming", for lack of a better term. Combing through the countless alternate realities for options that lead to his desired outcome.
I would happily recommend this game, were it a complete package. Currently, you only get a third of the complete game. And, as this third is embarrasingly short, I would hope the next two installations are both longer and included in this initial purchase.
If not, then I can't make an honest recommendation. It's a good game. It was easily worth the time I put into it. But paying the same price three times for three experiences separated by a significant amount of time is simply not fiscally responsible.

A very fun pirate ship battle sim. Upon joining a server, you become a crew member(or a captain, if your crew deems you worthy) and have to deal with all the details that go into running a ship during a naval battle. The game looks great, runs very smoothly, especially for an Early Access, and has a very fair price, even without sales. What's most impressive is that it's made by a 2 dev team, who put in more effort than just about any other game i've ever seen into making sure the player's input is heard.
Edit: Having since watched the intro of the ships updates and some gamemode experimentation, as well as having captained a bit of all the boats and done my fair share of swording-and-boarding, I can honestly say that this is without a doubt my best EA purchase to-date. The game looks good, feels good, and is fun to play. The combat is short enough to where you don't feel too committed, but long enough to where your individual actions matter. Captains are the high/low point of this game- if you're having a bad time, you probably need a captain change on one of your ships. Go to a good server at peak times after getting down with the basics- you'll have the best time when the score is neck-a-neck the entire game!

This game is great. I was immediately surprised by how easy it is to play with multiple combinations of weapons and skills, especially since each weapon is rather well balanced, and it is both possible and feasible to use any combination you can imagine, except perhaps in the case of weapon-specific skills. Also, the dynamic narration and music (also dynamic!) really help with the atmosphere, and the decisions you make actually have consequences. This is a fine example of a game where YOU get to choose how you will play. Will you bring a pair of ranged weapons? Or will you go full melee? Maybe you prefer a ranged weapon and a melee weapon. This game lets you play with any combination! The roll ability especially adds to the gameplay, allowing you to gain distance for a ranged strike, or move in for a quick melee attack. It has been a while since I played a game this dynamic and fluid, and I happily recommend it to anyone reading this.

Blackwake itself is a remarkably complete alpha with a refreshing concept horribly marred by an almost intolerable community. The awfulness of the people who play this game is exacerbated by the baffiling decision to let any player broadcoast their horrible microphones to everyone on the server. I'd guess about half of games have a ship named with a racial slur or some sexist tripe.
The captain system is poorly executed. The player who steers the ship is elected and called captain. The problem is at the beginning of the game, often only one person runs. So what really frustrates me is that I never run for captain because I have no interest with talking to these people, yet since I'm fairly high level I often get appointed after the captain leaves since no one else ran. When this happens, I'm rarely given a chance to do my job.
The most aggravating example of this is when I was appointed captain, mutined for being captain while the ship sank as I ran to the wheel, mutined twice more, and then votekicked because the mutinies didn't work. I was captain for less than 5 minutes. There's no way I could have done anything in 5 minutes to warrant that. Direct democracy is a terrible idea when the voters are on average ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s with no information and often trolls.
Making a game about teamwork and then having no meaningful system to keep the trolls at bay is not something that can be fixed with later features. I hope I'm wrong because I want to like this game, but if you create a culture of sexism, racism, and troll-celebration now boarding pikes later aren't going to help.

Very boring, yet utterly annoying Roguelike MMORPG.  Holy ♥♥♥♥ I hate it.
All you do is going through Grinding Hell by shooting things until finally battling the final boss of sort, Oryx, all while praying that the enemies just don't drain all of your life in one second (which happened to me a lot).  It bears repeating, that's literally all you do, nothing glamorous at all, little to no variety, you just shoot things, it's boring as hell, my god.
**In-depth mode, GO**
You could argue that fighting multiplying cats and then hordes of dwarves leads to different situations, which may be true, yeah, but Jesus Christ, there's no way, nor a reason, to use different strategies, it all boils down to aim at some blocky piece of crap and avoiding its pellets until it's gone, hoping there isn't a clown car full of unnecessary roadblocks offscreen, trying to ambush you.
There are classes to unlock, but whenever a game has multiple characters to choose from, they better have heavily different abilities to be worthwhile, and not just a carbon copy of each other.  And guess what?  They all pretty much act the same way, they all shoot some arrow/spell, and the only real differences being the statistics, and they have a different special move, which may change their playstyle, but not by much.  You're locked to a class until its inevitable end as well, so you can't alter the experience ever so slightly without having to die.  Such a worthless feature.
There may be Pets, and they may useful, but they don't deepen the experience much either.  You can't do some crazy chemistry like Palicoes or somethin, it's either they attack or they heal you, and you need Fame (or real money) to feed them stuff and fusing them, Fame is the only "free" form of money that you get by, again, Grinding Helling these, and then dying, meh...
Since it's a roguelike, if you die, you lose your character for good, but the problem is that you don't just lose about an hour of gameplay, oh noooo, your "oh-so-many" days character can just be gone due to some organized gangrape, where all the wildlife decided to all rush and shoot at you from offscreen, without any warning despite the map pinpointing them, and you have to start everything from scratch.  Geez, who the ♥♥♥♥ likes to lose so much (non-)progress?  I mourned more over my dead 10 hours character than on my grandma, knowing that I have to bore myself to death again.  I also find it hard to imagine that you have to not be messing up at all for many hours straight, like some MLG god, seems too hardcore even for difficulty.
And YES, I know of the Nexus Key, where you can go back to the peaceful lobby by the press of a button, but that is no excuse for poorly designed difficulty.  If some Cthulu wannabe with its Golem orgy decided to rush at you, you can't save your sweet rear with skill, without wussing out.  That's not good gameplay.
"But dude, you just suck at the game, it's the point to die and start all over."  Oh yeah sure, I could have gotten better, there is after all leveling to do and better equipment to get, like any self-respecting RPGs, but do you REALLY want to know how you do that?
Shooting things nets you experience points, but you can only go as far as Lv 20, which is still not high enough to confront the gods.  So what do you do then?  Get better equipment by defeating bosses, however it's completely random what they drop, more often than not they drop stuff for other classes, which your current class can't wield, completely useless.  I don't care if I can save these items in the Vault for future runs, as I want better crap for THIS character, it's utterly poor RNG, and even then, what would I do with an UT Skull if I don't also happen to have a good defense item to wanting to use it without dying in the process?

I swear, I grinded for many, MANY unholy succubus-fisting hours, spreaded throughout days, killing gods, and yet my equipment and stats were still too crap to deal with the quest monsters, and I got wrecked damn hard in the same fashion.  I'm completely clueless as to what I'm doing wrong, unless I have to cough up some dollars to get better crap that I assume I'd lose anyway if I would inevitably die.

First off, if you want this game, I HIGHLY recommend you buy all the DLC's with it as well.
I do not want to get into ultra detail as I try to keep this short and sweet. If I dont mention it, then I probably don't have any problems with it.
+ = Positive
- = Negative
Quality:
+You would never expect a small little company such as Coffee Stain Studio to make such high quality visuals like these. The world is extremely well done and dynamic as you can see buildings crumbling in the background and other cool events unfolding as you fight off the "lumes". I do have to admit that for me, I cant play for too long as it does give me a sense of motion sickness, even with motion blur off. I would also like a quick note that voice acting and inaminate object sounds are very realistic and doesnt seem to be bothersome.
Gameplay:
+A nice twist on tower defence + FPS. with a variety of weapons and perks, there are many customization to your character, (a choice from 4 characters) that you choose every level. There could be more customization, maybe in sanctum 3 ( If they plan on it :p) they could add armor customization and equipment upgrades.
+The towers also vary quite a bit as there are towers for utility like slowing enemies or mind controlling them. And there are towers for your everyday mowing as they turret down targets using lasers or rockets. I think it's also neat that there are flying and ground monsters (called lumes) that are affected only by certain towers as well as armored and metal lumes that have weakspots, and for the metal lumes, places where they cant take any damage.
+Oh, and did I mention all the lumes have weakspots? Yes, every lume has a weakspot, that indicats that if you hit that targetted spot, you will get bonus damage on them, also indicated by the red damage indicators flying off of them.
+The campaign will be the main thing you play as you are following a storyline and a neat little comic as you progress through the game. There are many difficulties you can choose from, like adding the difficulty for monsters to have more health or the difficulty to only have one life and or maybe all of them together. Which will give you more experience when playing, but makes it a lot harder to beat.
-The level up system is alright I can say. There's a max that's not terribly hard to reach as you unlock weapons, towers, or perks with every level. What makes it alright is that when you reach the max level, there's really no point in playing the harder difficulties for more xp, just for bragging rights. And survival on the other hand, also turns into just bragging rights, but you can get onto a scoreboard if you're smart enough.
+A little bit on the tower-defence part of the gameplay is that you place blocks to re-route the monster, you're basically creating a obstacle course for these monsters to run ( fly over, or destroy as certain things can do that). With the obstacles being the towers you place on the blocks. With a max of 10-15 towers on the level, and the ability to upgrade after every wave is done.
My main issue:
-One problem you might find is in surival. The campaign can be played with your character cleaning house and towers to back you up as you choose the perks that suit player strength and not tower. But when in survival, your character will never get strong enough to last forever, because there are no character upgrades. So you will have the first couple of waves actually doing something. But in the later stages, will find that towers are the only hope, as they can be upgraded (Over charged). So this once towerdefence+shooter, turns into a towerdefence+tickler, as you will take the most minuscule health off these lumes, like you're just tickling them.
-Soo... That leaves you with campaign mainly, which will keep you occupied, but is rather frustrating as it can be difficult to beat certain levels on the highest difficulty, even with your friends.

Conclusion:
+Still a very solid game if you are into shooters and have a knack for some strategic gameplay. It's definitely a very unique experience and would definitely recommend you give it a try for yourself.
PS:
+The ingame chat is hilarious as there is a robot voice saying everything you and others type. Good luck raging to others, haha.

When I first played Sanctum, I thought it was a peculiarly interesting game with a solid twist - being able to fight against the monsters themselves as they trudged through your maze, exploding into orange and purple chunks under fire from all kinds of crazy weaponry. When I heard about a Sanctum 2, I thought, "What could they possibly do to this niche genre that would warrant a sequel? What could be added to this that would make a significant impact to how this game is played?"
As I see it, Sanctume 2 is the only possible answer. While Sanctum had a huge focus on choosing a right maze and manipulating every type of enemy into a big pile to be bombed to Loek-come, Sanctum 2 places much more presence on your involvement and gives a large variety of ways to contribute strongly to the success of your maze other than a mass pile gib-fest.
There are still some wonky parts about it - such as one of the characters being far too OP on their own and anyone playing alongside that class is launched out of the arena and to their deaths - but it is a far more balanced, far more involved Sanctum than the original could hope to be. It stays true to its own quirky genre but doesn't hold onto what worked before so tightly that it is a complete rehash.
With lavish visuals, a great soundtrack, stellar level designs and lots of them, slight tweaks in customization to fit your play-style along with solid expansions packs that are well worth picking up, Sanctum 2 is a game that really puts the defense in Tower Defense. Probably not as much depth as your typical AAA game delivers, but you'll probably put more hours into it than you would one of those games.

I have played Starbound for more than 3 hours. I couldn't press the play button at the time because 64-Bit version of starbound for linux was broken. Anyways lets get into the review.
Before you think about buying this game, please read the reviews. Starbound was alright for an early-access game when I first bought it. This was around 2014, and when the winter update just happened. At the time, there were performance issues, missing features or just very narrow features, and "alot to explore". But now, it is just pathetic, and progression is very♥♥♥♥♥♥
To start off, when you first play this game, you are introduced to a tutorial. It might teach you a few things or might teach you nothing; to me there really isn't a point in the tutorial. When you finish the tutorial you are congratulated by your "first mission" which Starbound still calls part of the tutorial. In your "first mission", you will have to dig to the core for 20 core fragments. This has to be so ♥♥♥♥ing boring because you sit there for an hour with a copper pickaxe or two from the crates you looted on the starter planet and your matter manipulator. The copper pickaxes break way too fast, and your matter manipulator is so helpless. It is like punching your way to bedrock in Minecraft. Note that you are forced to the tutorial for every new character you create.  Once you collect these core fragments, you have to find a way to get back to the surface. if you dug a hole straight down with a few turns, I have some bad news for you.You can't beam up to your ship if you aren't directly under the sky.  So you then spend another hour or so diging your way back up, and finally you are done with the mission. Congratulations, you will have to this about 20 more times for missions with pointless lore. You will have to travel planets to get a guy a cup of coffee, a women a bug in a jar, and do this to get upgrades from your ship.
Combat has to be this games biggest failure, and sitting next to combat is exploration. Combat is NOT based on character progression. This means that you will see some lucky people that haven't even played the game for more than 10 minutes carrying around 10K damage weapons they found on some planet. Combat is very plain and basic. If you have a sword, you just swing it until you kill someone. 2 handed swords have parry, where you can block with the sword, and you can use a shield with one handed weapons, including guns. There is no point in dodging because the collision boxes are ♥♥♥♥ed up. Even if the collision boxes are ♥♥♥♥ed up, if you go online and PvP someone, the latency is unbearable no matter how close you guys are. Guns aren't even that special, the bullets are pretty fast you don't really need skill to aim them. Even firing a bow or a javelin/spear feels like firing a bullet. If you prefer bow and arrow, good luck finding some with quality damage in treasure chest. The magical weapons aren't that impressive either.
One issue I am having with this is game is it's main selling point- exploration. This is has to be the lamest feature in the game. Even though the mobs have random limbs and faces, you can still predict their attacks like you are a prophet. But in the end, it doesn't matter what mob you come across, you can blow them up or cut them up in 3 mouse clicks.There are only a distinct number of biomes, barely 10 biomes exist. Also there is no point in building a base on a planet or building period because once you finished the missions and fully upgraded everything, your ship will become the size of a planet itself.
Progression in Starbound sucks. You progress by doing missions, missions that consist of grinding. Every few missions comes a boss mission, which aren't that competitive. You can start "exploring" the universe as soon as you finish the "first mission", as long as you have the fuel, you can just start romaing around.
This game is also terribly optimized too, been like that since I first got it. Even from other reviews, people say this game can't take on the outpost on their rigs.

XCOM 2... XCOM 2... XCOM 2... How do I describe you?
But anyhow, XCOM 2 is probably my overall favourite game at the moment and has been for quite a while, at least since the summer. However, before I start talking about pros and cons, I would like to address the biggest reason why this game gets negative reviews, at least what I think that reason is.
Mission timers. The amount of turns that can take place before an objective becomes unfinishable.
I really do understand why this is such a big problem with a lot of people, and when I first started playing this game, I hated it as well. However, since then (and I have no clue if this is something added with the War of the Chosen DLC or not), Firaxis has added a new modifier for every new game, the choice to double that timer for every such timer that you come across. I think this is one of the best additions to this game because it makes the game a lot more like Enemy Unknown (EU), whereas you can take your sweet time with every mission, while still being slightly hurried by the timer (and I enjoy the game a lot more with this enabled).
Now that I've talked about that, let's move on to pros and cons and why you should buy this game.
---------------------------------------------------------
Pros
---------------------------------------------------------
-Great turn based strategic experience. Probably the best along with Civ V that I've ever seen.
-Great managing strategic experience. When out of missions, this game turns into a real time managing strategy game, which is a great blend with the fun turn based missions.
-Great progression. Your favourite soldiers level up (or are wounded or die), gain new weapons, abilities, etc. Enemies level up, or you encounter new ones. And all this is done in such a way that the game is still kept fun and it doesn't progress too quickly or too slowly (although there is a modifier which might increase progression time if you choose to use it).
-Great continuity. This game continues very well from EU, especially with the mechanics of the game, which have been slightly redone and new ones have been added.
-New mechanics. As mentioned above, the added new mechanics (such as concealment), make the game heaps better mechanic wise (especially with the mission timer modifier enabled) than EU.
---------------------------------------------------------
Cons
---------------------------------------------------------
-Badly optimised. Without the War of the Chosen DLC, this game can be pretty demanding, even though my build can run newer and more demanding games at higher frame rates.
-Mission timers. I did address it, however, I still want to talk about it. This game is amazing, but it is really hard to get over these damn mission timers. With the modifier enabled, this issue it basically deleated, however, beware if you cannot or willnot enable it.
---------------------------------------------------------
No Man's Land (neither good nor bad)
---------------------------------------------------------
-The story. While the story was better than EU, I wouldn't play it completely for the story. However, when added onto all the mechanics of the game, the story is a great added layer.
---------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
---------------------------------------------------------
-Like I said above, this game is probably my favourite as of now. I really enjoyed playing my first play through (however emotionally defeated I might have been by the end) and still enjoy playing different play throughs. To a new XCOM player, the game is very demanding and the choices you end up going with are (if you don't just re-run an old save) final. This game made huge improvements to EU, although others might disagree. I recommend you play both of the games at some point, especially if you enjoy strategy games. However, beware of the performance issues.
Final Score - 9.5/10

Close to 800 hours (and two playthroughs) into the game, I can say that I love the game but dispise the company that made it.
The Good: It's a breathtaking new edition in the series and gives a fresh new take on the game. With just as much time in here as I have with Fallout 3 and New Vegas, I can say it continues the story of post-war life in a fantastic way. Free mods take what Bethesda did to a whole new level, almost as far as what New Vegas became. Knowing to go to Nexus Mods is essential to getting the most out of the game.
The Bad: If you've played any of Bethesda's other "open world" games (Oblivion, Skyrim, Fallout 3/NV) know that there are bugs and crashes. The more modded up your game is, the worse it gets. That's the only major issue I have with the game and the trade-off of stability for new content is well worth it.  The only other thing that bears mention is that since the player character has voiceover (not just text) your choices in the game are severly limited over previous Bethesda titles.  I enjoyed hearing the player speak for a change, but this puts the breaks on what mods can do with new quests.
The Ugly: As the game now has been out for a while, Bethesda continues to try to push "Paid Mods" into the game. The catch is the way they've implemented this is lame at best and a PR nightmare at worst. If you google "fallout 4 creation club fiasco" you'll see why there is a rash of negative reviews, a lot of them are justly deserved.  Mods on the Nexus are better than what's in the Creation Club, and they're free to boot.  The other issue is that they're pushing "Creation Club Credits" instead of using actual currency in the game, forcing you to spend more on credits than if they just charged a flat price for the content.  They should have learned from how Microsoft used to use Microsoft Points for currency on Xbox, this type of payment scheme sucks.  The one shining point here is that the Creation Club can be ignored, it's not essential to the game at all.  If it really grinds your gears, there are mods on the Nexus to remove the interface completely from the game.
The Bottom Line: Fallout 4 is a fantastic game that's marred by Bethesda's ham-handed attempt to monitize additional content for the title.  The recent negative reviews are 100% driven by the public relations disaster of it's rollout, how they treat the authors of their paid content and not the game itself.  I still recommend it, but don't be fooled into the Creation Club.... Learn about the Nexus and you'll have a better trip through the wasteland because of it.

This expansion, as you might guess, adds titans to the game, which boast epic levels clear over nine thousand. Other additions are fleshing out of each of the factories' unit rosters with, as far as I can tell, one or two new units that add more options to the game. And the other addition I'm personally most impressed by is the huge expansion of orbital layer gameplay. Again, as far as I can tell, the orbital layer gets a whole host of new options to create epic 'splosions with, from energy collecting solar arrays, to interplanetary scout probes and radar satellites, to orbital cruisers capable of cementing your control of the layer, scouting and even bombarding the surface.

Something like Sins Of A Solar Empire's blend of RTS and more macro strategy I think would've resonated wth me a little better, but this is still very much a traditional base building RTS refined to a high level of multi-dimensional depth and complexity. When the Mass Effect trilogy controversially ended with a seemingly arbitrary final choice, it also felt like it invalidated all the choices leading up to it. Players were outraged because the game offered them a glimpse of something truly awesome and then snatched it away, right as the game came to an end. To be fair to the trilogy, what players felt they deserved was something most a games don't even
to provide: a true sense of player agency.
There's an obvious reason why giving players non-trivial choices is so rare. It's super hard. Every time a player makes a meaningful choice, the developer has to create all of the content for the path they chose
all of the content for the path they might not ever experience. The amount of content that needs to be written is literally exponential to the amount of content that the player experiences.
CONSORTIUM ambitiously tries to meet this goal and it actually mostly succeeds. The most common complaint is that it's short. Of course it's short. It has to be. For every chunk of the game that you see, the devs had to make many that you don't. This branched story structure is essential for creating the kind of fun anxiety that comes from making real choices with incomplete information. The tradeoff is that you're paying for a lot of content that you'll never see.
The developers have tried to address this issue by making the game highly re-playable. Not only can you return to saved games to check out different paths, some elements of the game are actually different on different playthroughs. This solution sort of works, but the bulk of the dialogue never changes so replays can feel pretty tedious. The repetitiveness feels especially punishing when you have to re-load a game due to finicky dialogue and quest triggers. The game shipped with a ton of bugs, many of which are now fixed, but the triggers still require some babysitting.
Overall, it's an ambitious game and a worthwhile experience. I'll definitely check out the sequel.
One final thought: CONSORTIUM advertized a large library of in-game text to read. It's theoretically optional, but there
information in there that can affect your game. Another important thing to know about it is that it's extremely boring. As much fun as I had playing the game, the world outside the aircraft is not particularly compelling.

It's not often that you play a game that feels fresh, but it's a magical experience when you do. CONSORTIUM is one of those games. You're plunged into a world you don't understand, hearing terms you don't recognise, encountering a ranking structure that is unfamiliar. You get the greatest feeling you can get in a game: the need to explore and learn more about this fascinating universe.
Suffice to say the opening is excellent at drawing you in and the music of Jeremy Soule is well utilised here.
It's a game about people and relationships. You will spend most of your time walking around the ship interacting with the crew, and every member of that crew has their own voice, personality, relationships with other crew members. Everyone feels like a real person, there's no lazy stereotypes here, no accented characters firing off lines about "in my homeland" or anything like that. They're just people.
The dialogue system helps with this feeling of a living vessel. Conversations don't pause the game or take control away from you. You can walk away, they can walk away, people can interrupt, other conversations carry on around you, they keep working on whatever task it was they were doing. Rather than taking you out of the game, conversations draw you deeper into it. And, hallelujah, keyboard shortcuts for dialogue options!
This game is part one of three with a larger meta arc straddling the series, but this game features a central mystery around a traitor aboard the ship. And this is my favourite bit: whether you discover who that traitor is is entirely up to you; you can end this episode not knowing. And it's not easy, you will most likely fail. How awesome is that?
It's reasonably short with about five hours of gameplay (though there's tens of hours of material in the console if you want to read it all), but it replays well. You're going to miss events, things play out differently depending on your choices, conversations might not happen, characters might not appear. I think you could easily get three playthroughs out of this without feeling bored. While I wouldn't recommend browsing the achievements before playing this game, they give you a good idea of the number of different things that can happen and how many of them you've missed.
The game isn't without weaknesses and there are a few biggies:
1. Combat isn't great, primarily because the entire episode takes place on the ship and the ship makes for a really poor combat environment. There's not really any cover to work with or great ways to maneuver, you will generally just hold down the trigger or find ways to cheese the AI for the tough bits. It is supposedly possible to make it through the game without firing a shot though. I've almost done it.
2. The inventory doesn't feel like it has a reason for being and is incredibly clumsy. It has that Mass Effect vibe of existing because people expect to see it.
3. The game just sort of ends without any feeling of closure. Sure, it's part one of three, but games like Mass Effect and The Walking Dead have shown how you can be part of a larger arc while still managing closure at the end of your game.
4. I have concerns with the meta element of "you are playing a game" which is being worked into the story. It works in dialogues in a jokey "are you mad?" kind of way, but it seems to be becoming a larger part of the plot in a way I'm not that keen on.
All-in-all though I'd recommend it. It feels new and exciting, and setting the whole game in one location works really well.

I will recommend this game, but be cautious. This game gets insanely difficult, and fast. Once you get access to basic utilities, like water, power, and oil, it can be so easy to bankrupt your city by trying to offer all of these to your city at once. This game runs on supply and demand. If you're producting a lot of oil, and your city can't pay for it (not that your city won't demand it; they just won't be able to pay for it), your city will lose money by extracting more oil than what it can pay for. This goes with about a dozen different resources the game takes into account. You can also have not enough resources. This makes things rather complicated, because you will always run into a scenario in which your city needs more resources than it can pay for, even if you trade with other cities.
Your city will always be plagued with problems once you get to a significant population. Traffic is always a problem. Always. There is no way to really mend the traffic problem. The tourism also really doesn't make much sense to me.
However, I recommend this game because it's kind of realistic. You can't make everyone happy. You can't "pre-plan" your city by making interstates in a town with 200 population. You have to build your city up and then create those, causing you to have to re-route traffic and demolish structures so you can work on your interstate system, which is a headache I bet most leaders in transportatioon have. You will have to have a ghetto and also a rich population. Your citizens will get bored. The game is also beautiful and zooming into ground level gives a lot of awesome views.

Let me start off by saying I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of fighting games. If you're still on the fence I believe I can elaborate as to why this game is getting mixed reviews. People are expecting day 1 amazing netplay, and considering the scale that Street Fighter V is going for, its simply not reasonable to set your hopes so high with it being only 2 or 3 days after release. This game is doing cross-platform play (which VERY few games attempt) with global matchmaking (this cant be simple as other games opt for a region-based service). I recall playing World of Warcraft on opening day... Diablo III on opening day... didn't these Triple-A, 60$ games have problems? or am I trippin? Capcom has been diligently working on the online portions of the game as people provide feedback. They are also working on non-network related issues as well (you can always check with @SFVServer on twitter to see for yourself). As of this writing their last update was 1hr ago (from 9am EST). In any case, I have the utmost confidence that these issues will be resolved with urgency.
Currently, we have :
- Survival - (easy : 10 fights , normal : 30 fights , hard : 50 fights , hell : 100 fights)
these are used to unlock color palette swaps and 2 titles. They are done on a per character basis, and using the points you earn per 1 round fight, you can purchase boosters such as health up , attack up, etc to carry you through the ranks
- Training - you go here to 'git gud'.. there are multiple recording slots, the usual attack data read-outs and gauge set-ups. I haven't personally utilized all that training has to offer, but it is more than adequate.
- Story - For each character you can do a prologue of sorts, which lets you earn an alternate outfit (however at this time, the outfits are not readily available.. I heard they will be next month due to them still testing their Fight Money).
Net-play modes :
- Battle Lounge - You make a lobby, invite someone and have at it without points or rank involved (Currently 1v1 only, as I imagine they are still doing testing)
- Ranked Match - You battle opponents via matchmaking to gain rank and Fight Money
- Casual Match - Like Ranked, this uses matchmaking but rank is not on the line here
Speaking of Fight Money, capcom has stated that all up-coming content will be unlockable with Fight Money~
*angelic music playing* Poverty, rejoice!
and finally, the Capcom Fighters Network.. CFN tracks a bunch of stats, and its also where you'll go to view replays, add a fighter to favorites (so you can invite them to your lobby), or possibly plot revenge as you study their weaknesses? lol? :steamsalty:
I recommend this game because its solid af, and really puts your fundamentals on blast while offering up new features like V-Skill / Trigger and Crush Counters.. we E-Sports, now~ :D

Despite lack of content, with Story Mode coming in June and Single Player Challenges and Shop unlocking in March, the gameplay in SFV is a tight and competitive as ever. If you're buying this game for a quick single player fix, this won't do it for you. Further down the line after release you'd be better off with fleshed out "Story Modes" and a potential "Arcade Mode" hinted at by Capcom.
Fighting games are essentially about 2 things: Training & Competeing against other players. These are 2 things SFV will provide right now, regardless of online teething. If you enjoy fighting games allowing you to learn characters and feel yourself improving every fight, SFV is for you. Yes it's lacking content and yes we are relying on Capcom releasing the updates on time and delivering on there promises. It's a difficult situation when your money is on the line.
It's entirely up to you. Value is subjective. I for one bought the game for £25 and have sunk 19 hours since launch, with 3 in training mode, 3 in Story/Survival mode and the rest in Matchmaking. I have not regretted a second of that time, even though Day 1-3 netcode wasn't spot on.
Gameplay is fun, and for me thats all a fighting game has to do to sell me. More free content is coming but for now you're still getting the wonderful SF combat you know and love, with several adjustments tailored to make it easier for newcomers to get stuck in.
If you're hesistant wait it out for the next few updates. If you enjoy fighters, learning characters and want a headstart you'd be mad not to jump in.

Just started playing this game, about 3 hours in as of this review. I have to say, this game is rather addicting, I can't seem to stop playing! Right when you start, If you've ever played Utlima or Runescape Classic, you get THAT kind of nostalgic feel from it. I knew I would like this game the moment I played it because Runescape Classic was fun as well, although I never played Ultima before. Currently, there are 15 skills you can level up, all of which have NO level cap. However, the SOFT cap is 120, meaning 120 is basically a practical maximum, but no absolute, so you CAN have say 200 mining potentially, but it would take a really long time as anything past the soft cap is pretty hard to obtain.
Starting the tutorial, it looked really close together, and the text i couldn't really focus on with everything else around me. Hopefully that gets refurbished soon. But the tutorial explains mostly everything considered you actually paid attention. One thing I don't believe they explain much are the shops around RPG MO. In the starting town, Dorpat, there are a number of vendors you can sell your items to. But beware, these vendors only buy low-level types of things. So, low level fish, low level weapons you forge, etc. To sell other types of items you can either click on your chest (bank), and then the market to sell your items. Or you could move to the other towns in RPG MO, where the npc's buy higher leveled items.
If you want to make money fast right when you start this game, I suggest mining/forging once you get to the iron stage (not very high ) you can sell iron helmets and make around 200k in an hour (considering you successfully make them with a high chance, and not fail most of the time.) With Iron, (like Runescape) There is a chance they do not get forged into bars. Fishing is okay, but at a high level. You could try your chances and sell your fish in the market.
I saw some negative reviews about people being banned because they posted some things in the chat. There are about 5 types of chat. All you really need to know is EN (English) is the PG chat, meaning no language, no talking about other games, and more. Try using the ST (Steam) chat, or /join 18 for the 18+ chat. It's not my fault you didn't read the rules, or the tips that appear throughout the game.
The games virtual currency, MOS can be bought or earned (in extremely low quanities) from quests. MOS can be used to buy all types of goodies in the MOS shop. One of the most used items is the 2x EXP, which cost $5 and yields 30 minutes of EXP. Ever since the steam release there has been a LOT of this stuff bought, even 10 hours at a time. Usually when one gets going, people add on to it and it builds up. So take advantage, play now!
tl;dr: Old school game is awesome, nice community. I recommend this game, 8/10.

Before we begin let's get this straight: This is a game very heavy on story and interaction with NPC's. If you're the kind of person whom likes to skip as much dialog as possible and just want to spend hours shooting things up, this game is not for you.
Also, AT THE TIME OF WRITING, there were bugs in the game that made you save often should something go wrong. However, the devs pretty much responded to them instantly and I'm quite confident this game will be fixed by the end of January 2014. (Remember this is a small Indie team game with limited testing resources pre launch.) If you're worried, check the forums. (Try to avoid spoilers however, since finding out everything for yourself is 90% of the fun in your first playthrough.)
That said:
This is one of the most refreshing games I've played in a while when it comes to an ACTUAL First Person Role Playing Game. You have the basic, an inventory system, your quickbars and as the items you require get stronger, so do you. But feature is used in probably only 10% of the actual game, and even that can be skipped if you play it like a smooth criminal and talk your way out of things. (Remember this is the first episode, the next 2 might contain a lot more combat)
But the real juicy part is the dialog system. As you make your way though the game, you gain and lose status with people. if it gets bad, you have less options, if it gets high, you'll have an easier time interacting with them. The problem? Certain actions boosts one, but lowers the other one. So be careful what you say.
There is no hand holding in this game, do you make the wrong choice, you'll have to live with it (unless you reload a past save, you cheeky basterd). Conversation is fuild, engaging and unless you do a blanc carbon copy of your last playthrough, not one playthrough is the same. You'll have to actually think, consider or ignore facts, make split descisions, explore and live with the consequences if things pan out badly.
The conversation system gives you a pretty diverse amount of conversation directions, and there are events that happen that can change the course of the game if you react badly. A crewmate could be injured, and you have about a second or 2 to heal them, you don't get prompted for this, you don't get warned this might happen, but it will impact your story on a decent scale. Especially if you consider your story will continue in the next episodes.
The lore behind the game is pretty vast. And there is a reason why the description talks about satalites and such, and the game will remind you of it through hints and events now and then.
Is it worth the price? Remember this is an indie game, and all money they earn will be funded mostly towards the next episodes. But then again, it really depends your tastes. For me, I had a lot of fun with it, and with multiple playthoughs, the game will last you quite a while. However, it might be a decent sum if you're not sure if it is the game for you.
The Graphics are a little outdated, but their cartoonish look, combined with a calming enviroment, make it easy on the eyes and you won't even care after 10 minutes. It has a Star Wars the clone wars cartoon series vibe going on in the looks department (Jar Jar free).

Bastion is an action role-playing game where you take control of "the Kid" as he tries to discover what caused the catastrophic event that starts the game off.
The gameplay consists of using two selected weapons from a varied arsenal. This naturally creates a plethora of playing styles and strategies to explore. As you progress through the game, you unlock more game systems: from various challenging effects that make the game harder and reward you with more experience, over a forge that lets you upgrade your weapons to various boons in form of a distillery and plenty more. Enemies come in only few forms, which is one of the few weaknesses of the game, but this is compensated for by placing them in carefully planned combinations and strategical positions which make for fun and engaging combat.
The game is set in an intriguing and dismally empty world that is depicted in a beautiful, vibrant hand drawn art style. Often times you can't help but just be in awe of the artistic talent on display. Another great strength is the exceptional soundtrack that always creates a seemingly perfect atmosphere. This is accompanied by a similarly impressive narrator, who delivers the story in a captivating one-of-a-kind fashion. The story is interesting and keeps you moving forward, exploring the often times troubling pasts of your companions. This all culminates in what is one single awe inspiring scene that on its own makes the game worth playing.
The short length of the game might be seen as a weakness, but one could argue that it benefits the game more than it hurts it, as it allows the story to flow at an appropriate pace without the gameplay becoming repetitive.
This game shows very clearly how much love and passion the developers put into it and I can't help but feel respect for them.

TLDR: A great city building game that could've been the best for years to come. There are too many issues though.
I still rate it 3rd for me after Simcity 3000 and 2000.
Beware of the compatability issues, performance issues, bugs and illogical things (the save menu WTF).
The city building is solid and all the info you need is available. Sometimes the city's management information is a bit hard to find, but it's there. You don't have to lay down power lines or water pipes, which I didn't like at first, but got used to. The roads can be curved in any way you want which is really cool.
The game is easy at first and the tutorials are good (not voiced though), but there is a big difficulty jump when your basic utility facilities aren't enough for your city anymore. The city will start to demand more electricity, fuel, water and waste disposal very suddenly. Also when you start building high density stuff the demands go up quite a lot.
The game also seems laid back and fun instead of taking itself super seriously. Just like Simcity 3000 did (And Simcity 4 didn't). It doesn't mean it makes the game any worse as a simulator, but more fun to play.
Graphics look really nice and are freely rotatable and zoomable 3D. You can tilt the view upwards/downwards with only 2 presets though.
I can't really get why some people complain about the graphics.
You can zoom in to see the details, which I didn't really care at first, but I found it's really cool to see your cities from the street level in the "postcard" camera mode.
Sounds are what you'd expect in a city builder and music suits the game nicely. The intro song does play a bit too much though.
I have not run in to any compatability issues with Win 7 64bit, but there are many people reporting them on the forums.
And the to the negatives:
The game runs fine when building a small city, but when the city size reaches 500k people or so it brings any computer down to below 10FPS in some situations (like making bus lines or zooming way out).
It runs only in single threaded mode, but also must be optimized poorly. Some tweaks to the game files help, but not enough to make building big cities fun.
There are some bugs like sometimes the trading does give or take more money than it should, some special building names or descriptions not showing up properly and one or two sounds not playing properly (police station is one).
And then there are these logical issues. When you click a diskette image in the menu that is labeled "Save" and in the following interface click a save thumbnail, it LOADS the save instead of saving (there is a confirmation dialog, but it's too easy to just click ok). Also it overwrites the autosave instantly at that moment.
There are more of these issues, but they're just annoyances, not wasting hours of city building!

Engage in a First Person Shooter game over a voxel-based world.
Equip your character with the variety of weapons to choose from including guns, knives, explosives, and even tanks.
Progress your level by winning the matches, and set your mark against the world's top ranks.
Similarly themed voxel-based open worlds have spurred out of control since the hype from the founding game Minecraft. Though as many rendition or clones come out to the market, every once in a while, one will surely grab your attention. Such is the game Blockade 3D. Sported to be a First Person Shooter type of game, you will be amused to what simple graphics can offer as it will rack up against high-end titles with top notch visuals in its aspect of entertainment, and fun-factor in general.
As an FPS released game over an online infrastructure, rooms are organized over the selection menu to provide the battlegrounds of the participating players. Every room displays the number of active players enlisted to it, and the battle space that you may expect to see as you get used to them. There are also several game-modes where you can enlist over Group Battles, Creation mode to build your own map, survive at the Zombie-Mode, or engage over tank battles in its Tanks Mode.
The main meat of the game is to take part into the battles, secure victory, earn resources, upgrade your weapon, customize your looks, progress through the levels, set your mark through its ranking system, and do everything all over again. There is so much stuff to get one’s self to be addicted to the game or simply engage over its creativity mode, just as offered in other voxel-based games.
Upon signing up your account, you’ll immediately be prompted to the game’s lobby of servers. It may take a few clicks and tries before you get the hang of it as the game does not provide any sort of tutorial to introduce you to its several play modes. Instead, a simple control guide at the lower portion of the screen is provided depending on the mode you play.
As you get to the game itself, beginners are basically given with 1 free gun. Upon completing your novice setup, you are ready for the killing as you get to the selection of different rooms and servers to enlist your character into.
From here onwards, you are thrown into your group’s spawn side of the map and scour your way to the enemy lines doing the usual gun-fights etc. As you win the tourneys, you will gain some in-game resources that will earn you the upgrades, weapons, and other custom features of the game. For some, it may be comforting to know that this is also available outright with the help of micro-transactions in the game.
From the graphics standpoint, you know what game you’re getting into. The title sports graphics that do look pixelated, blocky, and deprived of curved lines. Although that is very much the exact appeal of these games - spanning out on a massive world designed with only the use of square portions of blocks. Thousands and thousands of them.
Blockade 3D is a sleek free-to-play MMOFPS that can easily be played over facebook upon installing a unity plug-in to your browser of choice (except chrome of course). The title enlists a lot of great game elements to engage its players, plus the excitement of a heart-pumping action from a first-person shooter game that is truly capable of delivering great fun among its participants.

If you played Terraria and liked it but got bored, give Starbound a try. I was skeptical at first, taking it as a Terraria clone set in space, but when I got into it I found the mechanics a lot tighter, the lore is present, and the variety in options to the player varied and interesting.
There are a number of races to play as, each with their own backstories(although some are definitely more fleshed out than others at this point), racial armors and weapons, and unique ships and pets. The choice to largely forgo traditional pickax, wood ax, and shovel setup makes it feel a lot less cluttered, and less of a factory-simulation where you have to meet a quota of materials mined to stay mining.  There are an insane number of procedurally-generated planets in the universe for you to explore, and none of them are identical. They have unique monsters, unique weather, and unique geography, as well as unique structures both on the surface and subterranian.
It grabed me on a fundamental wanderlust; even though I have a character who is at the highest currently-available tier, if I don't feel like building a world I can go explore the universe, flying from planet to planet in search of who knows what.
I enjoyed my time with this game, and am looking forward to the release, although be warned it has been in development for a very long time and some members of the community are getting frustrated by that fact.

In current times I often find myself unable to stick to games. I tend to usually put maybe 10 hours into a game and lose interest, but this game has officially made itself an exception. This game is truly something i never expected to get in a video game. Very reminiscent of a type of game my friends and i might play as a board game of some sort while sitting at a table, this game makes itself special. There are very few games that are able to constantly have you put in a unique situation every single time you play. Town of Salem, of course, manages to pull this off because the entire premise of the game is that the entire game is molded by the players in each game.
Now sometimes you may encounter the occasional annoying or bad player online, but it's made up for because for the majority of the time, they are unable to COMPLETELY ruin a session. They may cause some loss of immersion into the game, but the other 13 players will tend to for the most part remain immersed in the game along with you.
Having a large list of roles, this game has portions of role play i haven't yet gotten to experience even after more than 100 matches, and i expect nothing but more fun in the future for other sessions i play. This game is incredibly amazing, and even if you do not feel like spending money on the game, it is free to play online on your browser. Give it a shot, invite all your friends (you get an awesome grim reaper skin if you refer 5 friends), and you won't regret it.

All in all, it's a wonderful game with a lot of exploration and a universe that the player should explore if they want to experience all the game has to offer.

Oh boy, let me just start this "review" (If we can call it that) by warning you to stay away from the PC version of Burnout Paradise!
No, not because of its gameplay and/or visual quality (I owned this bad boy a few years ago on the X360 and it was indeed a fun ride), but because this game is the absolute definition of garbage on the PC!
...and why is that you might ask?
Well, where do I start?
First off, I cannot for the life of me start this game up by conventional means without it crashing instantly, and trust me, I'm not the only one experiencing similar problems, browse it on the internet if you must.
...but of course, such could be fixed easily, just give the game a try in "compatibility mode", and you should be good to go right? Wrong!
Running this bastar♥ in compatibility mode for "Windows XP Service Pack 3" (the recommended) or even going as far as adventuring your self in the ancient ruins of "Windows 95" will in fact boot you up past the start up screen, but good luck playing the game for about 10 or so minutes without it freezing dead on its tracks!
On top of it by running it in compatibility mode you can kiss your steam overlay tab good bye.
I didn't gave up though, upon some research, I discovered that many other things could cause the game to crash such as programs related to your Webcam, which you obviously shouldn't bother with if you don't have one, that is unless you happen to have "Dxtory" (which is kindda like good old "Fraps") installed, as for some odd reason "Dxtory" appears as a Webcam, and yes even if it's turned off it'll affect the game (I heard "XSplit" might cause the same symptoms as "Dxtory", but I'm not sure), uninstall it and see if it does the trick.
...but it could maybe even be related to your multi-core CPU, which if so, it could supposedly be fixed by doing as it follows...
- Right Click "Burnout Paradise" > Properties > Set Launch Options > (type in) -multithread (and press OK).
Of course, such didn't work for me either and sadly, as of now, I can only play the game 10 minutes at a time, on top of that, the game does not support classic "Window Mode", which might not seem like a big deal, but sometimes you might need to do such because reasons...
As a final verdict, do NOT waste your greens on the PC version of this game (unless you're still rocking little old Windows XP, wich I think might play Burnout Paradise withouth any problems, but I'm not sure of it), it's simply not worth it, have a good one.

Do you like grind ? You can have as much grind as you want.
You can grind wood, grind food, grind loot, grind plants, grind magic, and so on and so on.
This game starts and from the begining, when you is open to grind and goes with it. No quests, except grinding mobs and whatever you can decide. No grafic fidelity. No skill based dodging and combat. Ultimate grindfest.
So if you miss old days Linage II c1 you can have your grind here.
Is this a bad thing?
I think not. It's grind you see, but with clicker games expanding nowadays, this game stand it's ground. Yep it is essentially numbers grindfest, but it is more complex, than clickers. If you want to mine lets say iron, and not cooper - you need to find a way to do it, passing through or killing mobs. You have inside game wiki, that shows drop rates and all item stats, and you quickly start to understand that 0.25% chance of drop is pretty high. And the best thing that game is very rewarding and funny, when you start to grasp its mechanics.
Let me give you some examples.
As an mmo this game have a pet system. Do you know fastest way to get pet here? Grind and buy? Grow from cheap pet? No. Buy 10 ham, take a hammer, go to anville and bash ham into a piglet. With 1% you will succeed. 1% is a very high chance for this game. And ham is cheap.
There is heaven and hell, and ancient dungeons.
To go to heaven and kill some angels you will need wings.
Do you know fastest way to get wings ? 0.25% chase drop from some fairly weak mobs. But they will not let you go to heaven. To get to heaven you need to grind some lvl 1 chickens to get 8 feathers (drop chance 0.25%), and then craft wings of path with 50% chance.
This game have high imagination involvement. Just imagine how badass will you feel, when you go to heaven, kill a lot of angels and archangels, adopt some smaller angels and rise them as your "pets", then go to hell and do the same thing with demons, then breed angels and demons to get some awesome genetic modified pets with some cool wings, and then freaking rip their wings off to wear them yourself.
Potentially you can kill, raise and breed dragons, you can kill titans, demons, angels, and death itself, you can do whatever hell you want and feel total badass.
Plus this thing works on mobile devices and tablets as far as I know.
Conclusion.
Is this a game you will enjoy? Depends on how well can you setup and follow your own goals, and how persistent you are, until you get there. If you want story driven experience, and "everything on a plate" this is not a game for you. If you can google, use wiki, analise drop chances and best grind roots, optimising loss/profit balance (or you wish to learn it) - you will like it a lot.
