CONSORTIUM is without a doubt one of the most unique experiences I've had in my years as a PC gamer. With elements of Mass Effect, Assassin's Creed, and Deus Ex thrown in to a weird-filtered, post-state one world government blender and given a good whirl, it is certainly a beast of its own. Combat is fun if a mite simple, but thats not where the depth of this experience is. This is a game that respects your free will. Make the choice to kill, to spare, to enrage, to befriend, to say nothing at all. Everything is valid and have consequences that make sense. Characters are likable or believable. Backstory is provided in veritable heaps if you care to read it. This is a game for someone who wants to digest a world, not someone who wants to shoot a whole bunch of people. I imagine you could speed through this game in a quarter of the time it would take you if you took your time reading files and talking to the crew. If you want an action game I suggest you go elsewhere, but if you want a game that immerses you in it's story with good voice acting, extensive backstory, and player choice this may be right up your alley. Reccomended, and I look forward to future installments.
Note: I am aware of the issues others have run into regarding game breaking bugs. Having not witnessed them myself, I cannot speak to them, but Caveat Emptor.

Tales of Berseria is probably one of the best mothership title of the Tales of series. A huge improvement on gameplay since Tales of Zestiria (Goodbye weird camera angles!) and it is one of the rare to have a full song in the intro animation ( Burn by FLOW, a treat for your ears ).
Every protagonist are likeable in their own ways, the fact that Velvet is pretty much an anti-hero makes the thing even more interesting. The concept is cool, too!

Interesting concept and an enjoyable experience, especially as it is possible to test out a universe in just a couple of hours. Likely will draw you back to complete multiple times, BECAUSE it is so quick to do so.

One of those games where communication is key, actions can get repetitive and the effects can get jarring.  However, captains are motivated to communicate clearly with their crew and other ships, those repetitive actions can be honed and timed with tactical effect, and the effects add another element of depth that forces crews and captains to adapt strategies on-the-fly, making those tense moments where the ticket-tally flips at the last moment with a massive cathartic pay-off, so you can chase that catharsis into the next round and the next.
Early-acess at time of reviewing, but a game like this is long overdue.  It relies completely on a community that has exploded onto it with enthusiasm.  Get it while it's fun.  Ignore the dust under the rug.

Only one playthrough so far, but this eclipsed Tales of Symphonia to become my second favorite Tales game.  Had a bunch of fun beating the crap out enemies as Velvet.  If you like the Tales series, you should enjoy this one.

I had a hard time to decide if i should write a (as of now) negative review for this game.
First of all i really like the concept of the game as well as the background of it.
Sadly the execution is somewhat lackluster.
This sadly impacts the game on nearly every level.
In conversations you sometimes have options, which shouldnt be there (since you don´t know this things), something which should be taken care of in a so dialogue heavy game. Also on other times your options are limited to only go against one side, i´ve often missed a neutral way (and saying nothing is not the option i want).
Even more hurting is... the relations to the crew members are there.. but they don´t change anything, as far as this game is going.
Then we come to the graphics and UI... both are underwhelming to say the least... the Virtual training enviroment hurts the eyes, also the normal game graphic looks in some ways like a ten year old game.. with the shooter part, they included in this game, this really hurts a bit. Also the action itself is very limited and basic.. no cover, only very basic healing and due to the basic graphics a very rudimentary gameplay in general, add to this an extremely clunky inventory as well as a heavy set move control, which likes to keeps hanging on the many small doorways - all this makes the game a not so great experience.
Furthermore it naturally has many bugs (some of which are game breaking.. at least two which i had in the last part) and a very short and abrupt ending (it ends, when it is just really beginning). This game seems really like an intro, which is supported by the many things you can´t even use as of now (and that you get some advanced equipment, just before the game ends).
So to conclude this, the story/setting is - as i said in the beginning - something new and innovative, though it surely won´t be for everyone, as some of the conversations (with the King for example) are kind of odd. And i really would have liked to enjoy the game, but in the actual state it´s more annoying than enjoyable.

Bastion is an action role-playing game where you take control of "the Kid" as he tries to discover what caused the catastrophic event that starts the game off.
The gameplay consists of using two selected weapons from a varied arsenal. This naturally creates a plethora of playing styles and strategies to explore. As you progress through the game, you unlock more game systems: from various challenging effects that make the game harder and reward you with more experience, over a forge that lets you upgrade your weapons to various boons in form of a distillery and plenty more. Enemies come in only few forms, which is one of the few weaknesses of the game, but this is compensated for by placing them in carefully planned combinations and strategical positions which make for fun and engaging combat.
The game is set in an intriguing and dismally empty world that is depicted in a beautiful, vibrant hand drawn art style. Often times you can't help but just be in awe of the artistic talent on display. Another great strength is the exceptional soundtrack that always creates a seemingly perfect atmosphere. This is accompanied by a similarly impressive narrator, who delivers the story in a captivating one-of-a-kind fashion. The story is interesting and keeps you moving forward, exploring the often times troubling pasts of your companions. This all culminates in what is one single awe inspiring scene that on its own makes the game worth playing.
The short length of the game might be seen as a weakness, but one could argue that it benefits the game more than it hurts it, as it allows the story to flow at an appropriate pace without the gameplay becoming repetitive.
This game shows very clearly how much love and passion the developers put into it and I can't help but feel respect for them.

Summary: Beautiful music and art but can't zoom in; story not extremely original but well done; floating maps are interesting but easy to fall off of; customizable controls, gameplay styles, and loadouts; minigames and side missions for loot and money; using idols changes play difficulty.
------
1) Art. Basically what first drew me into the game. Even though the drawing style is "kiddish" with brightly colored maps and big-headed characters (I think it's easier to animate and stay visible on the map), the art is digitally painted SO beautifully. In fact, I wishlisted this game immediately upon browsing the selection of profile wallpapers available from crafting the steam badge. The isometric map design imposes permanent bird's eye view which cannot be rotated. It's a real shame that the you cannot zoom the camera in and out of maps besides the Bastion, but you get used to it.
2) Music. Amazing soundtrack which greatly enhances the atmosphere of the game and your immersion into its world. When Zia's theme first played, I was taken aback by how perfect the moment was that I stopped walking around and simply listened.
3) Story. Looking back at the concept of the "Calamity," I realized that it's not particularly innovative or original, but it is successful in the way that the backstory is slowly revealed and keeps you wondering for more information. That also opens itself to fitting with the fantasy steampunk theme. At the end, there are choices that you make based on opposing moral values. That said, there are also serious themes in the story which contrast with the bright colors and cute art style. There's death and the loss of loved ones, but the biggest overarching question is whether the ends justify the means: How comfortable are you, The Kid, with sacrificing the lives of others in order to secure your own survival?
3a) Rucks narrates the game while you play as The Kid in a deep voice that's as smooth as BUTTER. He provides much of the backstory to the game and its characters. It's actually helpful sometimes because he alerts you to incoming enemies or a part in the map that will kill you.
3b) So many little quirky details made me smile. Most notably, The Kid always soars through the air and invariably lands on his face. Rucks also says the darndest things. The first time I died, he said something like, "And then The Kid falls to his death. Nah I'm just foolin'." You hear "Kid just rages for a while" if you destroy objects in the beginning. When Rucks tells you about The Kid's tutor: She "taught Kid some good manners. “Never used 'em though."
4) Gameplay. You travel between your home, the Bastion, and other areas of the globe via Skyway. Your goal is to collect items to restore the Bastion, but exploration of the map is encouraged in order to get loot, fulfill a particular side mission, collect upgrades for weapons, and domesticate pets for an achievement. On each map, the pathway is built out as you walk near the end of it. Maps are designed to float in the air, which is a blessing and a curse: It's easy to fall off, but you can push enemies into the abyss.

4a) Controls are simple and easily reconfigurable. There is an option to move using keyboard (WASD), mouse (kind of like playing League of Legends), or controller. Controller support is xbox only, but using a 3rd party program on PC to get my PS3 controller recognized as such did the trick. Playing with the analog stick felt more intuitive for me.
4b) Fighting style is hack and slash.  You can rambo, defend, camp, hide in a corner and snipe; whatever your play style is. Countering is rewarding in reflecting damage, but not necessary.
4d) Various weapons, skills, and alcohols, which give passive bonuses, make for a myriad of loadout combinations. Upgrading weapons is easy if you loot alot, and it also allows for customization because there are two choices on the left and right per tier unlocked.
4c) There are different types of side missions. You can go to Proving Grounds, where you use a specific weapon to complete a goal under certain conditions and are rewarded with upgrade materials. Other challenges, which you earn money from completing, are like mini-achievements. Battling waves of enemies in the 3 "Who Knows Where" maps, also known as The Kid's Dream, The Singer's Dream, and The Survivor's Dream, nets you money. (P.S. I found the context for getting to these Dreams hilarious--The Kid basically gets high in the first one and food comas for the second. P.P.S This is where you learn character backstories.)
4d) Idols can be invoked in order to increase the difficulty of the game since they buff enemies. Each idol invoked adds +5% to experience and money earned.

While they are both amazing games, and both equally worthy of praise, this review is all about Bastion. If Bastion and Transistor are anything to go off of, then we can expect great things in the future from this developer!
Bastion puts you in the role of the Kid, as he fights to uncover the secrets of "the Calamity", an earthshattering catastrophe that leaves the world in pieces. Bastion redefines storytelling, with reactive narration and superb voiceover work - simply playing the game and listening to the narrator is a joy in and of itself. The game also features a critically-acclaimed soundtrack, which is available for purchase along with the game.
The controls are extremely easy to use and get used to. Bastion features the typical but tried-and-true method of using the WASD keys for movement commonly found in many game, along with point and click input for combat. The direction you move the cursor is the direction the Kid will attack when you click. Left clicking uses your main weapon, which is more often than not a melee weapon, such as a hammer or machete; while right clicking is generally a ranged weapon, such as a bow or gun. Holding down either mouse button for a brief period unleashes a charge attack, dealing more damage than usual. Spacebar causes the Kid to roll in the direction of your cursor, allowing you to dodge most attacks. Some enemies have the ability to knock you into the air, at which point you have the opportunity to perform an air recovery by hitting the Spacebar.
There are many varied, handpainted environments, each crawling with savage creatures hell-bent on putting an end to your arduous journey. At your disposal is an array of different weapons and abilities, which are all upgradeable as the player progresses through the game. Also available is an assortment of Spirits, which grant various passive bonuses, such as an increase in Max HP, or increased critical hit chance. The game also has a New Game Plus mode, where you can replay the story carrying over all the items from your previous playthrough.
From an enthralling story told through superb narrative, to lush, detailed environments and deadly enemies, Bastion has everything you could want from an indie RPG. It's definitely worth adding to any game collection. It's the kind of game that will turn anyone into a gamer.

Don't let the nerd rage hate put you off from PA:Titans.
This game is a stand-alone expansion, much like Forged Alliance, Brood War, Frozen Thrones, or Heart of the Swarm/Legacy of the Void. Apparently if anyone else does that is is completely acceptable, but not Uber, no way. They shouldn't expect any more for their work, nope, not at all!
PA:Titans expands on, what despite other people might say, an already solid game. Planetary Annihilation throws you into a universe in turmoil, torn apart by great machines of war, reawakening to bring about destruction once again. The game has one faction, the robots, all these units are the epitome of perfection. Each unit has been honed through years of war, why use anything other than the best? This allows for balanced gameplay without worrying about which faction is the "best". Unlike most RTS games you fight on a spherical planet, this can be challenging for new players at first, especially those who are new to RTS games in general. With this brings a host of new choices and challenges in regards to taking and holding a position. You might think that front line wall is secure, but watch your back, or for a sneak attack from bots emerging from the ocean floor! Taking it a step further is the fact that you get the chance to fight across more than one of these planets ranging from Earth like to, moons, volcanic, desert, ice, and ocean planets! You can even fight over orbital control of a gas giant! Then there is the almighty game ending metal planets which if brought online can blow up other planets with their giant lasers.
PA is a fast paced game. If you have extra resources, build more factories, if you have extra factories, secure more metal. You can never have enough of anything. More is better. More is always better!
Titans adds on new multi-tiered terrain features which allows for more interesting planets, which can be custom made in their planetary system editor. It also brings with it an expanded unit roster, adding 1 or more units to every factory in the game.
Then there are the Titans themselves and boy oh boy are they TITANIC! They are so large factories can't even build them, you must construct them with your fabricators as if they themselves were a structure, except that compared to a titan the buildings in this game are mere ants. There is a bot, vehicle, air, space, and planet titan each bring with them their own benefits and uses, but none of them are invincible. The bot titan is a giant mech that smashes the enemies to nothing, literally. The vehicle titan is a large armored hover tank mounted with large cannons that pack a punch and fire from a distance. The air titan rains down balls of electricy dealing splash damage the enemies below. The space titan can be linked to ground teleporters and beam units to the surface from orbit, this is a great new addition for breaking planetary defenses which stop games from dragging on into stalemates. Finally the planet titan is a structure that upon completetion begins a countdown to destroy the planet it was built on! Make sure your commander is safe and sound off planet should you choose to build this guy!
This game was new and risky. It required an engine builts specifically for it. They choose to do this game via Kickstarter to escape the deadlines and expectation set by a publisher and the trade off was giving fans access to an incomplete game built on new and experimental technoloy. Making a game is not easy, it takes time, and dedication. Uber has proven that they listen to the community (just hop on over to their forums!). Even after the release of this game they released countless bug fixes and patches. Even with the release of Titans PA:Vanilla gets the performance and balance patches, they haven't abandoned it. In the end Uber has done the best they can with what they've got and IMHO they have been doing a great job, despite the roudy crowd who feels like each individual is the publisher for Uber and thus deserves a bit more.

I didn't realize this game was free to play in browser until after i bought it, and to be honest I don't really care.  It's worth paying money for it because you get $5 worth of the in game currency, which is purely cosmetic, in addition to faster loading times, although even in the browser version the loading times aren't bad at all.  You also get to support the developers of this fantastic game.  So even though this game is available for free, I really suggest supporting the developers and buying it on Steam, but maybe try it out for free if you're not sure.
Now for the actual review.  I bought this game on a whim during the summer sale because it was cheap and had a pretty good approval rating.  I didn't really expect to play it that much, but now it has more hours logged than any of the other games I bought during that sale.  This game is super addicting, and I play a game of it almost every day.  The rounds are fairly short, and usually last 15-30 minutes.  If you just want a mindless game without a lot of thinking in it, or a game where you don't have to communicate with other people, then this game isn't for you.  This game requires that you work with other people and strategize, deceive, and often try and mess with their heads.  This does come with the downside of working with other people though, where there will be the occasional troll, and sometimes people can be fairly annoying, and offensive at times.  There is a chat filter to block out some of the stuff people might find offensive, however I have noticed there are some words it doesn't block out that it probably should.
Town of Salem is pretty easy to pick up, although there is a bit of a learning curve.  I was really confused my first few games, but I picked it up pretty quickly after that.  While it can be pretty easy to play this after a few games, it takes quite a while to learn enough to be really good at it.  You have to not only know about your own role, but you have to know about the other roles in the game as well.  Knowing whether a role is town protective or town support can help weed out who's lying and who's telling the truth.  I really recommend taking a look at the role list on
to get a bit more familiar with some of the roles.  There's also a bit of a learning curve in learning how to strategise and manipulate properly.  My second round in this game, I was the jester, which is a role where you want to be lynched my your fellow townspeople.  I claimed I was the serial killer on the first day, and it became really obvious that I was the jester.  You have to think a lot about ways to manipulate the other people into doing what you want.
This game is definitley not one that was created by the developers and then left to die.  This game was updated just recently, with a new role, the forger, and a bunch of new cosmetic stuff in the shop, as well as some bug fixes and a bit of a UI change.  The developers also have more stuff they are planning for Town of Salem, so dont' worry about never getting anything new with this game, because the developers have shown they actually care about this game.
I could go into so much more detail with this game, it has so much depth and I've never played two games that went the same.  I could talk about the pros and cons of each role and how they work, but this review is already too long, so I'll let you play the game yourself and figure it out, which really is one of the best parts of this game.  I cannot recommend this game enough, everyone should at least give it a chance, especially because you can play it for free.
Pros:
+Addicting
+Lots of depth
+You can try it for free
+Easy to play, difficult to master
+No two games are the same
+Short rounds
+Lots of strategy and thinking
+Dozens if not hundreds of hours of gameplay
Cons:
-People can be annoying
-Confusing at first
The pros definitley outweigh the cons for Town of Salem, and I really cannot recommend this game enough.  It's a brilliant and unique game that anyone can play  and enjoy.
Edit: I previously had the reporting system listed as a con, however since then the reporting system has been significantly improved, allowing you to select an actual reason for reporting them and list comments.  In addition, the chat filter, while still not perfect, has become considerably more humerous, switching out offensive words with words like flummery and tarnation.  It automatically replaces "You Suck" or "X Sucks" with "You are a great player" or "X is a great player," which is always funny.

After nearly 1300 hours of playtime on this game I wanna tell you my honest opinions/thoughts on it.
Positives:
+ It's free
+ It's kinda like Minecraft, but with more RPG Elements.
+ A bunch of classes to choose from, you will probably find one you like.
+ Decent amount of customization options for the classes.
+ Alot of players, customizable club worlds and special chats for nearly everything.
+ Tons and tons of collectibles.
+ Alot of movement options, like Mounts, Wings, Dragons, Boats and Rail Karts.
+ Offers RPG elements, PVP elements, Arena Elements and Building/Crafting Elements.
+ The Endgame feels very rewarding once you get everything you wanted/needed.
+ Updates are coming every 3-4 weeks with more stuff and quests to do.
Negatives:
- It is really hard to get into the game if you are a new player without any experienced/ high-level friends.
- You are going to have a hard time making progress in this game without spending at least some money.
- The Game can feel really 'Pay-to-win'-ish sometimes (They are already trying to fix that tho).
- The Gem System is way too random while being pretty much the main focus of the (End)game.
- The game is more about grinding Gems and Gem Dust than anything else.
- The servers are not optimized. Expect alot of lag and even disconnects.
- The last few updates made a bunch of items untradable, disrupting the flow of the ingame marketplace.
I can recommend this game to all players that have either alot of time on their hands or a bunch of friends to play with.
The game is fun, looks nice and has a huge community.
It offers alot of options for creative players, adventurers and all you hardcore grinders.
But it is a game that you have to put quite alot of time into to make any progress.
But be warned; The game is FAR from flawless.
That's my review for the game Trove.

I played around 3 hours as of the writing of this review, and any of those who know me on the game, I am Nightcaper. I was skeptical of the positive reviews, and decided to see for myself; What did I have to lose? RPG MO would not be the first Runescape-like browser MMO, there's also RPG Reborn, and a couple others I cannot name off the top of my head, one of them being for Macs specifically. I've been on a long search for an MMO that could hope to capture what was so awesome about Runescape, while taking out some of the tedium. RPG MO is a 2d isometric MMORPG that has, as of this writing, 15 skills that you can level without limit; That's right, NO level cap! The world looks very nice, the community is pretty casual and laid back, and for those who knew Runescape's community long back, they would know how toxic it was. RPG MO has one of the more friendlier communities I've seen. RPG MO is free to play, and I should say that it does actually offer a shop for you to buy "MOS" with real money or Steam Wallet cash. Note this however: To my knowledge, anything you can get there, you can also craft. RPG MO is the furthest a browser MMO with a real currency shop can get from pay to win, as it forces you to still do the work to get anywhere, and in the end your work is the deciding factor of progress in the game, not MOS.
On the particular day I started playing, which is the day I am writing this review, people were chipping in double XP potions, which aren't exactly cheap to get, from the currency shop. When one person uses such a potion, EVERYONE gets double XP for the duration of the potion (30 minutes per potion?) This makes leveling skills notably much faster, for everybody, and people always give thanks for the double XP. I feel this shows how connected the community is, as a lot of things on that store are less than those potions and can serve you personally much better, yet they chose something that would benefit everyone involved.
I decided that this was a game and community I wanted to be a part of, and following the Double XP spree (which was 2+ hours), I added in a few of my own before taking my leave to write this review. Play this game, try it and see for yourself. It's fun, skill grinding won't utterly kill your interest as it's pretty fair overall... and remember to thank those who give 2x experience!

One of the best JRPG i've played! Great story and characters, good gameplay, combat, the only thing this game lacking is probably the exploration.
Tales of Berseria takes place in an empire ruled the by the "Abbey", a holy organization that hunts daemons. Their soldiers, "Exorcist", are people who used the power of a spiritual beings called "Malakhim" by sealing their will, allow them to use magical power. Our main character is Velvet, a normal human with generic anime elder sister trope, that turned into a Daemon, and her main goal is to take revenge to the man that turned her into a daemon.
Pros:
- Storyline
This is a long game, just following the main story will take 20~30 hours of gameplay. The story doesn't give you a unpredictable plot twist or anything, but the dark turn of the storyline makes this game different with the usual JRPG.
- Characters
Each character have their own purpose instead just be "there" to fill character quota. Along the story progresses, there's actual change in characters' personality. And the voice actors are just perfect.
- Soundtrack
Memorable soundtracks, composed by Motoi Sakuraba (Dark Souls and older Tales games) and opening theme by FLOW.
So-so:
- Combat
The combat itself is pretty good, you might like it, or just "okay" with it. You'll see number of enemies on the field, you touch them, then turn into the battle screen, pretty much like most of JRPGs. It will take time to master the combat mechanic, it is quite simple to learn, but the number of skills and mechanics might overwhelms new players, especially if you never played another Tales games.
Con:
-Exploration
The exploration is a bit dull, there are nothing much to do on the open field execpt monsters, and the dungeons have a little variations to each other. Towns have a great and unique design, but it doesn't feel live, and the NPCs looks almost all the same in contrast to the uniquely designed main characters. Hidden treasure chests, herbs, and katz boxes (treasure chest for costume) makes up for it.

There is multiple ways of playing this game. very dynamic. the dialogue is well written and you can even say nothing at all to the NPCs. what you choose to say or do can drastically effect the way the NPCs react to you. its an interesting concept and if you are into story driven games I suggest you try it out.

I have 330 hours in this game as of now. And somehow I wish I hadn't. You would think Bethesda, with it's surprise announcement of the fallout 4 release date and everything they went on about "waiting so long" because they "wanted to get it right" and not make the "mistakes other developers" were making would publish this amazing, new fallout, right? Because FNV and F3 were these incredibly immersive open world RPGs, right (although the combat system and the weapon repairing was a total drag)? But no.
I love some of the things they've done here. The graphics are great (and although I get why people are annoyed with the crappy hair choices it doesn't bother me one bit). The fighting system is nice, a lot crisper than the previous games. There are some great stories to unravel and small, humorous things to find in this wasteland - much like with the previous games.  And the weapon modifications introduced in FNV got a nice expansion, although it quickly feels repetetive. But the comparison kind of stops there - and I dont really know where to begin on the things that bother me: dialogue options that have no consequences 98% of the time (in a f*****g RPG)? Pistols that outrange sniper rifles in accuracy and damage? The mostly shallow character design of your companions where you basically just do drugs or pick locks or are nice to people and they suddenly give you a perk that is sometimes awesome and sometimes really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ (looking at you, Codsworth)? The main story line that in 330 hours worth of game play never got me interested so i never even finished the game once?
And then there's just this FUBAR history of the DLCs, their pricing and the CC. I got the Season Pass before it's price went up. That price was OK-ish for what you got in DLCs. However except for Far Harbor and in parts Nuka World and Automatron, nothing included there was anything worthy of even this reduced price. And Bethesda even raised that to heaven and beyond. Five bucks a pop for some new wall texture and a feature or two that should have been in the game originally? No, thank you. That's exactly the mistakes those "other developers" were making when you announced F4s release. And then there's these amazing lore inconsistencies - as in stuff that should be in f4 but isn't - or wouldn't be, if it weren't for community mods.
Seriously, community-made, free mods, are what make this game playeable and enjoyable (my played hours are more a testament to the modding community than anything else) - by providing necessary balance overhauls, bug fixes, a proper building system and adding items from the Fallout games to this one that should have been included in the first place. And now we get CC. Which is basically a skin-adding-feature for making even more loads of cash for Bethesda - and a little bit of extra money on the side for some community developers. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy skins. And games that finance themselves through skins. Except I didn't already pay 80 Euros for those games I can buy skins in and the game developers are actually the ones providing the content.
If you could get this game with all "DLC" and CC content for 30-35 Euros-Dollars I'd say it's a fair price for how long it's been about by now. But as it stands, this is a game from an incredible game series, with a great engine, some good ideas and♥♥♥♥♥♥poor execution of all of those and not worth any of you still shoving money down Bethesda's throat. There's just so many games out there where you'll get more "bang for your buck" than with this. I have reverted to playing New Vegas again. It's terribly buggy, the graphics and the fighting system suck most of the time, but at least it's immersive as heck and still a better Fallout than 4.

Close to 800 hours (and two playthroughs) into the game, I can say that I love the game but dispise the company that made it.
The Good: It's a breathtaking new edition in the series and gives a fresh new take on the game. With just as much time in here as I have with Fallout 3 and New Vegas, I can say it continues the story of post-war life in a fantastic way. Free mods take what Bethesda did to a whole new level, almost as far as what New Vegas became. Knowing to go to Nexus Mods is essential to getting the most out of the game.
The Bad: If you've played any of Bethesda's other "open world" games (Oblivion, Skyrim, Fallout 3/NV) know that there are bugs and crashes. The more modded up your game is, the worse it gets. That's the only major issue I have with the game and the trade-off of stability for new content is well worth it.  The only other thing that bears mention is that since the player character has voiceover (not just text) your choices in the game are severly limited over previous Bethesda titles.  I enjoyed hearing the player speak for a change, but this puts the breaks on what mods can do with new quests.
The Ugly: As the game now has been out for a while, Bethesda continues to try to push "Paid Mods" into the game. The catch is the way they've implemented this is lame at best and a PR nightmare at worst. If you google "fallout 4 creation club fiasco" you'll see why there is a rash of negative reviews, a lot of them are justly deserved.  Mods on the Nexus are better than what's in the Creation Club, and they're free to boot.  The other issue is that they're pushing "Creation Club Credits" instead of using actual currency in the game, forcing you to spend more on credits than if they just charged a flat price for the content.  They should have learned from how Microsoft used to use Microsoft Points for currency on Xbox, this type of payment scheme sucks.  The one shining point here is that the Creation Club can be ignored, it's not essential to the game at all.  If it really grinds your gears, there are mods on the Nexus to remove the interface completely from the game.
The Bottom Line: Fallout 4 is a fantastic game that's marred by Bethesda's ham-handed attempt to monitize additional content for the title.  The recent negative reviews are 100% driven by the public relations disaster of it's rollout, how they treat the authors of their paid content and not the game itself.  I still recommend it, but don't be fooled into the Creation Club.... Learn about the Nexus and you'll have a better trip through the wasteland because of it.

While Sanctum 2 is a good game, I think the original is better. If you enjoyed the original, the sequel is worth playing. But if youre new to Sanctum, start with the first game, especially if you plan to play alone. There have been several changes to gameplay mechanics, a couple of which are improvements. Some enemies will attack the player instead of just running to the core, and bosses can destroy towers. If you cant afford to fully upgrade a tower you can partially upgrade for a small stat boost. But other changes are restrictive. You can only build 15 towers per map. There are no mid game checkpoints - fail and its back to wave 1. Loadouts are smaller (2 weapons and 4 towers compared to 3 and 6 previously) which means that you cant fully appreciate the tactical depth unless you play with a coop partner who brings different gear. A new range of perks have been added, but the ability to upgrade guns has been removed, and many weapons/towers/perks are locked until you grind enough XP.

Most MMOs have a very generic setup, but Realm of the Mad God manages to mix Rogue Legacy with an arcade style free roaming RPG. It is very simple to play and brings in even newcomers to the MMO genre without throwing too many techicalities in their faces to deal with.
The large selection of classes, many of which are unlockable are nicely built. Each is special in a certain way, and mastering one will certainly unlock another for you to try. The permanent death mechanic adds a feeling of tension, and a good touch of realism. That said, the game has a chaotic fun factor. You roam about either by yourself or with a party blasting at everything in sight, gaining experience and finding loot. Everything that this game stands to be is accomplished very well.
However, I have a few gripes.
-Firstly, I don't have a problem with classes like the Wizard having projectile attacks, but those like the Knight don't feel right. Having these kinds of classes have a melee attack would make them sit much better with me. After all, Knights and Warriors typically slash with their weapons, not toss them into their enemies faces.
-Secondly, the coin system and the ability to purchase premium items with them seems counterproductive, as you will surely lose them if you were to die. I suppose this is what the vault system is for, but I'd rather use that sword I just bought rather than lock it away forever for fear that I will lose it. Instead, a lineage system could be added where the weapons of the ancestor are given to the newest member of the bloodline as long as they are able to hold the weapons (like if a Wizard dies, he can pass on his weapons to another Wizard, or another Staff user like the Necromancer).
-Thirdly, talking about the currency again, it completely ruins the collectability aspect of the game. The worst example of this the 'unlockable' skins. The game lulls you into thinking that if you reach a certain level, you unlock it. Nope! You have to buy it too! What?! Why?!
-Fourthly, the method of joining friends is incredibly disappointing. You can join the same server, and teleport to people (with some difficulty), but what if I want to go right to where my friend is, like in a dungeon? Can't do that in this game apparently. This is especially aggravating because I want to be able to play this with friends, but I really can't because the whole system is set up poorly. Not everyone wants to lone-wolf in an MMO and a lot of classes are supportive anyway, so it almost encourages you to use a playstyle that isn't there.
If these issues are addressed, I could raise my rating, but for now, Realm of the Mad God is very good, but it isn't phenomenal just yet. The key word there is 'yet', implying that it could be if the developers put enough effort into making it amazing.

I bought this in a Humble Bundle pack about a year ago and just let it sit idle on my account, never even installed it.  When I saw my Game Database say I had 53% of my games never played I decided to start playing, and Bastion was the first one
Basically the world has been destroyed by the "Calamity" and its up to you to go through the game collecting Cores and -spoilers-, new enemies are gradually introduced during gameplay and new weapons(that can be upgraded at the Forge) are picked up here and there, providing new types of gameplay periodically.  Theres a few other areas in Bastion, the Distillery, where you can be given one of many perks depending on what level you are, the armory which allows you to change your primary and secondary weapons and your secret skill, a memorial that gives you a bunch of rewards for accomplishing various tasks throughout the game, a shrine where you can invoke the power of the gods(makes enemies harder but gives you cash and xp bonuses, theres 10-12 different statues you can activate, each doing something different), and a lost and found that will have new things you can buy occasionally to upgrade your weapons/skills or the Bastion with.

Planetary Annihilation is the latest in a family of fantastic games (except for that weird nephew who nobody likes to talk about; I'm looking at you Supreme Commander II).
I really REALLY want to like this game, I want to love it, I want it to be what Total Annihilation was, with all the good bits from Supreme Commander added in, along with some cool new stuff all it's own. Unfortunately, it just wasn't meant to be.
While it has some really cool features, like slamming asteroids into planets with massive, world-shattering explosions, or just vaporising planets with your very own Death Star, all that shiny goodness is not enough to make up for what it lacks in gameplay.
The maps are boring, and terrain features make little to no difference to your tactics. You might as well be fighting on the surface of a billiard ball. The economy, while similar to TA and SC, somehow doesn't play quite the same way, meaning that the carefull resource management that was needed in Supreme Commander is not much of a factor anymore.
Combine that with small maps that are also wrap-around, means that if you prefer to play turtle you are shooting yourself in the foot. Rushing is the only viable option, since defending your ever expanding base on all sides is all but impossible, especially since terrain features hardly offer any bottlenecks that you can use.
I love blowing up planets, I love the way the game looks, but I hate that it lacks the depth, size, and scope that TA and SC had. Battles do not feel epic because the battlefields are so small and fights are over in seconds.
As an RTS, Planetary Annihiliation is a good, perhaps even a great game. As a descendant of its ancestors, it is merely so-so. So buy it if you are looking for an RTS with inovative features and quick combat. Do not buy if you are hoping to recaputre the glory of Total Annihilation and Supreme Commander.

***Very Possible Minor Spoilers***
This review will cover what I think are the most important aspects of the game. If you feel like Tl;dr then here is the basic rundown. Get the game. Be sure to remember that this is only one part of a planned trilogy. So buy it with that in mind. Wait till discount if you must (I did). The gameplay and music is superb. The aesthetic is excellent if a bit unpolished and over the top. The story and writing is a bit generic and over the top at times but it will make you smile at points. Its short but sweet and it has a lot of heart. Overall, would recommend.
Pros:
- The music is great! You can't go wrong with Jake Kaufman. He balances the demands of a retro sound with a Western feel superbly.
- The gameplay is absolutely solid. It is essentially a variation of the active time battle but instead of waiting for the character's turn you are waiting for their moves to charge. The same can be said for the enemies. This requires you to plan and strategise during battle as you have to not only decide what moves to do but to also anticipate what the enemy is going to do. The gameplay also borrows an aspect from games like Earthbound and Lufia 2 in that there are no random battles. Instead you encounter enemy sprites in the overworld and you enter a battle with them if you touch them. This gives you a chance to avoid battles entirely if need be. There is also a degree of customisability in the gameplay. You learn moves using hats in the same way that you would learn moves by being in different classes such as in the case of the Final Fantasy games. So you get to pick and choose what moves to bring to a fight as you are only allowed to use a max of four. Additionally, you can imbue your weapons permanently to inflict a variety of status ailments to enemies. However, different weapons have different amounts of slots to fill with imbuements so you have to choose wisely.
- The aesthetic has a retro feel to it (especially in reference to Earthbound or Mother 2). While I personally think its pretty decent as it has its own unique Western charm, I do feel that it requires a bit more polish, eg some enemy sprites just look janky. The character design however is generally pretty decent especially in regards to the Saints-Little Gang despite some of the characters being very over the top. Also every character, including the NPCs, are unique. They even have unique looks and names. A lot of heart has gone into this aspect of the game.
Cons:
- They should have made it more explicit that this was the first part of a planned trilogy. While they do mention this in the description, it is highly misleading to not include something along the lines of "part 1" or "episode 1" as part of the title. This admittely a minor point, at least in my opinion, as I still think its worth the price although I would still recommend getting it when its discounted (I did).
- The game is pretty damn short bearing in mind that I've finished the game and completed all the additional content, including the DLC. What do you expect for the first part of a trilogy? Seriously though I was completely blue balled that it ended when it did. I had just gotten the whole party together and the game ended. Overall though its still very enjoyable for its length.
- The story and writing is ok if generic but they serve their purpose. A lot of the characters were downright silly and cheesy, like Blaze and Templeton Howl. Of course, this being a Spaghettti Western kind of I can of thing I can sort of forgive some of this as it is meant to be over the top I assume. There were no positives. Some of the dialogue made me smile and the mystique they built around the original Boot Hill Posse and the Saints-Little Gang was dealt with well I think. Also Doc while at first seemed like a Clint Eastwood man with no name rip-off (I mean come on he even looks like him) actually ended up being the most interesting character for me by the end of the game. *Minor spoiler* We learn what he was before in the old Boot Hill Posse, a doctor, and that he had a connection and possible grudge against one of the Saints Brothers. *Minor spoiler end* This created a pretty interesting dichotemy to his character and instantly made it so that he was the least two dimensional character in the game, of which there were many, at least in my opinion.

I didn't realize this game was free to play in browser until after i bought it, and to be honest I don't really care.  It's worth paying money for it because you get $5 worth of the in game currency, which is purely cosmetic, in addition to faster loading times, although even in the browser version the loading times aren't bad at all.  You also get to support the developers of this fantastic game.  So even though this game is available for free, I really suggest supporting the developers and buying it on Steam, but maybe try it out for free if you're not sure.
Now for the actual review.  I bought this game on a whim during the summer sale because it was cheap and had a pretty good approval rating.  I didn't really expect to play it that much, but now it has more hours logged than any of the other games I bought during that sale.  This game is super addicting, and I play a game of it almost every day.  The rounds are fairly short, and usually last 15-30 minutes.  If you just want a mindless game without a lot of thinking in it, or a game where you don't have to communicate with other people, then this game isn't for you.  This game requires that you work with other people and strategize, deceive, and often try and mess with their heads.  This does come with the downside of working with other people though, where there will be the occasional troll, and sometimes people can be fairly annoying, and offensive at times.  There is a chat filter to block out some of the stuff people might find offensive, however I have noticed there are some words it doesn't block out that it probably should.
Town of Salem is pretty easy to pick up, although there is a bit of a learning curve.  I was really confused my first few games, but I picked it up pretty quickly after that.  While it can be pretty easy to play this after a few games, it takes quite a while to learn enough to be really good at it.  You have to not only know about your own role, but you have to know about the other roles in the game as well.  Knowing whether a role is town protective or town support can help weed out who's lying and who's telling the truth.  I really recommend taking a look at the role list on
to get a bit more familiar with some of the roles.  There's also a bit of a learning curve in learning how to strategise and manipulate properly.  My second round in this game, I was the jester, which is a role where you want to be lynched my your fellow townspeople.  I claimed I was the serial killer on the first day, and it became really obvious that I was the jester.  You have to think a lot about ways to manipulate the other people into doing what you want.
This game is definitley not one that was created by the developers and then left to die.  This game was updated just recently, with a new role, the forger, and a bunch of new cosmetic stuff in the shop, as well as some bug fixes and a bit of a UI change.  The developers also have more stuff they are planning for Town of Salem, so dont' worry about never getting anything new with this game, because the developers have shown they actually care about this game.
I could go into so much more detail with this game, it has so much depth and I've never played two games that went the same.  I could talk about the pros and cons of each role and how they work, but this review is already too long, so I'll let you play the game yourself and figure it out, which really is one of the best parts of this game.  I cannot recommend this game enough, everyone should at least give it a chance, especially because you can play it for free.
Pros:
+Addicting
+Lots of depth
+You can try it for free
+Easy to play, difficult to master
+No two games are the same
+Short rounds
+Lots of strategy and thinking
+Dozens if not hundreds of hours of gameplay
Cons:
-People can be annoying
-Confusing at first
The pros definitley outweigh the cons for Town of Salem, and I really cannot recommend this game enough.  It's a brilliant and unique game that anyone can play  and enjoy.
Edit: I previously had the reporting system listed as a con, however since then the reporting system has been significantly improved, allowing you to select an actual reason for reporting them and list comments.  In addition, the chat filter, while still not perfect, has become considerably more humerous, switching out offensive words with words like flummery and tarnation.  It automatically replaces "You Suck" or "X Sucks" with "You are a great player" or "X is a great player," which is always funny.

Wizorb is a pretty solid game. I recommend it if incredible sprites and artwork will carry you through a very difficult game. I cannot recommend it, however, if you're looking for a casual puzzle game. Or even a difficult puzzle game. Due to a number of strange design choices, the game is a gauntlet of very frustrating puzzles that you will either embrace or hate.
In this breakout clone, you use your "wand" to bounce orbs around the stage to break blocks and damage enemies. Using your limited magic meter which can be refilled by potion powerups, you can perform the expected maneuvers: shoot a fireball from your cursor and break a block, fire a beefed up orb that will break multiple blocks, control the direction of your orb by moving the mouse, and so on.
Again, the graphics are stunning. The animation is smooth and buttery, from the monsters you'll encounter to the charming and lively sprites you see when exploring town. The environments feel diverse and colorful. Sound design is good, though there are a few music tracks that are a little annoying. The castle music is particularly arythmic.
Wizorb is supposed to feel like a throwback and the difficulty is tuned to become more and more punishing, and on both accounts it definitely delivers. This game will make you feel like you've just shoved a grey cartridge into a game console and snatched up a controller with a d-pad.
Your progression is measured by an overworld map, also beautifully presented. And that's about all the progression you'll enjoy. You can throw your money at a ruined town and watch it rebuild, but the rewards they give you are absolutely paltry. Powerups that you can purchase from shops only last until you lose a life. This raises the stakes for every encounter--if you slip up, you definitely feel the loss. For beating the grueling dungeon challenges, there is really nothing by way of a reward to help you adapt to the next challenge. I wish there was some way of getting even small perks--Increase your magic meter, make your orb permanitely hit harder, unlock new abilities. You get nothing to help you along as the difficulty ramps up. It's the same gameplay from dungeon to dungeon.
An even more baffling choice is that every dungeon sells the same powerups in its shop. You can only get the multiball powerup in some areas, and the "longer wand" powerup ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) is only available in others. This consistency makes the game far less enjoyable to replay. There's no randomness, and the only clever powerup combos available are the ones the game maker decided to provide.
I don't understand the decision to turn the game into a series of gauntlets. When you begin a dungeon, you'll need to beat 10 or more stages consecutively. If you run out of lives, you are allowed 3 "continues" which gives you a healthy safety net to complete even the most difficult missions, if you can muster the patience to do the failed level over again. You cannot save your progress or quit between levels. The result is that Wizorb feels like a challenge of willpower. This cranks up the intensity, but there is so much of a time investment in each dungeon run that failure is absolutely crushing. Combine this with mechanics that are designed to frustrate and it's a tough game to recommend, and an even more daunting challenge to beat.
Having played lots of Breakout clones, the first problem I encountered was that the cursor feels different. The orb does not bounce off the cursor the way I expect it to; it never occurred to me that most Breakout clones are consistent about the angles at which the ball bounces off your cursor, and this game breaks my expectation of the genre. Another baffling decision is that you cannot remap the keybindings. You can control the cursor with WASD, the arrows keys, or your mouse. Left and right click activate your abilities. If you want to use the kayboard, your abilities are on J and K. Why J and K? I have no idea. Maybe the controls make more sense on a gamepad.
I can forgive the game for having its own style, though I was often frustrated by how little control I seemed to have in fine-tuning my shots. In the later levels, you routinely need to bounce an orb into a one block wide gap. The problem here is that the game does not allow you to hit the ball in a straight line. Even when you hit it dead center in the middle of your wand, it always deviates slightly left or right. This means that sometimes it is impossible to land an orb in a particular spot from an angle where it seems like you'd be able to. Now try to get the orb into a one-wide gap while the ball is moving at top speed. Whether or not it goes in is at that point a matter of blind luck because the ball does not travel in a straight path.
Keeping every movement of the orb strictly angled is the game's method of eliminating infinite loops. If the ball always moves at an angle, it will never get stuck forever (it can get close, but it will eventually work itself out). However, as the game progresses and there are more unbreakable blocks on the board, it becomes increasingly common to get the orb stuck bouncing in a long, circuitious pattern. Plenty of breakout clones I've played have a "speed up" button for just this reason--instead of waiting it out, you can make things go faster. The absense of such a feature here makes some stages take an unbearably long time, especially when the orb gets stuck among unbreakable blocks or when there are only a few blocks left.
Some stages have colored rubies that change color every time they're hit with an orb. In order to break them, you need to turn them all the same color. I have no problem with it in theory--it's a challenge of marksmanship. Mess up, or hit the wrong block, or get a bad bounce, and you'll have to go for a different color match. Because the orb always travels at an angle, however, trying to hit one particular ruby while leaving the others alone can be nearly impossible. Depending on how the orb bounces before it hits your wand, it may be impossible to hit your target from the position you've chosen even if it's a straight shot.
Wizorb is not a bad game. It is very challenging, and it will satisfy players looking for a puzzle game that will truely test them. Because of some frustrating design choices that stretch out the game, however, I can't recommend it for someone who is looking for a light, consistently fun experience.
TLDR: Wizorb looks beautiful and delivers on its promise of old school atmosphere, but it will likely pose a difficult test of your fortitude and patience.

Burnout is my favorite racing franchise of all time, I've played the previous titles and loved them to bits. Quite literally. I was always astounded at how beautiful (ironically) crashes in the game can be. The crash physics are wonderful and smashing into cars in road rage is a very pleasant feeling to me. The cars in the game are for the most part, unique and handle differently. Some cars cannot turn fast, forcing you to use the handbrake at sharp corners, and there are some cars that slip and slide everywhere, making it easy to swerve into oncoming traffic, but can drift without issues at sharp turns. The drifting in this game feels amazing; especially when you're driving real fast in a race late in the game when you get the really fast cars.
There are 5 different race types in this game: Race, Road Rage, Stunt Run, Marked Man, and Burning Route all of which are special in their own way.
Races (AKA: Point A to Point B) always make you feel like you're going fast, and doing multiple burnout chains is satisfying. Stunt runs are what they are implied to be, just jump off ramps, boost, and drift to rack up points (these are my least favorite). Road Rage is basically a timed, fast paced demolition derby, and holy crap, it is awesome! Just wreck other drivers and reach the takedown score to win. Marked Man is a bit of a spin on Races and Road Rage. In Marked Man you have to race from point A to point B. The catch is there are drivers trying to prevent you from reaching your target by smashing your car, survive till the finish and you win. Burning Routes are probably the simplest to grasp, just make it to the finish in time and win an upgraded version of the car you're using.
The core game is fantastic in and of itself, however I think it would be best for everyone if I mention how well the online portion of the game is. Freeburn online is a very enjoyable experience
the host actually makes the experience fun for everybody. What I mean is when you're playing online the host can make events that everyone can participate in, and these while limited are very enjoyable when alot of players partcipate. Marked man online is so much more thrilling than offline in my opinion, especially when there are 7 players trying their best to take you down. There are loads of challenges that the players can particpate in, and the challenges change with the amount of players, so there's always something to do.
(As far as I know, you can't join a friend's server via steam, you have to it from in game, via the search option.)
The thing to watch out for is that this game does NOT come with all the DLC. "The Ultimate Box" just gives you access to
online
cars, that don't even have boost. It also gives you party mode, which is useless to anyone, unless they share the computer with a friend; it's kind of like pass the controller. A mode with bikes, which is completely seperated than the cars, they have their own races.
I heartily recommend Burnout Paradise to anyone who loves a good racing game, with great crash physics and a fun online mode.

As my name suggests, I enjoy brick breaker games. They are far and few on PC these days, which is why I have mixed feelings about this game. The fact Wizorb has a story and allows you to purchase items is really awesome. The game plays well enough, meaning it doesn't do anything to really advance the brick breaking genre. My biggest grip is the lack of information about what you're doing.
Maybe that sounds strange, but in this game you start a quest, then 10 levels of brick breaking later I'm wondering exactly what it was I was supposed to be doing. I was on a quesst, but now I'm stuck in endless brick breaking levels. If this is a story driven game, please include more story as motivation. If it's just a brick breaker, then don't give me a glimpse of story.
As far as the gameplay it's nothing new. The control of the paddle feels like it could use some tweaking. The ball movements are arbitrary. It would be nice to see the dev help us cheat by attracting the ball to the last 2 or 3 blocks as this game suffers the same fate of it's older brothers. There are times you are bouncing a ball and not hitting anything. Pill drops don't really explain themselves, which is a normal mechanic for these games, but it would be nice to have a little text telling me what does what. The magic mechanic is nice, but nothing to really write home about.
Honestly, in the end, this is a game that could have been a huge hit and perhaps even revived the brick breaker genre. But it's teadious gameplay, lack of solid story, and no innovative mechanics hold this game back. What we're left with is a mediocre game with just a glimpse of greatness.

To start:  I love this game.  But, it can be little rough at the moment.
I was a backer on this game during Kickstarter, I was very intrigued at the setting, art style, and gameplay premise.  It seemed to be a unique take and full of great new ideas.  In this respect the game did not dissapoint me.  The weighted crew interactions are very well done and I found the voice work to be pretty good.  The first core gameplay centers around conversations with crew members of the Zenlil, navigating dialog trees to increase or decrease approval with different crew members and opening up new lines of inquiry and knowledge.  The second is exploring the Zenlil craft and interacting with it, though in this game it is a bit limited by what the scripting allows.  Third is the FPS combat, and in my particular playthrough it took a backseat, though depending in your actions you could get a lot more.
The story and plot started off well and became more and more intrigueing as the game progressed.  It takes place in the future, where your psyche has taken possession of a soldier on the combat aircraft Zenlil of the international Consortium.  Your mind has been sent forward to this realm through a special satellite system presented as a game.  But is it really a game?  What are the true motives of those who control the system?  And what might happen if you try to test the limits of that control?  Play to find out.
The world of Consortium is surprisingly deep, and there is an in-game knowledge center for those who really like to dig into the lore.  Multiple in-game hints also indicated that there is an ARG that links to the world that provides more background.  By the end I found myself with a few "Oh Wow" moments that really have me looking forward to the second Consortium game.
Now for a few negatives.  Despite the tremendous quality of the game from a small indie developer, the many branching pathways and moving parts are pretty complex, and I ran into quite a few bugs right off the bat.  I began playing with the Humble Bundle download version, and it seemed to have several issues with NPC pathing, especially getting stuck in doorways, blocking access and forcing me to start over.  I also ran into situations where the scripting would get out of sync and I would, for example, get caught in a loop where I ended a conversation and then the airplane exploded, only the reload at the last save and explode again.  The solution?  Save, save, save.  Once I got into the old school habit of making an incremental save between different encounters, I was able to work around various issues and continue playing.
When I got my key and changed to the Steam version, I noted it seemed to work better and several bugs present in the Humble version were not present.
Overall I am extremely pleased with my decision to back these fine folks on Kickstarter and have greatly enjoyed the game.  Those who are not patient enough to deal with progress halting bugs should avoid for now, and await patches which are swiftly being worked on.  The setting is incredibly rich and begs to be expanded in future titles, which I eagerly await.

It's been a long time since I felt fully trolled by a game. Lets ignore the game breaking bugs and the fact that most people seem incapable of finishing the game. Lets ignore the peculiar graphics choices since they're functional and graphics arent important as long as they perform all the tasks you need them to in the game.
Here be spoilers.
This entire 'game' is the intro sequence to a game they havent made yet! You're told bishops are essentially a warrior class, you're given a powerful suit of armour, several weapons and several pieces of equipment that you plug into your armour for various effects...and there is no combat in the game. The combat takes place in a virtual reality suite, there is one opportunity for actual physical combat in the game and it only happens if you screw everything up. Also, the special equipment you get for plugging into your suit that gives you different abilities? that is only given to you AS THE GAME ENDS! Meaning they put work into coding items you are physically incapable of using in the game at any point. They constantly talk about the combat system, the equipment system, your role as a warrior in this alternate society...and before you actually engage in any combat the game ends. This game would have been perfectly fine as an interactive story game. If they had included none of the taunting allusions to combat, none of the equipment and several guns you will never use in any situation (they're even locked down during the game with the safety on, I never even fired them) and focused on the one thing the game delivers, a good narrative and great voice acting, it would have been a good game. But constantly promising that this is a first person shooter with role playing aspects when it is in fact a socialization simulator is misleading and a direct attempt to lull in a different audience.
In short it's 2014 and having a dialogue tree in a game is not a selling point, we've had those functioning at this level since the 90s. You cant sell a game entirely on the point it has a dialogue tree in it, so they clumsily tacked on some pretend first person shooter aspects to use guns to sell it. The entire 'game' is a sham. It's an interactive movie, which would be fine if they marketed it that way. Including features it isnt possible to use anywhere in the 'game' whilst constantly leading you to believe the game is a first person shooter in the advertising and in the game itself is dishonest and frankly insulting.

I guess I am a fan of the Tales game series even though I usually end up being fed up with them. Having said that, Tales of Berseria did greatly surpass my expectations. The battle system works smoothly which is par for the course but in addition to that the characters, while a bit edgy, aren't completely idiotic or one-dimensional and they have good chemistry with each other. The plot is okay and unlike usually, it doesn't go to a stupid place towards the end. The villain also stays cool to the very end. Berseria is a prequel to the previous game, Tales of Zestiria, but I haven't played it and as such can say that Berseria's story works well with no knowledge of Zestiria. Knowing what will happen later could make some scenes have more impact though.
This game is still far from perfect. The plot suffers a bit from pacing issues. There are long stretches where not much else happens than dungeon crawling and monster hunting and then you suddenly get huge plot dumps and everything seems to happen at once. It isn't a huge deal in itself, but combined with really monotonous dungeons the game could be considered a bit boring at times. The excellent battle system carries the game well during these stretches. There's also the weird experience level discrepancy between main story progression and the late-game sidequests. I guess the later sidequests are meant to be post-game content, but it is a bit annoying to have a decent or maybe even somewhat overleveled team for the main plot that suddenly gets completely creamed in some random optional boss battle. I know this is normal for jrpgs, but I wonder why they didn't put all of these bosses to the actual post-game dungeon that was already filled with crazy overleveled monsters. As a final minor quibble the minigames are for the most part really uninspired.
All in all Tales of Berseria is a decent jrpg carried by its excellent battle system and fun characters. As a Tales game it is probably the best in the series. This PC port is high quality but be warned: using a gamepad is highly recommended.

Street Fighter 5 is a game which dispenses with the complex without sacrificing depth; all this while remaining the most accessible game in the franchise to new players that I am ever aware of.
Gone are the focus attacks and "come-back" ultras of Street Fighter 4; replacing them is the V-system: essentially a way to make every fighter play a little more uniquely and add another meter to manage. This increases tactical depth in a way in which new players can quickly access without complicated focus cancel combos. Simply pressing two buttons activates a vskill, while another two buttons activates the v-trigger and its associated effects.
This is huge for people who don't benefit from years of fighting game muscle memory (usually the highest bar to entry in any title).
Speaking of things that are good for people who don't have amazing muscle memory, Capcom has seen fit to give us combos of lesser complexity (most are three inputs!) and extended frame buffers with which to input our various commands.
Lesser complexity combos means the barrier to entry is lower than ever and even a new player can enjoy the feeling of mastery that comes with mastering a simple "bread and butter" combo of a character without much grief, but it is the extended frame buffer which truly helps.
In offline play, this is huge as it allows players more leniency in inputting the complicated movements required of a fighting game. Other great fighting games such as BlazBlue and Persona Arena already utilized a similar system to great effect, but to my knowledge this is the first time it has shown up in a Capcom game.
Whether you're a highly skilled player or a complete "scrub" (new/casual player), you will appreciate the extra leniency in inputting your commands, but where this really shines is in online netplay. Netplay often has lag which can't be helped, often messing up a player in the middle of inputting a complicated input. Frame buffers provide that extra "cushion" which help guard the player from dropping commands due to lag. This creates an incredibly solid online experience.
And speaking of the netplay, the game has some of the best I've ever seen in a Capcom title (a lot of firsts going on here). I have been playing people I know to live on the other side of the continent from me (southwest to northeast america) and have very little lag at all, even crossplatform...
And ah, that is the real draw here. Most fighting games are relegated to their respective "boxes" of PC, PS4, and XboxOne. Since the communities are fragmented across games, the online lobbies quickly become a ghost town and ranked becomes something of an impossibility; this is especially true for PC fighting games who often suffer from smaller populations than consoles.
Street Fighter 5, on the other hand, can play crossplatform against Playstation 4 players with no problems. This is huge for keeping the community alive and vibrant and it means that, at least in North America, you will never suffer for a lack of opponents at all hours of the day.
So, I've touched on the actual gameplay being excellent, the netplay being solid, and the crossplatform play ensuring a long competitive lifespan.
Doubtless you want to know what the problems are.
This depends on what kind of player you are.
There is a class of player which expects a certain amount of singleplayer content in a fighting game. These players are very unhappy that, at the time of this writing, the game's singleplayer modes include training, survival, and story. These modes are not very fleshed out at the moment; survival has the dubious distinction of being the only way to unlock additional colors for a character and many of the competitive crowd don't want to touch it.
Even though it's designed for the singleplayer crowd, they are not happy with it and are stating that the game should have released with more singleplayer content.
If you are one of these players who plays a fighting game for singleplayer content, I agree; do not buy this game yet. Capcom has promised additional modes, but they released the game early for the competitive crowd so that we could enjoy the tournament season.
If, however, you are at all interested in the competitive aspect of this game (that means both competing and watching people compete!), then you should absolutely purchase this game. Don't think for a second that "competitive" means soul-crushing competition or a grind; I've been playing fighting games casually for nearly two decades and I enjoy it now more than ever. This is absolutely a game to play with friends, both old and those you make in the scene. The feeling of "mastery," that is to say of getting better, is incredible and you might very well never stop learning new aspects of the hobby.
And that's what this is ultimately: a very cool, very accessible entry point to a great hobby.
Again, this is by far the most accessible street fighter ever; there is nothing quite like watching a tournament via stream and then replicating on someone else something you saw a pro player do.
The feeling is euphoric and makes the hobby truly shine; if you are at all interested in the competitive or multiplayer aspect of fighting games, this is the best game yet to get into and you should buy it post haste.
