Wizorb is a fundamentally flawed game. This, however, isn’t entirely the fault of the developer.
Wizorb is a game which takes the old Breakout gametype and adds a level-driven, Legend of Zelda themed design, seeing you play as a presumably experienced wizard who is tasked with saving the land of Gorudo from an invasion of monsters. While this concept is initially fairly compelling, Wizorb doesn’t do much to iterate upon the offerings of the original Breakout in terms of gameplay, acting instead as a fantasy themed clone of the original. That isn’t meant as a tear at the developers though, as I imagine that the game probably wouldn’t be as enjoyable as it is now had they instead chosen to introduce some arbitrary, RPG inspired leveling or magic-based progression system to the game. Instead, most of the original ideas present in Wizorb culminate in mostly non-game affecting ways, barring the interesting-yet basic magic functionality which I will touch on later, with the most notable example being the town which gets destroyed by monsters in the tutorial sequence of the game. The game gives you the option to help rebuild the town by donating gold earned in levels to the townsfolk, sometimes gaining you rewards like a temporary safety net in the next level or a shop you can visit at any point during the game. Other times, the effect your charity has is purely cosmetic, adding a pretty new house or statue to the game’s hub town. I use the term “hub town” quite liberally here though as there really is nothing pushing you to return to the town once you have begun your quest, lest you consider the unfortunate situation of the townsfolk motivation enough, resulting in one of the more detailed areas in the game feeling quite redundant.
Speaking of detailed aspects of the game; the level design in Wizorb often feels quite polished, with most early levels introducing new types of stages and bricks to the player and most mid to late game levels iterating upon these initial designs. While some levels can feel unnecessarily challenging for the type of game Wizorb is (level 5 from world 4 comes to mind), most levels are fairly balanced and leave the player feeling quite rewarded. The aforementioned magic system also adds an interesting layer of depth to Wizorb, giving you a primary spell which allows you to shoot brick-breaking fire balls from the paddle/wand and a secondary spell which allows you to blow a gust of wind that changes the horizontal trajectory of the ball; these spells change if used when the ball touches the wand as well, with the primary spell morphing the ball into a bounce-resistant, damage-dealing orange menace and the secondary spell allowing you to temporarily control the movement of the ball with the movement of the wand. Finally, you can also use a teleport spell on the ball in place of shooting it out normally during its initial sendoff, allowing you to choose where the ball will start in the level.
However, as mentioned before, despite the best intent on the part of the developer in creating well designed and challenging levels for players, the otherwise acceptable level design in Wizorb feels greatly challenged by the limitations of the old Breakout type of gameplay that the game is based upon, with the old system seeming mostly unchanged from its initial iterations. The paddle in Breakout games tends to not hit the ball in the way you intend for it to quite frequently, often sending it flying off at a fair greater or lesser angle than you were hoping for, a problem Wizorb suffers from as well. This renders skill-based gameplay nigh impossible, a sad misstep for a game whose level design and difficulty scaling seem to beg for constant improvement on the behalf of the player.
Another example of counterintuitive game design apparent within the Breakout formula is the fact that the speed of the ball increases the longer it is in play. Rather than provide an increased challenge for players who manage to keep their ball out for long enough in a level, it serves instead to make failure feel like an inevitability in Wizorb, with the speed of the ball often reaching a point of unmanageability where the player can do nothing but watch as their labor is rendered completely meaningless. The incredible lack of control the player has upon the ball once it’s already in play does nothing but amplify this problem to a nearly game-breaking degree. Further worsening this issue is the otherwise minor annoyance of the animation which triggers when the ball destroys a brick: this animation appears quite similar in color to the ball and often overshadows it in size, making it difficult to see the trajectory of the ball, thus rendering it yet harder to hit.
It’s obvious that the developers behind Wizorb put quite a bit of work into the design of their game, rendering it an obvious work of passion rather than an attempt at a cash-grab. The graphical fidelity of the game is quite nice and, besides the awful music present in the secret rooms, the music and sound design within the game is nice, albeit fairly repetitive. Unfortunately, the poor choice to use the Breakout gametype without improving it to better fit the skill-based nature of the levels within the game leaves Wizorb feeling quite unenjoyable at some moments, and nearly broken in others. However, for the price point, I think Wizorb is an interesting look into a new type of game that has yet to be fully explored and developed upon.
Also, for God's sake, make sure you use the mouse while playing the game and not the keyboard. It's going to make your life a hell of a lot easier.

To start. I've loved Planetary Annihilation since the alpha, and I'm going to continue loving Titans. I've played hundreds of hours of solo, although not a ton of multiplayer. Unfortunately, i have terrible memory, so i don't know all the unit names.
I can understand that a lot of people don't see the variance in the units in the game. It's small, but what a lot of people don't realize is they have specific uses.
Vehicles are slow, have more hp than bots, and generally hit harder. I say generally, because they're also more expensive than bots. A swarm of t1 tanks is more than capable of rolling through a horde of t1 bots in a head to head fight.
But that's because bots aren't designed for head to head. They're for hit and run, harassment, and swarming. Sure, they can't take on tanks (especially flamers), but they're great for taking out unescorted engineers and undefended structures, and they're cheap as dirt.
Air is interesting. Its fragile, expensive, and doesn't hit as hard as land. But it can stack, and a swarm of bombers can assassinate a commander that isn't paying attention or who doesn't have enough anti-air. Not to mention, air fabricators can easily sneak around the map, quickly building extra bases wherever they please, and running away whenever enemy land comes in.
Naval is a hard to use commodity. Most planets don't even have water to begin with. But on the planets that have it, naval is the way to control any patch of water, hands down. Huge health, huge range, and huge damage. If an ocean has a lot of metal spots, or if someone makes the mistake of building a base next to the water, naval is how you deal with it. Nothing is more satisfying than watching a fleet of destroyers munch a base to bits from long range, and a battleship or two is a good way to seal the deal.
Orbital serves one purpose in most situations: getting to other planets, and preventing people from getting to yours. A handful of orbital landers with t2 engineers can get a teleporter up in no time, followed by defenses to keep it up long enough to get the rest of your army through. Super expensive, tiny health,  and annoying difficult to control. Anti-orbital weapons, despite their limited range, are extremely strong and very capable of wiping out numerous orbital units at once single handedly. On the other hand, orbital can also stack like air, and when you move between planets, your entire force can stack on a single point. When 20 STX lasers suddenly appear over an enemy commander, that commander has a great tendency to disappear in a ball of plasma followed by a nuclear fireball.
I've also seen people comment that the game is just a rush to get to higher tier units, and stomp people with them. What they fail to realize, is that t2 is expensive (and titans are worse), and producing enough of them to stop equal-priced hordes of t1 is difficult to say the least. I've gone up against people who tried rushing straight to t2, got 20 ish t2 tanks onto the field, and then I rolled up with 400 t1 bots and absolutely crushed them. There have also been games where I've been seriously out-played, pinned into a small base, and crushed by t2. What people need to realize, once again, is that t2 has its uses. It's not a straight upgrade from t1 (although it seems like it for vehicles). A mix of t1 and t2 is so much more effective than just one or the other.
And finally, the variance between individual units. It seems like a swarm of 400 doxes is just as effective as a mix between doxes, grenadiers, and boomers. But then you watch as that swarm of boomers obliterates half the enemy defensive line, your doxes move in and distract the other half, and your grenadiers fire right over their heads. With vehicles, you have normal tanks mixed with flamers, and you realize how much more hp the flamers have, that they're great at absorbing incoming fire.
My final thought is the titans. At first they seemed underwhelming, but then I realized: they've just another layer of firepower application. Orbital battleships aren't great at shooting planetary targets, but damn they're great for dealing with swarms of orbital fighters (but countered by railgun platforms). The atlas is hysterically strong at dealing with swarms of ground units, but they can't do anything against air. The same thing applies to the super bomber, strangely enough. I don't know much about the drone carrier, other than it seems great supported by leviathans. All of the other "titans" (unit cannon, ragnarok, catalyst) are utility and doomsday weapons, respectively. Having trouble getting your orbital landers to another planet? Build a dozen unit cannons and drop some boomers onto the umbrellas, problem solved. Feel like trying to blow up another planet, but there's nothing a halley will fit onto? Drop a handful of t2 builders with a few dozen orbital builders above, crank out a ragnarok, and vaporize the enemy planet. We all know what the catalyst does (makes the Death Star).
In closing... Planetary Annihilation is a great game, but it has a learning curve to understand the finer points of ANNIHILATION.

If you played Terraria and liked it but got bored, give Starbound a try. I was skeptical at first, taking it as a Terraria clone set in space, but when I got into it I found the mechanics a lot tighter, the lore is present, and the variety in options to the player varied and interesting.
There are a number of races to play as, each with their own backstories(although some are definitely more fleshed out than others at this point), racial armors and weapons, and unique ships and pets. The choice to largely forgo traditional pickax, wood ax, and shovel setup makes it feel a lot less cluttered, and less of a factory-simulation where you have to meet a quota of materials mined to stay mining.  There are an insane number of procedurally-generated planets in the universe for you to explore, and none of them are identical. They have unique monsters, unique weather, and unique geography, as well as unique structures both on the surface and subterranian.
It grabed me on a fundamental wanderlust; even though I have a character who is at the highest currently-available tier, if I don't feel like building a world I can go explore the universe, flying from planet to planet in search of who knows what.
I enjoyed my time with this game, and am looking forward to the release, although be warned it has been in development for a very long time and some members of the community are getting frustrated by that fact.

I budgeted a whole two hours for games when I picked this up and I spent like... four on it before I knew what had happened.
It's a little rough around the 'indie' edges, but the conversation tree/affection-rating systems clashing with your goals of playing detective, diplomat, and warrior? All good fun. All while trying to figure out what's going on with the metagame without letting slip that you're actually a remote-control operator from the past in 2013.
The 4th-wall-breaking conceit behind the game is that the entire game is apparently a VR simulator delivered to you at your PC via uplink to a satellite which is making use of tachyon bursts or some♥♥♥♥♥♥to transmit temporally-adjusted data with an advanced, benevolent AI in the future, allowing you to remote-control an specific, nominated avatar at a fixed point in the future, generating a number of 'branched' alternate realities - based on your decisions - which the AI can track via other satellites in other parallel universes, spreading itself as a single entity functioning on nodes across all of them.
The rest of the story is best kept a mystery because it's kind of fun getting clues from the crew about the world lore and politics etc, without asking the standard, "Duh, so what is the deal with [Major Faction even a child should know about]?" RPG questions. Those options are still there but the crew will think you're a bit dozy or incompetent because of it, and start to regard you suspiciously or with hostility.
There's an in-game encyclopedia, but it seems like it only decelerates time to a certain degree to allow you to catch up, meaning that significant events and conversation opportunities can pass by or run their course without you. A veteran can probably see where most of the threads are underlying all this, and manipulate things appropriately, but if you let the smoke and mirrors do their job, I'd say this one's a fun one to get into.
The mechanics of combat and the rest are not the smoothest, occasionally fiddly and unintuitive, but you can avoid most twitch-dependency if you're so inclined, through game-choices. It's definitely more substance than style, with some kind of dated graphics.  Either way, none of this got in the way for me, so I can pretty confidently give this an overall thumbs up.

CONSORTIUM is absolutely fantastic.
It's very like one of those well loved but sort of clunky RPGs, like Deus Ex, Vampire: The Masquerade Bloodlines or EYE: Divine Cybermancy. If you can look beyond the flaws, which I personally haven't really suffered, it's a fantastic game. I've only played around 3 hours (so Steam tells me) but I could swear it's been more. It's absolutely astounding, the visuals are interesting, and the world is so rich! There's a computer bank with literally thousands of ebooks in detailing the world. There's so much there I really can't even begin to absorb it. It's got a real diversity in playstyle, too. For example, the big bad of the first act, I looked him up, worked out a bit about his personality, and when speaking to him, played his ego and curiosity. This meant I could defeat him and his army, then his fleet without firing a single bullet or hurting anyone.
Alternatively, I attempted a more violent approach, but I personally never found that to be the best way. The richness with the way you interact and chat with the characters makes you genuinely develop emotion towards them, not forced emotion, such as in The Walking Dead. They each have their own metric ton of things to say, and your behaviour changes their thoughts towards you, and the same will go for you.
The setting is very rich, like a Gerry Anderson serial, or something. I was strongly reminded of Spectrum, with the whole codename system and flying base. The only sort of problem with this is that nearly every character is designated as Pawn and then a number. This means I got very confused when investigating an incident that comes out through the game. I actually ended up screwing my alignment utterly with two characters and failing to find the bad guy. This did sort of annoy me, but the game does tell you that regular saves are a good idea, and I decided to not do that to add a more permanent level to my choices.
I can imagine that there's so many ways to approach this game, so I can't comment on the scope of it. It can also be very tense in some parts, like when you're being interrogated about your name and stuff.
All in all, this is one of those games you will love if you can focus past things like attempting the usual tutorial and introduction dialouges with NPCs being met with "Are you feeling okay? You've forgotten everything" and other things. The developers have also promised to fix the bugs that have damaged some people's experience, too.

Synopsis: Explosively fun multi-player game, in which teams role play as either the Pirates or the British.
Deplete the enemies' seamen lives or materials.
Pros:
+ Very well-fleshed out game, despite being in beta.
+ Fun role-playing community.
+ Quality Graphics.
+ Numerous combat options.
+ Easy controls (can pick up controls within 2 hours)
Cons:
- Matches can be repetitive and boring.
- Server issues and lag can make the game unenjoyable.

- Complex, well-developed characters.  Voice acting and scripting is done very well and they all feel to be believable people with individual goals, desires and motivations.
- Simple, intuitive controls.  It uses the WSAD movement with hotbar standard, but I like that the inventory screen doesn't stop time so much as vastly slow it down.  It's far more believable than Skyrim's stop-time-sort-through-inventory-resume-with-opponent-naked while still getting the job done.  It also forces you to make quick decisions while in combat while still acknowledging that you're a human being who might take some time to think.
- Incredibly deep backstory and history.  While not everyone will be interested to read into the pages and pages of historical documents, I found them to be great reads that really helped define the world and paint a vivid universe in which to live, breathe and play in.
- Notable attitude and path adjustment.  Unlike Mass Effect (which I did still enjoy quite alot) it's not good/evil/neutral in black and white.  Killing vs Incapacitating does much of the morality course adjustment, but social encounters between characters also play heavily into affect.  There are more branches than the three standards, or at the very least, it appears to be as such.
- Simple, intuitive ship design.  It's a little confusing at first but once you figure it out, you can get anywhere and everywhere quite quickly.  Also, it all makes plausible, practical sense; something of a rarity in game design.  There's no wasted space, no unexplained areas that defy the overal structural design.
- Fantastic atmosphere.  The music, the occasional static surge in the linkup, the turbulence that the plane suffers, it all makes the experience far more believable.  When you hit a pocket of turbulance, the plane shakes and people react to it.  When you get signal interrupts, your view goes staticy and people sound as if underwater.
- Clever balance of inventory to sustainability.  Your energy bar is used to heal yourself and repair your armor, but it also serves as a 'carry weight' limit to your inventory.  You can only store so much in your PCU before you run out of energy buffer; energy that could be used to heal you and fix you up.  Energy is relatively easy to get but healing is expensive, so it makes for a unique mmicro-meta.
- Very short.  While doing every possible path can really make the gameplay quite long, if you take a direct course the game finishes very quickly.
- Graphically average.  You won't see this thing rivalling Crysis or getting any visual awards.  The colours are very primal, really makes me think of classic Star Trek with the polar blues and whites and reds.  It gets the job done, and I mean no offense to the graphics team, however it is 'average' by big name standards.
- Minimal combat.  Personally, I love the amount of conversation and depths in the game, but I would have liked to see a bit more action.  I expect far more of it in the second game, considering the ending of this one.
- Bugs.  They exist.  This is a temporary Con, but one that should be mentioned all the same.  However, it is a mild one as the support staff seem quite responsive.
- Graphical hiccups.  There are shadows cast by crew heads that don't react well to the texture meshes or the general line of the neck.  I'm not an artist, I'm not sure what the issue is.  Still, it's rather distracting.  Technically a con but super super minor.
The game was worth the money spent.  It was a wonderful delve into a rich universe where I sincerely felt that my actions would cause a multitude of paths to open up for future content.  How well that translates into the second game will be a strong determining factor in this one's final value, but I feel it was worth my time and expense.
- Get it if you like story over action.  If you want a many-levelled shooter, not the game you want.

Consortium is a really wierd game. It has enough going for it to warrant a reccomendation, but it comes with some warnings.
Both the writing, and the graphical fidelity are pretty decent; from what I've seen so far there isn't anything that stands out too starkly as cheap looking or terrible sounding. The characters, while overly perky to the point of mild irritation are voiced well and move smoothly more or less.
If you don't like stories where the game talks freely about it being a game and breaks the 4th wall while attempting to work such breaches into the lore itself, then this isnt for you. It's quirky and funny but it can come off as a bit trying and boring at times.
The UI, on the other hand looks like it was made in flash, or paint or something and isn't all that great and is fairly confusing to navigate, especially in combat. Equipment is also sort of oddly priced. For some reason your basic armor you get at the beginning of the game costs 72 MILLION dollars yet your helmet - of equal technical complexity- costs a mere 75k.

Combat feels wierdly tacked on. Your suit is essentially this big vaccum cleaner that just sucks up EVEYRTHING and converts it into 'utility energy' This is then used for healing and weapons, but has modes where you can just passively heal/repair or repair/heal specific parts of your body. It's just unecessarily complicated and does not really translate well to the general flow of combat.
Enemies have a similar system although here the complexity is welcomed and you can maim them in a variety of ways rather than just killing them outright. I personally like this because it makes combat more interesting and engaging than simply pointing and clicking.
Those small nitpicks aside, I would say that this game is certainly worth it with a 10 buck price tag, so wait for it to go on sale.

Short version: This game is for those looking for great memorable characters that have always something interesting to say, a game with a good story that get better, a game that involves some phylosophic themes such as "what it means to be alive?" "live a happy life in ignorance or face the harsh truth?", hilarious dialogue, a battle system that isn't turn based, unique secondary quests.
This is no hack and slash game, it requires some strategy in battle (organizing combos, using right elements against enemies).
Edit1 - OBS: I still haven't beaten the game, so this review will change
Edit2 - Almost beating the game.
Edit3 - Beat the game. Added complete opinion of the story.
Long version:
+Story
A strong point in this game, I felt connected to the characters and the game made me care of what was hapenning to them.
The story starts simple: The main Heroine lost everything she loved, but that didn't left emptiness in her heart: There was hatred, the thirst for revenge. And so her journey begins. The game world have monsters called Daemons or Gouma (in japanese) and a organization called the Abbey appears saying it wants to save humanity from the Daemons.
The story is more about the journey than the destination, is how the characters develop. Is not about good or evil, as many things are morally grey. There are no villains and heroes, only our protagonists and the antoganists. Velvet's party are not a bunch of people trying to save the world, they kill guards and leave a mess behind sometimes, yet they are not completely evil as they can show mercy. The Abbey says they want to protect everyone, but they commit morally dubious things to get things done: sacrifice a few to save the many. For an outsider this seems OK, but what if in the midst of the few there was someone you loved? Would the act of sacrifing a few, still be considered right?
This is one of those games that get better the more you go further into the story. The game makes you question different beliefs, morals and ways of life, it tries to make you see things as they are. Is better to be a happy ignorant or face the truth even if it's ugly? Live a lie, an illusion or face reality? (kinda ironic as some people use video games as escapism)
Would it be right to try to run away from the truth, to not accept the world as it is and force the world to change? Or accept things as they are and keep moving on? There's much symbolism in this game and much to learn from it.
In my opinion the ending was good, as it wasn't your typical "they lived happily ever after" there's some sadness to it but there's also hope and joy. Just like real life.
+Dialogues
Well written as they show the characters personalities very well. Dialogues can range from many topics: Food, history of the world, some character (generally Magilou) mocking another character, etc. Dialogues play a important role in the story, there are times where an "y" icon (if you are using an xbox controller) will appear on the down left corner indicating that an optinal dialogue is avaiable. It's very recommended to watch them all so you get know the world and the characters better. There's also optinal dialogues through the map, which again, I recommned watching.
+Voice acting
Japanese voice acting is great as you can feel the if the character is being ironic, joking around, threatning, etc.
English is OK, but I heard better english voice acting before (but I also heard worse).
I think the Japanese voice actors understood who their character were and "became" them thus making it more enjoyable.
+Characters
Very memorable characters, they are not yor generic characters with lack of depth. Each one of them has their own story and journey prior to Velvet's journey. At the start the characters unite because their goals are similar/close to each other and out of necessity as well because they are a band of outcasts and outlaws. The characters seems simple but they are deep and it's a joy to go through their journey.
Each character is unique. I don't have favorites because each one of the characters are very important pieces of the story.
+Music
Soundtrack is good, fits the situations you find pretty well. The soundtracks range from classical instruments such as violin to more modern stuff such as guitars.
+Playtime
Around 72 hours (or more if you want to complete more things) including side quests and going through all the optional dialogues. It may not seem much for some people but the quality of those 72 hours is great because of the story and characters. There's a new game plus mode.
The only bad thing is that most secondary quests only beccome avaible once the last dungeon/level is unlocked, so from 0 side quests to OMG MY CHECKLIST. To make it worse you have to talk to certain NPCs through different towns to unlock those so if you skip to the last dungeon thinking "I've done everything" you will regret it after discovering this. Is almost like the developers forgot to add the secondary quests resulting in the following situation:
Dev 1: Yes! We finished the game!
Dev 2: YAY!
Dev 3: Grab the beer!
Dev 4:......
Dev 2: hmmm, what's up Dev 4? You don't look excited at all!
Dev 4: I noticed something.....
Dev 1:?
Dev 4: we.... forgot.... to add the rest of the secondary quests....
Dev Team: Oh sh*****! OMFG! WE WILL HAVE TO REDO THE ENTIRE GAME SCRIPT!
Dev Team leader: Calm down guys! I have the perfect sollution! Just add these quests right before the last level so we don't have to rework our script!
Dev Team: *applauses*
Dev Team leader: It's settled! Now let's have some beer.
-upgrade system
Every equipment has an skill the character can learn, after some battles he/she will learn and permanently earn that skill. This mechanic is interesting but makes you change equipment frequently which makes the upgrade system pointless most of the time until you are are at the end of the game.
-materials
Sometimes gathering materials for upgrading is a paint in the rear, maybe if gathering materials were easier this would have made swaping equipment frequently more bareble and feel less of a grind
Combat
-can be confusing for begginers who never played tales of series (me) since there's many game mechanics that you have to learn.
+using the party and right combos can cause you to wreak havoc and ensure total chaos in battle.
+when nothing absurd happens battles are fluid and fun
-sometimes enemies have 100% chance of inflicting negatives status on you, while you hit them 10 times and nothing happens
+characters controlled by AI are good and will support you in the best way they can (but sometimes they brain fart, but are still much better than certain AIs like Resident Evil 5)
-I feel combat shouldn't have been combo based as it can make it repetitive at times
-minigames
Not really fun, you earn tales coins but everything in the minigame shop cost a ton of tales coins making you grind through the boring minigames. Is not rewarding, it isn't fun. I don't even know who the f### thought this was a good idea.
final level
-/+ The final map is huge. Can be a good or a bad thing depending in how you like your games, for me it annoyed me cause I had to backtrack a lot in order to defeat optional bosses that rewarded me with a third mystic arte which increased play time but not in a good way.

A retro RPG set in a whimsical take on the old west. The graphics are quite good with some expressive sprite animation that reminds me of good SNES era RPG's. The story is fairly straight forward and full of the usual western cliches, but its well enough told and builds to a good conclusion at the end of this chapter, certainly setting up interest for whats going to happen in the next chapter. The combat is turn based but each action needs a certain charge before it will perform, so a large part of the strategy in combat is timing, picking what moves to use and when. This really makes the combats quite tactical and raises them above the usual "Pick an option from the menu and wait" fare thats typical of older JRPG. Skills ("vantages") are learned by wearing different hats, after each combat you will get a certain amount of skill points that will be assigned to the skill set the hat gives you, once you have earned enough for a skill you learn it permanently, even if you take the hat off. You can only have four skills equiped at once so this adds another wrinkle to the already interesting combat. All in all I had a great time with this game in the 15 odd hours it took me to complete, well worth the price.

Let me tell you a story about Bastion.
On one of my old computers, there was this little program which let you play demos of random games such as Diner Dash etc. Bastion was among them and the narrator immediately captured my interest. I can't imagine I was that great at the game (having never really played a game) but I remember really really wanting to buy it and finish it.
Fast forward a few years, I see it on Steam and although half of me is estastic, the other half is a little wary. It was an old game and I was hesitant to whether my memory was tainted by rose-tinted glasses. Fortunately I was not disappointed. Although the game is a few years old, the graphics are absolutely gorgeous and, the best part, the narrator's voice was exactly how I imagined it. Humous, witty, and a touch of nostalgia, I feel like the narrator really tied the game together.
Now, about the game. There is a touch of replayability in this if you want to see all sides of the story as well as complete all the challenges perfectly. However, the game is a largely somewhat linear style action game with loveable characters and an intriguing story.
Highly recommend it. One of my favourite games on my list.

Boot Hill Heroes is great because it takes classic JRPG elements and applies a western theme, while managing to bring back some beloved elements that the famous Earthbound game possessed--mainly a real time battle system (or close). Though Earthbound allowed you to take moves while hit points changed, Boot Hill instead shows a timeline of power for all characters with moves costing different amounts. In this way you can time yourself to be more effective, much like Child of Light. The story is cliche western, but still very fun and interesting. You also get different hats that let you learn new moves for all characters, and collect materials to put effects like fire or poison on weapons.
The bad part is it ends fast. The game is cheap, but you expect a little more and it's sad to end it without finishing the story. I hope they finish it soon, because it's a really good game.

As a long time Street Fighter fan I can not recommend this. The reason why... I can only explain it like this:
Imagine for a second that your favorite restaurant for making omelets was called Capcom. Over the years Capcom has made you the best damn omelets you can imagine. Some of them not as good as others, but generally speaking they are damn good omelets.
However, today, you are promised the best and newest version of your favorite omelet. You are as excited as can be after ordering it, but after only a few short moments the chef comes out with an egg in one hand and a plate in the other.
To your surprise the plate is set in front of you, and the chef just takes the raw egg, and cracks it open onto the empty plate in front of you.
"The♥♥♥♥♥♥is this?" You ask.
Capcom replies "O trust us, this is exactly what you ordered!".
"No, this isn't anywhere close. This is a raw egg."
Capcom replies "Well sure, right now, but trust us, over the next few months it will be the best omelet you ever had."
"Well that is all fine and dandy, but when I order an omelet I expect it to be finished after making the purchase."
Capcom "O, we know that. But trust us, we have things planned!"
"That's really nice that you have things planned, but this raw egg on my plate isn't even comparable to any other restaurant that serves omelet's! Not to mention, this is completely unacceptable based on your previous omelets!"
Moral of the story, don't eat raw egg. Wait until its cooked. Especially if you ordered an omelet.
UPDATE 2/23/2016:
Now that I have had more time with the game (on PS4), Im going to give more specific problems with the game:
Steam Store Page:
-Still incredibly vague, and doesn't give enough information about the product. Capcom is selling this as a completed game with DLC plans, not as an incomplete game that is planning on being completed sometime in the next few months.
-Aside from us diehard SF fans, the average consumer would have no clue what they are actually purchasing. This should clearly be listed as an early access title! Doesn't fit the $60 price tag for most consumers at this point in time.
Story mode:
- AI is absolutely terrible.
-No difficulty adjustments
-Extremely short. Out of the ~5 characters I have done, the average completion time when not skipping dialog and fight intros ends up being about 5 min. With only ~3 fights per character, that last at most 30 sec each.
-No real replayability
+This ~Might~ be updated at some point. Arcade mode ~might~ make it into the game eventually. A 2 hour cinematic story is planned to be added as well.
Survival:
-Again terrible AI. Most fights can be won by simply timing jump in HP or HK -> knockdown -> stun.
-Difficulties don't really appear to add any difficulty. Aside from Easy being 10 fights, and Hell being 100, its more about RNG and patience then it is about actually enjoying the game.
-Awards for survival are minor, and don't really warrant the grind to complete...
-Required to complete with every character to unlock 100%. Arguably the worst way to implement   color unlocks that capcom could have done
+This game mode DOES have allot of potential.
-The end of round perks are interesting, yet currently you get so much credit per round that you can always afford the most expensive upgrades for the next round (with exception to full health, which doesn't always show up).
-Not really worth playing in its current state
Training:
-Purely target dummy at this point in time. Not a Con by itself, but it is lackluster compared to the training options available in previous SF games, and most other fighters.
+This is going to be updated soon
Online:
-Connection issues still a problem, but getting better
-No lobby support for more then 2 players, and no spectating.
+This will be updated soon
Bugs:
-Capcom still hasn't released a patch for those of us that are effected by frequent crashing.
Gameplay:
++The game DOES play well, and so far looks to be balanced. Eventhubs early rankings also show a decent balance across characters.
~~Neutral at this point, but as a player that has mained Vega since SFII, I'm still not sure If I really enjoy all the changes. This new Vega plays well, but I do miss his old toolkit, and especially miss him being a charge character.
In general, the people that have already purchased this game are really the only people I could recommend it to. For everybody else, if you are planning on playing primarily with friends (in a lobby bigger then 2 people), wait until the March update at the earliest. For those that are looking for the finished product with all its training tools and other features intact I would assume the June update and any unannounced changes might put this game in a position where it would be worth your $$$.

The biggest problem with this game is that it's very passive. There's little you can do to affect the path of the ball. It flies up, hits a block or two, then comes back down. A lot of your runtime, you will be sitting there, watching the ball bounce around without anything productive to do in order to impact gameplay.

If you want to play a modern take on this classic game, try Shatter. It's a lot more proactive of a gaming experience.

Let me preface this by saying I was originally dissapointed in Planetary Annihilation. I certainly got my moneys worth, and I have no qualms about supporting a studio simply so they may make more games that I may like in the future. Titans is that game.
In PA vanilla, I felt that all of the matches were much to simplistic, with too much emphasis on rushing - first to scour your local planet, then to acquire a superweapon. If the map lacked any moons or metal planets it seemed like any match in which the initial rush failed would be a terrible grind to even form a lasting beachhead on an enemy world.  This was ameliorated slightly once I understood the orbital layer better, and the addition of the unit cannon was at least an attempt in that direction as well.
Now, in Titans, I find the greater unit variety makes for a more interesting choice as to your initial build order: Nearly all of the factory choices are capable of building solid, interesting armies and have worthwhile units to unlock with the advanced factory. I do feel that naval combat is a bit of a superfluous niche, and while I do like the units that are available I find very few situations in which building a navy confers an actual advantage over just stylistic considerations. I do feel that there may be some reasonably simple remedies, such as generating planets that are both large and 90+% water with only small islands, or perhaps just allowing the creation of giant terrestrial planets such that the oceans can be more prominent as strategic features without totally overshadowing the land.
I find stalemates to be almost nonexistent now: the increased unit roster depth and the addition of the titans means that there is always room to escalate, and the sight of a large mixed unit force led by your titans is a delight.
I bought Planetary Annihilation hoping that it would be a bigger, badder supreme commander and it did not deliver; I bought Titans only hoping to find some small improvement that might make the game bearable, and I found exactly the game that I was wishing for when I first heard of PA.
Thank you Uber for what I am sure will be one of my favorite games for quite a while, best of luck in your future ventures whether they be entirely new products or just expansions of PA (yes, please). Don't get too down on the negative reviews, though if I think they have on valid point among them: For a strategy title such as this, depth is almost the most important quality after basic funcionality. PA worked great, but was percieved as shallow, and there are far too many shallow strategy games around. The planetary aspect of PA was a great, interesting idea; now with Titans it feels deep enough to enjoy, and given your track record I'm sure there is still some depth unplumbed in this IP and I am finally excited to see where you take it.

I had mixed feelings after finishing Tales of Zestiria so I did not know what to think about Berseria at first. When I heard that suppose to be a prequel to ToZ I was a little bit skeptical. Unnecessarily. This is one of the jRPG that put genre back on right track in last year (together with Persona 5).
This game contains the most bizarre party I ever seed in any jRPG. Velvet, protagonist, woman filled with rage and hatred towards her brother-in-law Artorius. Eizen, the pirate,
, Rokurou a demon
, Magilou an unpredictable witch, Eleanor the exorcist and Malak named Laphicet.
Story is interesting with couple interesting plot twists and takes about 40-50h to complete.
Combat system was improved from ToZ, it is much more dynamic. You can choose either of characters that suits you during combat and you can swap them immediately when needed. Personally, at most of time, I was using Eleanor but I had no trouble to adapt with any other character. When you progress the story you are going to notice that battles become too easy (no problems with enemies 10 or more levels than your party) and only way to challenge yourself a little is to set difficulty a little higher.
In overall this is highly recommended position for any jRPG fan.

Simply put for a simple game, It's good. Not only good though, It's great. It has a very simple art style and a lot of content to enjoy. There are three problems I have with RotMG:
1. Spam bots. In the Nexus, or the games hub, there are bots spamming you to buy their items. How to fix: a simple chat limit in the nexus, one message every minute, and a faster rate at which messages go away.
2. Gold. Any Free to Play player can be just or almost as geared as any paying player. I just feel that there should be a way for free players to get gold, maybe by selling their own items on a "Auction House" to other players or Daily Log In Bonuses.
3. Content. Realm is a great game and can provide many hours of gameplay. It almost feels like it's not repetitive and Grundy because you never quite know exactly what you'll be doing. Still, the game needs new content, maybe DLC, even if it's $5.
In short, Realm is a fantastic game that is a perfect mix between an Arcady 8bit game and an MMO.

Let me tell you a story about Bastion.
On one of my old computers, there was this little program which let you play demos of random games such as Diner Dash etc. Bastion was among them and the narrator immediately captured my interest. I can't imagine I was that great at the game (having never really played a game) but I remember really really wanting to buy it and finish it.
Fast forward a few years, I see it on Steam and although half of me is estastic, the other half is a little wary. It was an old game and I was hesitant to whether my memory was tainted by rose-tinted glasses. Fortunately I was not disappointed. Although the game is a few years old, the graphics are absolutely gorgeous and, the best part, the narrator's voice was exactly how I imagined it. Humous, witty, and a touch of nostalgia, I feel like the narrator really tied the game together.
Now, about the game. There is a touch of replayability in this if you want to see all sides of the story as well as complete all the challenges perfectly. However, the game is a largely somewhat linear style action game with loveable characters and an intriguing story.
Highly recommend it. One of my favourite games on my list.

this is great game, loads of fun, runs great, have played it for hundreds of hours.
even better if you go to
you will find hundreds of mods for it, everything imaginable and a very active community over 40,000 members!
i also want to say that there is no serious memory leak or programming issue like some people are posting. what issue that people are having is that the game allows you to build huge i mean huge cities, ive seen some with population over 90M and basically they do not set limits other than the hardware you have. so as you add more and more buildings and roads and the cities get larger and more complex sure its going to use more and more memory until you run out of memory and until your cpu/gpu cant handle the size of the cities and complexity and the framerate goes down. It's hard to put in words just how large and complex your cities can get, they can look so real that you can't distinguish screenshots from real world images of some of the worlds largest cities. in fact i cant think of a real world single city that has a population of over 90M. so what you have a people with low end hardware trying to build cities they can't support. and since its a 32-bit application, like most games, the cities can only get so large and complex before you hit the 2-3gb limit that windows imposes. the trick is to balance city size and complexity and not try to build cities that don't make sense and would not be practical even in real life.
so yes the game is a 32-bit game with the game logic running in a single thread, but most other games out there have the same limitations. the only difference between those games and this game is that this game does not impose limits on you like simcity or tropico or anno does. also this games lets u pack the density of the cities to real world levels and beyond. in this way its more a city builder than a sim i would say.
having said that the game, like all other games and software, does have bugs and issues, but luckily they are for minor and can easily be ignore of worked around.

Seeing the negativity around the latest Simcity, I was hopeful when trying Cities XL, but it just frustrates me in a lot of little ways. For one, it plays like it's in beta: text on the UI gets cut-off awkwardly, there are weird texturing issues with roads fairly regularly, it feels like it needs more polish. And this is a game that was first released in 2009, and has had 3 re-releases including this one! I've no idea what they've been doing all this time.
For all the efforts at making you vary-up your cities, with different resources available in different areas, specialising is difficult - I needed fuel, so decided to start a second city just for that, and found that oil-extraction isn't unlocked until you have a fairly large city built.
There was nothing pushing me to expand, and no real consequence to failure. My man city has nowhere near enough power, with -5 electricity tokens, and yet it doesn't really matter, and things carry-on as normal. It's trivial to make a city profitable.
I'm also not a fan of the art style - the lighting makes everything quite grey, and it's hard to tell different wealth levels apart. It all just ends-up a bit bland.
I'm sure if you're after a game that lets you be creative with building, you'll enjoy it - you can individually decide exactly which building goes where, and the curved roads are nice. But as a game, it's a bit lacking.

The game is really fantastic. I've played some retro stuff, but I really can't recall ever playing a game that made me feel the same way I did when I played Chrono Trigger. The story is engaging and right off the bat sets up some characters (just at first glance from their sprites) that you immediately want to know more about.
The old west setting, for an RPG, is both very unique and adapted well. The combat is excellent (I remember the first menu-driven combat where there was queue times for actions that you could affect in Grandia, I think...) and actually keeps me thinking for most of the battles rather than devolving into select Fight, select Fight, select Fight.
A good way to sum it up is that if this was released for the SNES, it would be in the top 3 or 5 RPGs for the system. (Just to clarify, that's because this is the whole package. You could take any game today and just because of the graphics alone, it would have been revolutionary.) This would alos be an example of a game that would be on everyone's "please make a sequel" list.
About the only issue I have with the game is that I wish the character sprites were a little less detailed - because I think you can get a lot of expression from the sprites in Chrono Trigger and FF Tactics even though, for instance, those sprites lack noses and sometimes mouths. Trying to make the sprites 30% larger in order to fit in the extra facial detail - while it works in theory, it loses some of the charm.
So in short, I've seen retro games that are decent and give you an experience that is fun but largely relies on following tropes or tongue-in-cheek mocking them. But this is different, this actually feels like a new mid-90s Squaresoft RPG. They put in the effort to make use of the tropes, have some humor based off them, but more importantly go far, far beyond that to make a game that doesn't actually need nostalgia to get you to enjoy the game.

[Spoiler-Free Review]
Boot Hill Heroes is a modern RPG designed as a sort of homage to the glory days of the Role Playing and Wild West genres. The story is easy to follow and progresses at a snappy pace, the difficulty is forgiving (for the most part), and while it doesn’t allow for true
functionality, you’ll never feel locked-in to a play session beyond what your time allows. Despite being a linear experience overall, the game still manages to deliver a large scope RPG
(complete with unique characters, game mechanics, and plot twists and turns throughout).
What really distinguishes this game is the setting. Everything from the types of enemies you encounter, to the locales you visit, and the weapons at your disposal remain faithful to the genre and lend a sense of authenticity to the entire experience. It's charming and cohesive, with big entrances and over-the-top performances from a cast of characters the likes of which you’d expect to find in Vaudeville. I won’t give anything away but the characters (esp. the villains) are the true stars of the game and they don’t disappoint.
Every character in the game is completely unique (in appearance and dialogue). It’s hard to imagine how much work went into creating a world, one character and one house at a time, but you'll notice how meticulously places are decorated and arranged. It's a small window into who they are and the way they live. In addition to the dinnerware, you’ll find livestock penned in barns and stables, people working the farms and such: towns feel alive.
Hats are the means by which your characters change their appearances and acquire new abilities. They’re equipped, but don’t produce any defensive bonuses. This is crucial to what makes them work, once you've unlocked the skills associated with a new hat, you can choose to wear another hat for purely aesthetic purposes. In this way, you'll never have to worry about hats being outclassed by others discovered down the line. It’s a system that encourages experimentation. Receiving new hats throughout your adventure never feels old, you'll rush to try each one on as soon as you get them. Unfortunately there is some overlap in unlocked abilities so not every hat provides you with a completely new set of unlearned skills.
Especially in battles where enemies are introduced and later eulogized depending on your performance. I wish there was a greater variety of phrases rather than one or two for each type of foe, but I always looked forward to seeing how they would come to grips with being defeated: I know at least one or two lives were changed thanks to my relentless beatings.
Dialogue could use a bit of tightening up overall. In battles you'll sometimes get a message detailing every aspect of what an enemy attack does. Lick is probably the most egregious example of what I’m trying to describe here, “Weak physical damage with small chance for confusion that slightly heals the user.” Thankfully, the developer has demonstrated a willingness to address issues as they're identified.
A bit rough around the edges shall we say? Don’t expect to be blown away. Some of the enemies look like they were created in MS Paint. In addition, the font style (all caps, some spacing issues) makes it somewhat difficult to read what’s being said at times. I’m not saying you can’t read it, I’m saying you’ll appreciate how easy it is to read text in other games.
Does the industry have an award for Videogame Music of the Year? What won? This is better.

Planetary Annihilation: TITANS is a standalone expansion to the original Planetary Annihilation (which is now no longer available for purchase). If you backed the Kickstarter, it's a free upgrade. If you bought the original Planetary Annihilation, like I did, it's a cheap upgrade (with a 66% discount), making it more like a DLC. I feel the added content was worth the price that I paid, and the game overall has been significantly improved from the original game. It just feels like there's more meat on the bones.
I love RTS games, but would never claim to be particularly good at them. I therefore usually don't play them online and Planetary Annihilation is no different in this regard. For singleplayer, the game offers a Galactic War (a map of a galaxy where you jump from star system to star system and try to conquer them all) in addition to regular skirmish battles. I've had lots of fun going through the tutorial and playing Galactic War.
The game takes obvious cues from Total Annihilation and the Supreme Commander games. The factions are basically all the same: everyone gets to play with the same toys, which some people bemoan, but I think it's perfectly fine. The units are varieties of vehicles (mainly tanks), bots (fulfilling a role similar to infantry in other games), air units, naval units, and "orbital" (space) units. There are more than a hundred units, divided into two tiers. The expandalone adds "Titans": gigantic units that essentially function like the Experimentals did in Supreme Commander. As in the latter game, you start every game with your powerful commander unit (which you pick at the start of the game). If you destroy your opponent's commander, you win the game.
Planetary Annihilation has you fighting on planets, so the battle maps are spherical. The expandalone adds much-needed height to terrain, so you can get choke points on ramps (similar to Starcraft). It helps makes the terrain more interesting, both visually as well as tactically. Some people complain about the fact that the maps are spherical and therefore offer no edges to hide (you can't put your back against the wall, so to speak): I personally like this feature, and it makes scouting essential. The game favours an aggressive approach, but you can build impressive defences if you prefer to turtle. The game also offers plenty of tools to keep you from getting surprised: issue "area commands" to have your units scout and patrol the planet, and bookmark camera positions if you want to quickly switch from one point to another.
Things can get pretty hectic when there are more than two planets in a system, but I would recommend you play those in team games, so that you can each keep and eye on one to three planets each. Personally, I feel like the sweetspot is about one to three (maybe four) planets for every two players (not counting moons). If you play a skirmish on a single map you're essentially fighting a classical RTS battle (except without edges). Camera controls are fine and it's a smooth game to manoeuvre. There are buttons to quickly switch from one celestial body to another.
The ANNIHILATION part of the game comes to the fore when you add engines to moons and other small(ish) celestial bodies and use those basically like guided missiles to ram another planet, utterly destroying it and whatever was on its surface. It's always exhilirating to see a planet explode and that alone should be of sufficient interest to have you at least look at some YouTube videos of the game in action!
Graphically, the game is appealing, with a stylized, almost cartoony look to everything. The terrain is a little blocky, reminding me a bit of Endless Legend; it almost looks cute. The visual look is very clean overall and I didn't have any problems telling units apart. If you zoom out a bit, the game overlays the units with icons, which further helps making everything intelligible. The backstory is perfect in its simplicity: AIs awake to find that their creators have long since gone extinct, but they nevertheless decide to continue following their original orders by building robots to annihilate the enemy. It's almost satirical.
If there are any criticisms, I'd say that the naval units are perhaps the least useful. You really need a planet with a lot of water to feel the urge to construct any water units (and the fact that some land units hover across water doesn't help in that regard!). Flying units are generally a good alternative to naval units, especially since the enemy will need to build anti-air defences. Still, getting a big fleet out looks impressive, and I enjoy the fact that the commander can walk along the bottom of the seas to construct metal extractors and the like. The amount of units in the game can also be a little overwhelming, and often you start to rely on only a small subset of all the units available. Another minor point is that it's difficult to get the Titans out: by the time you can start building a Titan, the game tends to be over.
In short, though, I'd say this is a great RTS, and well worth the purchase, especially if you've never played Planetary Annihilation before. The visuals are great, the game plays very smoothly, and it's not hard to pick up and play, even though learning the finer points of the structures and units will, of course, take some time.

After seeing the massive amount of negative reviews and flak Bethsoft is getting for it's creation club fiasco, I feel that an honest review of the game is needed.
The good: The atmoshpere created in postapocalyptic Boston and the surrounding areas is amazing. The exploration is wonderful, with a feeling of "oh, lets check this out" almost constantly, and the companion s are well-written, with stories and emotions being unique to each. The combat is excellent, if a bit repetitive, but the combat AI seem to be well-developed. The Far Harbor and Nuka-World DLC add a lot of worldspace and content, with each being very original and well-made. The settlement system is decent, some things being locked behind perks, but overall very well done. The scrap system and the modification system
The bad: Nealy every 'cool' weapon/perk/playstyle is locked behind a leveling system that forces you to pretty much grind for the next rank of a perk. Playthroughs can get repetitive(mods help to bring more spice), and the story suffers a sort of "New Vegas Syndrome", where you must pick a faction and complete their questline. World limits are a thing still, and eventually exploration becomes a "oh, we're here again" between playthroughs. The Wasteland Workshop and Contraptions Workshop DLCs add stuff that, honestly, should've been in the game to start, with the only semi-original one being the Vault-Tec Workshop DLC. Removal of weapon/armor condition/karma system.
The ugly: Paid mods. Apparently Bethsoft didn't get it the first time they tried it so now they're back for round 2. While (most of) the Creation Club content is good, it's still paid. And if I'm going to be blatantly honest here, it's unnecessary to use. Nexusmods still carries only free content, and plenty of it to spice up the game. The paid mods fiasco thats causing the influx of negative reviews is people yelling at Bethsoft about Creation Club. Let Bethsoft figure out on their own that we don't want them by not buying for mods. That simple. Moving on, the game has some rough spots as far as FPS, and the Automatron DLC essentially adds a combination of a questline and a little bit of settlement stuff, and both should have been in the game for free anyways.
The final verdict: It's a great game. Most of the bad can be fixed via free mods and a change in playstyle. I'm usually a sneaky character, but my favorite playthrough so far was me running into raider encampments hopped up on Jet and Psycho wielding a Super Sledge. While the storyline is fairly rigid, it still is well done, with each faction feeling different.
I highly recommend this game, and at least Far Harbor and Nuka-World. The other DLCs aren't necessary, but are nice to have.

Consortium is a sci-fi'ish game set in the near future (there's more to it than that, but that's the easiest way to classify it). You play as Bishop 6 quite literally. It's a meta sort of thing, though that's not spoilers.
The Good: I loved the plot and the character interaction. It reminded me a lot of Mass Effect 2 in that regard, but with more life to it because people aren't always in the exact same spots. The graphics are nothing special, but they do fit with the art style. I loved that every choice in this game seemed to matter (we'll have to wait until part 2 to see how much), but it was nice to see immediate consequences and not just a change in an arbitrary karma bar llike some games. Yes, I'm looking at you Mass Effect 2. Speaking of a sort of karma bar, there isn't one, at least not one visible to the player and I for one loved it for that. As long as it's done well having no number attached to your actions that the player can see makes it mroe immersive and stops the player from "counting karma". The choices make a difference and aren't just things referenced in one line of dialogue lateer and forgot. A lot of your choices determine who lives and who dies, a thing most games are afraid to do and save for the last minutes of a game.
The Bad: Glitches. There are quite a few, but there's nothing that can't be fixed fairly easily. Aside from the game crashing when you alt-tab, there's no crash related bugs I've encountered. I run two 660 ti's in sli so I fully expected crashed and other stupid stuff, but it never came to that. The framerate is a bit choppy and others have mentioned it as well. I don't know if that's because of sli or just some other weirdness. It wasn't ever bad enough to where I couldn't play the game. It's a bit on the short side for 19.99, but I think the replayability makes up for it. Going through the game again with vastly different choices should have a huge effect on the story and make your game completely different.
The Ugly; I don't really have anything for this section. There aren't any really bad bugs, at least nothing on the scale of bluescreening or anything that severe.
In summary I loved this game. It is a little weird, but if you like the idea of a plot driven game then this is it. By plot driven game I mean it's not like most games where they wait for you forever and ever. This game will go on without you to a certain extent, but not to the point of where you feel like you're being dragged behind a car. I would say right now, get it on the sale that is going (at the time of this review) if you think you might want to try it and then wait for a patch. Like I mentioned before the glitches aren't super bad, but they may irritate some people. The developers seem quick on the uptatke and seem to care about fixing the bugs however. :)

This is a post-patch revisitation review. It contains no plot-revelation spoilers.
Consortium is a game I very much enjoyed, and I plan to play the future installments, but the game is also a victim of its own ambitions in certain ways.
The game concepts and mechanics are often novel and welcome, and the dedication to rpg storytelling is evident and appreciated.
And yet ...
... not all of the storytelling concepts are executed as well as someone seems to think they are. Nowhere is this more evident than in the mystery featured in chapter one.
You are charged by your superiors to investigate the possibility of a traitor aboard the Consortium aircraft. I spent real-time hours trying to perform due diligence on the investigation; reading files; questioning suspects; and the like.
The end result was only mountains of contradictory "evidence" any court would dismiss as circumstantial at best. Certainly not enough to assuredly accuse anyone, let alone convict them.
To compound the problem, even though you are investigating on the authority of the three ranking Consortium members aboard the aircraft, potential suspects routinely evade lines of questioning, or are flat-out uncooperative (however politely) -- even though everyone tells you that they want to see the problem solved.
Worst of all, the very people who set you to investigating shut you down when you complain of lack of cooperation -- but subsequently demand you produce a suspect, and express annoyance when you refuse to offer someone up on little more than a hunch based on circumstantial evidence.
It ends up making your superiors seem corrupt at worst, and heavy-handed fools at best. On my first playthrough save, I actually resigned from the Consortium over this.
I only solved the mystery thanks to a hint a fellow player gave me -- when you first arrive aboard the aircraft, look around. Someone appears to be working in a place which may later prove to be ... problematic.
None of my detective work led me to the suspect. Only this.
So, yes, Consortium is an enjoyable, and often novel, take on the rpg genre, and worth its price (in my opinion) -- but the game's clever systems and techniques are only as good as the content powering them -- and someone needed to spend a little more time inside the mystery plot to insure that it hung together as well as they believed it did.
When you succeed in drawing the player into your game-world -- as Consortium did with me -- it's important that the game world maintain its plausibility and consistency once the player has engaged.
My opinions, anyway,

Ну что ж, примем за факт, что многие японские игры довольно ДОЛГИЕ для прохождения. Около 70 часов лишь на первое прохождение. Ну и что же получается в итоге?
Tales of Berseria весьма самобытная JRPG в хорошем смысле этого слова. Она дарит чувство приключения, погружает в свой мир, и не отпускает до самых титров. В отличии от прошлых игр Tales, где сюжеты были по большей части детскими, Tales of Berseria же рассказывает нам более взрослую и суровую историю про предательство и отомщение, и показывает, что в мире нету абсолютно белого или черного. Отличным примером будет Велвет, главная героиня, которой движет лишь жажда мести, но несмотря на это, в ней еще остаются человеческие эмоции и качества. То же самое можно сказать и про других персонажей. У всех своя история и свои мотивы, но в конечном итоге, их всех объединит общая цель, к которой они будут идти на протяжении всего этого приключения.
Если с сюжетом нареканий нету, то вот к однообразной боевкой и дизайном уровней есть претензии. Иногда в игре попадаются хорошие пейзажи, но в целом многие локации играют роль лишь в виде сменяемых декораций. Тундра, степи, тропики... Все бы ничего, но вот тупо расставленные мобы напоминают, что это все таки типичная JRPG. А теперь представьте, что вы будете примерно часов 60 ходить по коридорным локациям и активно месить в капусту всяких мобов.
Однако боевку в Berseria нельзя назвать плохой или же однородной и монотонной. Даже напротив, бои очень динамичные и иногда даже захватывающие. Благодаря различным комбо-приемам, которые можно настроить под себя, можно довольно красиво убивать, делать всякие сальтухи и финты ушами. А еще тут в бою можно менять активного персонажа как перчатки, поэтому если вам надоест все время играть одним персонажем, его можно тут же сменить.
Я играл на "Умеренном" уровне сложности, поэтому игра для меня оказалась в некоторых местах довольно потной и приходилось действовать по уму. Лишь благодаря этому однообразная боевка, внезапно, становится довольно гибкой и умной, со своими нюансами, вроде правильной подборки снаряжения, смены контролируемого персонажа в бою, настройки комбо, и поведения неконтролируемых в бою персонажей. А еще тут можно приготовить похавать, и тем самым получить различные одноразовые бонусы на следующий бой.  Эти бонусы могут различаться, в зависимости от того, что приготовлено, кто это приготовил, и какой у него прокачанный уровень кулинарии. Привет, FFXV!
В игре есть еще всякие мини игры со своими наградами, немного сайд-квестов, боевые испытания, охота на элитных монстров и даже аналог рейд-боссов (но это не точно). Если играть на низких уровнях сложности, и вам не особо интересны все эти побочные штуки, то вся эта морока вам может и не понадобится. Вобщем, тут уж вы решайте на свое усмотрение.
Под конец скажу, это моя первая пройденная JRPG. И я ею доволен. Звезд с неба не хватает, но тем не менее, является качественным продуктом на рынке игр. Любителям данного жанра - это определенно "Must-have", а вот тем, кто знает о JRPG лишь по наслышке... Дайте игре шанс. Благодаря настраиваемой сложности, игра лояльна к новичкам. Да и не только поэтому, но и по сюжету. Для понимая сюжета проходить предыдущие игры серии не надо. Tales of Berseria это самостоятельная игра, со своим сюжетом, прямо как игры серии Final Fantasy, где в каждой игре своя история, не связанная с другими. Тем не менее, пара отсылок к Tales of Zestiria все же будет, но не более.

So here I am... Trying to get KOTOR to work on my computer and failing miserably. I go to the store with $20 in my Steam wallet. Fed up and tired to pick an indie game that looked interesting.
I run into CONSORTIUM.
I decide ah, what the hell and buy it. To my surprise, it actually turned out to be a great game.
The story goes as follows: You are you. The game itself is actually a portal to an alternate reality's future where you inhabit the body of a man codenamed "Bishop - 6" a high ranking officer in the CONSORTIUM. That's all the game tells you about the character (at least in the time I played it) The game physically cannot let you know about Bishop's past, as it glitches out when people talk about it. The characters and the writing are better than a lot of triple-a titles out there and can be very humorous at times.
The music is beautiful, it sounds like it could go in KOTOR itself, and there is a reason for that: Jeremy Soule composed this game's soundtrack. As an admirer of his work I was pleasantly surprised.
Other than a few minor bugs, the CONSORTIUM is a fantastic experience in my honest opinion.
Check this game out! You'll be glad you did!

Long time player of SC 4 here, heavily modded (keep it mind when reading, I ll be biased in that sense). Also, if anyone is color blind read 2 straight (there is the game breaker).
I really, really tried to like Cities XL. I tried it more than 4 different times. I really love city building games but I always felt CXL was unpolished and unfinished. My game breaker were always the same 2.
1- Roads and road layout. I am used to a grid like set up from SC 4, I can admit that. But I was never able to get used to not being able to make at least some consistent griding (it was always off and wouldn't stay stright and parrallel, so in the end I had less building space on one end than in the other). That wasn't that terrible. The REAL ISSUE was that I had to manually demolish each and every building to build a road expansion. And given there was no grid for reference placing was always odd. An avenue would not sit on one side as any 2 gridded element might but in the middle, taking up some space from adjacent building. And given that I had to expand a lot this was a nuisance that meant demolishing huge parts of my town just to fit a small avenue, casuse I had no idea what space it would take. If you are used to superposition building (that is to say, build on top of something else and the game make necessary demolishing) be advised, it won't work. (There is a mod that helps partially with this: you dont need to demolish a road if you want to replace it with another one of the same size, the rest of the issues remain).
2- Lack of colorblind-friendly interface. Road traffic is codified in red, green and yellow strips over the roads (changing zoom distance makes it a little bit more clear, not that much). I am color blind, I can tell up to a point the difference between these three colors, but it is really hard for me when the colored area is as small as in some cases is. And there is no easy way to have the camera move to the problematic zone. You have to use the map to navigate using the color scheme I mentioned above. Also, when you click a road stretch you get the info on that specific stretch, including a colored ball with the usage. The ball is completly impossible for me to use but if you hover over it you get (at last) a readable tooltip saying usage in percentage. This a too repetitive task to be so hassle ridden, so each and every time I uninstalled the game and went back to play SC 4 that gets this fixed in some simple steps such as using blue-green-yellow-red for traffic congestion (not perfect but it helps a lot).
3- Transportation options are really lacking for any SC player. Check the list, many sensible choices you may want may be missing.
Very specific reasons but some may agree they are important. On the up side, farm building is quite fun.

Street FIghter Alpha! Scratch that, even alphas are in better condition than this game.
Single Player:
This has to be the most barebones offering in a fighting game ever! Even some early access games are in much better shape than this.
There is no Arcade mode or even versus CPU mode, which is something that has been present in games since the days of Street Fighter I.
You're thrown into the tutorial without the ability to select settings on PC and said tutorial mode is also lacking. and speaking of settings, no option to connect my PS4 fightstick!? The game only launched on PC and PS4. Why the hell does it only support Xbox controllers and sticks? You had one job Capcom!
The use of V-Skills/Triggers is not explained properly at all. Not everyone is going to play with Ryu, Capcom.
The "Story" mode is laughably short, with no option to select difficulty. The voice acting is cringeworthy, the presentation is horrendous and replayability is ZERO.
The training mode is also lacking. There is no explanation on what a specific characters V-Skill or V Trigger does, even in the command lists.
Only Survival mode is worth playing as of now. But you lose all progress if god forbid Capcom servers are on the fritz, which they are more often than not.
Oh, and you also lose single player progress for disconnecting from the server. Perfect!
Multiplayer:
Unless you have friends on hand to play with, tough $hit! Battle lounges are finnicky at best and as for finding a Ranked or Casual match, I wouldn't know! I haven't been able to play a single one of those since launch.
I've had the game searching for a match since before I started writing this review, which was over an hour ago.
In that time, I've read three chapters of a book, read through my entire Feedly feed, had food delivered, ate that and then took a dump. Oh, and finished writing this review I guess. Weirdly productive, I know!
But as I sit here writing this, the game is still "Waiting for your opponent..."
I have not been able to play a single ranked match since launch.
And yet, Capcom says: "Matchmaking is now working as intended and users should be able to find online matches without much of a wait in both Ranked and Casual mode."
Capcom, matchmaking is not fixed. It is the exact opposite of that and then some. As of right now, the game is just a match-finding simulator, and not a very good one either.
Shame on you Capcom for exploiting our love of Street Fighter and giving us this piece of garbage.
For the love of all that is holy, please fix this pile of horse crap!
Edit:
I should explain that, technically, the game is amazing. I've had the pleasure of playing matches against friends in versus mode and battle lounges. The graphics are great and controls are amazing.
It's a shame though that I cannot level up or gain any LP because the match making component is broken.
The 14 hours I have on record playing this are from leaving this on decicated search for a match overnight. and yet, it did not find a single match! Match making remains broken 5 days after launch.
I have tweeted several times to SFVServer, emailed capcom and also posted on their upates on the capcom-unity forum. They are totally ignoring the fact that match making is completely flawed.
