With nods to Earthbound and Classic Westerns, Boot Hill Heroes part 1 is a well-done entry in what could be a really good trilogy.
10 years ago, a hero averted disaster by bringing the leader of the Saint's Little  - the most ruthless gang in all of Bronco County - to justice....but that was 10 years ago. I mean what is that? A decade? That's a mighty long time. It's time enough for all the Saint's Little Gang to plan for their return. Chaos is brewing, and it's up to a new generation of heroes to put a stop to it. Will they succeed? Or is it going to be their last round-up? Well, since this is just the beginning, I'd hate to imagine they failed their quest before it even started.
Earthbound gets mentioned often when discussing this game, and for good reason. Both games share similar aspects such as perspective and enemies appearing on the map rather than at random. BHH also has some obvious call-backs, which can be found in Kickstart Creek, but we're getting a little ahead of ourselves here. Let's talk about the biggest difference, the battle-system.
This game uses an active battle-system. Each character (up to 4) can equip four vantages. These can consist of attacks, healing abilities, stances, and so on. Having the right combination of vantages for battle is a necessity. Attacking is more than just stabbing or shooting something until it falls over. You gotta figure out a strategy. Do you pick the enemy apart with a thousand cuts? Debilitate them with several status effects? Or save up for those powerful attacks? There isn't an "item" option in battle. You can't hand someone a sarsaparilla if their health is low. Either have someone equip a healing vantage, or make proper use of stances. Stances are the cheapest abilities, and for good reason. They put characters on the defensive, reducing or outright avoiding damage. There are many stances, some not even defensive at all.
Meter management is an essential tactic. Using abilities requires power, and it can take awhile to use the most devastating attacks. The same goes for the enemy. Even when you don't know their next move, you always know how long it'll take them to perform it. That's the key moment to go in any stances that you have. Not doing so is a fatal mistake. Still, death isn't quite the end in battle, your characters will recover given enough time, but they'll be worse off. Wounded party members tend to bleed out, become less resistant to status effects, and generally have a tougher time staying alive. If they accrue too many wounds, they're permanently out. Okay, I mean permanent as in: "until they see a doctor" but whatever. Basically, you have to go into battle with the mindset that anything you can do, the enemy can do as well.
Like I said though, this is just the beginning of the trilogy. It only takes about 7 or 8 hours to reach the end of this chapter, and that's hardly enough time to get your boots wet. However, there are several battles that will require an understanding of how the west was won, and they're not the kind you can grind enough experience to breeze through. I expect battles in the next two entries to emphasize this unique and fun battle-system.
Some other things I'll note:
-There are no clone NPCs. Usually with these 16-bit RPGs we see 20 dozen of the same townspeople everywhere. Not so with this game, everyone is different.
-I'd be lying if I said that the music doesn't elevate this game. Jake "virt" Kaufman provides a great soundtrack.
-Easy (and missable!) achievements. Pay attention to your surroundings.
In short, Boot Hill Heroes is on the right track. Hopefully subsequent entries are even better, I'd hate to see such a promising start go to waste.

This game should not be $40. First off, adding a bunch of units while barely changing anything else does not warrant an entirely new game, and secondly, a lot of the features and content in this "game" (read: DLC) were promised in the original kickstarter for the first game.

At most, this game should be a $5-10 DLC, and really could even be released a free patch.

I originally had massive problems with running this game, and plenty of others did as well. In my frustration i wrote a negative review because of its near unplayable state.
Interdimensional Studios themselves admited ( and apologized ) that "Consortium's" launch was horribly buggy and thankfully this is no longer the case. With all their hard work and dedication to the project all bugs (game-breaking or just weird) are now gone.
I intended on fully editing this review if the problems were solved and now they have.
I can best describe 'Consortium' as a mix of the original Star Trek and Mass Effect with the shooting mechanics and engine of Half Life 2 and if that mix doesn't sound good to you ( or you didn't like any of these examples ) then it's hard to recommend. However if you're looking for epic 1st person sci-fi romp with an emphasis on story, dialogue, player choice story and wrapped up with some decent shooting mechanics look no further.
'Consortium' is also the first in a trilogy and only lasts about 10 hours at the most, however it never feels "too short" and i'm very excited for what's to come. The story is brilliantly written, the game has marvelous presentation and the characters throughout the adventure are interesting and their dialogue throughout it is well done. Combat is a bit like an old school shooter mixed with Half-Life 2 (which i find works well enough) but it's hardly the focus of the game.
No, the focus of 'Consortium' is the interactions between you and the other crew aboard the ship with multiple dialogue choices and the dire consequences for most of them, and Interdermentional studios have done it brilliantly. Even with my previous frustration at launch it's obvious how far 'Consortium' has come and the Master Edition truly is worth anyone's time especially for only $20.
This is the type of game i've been wanting ever since Mass Effect came out, and it certainly doesn't disappoint.

This game takes the concept of grinding far beyond the celestial realm of grinding as you have already known it to exist in other games. It is exceptionally more grindy than it initially leads you to believe; you're lured in with skills that level very, very quickly because of the constant double experience time that freemium players pay for. Seriously, someone just paid for 26 hours of 2x exp - $420 worth. There is a massive plateau from about combat level 50 to combat level 100, at the very least, where the seemingly efficient way to gain any money or combat XP is to farm Efreet spawns. They're high leveled but drop the illustrious Efreet 'pet', which can be sold on the market for about $400k gold. Unfortunately, they have a 0.25% drop rate, like practically everything else in the game.
The creators of RPG-MO are sadistic in their pursuit to make you grind and grind and grind your life away to get that one Efreet pet, or that one Paladin Shield, or that one ____ (any item). In other traditional RPGs, a high level skill like mining or forging should yield a steady income of gold that increases in proportion to the level. RPG-MO works on a leveling system that exponentially makes leveling harder while providing minimal, if even at all, positive gains. Want to be a high level forger and make sapphire weapons? That sounds great! You only need 60 forging, but how are you going to get to the azurite ore if the only two azurite spots in the game are guarded by level 150 mobs? The sad part is – sapphire isn't even high tier weaponry. And if you finally do survive long enough to start smelting azurite bars into sapphire weaponry? Well, the game has such horrid 'success rates' for most forged items that you're probably going to waste most of the bars you just painstakingly made. And if you do manage to make a sapphire sword? You get just about the same XP as if you had made a lower-tier steel sword.
Ultimately, I don't recommend this game until the creators make all the drop rates much, much more tolerable. Once you hit about combat level 60, the game becomes frustratingly hard to make any sort of vertical progress in terms of new gear... unless you farm Efreets. But even if you're farming Efreets, good luck with that 0.25% drop rate!

My last game from Tales Series on PC, this one was truly  wonderful. It improves on Zesteria in almost every way, and while its story didn't have the same massive impact as Symphonia did,  the great characters, in my opinion, make up for it. What you end up with is a Tales game with a great story, great characters, and the best gameplay so far.
The game is easy to get into, as the equipment system is streamlined from Zesteria's overly compliacted skill system, with enhancement being a linear process with the materials required being somewhat difficult to come by. It's also quite obvious which items are safe to sell, most of the time - being equipment you have copies of or "miscellaneous" items you can mostly find by picking up everywhere.
The combat is a little more complicated, in that souls limit the length of your combos, and your combos are almost completely customisable, provided your controlling a character manually. This is mostly good, though it can be difficult ot figure out which moves flow together well, and to construct a moveset that'll cover most enemy types and weaknesses. However, the AI is so good that sometimes it's better to let them handle controlling your character. You also rarely need to worry about taking care of your other members in combat because of this.
The story is refreshing darker than the last games, as the protagnist is for once not a bright, cheerful and optimistic hero. More of an anti-hero, Velvet and her party's adventures are different and kept me guessing on how their journey would go. The outfit though... was a bit too striperific, know what I mean? Oh well.
The chracters were great, and the dialogue this time was well written... though the subtitles had quite a few errors, which may have been due to localisation errors. Still I loved the skits more than ever between the characters, and was mostly sucked into the story due to these great characters, not so much the story itself.
Lastly, the graphics were great, soliid 60 FPS throughout the game, and the environments look gorgeous. The only real negative of the game is how each environment doesn't change much as you go through, making it somewhat boring to navigate dungeons and fields. Music is OK, though it really shines during the emotional moments.
Probably one of the best JRPGs I've ever played, I'd recommend this to any RPG fan, or anime fan that like games too. I will miss this game, and its characters, in a similar way I loved Symphonia, and other great RPGs like Baldur's  Gate 2. A truly wonderful game.

Here is a detailled review to help you in your choice :
Detailled review (pretty long, and from a non-english native, be prepared!) :
The world is filled with bad guys, demons, corrupted nobles and wars everywhere. But one man stand against that. And he's ready to everything to stop this madness and bring peace to the world.
How Classic.
But that's not the story we are going to play. We are going to see what happened
.
And not with good guys, but with a team of people who don't give a f*ck about what's good and bad and only care about their own desires.
Just for this, the game is worth it : You're not following people who fight for the "good". And this create a lot of interesting situations you will not see in any other game.
Add to this a team of characters with strong personalities (and especially different goals for everyone) and you get really fun cutscenes where no one agree on anything. Talking of cutscene, there are a
. Always, and for all kind of subject, most notably on non-important stuff, which help seeing our characters in their every-day life, their are not just puppet meant to reach the end of game.
Add this to a 70-80 hours of main story, and you've got a tale you will remenber for years.
Like most JRPG, gameplay goes into two parts : Exploration and battle.
Not much to say on exploration : you travel through towns and dungeons, gathering stuff, getting informations from NPC.. classic stuff. And there are a few mini games here and there.
As for battle, this is also a big point to the game : you control one character with 3 others helping you. You move freely trought the arena, dodging ennemy's attack and looking for the best opportunity to strike back. Or you can go head-on and pray the ennemies dies before you, works too. You can choose the comportment of your teammates too, will they attack the same ennemy as you? The weak one? Stay back and use magic? it's up to you to tell them.
This game also has a interesting system of weakness : each ennemy is weak to one or several element (fire, water, wind, earth) and has a type (beast, snake, undead, human...). Each of your attack is gonna hit one of those weakness/type, and the more you can hit in a combo, the more the damage can go up. This force you to adapt your combo to each new ennemy, preventing the game to become stale. Which is quite needed considering how long this game is.

Pros:

Very fun and addictive. I like pretty much all the gameplay changes compared to SF4. The input buffer makes combos much easier so there is less of an artificial barrier between players. There also is no more priority linking where you tap multiple buttons in a row which is just asking for a repetitive stress injury. In general, the higher damage combos start with heavier moves than in SF4 so more risk = more reward. V-skill is much more fun and varied than focus attack. V-trigger is more interesting and less of a revenge mechanic than ultra combos. Only supers can kill with chip damage in this game. Backdashes are no longer invincible. No more crouch tech and many option selects in general.
The roster is very fun and diverse, no clones, no terrible joke characters, and only two shotos (Ryu and Ken). And six more characters coming this year.
The matchmaking is very quick, with ranked points and leagues. You can join matches automatically in the background, in the main menu or in training mode or anywhere basically which makes it very easy to get games.
I like the art style, costumes, animations, stages (especially the stage interactions if you kill someone in the corner), and music.
The character backstories are really short but they have some funny lines and handdrawn art. The larger cinematic story is coming as a free update in the summer and the trailer looks good. I don't buy fighting games for these things anyway so I consider them a bonus. You should have a decent internet connection for this game. (btw the launch day server issues seem completely resolved for me anyway)

The game is pretty, plays well online and offline, and is really fun to learn and play. It might be a bit incomplete at face value in terms of single-player content, but if you take the time to explore the diverse cast of 16 characters, you'll see that you'll have a lot of time to do solo stuff. But let's face it, playing with other people is where this game shines, and that experience is amazing with friends, or against people online. Plus, free content is planned to be release regularly during the game's lifetime which the developers say will be quite a number of years from now.
At launch, a few days ago, it would have been harder to recommend, but "Crapcom" is actively listening and responding to fans both on PC and PS4, so I trust that their support in the coming days, months, and years will help make the roughly 60$ purchase justified. They've already fixed a lot of the initial connection issues and finding a match online is quick, and playing online is a joy. It's not a bad buy. If you're willing to put your faith in Capcom, as hard as it may sound, you might just end up with one of the finest fighting game experiences ever made, as well as help build the community for even more fun.
UPDATE: After 87+hours into the game, 4 characters, some stages, story mode, trials etc...
I think this game is now most definitely worth it for people.
Even in the single player aspect. For people who like challenges, Survival mode is actually good (NO IT IS NOT CHEAP AND IMPOSSIBLE TO WIN). Yes it can be frustrating at times, but look at Dark Souls, Darkest Dungeon, and those kinds of games. You lose and learn from your mistakes. Then try and try again to unlock all that fight money for characters and costumes. For story-driven people, the story mode here is... okay. It's entertaining enough to go through, and nets you a ton of Fight Money.
If you think this game doesn't have value, you're wrong. Capcom is not cheating you out of the money you'll spend on it.
I put my faith into this game even before launch, and so far I'm satisfied with their service, despite a few hiccups here and there.
PS: My 87 hours are mostly hours spent practicing, playing survival, and playing with friends :)

These are the strengths and weaknesses of the game and having obsessively played it and beating it start to finish I feel I have a fairly good comprehension of where the game excels and in some areas underwhelm for those who don't want to read everything I have to say I will sum things up first with a 8/10 score although this could be subject to change as some of the gripes I have that hold this game back from being a masterpiece could easily be remedied as this game is not yet complete as previously mentioned.
Strengths:
1) Local Multiplayer is something that is lacking in a lot of new games, I feel that Dave definitely knew what he was doing not just in getting a game to function for multiple people but also to have it flow well. I like the fact that locally I can still change my gear and skills while my friend may be running around or vice versa if we alternate party leaders. The menu system leaves a bit to be desired in terms of it's looks in my opinion but in terms of functionality A+
2) The pacing is done well, I strongly dislike how part one ends in that it feels like you are cut off right as the story is getting started but aside from that I never felt bored or that I was in a certain area for too long, I have this listed as a strength because once part 2 and 3 come out and the game is finished my main issue with the pacing (the end of part one) will cease to exist
3) Level Design, again keeping in mind that there will be more content to come I feel what is there is done well the areas are colorful and are quite different as you travel from one main hub to the other considering that all of this takes place in a western setting the variety within that is quite vast. The towns feel like the right size and the different dungeons feel like the right length, the only part I felt was tedious was the bonus dungeon at the end (without any spoilers you'll know why when you get there) with that exception though as I said what is there works great.

Decent but could be better:
1) The story is not bad but not great either. That could have a lot to do with the fact that by the time you finish part one it is just barely getting started, it's too early to say in terms of the overall scope but having said that I think you should have done and seen more by the time you reach a third of the games length. The characters are servicable and have their own motivations as to why they join up with the protagonist but to be honest I feel like every character in this game is a character I've seen a million times before. It's not a big deal but for the longevity of the series I hope these characters can break out of their stereotypes (Kid and Doc and the antagonists come to mind) I feel like there is potential in all of them to be something more but Moon in particular as a native american is not someone you see in a games story too often and I think there are a lot of interesting themes that could be explored with some research now that the story is starting to take off as part one ends.
2) The music wasn't bad, it definitely suited the theme of a western well, this really just comes down to my own personal opinion but I wish there were tracks that were a bit more catchy. When I think about games that this one was based off of like Earthbound there are just things that make you go "oh wow" and make you stop and listen to the track like Onett for example. The music does its job but I'm hoping that some tracks will come along that stand out a little bit more as the game picks up.
3) The first playthrough getting new attacks was interesting and the there is nothing wrong with a turn based rpg but I feel like there could be more variety, you learn a lot of different skills with different hats that you unlock as the game progresses but when I tried playing through a second time with a friend it was almost agonizing that there was usually just a go to move that was better than everything else or offered no real tactical change, kick kick kick dodge, or kick kick kick heal, etc. I feel like the core combat system and the idea of using x amount of points based on how strong the attacks are is a great idea but it needs to come with some skills that have a bit more variety. Also the customization of the weapons leaves a bit to desire, maybe it's because I never really liked grinding to gather materials to improve gear but I also feel like the options there are kind of limited, I would like to see it expanded upon in the latter 2 installments.
Weaknesses:
1) The overall presentation of this game was pretty good but I feel like the menus look very ugly relative to the characters and the buildings. I think the health bars etc. should be redone as they stand out as something not quite on par with everything else, The dialogue boxes are not as bad but it wouldn't hurt if they were spruced up a bit.
2) The length of the game is very short, I completed it in a couple of days. I think there should be some extra things for you to do outside of going to a dungeon or grinding for materials. This would take some work but it would be cool if there were some random side quests or other interesting things to do while waiting for part 2 or part 3 when part 2 is out. Random encounters and the like to make the world a bit more lively. Maybe some bandits roll into town and you get some perks for beating them or something. Just something to break up the monotany of town/dungeon over and over.
3) There is no online multiplayer I feel like with how well the local multiplayer was designed this was a missed opportunity, Though I understand the reason why it was not included (most likely down to resources)
4) I feel like the game and a lot of games like this are lacking the innovations that it was inspired by. If you just want to go back to the old days and play a game like the snes days then this is right up your alley, and for me I did enjoy it quite a bit because of the yearning for nostalgia but to me I would like to see some new interesting ideas. I'm not talking about mind blowing graphics or state of the art effects but innovation in terms of gameplay. Things to do, places to see. Just because it was inspired by old school games doesn't mean it should be limited by those same conventions. The art style? makes sense because it's one main guy and a couple of outsiders helping him work on the game, completely makes sense. As an example and I'm just throwing it out there I didn't think about this in depth or anything but just something to inspire, what about if you could duel people in the game? Maybe a mini game to clear a town that has been raided by bandits with a timer and then you can have a gun duel with the leader it could be a weekly or monthly event where you could unlock new gear. How about horse races with your friends? These may sound bland but elaborated upon I'm sure they could be something interesting that could help elevate the game. If they don't work don't put them in the game but It'd just be neat to have something on the side to do and look forward to.
Final Thoughts:
I do really like this game, despite a lot of the things I have said there is nothing wrong with what's here, I just figured I could contribute some ideas and as parts 2 and 3 are completed maybe some of them will find their way into the game in some form. I'm not really complaining more just constructive criticism as I feel the foundations for a strong game are definitely here. If not this is still worth $10 easy.

The store page does not do a very good job of clarifying that only the first third of the game is actually complete (except for a single line at the very end of the description), and as such, there really isn't that much of a game here yet.
Minor Spoilers: Right as the game is about to really start, when you finally have all 4 characters in your party and a clear goal, the game abruptly stops. You'll have to either buy BHH2 or pick up the DLC to have any real full party content.
The part of the game that is there is a solid, fun RPG, but I would not recommend buying this game until June 2015, when the final segment is slated to come out.
About the parts of the game that are complete though, the combat system is pretty strong, allowing a decent amount of customization, and a cool stance system adds timing and defensive elements typically not found in this type of RPG.  Enemies also use stances, but the game does a pretty terrible job of explaining what your enemeis stances do when they're not the same stances that you can use.

This game shows promise, but I would wait for the trilogy to be completed before picking it up.

It's free, so it earns a positive review from my end.
The game does a lot of things well. The atmosphere is nice and mysterious, a little eerie at times, too. It's rather macabre, as well, especially in hindsight now that certain things you discover early on make horrific sense after you'd beaten the game.
It's a nice game to help you relax, since you're just pointing and clicking and it's impossible to lose. There's also a nice little progressive pace, as you keep doing the same thing over and over, but the results keep getting darker and darker. Just play this and relax, unless you get too freaked out by the ominous atmosphere.
The game also does a lot of things bad (which I don't mind forgiving, since it's free). Getting around in the cabin doesn't have a good and sensible flow. I found myself having to get around in zigzag patterns and I couldn't get used to this broken mobility, at all. As I said before, you keep doing the same thing, only with different results. To be more specific, you keep clicking on the same objects and you get different results, but it's not always clear which object you have to click on and it doesn't require any sort of thinking to know which object you have to click on, so it's all just trial and error. It does get frustrating after a while, especially since you keep walking around the cabin in a broken, zigzag flow to get from one object to another. Also, I like unveiling mysteries, and I'm more analytic about it than the next guy, but I really didn't feel like thinking too much in this game. I'm sure I came across many subtle messages in the game, but they were maybe a little too subtle for my liking giving that I couldn't take this game seriously enough, since it's not really that much of a good game.
Nothing special, but I definitely got my money's worth.

I love this game. They've polished it up a lot since the original PA release. Galactic War is now fairly entertaining and playable. The UI enhancements are many and appreciated. I like this a lot better than SC II and similar games for a couple reasons. I like the 'flow-based' economy more than the harvesting economy present in the majority of RTS these days. I also like the focus on large scale in terms of unit and structure count. Build queues can be set absurdly deep, or you can just set a mix and put unit-producing factories on endless repeat.
The result is really huge engagements and lots of flexibility.
There is a great co-op mode (this was present in the original PA), where you share resources and units against the opposing team. It helps if you have unequal skill levels--you can have the less skilled players micromanage battles or invasions or economic expansion and they'll still have fun.
I consider this an improvement over PA. I believe there is a discount available if you own the original PA. If you are a Kickstarter backer I believe you get it for free!

Half-Life, the game that redefined the future of the first-person shooters again.
is the impact it had on the history of video games. From this point all FPS' took Half-Life as reference for its revolutionary gameplay and brilliant narrative. This series is very important to me, in fact it's my favorite. I'll explain why.
For starters, even though there are scenes in the game in which there's narrative and interaction with NPCs the player's control is never taken away, with the exception of two scenes. Something I like a lot about Half-Life's narrative is the way it is treated. Throughout the game you don't notice anything strange to the naked eye but if you look closely you'll see some pretty subtle details which probably are a hint to something bigger. There's an answer to that, but I won't tell you exactly at what time.
Despite all this the plot of the game is a complete enigma. We can get answers to some questions but we'll never get to fully know why all this happened. Even in Half-Life 2 we won't get an answer (hence all the begging for HL3). It's because of all this that I think Half-Life's narrative is brilliant. It has a superficial plot and also something deeper going on behind the scenes.
As I mentioned earlier, the gameplay was revolutionary for its time. The movement, the gunplay, the level design, the enemies, everything was incredible. The mechanics are fluid and responsive. There are also some puzzles to vary a bit, although nothing too difficult. The gameplay in general is pretty polished so any fan of FPS' will feel like at home.
The graphics for its time were pretty good. The FPS' were still developing aesthetically and Half-Life was a step forward without a doubt. It's obvious that by today's standards it isn't impressiveHowever for me the visuals of this game are a classic, a stamp that was won over the years product of the nostalgia of players like me.
Both, the sound effects as the composition of the music are excellent. The SFX are amazingly characteristic, whether it's for the weapons, background sounds, characters or enemies. The use and placement of these sounds is something that can't be overlooked either. There are scenes that felt incredibly atmospheric due to the placement of these sounds and use of filters. It's simply incredible, it's the quality that I would like to be able to replicate in my own video games someday.
As for the music... I don't have much to say. It's perfect. Each piece of the soundtrack is incredible on its own and is used at the precise moment in the game. I'm delighted by the quality of this- no, every aspect of the game.
In conclusion, Half-Life is a perfect game, as simple as that. Any fan of first-person shooters should have tried by now this game or its sequels. It's one of those classics that you have to play at least once in your life.

Heck yeah! This review is for long-time Burnout fans, although new players will find the advice to be just about as helpful. If you're thinking about buying this, read on!
BURNOUT FANS:
First off, rest assured that this game stays true to the classic Burnout style: lots of shiny pieces. Burnout has always been proud of lots of shiny pieces and they still are. The 3rd-person is identical to the previous and the boost has the same starts-slow-but-gets-really-fast-quick effect. However, the handling has one big change: THE E-BRAKE. All previous games had a single brake button that let you drift, slow down, stop and go in reverse. The brake button now does all of those except the first. It took a while for me to realize the change. Now, all drifting is done with a second e-brake key. It is WAY more powerful than previous versions, as it literally locks your wheels and puts your car in a 180-degree spin instantly. It takes some serious getting-used-to, and every car handles a little different.
Let's get the Cons out of the way first:
1. Events are no longer in a menu. They are placed randomly around the map at intersections. Some of them require a specific car, which can be frustrating because you aren't sure until you get to the stoplight.
2. Cars are more random. Revenge eliminated the organization completely. This one is even moreso. You have no idea what car is next and no way to organize them properly.
3. Lots of slow-mo, even in menus and car-changing screens. Get used to it.
4. Every time you crash, take down another car or do other cool things, the game slows down time to focus on that event. Another person complained that this interrupted the flow of races, and it does.
5. The city is huge. Finding specific things can take a while to get to.
6. You can take down custom cars that drive randomly, but they are unmarked and can be difficult to find.
7. The E-Brake takes some serious practice. It's a whole new feature with a lot of power.
8. The online store is now closed. Personally I consider this lazy, but then again I don't spend real money in-game anyway.
I just now realized how long the Con list is. Don't worry, a few show up in the Pro section.
Now for some Pros:
1. The city is huge. There are tons of jumps, shortcuts and other sweet stuff to find along the way. Rather than try to find them mid-race, as with other Burnout games, all races take place in a wide-open city that you can explore for yourself, meaning you can locate all the shortcuts and nasty areas (I hate pillars) far in advance, giving you a massive advantage.
2. "You found a giant BURNOUT sign. Smash all of them." Cool, how many of them are there? "200."
What.
"You found a shortcut! Find them all!" Okay, how many are there? "400."
What.
Yes, the number of shortcuts and bonuses is off the charts. This can be bad if you're OCD and need to find them all but it's also nice to just drive around and nail them as you go, rather than drive from event to event with nothing to do.
3. I mentioned the slo-mo interrupting gameplay. In reality, it only lasts three to five seconds in a race. Takedowns are two to three seconds. I don't even notice it affecting the flow. Plus it shows you whatever bonuses came from it, which is better than it showing you the bonuses without the cutscene and distracting you. Lots of flying parts, but that's what we love from the series. The in-menu slo-mo can be a bit distracting, but it doesn't slow down the selection speed and will skip the cinematics if you want to get back on the road.
4. There are custom cars to hunt down and takedown. I mentioned it in Cons because it can take a while and you honestly don't know where they are (they aren't marked on your map). However, the custom cars have a habit of finding you. They will fly past you, honking their horn and driving like maniacs. This happens randomly, but once you get into a chase, you should be able to take them down (with a little practice with the e-brake). I actually prefer the random incidents because it keeps you on your toes. Don't worry if you don't catch them: I lost track of one, and it showed up again less than five minutes later.
5. 75 cars. Nice number. Expect to see tons of classics (something the other games have been seriously short on), customs, supercars, trucks, etc. And motorcycles, which are separated into their own category.
6. The sound effects and graphics are all fantastic. No cheap repeats on a ton of cars.
7. Cars have different stats. Unlike previous games, the stat changes are very noticable. Different types of cars handle VERY differently. You find yourself getting attached to a car, trading up, then learning how to drive all over again. This may seem irritating, but again you have the whole city to drive around in for practice. No punishments for wrecking your car, either.
8. You can customize all of the controls. Personally, I suggest the following set-up for comfort and control:
Turning: Arrow keys
Acceleration: Spacebar
Brake: Left Ctrl
E-Brake: Left Shift (I find myself using it more often than Brake)
Boost: D (just to keep it comfortable)
9. The E-Brake is a lot of fun. As tricky and powerful as it is, it makes emergency 180-degree turns a cakewalk with some practice. Rather than the other games, where you tapped the brake to drift, you tap the E-Brake for a nano-second, as it actually engages the emergency brake and has a much more realistic effect. Experiment!
10. No actual course maps means no hitting those obnoxious XXXXXX barriers. You can take any route you want to get from A to B. The game has an ingenous feature that helps with staying on course. Rather than looking from the road to the mini-map to stay on course, the game shows green roadsigns at the top of your screen. When you're racing and you hit an intersection, it will show which roads are available and the best option will blink green-to-white slowly. You can ignore the mini-map completely and let the game keep you on track. Extremely useful if you get off-course, which is loads of fun, as you can use the E-Brake to make a 90-degree turn at 120 mph without losing control, then do it again in the opposite way to get back on course.
Overall, I recommend this to any long-term Burnout fan. It is VERY different, but it keeps the same style and overall laid-back attitude about racing. The freedom takes some getting used to, but I find myself just driving around for the heck of it, looking for new stunt ramps and practicing with my car, which is an extremely valuable feature. I know my Cons list is long, but honestly they are very much outweighed by the Pros. It has plenty of amusing in-game content. For example, instead of getting a new car in your garage and seeing it shown off, new cars are dropped out of the sky, totally trashed. Drive them to a mechanic to a repair (they are drive-through and it takes exactly 0 seconds to make the change, plus a short 360-degree cutscene that doesn't slow you down).
Go for it. If nothing else, it's worth the experience. Best of luck!
-Matt

Not gonna lie i am really enjoying this game...there are a few problems to do with balancing in some areas of units, seen as they can be built so quickly early game and can end up dominating, however these units can be countered if eco has been balanced and you have built up a force to counter it. I have found that the hard difficulty AI is quiet challenging especially when they use rush tactics early on and nuke spam/zeus spam late game...but the challenge can create some intense games if looking to play on your own or with friends. In terms of chrashes; i have only experienced one crash and it ended up restarting my computer, however i think this was due to the fact i had run the game for almost a day playing with friends with up to 16 planets + an asteroid belt.
I have found this game to be one of the best ive played in my opinion, if you love rts and mass destruction, then this game is for you! Just make sure that your specs are up to the requirements cause the game can be quiet demanding when massive scale battles are taking place. Also the system designer is amazing! So far ive been able to create our solar sytem...including Saturn, it is just a shame that the asteroid belt cant be placed around planets and instead four moons took its place. Apart from that i cant wait to get importing new systems and planets and maybe getting a few mods from the old game to add to the experience!
Overall this game isnt a master piece and it is a little overpriced...especially when it already has the vanilla game from the original (which i did not have chance to play) however the newer version has just improved in almost every aspect...but it does earn a positive review from me as it is my dream game and im glad the developers listened to the feedback from the original and have followed up with a much better game experience.
Edit : Orbital combat could be more fleshed out; for example, when playing on a large system that takes 5 or 10 minutes to get to the outer planet, it is frustating if an enemy that is almost defeated (the base is destroyed but commander remaining) sends their commander to that planet just to lengthen the game when it is not needed...also the unit variety is good but there are spaces left in the factories for units which makes me wonder if the developers are still thinking of adding more units to the game to further increase the roster! Which would be greatly appreciated. Even through these flaws or design choices it is still an excellent game, with good unit variety (especially naval <3), imaginative graphic design, an intuitive system designer and an overall grounded rts! What more could you ask for...oh wait a drop in price please ;D

Sleeping Dogs is a game that doesn't have anything to envy from other sandboxes. It features many aspects seen in other games: it's open world, based off a city (Hong Kong), you can buy cars, you can steal them, you can engage people in fights, rob them, basically anything you see in games like True Crime, Mafia or Grand Theft Auto. But the big point this one has is that the fighting is martial arts. While also having guns and all that, they are not as primary as punches and kicks.
The story is wonderful and has many plot twists I didn't see coming. It is very well explained, the cinematics look really beautiful and well made, and the ability to customize the character and his safe houses is great, featuring a wide range of clothes and decoration.
The only downside about this game is the insane amount of DLC it has, and the DLC cost more than double the base game's price. It is sad that such a great game has fallen into this stupid money milking practice that scourges the gaming industry.
Anyway, most of them are just clothes, bonuses and vehicles, so they are not necessary. The only ones I recommend are the Year of the Snake DLC, the Zodiac Tournament DLC, the Nightmare At North Point DLC and the High Resolution Texture Pack DLC (this last is free). And maybe the Ghost Pig DLC which is also free.
All in all, Square Enix did a great job in this game. Any fan of kung fu movies, triad mafia games, and open world crime based games should get this awesome game.

At the moment, this game feels like the empty husk of what could be a great game. It's plagued with server disconnects, broken game modes, and unfinished features. I love Street Fighter, but this game, as fun as it is offline, should not have been released yet. It simply lacks too much content to be called a full release.
Additionally, to unlock a color for 1 costume (yes, just one costume), you have to play Survival, which is pretty tedious. 10 rounds on easy earns you costume color 3, 30 rounds on medium earn you costume colors 4-6, and 50 rounds on hard earn you costume colors 7-10. 50 rounds. Easily an hour to an hour and a half's gameplay time in order to unlock those costume colors. That's not even considering the fact that rounds 1-45 are all cannon fodder, then suddenly the CPUs activate input-reading cheat mode and completely blow you up. That's at least 90 rounds of Survival to unlock all the colors for one costume. Ridiculous. Although I guess it's not really a problem when you consider the fact that the other costumes are all locked away in a store that hasn't been released yet.
Street Fighter V is fun, but it's currently too broken to be recommended.

For a game that very much wants to be an engrossing, artistic narrative that guides the reader from point A to point B, Serena has the subtlety of a cannonball. It attemps to bring into conversation ideas of self and work and compromise in relationships, but stumbles its way through ham-fisted dialogue and bad, bad voice acting (two things which, for a game that is almost entirely voice/word-driven, should be the most important things to get right). The story has some merit at its core, and the twist lands well enough, but even in the short span of the game's playtime (1 hour or less) it manages to fit in unnecessary dialogue and tedious steps to keep the story moving. There are a handful of genuinely moving/disturbing/interest moments in here, but these are thin (and I don't want to spoil the two or three of them because they all happen at key points in the narrative).
It's a free game, so, y'know, to a degree you get what you pay for, but this could have been far better with more editing and care. There are better narrative games out there; play Gone Home or Dear Esther or Firewatch instead of this. Dear Esther is probably the closest to this, while being very well-written and gorgeous. I wanted to like Serena more, but couldn't. Really, the writing/dialogue is surprisingly bad.

In Town of Salem, you are given a role. Your role could be part of the town, like a doctor or a veteran, or part of something much more evil, like a serial killer or a mafia member. The game plays like a metaphorical game of cards. You could be the doctor, and be pressured by everyone else into revealing yourself; if you do, you could become a target for the bad guys, and if you don’t, the town could decide to lynch you.
Each game consists of a day/night cycle. During the day cycle, the players discuss the night’s happening and share their suspicions or evidence an evil character. During the night, everyone’s ability is used. Some abilities kill other players, while others simply block another person’s ability or discover a player’s role.
If the majority of players agree that a player is evil, then they could vote to put him on trial. When the trail is in progress, the accused can plead a case: then, the town votes if they believe the player is guilty or innocent. If the player is found innocent, the town can vote to put another person on trail. If found guilty, the player will be hanged and the day will immediately end.

I'm enjoying this game.  The western setting is noticably different from other RPGs.  The graphics are deliberately retro, which fits both the setting and the inspiration.  The hat-based skill-learning system reminds me of Final Fantasy 6 and 9 (which happen to be my favorites of the series).  The combat mechanics are something new and refreshing, and should present some good tactical options once far enough along in the game to learn the necessary Vantages.  The dialogue is playful, with some fun old-school gaming references and playing with the Kickstarter backers.  The story gets off to a good start with a destroyed town, an obvious scapegoat, corrupt business interests, outlaws in hiding, and protagonists thrust into the whole situation by circumstances beyond their control.  The classic "go kill some rats" starting quest is fitting for a farm boy, and the second party member's rodeo-inspired abilites are useful and flavorful.  Riding a horse is a fitting fast-travel option, and easy to work with.
There seem to be some exploitable item-farming oddities (on an actual farm, for once), but not really any more so than the respawning Rupees in any Zelda game.
I also find making the achievements match up to a deck of playing cards very amusing, and appropriate to the setting.

A much improved, expanded PA. The expansions to gameplay are very satisfying and give you a host of new options.
Planetary invasions are more streamlined, new units really bulk up and fill out the roster and provide a satisfying variety. Orbital play  is far more engaging, and combat on gas giants (which are orbital only) is much more interesting now that we have more orbital units to play around with.
The game also has continuing support and content updates, and devs engage heavily with community feedback. Most new features found in Titans started out as community suggestions or community mods.
Speaking of mods, while it requires the 3rd party "Planetary Annihilation mod manager" (or PAMM), this game has a huge degree of mod support. There's more variety and utility to be found in PAMM's mods than most steam workshops i've seen. Mods exist between everything from tweaks to the hotkeys and UI for personal preferance, to reworking of some visual effects, many mods even go so far as enabling entirely new game modes which function entirely different from the base game, as well as mods that offer completely differnt sets of units and balance.
Quality product that continues to improve.

The setting is memorable and atmospheric, the story is simple, yet compelling (and is told through gameplay rather than cutscenes), the level design is organic and creative, the weapons feel satifying to use, and the puzzles are challenging enough to feel rewarding, but also intuitive enough to avoid frustration.
That is until you reach the Xen.
The final segment of the game takes everything great about the rest of the game and completely throws it out the window. The levels are confusing and drab, filled with enemies that can suprise kill you in one hit and often blend into the background due to the mushy brown and gray color scheme, with extremely unintuitive and frustrating puzzles that often rely heavily on imprecise platforming and random leaps of faith.
What should be only a small portion of the game stretches into a tortuously long and frustrating exercise in tedium that crushes your spirit and meticulously destroys every single bit of goodwill that the rest of this excellent game has built up, and for this reason I can't recommend it.

This is a pretty entertaing solo or co-op Tower-defense/shooter game.
It has a lot of the same fun things going for it that Orcs Must Die! 2 has but it's more serious than OMD!2 is.  I think it's pretty good if you're interested in that sort of play.  With all four DLC, it has well over 40 hours of puzzle-solving and exploration before the game devolves into grinding for Survival times.
Sanctum 2's solo and co-op gameplay is an evolutionary step away from Sanctum 1.  The primary differences are in scale and player utility.  That is, the scale is more intimate (close and smaller) while the player characters are specialized for certain utilities (sniper vs. AOE vs. close-range).
Although it's still a Tower-Defense game blended with FPS elements, they philosophically moved away from how the first game worked:
.... towards
.
Rather than every player being exactly the same, now there are four (five if you have the first DLC) different character classes to choose between who have different specializatons (such as sniper, rocketeer, soldier, and close-quarters).
The developer is very open to changing the game in ways the vocal fan-base seem to want it.  When S2 first launched, it received positive reviews by critics, but many fans of the original vocally didn't like it, because it had changed quite a bit from the S1.  Since then, the developer has modified the game to mollify the fans (allowing 15 towers per map instead of 10 like at launch, as well as other changes).
The developer is also continuing to add features free of additional charge such as the server browser for co-op players.
Lastly, I just finished the final DLC today, and I really liked it.  All four sets were well done: a good mix of interesting locations and enemies; a solid difficulty; and a good sense of satisfaction after winning some tough fights.
(Updated 15 Dec to account for final DLC release)

<edit>
I am adressing this as an expansion, not as the original game, stating that I would not recommend buying the expansion if you already have the original.
I got the expansion for free as I backed PA very early on.
If you don't own the game and are looking for a quirky RTS following the Total Annihilation line then this game is certainly worth a look.
The following is a bit about my background with the RTS genre as well as a few of the gripes I hold towards the game.
</edit>
I herald back from the time of Total Annihilation, the RTS that got me into RTS's, a fantastic game that I would suggest it to any RTS lover who's willing to deal with the somewhat dated graphics.
I moved onto Supreme Commander, which was in essence an enjoyable evolution from TA, SupCom being great for competative and social play, with its many facets. Then came about Forged Alliance, a stand alone expansion from SupCom, which brought a new faction, SP campaign and features, whilst still holding onto the core principles that made SupCom a great and worthy successor to TA.
Then there was SupCom 2...... ok ..... that game was a massive let down, being thrown into the casual pit, it wasn't in the same boat as TA and SupCom(/FA) and although it had some "interesting" things, it was in essence very bland.
When I saw the kickstarter for Planetary Annihilation, I thought it looked amazing, I thought it looked like TA but being over multiple planets... large solar systems and galaxies to wage war across.... perhaps a place where large numbers of players could be part of the same galaxy, holding worlds for their respective factions/clans..... I know a man can dream right.....
So, I got onboard the kickstarter, dreams of conquest and strategic complexity whirring through my mind....
As you can imagine I was a little disapointed with the initial game, but I thought that it could grow into the competative powerhouse I had invisioned...... I waited so long...... then TITANS.....
This isn't a really good RTS from a competitive standpoint.... a lot of the wow and awe moments of this game don't actually come across if you are "playing to win". Winning is easy, just take out the commander, which has been the goal of all previous games of this theme, but in past games, turtling up and protecting your commander was a doable task, but not here... when you have intel on a commanders location is ridiculously easy to take him out as he is nothing more than a large fabricator bot.
The only time the commander is safe is in the first 3-4 mins of the game where his weapons are such that it can take out the small number of early units sent his way, able to fend them off whilst constructing.
When the game gets to min 5 however it all changes....
Depending on your build strategy in the first 4 mins will determine whether you will win or lose the game and it is all based on numbers, not economic number as was the case with SupCom, but the number of factories you have setup and the amount of tanks you have.....
8 early game flame tanks is all you need to kill the commander... aproaching from at least 2 vectors can almost guarantee you a win unless your opponent has also built flame tanks.
The risk/reward for just spamming flame tanks is so greatly in your favor that there is little point doing anything else.... heck even if they are on another world, it just takes a little intel and a handful of flame tanks and even the most developed worlds won't save your commander from utter destruction.
No amount of defensive structures will keep you alive..... you can't turtle in PA, there is only one viable strategy and that is rush and that makes this a very boring RTS, which is why I cannot recommend it.....
<edit>
Thanks to SKaREO for pointing this out.
The game is not without its complexity and resource management is cruicial if you are to succeed, but as that is no different from SupCom or TA, I didn't feel it was required in my review.
</edit>

Half-Life, the game that redefined the future of the first-person shooters again.
is the impact it had on the history of video games. From this point all FPS' took Half-Life as reference for its revolutionary gameplay and brilliant narrative. This series is very important to me, in fact it's my favorite. I'll explain why.
For starters, even though there are scenes in the game in which there's narrative and interaction with NPCs the player's control is never taken away, with the exception of two scenes. Something I like a lot about Half-Life's narrative is the way it is treated. Throughout the game you don't notice anything strange to the naked eye but if you look closely you'll see some pretty subtle details which probably are a hint to something bigger. There's an answer to that, but I won't tell you exactly at what time.
Despite all this the plot of the game is a complete enigma. We can get answers to some questions but we'll never get to fully know why all this happened. Even in Half-Life 2 we won't get an answer (hence all the begging for HL3). It's because of all this that I think Half-Life's narrative is brilliant. It has a superficial plot and also something deeper going on behind the scenes.
As I mentioned earlier, the gameplay was revolutionary for its time. The movement, the gunplay, the level design, the enemies, everything was incredible. The mechanics are fluid and responsive. There are also some puzzles to vary a bit, although nothing too difficult. The gameplay in general is pretty polished so any fan of FPS' will feel like at home.
The graphics for its time were pretty good. The FPS' were still developing aesthetically and Half-Life was a step forward without a doubt. It's obvious that by today's standards it isn't impressiveHowever for me the visuals of this game are a classic, a stamp that was won over the years product of the nostalgia of players like me.
Both, the sound effects as the composition of the music are excellent. The SFX are amazingly characteristic, whether it's for the weapons, background sounds, characters or enemies. The use and placement of these sounds is something that can't be overlooked either. There are scenes that felt incredibly atmospheric due to the placement of these sounds and use of filters. It's simply incredible, it's the quality that I would like to be able to replicate in my own video games someday.
As for the music... I don't have much to say. It's perfect. Each piece of the soundtrack is incredible on its own and is used at the precise moment in the game. I'm delighted by the quality of this- no, every aspect of the game.
In conclusion, Half-Life is a perfect game, as simple as that. Any fan of first-person shooters should have tried by now this game or its sequels. It's one of those classics that you have to play at least once in your life.

Think NFSU 2 and you will be on the right tracks. This is great, but you seem to spent a lot of time driving around for no reason. I would much prefer to just race and perform the stages without this unnecessary addition. The races themselves also suffer from the same problem of being given too much freedom - you will accidentally go the wrong way because you are concentrating on driving and not constantly looking at the map.
O yes, and no 2 player split screen? Not good :-(
Bar the problems I have with it though, it's still a good game. Burnout fans will find something to their liking here.

As far as GTA clones go, Sleeping Dogs is one of the better titles out there. The story, in which you take the role of a loose cannon undercover cop trying to infilitrate a Triad organization using his checkered past as a cover, starts off as fairly engaging, but much like many sandbox games, eventually I lost interest in Wei Shen's story, and was just playing for the gameplay.
Which is actually very solid. Unlike most other similar games (GTA IV, Just Cause, Saints Row series), Sleeping Dogs focuses far more on melee combat than gunplay, and it benefits significantly from it. While not quite as fun and intuitive as the fighting from the Arkham series (which it is clearly trying to imitate), it definitely is a fairly unique and enjoyable mechanic for a freeroaming crime game. The driving and gunplay are decent as well (though I recommend a gamepad, as it is difficult to do the former with a keyboard).
Overall, Sleeping Dogs does a few cool things with the story and gameplay, but ultimately falls short in a lot of ways after the first dozen hours. Many things feel unfinished or lacking refinement. Hopefully this is the start of a new franchise and the developers work on the foundation here, because there is a ton of potential for something truly great.

One could call this a reimagining of the original Sanctums run and gun tower defense gameplay.  For those who played the original changes include enemies that actively attack you if you get too close, walls are now low enough for towers to be able to shoot across multiple rows and also make it harder for you to avoid attacks. Most towers are air and ground now. Weapons are now split into classes, and you can only carry four tower types so as to encourage team-work.
For new players and beginners, if you enjoy FPS combat and Tower Defense, then this is a great fusion of the two. Balance is perfect between towers and player weapons so as to ensure contribution from both. You also have the option of inviting three other friends for a chaotic good time of setting up towers and shooting monsters in the face.

Town of Salem is a pretty simple and straightforeward concept, 15 players, three factions (town, mafia, and nuetral), and one town. Durring the day, the townmembers talk amongst one another and can vote to lynch other members. Durring the night, however, the mafia, a crazed serial killer, and vengeful town members can kill and frame other townsfolk. The town faction have large numbers and have a wide range of abilities but have no idea who is a freind or foe. The mafia is a small but powerful group that kill anyone who opposes them. The neutral team are not one faction, but many individuals who have different goals, such as the serial killer and executioner. Town of Salem looses non of the dark themes that it is based off of, despite its innocent appearance.
Town of Salem has a semi-intricate set of rules that is given shape by the differnt abillities of town members, and these may give new players a hard time. Once these are learned, however, it becomes great fun to use these rules to one's advantage.
This game makes you deduct, decifer, and decive (see what I did there), and the stratagies that the community comes up with to win are always evolving. This game is great fun if you like thinking games that put your intelect against other people's. It has a pretty cool soundtrack too!
However, due to the nature of the game, you will often find yourself sitting through games as a dead townsmember that cannot really do much but watch the game. Allthough I find the risk of this to add a factor suspense, some people may find it annoying.
In my opinion, it is definitely worth the $5 price tag and your time.

My no spoiler review:
Boot Hill Heroes is a passion project funded by kickstarter and it shows in every aspect of the game (in a good way). The graphics have a "dirty pixels" style that really accents the western theme. The music is top notch and will instantly draw you in. Combine both of those and you will get a very atmospheric experience that you have to let yourself get lost in. This is my favorite thing about this game over all.
The game is high customizable in combat. it has all of the tactical thought and personal pace of turn based combat, without any of the waiting. Prefer active battle? You can do that as well. There are so many enemies you won't find in any other game, the art is very well done. From the way a ring of fire that enters you into combat, to the way enemies fall over (as if they were a hastilly constructed western movie setpiece), you can see very deliberate and very western themes. I wish more developers would steal this combat system, once you try it, you'll wonder why AAA games don't give you the amount of options you have here.
The game features an optional co-op combat system (I haven't tried it), and has 2 more parts scheduled for release. If you want to play a turn based western game that oozes charm from its every pore, this is it!

A complete 180 in game design for the worse. The original Sanctum was a great change of pace for tower defense games, putting you into the battlefield with upgradable weapons (a tower defense with shooting). Sanctum 2 takes the original's premise too far in the opposite direction in terms of game balance. Sadly, all the towers are too weak and this has become a first person shooter with towers. With very limited resources and base blocks, you will be building or upgrading on average one tower per wave with mazes only becoming effective near the end of the map. Even when you do finally make a great maze that is somewhat defensible, many of the bosses can smash their way through your base blocks, destroying your towers and creating a free path for enemies. The worst part is the difficulty curve; the early levels are tutorial-esque cakewalks which quickly drop off into frustrating trial-and-error tests of endurance.
The map design has improved significantly, including 16 levels with improved music and sound providing great atmosphere. While the drawn slideshow cutscenes are entertaining and provide some pretense for the missions, the story and characters are never really fleshed out. Sanctum 2 combines sub-par FPS elements with sub-par RPG elements and sub-par TD elements to create... a surprisingly mediocre game. Sanctum 2 does an amazing job of blending the tower defense and FPS sides of the game, especially when compared to the original. Instead of being an indestructable warrior left to destroy overclustered enemies or pick off enemies too awkward for you turrets to kill, you become a rather fragile player that easily incurs the wrath of enemies with few turrets to aid you. This change has you trying to do your best to distract the enemies and keep them close to turrets while being cautious to stay alive so your enemies can't have free run of your maze. Don't get wrong, I loved the original Sanctum and enjoy them both fairly evenly, but the second is better as a game.
In short: If you like tower defense or FPS games (much less both) this is probably worth buying. Even if you weren't a fan of the first than this is certainly worth a try.

Action buttons

I thought I would write a review to give my thoughts on a great little gem I just happened to stumble upon.
Some have likened this to UO or  Runescape.
This game is a 'learn skills as you use them' style.  You have to spend time playing the game game and using these skills in order for them to go up.  Want to be better at mining? Then mine, mine, mine.
There are a lot of different skills (Farming, Fishing, Cooking, Alchemy, Breeding, Mining, Jewelry, Carpentry, Forging, and Woodcutting.  There is no skill cap on any of these, just be prepared for the need to grind away at them to have them continue in going up.  You can make some amazing items just from farming the mats and practicing.  I actually made my own bronze armor/weapons as a lower lvl character just by spending some time mining, forging and smithing before I ran out and started killing things.
The gathering skills also provide you with the opportunity to earn money by selling them on the market to players who would rather pay for them vs gathering them on their own.  I made 60k pretty quickly selling sand and purchased my pet day 1.
There is a wide varity of pets which helps to increase your inventory size as well as adding some stats to your character.  They are limited in use by your stats/level so make sure you can use one before spending money on them.
Death happens.... In this game when you die you keep 2 items (based on their vendor value) and your pet.  The rest dissapear forever.  thankfully you shouldnt die unless you just aren't paying attention or you try to tackle something way beyond your means.  There is a potion (rare drop or ingame purchase) that you can buy which will protect 5 more items for those who feel the need.  Over all death isn't something one should fear after they quickly learn how to avoid it.
The community is a great one also.  Most will share their wisdom and will come help you if you got trapped by some high level monsters while farming goods.
The game has a captcha feature pops up occasionally.  enter the correct code and get 1 point which can be spent for exp on any skill or stat.  Get it wrong no point.  Don't answer it in 180 seconds and you get a - point.  Get 5 of those and you get jailed.  This is done to help prevent botting / farming.  It has a built in system to reward you for being there and for punishing those who would use it just to farm for other accounts.
The game has a built in currency (MOS) and store which isn't a bad system.  It doesn't feel like a pay to win game.  The items are helpful but not needed.  Most things can be gotten through the market and in game gold.  The only major item in the MOS store is the 2x exp potions which gives everyone on the server 30 mins bonus experience on all skills used during that time.
Overall the game is fun.  I have 2 monitors and watch movies on one screen and paly on the other.  You can also play on your phone or any tablet/ipad (which makes work playing possible too).
I would say give this game a go and tell your friends :)

As far as GTA clones go, Sleeping Dogs is one of the better titles out there. The story, in which you take the role of a loose cannon undercover cop trying to infilitrate a Triad organization using his checkered past as a cover, starts off as fairly engaging, but much like many sandbox games, eventually I lost interest in Wei Shen's story, and was just playing for the gameplay.
Which is actually very solid. Unlike most other similar games (GTA IV, Just Cause, Saints Row series), Sleeping Dogs focuses far more on melee combat than gunplay, and it benefits significantly from it. While not quite as fun and intuitive as the fighting from the Arkham series (which it is clearly trying to imitate), it definitely is a fairly unique and enjoyable mechanic for a freeroaming crime game. The driving and gunplay are decent as well (though I recommend a gamepad, as it is difficult to do the former with a keyboard).
Overall, Sleeping Dogs does a few cool things with the story and gameplay, but ultimately falls short in a lot of ways after the first dozen hours. Many things feel unfinished or lacking refinement. Hopefully this is the start of a new franchise and the developers work on the foundation here, because there is a ton of potential for something truly great.

There are no words in the English language (or any other, for that matter), to describe how much I loved Freespace 2. Especially Free Space Open from the modding community of the Hard-Light Project, which is basically the definitive edition of freespace, enhanced to todays graphical standards and featuring hundreds of hours of very high quality user made content they could actually charge money for. Writing, voice acting etc. the modding community did a better job at those than many AAA titles within the industry.
If it wasn't for Star Citizen, I would have had to play Freespace 2 until eternity, which would have been completely fine, considering it is, in my book, one of the best games ever to emerge into existence. For the last 17 years it has been the singlemost and best space combat simulation game of all time and it isn't going drop far from that position any time soon.
There are zero technical issues when using the Free Space Open mod with Win10 or any newer hardware and it starts looking actually gorgeous. Just to give a glimpse of the actual size of player modding: My Freespace 2 directory is 67GB large, the original game doesn't even have 2GB. That's the amount of user made content Freespace 2 has received over the years. And most of it is worth anyones time.
Not only an absolutely fantastic childhood memory, Freespace 2 Source Code Project remains one of the best space games until now. If you look back at titles like Wing Commander, Freelancer or Starlancer and wish there were games like that, Freespace is exactly like that, only even better. Much better.
Will remain in my list of all-time favourite games until I kick the bucket and I cannot stress how much I recommend this to anyone even just remotely being interested in space games at all.
Get it, download FS open / SCP, play the original FS2 campaign and then start looking around which user made campaigns might interest you and start downloading. You'll have something to do for months on end.
I've spent this much time with the steam version alone, but looking back at all the years I have played this game already, I probably spent more than 10000 hours in Freespace in my life so far. Not kidding. My original pilot profile had about 180k confirmed kills throughout all the campaigns I played over the years.
As you might have noticed, I'm absolutely fanatical about Freespace 2. There is a reason for that. Actually there's many reasons. Go check it out if you don't believe me.

Serena is definitely a different kind of point-and-click game. No puzzles to solve, just a (short) story to be told and played through. The game is SO stripped down that there are no settings to change in it (pressing ESC will literally crash your game to desktop without saving it).
This is not the game to play if you're looking for a jump-scare kind of horror game. This game has no such thing. What it does have is a mysterious story with a cringy (and maybe slightly disturbing) mood to it.
The game set takes place inside a little decrepit cabin, that you will need to explore thoroughly by interacting with the multiple objects inside it. The easiest way to progress in the game is to extend all dialog options for each object, move on to doing the same for all the other objects, and then starting the whole process again, as the narration for each object changes after you did certain interactions with your surroundings.
The atmosphere of the game (graphics, environmental sounds) is just amazing and it's fun to discover the way the story unfolds as you play and see how the narrator reacts to the same objects in different ways as his mood changes along the way. Really appreciated the little plot twist. And, last but not least, Josh Mandel's voice acting is absolutely outstanding! It really helps you get immersed in the story.

This game is beautiful and fun, with a narrative that is touching, haunting, and, at times, quite humorous.  Possibly, the most charming part of the narrative is the style itself, as the story is told to the player as they play, much as though they were hearing about it from a grizzled old man by the side of a fire; the narrator takes note of even your oddest actions, and is voiced brilliantly.  The controls are simple and tight, but the game affords even veteran gamers a bit of a challene, especially with totems you can invoke to make the game harder (much like skulls in HALO) and in the weapon-specific proving grounds you come across over the course of the story.  The variety of weapons and buffs are creative and usefull, giving the player heavy control on how they wish to play.  There are very few glitches or gameplay issues that I've encountered, and the game isn't too busy taxing your machine for you to enjoy it (no wasting time in the Video options).  It is nice to play a post-apocalyptic game that isn't a pile of ugly rubble and debris, especially oen that isn't so focused on teh apocalypse itself--Bastion is a deep look into the beautiful oddities of humanity, even in a strange new world.  Pick up this game for sure.  It's a brilliant work.

I don't want to have to not recommend this game but in it's current state, unless you really love fighting games, it's really not even close to worth full price.
Pros:
-One of the most solid fighting games in terms of mechanics on the market.  It's a bit of a departure from 4 but depending on what you want from the game that can be a good or a bad thing.
-Decent character roster.  With the exception of F.A.N.G. who seems to have a really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ moveset (demonstrated by the fact that in 6 hours I have not fought one single person using him online) the rest of the characters old and new are fun and varied.
-The optimisation on my PC at least seems excellent.  The game can hold 60fps with no noticable dips with all settings maxed on my i5 and GTX670.
-Being able to unlock future characters which would otherwise be DLC through in game currency.
Cons:
-Fight Money is not called Bison Dollars.
-There is no store currently available for me to spend my 200,000 Fight Moneys in.
-The story modes available for each character are frankly pathetic.  When it was anounced to be a mode comparable to MK9/10's story modes which were a good few hours long each with nice in-engine cutscenes and all the fancy trimmings I got excited. What you actually get when you begin a "Story" is a well drawn still image for a minute or so while one of the voice actors says a few lines, then another still image for another minute or two with some more lines, then another, repeat ad nauseum for every single "cutscene" for every character.  I got bored after the first two and just skipped them all for every single character which left me with 2-3 fights for each character taking me a total of 48 minutes to complete the story mode.  Before you say that doesn't count because I skipped cutscenes, I say a collection of 30 still images is not what was advertised.
-The netcode while better, is still not great.  Even having restricted my search options to only the most compatible connections available I still get matches with opponents teleporting around me, random slowdown mid-match and depending on the time of day wait times up to several minutes to even find a game.
-The servers flat out were not working on launch.  This is unacceptable for a AAA game and even though it is the norm it leaves a bitter taste.
-PC version is not compatible with any PS3/4/non-xbox sticks. This was a huge disappointment when I plugged in my Qanba Q1 and it simply didn't function.  There are programs you can use to fix it such as x360ce but with probably the biggest and most historic fighting game franchise in the world you simply shouldn't have to!
-The game is generally lacking in other game modes.  While to my knowledge SF games generally have at least a few different options for minigames and different things to do, in SFV there is no challenge mode, no minigames, you are limited to versus, story and a 30 match endurance/time attack mode.
Basically the whole game feels like they put time into the actual fighting, but everything else is pretty terrible and feels very cheap.
