Wizorb at its core is a block breaking game similar to Breakout and Arkanoid.  The difference from these classics is how it expands on their simple formula in almost every way possible.  You play as the wizard Cyrus who transforms himself into his staff to be used as your paddle.  Like any true wizard you have magical powers that will help aid you on your journey.  If its adventure you find yourself on you can bet there is a story too.  This game tries to do a lot of things and usually manages to do so quite successfully.
Wizorb is a very vibrate and colorful game with its 16-bit inspired, retro, graphics.  The different monsters, environments, pick-ups, and bricks all come together for a clean, uniform, style.  While the story isn't quite a enthralling as the visuals it does help incentivize your progression.  Tarot village has been ravaged my monsters and all the town folk need money to repair their homes and businesses.  By playing through the different levels you'll even money you can use both to help out the citizens and buy different power-ups.  The power-ups will give you a temporary boost that last until you lose a life.  The different power-ups from range from paddle extensions to sticky, slow and multi balls.
The long the ball remains in play it will move faster with each hit off your paddle.  At top speed its become quite difficult to keep your paddle lined up with the ball.  Thankfully, you have different magic powers you can to help make life easier.  As soon as the ball bounces off your paddle you can transform it into a burning ball that will pass through multiple bricks or give it wings and guide it into a certain area.  While the ball is flying around you can shoot fireballs from your paddle or blow a gust of wind to change the direction of your ball.  These all drain your magic bar which can be replenished with potions.  Also, if you go so long without hitting anything your ball will start to glow and the next time you hit it you'll receive some magic.
There are five different areas you must fight through to save the kingdom.  Each area has a unique theme, a set number of stages, and a boss battle.  Each level becomes progressively harder with bricks and enemies becoming tougher and harder to hit.  Look for rooms that provide bonuses and shops.  Watch out as any purple objects that falls onto your paddle with have a negative effect and could even kill you.  Replay levels for coins, score, and bonus stages used to free four sages who when reunited grant access to a special power.
Wizorb is a beautiful indie game with some really unique mechanics.  The sense of progression of the difficulty feels spot on.  Only in the last area does the game really start to almost too difficult.  There are times too where it feels the paddle isn't quite as responsive as it needs to be which can be frustrating when the ball gets up to top speed.  These aspects do make this game feel a little bit harder than it needed to be however Wizorb is still easy to recommend.  The magic abilities are a blast and there is a wonderful sense of adventure.  This is arcade style game is wonderfully crafted and thoroughly enjoyable.

The Arkanoid-clone genre has never been one to top any charts. Unfortunately, this game doesn't do anything to change. That really is unfortunate in this case because this game does retro so well. It's got music that reminds me of Legend of Zelda, and I could see myself playing this on one of the old consoles, with the game's title art prominently displayed on its cartridge. The controls serve their purpose, although that may be where the problems start to come in. Aside from the paddle, you only control spell casting/ball launching. It's all pretty standard faire here really, which when it comes to Arkanoid clones, means it comes up as short as the genre.
To give some examples of fine genre features that don't benefit the fun factor: why can the ball travel faster from left to right than my paddle under any conditions? It means I often get to watch the ball go kerplunk, and consequently I'm constantly left wishing my paddle was just slightly faster. I can literally watch seconds tick off the clock as I know I'm about to lose a ball and there's nothing I can do about it. Why not have a little stamina bar that I can burn down to move faster for a short time, and then wait for it to refill (manually or automatically)? Why in 2012 (the game's release date) do I still have to choose between getting a powerup and not dieing? This is perhaps one of the worst feelings: constantly watching your powerups drop off the screen because the only way to get them is to touch them with the paddle. Why not have them sit there and require me to hit them with the ball? Or why not pick them up automatically once I've destroyed whatever block contained them and they are revealed? Or why not have a little automated helper that picks them up? Players experience less of what the game has to offer in the ways of powerups and spell-casting (since one of the powerups restores magic) because of this mechanic.
I imagine the die-hard Arkanoid-clone fans would thoroughly enjoy this game and may even explain the number of positive reviews. I however felt myself wishing for something that better addressed what I (and likely many others) have felt are the genre's shortcomings. Not a bad game, but perhaps a little too much of the same ol' same ol' if you're not a big fan of this genre already. 5/10.

I get these unbearable headaches while playing these old FPS games. Maybe it's the graphics, or the old sound effects, or something else, but I don't have this problem playing classic 2D games like Super Metroid or Mario Bros, or newer FPS games like Fallout or Portal. It's happened with this game and with a few other classic shooters like DOOM and Duke Nukem 3D. I really don't have an explanation, so if anyone out there has a solution to this problem I would really appreciate being able to bring myself to finish this game without puking.

I bought this game long time ago and it was almost unplayable then. Recently I decided to replay it to check if it fixed.
It seems that nothing was fixed since initial release. A lot of crashes, broken zones where you appear surrounded by enemies, bugged visibility inside buildings, firing into the objects standing right in front the object having full visibility of enemy, etc.
But I have bigger questions. In original game we have some game mechanics like moving without looting, moving without changing looking direction, multiple attachments for weapons, enter through window, etc. I don't think that such things were hard to implement. To not to include them in the game was very bad design decision.
The graphics is unquestionably better then in original game and it is updated for today's technology, but loosing a lot of cool stuff just to update the graphics I can't agree with this. I even think that if they would just implement exactly the the gameplay and story as in JA2 but with updated graphics it would be much better then what they did in JA:BIA.
So I don't recommend this game. The authors just tried to make own average tactical shooter but for some reason poison JA brand.

Let me start by saying if you are not a fan of japanese style rpgs then honestly this game may not help you like them any more. I will say if you do generally like jrpgs then i highly recommend checking this game out. If its one thing that the tales of series does well it is the way the director tells the story.  The combat in the game is decent ( i prefer most other tales of games combat but thats just my opinion) and so long as you pay attention to the in game tutorials you will be ok. The visuals give the game that feeling as if your watching an anime but with slightly more detail. Music being played in the game is solid and really sets the mood easily based on whatever events are happening. Overall i give this game an 8 out of 10 because even though the story was very good it feels like something is missing in this game compared to other tales of games. If this game is on sale and your scared to spend full price on it I highly recommend checking it out. Its always nice to have games that really get deep into the story and even make you reflect on many things happening. I must say its been a while since a Tales game got this deep and im definitely glad I purchased this game. Here is hoping Namco Bandai releases all the Tales of games here on steam in the future.

My recomendation is based on:
- I played the game on Hardest difficulty, with the "Realistic Rebalance" mod installed, that made stealth combat much more enjoyable and improved many things in the game. Many thanks to Killatomate for his fantastic modding work.
- I played JA2 back on the '90s (original and Wildfire), and am a big fun of the original games, which I also recomment to everyone.
In general:
JA - Back In Action (moded) had me staying awake for nights on the row, with many fulfilling and rewording moments when my combined attack plan succeded in nutralizing six-seven enemies in a matter of seconds, when my stealth inflitration commado managed to get more than ten kills before remaining enemies even knew he was arround, and when my 'Boom Boom' squad cleared the batlefield with a rain of granates and RPGs.
Details:
The "pause-able real time" mechanic is not the "turn based" I loved in the older JA and X-com series tactical games. But it is more 'realistic' and can result in really nice momments . I am enjoying playing also JA2-Wildfire simultaneusly with JA-Back in action, since the different mechanics provide two fantastic but indepented game experiences.
One-time purchase cost of the mercs, and AI insisting on getting only two assoult routs (so no more than one-two sectors need defending), means that money soon will not be a problem. So, I got overenthusiastic and got more than 24 merks under my command (something almost imposible in JA2). At that point, micromanagment of their re-equipment took more than the combat itself, and I started getting a bit frastrated, even though I liked the huge variety of weapons available.
A critical fumble of the developers: They didnt include the option to create a character to be your avatgar in the game. I got angry on them, but afterwards I got over it...
Leveling with skill points and no training option as it was at JA2: As a result the local free-merks can never be super-merks. So I use them as packing-mules, while at JA2 games I always had the main squad consist of my character and the local fighters.
DO NOT PURCHASE THE "xxx Specialist Kit" DLCs. They just provide at the start of the game one above-average weapon and a one-time-use armor-helmet set. The variety of weapons and ammunition in my gamming, ment that really soon I had other alternative options, so the money spend on the particular DLCs were not justified.
Personally I value more the JA2 (Wildfire and original), so I propose you start with them, and afterwards go into Back In Action.

First off, bare in mind this that recommendation comes IN SPITE of Uber Entertainment's terrible marketing policies (and I'm not just talking about their initial £70 launch on early access!).
This should be a £10 expansion, not a £30 stand alone game.  And really, most of what they added here should have been a free update as PA:Titans is basically what most of us were promised, and expected with PA came out of KS and EA.  The only reason I bought PA:Titans is because they gave owners of PA the 66% discount bringing it in line with what I would expect to pay for a moderate expansion.
All that said, this is a good game.  If you like grand stratagy and the joy of big armies and huge explosions, then this is a worthwhile investment and you can happily sink many hours into the game.
If you already own and enjoyed PA, then get Titans while it's discounted for you.
If you were on the fence with PA, then Titans will not change your mind.
If you don't own PA, then watch video reviews carefully before buying to ensure it's what you want, then get this version and not the original release.
Titans is an all round improvement on the original PA.  Uber have listened to some of the community feedback and suggestions, while remaining totally deaf to others.
The planets are a bit better designed, and the multi-level battlefields make it easier and more fun to build defenciable positions.  There are now more ways to move aroudn the system, the orbital units now feel like a full class rather than a tack-on, and the new units add a pleasent bit of veriety.
Cons-wise, the standard AI still isn't as challanging as I'd like until you're facing more than one, and unit pathfinding can still sometimes go nuts unless you use shift-move to set waypoints.
So, overall a recommend for existing PA fans, and a recommend for non-PA fans who are willing to do their research first (even then it may be better to wait for a sale)

I have more hours than shown because of some problem where I had to launch the game outside Steam to get it to run properly.  This game was on my wishlist a long time and I was very much looking forward to playing it once I had some friends interested.  Ultimately I'm pretty disappointed with it.
Imagine Terraria.  Now take out the bossess.  Remove the difficulty and need to survive.  Abolish any uniqueness or variety among the different biomes.  Get rid of all sense of exploration and meaningful reward.  Make the crafting system far more complicated and frustrating.  Design your menu so that it blocks your view entirely, and even when you move it to the side of the screen, again and again and again, it still opens in the middle and blinds you every time.  Instead of one large and diverse planet, have a hundred or so small ones, each virtually identical to the last.  Imagine resources dropped ten times faster, but there were a tenth as many things to build with them.  Alter the difficulty curve so that within a few hours, you can have the most powerful weapons and armor in the game.  And add MMO style grinding to get through a series of meaningless fetch quests for rewards you not only don't want, but literally cannot use, because you have already maxed out the upgrade potential they provide while grinding for the randomly generated trinkets the questgivers desire.
And retrograde the multiplayer system so setting up games with your friends becomes a chore, much how Terraria was when it first launched, four years ago.
This game is not worth the money or the time.  It's not fun.  It doesn't handle multiplayer well in a variety of ways.  It has no sense of progression, challenge, discovery, or accomplishment.  There are a lot of 2D survival games on Steam, many of them cheaper than this.  I'd try one of those instead.

A highly enjoyable Breakout / Arkanoid type game, throwing in a light smattering of "rpg" to retro 8 bit graphic stylings.
The game ticked all the right boxes for me.  The single most essential thing for a twitch /skill based game was the controls are tight.  I use my xbox controller and everything just worked the way it should.  (No idea what keyboard gameplay is like.)
Some later levels become somewhat frustrating due to an over reliance on unbreakable and hard to reach bricks.
You get some handy spells to help compensate for these setbacks, however the Mana resource was always hard to acquire, meaning a lot of the time I was out of mana and praying  I could finally hit the last brick before the speed became too fast and I died.
That is one thing to note - there is a lot of times in endgame when you are waiting down the bottom like a chump while the ball bounces in loops between unbreakable surfaces.  There is even an achievement that celebrates it- "Infinite Loop - The orb bounces for 45 seconds before coming back to the magic wand."
The ball also has a nasty habit of being very hard to predict as it speeds up.  So after watching it bounce 30 times and suddenly shooting out at a random angle causing you to miss / lose a life, swearing becomes quite common.
I found myself in general having to "stockpile" lives for later missions by repeating easier levels.
However I had more fun than I had frustration.  I liked it enough to spend the last 10 hours playing it to completion, and there is still plenty gameplay left; masochistic achievements to obtain, personal scores to beat, and in general just enjoying a fun arcade game.

RPG MO is basically a more primitive version of RuneScape Classic, both in terms of aesthetics as well as functionality. I will cover the basics in sections below:
Like RuneScape Classic, the world uses a 4-sided grid-based system for movement and interaction, and unlike RuneScape Classic, which has a more or less seamless world, it is split into a number of square "regions" separated by loading screens. These regions seem to exist merely as a place to store the many mobs for players to kill as well as various resources, rather than seeming like a functioning world that could actually exist. As such, exploration isn't all that enticing unless the player wants a more difficult monster to kill or needs a specific material.
The graphics in RPG MO are by far more primitive than RuneScape Classic. The game is entirely 2D whereas RuneScape Classic was 3D with 2D sprites. Animations are basically nonexistent: I think I've seen one: the sparkling effect for magic spells. When walking, you just glide about. Even with combat, the characters just stand there as hitsplats pop up. For actions such as mining as fishing, images of fishing poles and pickaxes appear above the character just as in RuneScape Classic. You are very limited in the design of your character: there are about twenty styles of hair, with most of them just being recolors. When clicking to move to tiles, the selected tile's borders glitch out with pixelation. When moving, the edge of the screen shows a background image for about half a second before buffering in the actual tile contents. Resizing the game window only stretches what can be currently seen rather than loading in more of the world, and I get a good bit a screen tearing when I display the game at anything other than its native resolution. In short, it's ugly, and there is very little in the area of graphical options.
The audio in RPG MO is minimalistic. There is music, which RuneScape Classic lacked apart for the menu screen, which RPG MO has no music for. Each region seems to have a track each, and it does get very monotonous. As for sound effects, it's pretty much the same as with RuneScape Classic: a short sound plays when doing various actions, although the combat sounds are not nearly as annoying.
RPG MO's user interface is clunky. I have trouble controlling my character, and have to wait for each movement command to carry out before issuing a new one to get them to do what I want consistently. The local map constantly flickers with buggy pixelation, similar to what you might see in a poorly-compressed jpeg image. The inventory system is straight out of RuneScape Classic, where you have to hover over the button to open the inventory every time you want to access it, which serves no point when the game window isn't tiny. The smithing/forging uses a system similar to Minecraft, where you have to make a certain shape to specify what item you want, which, since there is a wiki built into the game, serves no purpose but to impede the player's ability to play the game. The shapes used are rather unintuitive as well, seemingly for no reason. There seems to be no way to close the chat interface, just reduce it in size to one line plus its title. Speaking of the chat, there is no local chat and the global? chat is essentially useless with how much spam there is. Luckily you can turn off player messages, and just keep the game messages. The most annoying part of the user interface, though, is when a Captcha randomly appears in the middle of your screen that you have to solve as an anti-botting measure. Fail enough of them, and you'll be banned. RuneScape Classic had this too, but in a much more seamless way with a system of fatigue that you had to sleep and solve a Captcha to recover.
RPG MO has many skills which exist in RuneScape Classic, albeit some are renamed, and a few that do not exist in it. You still have attack (renamed accuracy), strength, defense, hits (renamed health), magic, herblaw (renamed alchemy), woodcutting, fishing, cooking, crafting (renamed jewelry), smithing (renamed forging), and mining. Like RuneScape 2, RPG MO also has farming and construction (renamed carpentry). The most unique skill is breeding, which encompasses breeding pets which help the character, similar to how you can summon creatures to help you in RuneScape 2. RPG MO also has no thieving, agility, firemaking, ranged, or prayer skills. Training skills works much the same as in RuneScape Classic, complete with the enormous amount of grinding.
The combat in RPG MO is almost a direct copy of RuneScape Classic's. You click to attack, and hits are automatically exchanged. Magic can be cast mid-combat, albeit with scrolls held in a pouch in the shield slot rather than with runes. The system of choosing between attack/accuracy, strength, and defense experience via combat style is still in place, although experience is granted on hit rather than on kill, and you must cycle between them rather than choosing from a menu, making it easy to accidentally gain experience in an unwanted skill. Equipment and weapons use the same "aim", "power", and "armour" system. Unlike RuneScape Classic, there doesn't seem to be any sort of ranged combat whatsoever, and loot is automatically placed in the player's inventory upon defeating your enemy.
Like others have said, this game is very grindy. I'm personally okay with grindy, but the problem with RPG MO is that there really doesn't seem to be anywhere to go other than to the stuff that requires higher levels. I can kill 200 rats so that I can kill 200 orcs, so that I can kill 200 vampires, so on and so forth, but there doesn't seem to be any point to it all. The only quests I found were more tasks rather than quests, and with the lackluster exploration, dull combat, and lack of player interaction, there doesn't seem much point in playing rather than making arbitrary numbers increase.
In short, I simply can't recommend RPG MO unless someone really likes solving Captchas, wants to experience online gaming in 1997 without the dialup, or just really happens to like this sort of simplistic grinding game. It seems to be recreating the games of old, complete with flaws, rather than taking the core concepts and gameplay and improving upon them with the power of modern hardware, internet speeds, and programming languages. In it's current state, I feel that it's more of an inferior rendition of RuneScape Classic rather than its own game.

If you paid for Planetary Annihilation, you're not going to be crazy about paying another $40 for this game - but this is the complete game that you wanted Planetary Annihilation to be.
Every factory puts out basic units, in addition to kind of wacky units that give the game a bit more flavor.  Bot factories can put out high damage electrical units, air factories have transports, Bot 2 has weird swarm units.  The unit cannon and teleporter make taking over new planets refreshingly easy.  You can finally build sub-commanders.
But what you want to know about are the Titans, and the Titans are exactly what you want them to be.  Expensive, incredibly high health destroyers.  They're heavy to use and scary to see.  Incredibly, not quite as scary to see as the number of world-destroying superweapons, including a structure with one purpose: 1 minute after it's completed, it destroys the planet it was built on.
I hope whatever your experience with PA was before now, you can stomach the extra $40 - because this is the game that you were looking for in the first place.

It's still an enjoyable game, though. Less difficult of the city builders.

Let me begin by saying that PA: Titans is a huge step forward for the series.
In terms of gameplay many many things have changed. There are many many balance changes and a ton of new units were added rounding up the roster you previously had and not only is that adding variety, it completely changes the pacing of the game.
-In PA games often led to a slow death when people turtled a lot and you didnt have many way to break sieges and especially not to retake planets once someone secured them other than blowing them up outright by crashing a moon into it if the map allowed you to do so. Recent patches tried to fix it with moderate success.
-In Titans the games play a lot faster, the overall ressource gain is increased however certain units, especially engineers and a couple of buildings now have a hefty upkeep cost. There is no longer engi spamming to boost production, if you tried youd run into a ressource shortage and stall your production. Its a fine balance between trying to gain map control and trying to get a lead on your opponent. Choices like when to go tier 2 and when to try to produce a titan are huge game changers allowing for great comebacks or lead to defeat.
Overall it made PA a game that im really enjoying even in 1v1 ranked matches due to a new metagame that developed from the changes made. On top of that the ranked system allows you to watch replays of players regardless of league allowing new players to learn from veterans without the need to download things from other sources which is a feature many more games should have.
People might argue that the pricetag is unreasonable, but think of it like a stand-alone expansion that reinvents the game, allowing newcomers that don't have the original to get more value for the same price and giving former PA owners a fair deal for brand new content that goes beyond limitations of the original.

I often hear that Tales of Symphonia was the best game in the series, and as someone who had up until recently had that as my only Tales game, I could see why people would think that. It had a great caster of characters, a plot full of epic twists and turns, and a fun battle system with a good mix of action and strategy.
Now having played Tales of Berseria, its just amplified all of Symphonia's positives.
The characters are INCREDIBLE in this game. There's only six in Berseria compared to Symphonia's eight, but they are so much more cohesive and have some of the most comedic and close interactions I've ever seen in an RPG, with deep storylines to each one. The character development for the main two characters (no spoilers here) are so amazingly cathartic and moving that I was stuck watching, eyes glued to the screen, with that panging feel in your chest when your emotions have just spilled everywhere.
Graphics are decent. Sure, sometimes hair clips through clothes, body parts clip through other body parts (in cinematics where it really is kinda unforgivable), and that could've been improved upon, but its not in that kind of comedic glitchy light where its gone so far that you can't help but laugh and break immersion, its slight errors only.
Symphonia had really thick outlines and cel shading that this game does not have, and to be honest, I wasn't too comfortable with the look of Berseria at first, but it quickly grew on me to the point where that iffy feeling was but a memory. Once you're involved with the game (with a story like this, really damn quickly, mind you), you won't even care, if you ever cared at all.
Soundtracks are incredible; the protagonist's theme serves as a motif for her development throughout the entire game from the beginning to the end, with each section of the track 'unlocking' as she develops. I've never had such an uplifting feeling in a game from soundtrack alone, so Velvet's theme is probably my favourite OST from the past decade, and I've had quite a lot of damn good OST's in that time.
The opening theme 'Burn' whilst not involved in the game outside of the animated opening, was good enough for me to find it on Amazon for 99p and buy it a few hours into the game, but thats music taste and that's subjective.
On the other side of sound is voices. Rina Sato's Velvet is as amazing as it sounds (for those of you who know her, a similar role she plays though not nearly as deep is Misaka Mikoto from A Certain Magical Index or A Certain Scientific Railgun), and nails the range of emotions Velvet goes through convincingly and beyond that; it is her ability to empathise with Velvet's character that really made those cinematic scenes throughout the game and made them so engaging. Not to overshadow the other Japanese voice cast who are really just as amazing. The second protagonist (not to spoil with their name) is just as worthy of the spotlight as Rina Sato, though Rokurou, Magilou, Eizen, Eleanor, Artorius, and pretty much every character in the Japanese voice cast is perfection. I can't fault them.
Now for those wondering if you should play in English dub (I deliberated on this since Symphonia's dub was so good), I'd recommend against it. While I can appreciate Cristina Vee's voice in League of Legends as Riven, and she isn't horrible as Velvet, she doesn't nail it like Rina Sato does. Despite this, the main reason not to go for Dub is the REST of the voices.
The aforementioned second protagonist who was just as amazing as Rina Sato in Japanese, is outright horrid in Dub. Key scenes are ruined by their lack of effort, their lack of empathy for the character, and their inability to read the mood of a scene. They also can't seem to decide on what gender they are, when just looking at the character's profile would've sorted that out.
Magilou sounds too basic, compared to the absolute craziness that his her Japanese voice actress, but its not necessarily terrible like the previous character. Rokurou makes me cringe a bit sometimes, but not totally terrible; just not fitting the character's carefree attitude. Eizen is a decent fit, and Eleanor isn't a decent fit, but in any case, all of the protagonist voices simply are inferior to the original Japanese cast, for budget reasons most likely. Even the best voice actors like for Shigure in English dub pale in comparison to the Japanese cast.
On the other hand of localisation, there are annoying typos in the subtitles in the game's skits/dialogues. Whilst its most prominent in the smaller side quests, I have detected at least one in the main story which I didn't actually see in the first playthrough. A minor detail perhaps, but still annoying; its a sign of a lack of playtesting, and for some reason isn't fixed in an update. Sometimes the meanings of a character's words are changed a bit from Japanese to English, which is quite usual for English localisation since Japanese is often quite vague and relies on context more than English does, though there are times where what I'm hearing from the Japanese voices and what I'm reading in the English subs are quite different, where someone perhaps sounds meaner than they should, or someone sounds softer than they should. Its a minor detail, but just another point to add. None of this actually detracts from the game itself.
Overall, despite some issues with the English localisation, the game is, to me, perfect. I would play this once, then again, then probably again. For those who don't know, there's a good 50 hours of gameplay available and even more if you go through the sidequests, which you will since they expand on these amazing characters. It has a story that will stick with you for years after you play it, gameplay that will infuriate you as much as it will bring you joy (on hard difficulties, lets be real here), and characters that you'll never, ever forget.
I'd give it a 9.5/10. The only issues are graphical, and even then, only slight, so much so that many won't even notice or care.
Since I don't care either, I'd give it a 10/10 in reality.
And I suppose if you do care a bit much, then its a 9/10, since everything good about this game really offsets anything potentially bad about it.

One of the BEST all time space combat games i have ever played (if not simply the best GAME i have ever played).  Old school simulator(ish) style gameplay with basically everything done right.  Review will be for both Descent Freespace 1 and Freespace 2.
1) Gameplay flight mechanics and controls:  Flight is simplified to mimic atmosphere flight mechanics (Arcade style) but the controls are simulator style.  Power managment, shield distribution, ETC.  Joystick control is reccomended but the mouse can be used as well.
2) Story:  In my opinion, THE ABSOLUTE BEST STORY I HAVE EVER EXPERIENCED IN A GAME.  The story is told through Cutscenes, Pre-mission briefings, and sometimes even during your mission.  Oh...and the games intro scene is the best cutscene in any videogame ever.
3) Graphics:  Excellent if it were 1998-2000, however now the graphics do not hold a candle to current games.  However a dedicated group of programmers have created the "Freespace 2 Source Code Project" AKA "Freespace 2 SCP".  Simply explained, this project updates all the graphics to about modern day [2015 (ish)] standards.  In order to use SCP project you must have purchased Freespace 2.  Then the SCP project will allow you to play the following things with the updated graphics:   Freespace 1 (Descent Freespace), Freespace 2, as well as additional fan made campaigns.
I could go on and on about the greatness of the Freespace games but let me ask you a simple question instead.  Can you remember the last game you played where the graphics were amazing (now using SCP Project mod), you had no issues or complaints with the controls or game performance, and the story was so amazing that you can remember it 15 years later?  I can, and they are Freespace 1 and Freespace 2 (which i have replayed over 5 times now).
Oh, and whatever company has the rights to Freespace, PLEASE make Freespace 3.

I have more hours than shown because of some problem where I had to launch the game outside Steam to get it to run properly.  This game was on my wishlist a long time and I was very much looking forward to playing it once I had some friends interested.  Ultimately I'm pretty disappointed with it.
Imagine Terraria.  Now take out the bossess.  Remove the difficulty and need to survive.  Abolish any uniqueness or variety among the different biomes.  Get rid of all sense of exploration and meaningful reward.  Make the crafting system far more complicated and frustrating.  Design your menu so that it blocks your view entirely, and even when you move it to the side of the screen, again and again and again, it still opens in the middle and blinds you every time.  Instead of one large and diverse planet, have a hundred or so small ones, each virtually identical to the last.  Imagine resources dropped ten times faster, but there were a tenth as many things to build with them.  Alter the difficulty curve so that within a few hours, you can have the most powerful weapons and armor in the game.  And add MMO style grinding to get through a series of meaningless fetch quests for rewards you not only don't want, but literally cannot use, because you have already maxed out the upgrade potential they provide while grinding for the randomly generated trinkets the questgivers desire.
And retrograde the multiplayer system so setting up games with your friends becomes a chore, much how Terraria was when it first launched, four years ago.
This game is not worth the money or the time.  It's not fun.  It doesn't handle multiplayer well in a variety of ways.  It has no sense of progression, challenge, discovery, or accomplishment.  There are a lot of 2D survival games on Steam, many of them cheaper than this.  I'd try one of those instead.

It is impossible to deny that Coffee Stain Studios took just about everything good in Sanctum and amped it up tenfold for Sanctum 2.
Enhancing the coop mode by adding three new player characters alongside the original protagonist, each specializing in one of four weapon categories (Assault Rifles, Snipers, Shotguns and a big happy rocket launcher that blinds the entire right side of your screen).
Like the previous title, Sanctum 2 is a fast-paced FPS tower defense game that requires a heavy load of brainpower to keep the waves of alien enemies away from your core. In Sanctum 2 the challenge level is increased, giving the player less resources after each wave and removing the ability to upgrade weapons with resources, forcing the player to focus less on weapon damage and instead on carefully placed towers, walls and turrets to keep the enemy waves back, as well as the addition of a timer to mix things up and make the waves more chaotic.
With an immersive campaign mode playable in both single player or coop, Sanctum 2 offers mind-blowing gameplay complimented with a level-up system that rewards the player with unlockable towers, weapons and perks as well as a digital comic that offers insight into Sanctum's world which reveals a page or two before every stage.
Sanctum 2 is a direct upgrade to Sanctum, and is well worth the time for any fans of the original.

This game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ It takes everything that made the first game great and throws it out, focusing instead on the first person shooter aspect, which is horribly mediocre. The towers in this game are worthless coupled with the fact that you are limited to only a handful in number at any time anyway. Also bosses will smash through very limited mazes that you can build, destroying swathes of blocks and towers like they aren't there, forcing you to full engage enemies with your hand held guns, which as stated previously are barely passable.
A strange design choice was to also add player death, which means that this time around mobs can attack you. While this in itself isn't a bad thing, alot of mobs will throw you around like a ragdoll or nuke you down in seconds - you have very little health. If you are thrown off of a bridge or cliff into the abyss, you will die. Some mobs will do an area of effect throw, throwing anyone near them.. it makes some mobs almost impossible to kill if they are on thin ledges and are immune to attacks unless you hit the weak spots. Often the respawn point is right near the core too, so if they are at the core, doing the AoE, you will respawn and instantly get thrown off again. If you are lucky enough to survive you will probably land in scenery and glitch into it, unable to move, unable to respawn (and did I mention that they removed televators? So you can no longer teleport like you could in the first game)
This game was obviously designed with consoles in mind due to the limited number of things that you can do and the unintuitive interface; A bizarre decision by the developers considering that the first Sanctum did really well on PC. It tries to dazzle you with ragdoll physics and huge bosses but ultimately fails to provide the gameplay to back it up. This game is less about tactics and clever maze building than the first, in favor of bouncy, flashiness and guns. Buy the first game instead, Sanctum 2 is a wasted opportunity and not worth your time. A shame because I was really looking forward to it after the fun and original game that was Sanctum.

Well detailed game. You can read (albeit dangerous) the license plates on other cars. The lighting from the sun shines off high gloss paint jobs like in real life. The small detail damages are realistic; if you broke a headlamp it stays broken and doesn’t light up. The back ground is realistic enough to tell distance. I’ve played this at both regular television and hi definition 1080p while it is still good at the lowest setting I highly recommend the playing at the highest possible detail.
You can tell from just driving around what types of cars are around you with even having to look at that area. The screeching of the tires to the roar of an engine is clear with any vehicle you use. Now the music, quantity or quality wise you will not be disappointed. There are a lot of songs that play while driving around so chances are if you play for an hour or two, you will not hear the same song twice. And you don’t like a particular song you can always take if off the play list. One should note that a good portion of songs are the same songs from older Burnout Games.
As you win events you upgrade your license. The higher the license, the larger amount of vehicles you will be able to use. These events are littered all thought Paradise City. To start the event simple pull up to a light to start it.
Here is the events.
Races: Standard Race. From one to seven other opponents you drive to a specific end point.
Road Rage: Timed Event. You use your vehicle as a battering ram to smash other vehicles into traffic, walls or other hard objects. Target amount is usually displayed. Event ends when either you take to much damage or time ends.
Marked Man: Almost like a race. You goal is to reach one destination while four other computer cars try to inflict enough damage to keep you from reaching your destination.
Stunts: Use your vehicle like a little acrobat, jumping off ramps, crashing bill boards and doing spins. The more you do in a sequence the more points you get. There is a target score to get per event.
Burning Route: One route per vehicle. It’s a timed race where you just have to get to the finish line by a certain time using a certain vehicle. Every route you finish unlocks a upgraded version of the vehicle used.
All these events get a bit more difficult as the game wears on but not that much more. I would say once you get used to the way the game plays you find that most of these events range from easy (one or two attempts) to medium (fifteen minutes maximum).
Now there are a few side events or tasks that are fun to do. Running certain billboards, barriers, and super jumps. They are littered everywhere, cant be avoided just driving around. There are few hidden but find to fun all of them and as a reward for finding all it unlocks more vehicles. There are also two events per street, one is time trails and the other is showtime. Showtime is just you bouncing around hitting vehicles for points.
Online play is quite fun with tasks and races, connections are usually stable. One thing I like is with Xbox Live Vision take a photo of you when you get taken out by another drive and sent to the aggressor. The online experience is a whole new game in itself and worth playing.
Although it’s a very good game here is a few of the things I didn’t like. Showtime is very repetitive in the sense you have to do it to all 64 streets of Paradise City. Also Showtime replaced Crash from previous games. The on line challenges are very repetitive where if 2 players you have to do it for 7 players. And some of them are very very basic like driving in oncoming traffic. Also while doing online challenges if one person get disconnected, the challenges are cancelled. The difficulty level is somewhat misleading as the more cars you unlock the easier the game is when trying to do the events.
One last thing that kind of surprised me is the amount of advertising in the game, from billboards to vans there is way too much advertising in this game. To show how much advertising there are four unlockable cars, all of them are plastered with the names.

Jagged Alliance - Back in Action is by far not a bad game per se, but it does suffer from one completely fatal flaw: It tries to appeal to the old Jagged Alliance fans by delivering a remake that is a good tactics game, but has literally nothing to do with Jagged Alliance core gameplay wise. If they had made the whole game old-school-fully-turnbased combat, it could have been absolutely amazing. If the AI was working better and balancing wasn't extremely wonky, it would have been great.
The way it is, it is solely not bad and can fill the void of tactical iso-combat within the heart of the older generation of gamers, but being a diehard Jagged Alliance fan since the first game, I was let down by this fundamentally flawed remake. Only after just ignoring the title name and the fact that I do remember the story vividly from the original game, I was able to start to look at Back in Action in its own right and stopped to compare it with its original successor.
And after doing that, I did actually manage to sink in quite a bit of time into it and after getting used to weird AI range proficiency and being in cover at all times, it suddenly started to be more and more fun.
If I ever had really mixed feelings about a game, then it was Back in Action in the last two to three weeks. It's not a worthy Jagged Alliance game, but it is not a bad game either. If you like semi-turnbased iso tactical combat, it could be for you. If you want to relive Jagged Alliance, you'll have to replay the original. And don't do the same mistake of comparing titles like I did, because it will ultimately make you feel let down.
All in all, I still had fun and even with those mixed feelings I feel like I can recommend this title to genre fans.

The new expansion of PA is getting bashed by haters just like the core game, but this time it's uncalled for. Original PA was in a terrible state on its initial release and the devs deserved all of the criticism for delivering a lacklustre product, but over the past year it was updated and polished to become a stand-alone expansion. I often hear that Tales of Symphonia was the best game in the series, and as someone who had up until recently had that as my only Tales game, I could see why people would think that. It had a great caster of characters, a plot full of epic twists and turns, and a fun battle system with a good mix of action and strategy.
Now having played Tales of Berseria, its just amplified all of Symphonia's positives.
The characters are INCREDIBLE in this game. There's only six in Berseria compared to Symphonia's eight, but they are so much more cohesive and have some of the most comedic and close interactions I've ever seen in an RPG, with deep storylines to each one. The character development for the main two characters (no spoilers here) are so amazingly cathartic and moving that I was stuck watching, eyes glued to the screen, with that panging feel in your chest when your emotions have just spilled everywhere.
Graphics are decent. Sure, sometimes hair clips through clothes, body parts clip through other body parts (in cinematics where it really is kinda unforgivable), and that could've been improved upon, but its not in that kind of comedic glitchy light where its gone so far that you can't help but laugh and break immersion, its slight errors only.
Symphonia had really thick outlines and cel shading that this game does not have, and to be honest, I wasn't too comfortable with the look of Berseria at first, but it quickly grew on me to the point where that iffy feeling was but a memory. Once you're involved with the game (with a story like this, really damn quickly, mind you), you won't even care, if you ever cared at all.
Soundtracks are incredible; the protagonist's theme serves as a motif for her development throughout the entire game from the beginning to the end, with each section of the track 'unlocking' as she develops. I've never had such an uplifting feeling in a game from soundtrack alone, so Velvet's theme is probably my favourite OST from the past decade, and I've had quite a lot of damn good OST's in that time.
The opening theme 'Burn' whilst not involved in the game outside of the animated opening, was good enough for me to find it on Amazon for 99p and buy it a few hours into the game, but thats music taste and that's subjective.
On the other side of sound is voices. Rina Sato's Velvet is as amazing as it sounds (for those of you who know her, a similar role she plays though not nearly as deep is Misaka Mikoto from A Certain Magical Index or A Certain Scientific Railgun), and nails the range of emotions Velvet goes through convincingly and beyond that; it is her ability to empathise with Velvet's character that really made those cinematic scenes throughout the game and made them so engaging. Not to overshadow the other Japanese voice cast who are really just as amazing. The second protagonist (not to spoil with their name) is just as worthy of the spotlight as Rina Sato, though Rokurou, Magilou, Eizen, Eleanor, Artorius, and pretty much every character in the Japanese voice cast is perfection. I can't fault them.
Now for those wondering if you should play in English dub (I deliberated on this since Symphonia's dub was so good), I'd recommend against it. While I can appreciate Cristina Vee's voice in League of Legends as Riven, and she isn't horrible as Velvet, she doesn't nail it like Rina Sato does. Despite this, the main reason not to go for Dub is the REST of the voices.
The aforementioned second protagonist who was just as amazing as Rina Sato in Japanese, is outright horrid in Dub. Key scenes are ruined by their lack of effort, their lack of empathy for the character, and their inability to read the mood of a scene. They also can't seem to decide on what gender they are, when just looking at the character's profile would've sorted that out.
Magilou sounds too basic, compared to the absolute craziness that his her Japanese voice actress, but its not necessarily terrible like the previous character. Rokurou makes me cringe a bit sometimes, but not totally terrible; just not fitting the character's carefree attitude. Eizen is a decent fit, and Eleanor isn't a decent fit, but in any case, all of the protagonist voices simply are inferior to the original Japanese cast, for budget reasons most likely. Even the best voice actors like for Shigure in English dub pale in comparison to the Japanese cast.
On the other hand of localisation, there are annoying typos in the subtitles in the game's skits/dialogues. Whilst its most prominent in the smaller side quests, I have detected at least one in the main story which I didn't actually see in the first playthrough. A minor detail perhaps, but still annoying; its a sign of a lack of playtesting, and for some reason isn't fixed in an update. Sometimes the meanings of a character's words are changed a bit from Japanese to English, which is quite usual for English localisation since Japanese is often quite vague and relies on context more than English does, though there are times where what I'm hearing from the Japanese voices and what I'm reading in the English subs are quite different, where someone perhaps sounds meaner than they should, or someone sounds softer than they should. Its a minor detail, but just another point to add. None of this actually detracts from the game itself.
Overall, despite some issues with the English localisation, the game is, to me, perfect. I would play this once, then again, then probably again. For those who don't know, there's a good 50 hours of gameplay available and even more if you go through the sidequests, which you will since they expand on these amazing characters. It has a story that will stick with you for years after you play it, gameplay that will infuriate you as much as it will bring you joy (on hard difficulties, lets be real here), and characters that you'll never, ever forget.
I'd give it a 9.5/10. The only issues are graphical, and even then, only slight, so much so that many won't even notice or care.
Since I don't care either, I'd give it a 10/10 in reality.
And I suppose if you do care a bit much, then its a 9/10, since everything good about this game really offsets anything potentially bad about it.

No, but in all seriousness I do have some real thoughts about the game. First of all, the artwork is beautiful. It's a bright and colorful world set behind a fairly dark storyline, which is kind of a nice contrast. You can tell in the cutscenes that the artwork in general isn't supposed to be super realistic like you see in some of the newer Final Fantasy games - it's actually really reminiscent of Windwaker; a nice, elegant cartoonish style. The voice acting is also superb, by the way.
The gameplay is very smooth, and you might say the same for the combat. The movesets you get as the main character Velvet are AWESOME. I've played a fair number of hours in the game so far and I haven't grown sick of them. But now I have some critiscisms.
A lot of the game can be very, very tedious. And that begins with the combat. Although the gameplay is smooth, when fighting enemies they can sometimes block your attacks. Which is fine, but when this happens, your attack is completely cancelled out and there's a second of a delay before you can attack again. When this happens consecutively for every attempt you make, it's maddening. Now I get that the game is trying to prevent players going out and attacking really high level enemies without better gear or tactics, but it completely disrupts the gameplay and there are some enemies where you can only get one or two actual hits on them before the rest of your party takes them out. Also, whenever one of your party members uses one of their 'special moves', combat stops and you have to watch the entire 5 second cutscene before you can continue fighting. That seemed unecessary.
Lastly regarding the tediousness, traveling is a pain in the bum. I don't believe you can actually fast travel until much later in the game, so up until then you have to do it the old-fashioned way. If done right, that isn't a big deal. But in Berseria you aren't allowed to cross over the tiniest ledges, yet your character can literally jump off of 50 ft tall ladders. This leads you to spend minute after minute walking through several loading areas to get to a place you practically just were. Plus, new quests send you to opposite sides of the map, only shortly after finishing you're required to walk back to turn it in.
Overall, it's a great game with an amazing story and a lot of material - an overwhelming amount, really. If you like action RPG's, give it a shot!

-The UI. there are several bars that can expand to show you the full options available and be hidden when unnecessary. this can be quite useful when you have a lot to look at, and dont want all that other crap blocking your view.
-i like the fact that there are multiple ways to view your city, with the satndard camera and the postcard view, which helps you see a more....well.... postcard view of your city.  you can also switch the time of day to see what your city would look like at night or watch the sun rise and all that romantic stuff.... this helps add to the feel of reality, that your city is actually a city and not just a random map generator.
the map selector is also quite nice as you can filter which type of resource you want to focus on, like food or holidays, and get a description of each. there are also city templates like New York and Hollywood so you can attempt to copy / make your own version of each.
the bad:
get comfortable because we might be here for a while....
-you know how i said that the graphics were good? well thats from a distance. up close, the animations of the people are horrific, and make me want to never go down to street level again. For such a beautiful game, the people, and cars, that they are filled with are more reminiscent of team America puppet dolls than real people.
-whilst we are on the subject of up close and personal, when you get down to the ground level of the game, the failures of the game become that much more apparent, to the extent i will have to create another sub level to this review:

1) The buildings. whilst the genral view of the city will be nice, some of the buildings just dont make sense. some are horribly out of place, like a snowy resort in the middle of the desert, whereas some are more of the "what the f*** inspired you yo do that?" type. i am spekaing, of course, about the futuristic building that pops up at random, and completely ruins the suburbia feel i had going on. its poorely drawn and makes me think the creators were high when they were designing the game.
2) The landscape. yes i know i said it was nice to look at and yes, it is nice to look at....... from a distance. once you get up close, the "hills" become more irregular, and turn out to be weird bumps in the land that you cant build on. seriously, it completely puts me off and since there is never 100% flat land, you'll always find those hideous goosebumps around and about.
Another problem i have found about the game and people on youtube have mentioned this aswell, is that when you zoom in on the road, no matter what type or whether or not there is a single car, you will always hear the doppler effect of the cars going past, or the horn being honked at nonexistent drivers, by nonexistent drivers. again a sloppy mistake, but considering the grand scale of the game, it's okay to overlook something like this.
something else, however, that everry city builder should have nailed from the beginning, is terraforming. whilst you do have the ability to flatten the landscape, it is expensive and often makes the problem worse, making me wish there was a undo button, which there isn't but would make the game so much better. so i tend not to use that when building. fortunately, the placement of buildings does flatten the landscape somewhat, so that you are building the item on a level area. unfortunately, this doesnt change the landscape around your building, and so i have been left with houses surrounded by huge slopes of earth or a jagged drop to the street. all of which makes you again, consider why the developers havent done something about it. but i am not a developer, so i dont know if thats something that possible to do, only that it's something that needs adressing.
once more, there are rather basic things in the game that are missing. for example the notices that appear. whilst helpful at identifying what i need to do like "more housing for skilled workers", sometimes its general like "something is wrong with the hotels" right okay then . what ? and it wont tell me. and sometimes it starts to tell me what to do, but then runs out of space and cuts of the message half way through. this is one of the most blatant and unforgivable failures, that the developers couldnt be bothered to extend the boxes for one or two lines, and really annoys me. and i dont know if there is any way to see it or im supposed to guess.
so you might say: But then why dont you go through the tutorial and find out. i did and i didnt find out and it was nightmarish. the tutorial is a shoddy excuse for  a guide, and left me no better than before. the crap attempts to be funny with their stage directions and childish humour makes me really just want to get stuck in and find out for myself, which is shame becuas that is bloody difficult to do. there are so many complex things to work out like bus networks and trade that i feel arent explained in the tutorial to an acceptable level, leaving me to painstakingly trial and error with cities until i figured out how to make money properly.
Conclusion.
as odd as it might sound, i actually enjoy the game , with its quirky music and beautiful skies. there arent many citry building agmes out there, so i commend cities xl for attempting to make such a complex one, even if they do fall short in some areas. as far as improvements go, i would like another cities xl game as  i feel there are definite ways they could make an even better game which would be well worth the £14.99 on steam (hint. wait until it's on sale). for example, weather features like rain or cloud, more detailed forests, not just some sporadic woodland.
NOTE TO ANYONE NEW TO CITY BUILDERS. IF YOU ARE, LIKE ME, UNFAMILIAR WITH CITY BUILDERS BUT WANT TO TRY THIS OUT, GO FOR IT. IT IS A FUN GAME ONCE YOU GET THE HANG OF IT, AND THERE ARE ALWAYS PEOPLE ON YOUTUBE WHO DO  GAMEPLAYS OF IT FOR HELP. KEEP PERSISTING WITH IT, AS IT DOES TAKE SOME TIME, BUT IS WELL WORTH THE MONEY.

One of my all time favorite games was the Descent I and II.  I loved how you could smoothly circle strafe around corners and enemies, it ran silky smooth, and had great music and insane maze levels.
I was really hyped to try Descent Freespace 2, but the excitement left after two things.  One is how complex and difficult is it was to get set up.  Multiple downloads, patches, and obtuse directions.
The second thing was the flight model was not newtonian,  you could not side or circle strafe smoothly.   The flight model was almost the same as Star Wars X-Wing Alliance which is smooth and fun, but leaves no room for side strafing.
Freespace does have a switch to allow your ship to rotate around it's axis, but was very hard to control.
Some forums claim a Battle Star Galactica conversion fixes this, but again,  I took one look at the install and patch directions for that and decided if it is not push one button install, I don't need the grief.
Another reason I stopped playing it was it was not exactly friendly in terms of setting up and customizing your controller settings. It is an old school space sim, with lots and lots of minutia controlled by lots of hotkeys.
I have both a good joystick and a game controller and found, the whole process of trying to get so many hotkeys to work the way you want was time consuming and tedious.  Make this change, reboot the game, see if it works, rinse and repeat.
I am not saying you should not buy this game, it has great promise and I have had lots of fun with it, but there are so many other games out there that are more polished and don't require you to spend hours tweaking control settings and patching the game exe.
I recommend it only if you are comfortable with that kind of hassle, Otherwise I would instead recommend Star Wars X-Wing Alliance which came out the same year, but has a much better and relate-able story.

Core mechanics are true to the SF formula: easy to learn, hard to master. And the fighting is just brilliant: based on fundamentals, rewards reads and intuition, rather than execution and practice.
Cheap ways to get out of risky situations are gone, low-risk high-reward attack/combos are not there anymore, vortex that put the opponent into a 50/50 situation costantly are extremely limited due to the 2 new ground recoveries ( or tech).
Crush counters, v-reversals/v-skill/v-trigger are new addition to the gameplay.
Crush counters will cause the opponent to dizzy for a second if the player is able to counter his attack with one of his own, thus rewarding a good neutral game and read.
V-reversal is a defensive tool that will put the pressure off the defending player at the cost of one v-gauge bar.
V-skill is a particular special move performed by pressing mid-punch and mid-kick, an unique tool for each character.
V-trigger is a special state in which the player is put upon activation, the effect of the trigger are unique for each character but they can deeply change the pace and the outcome of the match.
All of the new addition blend perfectly into a masterfully crafted gameplay.

The launch of Street Fighter V was an unmitigated disaster. With my arcade stick hooked up and ready to go, I faced my first challenge on my road to becoming a world champion: getting past the User Agreement screen. The game would not respond to my joystick inputs, so figuring I had to pass the screen to get into an options menu and enable it, I tried using my keyboard to get past the legalese threshold guardian. The arrow keys worked, but hitting 'Enter' would not advance the game. I'm lucky enough to have a second arcade stick, so I plugged that in. No dice. The mouse fared no better, so I fell back on years of gaming experience and proceeded to press every key on the keyboard. Finally, I was making progress. Protip: it's 'B'.
This was the first stumbling block in a comedy of errors. Turns out neither fight stick I own is supported even though Windows certainly recognizes them as functional. Bold move for a fighting game. Then I got to witness the joys of launch day server problems: they didn't work, either. Granted this is unfortunately common, but Street Fighter V is a game with next to no fallback plan for when the online portion is out of commission. There are a few (very few) single player options, but if you're not connected to Capcom's servers you're not earning “fight money”, the game's currency for buying future DLC characters and costumes. I say “future” because right now the Store option is blacked out, promising to open at a later date. So what that fight money is actually worth... who knows? The game isn't interested in telling you. It's not interested in telling you many things, actually...
So, despite not racking up Capcom funny money, I decided to dive into the few options available to me, starting with the Story mode. You could easily confuse this to mean Arcade mode, but don't get your hopes up. What's on offer is almost hilariously awful. Almost. I've played enough fighting game stories at this point to appreciate some cheese, but Street Fighter V's Story Mode is offensively bad to the point I had to skip most of the “cutscenes”. And by “cutscenes”, I mean static, hand drawn illustrations that appear to drawn by a middle grade student who checked out a “How to Draw Anime” book from the library. It's bad, and the story and dialogue aren't much better. Each fighter is tasked to complete roughly three one round fights, starting with full meters, in what has to be the easiest of Easy difficulty settings with no option to tweak any settings. This mode lasted all of an hour.
What caught my eye next was a Training mode that promised numerous different options to hone your skills. I adored the training mode in Street Fighter IV, so I was looking forward to hopping in and challenging myself to some combos. Nope. It's just a dummy AI mode where you can set the CPU to different states. No combo lists or actual training of any kind. There's not even a VS CPU mode, so all that was left on my plate was Survival, which is easily the strongest of the offline offerings. Here you fight through a set number of CPU opponents depending on your difficulty setting, and spend the points you earn through winning matches on “supplements” which range from health gains to offense, defense, and meter boosts. If you're trying to practice anything else besides health boosts kind of screw up the game, but it's better than nothing.
Days later, the servers seem to be somewhat functional so I've been playing Survival mode with Fight Requests turned on... because there's not a whole lot else to do in the game. Every now and then I even get to fight online, and sometimes it's playable. For a test I set aside an hour to gauge my success: Ranked requests on, all platforms, regions, skill levels. In that hour, I had a whopping one match come up against a fine fighter named PoopyPoopFarts. To the game's credit the match was very smooth. After that hour, another fight popped, but it was laggy to the point of unplayability and got disconnected after about thirty seconds. Going into straight Ranked matchmaking is painful, staring at a spinning wheel for three to ten minutes on average, and about two thirds of those games ran very poorly as well.
The core mechanics of Street Fighter V seem okay. I find them simple, but I'm not a hardcore fighting fanatic so any depth beyond generic strategies and spamming specials is lost on me, and it's too much to ask the game to actually teach you anything in-game, apparently. There are promises of a true Arcade mode, challenges, and loads of “free” content coming to Street Fighter V in the future, and who knows? Maybe this game will be a complete package someday down the line. As it is now, it feels rushed, unfinished, and outright broken in many cases. The problem with waiting for these updates is the game was released as a full priced product, and by the time those updates roll out there will be better, more complete games already released (there are already plenty), so I don't know who this game is for. Not me, anyway.

A well done game and the best space fighter simulator i have ever played to date after doing the bug fix it suffers from.
The story picks up years after the events of the first game and unless you play that first you are going to be a little in the dark about the plot, but other than that is a good and enjoyable plot.
The fights that you will partake in will range from engaging fighters and bombers to taking down corvettes and cruisers and is always entertaining watching them blow up
. The AI in this game does not suck and can excel at dispatching your teammates and you if you are not careful and the same can be said about your own teammates, although they will sometimes need a helping hand when an enemy gets behind them and will inform you of the same thing.
The guns and missiles that you will unlock as you progress through the game will allow the adding (if the ship allows it)  of individual guns into slots to complement eachother such as a gun with good hull damage but not very good shielding damage with a gun with the opposite properties. Missiles range from lock ons, fire and forget and dumb fire and are useful in quickly taking down enemies or turrets.
The line up of ships vary from space superiority fighters, intercepters, heavy fighters and bombers and in most cases have multiple versions of the types with differing armoring, speeds, manoverability and gun and missile (and differing amounts of the same missiles you can carry) slots.
The actual playing of the game is smooth and other than a few hiccups in framerate runs incredibly well and the fights can become challenging and exciting for the player with the right difficulty, the HUD on your screen will keep you up to date with monitoring crucial ships to protect and constant tracking of any ship that you can target.
The joystick is a very effective tool for this game as with the mouse i found that the fighter would zoom of my screen
and i would have to swipe the mouse a few time in the direction i wanted to go before I had visual contact again but unlike the mouse i found myself overshooting the target lead multiple times with the joystick but thats probably because i'm bad at using it.
The game also has a mission editor called FRED2 that I personally enjoyed playing around with but requires a understand of how the coding in the engine works, for example the corvettes will not fire their main lazers until you give them the ability to by going into the events editor and enabling it there by replacing the operators of the event I made for it, despite that you can change the name of the ships in this program and had fun giving them wacky names.
Overall the game is impressive and is highly entertaining. The only negatives i have for this game is that:
1. I bought this a day before the special

2. once during a mission a prompt in the coding did not activate as it should and i flew around for a few minutes while nothing happened before deciding to reset which fixed the problem the second time around.
3. Resolution...but that's just nitpicking at an old game.
But other than that i could not give a higher recommendation for anyone to at least pick up the game for a little bit to play through.

Tweed says it all:
Terraria was developed between January 2011 and May 2011 yet the Starbound apologists compare release Starbound to release Terraria.  The better comparison is Terraria after the last major content update in 2015 and release Starbound... and Terraria blows it away.
Chucklefish scammed a bunch of people out of money to set themselves up as a small publishing outfit.  Marketing as a 'spiritual sucessor' to Terraria; Starbound offers little to anything other than hardcore 'builder' types who like playing with virtual ant farms.  Boss fights are in fixed mission areas.  They have no loot (aside from a couple of hard coded drops).  You can replay these missions but there's no point in farming.  The mechanics are straight out of a 1980's Capcom platformer.  In the end this game is little more than a 15-20ish hour side scroller with nothing in the way of character progression or meaningful itemization.

Now, I'm not normally all that big on GTA-esque games, as they tend to really only be good for derping around in. That is not so with this game. The combat and free-running are smooth as silk, the story is well paced and written, and the game world feels alive and is big without being overwhelming. I'd highly recommend this game, 20/10

Potentially fun little game that could have been so much more. The breakout/RPG mashup is potentially very fun but not enough was done with shops, bonus power-ups, and special abilities to make the game truly shine. Shatter is a modern example of power-ups done better but you can go all the way back to Arkanoid and that game still does a better job with power-ups/-downs in 1986 than Wizorb in 2011. There could have optional side-quests, rewards for helping the townsfolk, a lot more buffs/de-buffs to be used on the fly but instead this game ends up being a basic breakout experience with a little flair and a thin coat of RPG paint.
If those were the only issues, I could recommend this with some minor hesitations but what pushes this title into the "Not Recommended" category is the way the quit and save features work. This game would lend itself very well to a quick play session now and again but instead forces the player to play through an entire world (12 levels and a boss) if you want to keep the gold you've accumulated. That alone is terrible and is, unfortunately, why I can't recommend this title.

A highly underrated game and one of the best looking in recent years (especially in rainy,night scenes),Sleeping Dogs is pretty much a Hong Kong version of GTA with many of the same elements. You play as loveable badass Wei Shei,both as an officer and undercover cop in a story packed with high speed chases in awesome cars and other vehicles,shoot out's,gang related activity,hacking equipment,drug busts and other random things like singing karaoke haha. There is a large focus on hand to hand combat,especially earlier on in the game. The story is great as is everything in between,with the soundtrack and surrounding world making you feel like you're actually in Hong Kong. As much as I love this game,after completing the campaign,the side missions can get somewhat monotonous as there is just so many of them and they're all pretty much the same after a while. This isn't a game breaker though as you can choose to just not do them (If you're not after achievements) and they do add a large chunk of extra gameplay If you enjoy them. DLC wise,I recommend the item's packs as they give you a big advantage in the game money/purchasing wise and equipment wise (better car's for race challenges and outfits that reduce damage etc.). Story DLC wise,If you got sick of the side missions I mentioned earlier,they're not really necessary as they are pretty much just more of the same in-game one's. Good If you want to add a few extra hours of content though. Overall,It's a must purchase for action fans and one of my new favourite games.

Half life changed the way that we play first person shooters, by allowing us to step into the shoes of Gordon Freeman, we were able to see the story unfold bit by bit. This was truly the first FPS game to introduce a deep story, and excellent immersion.
Though it is old, Half Life stands the test of time. From the intense yet satisfying combat, fun puzzles, immersive atmosphere, interesting storyline and more, Half life is truly a legend; one that can still be enjoyed even today, and remains an important piece of video game history.

In my 40 years of gaming I have seen titles come and go. Both independent publishing and Mega productions that promise to change the face of the gaming as we know it. With baited breath I look now to an indie browser rpgmmo called RPG MO.
While my time in game, (RPG MO) has been somewhat limited; I find myself transported back through time to an age where my favorite titles consumed every free moment I could spare. Dragon Warrior-(NES), Telengard – (Atari 800XL), and of course the vaunted Ultima series from the original pc days all comes to mind when playing RPG MO.  The magic these games held was partially due to the love of the, “Grind”. That love has been neatly re-created in this polished offering from the RPG MO team.

The love and care the Dev team along with the staff has put into this offering can clearly be seen from the moment a new player steps into the tutorial. A deep crafting system along with applicable time sinks to farm materials makes for endless hours of enjoyable reminiscence. This has taken many aspects of the past and improved them to fit for today’s discerning gamer!
This game is well worth a look for just the community alone. The staff and players are both informative and well behaved. I don’t have to tell you just how rare that is these days…

The verdict!
If you are a fan of fast paced instant gratification with no community save the smell of your own stench, stay away! This game in many aspects will not speak to you.

If you are a fan of retro gaming, a helpful and friendly community along with the beauty of a smoldering slow satisfying grind, then welcome my friend!
Hands down this is a title that is welcome and I am glad I have the chance to play it!

This game doesn't allow you to trade with anyone on the same IP and if you play this game while someone else is playing it on the same IP at the same time you run the risk of both accounts getting perma banned.
"3. No Interaction Between Multiple Accounts
Although you are allowed to have multiple accounts (A maximum of FIVE), and are allowed to have more than one account training at one time, you may not use secondary "slave" accounts to gather resources to give to a "primary" account for skill training. This also includes using accounts for storage space, and selling the resources gathered on one account to gain money on another. Any accounts that are found to be interacting with each other who have the same owner will be permanently jailed and banned. You arent allowed to give items to your firend so he/she gives them to your alt account, in the end it's still trading between same player accounts."
I asked a mod about it in-game and he told me they have no way of knowing if both accounts are from the same person or not, so even if you have them registered to two different emails and are playing from two different computers the "alt" rules apply to all accounts on the same IP.
TL:DR - You can't play with any family members or friends/roommates in the same house (same IP) without running the risk of getting perma banned, and even if you don't get banned you'll be unable to trade with them.
Edit: Both issues have been addressed by the developer, I sent in an email as directed and within a short time they responded to sort out the trading issue for me. (changing my review from negative to positive)

This game is flawed. It is better than Sim City 4 in many ways, but it is flawed in that it was built many years ago for single core systems. The main thread of the game handles most everything and becomes overwhelmed with you city gets to be about 1/3 the size of a city's maximum footprint. It doesn't matter how many cores, how much RAM, or what kind of video card you have. Everything is bottlenecked by the single game thread which will max out a single core and bring the game down to an unplayable single digit frames per second.
If it wasn't for this one show stopper issue, I would recommend this over Sim City. It is a shame they don't rewrite their game engine to work with multiple cores.
