I got the original Descent: FreeSpace and Silent Threat from one of those bargain-rack displays in the video game section at Wal-Mart in the early 2000s. Remember, when Wal-Mart still had PC games? One of my friends had been raving about it, and he was a pretty big nerd, so I figured I'd give it a try. I didn't expect much from a game released the same year as StarCraft, but it was only $10 so what the hell? I took it home, popped it into the CD drive of my 200MHz Pentium MMX machine with 32MB of RAM and a video card with 4MB of memory...
AND WAS BLOWN AWAY. The explosions, the lasers, the enormous capital ships...It made X-Wing vs TIE Fighter (my other big space flight sim crush) look like a cartoon. Not a good cartoon either; more like something I would draw. I loved it. I lived it. I wanted the sequel. But FreeSpace 2 wouldn't run on my old girl.
Then, one day browsing Steam, I said "I wonder if they have FreeSpace 2." OMG, yes they do! And there's a mod project for it called FS2 Open, with a ton of user-generated content and tweaks? That lets me play at my monitor's full resolution? AND SOMEBODY MADE A MOD TO LET ME PLAY THE ENTIRE FS CAMPAIGN USING THE FS2 ENGINE? SHUT UP AND TAKE MY MONEY!
I had some trouble getting FS2 Open to launch. What worked for me was downloading, in addition the FSOpen stuff, wxLauncher for the FreeSpace 2 Source Code Project. It's pretty awesome and I'd recommend it even if you're having no trouble launching.

Disclaimer: Ive been playing street fighter games since i was a wee baby.
Early reviews for the game on steam mostly talk about a few thing.
While this may be for the most part true i must state that the idea that you may be looking for a deep engrossing single player experience you will be deeply saddened and dissapointed. This isnt "The Witcher" or "Fallout". there is no vast open world to explore, and there definetly are no skill trees here.
However you will find something within this title that you wont find in those titles, and that is a game that works both on a casual level in your living rooms with friends, as well as a competive game you can spend thousands of hours learning the nuances to playing specific characters, matchups,
While the roster currently is nothing to brag about in size (although an additional 6 characters will be added in this year alone with promises to continue to support this product), its worth stating that each character in the roster is very unique in playstyle, appearance, and overall usage, Character designs that were used in previous games are completely new and different, with no copies of play style in the roster. where as if you were to compare it to other similar games or previous games you would find that most characters on the roster fit one of a few designs or archetypes and thus would be clones of each other with slight differences.
As for Controller issues and binding issues there are work around and while it seems silly will be a non-issue in a month's time, its worth noting that it is inexcusable that you are not even able to use a Playstation 4 fight stick for this title without 3rd party software, concidering the playstation 4 fightstick is branded for Street fighter V. The fact that you cant change the keyboard binding is another wierd thing that would seem like a no brainer.
In conclusion if you are looking for a VS fighting game for your livingroom for casual play with friends or if you want something more out of this title, you can find it here.

Ever had a dream where you could be a pirate? I remember seeing pirate movies where it looked really cool to shoot ships with cannons, ram and board, and, of course, lead your very own ship and crew. Blackwake definitely brings all of that to the table, properly executed and well-established, but there are still some issues about it.
is solely a multiplayer, first-person, strategy, naval-battle game where you could take on the role as either one of the crew mates of a ship, or the captain of the entire ship. Your objective: sink the enemy ship before they sink you, and to achieve that, you have to go through intense broadside-fights, insane ramming scenarios, and grapple-on-grapple deathmatches.
As of now, that is what the game currently is: a deathmatch. Even with the new gamemode added, which is basically a treasure raid, players still play Team Deathmatch (TDM).
Players could be either the Pirates or the British Navy, and in two teams of 32 players, 3 ships will go head-at-head to achieve that sweet, sweet “B-double-O-T-Y.” Each team will have a large Galleon ship and two smaller ships, which could be a Hoy or Schooner for the British, or a Hoy and Junker for the Pirates. And that is basically it, the rest of the gameplay is repetitive back and forth, non-stop, first-person action that will keep you on your toes, so long as you are awake.
Not only does this game have great graphics, but, in a way, it’s fun. Not many sole-multiplayer games can possibly achieve what
has accomplished here. There will not be one scenario where you are sitting at your screen in silence because in
match, you would have talked the entire time; this is especially true for the captain.
The developers have executed naval ship fights pretty well in
, and for those possibly hardcore history players, it’s important to understand that the timeline setting of this game is real, but how the battles were at this time are not. Combined with uproarious ragdoll physics, intense boarding fights, really stupid-fun ramming situations, and leave-them-for-dead overboard events,
is that type of game where you can have fun, and with friends, it’s a whole lot more.
You could establish your own crew, hop on a server, and prove you and your crew the best of the best, sinking enemy ships and having a blast, all the while laughing at one of your friends being blasted off the ship by a cannonball, sent soaring across the sun, or even over your head.
Best of all, this game can be played casually or competitively because there is no real Ranked Multiplayer system. In
, there is less toxicity among players, and you are allowed to leave a match
if a game turns sour, you aren’t glued to your desk like how it is in many other multiplayer games. Additionally, the game invites and embraces teamwork, something that a lot of games fail to execute, but this one does it well in a way. You
to work together to win; you can’t win alone, which I praise the developers for making a shining reality. However, that could be its ultimate downfall.
Currently, the game is in Early Access (EA), so for most of the issues that I see in-game, I can turn a blind-eye. However, even after playing 50+ hours, I still don’t see this game as something I can have a blast with for hours without getting angry.
As I have stated before,
encourages teamwork and cooperation to successfully play the game and have fun, and while that is all fun and good, that is also the greatest issue of this game. Like any all-multiplayer game, there are those that will troll, fool around, and purposely be jerks for no reason to either the captain or the crewmates all because he/she has a hate-life. This is the Internet, that is bound to happen no matter what. The problem is that Blackwake is
on teamwork for people to actually play the game.
You could have a captain who is clearly trying to sink his/her own ship. You could have a crew member randomly and intentionally firing off cannons on the portside, starboard-side, and/or the aft for no reason at all, wasting ammo and angering off the captain. Worst of all, in Friendly-Fire-On servers, you could have a troll who shoots
on his/her own ship “for the fun of it” and kill them. I’ve seen it happen. As someone who loves to play captain, I had to deal with it, and it isn’t fun for me, nor the crewmates trying to actually win. And even with the game receiving more and more players, this is becoming more and more apparent.
Moreover, the way teams are divided is currently not in a stable-state. If you played Team Fortress 2 or CS: GO,
’s team selection is similar to both. That is not the issue. The issue is you could have Prestige 5 players, all of them, on one team, and all-new players on the other team, crying as they get rekt. The point of this game is to have fun
not just one, but I’m hoping to see that change.
Furthermore, this game is heavily-repetitive. Please understand that you will likely be bored of the game after 5 matches of the same shoot-and-kill unless you switch to the other gamemode, or stop playing all-together.
Worst of all, there is an unusually large amount of racism from the players in this game. I have no idea why, but be prepared to listen to 10 straight minutes of racist remarks per game round.
makes me wish other game developers came up with something like this years ago because this game is really,
fun. Seriously, you have all these other complex games… why not go with this one? I praise Dakota and Tyler for making, drawing, and coding such a wonderful game, so well-established, properly executed and deployed. And for an Indie game, my gosh, this game blows other games away as it takes charge, and it will always be a part of my heart and soul. That is my word.
For 20 USD, or 25 Canadian, yes. In its current state, there is enough content to compensate for the price. Trust me, it’s worth it… so far.
Constant trolls, unbalanced teams, all-multiplayer with no practice games, so much racism, and overly-dependent teamwork currently sabotage this game. I know it’s in EA, and it will be fixed because these developers are talented, but I just can’t give the developers what they want to hear right now: a thumbs up. They need to fix what needs to be fixed, maybe then I will say yes.
I still say buy it and give it a shot, just understand what you may go through.

I have been sitting on the fence with this game. First - with the decision to buy it (seeing as it garnered so many negative reviews), until the publisher relented and I got it for around £2. Second - with my own recommendation. After careful consideration, I have decided to give this game a reluctant 'thumbs down'. Allow me to explain why (please be forewarned - some spoilers ahead).
Jagged Alliance: Back in Action is a third-person-perspective strategy with emphasis on team tactics and with strong elements of RPG (pun not intended), and the game that happens to also be a franchise re-launch. Veterans of the genre will remember the hallowed original Jagged Alliance 2, which was, and for many still is, the pinnacle of turn based tactical games. Various J.A-related titles tried to ride the same gravy train afterwards but almost all of them inexorably failed to deliver. Russian developer Apeiron made attempts to bring the gameplay to the next level, introducing real-time tactical combat (with active pause), with the Brigade E5 and the 7.62 High Calibre - both of which are highly enjoyable and bring about the whole new meaning of the word 'micromanagement' but both somehow failed to find wider rapport with the gamers.
Fast forward some years and here is the Jagged Alliance: Back in Action, hailed as the 3D improvement on the original. As it turns out the game did improve on the visual aspect somewhat, whilst fouling/simplifying/streamlining almost everything else at the same time. The BiA literally looks as if the old content was ported into a new 3D engine in haste and in the process some bits broke off and were left scattered on the floor.
First of all, Jagged Allience has ceased to be a turn-based game. It followed the footsteps of other titles and introduced real-time decisions (albeit with highly configurable auto-pause) and partially replaced the turns with 'active pause', where you can - and will - create tactical plans for your mercs. This is a double edged sword. It speeds the game up enormously whilst retaining the possibility to plan and execute minute plans BUT it is much less focused on details and makes the gameplay that much less immersive (merc on auto-guard equals low-maintenance gameplay).
Secondly, many layers of complexity have been lost. As it stands, almost all features present in the original J.A are included in J.A:BiA, but simplified.
Guns? Yes, good selection but with less custom options. Armour? Yes, much larger selection, but with less interaction and now non-repairable (which is actually more realistic). Mercs? Uhh... A.I.M. only? And forget your custom-made character - this feature has been axed. Gun accessories? Yes, smaller selection, simplified impact. Quests? Yes, plenty to choose from and rather logical, however less varied and rather simplified. NPC conversation and interaction? Oh, a lot, but - incredible as it sounds - with even less options than original J.A.2. Ammunition? You'll probably go through truckloads of 5.56. Simplified choice - no more AP/HP/Buckshot/Slug choice.
...and so forth and so on. (Almost) every aspect of the game has either smaller selection or is less complex or has been 'streamlined'.
Pros:
- The game is (somewhat) engaging and challenging, especially mid-game onwards.
- Plenty of equipment to choose from. Granted, it is not as broad selection as you're used to but still... The developers added plenty of different clothes, shoes and hats to the game and added few parameters (ie. camo values) to augument mercs' survivability.
- Overhauled militia system. Instead of training done by your mercs, you simply arm the (marked) bystanders. You can then train your militia for a fixed fee using interface on the world map - five levels of expertise - as well as update their equipment as soon as you get your hands on better guns - every fighter has similar slots to your mercs, which accommodate weapons, uniforms, hedgear and personal armour. The availability of recruits is generally tied to loyalty level of the 'settlement'. Some recruits might start trained to higher level, but they usually require additional tasks to be performed (ie. picking the lock on their cell door) and their existence is more or less random.
- The 'active pause' planning system, which allows one to enact complex, synchronous tactical plans.
Cons:
- The game lacks polish. Really. This is my single big issue here - starting with descriptions copied straight from the original JA (which sometimes state things contrary to the obvious), through dysfunctional and basic interface and ending with pathetic glitches - such as silencers not aligning with the hand-held gun and bullpup-style weapons being held the same way as the classic configuration rifles. This leaves bad impression, almost as if the developers just couldn't have been bothered to put that extra five minutes of work. If you're willing to overlook the visible seams, you still have to contend with:
- Quirky, awkward and counterintuitive controls. You have to master several keyboard + mouse shortcuts to turn the view around to see the only door to the compound you're assaulting. And then navigate the maze inside whilst constantly battling the automatic roof overlay toggle, which obscures the view on parts of the building. Rather frustrating to say the least.
- The novelty of the 'active pause' feature wears thin quickly and becomes a chore on its own.
- The game feels like walking through your favourite park or forest, where you know every tree, bush and anthill and finding that since hte last time, the council cut half of the trees down and relocated all the wildlife to different corners. IMHO, the developer would have been better off creating a spin-off based on JA2 instead of blatantly copypasting the content and story.
Overall:
Whilst the gameplay mechanics and some ideas might be refreshing, the delivery is bad. Most often than not I was battling the UI instead of the enemie. 4/10 overall. I'd rather download and play Jagged Alliance 2 with the newest community patch.
And last, but not least, a glimmer of hope: there is a community patch available which brings about a plethora of improvements and new content - should you really want to play the JA:BiA, I strongly suggest downloading and applying it before you even start a new game. 6/10 with the patch.

Fallout 4 has been controversial as a significant departure from the typical Fallout games. It is no longer the roleplaying joy of Fallout 1 or 2. It is no longer the immersive worlds of 3 or New Vegas. Instead, Fallout 4 is something of a Shoot and Loot type game with basebuilding mechanics, which seems to be a natural progression of things as making the game more accessible. As a guy who's played 1,2,Tactics,BOS For the PS2, 3, and New Vegas, I'm of the opinion that despite all the changes, Fallout 4 in itself is a good game.
As far as the base game plus DLC is concerned, it's quite fun and one can easily lose many hours enjoying the gameplay, in a similar manner as a more slowly paced Borderlands title. The shooting, after installing the Stronger Weapons mod intended for the Modern Firearms mod, is truly satisfying and by putting points into one's selected weapon area of choice one can increase their ability to deal with threats in the later game. The overland travel is something of interest, with plenty of unmarked areas to explore, especially with the addition of the Beantown Interiors Project which turns some of the boarded up houses into areas of intrigue. The crafting is of particular note, and I have spent hours swapping parts of the many weapons afforded by the base game and many MANY mods available via Bethesda. One area of the game I myself have spent most of my time in is the settlements system, where I would try to make some of the best settlements for either myself and my selfish enjoyment, toying with the plebians that for some reason never think to leave, or being a benevolent dictator who loves to return to save everyone's bacon because it means more looting. Heck, I dedicated most of my outings in the wastes of the Commonwealth entirely to getting more tin cans so that I can reinforce my bases even more for whatever little crafting projects suit my whimsy.
With all that said, why can I not recommend this game? Because as James Rolf of Angry Video Game Nerd fame puts it "What's the most important thing about a video game? Well, being able to play it!"
I stopped playing Fallout 4, not because of ennui or disinterest but because after the patch that introduced the Paid Mods system, I could no longer use the settlement system. Supposedly this bug has been around, reported as early as August 2016, and has to do with a poor job done on the scripting of the Settlements system, where every one of the 30+ Settlements of the game shares a single action queue with one another, and the issues of this manifest initially as input lag when commanding settlers and finally culminating in them refusing outright to do as their told. Now, if this is a bug that's happened before paid reskins were introduced, why should I mention the latest patch at all? Because this problem has existed for more than a year, and instead of fixing it Bethesda would rather introduce paid reskins.
This gets even worse, since making a new save file doesn't work, so I guess the queue is shared across save files also. To put this in perspective, the first Sims game had queues that were individualized. A game some twenty years old, had enough innovation to not be built with this problem. So, I guess I'm left with totally uninstalling the game and deleting all files from it I got, but I'm wary of even that since I wouldn't put it past Bethesda (The company that decided paid reskins was a good idea) wouldn't also pull a Myth II situation.
So, in short, Fallout 4 is bad because Bethesda has no intentions to fix it. So, it's not a question of if, but when your game will break, and it will with a certainty.  Bethesda's quality has sunk in recent years, and it's clear they have no intention of improving, if the deleted save files of 2017's Prey are to be believed. So, consider this summary to also be a review of all of Bethesda's post 2015 catalogue. Don't buy unless they and their DLC are under 10 bucks.

Fired this game up after a pause(~6month) and LOL-d hard at the very beginning, on the first hire: "Fidel is not himself lately. And it´s not a bad thing".
Haven´t finished the prequels- tried them as a kid a bit- and maybe this game isn´t like the prequels, but it doesn´t mean it´s bad to the bones. The characters are funny and the whole game has the "parody thing" going on.
The best thing about JABIA is the camera handling imo. With ALT key it´s possible to peak behind every corner and with aided aiming lines it´s possible to precisely plan my actions.
And for the good camera work I´ve ditched "other" turn based games to come enjoy this one.
In general if you know the rules the game sets for you, then it´s more certain in outcome than other tactical turn based games. And that´s what I like about this game; if I choose the right team with right equipment for the job then the outcome is mine to decide. Main factors to take into account are equipment+skills which decide my mercs aiming time and enemies are wallhacking aimbots.
But both sides hit if the teamwork is planned correctly. If the rules are accepted from the very beginning then the game can be entertaining- can´t be anything better than setting team to nade the room and then rush in to clean the room with pump action shotguns and all that executing out in a few secs.
Now to the AI part. Yep the AI and game mechanics is unfinished. It´s actually possible to go on stealth kills against lvl 1(maybe 2 also) enemies but but later in game against higher level AI the only way is rambo style. (DLC Point Blank was fun bc I could go with 45 cal silenced pistol and take out the whole garrison alone). In the early stage it´s important to choose correct merc for certain tasks, if it says expert in stealth, then stealth approach is doable etc...
The most fun part is the start of the game, where I can play out different approaches till it goes rambo style with 2 squads of rambos.
And for as old a game as this, it still looks good though unoptimised.
Later in game there is indeed lot´s of micromanagement- all actions must be double checked on mercs, mules have to carry equipment over the map etc. But grinding money for equipment can be fun too.
One good side of the game is that when I return to my favourite multiplayer FPS I always think more tactically and am doing much better. Haven´t experienced this with any other tactical turn based games, so it must do something right in the end...

I would recommend this game to anyone who purchased Planetary Annihilation to get the game for cheap.  I wouldn't recommend someone to get the game without it.  Why?
The AI is not very good.  The game takes a best of a machine to run well.  The single player is very bare and not very fun and not only because of the lack of AI.  I would see the AI turtle all their forces and never move, I would see them consistently try to build a teleporter on a planet in the same area every time with only one construction bot, even though it was covered by turrets.
The planets have had terrain heights added but it doesn't seem fully implemented.  Naval gameplay can be completely ignored as there are not many water planets.
The multiplayer is fun, but it is hard to find a game and get into a game.  Disconnects are common.
All this and I'd still recommend.  It is great fun to break onto an enemy held planet and establish a foothold.  The battles look pretty, especially if you add mods to make the battles look even better.  They even have a mod manager available that makes mods as easy to install/uninstall and update as it is with the Steam Workshop.  You can get a lot of time out of this game.

Don't buy this peace of garbage if you want smooth gameplay. Go play Fallout New Vegas, at least I didn't had input lag there.

Oh gosh... Where to start? Well, you take the original epicness of Descent: Freespace and add in new ships, weapons, vastly new and improved lore, more combat variety, and more customizations to your ship controls. On  top of that already well-seasoned game you throw in some new spices by adding Freespace Open, a free customization/modernization program maintained by diehard fans of the series, improving the graphics and allowing modabilty for even more gameplay.
There might be issues with the startup of the game but with Freespace Open these issues were corrected and even without it a simple fix can be applied to get you up and running.
And do not let my hours deceive you, I played the game through the Open Launcher and had one of the most epic times of my life playing this revamped classic.
I give this game 10 Sathanas Juggernauts out of 10.

A difficult, but enjoyable MMOPRG experience, with plenty of bullet hell and rage elements that keep things intense.
Will you die a lot? At first, yeah.
Is it hard to get good items? Unless you pay IRL money or some kind soul gifts you some, yes at first it's very difficult.
Are deaths big penalties? Oh yeah. You lose whatever dyes or cloths you used on the character, you lose everything in your inventory and your backpack, you lose the backpack itself, you lose the character and all it's stat boosts. You start completely over unless you're a smart one who keeps their expensive gear in their vault.
But once you get the hang of it, Realm of the Mad God can be one of those gems in the MMORPG world. Microtransaction'd to hell, but is still a really good game that people should try at least once.
Get it with no regrests!

The limiting factor in this game is that it is optimized running using a single core. In short, if your system unit is Quadcore, this game only uses 1 core. This game runs well for the first 20-30 minutes with a population of 70,000 to 100,000. However, the population growth increases the demands for it to run. Then, it lags horribly as the population increased to 200,000 more. One fix is to restart the game but it only takes 10-15 minutes before it lags again really bad. If only I knew this is still persistent in this edition, I would've not bought this game.

Four hours into this game and it's definitely worth saying a few things. I'll start with the graphics only because the style in which this world is built is breathtaking. The art direction is watercolours, and do they ever add a fluidity to the movements of The Kid, the silent protagonist of whom you are controlling in this adventure. The colours themselves either have an undeniable shine to them that gently turn into black and white as your health decreases. So does your vision, which I found to be a great mechanic to have.
The story is unique in where a narrator occassionally comments on your actions, while giving the player a sense of direction of where they are going and why. Honestly it's the only sense of direction you are likely to receive, given as to how each level is "summoned" step by step.
A final word would be on the soundtrack. It goes with the game perfectly. What else is there to say?
Get yourself this game if you're a fan of Adventure games!

Ever had a dream where you could be a pirate? I remember seeing pirate movies where it looked really cool to shoot ships with cannons, ram and board, and, of course, lead your very own ship and crew. Blackwake definitely brings all of that to the table, properly executed and well-established, but there are still some issues about it.
is solely a multiplayer, first-person, strategy, naval-battle game where you could take on the role as either one of the crew mates of a ship, or the captain of the entire ship. Your objective: sink the enemy ship before they sink you, and to achieve that, you have to go through intense broadside-fights, insane ramming scenarios, and grapple-on-grapple deathmatches.
As of now, that is what the game currently is: a deathmatch. Even with the new gamemode added, which is basically a treasure raid, players still play Team Deathmatch (TDM).
Players could be either the Pirates or the British Navy, and in two teams of 32 players, 3 ships will go head-at-head to achieve that sweet, sweet “B-double-O-T-Y.” Each team will have a large Galleon ship and two smaller ships, which could be a Hoy or Schooner for the British, or a Hoy and Junker for the Pirates. And that is basically it, the rest of the gameplay is repetitive back and forth, non-stop, first-person action that will keep you on your toes, so long as you are awake.
Not only does this game have great graphics, but, in a way, it’s fun. Not many sole-multiplayer games can possibly achieve what
has accomplished here. There will not be one scenario where you are sitting at your screen in silence because in
match, you would have talked the entire time; this is especially true for the captain.
The developers have executed naval ship fights pretty well in
, and for those possibly hardcore history players, it’s important to understand that the timeline setting of this game is real, but how the battles were at this time are not. Combined with uproarious ragdoll physics, intense boarding fights, really stupid-fun ramming situations, and leave-them-for-dead overboard events,
is that type of game where you can have fun, and with friends, it’s a whole lot more.
You could establish your own crew, hop on a server, and prove you and your crew the best of the best, sinking enemy ships and having a blast, all the while laughing at one of your friends being blasted off the ship by a cannonball, sent soaring across the sun, or even over your head.
Best of all, this game can be played casually or competitively because there is no real Ranked Multiplayer system. In
, there is less toxicity among players, and you are allowed to leave a match
if a game turns sour, you aren’t glued to your desk like how it is in many other multiplayer games. Additionally, the game invites and embraces teamwork, something that a lot of games fail to execute, but this one does it well in a way. You
to work together to win; you can’t win alone, which I praise the developers for making a shining reality. However, that could be its ultimate downfall.
Currently, the game is in Early Access (EA), so for most of the issues that I see in-game, I can turn a blind-eye. However, even after playing 50+ hours, I still don’t see this game as something I can have a blast with for hours without getting angry.
As I have stated before,
encourages teamwork and cooperation to successfully play the game and have fun, and while that is all fun and good, that is also the greatest issue of this game. Like any all-multiplayer game, there are those that will troll, fool around, and purposely be jerks for no reason to either the captain or the crewmates all because he/she has a hate-life. This is the Internet, that is bound to happen no matter what. The problem is that Blackwake is
on teamwork for people to actually play the game.
You could have a captain who is clearly trying to sink his/her own ship. You could have a crew member randomly and intentionally firing off cannons on the portside, starboard-side, and/or the aft for no reason at all, wasting ammo and angering off the captain. Worst of all, in Friendly-Fire-On servers, you could have a troll who shoots
on his/her own ship “for the fun of it” and kill them. I’ve seen it happen. As someone who loves to play captain, I had to deal with it, and it isn’t fun for me, nor the crewmates trying to actually win. And even with the game receiving more and more players, this is becoming more and more apparent.
Moreover, the way teams are divided is currently not in a stable-state. If you played Team Fortress 2 or CS: GO,
’s team selection is similar to both. That is not the issue. The issue is you could have Prestige 5 players, all of them, on one team, and all-new players on the other team, crying as they get rekt. The point of this game is to have fun
not just one, but I’m hoping to see that change.
Furthermore, this game is heavily-repetitive. Please understand that you will likely be bored of the game after 5 matches of the same shoot-and-kill unless you switch to the other gamemode, or stop playing all-together.
Worst of all, there is an unusually large amount of racism from the players in this game. I have no idea why, but be prepared to listen to 10 straight minutes of racist remarks per game round.
makes me wish other game developers came up with something like this years ago because this game is really,
fun. Seriously, you have all these other complex games… why not go with this one? I praise Dakota and Tyler for making, drawing, and coding such a wonderful game, so well-established, properly executed and deployed. And for an Indie game, my gosh, this game blows other games away as it takes charge, and it will always be a part of my heart and soul. That is my word.
For 20 USD, or 25 Canadian, yes. In its current state, there is enough content to compensate for the price. Trust me, it’s worth it… so far.
Constant trolls, unbalanced teams, all-multiplayer with no practice games, so much racism, and overly-dependent teamwork currently sabotage this game. I know it’s in EA, and it will be fixed because these developers are talented, but I just can’t give the developers what they want to hear right now: a thumbs up. They need to fix what needs to be fixed, maybe then I will say yes.
I still say buy it and give it a shot, just understand what you may go through.

I'll go ahead and start with the cons.
1. If you play fighting games for the single player experience, you're better off waiting until the June update to pick this game up.  The single player experience in this game is severely lacking as it currently stands.
2. If you want comprehensive lobbies of up to 8 players with spectating features, you're better off waiting until next month when these features will be added.
3. While the servers have now mostly stabilized, there is still an occasional downtime, so if that's something that you just can't bare, I'd suggest riding it out for another week or so until they get everything figured out.
Now the pros.
1. This game is extremely comprehensive with characters.  Even with the currently "limited" cast of 16 characters, I guarantee you're likely to find at least 1 to your liking.  New player or veteran alike, every character is extremely diverse, with more to come monthly over the next 6 months.
2. I have had zero graphical problems, and this game seems to be extremely well optimized.  To be fair, my PC is relatively powerful, with an R9390 and a 6600k under the hood, but this game ran like a charm right out of install at 60 frames constant.  No frame drops or graphical lag in sight.
3. When the servers are up, my connections with other players are solid, and the netcode is actually very good.  One in ten matches or so I run into a rollback or two, but it's something you grow to accept playing fighting games online.  I play many fighting games, and this games netcode is probably the best I've encountered.
4. The training mode, where most players new and old alike should be spending the lions share of their time in a new fighting game is extremely comprehensive.  5 recording slots for dummy actions.  Wake up actions.  Great input and attack data displays.  All the data you need to learn a new character, practice your links or anti-airs, or even just commit special moves to muscle memory if you're new.  It's all here and better than ever.
To summarize, should you buy this game?  Well it depends.  If you're a single player warrior, I'd hold out for a bit longer, but if you're the type of player that loves to get their hands dirty learning a new game and playing other humans there is plenty here to sink your teeth into until more features come out down the line.  I've already gotten quite a few hours of fun out of this title, and I feel like I'm only beginning to sink my teeth into this one.  This to me feels like the evolution of fighting games, and it's about time.

If you came here looking for a review, you have come to the wrong place, but if you want some very ♥♥♥♥ing good brownies, you have come to the right place. You're welcome for an actual recipe, not a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ copy and paste pie recipe. Trust me nothing goes wrong with nutella.
INGREDIENTS:
1 c. unsalted butter
2 c. sugar
1/2 tsp. salt
1 c. flour
1 c. cocoa powder
4 eggs
1 (13-oz.) jar Nutella
5 Ferrero Rocher candies, unwrapped and crumbled
DIRECTIONS:
1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F.
2. Melt butter in a medium-sized saucepan over medium heat. Add sugar, stirring until combined. 3. Remove from heat and add salt, flour, and cocoa powder, stirring to combine. Whisk in eggs, stirring just until the mixture is combined into a batter. Set aside.
4. Spray an 8"-x-8" pan with cooking spray. Pour half of the batter into the pan. Spoon or lightly drizzle most of the Nutella on top of the batter, forming an even layer over the brownie batter. 5. 5. Use a spoon or silicone spatula to cover the Nutella with the remaining brownie batter. (If you pour the batter straight on top of the Nutella, it will sink into the Nutella and combine into one marbled—yet delicious—mess.)
6. Bake until the top layer of brownies has browned and set, 28 to 30 minutes. It shouldn’t jiggle when you remove it from the oven. (The toothpick test doesn’t work here, since the toothpick will hit the Nutella layer, making the brownies seem uncooked.)
7. Let cool for 15 to 20 minutes, then top with a drizzle of Nutella and crumbled Ferrero Rocher chocolates. Cut into squares and serve.

Titans adds a lot of new units and mechanics that are quite frankly, super fun to use. The content itself is a good adition, and adds a lot more strategy into the game. Most of the negative reviews stem from how Uber handled the release of Titans.
Uber released Titans as a standalone game from the original PA and stoped selling the original. I can think of a few resons that did this, obviously money being one, but also the fact that the original was flooded with bad reviews from when the game was not nearly as finished as it is today. I'm not saying that Uber did everything the best way, but the current game is much more polished and well done that it was for a long time in and after the Early Access. Having Titans as a new game wiped the slate clean, and maybe introduce a lot of new people into the game.
Many people also complain about how kickstarters get the game for free, while people who played the game only get a reduced price. The kickstarters took a much bigger risk in funding the game, as it was only a concept at the time, so it makes sense that the rewards should be larger. Even the price that it is with the discount is fairly prices for the amount of work that went into the update, including new music, units, mechanics, and large rebalances.
Despite all this I do reccommend Titans because it adds a lot of good content despite Ubers questionable tactics regarding it's release.

I both love and hate this game simultaniously. It took me a while to get into it. I can get behind a revenge plot, and i can most certainly enjoy a deep and dark storyline. In symphonia for example (SPOILERS if you haven't played that game but it's kinda old now so you really should have by now because its one of the best games ever created in my opinion) has your characters learn about 60% through the story that these items they have been collecting and granting them power are created by harvesting tormented human souls, horrible experiments performed on children that both stunt their growth and rob them of their free will and slowly and horrifically kill them, and chracters who feel like they need to punish themselves for the rest of their lives due to accidents they were involved in where someone they know and/or loved died.
None of these characters from symphonia however go full edgelord, frozen heart, dont care who i hurt in the process of my goals like berseria's main "protagonist" Velvet. She spends most of the story being a mostly heartless, self indulging ♥♥♥♥♥ until a major plotpoint of the story comes up about 75% through the game and finally breaks her, and she begins to soften up a bit.
Once she does however and all the sins of everything she does starts to catch up to her and she starts giving other emotions besides disdain and rage, I started warming up to her a bit.
I spent all this time talking about Velvet becuase she is the main character of a very highly narrative game. Oh i'm sorry, the gameplay? The combat revolves around putting moves of a certain element to each of your 4 buttons, holding a button to see which of the elements your target is weak to, and then spamming that button repeatedly till it stops moving, FUN! Oh whats that? Gameplay out of combat? Well there is running.... alot of running, going place to place, with most areas in the place your at looking pretty much exactly the same...
To put it simply I didnt finish this game for it's gameplay, in fact, I had a bit of a hiatus for a couple months about halfway through the game due to this and how insufferable and unlikable Velvet was, I didnt care for the main character or the gameplay so i just kinda stopped for a while. It wasnt until i got bored and picked it up just for the sake of finishing the still somewhat interesting story that i finished it, and now that i have, i'm glad i did.
Even though Velvet was a bit cold for my liking most of the game, she was acompanied by 5 other interesting and likable characters i genuinly did enjoy. And even though i saw quite a bit of the story coming from a mile away, (holy crap that intro was so sugar coated it just about gave me diabetes, i just knew from the get go that everyone was going to die horribly) There were still plenty of times when the story threw a curveball at me and make me go "OOOHHH! That explains EVERYTHING!"
Dispite all of my griping, the banter between the characters, the humor and the epic ending storyline cutscenes were amazing. The world is deep and the lore is heavy, and i had no idea how to actually set things right once i fully understood the gravity of the situation. It seemed like there was no way to acheive true peace or to foster well being within humanity for the longest time as the choices seemed to be either everyone losing their free will or massive global casualties. I feel like the ending was brilliant and was worth all of the suffering and torment to see it.
It wasnt until i finished this game that i found out Zesteria is directly connected to this game, and i am installing it now as i write this review.
TL;DR
Velvet is obnoxious most of the game till the end when she actually starts becoming likeable and i didnt care for the gameplay much itself but the banter between everyone and the story make it well worth it.
Overall I feel like the game is worth playing, just maybe not replaying.

Sadly as a fan of point-and-click games, i was sorely dissapointed in this one.
The game is slow... not framerate, but the pacing is slow.  There is no clear way to track progress as the plot is controled entirely my dialog, not puzzles and clues like most p-&-c games.  This sadly makes the story feels rather flat becuase of the backtracking to every clickable thing to see if it ever changes.
You will spend a lot of time randomly clicking everything hoping for the one line of dialog that is defferent from the rest so you can find something else to click on.  This is a bit normal for some p-&-c games but unlike an escape the room or even Myst, you arent randomly clicking to find that one magic pixel that lets you pick up a hidden note.  No you are skipping line after line of dialog without even listening to them until you hear something different.
This "game" isnt all that bad from a story perspective (yes i know I called it flat, hear me out).  Personaly I would have loved to see this made a short film.  The tone and atmosphere are perfect.  The plot (once you finaly figure it out) is nicely done.  Even the voice actors are done well.  The reason I call it flat however... as a p-&-c you have to make things re-clickable.  And since this game is 100% spoken dialog, you hear the same 3-4 lines over, and over, and over again as you try to find the next crucial line of dialog.  So even though the voicing is rather good, the script is dry and boring well befor the 9th time you hear the same line.
Tl:DR -- its free but meh quality... Would be better as a short film than a game.

TL;DR bullet points at the end. I don’t blame you, this is pretty long.
<No intro, conclusion, or good formatting due to space limit, sorry>
Story/Characters
The main highlight of this game is the story and characters. They're not your typical band of friends on a quest to save the world or whatever; they're actually very morally gray or sometimes bad people. For example, the main character Velvet just wants to kill one particular man really ♥♥♥♥ing badly and she has little to no remorse destroying, killing, or using people to her advantage. For most of the game you don’t even get the sense that your party are even friends, more like "allies of necessity", teaming up for survival and a mutual goal.
That isn’t to say id call the main characters the villains, since the "good guys" can also be morally gray also. This lack of a true "good guy" plus the fact that it’s Your Party VS The World gives the game a more somber tone than you'd see in other Tales games.
Despite all that though, I’d say the characters are very likable (or unlikable if the situation calls for it) and are voiced appropriately, with my personal favorites being Cristina Vee as Velvet and Ian Sinclair as Zaveid.
If I did have some complaints, it’s that one of your side party members is an annoying ♥♥♥♥ who won’t go away (you'll know when you see him), and that Velvet's talk of hate and revenge can get a bit too "crawling in my skin" at times.
During the course of this game you also learn about the origins of certain things from Zestiria, like the first Shepard, the Lord of Calamity, the Armatus, Malevolence, and the Seigfried gun. Ironically, this game does such a better job of world building that it makes Zestiria more interesting by proxy.
Something else I was surprised by is the script for this game. It’s big, really big. Not only are there numerous skits and cut scenes, but every sub event is fully voiced. Every single one. Unfortunately sometimes the sheer amount of dialog can be a bit much. There were a few times where I got access to 4 or 5 skits at once, and while most of the sub events are enjoyable or interesting, there were a few that I straight up skipped because it was telling me things I didn’t care about (no really, tell me more about how your town peals poisonous potatoes I’m SO interested).
Theres also a good amount of detail put into skits. The uh…”character artwork sprites? Yeah there is quite a few of those. Even side characters that are only in a few or even just one skit get their own sprites. That’s kinda awesome.
Battle System
The battle system is simple yet fun to use. Every character can do a certain amount of attacks each combo, but you can use one of your combo souls to execute special abilities unique to each character (EX. if Velvet has 3 souls she can do a 3 hit combo, or she can use one which will bring her down to 2 souls for a 2 hit combo). Velvet swipes with her demon claw to gain a power up and unleash up to a dozen special finishers, while Eizen can throw a giant ball of fire at downed enemies. It’s a kind of risk vs reward that makes you think about how you want to go about fighting the battle.
They also added in a new use for the blast gauge. Not only are they for doing your mystic artes, but 1 BG can be used at any time to switch to a party member in reserve, which is very useful if you're almost dead or are low on souls to attack with, and it can all be done with the simple press of a button even mid combo. This is the only Tales game I’ve played where I wanted to learn to use every party member, since switching during combat is very beneficial.
Bosses
The bosses and mini-bosses are very rewarding. Almost every one you kill gives you a unique passive item that does various things (EX. run faster, upgrade gear higher, get better gear on X difficulty). It makes you want to hunt down the side bosses just to get more of them and feel like you have more options. These items also give you an incentive to play on higher difficulties which can be changed in the menu whenever.
A glaring issue with *some* of the bosses though is that they can be cheap asshats. When they get down to the last bit of their health they start spamming strong multi hit (and possibly multi person) attacks that kill you very quick, and it feels very unfair when it happens.
Gear and Upgrade System
The gear upgrade system is…not implemented well. You can use spare parts that you pick up randomly or from dismantling gear to upgrade your gear to +1,+2,+3 ect, however there’s two problems with it.
First: the parts aren’t as abundant as you'd like them to be. I can upgrade a few weapons to +2 or 3 before I run out of supplies for some time. Some parts you will have literally hundreds of, while most others that you actually need to upgrade your current weapon you'll get a few of.
Second: gear mastering. Every type of gear as a special mastery trait that you fill by getting grade after a battle (EX. Iron sword has +5% chance to stun). Once you master that trait it’s on that character forever, and with the amount of gear that drops and how long it takes to master it, it becomes less about "what has better stats?" and more about "what haven’t I mastered yet?” You'll be switching out gear for the mastery so much that there’s no point to upgrading most things.
Level Design and Sound
Won’t sugar-coat it, Bandai Namco still hasn’t picked themselves out of the level design rut they’ve had since Xillia. Caves look like every other cave, fields look like every other field, and it’s all pretty dull and boring. Exploring these places usually boils downs to “press X to kick this rock/burn these plants/jump this gap”, and the game feels the need to explain to you like pressing a button to remove an object in your way is such a foreign concept.
There’s also some fair amount of backtracking in these places too. The game does give you portals and magic bottles to help you get around, but half the time these things will be disabled because the game wants you to walk and view a cutscene on the way to your destination.
Music is…there. It fulfills its purpose just fine. I’d say there are only a few standout tracks while most of it is forgettable. Not much to say really.
Graphics
Honestly not improved much from the last game. I get that they’re going for a certain art style, but at times it really feels like they’re dragging their feet on this. One could argue it’s for the benefit of having this game run at 60fps on consoles which is a fair point, but it still feels like they need to up their game.
PC Port
Plenty of options, and full keyboard and controller support as well as keyboard specific shortcut keys. It runs well (see graphics), and can actually hit 60 fps without the need for a mod like Zestiria. No real complaints, they’re getting better at this.
TL;DR Bullet Points
The Good
-Good story                                                                                                                                        -Good characters
-Interesting tone                                                                                                                        -Good world building
-Fun battle system                                                                                                                        -Very good PC port
-Rewarding bosses                                                                                                                         -Good voice acting
-Lots of dialog                                                                                                    -Skit artwork for a lot of characters
The Bad
-Sometimes TOO much dialog
-Same dull levels and environments the series has suffered from since Xillia
-Music serves its purpose but most tracks aren’t particularly memorable
-Bosses can be super cheap
-Pointless upgrade system with how much you’ll switch gear
-All the good alternate costumes are stuck in overpriced DLC. Again.

I am one of the original PA backers. I understand what Uber did with this release considering user reviews, but to be honest I personally don't care. For me, yea, the original PA had it's share of problems like CTD when you destroyed some planet if you did not have the latest graphics drivers (derp on my side), lags in very large battles, etc. I still remember early builds of PA when your land units sometimes became orbital units or fell to the middle of the planet.

I am an older gamer and I have seen many games come and go, some good, some bad or unfinished... I am not saying that this game is perfect, but at least for me personally it is enjoyable enough. There is no other game where I can destroy enemy by destroying the very planet he is standing on. When I replay the original Kickstarter video for PA, I now have what I have backed.
I have noticed some reviews where guys were complaining that they cant defeat AI, that it is too hard, etc. I regularly smash AI on normal difficulty, if they really do lose, then they are doing something wrong. Yes it is aggresive, but afaik, it does not cheat and it is beatable.
On the matter of bad reviews. I personally don't care what Uber did or did not as long as they deliver in the end. While far from being the strongest Fallout game, it doesn't do a half bad job of reinventing the franchise.
PROS:
+ Stellar graphics upgrade from previous installments.
+ Great story.
+ Colorful and interesting characters.
+ Companions are more than just cannon fodder this time around! You can get very personal with them and learn a lot, or they can just carry that Fat Man eating up your carry weight.
+ New enemies
+ New weapons
+ Greatly improved modding feature
+ More cinematic dialogue
+ FIXED gunplay! And it's smooth too!!
+ Constructing towns
+ Catchiest soundtrack (in my opinion) out of all the Fallout games!
CONS:
- Dialogue wheel greatly limits the possibilities of speech.
- Voice actors for the protagonist almost destroy the RPG aspect. (They aren't even that impressive)
- The transition from the less FPS-styled Fallout games is extremely rough at first. Took me about 20 hours to get used to it.
- The perk system doesn't feel special at all - you can suddenly become good at everything as opposed to picking your strengths and weaknesses.
- You can only travel with one companion at a time.
- While the graphics of the world look nice, some of the character models look a bit glassy.
- Some quests are just too. damn. repetitive. (I'm looking at you here, Preston Garvey.)
For the diehard Fallout fan, this game is worth looking at. It's a change from the predecessors - but a welcome one. People give this game far more flak than it deserves. By no means is it perfect - but that doesn't mean it isn't a great game.

Planetary Annihilation: TITANS is an expandalone to Uber Entertainment's previous title, the Kickstarter funded Planetary Annihilation.
Assuming you haven't played the original PA before, let me lay down what this games are about. Planetary Annihilation is about managing an economy and building up a giant base with which you build an even giant-ER army. Where some games have your battles span miles, this game has your battles span multiple planets. Vehicles come in a number of variations, from 4 archetypes; you have access to ground vehicles, robot units, aircraft and ships. In addition to those there are also the orbital units, which have often highly specialized roles.
With these tools you go about conquering worlds, destroying your enemies (lamentations of their women optional) and, if you are so inclined, BLOWING UP THE VERY PLANETS THEY CALL HOME.
That's right, you can blow up planets in this game. With other planets even. Want to be spiteful and throw one of your enemy's planets into one that belongs to their allies'? This game allows you to do that.
Now you might be thinking that this all sounds pretty sweet, and you'd be right in thinking that. But what of this expansion? What does it do?
It turns everything up to 11.
Not only does this expansion add a host of regular new units, including but not limited to a nanobot swarm and a younger brother to your already impressive commander unit, it also adds the titular TITANS. TITANS are basically super-units. Have you ever wanted to destroy your enemies by stepping on them with a giant robot? Now you can. Did all that talk about interplanetary units made you wish you could have giant space-battleships? This expansion has it. Giant teleportation deathstar satellite? Yes'm, all here.
It also comes with a bunch of smaller enhancements to the game that I won't bore you with here, look up the patch notes on those if you're so inclined.
This all brings us to the question of the hour: is this game worth buying?
Now you must understand that I was already quite fond of the original, having played it 69 hours (Ha! That's never changing now) so I came into this with that as the base to my experience. But it still surpassed my expectations and has wowed me with all the cool new stuff you can do now.
The best thing about this one though is that it added that one key thing that I always thought the original lacked.
If you've never played Planetary Annihilation, this game is unlike anything you've played before. If you have, you owe it to yourself to give this one a shot. It's got everything good about the original with everything that even I didn't know I missed about it. This is the way to do an expansion. It's the
to Planetary Annihilation's
.
It's worth your money, and may even prove itself worthy of your
.

One of my favorite examples of racing games. It keeps a good balance between realistic physics and absurd adrenaline fueled chaos. The open world was big enough to enjoy exploring and take skill to learn, but small enough that it was easy to traverse. The car roster was a bit silly, that there was a normal and a 'good' version of each car, with most of them becoming obsolete within an hour anyways, but there was always a car that would become my 'new' favorite. It's one of those racing games where you can barrel down a street at nearly the speed of sound, forgetting to blink until you plow into a civilian and send yourself flying into the sky in a million pieces. It's just cathartic fun, in my opinion
I will warn that the catharsis does take a big hit near the end-game, when the difficulty of the ai opponents is just ludicrous, but I just switched to bikes, and it remained a fun experience. If you like gran turismo or other simulation racers with a bit more crunch, this isn't for you, but it's worth a few bucks to spend an hour or two as a blur along a city street. It's never a dull moment

is a 3D space craft action simulator. Decades after the war that lost both race's home worlds, the new Galactic Theran-Vasudan Alliance is rebuilding its forces, up until the the discovery of an extremely ancient Jump Node, and the return of the Shivans.
There is little to say besides it is everything you liked about
. The engine was improved, both in terms of resolution, interface and control, and those improvement match in terms of in-game technological advancement of shield, firepower, and options. The story, once again told to an anonymous pilot recruit through mission briefings and in-game events, picks up some time after the previous game and digs deeper into the lore and origins of the mysterious Shivans, and includes multiple winks to missions from the first game. Control are just as pitch-perfect as they used to be, assuming you play in keyboard-only mode (early 90s style: no mouse).
Same flaws as the previous game: no exploration, little branching paths, ugly aged graphics (even with the better resolution). "More of the same" is accurate, as there is little innovation over the gameplay or game itself when compared to its predecessor. The game wasn't correctly ported to Steam and requires a manual intervention before working (luckily, it's an easy process well documented in forums).
★★★☆☆ - It's up to you

Ugh, why can't Steam have a 'mixed' review option? It's a good game, it just has a lot of growing pains and i wish I could say "wait til it develops more" instead of just "Yes or no". Anyway... there's a lot to like and dislike about Starbound. I won't drone on and on about it though, and try to sum it up.
It's got a good style, good polish, tons and tons of items, content, enemies, the map and word system generates procedurally and with a surprising amount of interest. There's quests and ship progression, item and skill upgrades... there's no shortage of content in the beginning. However, once you're through with the quests, have a big ship, and are free to explore the universe, it kind of... falls flat at the moment. I feel there should be, at some point, either more interesting quests, bosses, things to find and explore at the end game. Before the questing, this was more free-form and fun, experimenting and discovering. Now with quests it's a bit too restricted, but.. if they want to go that way, fine, just develop them more. The other part is the ship, making no reason to build on planets. While I like the ship upgrades and progression, I think it goes a bit too far and too much, as one other review said; you can put everything in your ship, so what's the point of building on planets?
The progression is alright, except I personally found the bosses to be INSANELY difficult solo. When you die, too, you re-navigate the entire level. Extremely frustrating and annoying... but customization is extremely high, music and visuals, polish and controls, all very high. I think the biggest problem is just later game content and some balancing, but it's a good game overall, I'd just still say wait on it.

"Terraria imma let you finish, but Starbound is the best 2D Sandbox Adventure game of all time..."
We all have some crazy aspirations as children - some will want to be an astronaught and explore the depths of space, some will want to be great architechts and build structures that rival the wonders of the world, some will want to be masterful warriors who are revered throughout the land and others will want to be...a fish person. Well good news because you can do all of these things and so much more in Starbound!
Pro's
- There are literally Quadrillions of unique planets to explore, each with different biomes and monsters/civilisations on them.
- Humans. Harambe's. Bird brains. Fish faces. Triffids. Johny 5's. Whoopie Cushions. 7 unique playable races each with great lore and backstory and unique armour sets and also unique architecture if you happen across one of their villages/dungeons. Also there are poo people in the sewer mini-biome...just thought I'd throw that in there...
- They say you should never bring a knife to a gun fight but if your knife is in fact a Violium Broadsword then you ignore the haters my friend and spin splash their feathery behinds into oblivion! The sheer amount of weapons and armour in this game is truly staggering - so many different kinds of unique weapons and abilities that all have their uses. Even the more obscure silly ones can be useful - I recently stumbled across a gun that shoots tentacles that literally slap things to death. Oh, you're shooting at me for smashing your vases? Well me Avian, let me tell you, Hell hath no wrath like a tentacle scorned! It's slappy time...
- There are so many crafting and building options that you will spends hours upon house building your perfect base/home and with convenient teleporters you can always zip in and out as you need, even if your ship is lightyears away. Which makes it very worthwhile and satisfying to find yourself a perfect little planet in the middle of nowhere with no inhabitants to pester you to build your house on. Or, if you actually enjoy the company of others, you can establish whole colonies of people. If you wanted to take it a step further and fancy yourself a bit of Universal domination you could theoretically make colonies on a great many planets and link them all with Starga...ahem, teleporters.
- So much more....building, crafting, fighting, exploring, mechs, farming, ship crews, side quests...there is just so much to do in this game - your only limit is your imagination. There is also an extensive campaign and story to top it all off!
Con's
- Honestly, it's very difficult to state any real cons about this game. It is truly the Mona Lisa of this genre. If you held a tentacle gun to my head and forced me to give a "con" however I would say that some events surrounding your colonies would be a nice improvement - such as a mass attack or something. When I've spent hours upon hours building a super-mega-hyperstrong-destructo-fort to protect my colony it would be spiffing if it protected them from more of a threat then the occasional deceptively innocent looking beastie wandering too close to the wall while whistling the starbound theme tune.
Overall, this game has more to offer than Santa at Christmas - I could not recommend it enough. On top of all that has been said, the game looks beautiful, has an outstanding OST and the devs continue to update it regularly. So, if you are still clinging on to any dreams and aspirations in lif, if you buy Starbound now they have already came true!

The game is very much what you make of it. If you don't make a story and get invested in your character(s) or set a goal for yourself, you probably won't enjoy the game very much! The base/progression questline is just that - a base. Most of the quests are very easy to complete, and it's usually clear what you need to do. Replay does, as is typical for all games, make some of the early quests annoying when you start a new character, but is something they've noticably been altering through the recent updates.
The quests and game-set goals essentially *force* you to do something fun, whether that happens to be digging deep below the ground, slaying monsters left and right, setting up a village and attracting renters, farming, or just trekking across the surface of myriad worlds. You can also ignore the quest line and just dive into the hundreds of thousands of worlds available to you - lo and behold, at some point you'll probably realise you accidentally picked up the stuff you needed anyway. Or, just hop onto one of the servers and trade for items. You'd be suprised what you can buy for nine hundred and ninty-nine potatos.
The starting planet is toned down compared to earlier versions, as some reviewers have noted, but overall the challenge is still there. You will die, probably a lot. Don't start on one of the hard modes. The endless arrays of weapons are immensely entertaining - everything from rocket launchers and machine guns and grenades to cursed bone hammers and weaponized lightning rods and vine swords that shoot swarms of bees is represented, and you never know what you'll find in the next weapons chest. One thing to note here is that the merchant mechanic is currently strange - instead of generating a weapon before purchase, you buy and then get a random weapon from the base loot table. They're talking about changing it to something clearer in the future.
Starbound started out with a very different feel than the one it has now: progression was closely tied with crafting level, and there was barely any guidance as to how to progress. The only story to be found was in the ingame books.
When the first big update happened, some people were upset because (in addition to wiping old characters) it totally changed the questing format of the game to something story-based. However, it also radically expanded the worlds around you - now, every planet you stop at has hidden treasures hiding around every corner, and every system has something worth looking at.
It really is still in dev, but getting to watch the new content being added gives you the feeling of being part of something special.

Before you play the game:
- Strict Rules about swearing in the EN (English) chat. Which yes, is somewhat strange since swearing can be found in any online game. Don't even try using acronyms that somewhat imply a curse word, still counts as a bad word and can recieve mutes for 30-60 minutes if done up to three times or more.
- Have to join the 18+ chat to have access to use acronyms that imply, or full spelling of swear words or anything that implies drugs. Also have to join 18+ chat to do anything above soft trolling, or type like an 8 year old even though it's 18+ chat.
- There is no such thing as Local/World/Global chat yet. So yes, the chat is always clogged up even if you turn on filters. Might as well made seperate chat tabs for system notifications+game events, and player chat. Especially when you want to private message a friend because it's almost impossible to follow a private message conversation.
- As of this current review, there are six worlds (Servers). They all basically share the same chat, so you can see whatever someone is saying if they are in world one even though you are in world six. They need a Local/World/Global chat soon, the chat is getting more and more cluttered and spammy the more players that play.
- No guild system and even if there was, there isn't enough things that a guild can really do together really.
- There is a captcha system in the game. You have to fill out the captcha whenever you are actively grinding a skill every once in a while. Missing or getting the captcha wrong at least five times (Or more depending on your captcha points.) can get you jailed in-game, or instead banned. This is a anti-botting system, it's fine since the captcha does give you bonus exp. Warning, the captcha can still appear in-game even if you go cook something on the stove or take a dump on the toilet. Happened to me once.
(Maybe try telling the moderators that your eyes are bad and they'll let you off with some kind of alternative system for anti-botting.)
- No animations or voice files for character, NPCs, or monsters. Suggest playing this game while doing other things so you can just play this game like an idle game. Like any other idle game, do other things while playing since you aren't really going to see much happening other than the feeling of progress.
- Suggest if you're not going to do other things while playing, try playing your own music while muting the game. Helps to get your mind to feel better rather than just looking at a screen that isn't really changing other than scenery and the occasional watching someone die.
- I don't reccomend this game if you're not going to, or try to put 168 or more hours into it. Game is very grindy once reaching Combat Level 35+, and you will need to spend a lot of time on other skills other than combat to make money for equipment, or either invest into skilling to make equipment. If you're too lazy to invest time to make your own equipment and items, it also takes time to make money to buy higher level equipment to kill those stronger monsters.
Grindy game that does award you for doing it, but only play if you're into grindy games where it takes longer and longer to level up a skill the further you go into it. Suggest using $5 irl to buy a double exp potion.

My first hour of playing this was actually relatively enjoyable. It has been a long time since I've played an mmo that uses skill based progression rather than throwing numbers at your stat counts. I enjoy the rogue-like feeling that the game has with the constant worry of death taking everything from you but your two most valuable items. Stats are a grind and the music can get repetitive after a while however I can forgive the music while watching my favorite live streams in the background (KPE3 at the time of this review) however I can truly enjoy the serenity that this game offers behind what is simply pixels. They also have ways to boost you and keep you from idling, example: after playing for a while they will jump you with a captcha, they give you two minutes to solve it and upon completion they give you a "Captcha point" Captcha points can be placed into any of the games skills and is essentially a free instant skill level. Now for the negatives I noticed within this first hour. I expect the tutorial to be a bit jarring and hard to understand for some people but if you have more than 3 days of accumulative gaming in your life for sandbox styled mmo's or 4 years of general gaming then it should be easy to understand (I have been gaming for 11 years). The second error is that the menu feels crammed and there is little space between your chat bar and the inventory bar, it's easily fixable however so no worries. Combat however does in fact feel like people throwing numbers at eachother. A positive that I failed the mention earlier was it's forging system, it takes the minecraft approach in which you shape out what you want to craft, luckily you only have to craft a piece of equipment once for it to be permanently in your list of known recipes, that's good because of the game stealing away all your hard earned equipment upon death except for your two most valuable items and pay to win doesn't seem to exist however as other reviews have stated I have done the same, I have not played PVP yet. Why? Because I feel that the true gems in a sandbox game come from it's worlds and what you can make of them.
7.5/10
EDIT: This game also used to be a browser game so theres that.
EDIT2: When I said that the captcha points were instant skill levels I was wrong, they grant 100 EXP to the skill you select to spend them on, which tends to be instant levelling up to skill level 9.

For such a cheap game, Wizorb has a LOT of content.
Pros:
- Excellent cost-benefit relation - a lot of content in comparison with the game's low price.
- Different powerups that stack with each other along with magic spells to use and debuffs to avoid makes the gameplay quite dynamic.
- Bonus levels and a few secret things make the game more fun than it already is.
- Boss fights, although a bit repetitive in comparison to each other, are pretty interesting with how the game is played.
- Interesting level design for each level.
- A new take on classic Breakout/Arkanoid games.
- The game looks beautiful.
- Good soundtrack.
Cons:
- Lack of RPG elements. The game looks like a combination of RPG and the classic Breakout/Arkanoid games, but there are actually very few RPG elements here. Mostly the magic spells the player can use. NPCs have very little influence in the game and rebuilding the town only provides extra lives, extra keys and two advantages (building ramparts on levels and opening a shop)
- Not many uses for money. You use it to rebuild the town and buy items and there are few items to buy - mostly powerups. After you have everything (which is pretty easy to do), the only use for money is buying extra lives and magic refills.
- Progress only saves when you finish a world. Worlds aren't too long but if you lose all your lives and go back to the map, you don't keep anything you obtained.
- Losing a life means you lose all your powerups. This wouldn't be too much of an issue if they were easier to re-obtain, but they aren't. Some powerups can only be obtained on certain worlds and because as mentioned above progress only saves when you finish a world, you have to replay entire worlds to re-obtain those powerups.
- In addition to the two items above, if you lose a life and your powerups and go back to the map before finishing the world, you don't keep what you obtained - but you still lose your powerups from the life you lost.
- Hitboxes for the ball and objects can be a little weird. Sometimes it looks like the ball is going to hit an object but instead it hits something else nearby.
This game would be a LOT better if there were more RPG games in this game and more uses for money. A leveling system with stats affecting things like ball speed and wand movement speed, buying and selling items with each of them having different effects on gameplay, etc.
Still, for the price this game costs, it's definitely recommended.

It is a great fighitng game let down by other issues.
The main points:
1. To progress in the game you need to be connected to a server.  However the server connection frequently fails and thus you finally win something there is a chance of reaping the reward or getting plauged by a server connection message.  This is extremly frustrating when you are not good or new to fighting games.
2. Matchmaking, right now is very slow.  The positive side of this is you can practice playing against the computer while you wait.
3. Matchmaking is not doing a good job of putting me in matches with people of the same skill level.  I do well against the computer but then get destroyed against other people online.
4. There is very little single player content, which is very bad when the servers aren't working.  Generally I would play the single player content while I waited for the multiplayer to get fixed, but since there was so little to do I wrote this review . . . while I am waiting for them to fix the servers.
5. The mechanics are great and fun to use.
6. The graphics are very good.  My gtx970 can run it on max settings at 60fps.
7. The xbox one controller works well.
8.  While it is still up in the air, it appears like the ability to earn fight money is extremly difficult after you beat the little single player section. It feels like players who are not good at multiplayer will most likely have to pay extra to get what the store has to offer.  In other words I don't think, as of right now, you win any fight money for losing at multiplayer and
you are not able to grind fight money in the single player mode.
Conclusion: I really enjoy the game and after they fix the server, add single player and the ability to do a match against the computer I would be able to recomend it.  I hope Capcom fixes these problems and gives the people who bought the game early some sort of perk for having those who paid practically full price practically serve as an other wave of beta testers (assuming that the plan on fixing these issues).

Multiplayer servers for me, are great. I am getting a solid stream of battles at regular intervals.
I think Capcom is doing great at communicating with the community and trying their hardest to make the game better. Though I would admit, the launch was not as well as it was anticipated.
Overall Pros:
-Solid Gameplay
-Characters are unique from each other (EG Ken and Ryu plays as different sort of shotos)
-A schedule for season pass, creating a sense of reliability unlike other developers who have season passes often have no schedule for their content.
-Delivering their promises (refer to cons)
-Anything core game related are purchasable with in game currency (EG Characters and balance patches)
Overall Cons:
-Sloppy launch
-Promised content is not as much as expected (refer to pros)
-Little offline content
Overall Neutral Points:
-Slowly, yet improving game
-Single game for future improvements (No Super, Ultra, Alpha editions of games)
-Some content that should of shipped but not as important (EG The June Story cinematic update)
