Absolutely brilliant. Most Tales fans started out young in the early 90's/00's, playing the original games which were clearly written for children & teens. But a huge chunk of us are now in our 20's and 30's and desire more mature themes in our games. Finally we get a Tales game to match our age. Berseria is the most mature Tales game yet. It has a excellent story with great character depth and growth. Gone is the typically self-righteous attitude of the main characters, where "right" and "wrong" and neatly in black and white. Instead, Berseria is more reflective of the real world, where the line between "right" and "wrong" is a lot more muddy, often only being a matter of an individual's own experiences and perspective.
The games runs in a smooth 60fps, and the combat system is fast and explosive. This is by far the best Tales game yet; rivaled only by Xillia for the PS3.
If you would like to see more mature themes in your future Tales games, let the devs know by showing your support and buying a copy of Berseria. You won't be dissapointed!

Don't pay the nay-sayers any heed, this is a GREAT game, especially if you use the Realistic Rebalancing Mod. This is sort of a community patch, changing some broken weapons and buggy systems for the greater good.
Basically, it's JA2's story. The government coup, payed for by a handful of diamonds late at night on the streets of prague. Dedrianna is still the main antagonist, though the cinematics featuring her and Elliot (idiot!) are missing.
You do NOT have a personal avatar this time around, instead you hire starting mercenaries with a small starting fund. It's about enough to get three beginner mercs with basic armaments. You'll see a lot of familiar faces in the merc roster, but they have a lot less personality than previous titles. The UI is a rather drab green colour, and there is less exposition in this game.
For balance reasons, mercs are now very expensive.
To make up for the lack of flair, BIA features a more streamlined combat and logistics system. There is only one airstrip, just north of drassen. You capture it straight away, and can start ordering guns and mercs in the first day with little difficulty. Shipping weapons and items to the front-lines can be done by one merc, and is a simple task. Though you may find it taking quite a while to arm up, this should come as no surprise to vets of the series. Capturing an area will leave any items discovered during battle in the item section of that area on the world map. No need to run around grabbing stuff.
Recruiting NPC militia is a little more annoying this time around. You have to actually run about in the map to each recruit, and hand them a gun. You can use the area inventory for this, or your character's personal inventory. It's annoying, but this makes it so you can have some pretty serious militia. If you leave just one merc in the area to help out with combat, a well-armed militia can make short work of anyone attempting to re-capture your towns. Upgrading the militia's skills is done from the world map, just click on the town or house or whatever, and you get a simple menu at the bottom left for progressively more expensive level-ups.
There are some hiccups with the combat system. Controls seem a little janky, as far as contemporary tactics games go. You need to manually enable auto-attack (guard) mode for your mercs at the start of every battle. Otherwise, they'll sit around yelling at you while they get helplessly massacred. Panning around the scene will prevent you from using buttons to change stance and such, and the queue-based command system that BIA uses during the Pause screen in combat can be tough to get used to. If you take the time to learn to use it though, you'll find each fight works itself out a lot faster than JA2 combat ever did. This can make easier battles fly by in a devestating hail of gunfire, instead of a protracted hour-long clickfest.
BIA doesn't let you zoom out as far as I would like, but you can zoom the camera down with the mousewheel, and view the combat from a sort of soldier's-eye view. This is good for longer-range engagements, and looks pretty cool.
The Rebalancing Mod adds some extra weapons, there's a pretty decent number of available guns in the game with that installed. They're all reasonably well balanced, and combat is a brain-over-brawn affair. You need to have really good unit placement and firing lines to be successful, especially when your enemy finally starts getting high powered rifles and body armor. Saving when you're in combat is impossible, so you can't cheese the shot rolls. It's a good way of doing it, as the game will auto-save every time you get spotted by the enemy. You can easily retry an engagement, and since the combat is so fast-paced, this really doesn't seem to be that big of a pain.
The entire map seems to be rendered in 3d, so if you encounter an enemy patrol in the middle of nowhere, you will fight in a forest or desert just like in JA2. That being said, the 3d world battle map is surprisingly small. You may find that starting combat in a field will also include the nearby town, and you'll end up on the side of a HUGE combat map.
Approach direction, and party location is very important for starting battles. You can easily place your squad in a specific street or courtyard using the world map, and then wait for the enemy to step into your auto-battle range. It's a really nice feature that works very well for multi-squad engagements, and planned attack missions. Want to approach from the west side of the village because it's got no sandbag walls? Load the game back to the map and circle around!
Really, seriously consider giving this game a go. Right now it's non-sale price is $15 USD. There is a LOT of fun to be had here for that price.

As other reviews have mentioned - this copy of the game is a crappy one. At minimum you need to set up a registry fix (which on the top of the store page, though it might've not been there then), however you'll most likely end up modding your game with FreeSpace Open which, thankfully, has a really easy to use installer. After installation you can rename fs2_open_<version>.exe to FS2.exe to play the game (I only realised that after playing it for a while, so Steam didn't even track my game time :( ). You can also use FS2 Open to play the original campaign using the second game's engine, and as far as I saw, you don't even need to own the first game for that (not sure how that works out for them legally).
As far as the game goes - it's a classic space combat sim that I still consider being the best in it's genre. Other games (read - X series, Evochron Mercenary, SpaceForce and whatnot) are great and all, but they're more about the economics aspect, while games that do try to be like Freespace (most recent one being Strike Suit Zero/Infinity) don't really come close to the way this game handles, although I'm still not sure how turning off your engines can cause you to go to full stop in space. With FreeSpace2 open the game's graphics aren't all that shabby either.
As far as the gameplay goes, there's nothing more to this game than flying in space, infiltrating behind enemy lines, escorting stuff and shooting stuff. In space. It's harder than you might think, as there is no right side up. If you don't think killing stuff in space is exciting, then this game might not be for you. There is multiplayer, but it's a bit tricky to set up since you need to use, you guessed it, FS2 Open to make it work, as the original implementation is kinda ancient and doesn't really work well. There is also a modding community that makes campaigns that try to extend both this universe and various other sci-fi universes. Also, this game did Reapers before Mass Effect ever did.
So do I recommend it? The game - yes, definitely. The steam release - not so much. Go get it on GoG instead as it seems to be the better version of the game.

Cities XL Platinum is at its core a solid city management game. Despite the several irritating glitches, the game plays fairly well, with occasional FPS drops. City management isn't difficult at all for anyone who has played a game of similar style before, however, for someone new to the genre, they may find it difficult to get a grip on this game for a short while. While the broad focus of this game is enjoyable, the one thing that started to become extremely annoying after some time was the focus on the needs of individual areas of your city. At first, it's easy to manage personal happiness, but after some time, it starts to get annoying. Parts of the city often do not respond to numerous attempts at improving leisure and shops satisfaction. It often takes at least 5-8 shops for me to get one area to be satisfied with the shops in the area, and then I get new messages telling me to decrease retail because it's too hard to sell. Trading with various cities is also a task that is more complicated than it needs to be, and it starts to become yet another tedious part of this game after a while. This game seems to want to educate you more on the boring, redundant part of city management than the actual entertaining, meaningful part. Cities XL Platinum was a nice break from EA's money-grabbing, but it's a game I can only handle so much of at one time.

2/24/16: Edited for more legitimacy and less memelorditude
+The fighting system is great.  Much more accessible than IV.
+DLC that can be purchased with either in-game currency or real-type money (soon)
+Looks dang beautiful
+Online play works (much better than it did at launch.  Not one server problem for me in days)
-Only support for XInput or keyboard, which the new SFV-themed Fightsticks are not (Use something like X360CE or Joy2key if using a PS3/PS4 fightstick)
-Severe lack of single-player options (Arcade mode, Vs. CPU, etc); not worth $60 (yet)
-Has story mode, but it not very in-depth.  Feels more like a build-up to the upcoming cinematic story.
-Takes a little while to find an opponent in matchmaking (or maybe I'm just impatient)
The gameplay is good, but the overall game is severely lacking in substance.  Features that have been a staple of fighting games are absent.  Capcom has stated that such features will be available in March, but these features are what most people would expect to be available at launch.  I personally like the game, but I'm sure most people want more of a single-player experience than this game has to offer.

For what it's worth, I enjoyed the Sleeping Dogs campaign. The combat that attempts to be dynamic is flawed but functional, much like the rest of the game. Some issues plague the PC version like some redundant controls and awkward camera placement. The sheer bugginess of the game can provide for a lot of entertainment, however situational it may be.
If you're looking for GTA-style gameplay, I'd say you're better off with GTA. Otherwise, Sleeping Dogs will keep you playing for about 16-18 hours on its campaign.

This is probably the best SNES game to be released on Steam. From the very first second of booting the game you are guaranteed a trip down the memory lane. The gameplay is solid and only hard enough to keep you entertained. Graphics are old fashioned tiles reminiscent of Pokemon and Zelda. Music is original but very much in the spirit of the 16-bit times.

The story was absolutely wonderful, intriguing, and did have some twists here and there. Whilst the city is fairly small, it has a lot of detail to it. The place is littered with back alleys and small sights to see. The driving is surprisingly pleasant (minus the quirks listed below) and responsive. This feels essentially like GTA in China Town due to the size (which is honestly rather small, although it's almost completley urban). Unlike GTA and most other games that follow this formula though, guns aren't exactly a mainstay of the game. They pushed the combat focus of this game onto melee. It feels reminiscent of Arkham Asylum/City, although not as refined (listed why, once again, below). There are also plenty of things to do besides just missions in the game. Everything from score attack (based on Steam friends list) to racing, to multiple types of gambling, and even Karaoke (Okay, so maybe that's all it has to offer...). Additionally, the voice acting is in my opinion superb, and the same can be said for most of the other sound assets. The music however is lacking, and not because of the lack of good tracks, but because of the limited quantity of tracks. Not only that, but the music isn't fitting. I love Machine Head and Soulfly as much as the next metal head, but it just doesn't seem to fit in with the setting... That said, they do have other music that is more fitting to the setting, but it would have been nice to get less (none) of the stuff we hear over here in the states, and more stuff that you'd hear over there (top 20 radio hits and the such).
Now, onto the issues...
A: The camera for driving absolutely sucks. It sticks when you don't want it to (when trying to go in reverse) and it doesn't stick when you do want it to (when doing sharp turns). It also flips wildly if you try to force it behind you while backing up as soon as you start going forwards, and then it ends up pointing backwards anyways.
B: The typical cliche of cops being able to keep up with anything you drive is here in full force... Be prepared to have a cop in a Crown Vic on your tailpipe while you're maxing out a Lamborghini in a straight line. You'll never be blatantly faster than the cops, unless you're a suicidal maniac on a 2-wheeler.
C: Combat is utterly horrid due to the hard-lock that can't be turned off (it doesn't change targets based on whom you're looking at, but rather which direction you tap prior to attack) and the horrid input detection that leads to many missed shots. Additionally, the most devastating moves (done by the "heavies" as you could call them) give you about a half of a second to respond with the proper key press. That said, unlike other games, the enemies won't wait and take turns attacking you. (I'm looking at you Assassins Creed)
D: The save system is a sin for an open world RPG, be prepared to reload and run/drive the entire way across the map, because it always puts you back at your house upon reloading, not the location you saved at. Thankfully the map isn't that large... right?
E: The game, at least the main story, is way too short. You can beat it easily in under 8 hours (main story only), but I squeaked by at 25 hours by doing quite literally EVERYTHING that the game had to offer by the time I finished up the last mission... and then I spent about 2 hours jacking around in the city. This isn't horrid by any stretch, but you can get much better value for the dollar with other open world games that provide many more side activities.
7.5/10 For a first attempt at a new IP, it was a good job. The game, while scarred by a lot of oversights, was great.
Buyers Note: If you pick this game up, I would highly suggest picking up any mission DLC. Additionally, the combat style DLC is good too. If you can pick up the entire lot for a discount on a sale, even better.

This game could have been a lot of fun but several design decisions really put the brakes on.
1) Defeating levels are more about luck than skill: often there is one brick left to hit, making it quite tedious. There are even achievements in this game for going longer than 45 seconds without hitting anything (that's a bad sign).
2) The batches of levels are WAY too long (~15 levels) and going back to the main town to hand in coin erases all progress of that level batch and clears your inventory. This is not a bug and there is no warning. I literally had to replay the levels all over again after thinking I would go back to town and hand in my stuff.
3) Part of the goal of the game is to rebuild a broken town, so that's what the player starts to do. Then, the player realizes there is an achievement for beating the game without rebuilding anything in the town. So... I guess we have to start all over again just to get the achievement?
4) The music is VERY repetitive and of poor quality, which makes it hard to listen to.
If this game is on for $0.50 or less, you might find some enjoyment, but there are WAY better Breakout games available, Shatter being one. Save yourself the trouble and play Shatter instead.

Love this game. As near as you can currently get to the real thing with regards to controlling troops on the battlefield. Unless you have played this makers other games prior to this, do not expect to jump in and take over the battlefield. The tutorial videos are really good and give you an idea of what to expect.Do them, otherwise you are in for a steep frustrating learning curve. Graphics are great. You can view the whole battlefield from miles up watching military symbols moving around or you can zoom right in and watch individual units in combat. Supply and comms are vital just like in real war. Lose these and you lose units and control of units. Likewise, neglect your units or ask to much of them and you are likely to get a real world response and you can watch your mission start to grind to a halt. The AI is pretty good also and will punish your mistakes. Finally don't expect a nice quick battle. This game draws you in and before you know it, you have run out of time to go to bed and it's time to go to work again. Graviteam keep up the excellent work

Absolutely brilliant. Most Tales fans started out young in the early 90's/00's, playing the original games which were clearly written for children & teens. But a huge chunk of us are now in our 20's and 30's and desire more mature themes in our games. Finally we get a Tales game to match our age. Berseria is the most mature Tales game yet. Instead, Berseria is more reflective of the real world, where the line between "right" and "wrong" is a lot more muddy, often only being a matter of an individual's own experiences and perspective.

If you would like to see more mature themes in your future Tales games, let the devs know by showing your support and buying a copy of Berseria. You won't be dissapointed!

First off let's clarify graviteam tactics is a ground warfare battle operations simulation like a fully realistic flight or tank sim. Don't expect a RTS like company of heroes or even men of war. Also the game is singleplayer only.  Also understand you need to read the game manual, if you don't know all the waypoints and movement type parameters or command and morale system you won't know how to effectively command troops in 3d tactical battles.
You start off in the campaign operations list, you pick a operation then start in  overhead 2d grid operations map that all your forces are shown in checkerboard style map. This operations map is where you will fight 3d tactical battles on and similiar to total war series that whats on map is whats in 3d battle. Understand this map is a persistent battle so every stat is saved and taken account for, if a vehicle gets destroyed and a town is leveled, next time you fight in that area you will see the all the map terrain damage, dead corpses, destruction all saved exaclty the way it was end of previous battle in that area. 2d operations map is turn based and you move you units around then after AI turn when they attack, ambushed or counter attack you will see a flame with all nearby invovled units with red dots on them representing battle to click on an fight. Then you go into the 3d tactical battle mode, or rts mode.
3d tactical battles are full on simulation. all tank simulated ballistics and armor values are represented historally accuratly. The movement speed is at a realistic pace, so thats why the time speed button is there for, the morale command system is very compolex and integrated. The distance to commander, nearby troops, enemy troops and under fire severly changes your troops ability to follow orders.
The movemnt types are critcal to use properly, you mave move by roads is key to keeping vehicles from getting stuck in rough terrain. the move fast or crawl under cover, formation of line, free blob, column and unit spacing of in file, spaced, or scattered. movent can have tanks in front lead as cover for infantry tofollow behind or infantry can ride on tanks. Commander units must use area fire order to spot for artillary to barrage point and better commander can spot the more accurate the artillary fire.
Units that don't move on current turn can intrench in the ground. The detail is amazing, building that get hit will catch fire and burn with smoke and after awhile will collapse, destroyed vehicles might blow up, or catch fire and crew bail out on fire screaming running around like chickens with head cut off for a few seconds until they burn to death. Also burning vehicles will start cooking off munition and see secondary explosions. Terrain is fully deformed with explosions blasting holes in ground, burning trees and buildings, tanks can smash down fences and trees. There is pools of blood and gore decals on shot soldiers. If morale low enough units will surrender and put hands in area or panic and route and no longer follow any orders and run away to save themselfs. Soldiers can be knocked unconsious from concusion of explosion or wounded and drop to knees holding there wounds on arm or stomach.
Also note there is a quick battle scenario that has a template to quickly whip up a operation to fight and there is a full editor (probably same one developers use to create campaigns) to create a operation as details as the ones in the game. There are modding tools to bring in your own textures and models.
Basically long story short if you want a hardcore ground warfare simulator to fight a battle operation on the eastern front in WW2 this games for you.
If your a casual RTS player, want a quick get in play and stop, or need lots of instant action, don't have patience, want to only or need to play multiplayer then this games not for you.

The Maps you play on, are recreated Areas, where the Soldiers fought while WW2 (No fictional Stuff, even the amount of Troops, that fought while the certain Battles, were recreated). Mostly open Areas, with some small Villages, with a lot of love to detail. The DLC's are also great, and add some modern Campaings, like the Soviet-Afghan war or while the Angola conflict. This game is still my go-to when I feel like some stress-free tactical badguy popping, but it's not without its issues.
I've tried picking up JA2, but it feels far too clunky for 2016. The remake, by comparison, is streamlined almost to the point of oversimplicity. JA:BIA combines the slightly crap humour and storytelling of a game from the late 90s (most of the voice acting is recycled from JA2) with the visuals and minimalist UX of a 2014 iphone game.
The mid-to-late game is almost unplayable without a rebalancing patch. I wrote my own, but I believe there are some downloadable from the interwebs. The maps are large and varied, but mostly unused. The AI - both enemy and merc - is almost nonexistant. Planning and executing a successful building assault or map clearance is still satisfying though, and while the game feels full of missed opportunities and never really lives up to its promise, it still has a certain charm.
If you like plan-and-go-tactics and JA:BIA is on sale, then buy it, mod it, and enjoy it for what it is. If nothing in the premise speaks to you, or you're not willing to do the work to make it shine, then avoid.

Builds on the origional PA with new units, new terrain and a new game mode. It feels like what I hoped the origional PA would be like - and is a ton of fun with friends!
Desprite the plethora of reviews suggesting this game is dire - I am here to recomend.
Personally I believe it is worth the money - avoiding the contentious moral issues for the moment - Titans add a new twist and the rest of the new units are a welcome addition to spice up game play. I've barley played 8 hours yet and I have already had a great time (about 5 in galactic war and 3 with friends).
I havn't encountered any game breaking bugs or crashes yet, mostly just a bunch of odd looking/narly graphics on terrain.
It does seem though that some people are running into more serious bugs - some caused by out of date GPU drivers, others caused by genuine issues with the game. These bugs include non-starts, various crashes ect. Fortunatly out of the 5 people I know playing PA:TITANS no one seems to be affected (I actually have the worst bugs with the narly texture popin-out) and there are a range of GPU's in use with both ATI and NVIDIA.
Relevant specs: 2500k @ 4.5, 290x, 32GB ram, SSD. (also running on a 4k monitor and considering I have everything on max the gameplay is pretty amazing).
I honestly hope that people dont throw the baby out the window... or drown it in the bath or whatever that saying is and destory this addon with negativity. I'm not Uber's biggest fan right now either, but this game is fun and putting its past behind it, it could be really REALLY amazing with a few more expansions (which I would personally be happy to pay for).
So if I'm recomending....why all the negative reviews?
Unfortunatly, some bugs asside, the situtation surrounding PA:TITANS release and is predecessor, vanilla PA, is very dissapointing.
It's pretty clear people are mad because vanilla PA was a dissapointment of broken promises (although I have been told this depends on your point of view and what you expected out of the origional game) which has now been abandoned in favor of a product people have to pay more money for.
Does that situation feel ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for a lot of people? Yeah it does.
And can I therefore understand where people are coming from? Absolutley, because I feel that betrayed/let down feeling too.
BUT -  and there is always a but - would I choose this situation over Uber giving Titans out for free and then having to close up because they cant pay people? Yes I would. A world where PA is supported in some form or another is a good one in my book, as despite its faults this game has some unique and frankly really fun freatures. There arent enough large scale Sci fi RTS games and despite its flaws (and history), this one is a good example of a fairly rare breed.
I should note I am one of the people (suckers) that purchased the origional PA on steam right after kickstarter, so I paid a ton of money (£90) for vanilla PA based on its godly promises (which are here to pay for in Titans) and I yet I still don't get the expansion free. Do I think thats a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ move by Uber? HELL YEAH I do, but at the same time I'd be lying if I said I couldn't understand it.
At the end of the day,♥♥♥♥♥♥happens, lines have to be drawn somewhere and people need to get paid!

As much as I would love to give this game a thumbs up, due to the problems the game has, I cannot. This is a serious review for anyone looking to buy the game, as you must be warned before you purchase this for $43.99 .
This game, is an extremely good release to try to bring back an old age of RTS games in an age of MOBAs. I must admit, it is a good game with a very good concept and idea. Its essentially a war on four scales. Ground, Water, Air, and Space. The overall idea based behind this game is a good one, however I do not feel I am able to give this game a thumbs up yet. For now I must give it a thumbs down for numerous reasons. Reason #1. If you have a solar system with 6+ planets, the game is laggy, crashes and is just generally unreliable. I will give you my system specs just so you can understand that I don't have a below sub-par computer, and my computer should be able to run games like these well. Reason #2. This game is basically a DLC for Planetary Annihilation, they should've just added it as a purchaseable DLC instead of forcing people new to the game to drop 15$ more into purchasing it. Reason #3. Extremely buggy AI pathing.
Intel i7 4990k Quad-Core 4.3Ghz Overclocked
Nvidia GeForce GTX 980 Graphics Card
16 GB Memory
1 TB HDD
500 GB SSD
MSI Z87 GD65 Motherboard
Back to the review. The lobby pre-game looks nice, unfortunately if the solar system is decently large it takes a while to load the system before you get in the game, its got horrid FPS, and you still have to load the system in a loading screen either way. Into the game, if you actually make it in (you have 6 or less small planets with maybe one large planet) then the game is fun, however large armies take the FPS down a lot as well. Not to mention that lots of ground troops (bots, tanks, etc.) have extremely horrible pathing. 50% of the time if you are trying to attack around a mountain, a large amount of the bots in your army will get stuck and are not able to move. However, the game is still enjoyable, it gives a fresh new taste to Planetary Annihilation as its own standalone game, but if you we're looking to purchase this if you have vanilla PA or are looking to get either of them, stick with the vanilla version as there are not enough new units and such to make this a decent buy. Even for $14.96 it's still a bit pricey.
TL;DR It's a fun game, but has FPS problems and crashes frequently, would not recommend, buy vanilla PA
Overall Rating 4/10

+/+ Graphics are great for a city building game.
+/+ Most game mechanics are well executed.
+/+ Great UI.  Very easy to pick up and learn.
+/+ Cities can interact (i.e. trade) with each other.  This allows you to create specialty cities.
+/+ Large maps.
+/- Not as difficult as SimCity 4.
+/- Not much different than previous Cities XL games.
+/- Includes Steam Cloud, but lacks other features such as achievements and the workshop.
-/- Lack of variety in graphic style.
-/- Not map editor or terraforming options.
-/- Roads & highways can sometimes very picky about how you place them.
-/- Game slows down once your city reaches a certain size (very processor heavy game).
-/- Developers have a bad reputation and have gone out of business.  Don’t expect new patches.
-/- Unfixed bugs and broken features.
Verdict: 6.8/10.  While Cities XL Platinum clearly fails to surpass SimCity 4, it does offer a unique and fun take on the city building/management genre.  If you can put up with the late game slowdowns or don’t care about creating larger cities, then I can easily recommend Cities XL Platinum to you.  If you expect more, you will be disappointed.  Don’t spend more than $10 and you’ll likely be happy.
Update 9/7/15:  Buy Cities Skyline if you want a city builder.  This game is no longer worth considering.

(For example, in a city that had no agricultural area, it was impossible to develop retail that theoretically covers other goods as well, and in another, heavy industry, manufacturing, offices and high tech constantly screamed for more of the others while none were being developed because they wanted the others to be there in the first place.)
On the good side, it looks good, is easy to get into and is satisfying until you run into the impossible-to-solve problems.
The game has potential, and if tweaked could certainly be a very enjoyable experience, but it ultimately got on my nerves more than anything.

What drew me into the game was the comparison of RS and UO which were both games I thoroughly enjoyed in the past growing up. Realized quickly that this game has absolutely nothing even remotely close to being like UO.
I would normally recommend this game as it's F2P, but it's got some astonishing flaws for a game that has been in development for 3 years. As for some of the things I liked. Gathering actually holds value in this game even at the very beginning which helps boost you up to being able to do more things quicker. There's a decent anti-bot system in place. The tutorial did not explain much which thankfully there is a built-in wiki that will constantly be holding your hand through majority of the first few hours.
As for the flaws. The game is built on an isometric map with 8-bit sprites that aren't animated whatsoever. Combat is clunky and all based on RNG. First few hours you'll be constantly in the wiki learning the basics of the game, which the game has a tutorial it just skips over the most important part of the ENTIRE crafting aspect. The game is free but has an item shop built purely for people to get mid-to-late game gear with just a few dollars. There's also packages that give you a large amount of coins, housing material, rare pets, etc. After seeing the item shop I checked out how often the game is updated and it's not surprising that they spread out updates several months in between.
TL:DR It's an old school RS clone with a crafting system similar to Minecraft with the added breeding of animals and the ability to purchase your own island and build on it. Fair warning it's a F2P so be weary that it's extremely pay to win. If that sounds appealing feel free to go nuts you'll probably spend 10-20 hours before uninstalling.

The first zone of Wizorb requires you to complete twelve levels and a boss in a single sitting; if you lose all your lives or quit in the middle of it, you keep none of your hard-earned gold.  Precise mouse control with left- and right-click is clearly a superior option to two-speed digital control, but the UI makes no reference to mice, instead displaying either keyboard or controller buttons. The music is droning and repetitive and doesn't stop if you alt-tab out. While these various quibbles aren't dealbreaking, the game clearly feels like a 90s era console game, but doesn't really take advantage of that fact.
On the gameplay side, hitboxes aren't nearly as clear as they should be for a genre that demands precision. Boxes, for instance, only have hitboxes on the top portion, as the ball is effectively floating off of the ground. This is probably the biggest dealbreaker, especially where enemies are likely to hover near the bottom of the level and liable to send your ball careening in a seemingly random direction.
In all, Wizorb feels like a poor PC port of a mediocre Xbox game.

An amazing sandbox/RPG style game that existed when I was in 8th grade(around 2 years ago). I would log in with one of my best friends and play, level, and build. Classes cost in game currency, so it only took around ~2 months for me of playing an hour a day to obtain every single class. Leveling was not difficult, mounts were not hard to get, and reaching max level was only a matter of time and not that far from people who spent money on this game. Market was somewhat balanced, item mall did not give too many OP items, and it was possible to see people reach max level without spending a single cent. Streamers were nice, loved the game(I was part of a streamer's guild and watched 20+ hours of his stream), and had massive giveaways that simply made every minute of this game fun to play. Grinding was not that annoying since drop rates were not unreasonable, and crafting materials were not so difficult to find or buy from others. When I would happen to get bored(very rarely), it would be a 'why not' to just go ahead and play some soccer from a stadium one of the guild members created. Toxicity and scammers were uncommon, since many people were flourishing and being quite successful both economically and emotionally. I was mastery 60/100 at that time after only about ~150 hours(before steam release obviously).
Trove created a "Patron Pass", basically a premium subscription based system that when activated, gave double drop rate, double exp, and multiple other benefits. This seemed miniscule at first, since not only was this given out two weeks for free, the buffs do not look that overpowered at first. However, at a deeper glance, trove seemed to slowly lower drop rates for rare items, and people would have to rely on Patron benefits to simply live like the old life of the f2p player BEFORE the steam release. However, this by itself was not bad, since trove gained more populrity, Trion struggeld to keep servers up. Level cap increased to 200. Absolutely fantastic game, there is literally nothing comparable on the market out there, even behemoths of the RTT (Real-Time-Tactics)/Wargames/Simulator such as Close Combat, Combat Mission, Theatre Of War and newer yet far more simplified entries like Wargame and Men Of War can't hold a candle to this unique game. The complexity, depth of tactics and operational scale are unrivalled, from destructible landscapes and weather-systems, to small-arms ballistics and individual solider injuries, to fully-fledge tank-combat with accurate penetration properties and modular damage-models are all present with a rather great degree of accuracy.
You are not some all-powerful diety who telepathically transmits your orders to your subordinates, instead you have to rely on radio communications, wire companies, or if all else fails flares and runners, there is nothing even remotely as accurate in portraying the complexity behind the chain of command on a tactical/operational level.
On top of all that it features also an extensive and cusomisable menu which allows for some further tweaking by the player to tailor the experience to their personal desires.
Even the visuals are appealing, although occasional they can be somewhat bland. The biggest downside in the visual and auditory department are the sounds, often lacking  the real "omph" of the effects they try to portray, however they often enough sufficiently succeed at enthralling the player into the atmospheric spectacle of the varied conflicts portrayed through-out the game(s) and its DLCs.
There are some downsides to it of course, quite a few bugs, the sim-typical unintitive interfaces with little in terms of tutorials, guides (within the game that is, the small yet loyal community has created a myriad of guides and explanations for just about all of the functions in game), or in general visual appeal can be somewhat off-putting to newcomers, coupled with the somewhat higher price when taking into account the DLCs and very niche-genre (much in the same vein of Paradox, although a far cry from the likes of DCS), it is understandable many are hesistant to try it out.
Nonetheless I can only whoelheartedly recommend the entire graviteam franchise to any wargames, RTT, or merely military-history afficionado, after the initial entry-curve you'll fall in love with the franchise and have a somewhat decent replay value given the mission editor and slightly randomised campaign missions.
I do hope Gaviteam aims for a multiplayer component for future releases, even if only limited to a 1v1, because despite the effort put into making the AI responsive and unpredictable, I comes nowhere near rivalling a real human opponent and to my mind it is a shame that such a fantastic game loses its longevity because of the lack of that kind of feature.
Anyway, this game is a rock-solid 9/10 even if only for it's uniquness on the market, were I to judge it entirely on its own merity, taking into account all the drawbacks, perhaps an 8/10 would be more adequate. That said, a must have in my book, you simply can't miss this, even if only for the fact it's one of a kind.

Jagged Alliance:  Back in Action is an exercise in compromises between improving an already good strategy game and keeping it true to the original. On one hand, the graphics are definitely better and the 3d aspect adds a lot to the overall look and feel of the game. On the other hand, the real-time battle system can be a real turnoff to purists looking for a straight upgrade to the original series.
Other than the graphical and audio updates, most of the game is the same. You still have to save Arulco from the evil Deidranna and must do so by recruiting mercenaries, liberating towns, and stocking up on the latest military hardware. Combat tends to be a bit more frantic this time around, since it’s no longer turn-based, and you will have to find whatever method gets you the most success with the least number of loaded saves. On my playthrough I found that having a trio of snipers and three assault-style mercs set up in a layered line formation in guard mode (auto-attack) tended to work really well and I could just un-pause the game while they murdered everything with very few interruptions needed (your experience may vary).
The game is unfortunately, not without its issues, hence the mixed rating on steam store. Determining line-of-sight is an absolute chore and the graphical interface does very little to help you determine the topology of the map you’re fighting on. This can lead to your characters being more exposed than you think they are and/or not able to fire on an enemy. This is aggravated a bit by the fact that your player must have a high perception score in order to automatically fire on far away targets in guard mode. While this isn’t a problem at the beginning of combat, when you suddenly have more enemies coming into the battle and have to start micro-managing forces it can become a bit of a pain.
JA:BIA is another one of those games that makes you wish that Steam allowed for neutral ratings. I managed an entire playthrough and even enjoyed figuring out how to clear some of the maps, but I still wouldn’t rate this as a particularly “great” game, just an “okay” one that’s good for one playthrough and really moreso for people who aren’t religious Jagged Alliance fans (who would probably hate this game to death.)

"It's one of those games", that's what I planned to make my review about. Until I put more thought into it and realised it's not "one of those games". It's the only game of its type.
1. Full, FULL command simulator. No pixel lives, no cursor-following 'units', you're someone behind the lines holding a map sending orders through radio, wire telephone, or voice. Through command-chains
2. The most realistic combat simulation I have ever seen in a strategy/simulator game
3. ♥♥♥♥♥ons of potential playtime (8 campaigns in stock game, up to 100-150 hours of play-time) not mentioning DLC's
4. terraformable terrain. A feature that I greatly appreciated in MOWAS.
5. Night-fighting, lots of it. Realistic, confusing, intense, pure unfilterd night-fighting.
6. I'm gonna have to resort to using the sentence "this is one of THOSE games" here - It's one of those games that don't cater to title-bait casuals, this is made by a small dev-team that doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about selling and more interested in spending hundreds of work-hours into obscure conflicts or battles that took place around their homes. It's not Normandy/Omaha beach or Stalingrad or Kursk or the Ardennes or whatever attention-grabbing battles to people with a very generic view of WW2, I never learned about things like Kampfgruppe Peiper until I played this game. This is one of those games that cover many conflicts some people never heard of
7. Cold war DLC's. Straight-up the most fun I've had with this game. Includes a massive fictional tank-battle set in an alternative-history scenario if you want to fulfill your western-vs-eastern massive tank battle dream.
8. Physics. This game is old, but their physics game is on-point.
I don't know what else to mention, but overall like I stated at the beginning. This is not "one of those games". This is THAT game, one-of-a-kind, only of its type.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I don't see what all the hate is about here. I do agree it is a bit silly that people who had the original have to now buy this to keep up but I wouldn't call it fair to judge the actual game based off that. As for all the complaints about the AI being too dificult I think this is just new player's frusturated with a very steep learning curve. The AI is actually very bad and does a lot of silly things, very easy to defeat with some experience. I also experienced frustration when first playing over a year ago in the difficulty of beating the AI on the lowest setting. It takes a lot to adjust to this game from more traditional RTS games. As for the game being buggy I have experienced some frustration with the game lagging and crashing. However the issues have been vastly improved since I began playing and appear to continue to improve. I run this game one a machine I built in 2009 with very few issues so I am a little surprised about so many people claiming that the game constantly crashes on their brand new $2500 PC. Most new players also don't realize that most of the game processing actually occurs on Uber's servers and not on the client's side. Doing certain things in game such as setting too many land units on too large of a patrol can cause too many pathing calculations for the game to deal with, avoiding certain (all very unnecessary) actions can prevent the game from lagging and freezing. Though I'll be the first to admit the game isn't perfect and does have a few programming issues there are a lot of great things that make this game stand out and in my opinion very much worth playing. Below I'll list some pros and cons;
Pros
- Three dimensional map allows for completely new strategy forcing players to change their strategies and defend from all sides.
- Single faction allows for highly competitive gameplay where both players always start on an equal field with no faction based advantage to impede upon the competitiveness of the game.
- No unit cap, build as much crap as you like, huge battles.
- Large unit variety allowing for virtually limitless combinations of strategies.
- Need for large build areas and lots of resources impedes players ability to 'turtle' and forces constantly agressive gameplay.
- Kill the commander objective forces players to re-think strategy from previous RTS experiences, keeping players constantly on their toes as a commander snipe can always be just beyond the fog of war.
- Orbital layer of gameplay adds again another level to strategy forcing players to defend their bases even from the space above them. Additionally with multi planet maps players can find numerous ways from massive teleporter invasions and nukes to planet smashes with asteroids and even using the annihilaser to lay siege upon their foes.
- Land, sea, air, and space layers of combat.
- 1v1 ranked matches allows players to quickly connect with another player of a similar skill level for a match on a mirrored planet allowing players to rise up the ranks on an always level playing field.
- Teleporters allow for moving massive number of units across map instantaneously adding yet another level of depth to strategy.
- Live economy forces players to be mindful of how much they are building and how much resources they have available or risk losing radar coverage and experiencing a proportional reduction of production capabilities.
- Mobbing through enemy bases with tons of units destroying everything around is tons of fun.
- Developers constantly improving/refining game, very actively.
- Can switch game mode to vanilla in settings allowing you to still play with friends who do not have the expansion online without having 2 copies of the game installed. Vanilla may also be a good place for new players to learn due to there being less units to manage and learn.
Cons
- Game sometimes buggy; pathing issues at times with complex terrain and large numbers of units, build units refusing to build in places they should be able (sometimes this is from previously queued structures), and very rarely the game freezing out player commands or disconnecting the player altogether but this happens to me very seldom, less than once in ten matches.
- VERY STEEP LEARNING CURVE; this game is not easy to pick up, the variety and scale, along with the live economy, make managing everying very difficult for new players. I would recommend new players watch a few replays on the leaderboards to see what the best players do to win.
- No 'Easy' AI setting. AI on lowest setting very difficult for new players to beat due to previously mentioned learning curve. My recommendation to new players on this is to lower the resource rate for the AI to .5 or lower then slowly turn it up .1 at a time every time until you are able to beat the AI, then when you are comfortable playing at 1.0 rate then turn the AI up to hard. When you can confidently defeat the AI on 'hard' difficulty you are ready for multiplayer.
- Singleplayer mode 'Galactic War' sucks. Don't bother playing it. This is a multiplayer game, the only reason to play singleplayer is for practice and for that I recommend skirmish battles against the AI.
- Internet connection required for gameplay due to way game runs. However as I previously stated this game is only actually fun on multiplayer so this shouldn't really matter.
- Lack of community support and game information due to small player base. The most complete wiki of the game,
is no longer kept up and all information is now very obsolete forcing players to look in game for information on unit meta. Hopefully this will change soon with the introduction of a new player base from the Titan Wars expansion.
- Had to pay $13 for the expansion. However I purchased the original during a steam summer sale for only $23 so I wasn't too upset.
In all I find it kind of disappointing that so many people have given this game a negative review after only playing for a few hours just because they can't beat the AI on the lowest setting. It took me at least 15 hours of practice before I was even able to beat the AI on normal mode. As for all those who have experienced so many gameplay issues I'm not sure what to say as I have so few on such an old machine. My only recommendation is to make sure your drivers are up to date and that you have at least 6GB of RAM. If you are looking for a simple RTS that is easy to pick up and learn with a fun singleplayer experience, and are not feeling up to a frusturating learning curve then this game isn't for you. But if you do want a very complex, fast paced, and balanced game with top notch meta look no further. This game is very strategy oriented and though shares some elements of gameplay with games like Supreme Commander the game overall is completely unique and a breath of fresh air in the long stale world of RTS games.
As for all the complaints about the Titans expansion being a standalone, I think most people are making a far bigger deal about it than it really is. From a business perspective and as a player I commend Uber for going the route they took. Since this was released I've noticed a huge boom in current players in the community. The PA subreddit is far more active and wait times between online matches has been almost non existent waiting at most a minute where before it was who knows when you would get a match. I think this move  was necessary for the game to continue being worked on. The vanilla game has a very poor steam user rating, which can be crippling to game sales, mainly due to the game falling short of promises made during the games early acess phase. Though Uber did finish the game late and still in patchy condition I do defend them on the grounds that over the last year they have been very consistent with updating, improving, and refining the game with regular updates. My only quarrel is making those who purchased the vanilla version on Steam early access... Continued in comments.

Paid mods aside, I'm going to have to hang my head in sadness as I write a review about the game itself:
I enjoyed the concept and setting. The idea of being on the east coast of the US is way more interesting than the wild-west theme that permeated New Vegas. However, the game really felt empty at a lot of points. It was repetitive to the extreme, to such a point that I felt as though Bethesda didn't even bother hiding it.
The main hook is that you have an NPC follower that you have to talk to, just to have him mark a new settlement that needs help on your map. On top of that, you have to juggle a little to get around the dialogue unless you do this mission.  And the missions are always the same, "help, X group is attacking us, go wipe out their base nearby and when you're finished we'll let you spend money to make our lives better."
In terms of controls: the game was OK. I didn't run into too many control issues or anything, though I'm used to changing with each new game that I pick up, so others may have more to comment on that.
I just keep coming back to the gameplay itself. It feels like a loot-based rat-race that has me walking around picking up as much junk as I can then teleporting back to wherever I have storage space and dumping it all until I can level up enough to craft gear to do missions. The leveling is even worse, as you can't really build anything uself (night vision, power armor parts, gun sites, etc.) until you're about level 14-20 depending on the equipment and how hard you push certain pathways.
Aside from crafting, there's the issue of settlements. These are a nice idea that I was really excited about. However, the execution is absolutely horrid. For one thing, you have to walk around and place buildings in 3D, but if you move too far it disappears so you have to play with it a bit. On top of that, there is no logical interface to manage all your people, especially if you have multiple settlements. In fact, there is NO ECONOMY either. You can build little stands where people work to generate some caps for you, but it's a paultry sum compared to what it cost to build and the fact that you have to travel back to each settlement and collect the cash is ridiculous. So with no economy you have no idea what kind of parts or items a settlment may obtain to sell you, which means you can't really easily setup supply lines or anything else that a mayor would actually have to think about.
In fact, it seems as though settlements were almost an after thought with no real purpose in the game. It's just a huge wasted effort and physically exhausting to try to position buildings properly, get things to mesh or draw any enjoyment about of it. There aren't even any roleplay opportunities or quests from any settlments after the first one! Where is the problem-solving? Where is the concern about supply lines or logistics? Where is the feeling of rebuilding the wasteland??
Overall, I'm very unimpressed with Bethesda's sequel to Fallout 3. The less-linear approach is nice, the settlments are a good idea, but in the end this game just feels like one great big good idea with terrible execution.
That's the end of my review! Flame on and hate me if you will, fanboys! :)

Characters and Items are really basic: There is nothing special to be found and better items are just more annoying to find and new characters just bring other abilities. There are even some classes that share the same equipment with just another ability and slightly different stats. For example: Playing Trickster and Assassin are basically the same thing, just that the Assassin can throw poison to apply a DoT Effect on the enemy and the Trickster can distract enemies with a decoy he spawns. They share the same Items and similar stats.
When you get into the endgame things dont change, you're just hunting for really rare items ,which will disappoint you with their lack of variety. They sometimes just add 5 damage to the attacks and they have a different sprite animation. Some Robes and Armors give you 1 or 2 stats aswell as some defense, but thats nothing special if you ask me. The higher tier the item is, the more attack/defense it has, thats it.
Some unique items have another ability to them, but unless you're spending 10 hours straight to get them, you wont even know about them.
You can increase your characters stats buy using stat potions, which are pretty rare if you're not a dungeon slaying master at this game and its really annoying if you die after you've almost maxed out one or two stats.
My biggest problem with this game is the repetetive gameplay and the lack of variety with the items. All youre doing is holding left-click on a monster until it is dead and while doing that youre spamming "A" and "D" to make it miss all of it's attacks. The dungeons are decent, but its still, always the same gameplay.
I usually like farm games like these, where you have to work hard for your gear, which is the reason I spent around 1000 hours of playing Diablo 3 and Im still enjoying farming items to get something out of it. But this game just gives you another Item with a different name and sprite animation to what you already have and those dont even change your damage too much.I played this game a lot and I just dont think I should have. I had a Knight witht the best Items and 6 out of 8 stats maxed, so dont tell me I didnt get to play the endgame enough or sometime. Im not saying it's a bad game, but it's missing something for me.

The game is obviously well-crafted and the atmosphere is wonderful, but I found both the script and the voice acting to be wanting. The gameplay itself amounts to just walking in circles and clicking on the same items over and over again in order to move forward, which may work as a cynical meta-commentary for gaming itself if there weren't such obvious care and effort put into other aspects. The use of the mutability of memory as a theme was admirable and could have been compelling, but in the end, this just did not feel like time well-spent to me; I would have appreciated if there was at least an illusion that any aspect of the game were under my control.

Cities XL is a great city builder, if you're willing to deal with lag.  Short and sweet, this game is what SimCity 2013 should have been, released a year earlier.  The game scales extremely well, allowing for truly MASSIVE cities to be build.  It has a billion different building types, large amount of road variations, and entirely different themes for all of them, depending on where you want to build.
Now, that's all great, other than the fact the actual developer for the game is dead and long gone.  It's got the same problems cities XL 2010 had, and will continue to have them forever.  Those problems are potentially game breaking for anyone willing to invest a lot of time.  The major bug that gets near everyone is the fact it's single threaded.  The game will not use more than one core on your computer, so no matter how well the rest of your system is, a large city will cripple you to single digit frame rates.
There are a few other much more minor bugs that people complain about, however I haven't come across.  Overall, I find the game to be very satisfactory.  I've gotten pretty large cities before the single digits hit, and even then it's still fairly easy to play.  For a veteran and novice to city building alike, I highly recommend this game for at least a short try.  It's just a shame there is no more development on it.

Sekhemre Khutawy Sobekhotep (appears in most sources as Amenemhat Sobekhotep; now believed to be Sobekhotep I; known as Sobekhotep II in older studies) was an Egyptian pharaoh of the 13th Dynasty during the Second Intermediate Period who reigned for at least three years c. 1800 BC. His chronological position is much debated, Sekhemre Khutawy Sobekhotep being either the founder of the dynasty, in which case he is called Sobekhotep I, or its twentieth ruler, in which case he is called Sobekhotep II. In his 1997 study of the Second Intermediate Period, the Egyptologist Kim Ryholt makes a strong case for Sekhemre Khutawy Sobekhotep as the founder of the dynasty, a hypothesis that is now dominant in Egyptology.[1][3] His tomb was discovered in Abydos in 2013 and was assigned to a king Sobekhotep I in January 2014.

Look, there's no beating around the bush here, this game is only going to appeal to a very specific group of people: People who like grinding, and people who like RuneScape Classic
If you like either of those things, then I highly recommend this game.
This game is more fast-paced than RSC, which makes it much more rewarding imo. Why? Because I can actually craft my own weapons and armor. Now you might be saying "Yeah you can do that in RSC too". Yeah, you can spend 20 hours leveling mining and smithing to a point where you can craft yourself weapons/armor that fits to your level, or you can just buy it with coins from merchants and players.
This is where the game separates itself from RSC: By relying more on individual skill and less on economy. You don't get gold drops from monsters, the only way you get gold is from quests and player markets. This means that you have to rely on actually leveling up your skills in order to better your character as a whole, which makes this game much more rewarding than RSC ever was. Also, since everything you could ever need is in the first town, its much easier to make your own items without having to walk across the entire map just to find a specific tool like RSC.
The only downsides so far:
reCAPTCHA interrupts your gameplay every once in awhile, which gets a little obnoxious
Bank UI is poorly designed, and took some time to get used to
Other than that, this game is truly free to play, unlike RS, where its "free to play to a point where you can't progress any farther without paying for membership", so I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a new MMO to play that's similar to RSC without all the junk that comes with it.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I am really not sure whether to give this game a positive or negative review. I finished the game and I'm not a hater for the series. I haven't watched the tv series but I try to reason my subjective opinions because you are most likely to feel the same way.
This game might have been innovative and super cool in 2012 but I'm writing the review now and because I know it's unfair to judge it based on today's standards, I will not take into consideration graphics and animation.
The first and foremost problem I have with the game is a subjective one but hear me out because it's very likely that you will feel the same. I have played every other Telltale game that was released after this one and the other ones were exploring stories in worlds I wanted and was interested to explore. The Walking Dead world isn't one in which I find pleasure exploring for obvious reasons. I mean you can totally understand why somebody would like to feel like Batman in the Telltale series, for example,  and would want to explore his world, or the magic world of Minecraft and so on, but this one, not so much because of the next poroblem.
The same problem I have with the Fallout series for same reasons but here comes the difference: you don't matter. The fact that this world doesnt have any hope for a happy ending worth fighting/playing for at the horizon feels bad and discouraging but the fact that you don't contribute with anything to the future of this world is even worse.At least in Fallout there's no way for things to go back to normal but you can feel your importance in making the world you're in better.
The ending, even though emotional, only confirms what I just said. The lack of a soundtrack through most of the emotional scenes feels off.
The GOOD stuff: The good part of the story is the relationships between the diffrent characters, part of your group. Getting to know what they lost and how they got where they are contributes to make you care for them.
Another problem though is that even though the characters are realistic and somewhat well-rounded, they all have a dominant treat that make your decisions hell of a lot easier to make. For example: one is selfish, one is always causing problems by making mistakes and one is nice and useful. If I will tell you to choose only one to follow you in this surviaval of the fittest world, the decision would be clear. The whole point in these Telltale games is to make you feel bad and in question no matter what choice you make. This game doesn't do that.
Also, way longer than it needs to be. Although the game will be enjoyed more by some than others I can only give it no more than  8.

Maybe a couple of $$ and some crappy pistol ammo. Ummmm what happened to all the gear you were carrying Mr. Dead Bad Guy?
Because of this, I started a new game 3 times and lost motivation each time I reached that point in the game, never going any further because it wasn't much fun.
HOWEVER! Using the Realistic Rebalancing Mod, it fixes all that and more! After getting this mod, I finally had fun and finished the game. My only flaw now would be the level design in some of the later levels isn't as good as the starting levels. A lot of big open spaces where long range weapons and high marksmanship stats are all that matter.
I would definitely recommend JA Back in Action, as the first few levels will definitely get you hooked. And if you want to improve the game balance, just simply use the Realistic Rebalancing Mod.

This review might upset some people. But first, I'll talk about why I keep playing this game and what pushes me to finish this game.
I'm not someone you can see playing JRPG's and this game was an exception I could make after hearing about it on Youtube and seeing the reviews. I told myself "what could possibly go wrong? I can always refund it if the game's bad", I'm not saying this is a bad game, it's a decent game but that's that. It's not great, it's not perfect. Why? Let's talk about the story first. Story is deep, emotional and serious and surprisingly it's far from being cliché as we're awfully familiar with other revenge-based stories. The story was what impressed me the most about this game, the game also successfully manages to keep the balance between dark-serious theme and humour and some of the jokes characters pull are really quality jokes. I haven't seen all there is to see yet but as far as I can tell, the story is on point. Secondly, characters. All the characters, even the villains, make you love them. They don't feel like robots and they certainly feel "human" so to say. Their dialogues are natural and they develop themselves over time and they really make you feel like you're playing a roleplaying game and not an action game. Expedition system is pretty cool too. If I am happy with these, why am I complaining? What initially brutally murders this game is the gameplay. Maybe it isn't a gameplay for me, maybe it's just boring. The combat doesn't feel fluid at times and it kind of gets repetitive after a certain point. Let's not forget to mention the game's not open world, you'll be teleported into zones as you pass certain "checkpoints" and you'll have an invisible loading screen. You're always limited with invisible walls, you can't swim and there isn't really much you can do in the game(at least for now, I don't know if something gets introduced after a certain point in the game). I got sick of the soundtrack that I had to mute it too, I don't know if it's a JRPG thing because like I said, I am not someone who plays JRPG and this was an exception but the soundtrack is repetitive in the sense that a song is made of the same tone over and over again and you keep hearing that same song every time you enter a new zone. Even if there's no action, you'll hear the music changing and getting faster and it makes you think as if you'll encounter a boss or something, I don't know but nothing really happens. The game sort of encourages exploring as it awards you with chests and souls in areas you don't have to go to, you'll also encounter "red daemons(?) I forgot how they call them", basically daemons that are VERY powerful and have the chance of dropping a quality item while exploring.
Do I still enjoy this game and recommend it? Hell yes, the story and characters alone can keep pushing you to finish this game and a lot of people still enjoy the gameplay so it could be me.

TLDR; Slightly arcadey for my taste, but there's nothing quite like it on the market.  I give this game two swollen missing heads out of two.
Okay.  A bit less tongue in cheek.  Anyone who's played Guns of Icarus (or, frankly, watched guns of icarus) knows the formula for this game for the most part.  The lack of verticality and classical naval style is what makes this particularly appealing to someone like me.  I've always enjoyed great naval engagements and although I've stayed away from World of Warships, I've had a lot of fun over the years in the naval battles of the Total War games.
As a captain, if I call out a ship, the gunners help me line up the sights so we get everyone a good chance of a hit.  The crew can get frustrated at times if I make a decision to try to help us survive as opposed to dealing damage because most of these can have the effect of allowing few guns an angle on the vessel (usually because I'm showing them the skinny side of the vessel).  It shouldn't have to be stated communication is key; when I tell the crew to get ready for a starboard broadside, they should all get ready to fire.  The primitive nature of the weaponry and extensive reloading procedures adds to the tension of the engagements, but the slightly arcadey nature of the sailing hurts the immersion.  I shouldn't be able to turn the entire vessel that quickly at that many knots.
As a crewperson the intensity is ramped up.  You seem to be given unlimited bullets in your carried weapons on the philosophy that if you fire and successfully survive the reload process, you deserve to fire and try to reload again.  The physics are more amusing than realistic and the combat plays more like an arcade game over all, but many of the problems appear to just be band-aid solutions while the rest of the groundwork foundation is being laid.  I'm a fan of this game, and have enjoyed playing all the roles.  Highly aggressive captains make for wild boarding party excursions, many of which go very wrong some of the time to hilarious results.
It's a partially built game but if the foundation is THIS fun, the finished product looks to be fantastic.  But, as always, buyer beware, as games with as much potential as Blackwake (if not more) have seen their potential stifled by singular decisions from amateur developers or greedy business models met with mob-mentality fans.  The future is bright, but far from certain.

Before my review. The game didn't run at first and gave the message: ""Freespace2/Fred2 cannot be run from a drive root directory!". After looking around and saw some crazy solutions finally came to this very simple steps (no need for you to edit anything just  click 3 times):
A) Go to the directory that the game was installed in
B) Go to the 'data' folder
C) DOUBLE click on the file 'FS2.reg'
D) Click 'Yes' When asked if you want 'Registry Editor' to make a system change
E) Click 'Yes' When Registry Editor asks if you are sure you want that change
F) Click 'OK' when Reg Edit says it's done
G) Run the game and enjoy

A thirty-minute point-and-click variant of the walking simulator, where a man sits in a remote cabin, struggling to regain his memories.  It's emotionally heavy-handed, but, when you're trying to tell a compelling story with only thirty minutes of clicking on various obects, there's not a lot of leeway for subtlety and restraint.
What made this game good, in my view, is the fact that it came prepared to face a genre-aware audience.  Nobody's introduction to PC games is going to be an odd indie like this, so the audience will be experienced gamers who know a thing or two about how this genre works.  By the time the central character first picks up the photograph, you
there will be some kind of twist and surprising revelation.  You'll already be cataloguing the various common tropes the story might be tilting towards, constantly thinking two steps ahead of the narrative.  So rather than expecting you to sit in blank befuddlement until the big reveal,
creates suspense by deliberately invoking several of the most common paths that this story might take.  Instead of being able to pick out the trope in play from the foreshadowing, you're instead offered too many plausible clichés.
can't possibly use
of the standard twists, so which will it be?  In essence, it takes your out-of-game metaknowledge which can spoil the suspense, and deliberately turns it against you.
Efforts at storytelling using a game as a medium are frequently crappy.
is not.  It only asks for a half-hour of your life, and is entirely worth it.

I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone at this stage. Like several people have mentioned here it actually does feel like an early access title. Sometimes even worse, considering that most early access titles are actually PLAYABLE. I've been unable to play more than 5 matches at most since the game's launch and even those were after I got tired of waiting in a queue for almost an hour and making my own lobby. Factor in the constant disconnects and errors regarding sending data to their server, and you've got your standard utterly broken-at-launch online title right here. Yes, I've noticed many people have had way more luck than me with getting matches, but the fact of the matter is MANY have not (feel free to check out any popular/common gaming forums to get a better feel of the current situation).
Besides the broken online play (which is BOUND to get fixed eventually... I hope...), you all should be fully aware that SFV is the most barebones fighting game I've had the displeasure of playing when it comes to offline modes. You can't even do standard VS. matches with a CPU, which has been the most common and basic feature in a fighting game since the very inception of its genre. Then there is an utterly useless training mode and laughably-short and cringe-inducing 5 minute-long "story" battles for each character, which can provide a small distraction before they are never used again. The survival mode is the only offline single player component worth a notice, but be warned that it kicks you out if you get disconnected from the server, which is very often. Yes, you lose single player progress for disconnecting from the server.
Long story short, this game is not worth buying at all in it's current state, not even for die-hard fans of the franchise, UNLESS you have people on hand to do local matches with. Let's see if patches and the many future scheduled updates fix this mess. Till then, shame on you Capcom.

After putting in some more time in this game. I apologize for the relatively positive review above. This game gives no liberties when it comes to methods of attack. you have one or two roads to major combo damage no variation what so ever. There is no individuality at all that can be applied to any of the cast. most of your combo options go through 2x medium punch, heavy punch, special/CA for alot of the cast. The game has potential to be sure but at present it feels like an xbox game and a shell of its former self, perhaps in time the devs will introduce some more PC friendly features but for now that $15 could easily be spent on a whole host of other games that were actually made for PC.

Hands down one of the best point and click games I've ever played.
LIKED:
- The storyline. It's engaging, emotional and just generally amazing. I really felt for the characters, what they'd been through and the choices they had to make. It made me cry more than once...
- The artwork. I love the comic book style graphics with slightly sketch line work which is reminiscent of the original comic book covers.
- The choices. Each choice is genuinely difficult to make. Weighing up the potential outcomes and later seeing how this has affected your gameplay is brilliant.
- Voice Acting. Nothing ruins a game more for me than poor voice acting, but throughout the entire game there had been brilliant choices for all of the characters and the delivery was spot on.
DISLIKED:
- Dialogue Options. I wouldn't say I particularly disliked anything about this game, but occasionally I found that the conversations that lead on from choosing a particular dialogue option for Lee wasn't always how I had assumed it would pam out from the choice I had made. Not really a problem of course, just sometimes surprising when you think you've chosen something supportive or neutral and you end up being argumentative.
Over all: 10/10

The original Sanctum was essentially a conventional tower defense game with a first-person user interface. Sanctum 2 is much closer to a true hybrid of FPS and tower defense. Teamwork and marksmanship are MUCH more important than they were in Sanctum 1, everything is much faster paced, and you will no longer be able to make huge, insanely complex, super-efficient mazes. Essentially, Sanctum 1 was maybe 20% shooter, 80% tower defense. Sanctum 2 is 50/50.
If you were expecting gameplay identical to the first Sanctum, you'll probably RAEG. But if you were hoping for significant evolution and change, Sanctum 2 is well worth a try.
