A masterpiece in storytelling, character development and presentation. The story in this game is hands down the best story  have experienced in a video game right up next to Nier Automata. There was never a dull moment throughout my almost 50 hour playthrough and I loved it. The characters are all very enjoyable to learn about and every single one of their personalities is unique and charming. You feel for every single one of them, whether it be sadness, anger, happiness, hatred, they all feel so real and relateable. The presentation is also very well done throughout the game. Animations are very fluid most of the time, dialogue is animated in a visual novel style and it always looks great and is pleasant to look at. The cutscnes, whether they be in game or the few anime scenes, are all very well done. The soundtrack is good, not great but nothing bad at all. The combat system is fun and is awesome to watch but I always felt like I was just spamming buttons and hoping for the best. The game is pretty easy overall which is a shame but it definitely makes this a good entry point for those who have never played a JRPG. My only real complaint for this game is that the world you travel in feels like a bunch of empty wastelands filled with enemies. Exploration isn't really something I liked doing in this game at all. This is also my first Tales game and I was genuinely pleased with it. I look forward to more in the future! 9/10 A Fantastic Game!

Well-structured world, albeit clashing, but if the ground itself blew into pieces it's hard to keep it from looking like 3rd time patched quilt work. The characters, that are introduced, are very well characterised and very human, very rare in games. Combat works ok, though I will argue that isometric viewpoint Action RPG combat (might as well call it Diablo-lite) isn’t really my staple, so I have no authority on judging it. Though I will state it’s different from most, since it is a (good) XBLA port from Xbox 360. Both choices you can make are well realised, but one still feels more satisfying than the other. It’s not perfect though: platforming does not go well in fully realised 3D games, in two that it really goes wrong are first person precision platforming (looking at you Half-Life), and what Bastion has in the last chapter which is the “oldschool predetermined jumping arc” in a 3D isometric world with pits. I still highly recommend Bastion to anyone trying to find a well-crafted interactive experience.

I see a lot of negative comments. Those negative comments are all largely due to the price.
I find this silly.
Those complaining say it's effectively only a DLC upgrade if you have the game, and not worth the full $40.
Well, the creators are making it 66% off for people who already own the game on Steam, or free for people who were in on the Kickstarter... so the price IS that of a DLC for those who already have the game, and basically a discount (since they're buying "game + dlc" for price of "game").
Could they have marketed it better by putting it as pure DLC? Probably. Definatey probably. But the reality of the situation is the way they're doing it actually makes it cheaper, and ensures those new to the game are more likely to have an updated version than putz around with an older version. For game enjoyment, not a bad route imho. But, unfortunately, reality and perception of reality are two very different things, and despite being a good deal for gamers, it really bad PR. In fact, if you're buying for friends too and you have the previous, you still get the discount for the extra copies, so it's even better.
That said, I do find this a solid upgrade from the old game. They sped up the pace of the game, it feels more intense, the Titans definately add a rush, and exploding planets happen all the more frequently. It's fun, it's fast-paced. It feels more polished now.
I say, show your love for an excellent made RTS and grab it.

Wizorb is a breakout game. If you don't like breakout games don't buy it. If this style of game intrigues you, read on.
The main part of the game is broken up into levels of breakout games. There is a story about saving a village and you only really need to pay attention to that if you're an achievement hunter. This is more of a side-story than anything.
The gameplay is good as far as breakout games go. Broken up into several worlds of about 12 levels each, offering differing setups and enemies. It is static however, so on any replay you will get the same levels. There is a "magic meter" which you can make use of to temporarily increase the powers of your ball, or you can use powerups bought in "stores". All of this is good. The only major problem is that if you wish to exit the game mid-world, it will save your level progress but you will lose your score. It almost feel like a bug marked as a feature.
Some of the levels, however can be a bit boring as you try desperately to get that last block, as is often the case in breakout games. And definitely don't play on anything but the hardest setting as otherwise the ball will be too slow and the game will become boring. On a faster difficulty, things are much more of a challenge.
The game is best controlled with a mouse, but if you are playing on a tablet, or streaming to a tablet, that will also be a good way of controlling. I wuld not reccomend using a controller, but that is well supported if you want to.
The graphics are very reminiscent of a top-down jrpg, in a pixelated style. It's all very consitent and well drawn out. Similarly, the music has a very retro 8-bit feel. The music and art styles vary across all of the worlds giving you a good variety.
Aside from data not being fully saved if you quit the game mid-world I found no bugs in the game. It is very well polished. [Although if you want to change volume levels it's not a slider, it's a click-to-change-by-1% deal, so that may take some time]
If you like breakout retro-style games then this is definitely worth a buy. (And, If possible, avoid buying this game with a discount. The price is a good one).
[edit 1:]
Notice to achievement hunters only: If you are trying to replay the game for sake of getting 100%, there is little to be gained by this. Upon replaying you will find it may be useful to have something like netflix running videos as having played it once, you will already know all of the trick and it may become very repetitive.

I play this game on a Mac and can only review it on the mac.
I've always wondered how someone can have 50 hours in a game and not recommend it... well now I understand. BUGS! I actually really enjoy this game and the tactical rts/rpg elements, however the game is too buggy and eventually became unplayable after all my saves became corrupted then plain dissapeared. I struggled through the bugs ti complete 55% of the game when my many saves just vanished.
Pros
Fun tactical rts style gameplay with pause
decent level up system with rpg feel. you can allocate points to stats or skills as you gain exp
wide variety of weapons (many of which just do not work as intended ie rpg has no blast radius)
lots of locations
large selection of mercs
Cons
Bugs galore. including but by no means limited to: All items dissapear (this bug is tough and even loading a previous save somehow does not restore the lost items.) Unable to enter any buildings in certain towns. Game locks up when interacting with certain NPCs.Characters sometimes do what you tell them...sometimes they just don't (seems not to be affected by increasing stats)  weapon stats such as range do not apply correctly (you will have a sniper rifle which will be out-ranged by enemy pistol) Many, Many more...but you get the idea.... lots of bugs.
Voice acting. A couple characters have decent or funny voices...but some of them are unbearable. Tip: Do not choose the merc "Fox"as your first merc...she will drive you insane.
Broken achievements: Many easy ones do not work others work when they shouldn't. ex I tossed a gas grenade... it hit a tree, even though the path for it indicated it would not hit the tree...the grende dropped at my feet and killed me... the achievemnet for killing a tank with the rocket launcher ticked! Haha, I had not even owned one at this point.
Icons often do not change after switching weapons.
so many things do not work as intended, or not at all
Other thoughts
I had not played any other Jagged Alliance title, so I can't compare to previous releases... but I had fun with this game despite the bugs. I got it in a bundle and probably spent under one dollar on it...so I certainly got my money worth, but I can't recommend it with all the bugs and especially the saves corrupting. I got my moneys worth, although I would say, don't spend more than a few bucks on this AND be ready to encounter a wide variety of bugs that may or may not make the game unplayable. Certainly think twice about purchasing if you plan to play on a mac

First of all I'd like to point out that this kind of game or genre is really fun but may not please every kind of player. You find yourself in a town named Salem, you all seem happy around the plaza and everyone is reunited. However, after the first night one or multiple people have been killed and you start debating on who could be the culprits. If you "all" (majority) agree on someone, you will put that someone on the hanging stand to give him a last chance to defend himself, convincing or not , you decide, majority will win again and this will continue on and on untill the end of the game.

You pay all of your taxes and you love the green grass of this town , the fresh air of it's surroundings and the butterflies, you have friends in this town and you gotta stay close to them, however you don't know who they are. As a town member you can be different types such as investigatives (Power of discovering part of someone's identity, "part" because it's rarely 100% because of sheriff's and investigator's flaws), protecting such as doctor, bodyguard or killing such as Veteran or vigilante. You have friends (or not if you're really unlucky and you play in chaos mode) which you know the identity of and will have secret council with them at night. Many bugs. Install bugs. Game play bugs.Very rough around the edges. Buy this game when it is on sale only. It has a lot of neat features but the UI and some game design choices make it frustating. You spend most of your time figuring out how to do what you want or trying to figure out what is going on. The UI feels like a beta game.
** Update ** After playing a while, the game does not get any better. The good parts dont out weight the bad. Ran into another bug, I will have to restart the operation or reinstall the game, AGAIN.
Just like George Orwell said, "If you want a vision of the future, imagine a boot stamping on a human face forever." This game is the boot and guess who's face it stamps...
The bad -
1. Battle maps too large compared to the forces available. You will find some battles where you have 50 guys to cover a couple square miles of battle map. The game, literally, will not let you concentrate your forces. The operations map (where you move your units before battle) limits how many units you can attack (or defend with). Every battle (EVERY one) will create a map too big for your forces. Large battle fields, 1 platoon per square mile, and a horrible battle field AI (more on this later), make for a pretty crappy battles. You might say, "well some battles were small unit action. Sometimes You wont have enough forces to cover the front." Well, what if I do have enough forces? I might be in a operation where my units are packed as tight as I can get them on the operations map. There are time when I have plenty of units on the operations map. Why would country send a couiple platoons into a town while the rest of the battalion sits and watches them die? If you have a battalion, why not send the battalion? Since you cannot concentrate any of your forces most of you battles will be one unit vs. one unit. Or two units vs. two units. Or three units vs. three units. All of the battles are pretty evenly matched. Most battles are battles of attrition. BORING.
2. HORRIBLE battlefield AI. Yes caps. The battlefield AI has no clue what it is doing. It has not clue what the strategic points are on a battle map. And the game mechanics are built with the AI's limitations in mind.
In one of my battles, I saw the battle map, saw a town on a hill (with a large objective marker), and I figured the AI just had to attack that town. There was not much else on the map -  some fields, a couple roads, some woods. My units sat in ambush, waiting for a battle royale. The AI slowly apeared from the left. My units waited for the perfect moment. But the AI did not advance toward the town or the objective point. The AI decided to take an open field to the far right of the village. The AI made a nice little parade in front of my troops. I openned fire, but since most battles are setup to be evenly matched (see 1 unit vs 1 unit above), the battle was not a slaughter. I might kill 2:1, but that is not enough.
The AI has not idea what points are important. But saddly, the game does not place any importance on map points that would make sense in real life. The game has objectives sprinkled around the map. If the AI takes two objectives in open fields, while you hold the town at the crossroads, on hill the battle will end a "total defeat". All objectives are equally important to the game design, so all objectives are the same to the AI.
This creates two new problems. One, it is hard to defend and win battles when the AI attacks random points on the map (it attacks random points and wins the battle). Two, since all objectives are the same (more or less) and maps are so huge that you can not cover it, the AI will win battles by sneaking squads around the map, capturing objectives. These ninja squads ruin the "feel" of the game. I have used ninja squads to take most of the points on the map...
The game relies on huge maps with few forces, so the AI has a chance to randomly attack where  you are weakest. If you were able to concentrate your forces in some battles (if you have the units available), and have a more favorable unit count to map size ratio, the AI would seem even worse. So, basicaly, te huge map size and very low unit count is there to mask how bad the AI is at attacking the most important part of a map.
*** Edit *** The good points, but my current campaign still has a ammo bug, so these good points do not out weight the many bugs of the game.-
The one thing this game does very well is line of sight and projectile modeling.
From what I can tell, very few things are abstracted in the game and this is a good thing. If you zoom in and it looks like there is a clump of grass in front of your soldier, then guess what, there really is a clump of grass there and he wont be able to see.
Luckily, the AI that controls how the individual soldiers act is not too bad (I would give it a score of 7/10). Your soldiers tend to get behind cover correctly, but sometimes your soldiers will run and jump, and go prone in the middle of the street. Sometimes your soldiers will deploy at the begining of a battle in the middle of the street too and this can take a surprising amount of time to force the AI to deploy in a better position.
As for projectile modeling, the game is well know for having accurate tank to tank modeling, but I lked watching infantry fire.
In one battle the AI tried to converge on an objective in the rear of my lines (serious error on the AI's part) and had to pass between two other objectives on the front line, which I was heavily defending. As the enemy was trying to pass my men, they were getting a beating. A lone bren carrier made it past the main kill zone but found itself in the middle of one of my platoons and they were hosing it from three sides. The game showed the bullets impacting the bren carrier. It was "funny" to watch. The driver was killed and the bren crew kept firing. One by one you could see the crew slump over dead (the game shows a red cloud of of blood when a crewman is hit). When it looked like all of the crew was dead (the game marked the carrier as still alive) my men kept firing. It looked like the game still showed red clouds of blood when ever the dead men were hit again and again by bullets.
Despite my disfavorable review, I will be looking for the next game in the series, Mius Front, to come on sale to see if it is any better...

Tales of Berseria is easily the best Tales game I have played so far. Berseria splits away from standard storytelling mold for Tales games by making the main protagonists antiheroes. The story is very well-told and the characters' motivations are not handed to the player via dialogue backstories, but shown to them through their actions and the twistedness of the world they live in. Although the character archetypes are familiar, the player is actually likely to develop genuine connections with them, unlike in some of the more childish (and sometimes melodramatic) Tales games.
Although you can play Berseria without playing its parent story, Tales of Zestiria, I would personally recommend playing Zestiria first. Berseria seems to be set hundreds or even thousands of years before Zestiria (I'm sure the lore lovers know for sure), and sets the stage for Zestiria. However, the actual landscape is virtually unrecognizable except for a few significant landmarks that tie the two stories together across time. Playing Zestiria first really makes everything fall into place, but doesn't give much of anything away. A lot of the side stories assume some knowledge of Zestiria to get the most out of them. The downside to having to play Zestiria first is that Zestiria is a much worse Tales game. It's much more predictable and has very obvious archetypes, annoying characters, and way too much melodrama.
From a gameplay perspective, I found Berseria to be quite engaging and complex, although certain loopholes seem to create problems. I have only played through the game once so far, exclusively playing Velvet. So while I can't comment on other characters, I can at least say that Velvet's combat style is very appealing and is the best example of a true berserker class I have seen. However, it goes a bit too far insofar as she makes standard encounters somewhat obsolete regardless of what difficulty mode you choose, due to how her break soul technique synergizes with the rate of soul gain. Conversely, bosses seem to have excessive skill cap walls with various difficulty modes. Some bosses have power links that make them virtually impossible to beat unless you keep one of the pair stunlocked until it's defeated (which your average player can't handle); however, to get rid of these links, you have to set the difficulty so low that the fight becomes a faceroll, even for very poor players. As a result, some of the most climatic battles in the game lose a lot of their excitement simply because many players are forced to choose between "impossible" and "faceroll" difficulties.
Overall, Tales of Berseria is still the best Tales game I have ever played though, and I strongly recommend it not just to fans of the Tales series, but to those wanting to see what Tales is all about.

I'm requesting a refund for this game (and all of its DLC's), because I did not understand the sheer over complexity of it. The trailers made me assume it would be a real time RTS using realistic damage models based off of real world conflicts. Sounded right up my alley.
After starting it, and spending ten minutes verifying the installation of each individual DLC and waiting for those to also install, I found that even navigating the menus was difficult due to the massive over complexity in it. Each menu selection in the campaign menu then has sub-dropdown menus, to select battles in the mission I think, which each can be clicked for a blurb on the battle. Finally after loading into the game, you are given a map overview, which shows the battle ahead, while a painfully dull popup in the corner attempts to teach you what each small symbol for the various mouse button bindings are. Strangely enough, I found I had to click different bindings and on different things to try and finally get anything done. I didn't sit in what I assume is the preparation screen for very long, because about twenty popups in, it still hadn't explained what I was looking at or doing. This didn't change in game either (or I guess in battle, as the prep phase is also part of the game).
Once I was in game it simply told me what each button on screen does (and out of about 40 buttons, that took quite a while) all the meanwhile acting more like a glorified tool tip, but still hasn't explained how most of it was relevant other than in number crunching parts. I finally skipped the tutorial by clicking a button that was labeled to start the combat itself, and found that the combat (which ran at a whole 9 fps) was duller than half melted butter. This game may have its appeal to some people, but I am not masochistic enough to try and tackle this behemoth. Despite the battle itself being real time, it felt like a turn based game. Over all I regret buying this, even when it was on sale.

While the game had some interesting story points, I couldn't ever finish it because of the controls. Evertime I went to the bookcase, it would't give me the ability to return to the rest of the cabin. So after multiple tries I had to just give up without finishing the game.

GAMEPLAY POSITIVES
PA has been a great game for a while now. I generally play the game for fun, exploratory ways to destroy AI or create awesome battle situations with friends in 1v1 or 2v2. TITANS adds my favorite thing by far from Supcom and FA in the form of giant world dominating mechs, and adds a ton of fun strategy and gameplay options to boot. AI can be absolutely brutal at the higher difficulties, and Galactic War is an interesting take on single player (even if it's not my favorite feature).
GAMEPLAY NEGATIVES
This is an RTS almost purely based on economy and multitasking, which can be a problem for some. It's not 300 APM Starcraft. Commanders are incredibly fragile, and unlike its predecessors, there is no way to upgrade them to have more health or better combat abilities (or create shield systems/etc). This can create victories that are VERY fast, especially on same-planet battles. I'd love to see an option for higher health commanders, or the ability to choose a path for in-game progression. Additionally, without classes, every match is going to be the same pool of units for every player.
OTHER REVIEWS AND COMPLAINTS
As someone who bought into the game shortly after kickstarter, I've never ever felt disappointed in the progress or pace of the developers improving the game. On that note, saying TITANS is "the game we should've had at launch" is entitled at best, painfully ignorant of modern game development at worst. The content in this expansion was never promised in the base kickstarter, but was still given away for free for early backers, and heavily discounted (to what would be an incredibly valuable DLC package if you want to view it that way) for anyone for has the base game.

I started the game in the easist mode (no life limit), as I wanted to view the storyline.  (I even personally didn't mind the melodramitic narrators voice, and even got a giggle from his comments sometimes-I read prior comments so knew what to expect anyways)  After solving the world on cake mode, you can start the story over on NormalPlus mode, where you save your weapons and the blueprints for the buildings you can eventually place.  Doing the Story a second or third time is the only way I could see it possible to get your weapon upgrades to the top tier (being able to stab though armor is sweet).  I don't think I missed much but even with buying the Something upgrade items at the Lost and Found I was only able to get 3 to 4 upgrades per story.  Anyways, game was an absolute blast.  I ussually don't expect much for such low priced games (a couple of Steam specials [less than $5] have ended up to be unsolvable), and as such was extremelly suprised that this game was a) solvable b) fun c) beautiful d) a good story (though disjointed and boring at some points).  Even worth it at regular price, if you have played it before and want it back in your collection.

This is one of the worst games I have ever played. There are so many disappointments in this game.
Story:
The story is pretty good. You play as a Hiro Miyamoto, a swordplay instructor who is down on his luck. One night he is visited by a homeless looking man. He explains to you, in the rain, that everything Hiro knows is a lie. Kage Mishima has taken a mystical sword called the Daikatana and has used it to alter time in his favor. He also says that Miyamoto is descended from the people who created the Daikatana, so he is the only one who can master it. He asks him to rescue his daughter from Mishima's fortress. Moments later he is killed by Mishima's assassins, so if Hiro didn't believe him before he does now. Along his quest he meets Superfly, a former security guard for Mishima, and Mikiko, the homeless man's daughter.
It turns out everything he said was true as, when you get the sword, Misihima shows up with another Daikatana and transports Hiro and this gang to the past. As far as I know you visit four time periods with the first one being the present.
Setting:
The levels I played were really nice looking, except for the first time period. You go to Ancient Greece, 18th century (I guess) European village and castle and I think you go to San Francisco later. I would like to mention now that I only played up to Dungeon in the European village. The music is also really good.
Gameplay:
This game was infamous for having many weapons. Basically there are six unique weapons for each time period. However none of these weapons are satisfying to use. Almost all of them are generic projectile weapons. Killing enemies is not fun and not really balanced either. In the first time period you can kill a robot with a shotgun. From the 2nd time period onward you wield the Diakatana. The Daikatana is the most disappointing weapon of the game. All you can do is swing the sword; the only thing unique about it is that the more enemies you kill, the more you level it up. When you level it up the only thing that changes is the damage it does. No fire powers, no poison, nothing else. You can also level up your character and increase your HP, weapon damage, attack speed, movement speed, and jump height.
The sidekicks are really bad. In the fan made patch, they "fixed" them by altering the maps and giving them infinite health. But they still got stuck multiple times and when playing I had to look back every five seconds to see if both of them were following me since you cannot exit the level without them. Other than killing things for you they do not really add anything to the gameplay. No combo attacks or any interesting dialogue.
Starting in Greece the levels get too long for their own good. In the first level of Europe you meet a monk who tells you that you not only have to find 3 keys to get into a castle but you must also find seven pieces of some kind of sword to defeat the necromancer terrorizing the land. Don't you think one is enough? The seven pieces of sword are collected across multiple levels in the time period. What if you miss one? Also what about the Daikatana; I thought that was supposed to be some powerful sword. It is not good enough to kill a magician? At that level I used no clip to get through a gate in the graveyard (I later found out I had to hit a button on one of the graves).
I stopped playing in the Dungeon. At this point Mikiko is unconscious so neither she nor Superfly can assist me. And at this level they introduce enemies that, as far as I know, do not die. They are super zombies or something and at that point I only had 3 weapons other than the Diakatana: the claw, the crossbow and the crossbow that shoots logs, which all suck by the way. None of them could kill those things. I got up to a door that would not open even when I flicked the switch. It turns out an enemy was stuck in the door, the one that does not die, and was still stuck even after multiple reloads. So I used no clip to go to the end of the level and found out that I could not teleport Superfly because in the fan patch there is a glitch that prevents him from teleporting if he is holding Mikiko. Even if that glitch were fixed and even if the enemy did not spawn in the wall I would've stopped playing (or at least gave this game a bad review) because I stopped having fun.
I appreciate that fans of this game took the time to patch out some bugs but that still does not change the boring gameplay. The main con of this game is how much your weapons suck. An FPS were it is boring to kill things is a bad FPS. You'd be better off with pretty much any other decent shooter, and I have played a lot of them.

Sleeping Dogs is ruff (geddit?), but it's worth playing.
The melee combat is a plus, but it takes some time to get into the swing of things.  Combos work with permutations of tap and hold.  A bit of lag and lack of knowledge about the frames can lead to frustrating defeat.  By the end, it was moot due to both my experience and the fact that my upgrades filled in erroneous button presses with new moves.  I went from dreading combat to enjoying it a lot.
I even found the racing tolerable.  It's perhaps even enjoyable.  I avoid racing games and loathe racing segments in open world games so this was a pleasant surprise.  Granted, quick sessions and the ability to slam cars away helps. ;)
Despite the quantity of DLC, the game could still use some polish and at times seems unfinished.  What can and can't be jumped over often feels arbitrary. The wayward GPS may add realism, but it's inconvenient.   Towards the end, there was an important conversation which got cut off near a waypoint and sent me into a rage as I witnessed umpteen YouTubers do the same. Earlier, there was even an optional mission with a conversation hinting at a prior, nonexistent event.
However, I can look past all of that.
The main problem is built into the game design.  Missions are graded, and unlocked abilities are based on those scores.  While the missions can be replayed, their prior reward is subtracted from their new one so there's no way to grind.  For the Triad, you have to either do extremely well or buy some special DLC.  Adding RPG elements just to replace them with a feedback loop for arcade perfectionists doesn't sit well with me.
I'm the kind of guy who likes to earn everything BEFORE finishing the story and then walk away with good memories of the credits rolling. Having already beaten the game and replayed missions to being just a fraction away from my final upgrade, I finally decided to just move on.
Fortunately, it was fun while it lasted.  I might pick up some DLC sometime when it goes on sale again.

It's a pixelated breakout game with RPG elements, a story, hidden levels, powerups, and a unique system that allows you to use collected magic power to cast spells. The ball increases in speed with each bounce until it is lost, keeping the game difficult and encouraging you to creatively use spells to finish each level as quickly as possible.
The biggest problem this game has is the length of time you have to play to make progress. Each level is composed of 12 stages with a boss fight at the end. There is no saving or returning to a level without starting over. This results in play sessions of more than 40 minutes before saving any progress, which is unusual as most would describe breakout as a casual genre.
Additionally, the life system is a little archaic. If you lose all of your lives in a level, you must start at the first of the thirteen stages again. However, the game carries over extra lives that have been earned in previous levels, negating any difficulty for players who have managed to save up lives when they are abundant in early stages, and making the game unusually hard to progress through for a player new to the genre.
It's a fun game to chill out with if breakout is your thing, but it's not worth trying if you aren't already down with the whole ball-and-paddle thing.

Overall I would say this game gets too much♥♥♥♥♥♥ It had some great things going for it: Good level design, a variety of enemies, and a few well implemented RPG mechanics. Each act of the game takes place in an entirely different point in the world's history, and you get new weapons and fight new enemies accordingly, which is great and stops things from getting stale.
The original game does however include alot of crap that really fell flat. Originally, there was a system of limited saves in which you had to find some kind of magic save cyrstal to get a checkpoint (which I found very few of in my playthrough). There was also 2 AI partners that would follow you through the whole game, often getting stuck in places, and dying.
WITH THE PATCH:
The AI partner's nodes have been reworked to stop them from getting stuck as often, and having them regenerate health. They still get stuck pretty often, but at least you can now just go through the entire level then akwardly guide them to the exit. OR, you can now straight up disable them entirely!
Also now you can quicksave anywhere you like!
Other features in the patch include better optimization, and more screen resolution settings (just be careful not to set the screen size to something bigger than your monitor, theres no easy way to revert the settings to fix that)
Overall id give this a 7/10, not nearly as bad as people say it is with the mods. I would reccomend giving it a shot whenever it goes on sale for really cheap

Immediately upon seeing this game on the store page, I knew I had to have it; the presentation is absolutely top-tier NES-style, on par with the likes of Shovel Knight, and though I wished for a Zelda-esque adventure game only with a wizard star rather than a sword-swinger, Breakout clones are few and far between today and I definitely don't hate them.  So when it was on sale I grabbed it without hesitation.
That was a bit of a mistake.  It was a measly $1-2 (I don't recall, but around there), and I do feel the developers deserve such a paltry sum for the superb graphic and art style alone.  But as for the game itself...?
Quite succinctly, it fails in one major aspect; the concept, though great in and of itself, utterly fails to deliver.  The idea is that it's a paddle-bouncing, block-busting game a la Breakout, Arkanoid etc. but with the twist that your player character controlling the paddle is actually a wizard, and can help his orb along by casting spells of both offensive and defensive natures.  Sounds fun, IS fun.  The problem?  Well, aside from a paltry four spells (plus a situational fifth that can only be cast upon death), which, as nice and functional as they are, leave a bit to be desired (and they only fall into the elements of Fire and Wind, where's Earth and Water?)... the magic meter is simply too meager and too difficult to refill.  Casting either of the smaller spells which, though useful, often need to be used multiple times for much effect, cost 1/10th of the entire bar.. and the really fun, powerful spells?  Nearly half the whole thing.  This wouldn't have been an issue at all except for the rarity with which you're able to recover magic at all.  There are really only three ways -- being lucky enough to get a magic potion to drop from a destroyed block which only restores a small amount of the magic meter and are very rare after the first couple stages of the first world, purchasing a fully-restoring potion at a shop (of which you'll be lucky to find two in an entire world and of course need to actually work your way into and then spend your hard-earned gold for it), and bouncing your orb against the paddle a grand total of TEN TIMES without it hitting any enemy or block for a tiny 10% 'pity' refill.  So more or less you're going to feel EXTREMELY strapped for magic and be very wary of spending ANY of it, EVER until you finally reach a point at which it's really needed, only to screw up and mis-aim an expensive strong spell then lose a life in your rage.
In addition, the worlds are very frankly too long.  With how time-consuming it tends to be to complete each individual stage, and the drollery of not even having powerups to look forward to since most are attached to your insanely stingy magic meter or bought for hefty coin from one of the rare shops (and then lost on death after that), you'll be more than ready to take a break after five stages.  But does it end after five?  No.  TEN?  Still no.  You're looking at a monsterious TWELVE long, boring stages AND a boss fight before you can even think about taking a break and shutting the game down.  I will at least admit that the bosses are pretty darn cool and I like seeing them in a game like this.
Bottom line: Gorgeous presentation is marred by woefully boring gameplay (that COULD VERY EASILY have been superior with changes as fall as a steadily-refilling magic meter to bring on the fun and a few less levels per world so you don't get hand cramps and/or overcome by drowsiness) and surprisingly lackluster music that again could have easily been knock-your-socks-off 8bit faire that could have alone, along with the graphics, picked the game up a bit, were they able to hire anyone even remotely as gifted at composing catchy 8bit tunes as Jake Kaufman or, say, any of the hundred or so comparably skilled composers who spend their days uploading free music to YouTube and probably would have done it for pennies on the dollar.  Alas.
If you want a great Breakout clone for PC, check out the superb DX Ball series, not this.

Amazing game! All the content was improved upon. Players can now draw aggro from some enemies and can do much more damage than in the previous game. New enemies are introduced in the game with varying abilities. There are four different characters to choose from, each with their own unique abilities and weapons (Assault rifle, Rocket launcher, Sniper rifle, and Shotgun). Each character has a primary weapon, based on the character chosen, and a secondary weapon. From what I can tell, you basically fire your primary gun until you need to reload and then quickly switch to your secondary and fire until you need to reload, rinse and repeat. The reload time is such that you should be able to immediately fire the gun you are switching to after fully unloading your current gun. There are also new perks introduced in the game, which are passive skills which may boost damage, make your character more agile, etc. Sanctum 2 also has a new leveling system which is experience based. You are able to unlock new perks, towers, weapons, and slots for these as you level up. Some of the towers are taken from the previous game, while some new ones are introduced. Same with the weapons and enemies. Some enemies from the previous game have been reintroduced with new abilities. These can be quite annoying, and force the player to devise new strategies to defeat them (I won't go into detail on the enemies, as I don't want to spoil it). The enemies also don't just die and take a certain percentage of the core's health away after they go in as in Sanctum 1. In Sanctum 2, they stand there and hit the core until they are dealt with. This may be a good thing if you can kill them quick, or can be devastating if you forget to look at the map and just a few take down the core health significantly. As for the building of towers and credits to spend on towers, this entire system has been redone. In order to build towers and tower bases, you need to find drops which fall out of the sky before every round. There are two seperate drops (sometimes more depending on the level). One is the cash used to spend on building and upgrading towers. The second is specifically for building the tower bases themselves. The tower bases in this game are about half the size (or less) of the tower bases in the previous game and allow you to easily jump up onto them, or stand behind them and shoot taller enemies (however this does mean that some enemies can aggro you and hit you on the tower bases). The tower base and tower cash allowance may seem meager at first, but it is designed to make you gradually build as you go, instead of building everything at once. Some may find this frustrating, but it really forces the player themselves to use their weapons to defeat the monsters and it boosts the FPS part of this game. As I said before, the FPS part of this game has really been improved and is a lot of fun to be more powerful and blow up the enemies. Some other tidbits about the game... There are several feats of strength you can try for on each map which can give you a 20% bonus to experience gained if you need an extra challenge or need more experience... There are three modes available on each map: Campaign, Survival, and Easy Mode. All of these modes give you experience whether you are successful or not, with easy mode giving less of course... Each tower can be upgraded three times, after you finish upgrading a tower, you can continue  to put resources into upgrading it for "overpowering" the tower, which continues to increase its damage... There are no weapon upgrades as far as I can tell, you can just use perks to upgrade them passively if you so choose. Overall, this is a fantastic game and a significant improvement over the first. There are some slight drawbacks, like the money and tower drops instead of getting automatic cash that some may not like and the lack of online game customization (at this point), but all in all I highly recommend it to anyone into TD and/or FPS games. 9/10

It has a seriously gripping story with very real feeling characters, the voice acting is super solid, the radio stations are unparalleled (I've discovered some great music through this game) and Hong Kong in-game is totally gorgeous (although a little small - damn you, budget constraints!).
Sadly those budget constraints are noticeable in a few areas - most of all, the would-be dating sim within the game. There are a few different possible romance-able characters but the dating sim was cut during production, so it doesn't go anywhere despite being initially well written. Sad times!
The action is entertaining enough that you won't ever feel like you're just going through the motions to get to more story and the upgrade system is both satisfying and simple. The game overall is a huge homage to Hong Kong crime dramas and you can read more about that with a google search - for a quick recommendation though, watch the "Infernal Affairs" trilogy. Super fun, well paced and I found it pretty inspirational! Made me really want to travel for one thing.
tldr; Play it! It's awesome and underrated.

[I'm going to keep this spoiler-free as much as possible] The first playthrough was a delight, mostly because it really felt like my choices were meaningful. But upon replaying the game (up to Chapter 2, now) I realized very quickly that there is a single narrative that's being told here. Your choices affect who lives, but the one that does live seems to replace the other character functionally-- that is to say that one character being alive over another doesn't change the plot. You just happen to have a different face with the same role.
There isn't anything wrong with this method of story-telling, and the story itself is alright (riddled with plotholes, but it's not a terrible generic post-apocalyptic zombie world story #85). The thing is, the major selling point (and the text splash at the beginning of every chapter) is that game adapts to the choices you make. This is simply a lie outside of the few "pick X character to save" moments. You end up in the same situations with the same people (more or less) using the same solutions and pathways. Nothing is unique and nothing you do matters. I would highly recommend watching a Let's Play of this instead of dropping 25 $%#@ing dollars on this (I got this via the Humble Bundle dollar deal~).
It's not a terrible "game", but unless you really like point-and-clicks and/or generic zombies, then I would say that you should look elsewhere for a custom story.

The Walking Dead video game by Telltale is through the roof. I can't believe it took me this long to finally play it all the way through. I played until the middle of Episode 3 a few years ago and stopped playing out of interest, but after a few years of growth and caring more about the story and characters in video games, I decided to return to give the game another shot, and I'm very glad I did. I played through the story and the 400 Days DLC in the span of about three days. That's how invested I got into this game. It's an experience you do not want to miss.
The story starts with Lee Everett, the main protagonist and the character you fill the shoes of. After riding in the back of a police car heading out of Atlanta, Georgia, your escorter crashes after hitting a walker. After awakening, you escape your vehicle and rush into a house. There, you run into a little girl named Clementine. She's all alone in her parent's house. After realizing this, Lee decides to take her along to look after her and make sure she is okay. After this, you make choices and take sides with various characters you meet in the world; all of this is going on while Clementine is under your care.
The Walking Dead is a game that you need to experience. It's unique to any game that I've played. It's a playable TV show that changes depending on your choices, and that's something that I am now a big fan of, and I am now a strong fan and supporter of Telltale. Please experience this game one day. You will never regret it.
Fun fact: I wrote this review while downloading Walking Dead: Season Two.

I sum SFV up in one sentence.
-There may not be a lot there but what is there is amazing.
That being said it follows the history of Capcom Street Fighter releases so here is a short summary of what you are going to get.
The Good
- The Fighting: No seriously this is easily one of the best Street fighters released. The actual fighting is fast and fun and extremely well-polished. If you are a fan of the SF series you will feel right at home and if you’re new it one of the easiest and cleanest Street Fighters to start with.
-The Characters: Every character is unique, interesting and pretty well balanced. They have a great and unique cast this time around bringing a lot of veterans back, some fresh faces, and some fun surprises.  The small cast is also great for learning match ups, and experimenting with playstyles, and learning the game.
-How it Runs: 60FPS, 0 Sound glitches, Beautiful graphics. This one is simple, it runs and it runs damn well.  Can't ask for much more there.
-Training Mode: In short, it’s what you've always wanted in training mode. Lab time has never been more rewarding.
The Bad
- There isn't much there: This is many peoples biggest complaint right now for good reason. 12 characters, 4 Modes, and a lack of costumes and colors is all you are really getting with your money. Treat it like early access, 60 bucks for more stuff down the road. Story mode is short, a few easy fights and some voice acted cutscenes. No Alts or colors for really anyone. It really is bare bones.
- Controller Support: There is no native controller or fightistick support. You cannot customize your controller settings either. That being said there are 3rd party apps that are very easily to download and use in order to connect with your fightstick. After using one I can now launch the game and have no problems using my stick.
The Ugly
-Server Issues: Servers are unstable at the time of writing this. Online matches are hard to connect to and can be very laggy and unusable. On top of that fight money to unlock the characters coming in the coming months are un-earnable right now due to the online connection problems. Hopefully this will get fixed soon.
In Summary
Regardless of its problems this is easily one of the best technical fighting games and one of the best Street Fighters Capcom has released. From the pure fighting aspect this game will not disappoint you. Its launch has been sketchy but hey it’s better that vanilla SF4.

I simply cannot reccomend this game to more average player. The issue is not in the complexity of the game, but how obsolutely attrocious it truly is at realism. The issue is that not only units have uncanny difficulty in fighting the enemy on their own, that is having company of heroes squad AI to actually have common sense for them to shoot at the same direction, but also the attorcious line of sight function which is very poorly implemented. You will find units struggling to cover lines they were ordered to, because few meters in front of them is a bush or a tree. That is not realism, but simply a poor game design. In reality a commander would not need to baby sit units and if we are going for realism, lesser control of the units and greater independancy would be they key.
Another issue is that this game is terrible at explaining stuff. I mean, simple tooltips, explanation of why and etc. Game certainly is poorly designed to help new players to get into the game. This game has a lot of going for it, but it sadly suffers from poor developers of not knowing where to put their own priorities. This results in the final shody product, with interface from 90's designed to fight the user rather than to help him. Maps and interactions with barely any notification of who they are. All of that could be made simple without loosing depth, but the truth is, this is simple game mascarading as something bigger. It certainly have the scale and right things in mind, but fail completely flat on execution.
Addition: my story which perfectly illustrates my frustration with a game.
Here is that broke my back. I ordered my antitank weapon to oversee flat terrain while hidden in the woods. Not only they had failed to approach Germans approaching through it which is of course ridiculious (since they had freaking half-track), but they also had failed to engage it then it had started to fight my squad in the left.
My mistake was, I did not made its engagement line correctly. I fixed that mistake. I made a correct firing arc. AT gun still ignored orders. I started looking the cause. Line of sight was the problem. So, I ordered AT cannon to be dragged to different position. Units could not effectively place the weapon in the desired direction, so it took a while. I, as a player, saw that there was a direct line of sight towards AT weapon and the cannon. Squad AI had failed to properly allocate itself multiple times and that is worse, it had failed to fire.
You see, at last then I got the cannon pointing into right direction, it could not fire. Why? I pressed the button to see what they actually were seeing. It was messed up view. In the flat terrain they could see very little, because a vegetation (nothing major, I pulled AT weapon out of the forest for a clear shot).
So, in the end, my cannon could not fire, because units view range, while realistic is broken. It is difficult to know what they can see exactly. If you for example move infantry from this building to the next and ask to engage them, they won't do it. Man of War does it, units are smart enough to take positions and fire upon enemy. In this, they will get into a trench. Since you ordered them to crawl or to fire from sit down position, now they cannot do that, because trench is too big. They cannot see♥♥♥♥♥♥and thus they cannot fire. Defense of the town is more a matter of figuring out terrain and puting everyone on the firing range. It is micro intesne game in a bad, unrealistic way. Such game should focus more on "commanding units". Just giving them mission like: "hey, you two squads. Go and protect that building and surrounding area. Enemy is coming from dat way, so place your machine gun covering that direction". In man of war for example it is far easier to do that. In this you have to fight interface, sight mechanics in order to ensure that every soldier can see anything at all.
In conclusion, if you want direct unit/squad control go for man of war. Nobody does that as well as that game. If you want to focus more on the tactical aspect, look elsewhere. This game is too focused on micromanagement in order to allow proper tactical gameplay as for example, wargame:airland battles allows you to achieve.

A lot of reviews will tell you that there isn't any actual gameplay in Serena and they're right. There are no items to pick up and use with other objects or locations within the cabin. Pros
+Excellent and emotive voice acting in the narrations
+Atmospheric location and sounds
+Immersive graphical design
Cons
-As stated, there's no gameplay. If you're looking for a traditional point-and-click adventure then Serena isn't for you.
-With few exceptions, horror is implied, not overt. If you expect jump scares and monsters in your horror, look elsewhere.
Add Serena to your collection if you appreciate a good narrative and/or are a fan of "art" games.

Like many others, I've played nearly all of them with mods, mods that not only enhance the games experience and add countless replayability and longevity to the game, but also mods that simply fix a lot of the main games problems and simply make it a better experience.
Bethesda's decision to retroactively change this game into paid mods has not only destroyed the saves and made modded games accessible for millions of players, but they also have once again failed to answer many important questions necessary for any paid mods scheme to even be viable.
* What happens mods are no longer updated, broken by a developer update, or conflict with other mods?
* What keeps the mod store from being flooded with $99 fake mods and $1 gun skins?
* What is and can be done about people who copy free mods to try to capitalize on other people's hard work?
* Thus far, it seems like the mod "store" uses in game credits which are basically never refundable.
If this is how Bethesda is going to play, I can't recommend this game.  Fallout 4 was by far not the best game in the series.  It was a game who only became a fitting addition to the Fallout IP through the use of mods that extended and corrected much of the games content.  Without it, it's just another one of hundreds of mediocre games most people have in their list already.  Without mods, there are simply better games to go play.

I got this game while it was on special for $2.99, absolutely well worth it.  OMG for that price you can't expect the world....  Game is very parent friendly.  Game runs great (I got Win 8), no hardware, or software issues.  Game never crashed.  I got stuck once-a monster knocked me over a wall, but monster came back and I let it knock me back over and I immediately thanked it by slaying it.  There is a function in the menu to return to town (Bastian) in case you get stuck, but I never used it for that.  Graphics are said to be hand painted scenes, very beautiful, and different.  I enjoyed the music track that came with the game.  How the world builds as you explore is a neat concept.  The game is sort of open ended.  I started the game in the easist mode (no life limit), as I wanted to view the storyline.  (I even personally didn't mind the melodramitic narrators voice, and even got a giggle from his comments sometimes-I read prior comments so knew what to expect anyways)  After solving the world on cake mode, you can start the story over on NormalPlus mode, where you save your weapons and the blueprints for the buildings you can eventually place.  Doing the Story a second or third time is the only way I could see it possible to get your weapon upgrades to the top tier (being able to stab though armor is sweet).  I don't think I missed much but even with buying the Something upgrade items at the Lost and Found I was only able to get 3 to 4 upgrades per story.  Anyways, game was an absolute blast.  I ussually don't expect much for such low priced games (a couple of Steam specials [less than $5] have ended up to be unsolvable), and as such was extremelly suprised that this game was a) solvable b) fun c) beautiful d) a good story (though disjointed and boring at some points).  Even worth it at regular price, if you have played it before and want it back in your collection.

Planetary Annihilation: TITANS is Planetary Annihilation + the TITANS DLC released as a standalone expansion. It's a separate client and a separate slot in your library. First: why the negative reviews all share a common misinformed opinion.
Planetary Annihilation: TITANS is PA + TITANS DLC. With that in mind, look at the pricing structures.
Early backers (kickstarter) get the DLC for free. Vanilla PA + TITANS. The new client will logically replace the obsolete PA.
Owners of PA (Early Access or not) get the DLC for 66% off. This means that they paid for the game (PA) and $13.60 for the DLC. Even the odd bunch that paid $90 for the privilege of supporting the developer through the process of making the game (which is what Early Access is) do the same. The new client will logically replace the obsolete PA.
Everyone else pays $39.99 for the game. PA + TITANS DLC.
This is a perfectly sound way of migrating to a new client and releasing a DLC at the same time, considering that vanilla PA players will be able to play with friends who own the new client with no problems.
On to the game.
It's just as much fun as PA was, only TITANS ramps up the action. The new titan units are a marvel to watch cause destruction. For example, the land bound Atlas smashes into the ground causing a massive AoE explosion, wiping out nearby units and buildings. My favorite addition to the game is the Ragnarok titan unit. It actually destroys the planet it is built on after a short countdown. This enables frantic battles to destroy the Ragnarok planted on your planet or a desperate attempt to get your units and commander off the doomed planet. The new units are interesting, notably a nanobot swarm that can rip through enemy armies and bases like a more efficient boom bot. The orbital battleship is a neat new unit as well, if not suffering from the same tedious management required for most orbital units.
You still engage in massive air, land, sea and space battles and naval combat has been improved. New handcrafted planets with variable elevation add a welcome change to the procedurally generated monotony of the base game.
It's everything PA was but bigger and better. And remember, you're paying for DLC and migrating to a new client, not buying the game all over again.

Like all good horror survival stories, 'The Walking Dead: Season One' is a game about the people - not the monsters.
*
At the heart of the narrative are the characters you'll come to care about - History Professor Lee Everett (who you play), and the lonely eight-year-old he stumbles across by happenstance, Clementine. They're joined throughout by a supporting cast of sympathetic, conflicted, and ultimately very
characters. It's the relationships between these characters - particularly the main two - that represent the real success of the game.
If you're at all familiar with 'The Walking Dead' as a television series or graphic novel, you'll at least know the key elements of the story before it even begins - survivors, resources, the road, and the search for safe havens - with a few not-so-safe havens thrown in too. It's well-trodden territory, but this doesn't take too much away from the surprises this particular iteration has to offer.
Unsurprisingly, Telltale's episodic approach to storytelling lends itself well to a franchise characterised by 'episodes' - a graphic novel series, and its televised adaptation. The episodes here work more naturally than in other offerings from the studio like 'The Wolf Among Us' - if only because it allows for the progression of time and events between instalments, rather than just a break in the flow of the game. In essence, each of the chapters is its own 'season', offering new locations, people, and problems.
For a point and click adventure, there's a surprising amount of action too - zombies to shoot, stomp, and stab, mostly. It's an extra gameplay element that suits the story, though I came to prefer the parts where I was given free reign to explore in the (fairly small) spaces each new location offers.
There are a few standout moments - tough decisions you need to make, characters to side with or against, unexpected events and consequences - and a few minor frustrations too, like Lee's irritatingly slow moving pace, and a few decisions that seem to be made for you. But 'The Walking Dead' always manages to drag the emotions out, even if it's sometimes a little heavy-handed. It's testament to the writing that several scenes took me entirely by surprise, either because they were funny, shocking, or more often - heartbreaking.
Recommended.

Daikatana is mediocre at its very best. There is simply no better way to put it. The level design is uninspired. The sounds are mostly weak and inappropriate. The flow of the game is choppy. The texture work is busy and looks as though entirely too much detail was crammed into resolutions far too small.
For a good indicator of how the entire game plays out, look no further than the very first level. It stands out as an example of almost everything wrong with this game. It takes place in a futuristic swamp, not exactly the most exciting place ever. It is painted in primarily two colors; green and gray. The first enemies you fight are (and I'm not joking) robotic mosquitoes, robotic frogs, and robotic alligators. They all behave in the same manner; hop, fly, or crawl directly at you and attempt to make a melee attack. Your first weapon is the ion blaster; an ugly green and gray pistol that looks like it's a bundle of tubes and wires all taped together. Shots from the ion blaster ricochet off of walls and explode in water for no particular purpose. Since you spend some time in the water because you are in a swamp, it is quite a surprise to be burned by your own weapon when you attempt to fight something there. You are left to fight alligators and frogs in water with your fists. There is one path through the level from beginning to end and it is not particularly interesting or exciting. This tepid start is how the entire game plays out.

Early in the game you are cursed with two AI companions. Had these companions any semblance of intelligence, they may have been useful. As they stand, they are walking liabilities. They get stuck in terrain, they get stuck in doors, they fall way behind so that when you are trying to exit a level, you waste time waiting on them to catch up. They can wield weapons but since they are often far behind you, they either do not get to the firefight in time to contribute in any meaningful capacity, or they end up shooting you in the back. Babysitting them is a miserable experience.

There is an experience point system in which you can level up your amount of damage per attack, speed of fire, speed of movement, jumping ability, and total health. Of these, the only one of any real use is increasing jumping ability. It is the only one that has any tangible benefits as it allows you to access some secret areas that you would not otherwise be able to reach. If you use the Daikatana, it takes your experience points to level itself up. Increasing the level of the Daikatana is not really useful. It attacks faster and does more damage, but it begins to glow and spark and these effects end up taking up more screen real estate than they're worth. The Daikatana is useless in any ranged fight and most of the enemies in the game are melee focused, so you can put yourself at a tactical advantage by using whatever your period specific pistol is and leaving the Daikatana alone.
As I described the ion blaster, so many of the other weapons in the game tend to bite you just as often as they do your enemies. The C4 launcher in the first episode is absolutely crippling to yourself more than Mishima's forces. It fires sticky proximity mines that explode in a large radius if anything comes near them, including yourself and other prox mines. Since enemies are often too dumb to follow you once you're out of sight, it is impossible to use this weapon to set any traps and it becomes a dangerously unhelpful grenade launcher. In the second episode, you get the hammer of Hades. It does healthy amounts of damage when charged, but places that damage right below your feet so you feel its power also. It'll even nuke your AI sidekicks if they get too close, which send you straight to the game over screen. The weapons in episode three are not particularly good or bad, and, in a surprising turn, the guns in episode four are actually fun to use. Episode four, however, contains one of the most personally dangerous weapons in the entire game; the metamaser. It is a thrown proximity turret that shoots out lasers at anything that comes near it, including you! However, its range is so great, and there are basically no encounters with anything more than one or two enemies at a time, and it explodes violently after a short period of time. It is far more dangerous than useful.

The level design can only be described as painful. As in the first level, there is typically only one path and it is rarely an interesting one. Platforming abounds and it is about as fun as pulling teeth. In episode two, there is an inordinately large area through which five runes are hidden. The player is rarely pointed in the direction of each rune and it becomes a long and boring game of hide and seek. While most levels took me only twenty minutes at most to complete, I spent over an hour on this area alone, and that does not include time lost due to deaths. At the end of episode four, there is a series of instant death platforming sections that serve only to drive the player insane. It is unfathomable to believe that someone at some point in time thought that these areas were a good idea, or even fun.
Story in this game comes only through long and boring cutscenes. Even though you carry two AI companions with you through most of the game, they rarely speak to each other or contribute anything to say about what is going on in the game. All meaningful dialog is contained within cutscenes that run too long. Thankfully they are skippable at any time.
There is no avoiding it; Daikatana was not a good game when it was released, and it does not get better with age. If you are feeling nostalgic, as I was, watch a playthrough on Youtube. Do not play it. This game is far more trouble than it is worth.

As of this review (February 17, 2016), this is essentially the "Arcade Release" of Street Fighter V. Right now it features standard online and local play, 1 extra game mode and a training room ONLY with a small-ish roster of 16 characters. Street Fighter V will feel like a traditional console release by the end of this DLC wave in August (with 6 new characters, multiple new free game modes/options,/features, new costumes and stages added, as well as many updates in March and the free story mode dropping in June). It will feel like a truly complete super full game likely sometime from April to June of 2017, with further additions on top of that.
The reason Street Fighter V was launched this way was because the gameplay was complete but the modes weren't and many dedicated Street Fighter fans like me want to play it right away. This way the developers can built the extra modes, characters and content while getting feedback on the gameplay of the game. In the long run this continuous development cycle will produce a better game than traditional "one off" developed games or DLC on and off development. But for now, the game isn't anywhere near that point.
Before I continue, I will offer a warning: If you aren't a super dedicated Street Fighter fan, don't have a console Gen 8 controller/fight stick/fight pad or newer, and don't have a remotely modern PC, don't buy this game yet. For the 1st group wait for more content, for the 2nd group wait for support to be added in March, and for the latter group, wait until you have a PC that can run this game at a consistent 60 frames per second.
If you don't fit into any of these 3 categories I said not to buy this game, I recommend you get this game.
\\
Now onto the 2nd controversial part, the character DLC. You can get every DLC character for 100k with an in-game currency called "fight money," which is easy to acquire (or you can pay $6 in real money). In less than 2 hours of gameplay I beat all 16 character's story mode and survival mode on easy and got roughly 250k fight money. If you play the single player modes, play online, and do the daily objectives (these haven't started yet), it is incredibly easy to earn fight gold and having enough fight money to buy characters with fight money will be easy. You will have so much fight money left over it will be crazy.
DLC stages will be available similarly, although the price of them is unknown. In addition to that, there will be a plethora of costumes, roughly as many as MOBA's have in the future, that you can get. Note that a few rare costumes will only be available via real money.
For the last controversial thing is the negative reviews. Much of them came because of reasons previously stated as well as the online not working very well for the 1st 24 hours. That has been mostly fixed.
For some reason of all the Steam releases in the last year this game got blown up the hardest for this. Newsflash: Fallout 4 wouldn't run properly on people's PC's for month; CS:GO's online was flat awful for at least a month after launch. Mortal Kombat X had inconsistent frame rates, tons of bugs, crashes, and online that doesn't function. Developer support for that game was dropped entirely recently with no patches coming in half a year for the PC release... and that game has a 17% higher rating than this game for some reason.
Many of the people who feel scammed by this game were simply uninformed consumers. Capcom clearly communicated this, although the amount of people who pay attention to these things is pretty small sadly. That is why I wrote this review.... to inform fellow consumers so they can make the best possible decision on whether they should get this game, or when they should get this game, as well as encourage them to do some research.
(Note: If I glossed over anything important or missed something, inform me in this review)
On to the actual game review:
Pros:
-The 16 characters are amazingly diverse. There's a character for everybody to enjoy, with 6 more to come in the next 7 months and more after that!
-The gameplay is incredibly smooth. This game has the content of an early access game yet the gameplay of a fully realized and finished AAA quality title.
-This is the best initial release of any Street Fighter ever and it isn't even close. In fact this is one of the best Street Fighter games ever.
-The DLC policy is amazing if you understand how it works (I covered this in an above section). All future game modes and features will be free, and being able to afford the DLC characters with in-game currency is relatively easy (although you could pay real money for them still).
-The visuals on most of the stages and the character models are incredible. Running this on max settings 1080p now is a blast. The graphical leap IV to V may not look like much from gameplay videos, but seeing it in person is night and day.
-The net coding is brilliant. Across over 400 beta matches I had only 1 game with lag (against someone on the other side of the planet), and that wasn't even that bad. There's not a ton of buffering either like other online fighting games.
-No random frame drops to report (sadly after MK X I have to report such things as positive instead of "100% necessary to even be recommended").
-The gameplay issues Street Fighter IV had are long gone (such as strong attacks trading with weak ones), and the gameplay is more simplified, yet the game mechanically is deeper and feels more rewarding for good play. The gameplay balance in this manner is very good, and the game feels deeper than IV already.
-Japanese and English voice options for the whole cast or each character individually. I'm glad this is becoming standardized in fighting games.
-The best Street Fighter soundtractk ever. This soundtrack is much better than I anticipated it would be.
-For Street Fighter fans this is the game you've probably been waiting for in regards to gameplay.
Neutral:
-This game is well optimized for most modern PC's (including mine), but some people are still having issues with it. Hopefully the March update fixes that.
-Character story mode is basically a visual novel teaser for what's to come. The gameplay in it isn't really gameplay. Sort of a trade-off there.
-If you don't play the game much, unlocking the fight money to get DLC characters may take a while in a year or so.
-The training mode and tutorial are well put together, but lack features. The training mode lacks some features for practicing specific techniques and moves, and the tutorial while covering most things for beginners missing a few things here and there.
-I like the pre-game and post-game character dialogue as well as the voice actors in both languages, but I wish there were more lines for every character.
-Unlocking alternate colors is locked to Survival Mode. While I enjoy Survival Mode, I'm not a huge fan of that.
Cons:
-Lack of support for many pre-8th Gen Gaming controllers/fightpads/fight sticks. This will likely largely be fixed in the March patch, but for now it is a bit of a letdown for many gamers using older controllers.
-The graphics of some of the background characters in stages are somewhat disappointing. Some of the background characters move at 60 fps, most at 30, and a few at around 15. Some of the background details are also pretty low res. This will be upgraded, but for now it is sort of disappointing to see on a few stages.
-Right now it only supports lobbies of 2; it will be 8 in March but right now it isn't suited for rotation play.
-Have to unlock color variants in Survival Mode seperately for alternate outfits. This is an unneeded grind.
-Match load times can take up to 15-20 seconds. If you got an SSD, store this game on that to eliminate this con.
-Not a game recommended for newer Street Fighter fans right now or people trying to get into the series. You'd probably would enjoy Ultra Street Fighter IV right now.

The Tales series has been a staple of JRPGs (Japanese Role-Playing Games) for a long time, and each installment has been its own beast, just with some familiar series markings.  Tales of Berseria feels true to this sentiment, though the idea of doing something different is wholly embraced by its developers.  It may get bogged down at times in genre tropes and long-time design traditions, but it makes up for it with an entirely fresh and daring plot with characters that are truly unique and complex.  If you have the patience to see it through and the ability to enjoy the ride for what it is, you'll be treated to one of the most captivating narratives in a JRPG in years.
The story follows Velvet Crowe and her quest for revenge against the man who killed her brother.  Along the way she meets various other shady characters who join her for their own reasons, most of which are similarly tinged with malice.  The characters in Berseria are not heroes, or even anti-heroes, but villains each with their own flaws, single minded desires, and histories.  That isn't to say that they are devoid of all good qualities and simply want to see the world burn, just that their goals are against societal norms.  It's an interesting dynamic, and thankfully, doesn't overplay its malevolent hand by shirking scenes of levity or emotional progression.  These characters may be villains, but learning their motivations and seeing them become more comfortable with each other along the journey is compelling and creates a welcome balance, allowing one to connect to the major players of the plot despite their irredeemable natures.
The gameplay involves adventuring through maps and encountering enemies in real-time battle.  The battle system is multi-faceted and generally consists of choosing attacks (or Artes) for each character as they unlock them in flashy and effective ways to combat foes.  You can take direct control of your favorite character and set up AI parameters for the rest of your party such as fighting aggressively or being more defensive.  As you play, you level up, collect gear, and engage in other JRPG staples, though a layer is added into the mix in the form of Master Skills tied to each piece of equipment.  As you use a piece of equipment in battle and gain experience (or Grade) points for the gear, you earn a permanent upgrade associated with that gear which applies to your character even when the gear is not equipped.  It adds an extra depth to the normal stat-raising gameplay that is typical of most JRPGs, though unfortunately, it doesn't entirely save the experience from being repetitive at times.  It's a trope that Berseria falls into when progression is very closely tied to simply raising stats to become stronger, and oftentimes, this can take the form of grinding out battles on the map in order to be ready for the next big encounter.
You can forgive Berseria for this though, and you should.  The overall experience is well worth seeing through to the end even if that means having to trudge through some repeated encounters for that extra level or Master Skill.  Perhaps this experience would've been better suited as an Anime however, because the story is stellar and hits many engaging beats along the way.  It may not have escaped the grating grind and restricting conventions of its contemporaries, but it propels itself high above most because its journey is just so different and well-executed.  Tales of Berseria is definitely a rough gem, but when viewed from the right angle, it can shine brilliantly.
