Long-waited revival of Jagged Alliance experience in full 3 dimensions. Jagged Alliance 2, simply put, is the king of the small, but proud sub-genre of strategies, namely, a squad-based tactical wargames.
JA Back in Action is the 3d re-vision of classical JA2, with new engine based on real-time action with commanding pause mode. To my regret, I wasn’t impressed with that cover-version, so I’m not gonna persuade you to buy it. Game’s decent, even engaging sometimes, but really not that much as original JA2. Even with the all downsides that original Jagged Alliance 2 have, it is still a much better game than its remake Back in Action.
Short audition of features:
1) 3d view works fine enough, but I can’t say same thing about control above the camera view. Due to real-time gaming pattern, I often was in the not-so-fun position where I can see neither enemies, nor my own soldiers in the middle of the shootout. Somebody’s shooting, but who? On whom? It was not obvious way too often. The biggest throw-down of the given 3D engine is not a bad camera, though. It is very limited destructibility. You have plenty of C4 there, but you only allowed blowing certain points at every sector. You can’t even open closed door with the shotgun!
2) All controls are giving the feeling that developers were in need to invent a wheel anew. Or at least, a bicycle. Even moving a map from side to side with the sliding of mouse was added after some patches. And when you‘ll make yourself familiar with the basic controls, you’ll still be wandering with some “decisions” about user interface. Like management of your mercs in teams, or management of inventory of taken sectors.
3) Smart pause mode itself is good, comparing only with the best examples in the genre. But crude AI behavior and sometimes ridiculous camera makes that modus not so desirable, so to say. It is still a good option, but not the essential, like in games on Apeiron engine (7.62, Marauder) or even in the Dragon Age titles.
4) AI of the enemies… they shoot precisely, even with the weakest of weapons, but instead of taking the advantage of those superb skills, they always tend to rush forward, by the shortest path available. And they don’t give much attention to the dead bodies of their comrades, if they don’t heard a shot or seen the shooter. In short, they are quite dumb. There are several maps in the game, where some additional rules were added to enemies behavior, and it is there you’ll probably meet some troubles, and get an urge to plan something ahead. 3-4 serious fights in the whole game, I’d say it’s not enough, but that’s me. Someone likes easy games, and the majority of games now are making for those casual players. So take a hint: buy some PSG-1 rifles and collimators, to shoot far and precise enough, and quite fast at the same time. With those rifles you’ll be having the upper hand almost in every situation that game has for you.
By the way! The AI of guards you’re hiring for defending your sectors… it’s the same as with soldiers, but even worse! They don’t use any tactical advantages of the defending position; they just rush on the bullets! And, unlike the Jagged Alliance 2, you can’t just hire new guards via global map. You need to get some guns, go to the sector where the fight with Deidranna forces was, arm manually each new volunteer… And if he dies, he won’t leave his gun on the body, you need to find or buy a new one. So you need to participate in every fight by yourself, and it will be faster that way.
I can keep up with that list, but that’s major things: the game went in 3D, but became much plainer in the process, if we compare it with the vanilla Jagged Alliance 2. Back In Action took almost everything that wasn’t so necessary and fun, like over-pompious music themes, and constant transitions of items between sectors. A 3D perspective is not bad to have, and smart pause mode can be tolerable. But illogical and un-informative camera views, clumsy controls and blunt behavior of any opponents are not giving the taste of satisfaction even when you prevail above them.
Take me right, I’m not thinking that the Jagged Alliance is a perfect game, even if I’m calling it the king of the tactical genre. Were it up to me, I’d cut or remade some features from it as well, and all that constant fuss with the inventory items, which need to fix, optimize, transfer from sector to sector, from drop zone to battle lines – in the first hand. I’d add some really fitting and atmospheric music to the background, just to fight the urge to fell asleep over the keyboard, while I’m planning another phase of ongoing war conflict. And to think more of it… Maybe the most challenging thing that was made under the brand of Jagged Alliance was not that 2nd game we’re so much talking about? Maybe it is the add-on to the first Jagged Alliance, the Deadly Games? There you have a line of separated missions for your squad of mercs. You have one map, where you fixing all your tasks, and after it, that’s all, you’re victorious! It feels much more refined, than questionable economic system of the JA2 game.
The developers of Back In Action thought in that direction as well. They made two DLC with such maps, in every case you have some quest to get in somewhere and kill there somebody, via some sub-stages on the way. Sadly, but both of those DLC’s are just shown how amateur those developers are. There are different reasons for this conclusion, but hear this: in the mission Shades of Red you need to storm some embassy where hostages are being held. The developers make the several ways to get to that embassy, and the cleverest one was from the basement, which you can penetrate via sewerage tunnel. That way you don’t need to dodge the rockets, which the insurgents will be shooting in case of direct assault. But, but, but… In the end the devs decided it is not good for balance, so now you can’t get to embassy via tunnel. You see it from one end near the river, you can get there with a C4 blast through the wall. But you can’t go further to the tunnel. After you storm the embassy in the hardest, direct assault way, you get down to the basement, and then you see another end of that tunnel, and you realizing, how far Back In Action from the real complete state. Even now, after 3 years after release, with all after-market fixes, like adding the possibility to use mouse to move the map… it is still far from complete, not only in the DLC maps, but in the major game as well.
Finally, so many words after, a conclusion: you CAN buy the Back In Action, if you have a thing for tactical games. It is not a bad game; it is playable and sometimes even brings some fun!
I’ll mark it 6.5/10. It looks good, it sounds and feels almost like old-good Jagged Alliance. Simple-sized for newer, casual players (who can forgot to reload gun between getting into the fights, for example) – but still you controlling a team of mercs, and still you’re in the lead of private war going in the colorful little Latin country. You may find many mods, honing the improvements Back In Action made to Jagged Alliance franchise. There are not so many games in the genre, after all, and Back In Action is certainly not in the worst part of that list.

Freespace 2 is, fifteen years later, still the finest first person combat-focused sim around. It's combination of exceptional storytelling, insanely satisfying combat and the best control scheme and H.U.D. around still make it the pinnacle of the genre. Whether you're escorting a convoy, flying undercover or destroying a Shivan cruiser, you're in for an amazing thrill-ride. You can see my own play through of the game right here to get an idea of what's in store.
This isn't simply a game you're purchasing, however, it's also a platform for more content. Thanks to the Source Code Project, you'll not only have access to updated graphics, but new missions, campaigns, and mods that extend the Freespace universe and help create new universes as well. This engine also powers the total conversions for the Wing Commander-based Saga and Battlestar Galactica-based Diaspora games as well.
So with Freespace 2, you're not just buying one game, you're purchasing a portal into years of fan-based work and content that goes well beyond the amazing base game. And heck, even if you never used the SCP, you'd still have one of the finest space games around. Do yourself a favor and buy this, whether you fly with a joystick or a mouse, you won't be disappointed.

It's unfinished. Not just in a slightly annoying way, but in a major chunks of functionality are just not there. It's only after a while of playing you realise that things like the leisure buildings and education buildings are either horribly out of balance for the game or just entirely non-functioning.
Examples:
* As far as I can tell, only one of the education buildings has any effect. There's no concept of levels of education.
* Water is derped. If you want to place water towers, pause the game, place them in a bunch, then unpause the game. The water vanishes if you place one tower while the game is running, but if you place them while it's paused the towers work. Which one was the original game intent?
* Roads clag up horribly. Since the roads have slightly different widths, you'll have to demolish vast swathes of city to replace them with wider roads, which don't add that much more capacity and then clag up again. I can't even tell if having busy roads affects the sim at all anyway. Everything seems to work fine even with most of the roads over capacity.
* You notice more and more buildings with mangled or missing titles and descriptions as you unlock them.
Recap: Water, transport and education appear to be borked. Pretty basic items for a City builder?
So that seemingly complex balance of budget vs city needs? .. Forget it.
Basically it's just houses for 3 types of people and jobs for 3 types of people. That's your main task to juggle for the entire game (yawn).
Add a bit of class X housing, add a few class X jobs. Wait for them to fill. Do it again.
Occasionally, add more power, and maybe pause the game, demolish your water towers, wait for the water to reappear, then pause the game and put more water towers back down ..
That's it.
That's the game.
Fun huh?

It was a smart move by developer United Front not to try and copy GTA but to make Sleeping Dogs an open world game of it's own. Main selling point is the martial combat, which is fun and actually more satisfying than gun play. And when you do get your hands on a shooting weapon it actually makes you feel that more badass.
Hong Kong is a great setting: it's pretty big and packs many beautiful or otherwise interesting areas. Sleeping Dogs's story is one often found in Asian crime cinema, with a hardboiled yet tormented protagonist going undercover with the Triads. Besides the main missions the game offers plenty of things to do and explore: hidden statues and cases, martial arts tournaments, street races and even karaoke. There are also all kinds of achievements to be made: drive X minutes at high speed without crashing, getting a 'killing spree' or jump X meters with a motorcycle. These scores are then automatically compared to those of your friends. So basically it's pretty hard to get bored with this game the first 30 or so hours.
A final good point: the world feels very much alive. There are always a lot of people on the streets having chats, doing shopping or reacting when you bump into them. When it rains people get umbrellas and the lights reflect beautifully in the wet streets. My only real critique could be directed to the driving, since the cars basically don't handle too well, even with a controller. Either they accelerate too fast, take corners like a brick or steer to jerky (even using a controller), or all of this at the same time. But otherwise this game is loads of fun!

While Street Fighter V might currently be somewhat lacking in single player content, it's one of the best fighting games I have played mechanically. Any issues with the online play seem to have been fixed as of the time of myself writing this review.
Gameplay - The gameplay is fantastically well-tuned, and thus far (over 50 hours including betas) it's some of the most fun I have had with a fighting game. It's well suited to new players because it's combos are significantly easier than SF4's, and there's a lot less hidden "tech" that requires experimentation and inside knowledge to discover. It's equally well suited to fighting game veterans, boasting a large and varied cast and gameplay that revolves around winning the neutral more than setplay and oki.
Graphics/Sound - The game looks and sounds amazing. At max settings the game looks phenomenal, with sparks flying from hadoukens and detailed textures on the characters' skin and clothing. The soundtrack is among the best of any Street Fighter game, with several genres including jazz, rock, electronic dance, classical, and latin represented in well-arranged remixes for each returning character and new stage and character themes. Having that said, you'll need a decent graphics card to run it well, and I recommend taking a look at the recommended specs before purchasing.
Story/Single-player - so here's a large reason why the game is getting a lot of flac, and understandably so: the story modes currently are very short, and other than that there's just a very tedious survival mode, and of course training mode. However, there are several new modes coming in March, as well as a fully cinematic story akin to Mortal Kombat's coming in June. Also, the training mode has some of the best features of any training mode I have seen, with complex options for recording wakeups and reversals.
Netcode - So on release date, this game's online functionality wasn't working at all, players were constantly dropping their connections, nobody could get games, and lobbies weren't working. However, Capcom has been hard at work fixing this stuff, which was likely caused by the massive amount of people logging on at the same time, and everything appears to be stable. I played for several hours getting games consistently without being dropped. Having all that said, this game has fantastic netcode. Capcom has implemented a rollback system for their netcode which is a marked improvement over SF4's, which was already pretty good. Almost all of my matches I hardly noticed that I was playing online vs offline, and that's including people I've played across the Atlantic ocean.
Other - Street Fighter V ships with 16 characters, but it's coming out with new characters every month, and these characters can all be purchased with in-game earnable currency. This is tremendous because pretty much every other fighting game releases new characters only as paid DLC or more frequently in expansions with new mechanics. But Capcom has already promised that there won't be a Super Street Fighter V, with all gameplay expansions being released for free.
In conclusion, Street Fighter V is really fun, and I recommend it if you want to get into fighting games or if you already know fighting games pretty well and want to try something new. If you want to play it for the single-player, however, I'd suggest you wait until June, as that's when the main story mode comes out.

[I'm going to keep this spoiler-free as much as possible] The first playthrough was a delight, mostly because it really felt like my choices were meaningful. But upon replaying the game (up to Chapter 2, now) I realized very quickly that there is a single narrative that's being told here. Your choices affect who lives, but the one that does live seems to replace the other character functionally-- that is to say that one character being alive over another doesn't change the plot. You just happen to have a different face with the same role.
There isn't anything wrong with this method of story-telling, and the story itself is alright (riddled with plotholes, but it's not a terrible generic post-apocalyptic zombie world story #85). The thing is, the major selling point (and the text splash at the beginning of every chapter) is that game adapts to the choices you make. This is simply a lie outside of the few "pick X character to save" moments. You end up in the same situations with the same people (more or less) using the same solutions and pathways. Nothing is unique and nothing you do matters. I would highly recommend watching a Let's Play of this instead of dropping 25 $%#@ing dollars on this (I got this via the Humble Bundle dollar deal~).
It's not a terrible "game", but unless you really like point-and-clicks and/or generic zombies, then I would say that you should look elsewhere for a custom story.

Almost everything about this game gives you a sense of what it was like. The look and feel segway you into a glimpse of warfare more than 70 years ago. From the interface screens to the planning elements, you feel like some colonel trying to meet orders with limited resources and equally limited intelligence.
The graphics are pretty good, with realistic environments and equipment. The physics seem to have been worked out fairly well, and movement and ballistics make sense too. The all important line-of-sight seems to have been treated well and you don't get a lot of spectacular through the trees and around the hill shots that spoil your day and make you say 'what the funk'!
The only beef I would have is in what seems to be a bit of a weak AI. It sometimes seems to sit on its♥♥♥♥♥and do nothing, which could also be considered realistic when you factor in that sometimes if you want something done right, you gotta do it yourself.
Another weakness is the interface for the 3D environment and for the map overview. Both are gorgeous and really give you that sense that you're at war and it's World War 2. However, the myriad of symbols and controls can be overwhelming and this leads to a steep learning curve in the game.
In fact, I think most people will not appreciate the game, or won't even be able to get into it, because of this very high level of realism and poor interface design. For me, it took a while to get into the game and I absolutely love realistic simulators.
This game is pure old fashion strategy and tactics: It's great at S&T, it's great at simulating mechanized warfare, and it's great at illustrating the past. However, for the more casual gamer it will overwhelm and possibly bore, but if its reality you're after, then welcome to the battlefield buddy...
Seriously, with more polish and a few changes, this game could be used to instruct at the troop or even squadron level for basic mechanized warfare.

THE BAD:
I'm just going to flat out own up: I hate the main character.
People can say she's interesting, people can say she's really deep but I found myself honestly wishing for bad things to happen to her. I'm 22 hours into the game and I've started to get close to where she's possibly maybe considering in the future the idea of character development by way of taking literally any new information into her paradigm and using it to evaluate her own thoughts. But, until that point it's 22 hours of dealing with the least self-aware, short-sighted, obnoxiously   hypocritcal main characters I've ever played. Sometimes she's so busy making threats she doesn't even consider that carrying out any of them would actively preclude her from the one goal she has.
It might as well be Climate Change Denial, the game: you follow around a person who's really sure there's no such thing as global warming as they encounter clear evidence of global warming scene after scene after scene after scene. Yes, I understand she has theoretical reasons to act the way she does... but literally any amount of self-reflection would have given her the insight that the game later provided. Yes, I understand that the thing she's against probably DOES pan out but it's very obviously not going to be for any of the reasons she thought.
My gripe with the main character, however, is a personal thing.
Outside from Velvet, these are the worst dungeons I've had in a game. There's a mechanic that changes from dungeon to dungeon where you find something and it tells you to press A to get passed it.  Then you do.  Then you continue on through the dungeons.  The sliding block puzzle in the opening of Symphonia was more involved -- I feel as if the game thinks I couldn't handle an actual puzzle. Instead, they're all mazes made more difficult by how the map works and you find yourself going through room after similar looking room until you find the right thing to stand in front of to press A.
THE GOOD:
The controls for the game are amazing. It's just fun to go through combat and the camera is really intuitive for where to be in order to get the most people in the shot.
The (other) characters are really interesting.  Eizen shows the same pragmatism that Velvet seems like she's supposed to have but is a lot more rational about the whole process. He doesn't seem to have evolved any since we started, Rokukou is still being defined... but Laphicet and Eleanor have clear character arcs that are interesting. I'm biased with Magilou; as noted before Velvet annoys me and Magilou calls Velvet out so much that I bonded with her.
The voice acting is really amazing. I'm not a fan of the English voices but from sound alone my friends were able to tell what each of the PCs were like with their Japanese voice actors despite not seeing a bit from the game. I LOVE the skits. Everything stops when there's a skit because I want to watch them all.
The game is really, really pretty. That's a weird thing to note for me as graphics aren't typically that important to me but it's gorgeous enough to mention.
I'm invested in the majority of stories of the characters. It's interesting seeing how they're panning out, what's going to happen to most of them, etc.  It's a bit telegraphed to me how things are going to happen and I'll update this if I'm wrong, but it's solid none the less.
If you can keep yourself from cutting your wrists on Velvet's edge, I highly recommend this game.

I am 50+ hours into this game, and I mean to complete it.
After going through all the mixed reviews for this game, I decided to wait for a sale and try it out. I have to say I was pleasantly surprised. IF you're expecting some sort of revolutionary (or evolutionary) successor in the JA franchise, you're going to be disappointed. Back In Action is not that -- it's a re-envisioned, updated version of Jagged Alliance 2, with the ultimate aim of liberating Arulco from Deidrianna. Graphics are now 3D, and the game engine is "real-time" but combat can be paused for you to issue orders/commands. The nice thing about this system is that you can simultaneously coordinate attacks from different entry points, create overlapping fields of fire, ambush enemies stealthily with a knife, etc.
Some things have been simplified too: you only pay for your merc once. Militia recruitment is simplified (all you need is to arm them). And you cannot create your own character (this was fun in the original JA2, but I'm not convinced absolutely essential).
The game focuses mainly on combat. In JA2 it was turn based, here, it's real-time with pausing enabled. Sight lines and physics seem ok. Can things go wrong? Of course. Just as they do in real life. So pay no mind to those who expect their tactics and plans to be executed perfectly. But that's part of the realism, and to me, the appeal of this JA title.
Some things I didn't like: no helo transport (am going everywhere on foot, which is a pain) thus far, no ETA for my online orders at Drassen, no crafting of special items, inability to repair anything except weapons (though this can be thought of as realism I guess -- how can your merc repair everything from guns to knives to armor? Seriously?).
Still I paid $11 for this title when on sale, got 2 extra DLC mission packs, and some mediocre firearms in some other packs. Based on that, I'm going to recommend this game. Get it when it's on sale. It's really quite fun!

First things first, the Freespace 2 Open Source Code Project has essentially brought Freespace 2 to 2014-era graphics. Find it through Google and bring this classic, masterpiece of a game to the modern day.
I will go on record and say it: Freespace 2 is the best space flight sim ever made. It has never been beaten and no game has ever really come close to matching the high-octane action and depth of control gameplay, nor have they ever matched the amazing sense of scale (Freespace 2 truly gives you large capital ships and swarms of fighters), nor have they ever beaten Freespace 2's incredibly atmospheric and surprisingly deep story of apocalyptic hubris. It is a game I have kept on my hard drive since first playing it in 2000.
The voice acting is solid and understated, befitting the professional military nature of the story. The music fits. The gameplay is fast-paced with missions ranging from dogfights to blockades to covering capital ships as they duke it out with beam cannons, flak batteries and torpedoes. No space sim has come close.
The fan community has kept the game alive for the past decade. So, while there is no final conclusion to the Freespace saga, many talented individuals have turned out many professional campaigns and mods. There are even huge projects for popular series like Battlestar Galactica, Babylon 5, Star Wars and Wing Commander. If this reviewer may make a recommendation, when you finish FS2, move onto the Blue Planet campaigns for a thrilling possible take on Freespace 3.

Pros:
-Relativly immersive story that keeps you wanting to learn more about the ADVENT and their Elder masters.
-Great squad customization both with the individual charactors and also the diveristy in abilities and tactics you are free to employ on any given mission.
-Graphics aren't half bad, but that is not the most important aspect of a game like this in my opinion.

-Controls are pretty easy to pick up on, learning that you can tab through squad mates to skip lengthy animations (such as on evacs) and ending turns without taking an action are the two things it took me to pick up on.
Cons:
-Campaign tempo can be irritating, though it's likely by design. You will not be able to really plan too far in advance as to how you will tackle landmark missions, or develop specific teams because you will contanstly interupted by retaliation strikes. You are basically always reacting. For instance, you will be prepping to attack an ADVENT blacksite and as you are traveling to or making contact with the region you will be presented with a "Very Difficult" mission where you run a high risk of losing a squadmate, you have to decide whether its worth sending your B-team to absorb the losses and possibly fail the mission, skip the mission and face the consequences, or send in the A-team and risk them being wounded or tired for the big mission you've been preparing for.
-The biggest pitfall of this game is RNG. Running on Ironman (auto-saves so no re-do's when a squadmate dies) this quickly becomes a downhill snowball completely ruining a campaign when you miss several 70%+ shots. You can essentially lose so many people over a short series of missions that you cannot recover/develop new Soldier's fast enough. Your MAJ and COL that had 90+ aim were somehow missing shots, and their new replacements are even less likely to get it done.

Im truly amazed by this game. The only Tales titles I've played were Symphonia and Dawn of a New World, both of which I really enjoyed. I bought both Berseria and Zestiria on sale and figured I'd go with Berseria first with it being a prequel, albeit a spinoff one before tackling Zestiria.
54 hours. It took me 54 hours to beat this game, and thats probably on the low end. I didnt grind anywhere near the amount I probably should have, though i did attempt to pick up as many side quests and skits as I could. Either way, this is an easy 60 hour time sink, a very rare instance of a game where every dollar you spent was worth it. I almost wish I paid full price for this.
Every character, with maybe the exception of Bienfu, are amazing. Each one have engaging backstories that expand even further if you pursue their questlines. When you manage to finish them, it actually feels like the character has developed outside of the main storyline rather than acting as if you just spent hours on them for seemingly no reason.
Also, Im very big on how well voice actors do in their roles and they certainly did fantastic in every instance. Especially Velvet. Good lord im now a fan.
My only "issue" with the game was the combat. Dozens of hours into the game and youre still getting tutorials on how to do x y and z, alot of which would have been great to know way beforehand. Im more of a comfort zone kind of guy, so I only played Velvet for my entire playthrough. I dont regret it, but it feels like her playstyle might be one of the more annoying ones to take on. There were no fights that were extremely difficult, but every new area did bring a minor challenge with it on normal difficulty. I'd be damned if I ever want to go above normal though.
Overall, if you want to spend the next 60 hours of your life on a pretty stellar journey, by all means pick this up.

If you care about getting online and fighting, training and discovering combos in training mode, and working to build the foundation of the community. Grab it now and play your heart out.
If you're looking for more single player content and data, more feature rich online multiplayer and other offerings that, for example, Ultra Street Fighter IV, offered, then keep your eye on this title for a future buy.

I'm going to review this as someone who wasn't a kickstarter backer, but someone who throughouly enjoyed the original Planetary Annhilation, thus I paid 13 dollars for this DLC. This is also going to be short and to the point.
The original PA had its problems. It had performaces issues, a lack of variety, and not enough content to engage for that long. It was engaging though, and for the time it held my attention, I enjoyed it a lot. Titans, as DLC, adds a lot of things that I wanted into the game. New terrains features make the planets feel more alive, rather than just flat circles with the occasional ocean. There can be ridges and mountains now, which adds a new layer to base building, Before, you could practically anywhere, but now you have to think where you are going to place yourself based on terrain features. This was a small addition, but the biggest thing was the new units. All of the units have their place, and I have found myself using some of the new units very frequently. All methods of combat have been improved, but what has been improved the most is Orbital combat. There are plenty of new Oribital units that make space battles a lot more interesting than before (as there was just one real attacking unit that could be in Orbit, which were those little fighters). Now you can have much larger battle cruisers that can also shoot beams down to the planet below. The new units have added a lot to the game. Sadly, I have not had a chance to try out using a "Titan" (I have been playing Galactic Conquest and have not unlocked the technology) but I have had them used against me. They certainly do live up to their namesake. They are collasal, and can quickly dispatch and entire army if you don't have proper defenes set up. Overall, this was definitly worth 13 dollars, and in my opinion, was not a cash grab. This is far more reasonably priced than a lot of other DLC.
My score for PA: Titans is a 8/10
If you can get over the performance issues, then this is a solid RTS that can be very engaging.

If you're having technical issues be sure to check out the Freespace Open project, which attempts to fix some of the bugs and update the graphics and lighting to a level contemporary players may be more comfortable with. For me personally, as-downloaded, my installation of Freespace 2 refused to run properly, but after installing FSO, it executes effortlessly.
In the space of a few minutes, you'll find yourself weaving between capital ships, trying to dodge flak, focus-fire on enemy capital weaponry to disarm them, and dog-fighting with customizable ships and loadouts. All the while, a grand narrative is unfolding with plenty of little twists and flavor to keep your interest.

Welcome to Black Mesa where we take the role of Dr. Gordon Freeman, a physicist recently employed at this research facility located in the New Mexico desert.
Another normal day for Freeman, until a new crystal is up for testing, and all hell broke loose by opening portals between our world and the extraterrestrial one!
presents a top-tier sci-fi storyline about a simple person who has to fight for survival in a complex facility infrastructure, fighting not only aliens, but also military and mercenaries who try to destroy the entire complex.
The game treats the player with a mist of doubt and mystery, as we travel from section to section in hope to find answers, but only to find most devastating effects of the invasion. Fellow scientists and security guards are as oblivious as us, but this doesn't stop the player from teaming up with them for survival.
As the plot goes, the game delivers hints in small amounts by leaving trails of information with each new objective, as we explore the facility compound.
The storyline isn't practical, but leaves a huge deal of assumption to the player, and The G-Man proves exactly that. This is deliberate, and I for one love Half-Life direction, as mystery suits extremely well within Black Mesa.
When I first started
, I knew it was going to be good, but not that good!!! We shouldn't forget this game was released in the late 90's, and back then, this game had much higher standards of gameplay from every other FPS. Even almost 20 years later, Half-Life is still an enjoyable first person shooter to new gamers, and this just proves to how advanced
was back in the day.
Although this game is a classic, to me, was a refreshing adventure, as I no longer find games as these on the market. A game with no RPG elements, and yet delivers different type of approaches thanks to impressive AI and other mechanics that even some games released in today's age, can only dream of accomplishing.
Throughout the adventure, Freeman must survive the alien attacks, which teleport to our world with nothing in their instinct but killing us. Each enemy is susceptible to noise, so it's possible to stealth kill each enemy as long as a one-hit kills the target. Some aliens, however, are also manipulated by the smell of other small dead creatures, such as the bullsquid. Others, such as the vortigaunt show a cowardly behave, and become easy preys at close range scenarios. Those are just some examples one can use to survive the Black Mesa invasion, but thru out the years, players have found numerous ways to survive!
From time to time we actually have to escort scientists to open doors, or extra locations for more gear. These escort missions are actually fun to do, and far from boring and tedious as games usually portray them. I always enjoy having a scientist with me, I find their remarks quite funny considering the situation at hand!
Although the crowbar is Freeman's trademark, the rest of the arsenal available is satisfying, from the standard pistol, assault rifle, shotgun, grenades, crossbow, and even some pretty cool prototype machine devices! If you think this is cool, you can even use some alien weaponry too.
uses smart gun positioning, that when used correctly, can deliver the player some pure amusing moments of satisfaction. It's also satisfying when we finally figure out what weapon to choose on each enemy, and thanks to quick-save, there's no excuse not to explore all possibilities.
The design shows its age, but an HD patch is available within the game, that significantly increases the game quality, and with pretty much any resolution at your disposal, plus external mods out there,
can really become next-gen. Personally, I never felt the need to, but it's a choice.
Overall visuals are good, old but remarkable and atmospheric capable of leaving a trial to everyone who plays, and this is exactly why I'm not surprised why so many players feel nostalgic when comes this title!
The game delivers a fantastic journey from a simple day at work, to finishing off an Alien boss in a otherwold location, through the radioactive swears, to desert canyons, and even several science labs. An epic science fiction adventure, from a time where simply playing the game was a conquest. With linear levels yet quite disperse, and some simple and small puzzles between, you'll never feel you're in the same area twice. Even labs have a very distinct feeling and visuals, and the deeper you go, the darker are the secrets and it becomes obvious, Black Mesa is not just another facility!
Although NPC's are just groups of scientists and guards, there is one special NPC that changed everything for me... The G-Man! This is probably the most iconic character (other than Freeman himself), and I can't stop having a massive vibe from
(
), and overall influence of one of my favorite TV Series. This is obviously a personal comparison, as Half-Life is extremely distinct and offers a tremendous identity on its own.
Other NPC's deliver small amounts of dialogues, keeping it short and simple, but doesn't really affect the game at all. The soundtrack is based on ambient, and key moments during the game!
Replayability is present, not only by mods, but also by difficulty, with the hard-mode proving to be a nice challenge!
Overall
is a fantastic title, worth it of all the praise from the fans throughout the years. I enjoyed every single moment I had with this game, and some of the mods I tried. My journey won't end here, as I'm sure I'll return to the original. After all; "
".

Probably one of the best free "horror" games I've ever indulged in! It's a great first person point and click game the delves into the depths of loss and true misery. I could not reccommend it more for those willing to explore almost an hour of storyline.
Pros:
- The ambiance and sounds are on point. It can give a nice immersing feeling as well as uping the creep out factor. It really kept me connected to the story.

Cons:
- Some of the movements got a little jerky at some points. Mostly when the bedside tables are closed. But it does not deter the viewer from playing.

Whenever i start to get into a series, my mind always starts wandering. What if so and so had happened, how would the story be affected, what would happen to characters? So when i got into XCOM, my first thought was that what would happen if humanity lost the war? (and no its not a spoiler, anyone can see that humanity always wins, one way or another, unless its an exceptionally dark game or whatever) When this game came out, i was psyched. I couldnt wait to see the next chapter. Humanity won the first time, who is next? Then i find out that this is entirely different. Someone at Firaxis must have been thinking the same way i do. This whole game is a big what if, and i highly respect that. Ive met few people who actually enjoy a series to an extent where they actually wonder about what could happen if events in that world were changed. The creativity of the story aside, the game itself follows the standard XCOM fomula. Carry out missions, do research, get better guns, build a base in between missions eventually reaching the final objective where there is a final showdown between your crack squad of shocktroopers who you've so lovingly trained and a threat that is greater than anything percieved. Although, just about every element has improved. Your base, for example can now fly while previously it was static and this adds a whole layer of strategy. Obtaining better guns is now much easier since all you have to is buy it and all units who can use it get it, instead of manufacturing individual units and handing them out. guns now also have a modding system giving them buffs for as long as the mod is attached.
Ive talked about the good, now the bad. Most people will complain about the mission timer. the reason it exists relates to the story and i wont go into details but it adds a challenge to the game where in the older versions you previously only had all the time in the world to finish. I personaly have had no problems with it (i play on easy cause i am a wimp) but i can imagine that on the higher difficulties it is pure hell. This in mind, the community has made mods which disable the timer so it is better for those casual gamers. Also, i have had start up issues relating to this game and murderous load times but i think it is problem with my computer and not the game itself.
All in all, this is a top strategy game that improves on its predecessors. I wont be biased and say "YOU MUST BUY THIS GAME" instead, ill say buy it if you are a fan of the series or a lover of turn based strategy. Otherwise you can choose to buy it for the story or any other conceivable reason a human can think of. I dont care what you, the reader might choose to do. its your money and your choice

Really like this game alreay. Picked it up in sale with DLC and just starting to get to grips with the basics. It has a learning curve - partly from a slightly non-intuitive UI and partly due to complexity/options involved - but underneath, the actual mechanics of playing are faily simple. Similar to Total War games in that you play a strategic layer and then resolve battles yourself. The battles are at a slightly abstract level compared to say combat mission, but much more realistic and (I think) more interesting than say a Wargame: game such as European Escalation.
It's obviously going to depend on your interests and game play style, but I've been looking for a game like this for a while.. and great to find this one. After a couple of early crashes (one solved in support forum) I've found it pretty stable so far (early days but some play sessions of several hours with no issues)..
Visually it is not cutting edge by any means, but somehow puts in enough authentic details for the battles to play out amazingly well and in the middle of a pitched battle it can really start to be immersive to zoom down into each conflict.
Control is more complex than a simplistic RTS style, but at the same time discourages 'micro' levels of control, making it feel closer to platoon or company leader levels of management, with some great sim mechanics including unit fatgue, state of mind, communication system (telephone, radio, flare etc) and as far as I can see ok AI for everything below your level of control (snipers automatically take cover in belfries, machine gun teams auto deply, soldiers ride on tanks etc).
At sale price definately worth a try, but if you like the genre and didn't know about it, it might just be a 'find'.. Plenty of lets plays on Youtube to watch before buying if still unsure

Graviteam Tactics: Operation Star is a WW2 heavily realistic RTT game.
You are taking role of a commander in a series of historical decisive battles taking place around Kharkov a Soviet megapolis and important industrial and scientific center. Battles are fought in two steps, first you make chess-like turn based moves on the operational map and then you fight a series of corresponding real time engagements.
Main game concepts and mechanics are direct descendants of Close Combat series. With squad level control, attention to morale, weapon loadouts and rough realism, however visual part of game is a huge leap ahead. You will find one of the best 3D scenery you ever saw in strategy game here. Lighting, shading, weather effects, complex landscape,terraforming, etc.. Everything looks great and really belivable here and Total War series is the closest what comes to mind if you want to compare visual style.
Battle part provides from \"little\" to \"no\" compromise in this game. Single bullet hit usually means dead soldier, mortar shell on your position usually means dead squad and enemy tank is your  worst nigthmare. Germans are mechanized, better equiped and organized, so all Soviet campaigns are even more hard to play. No balance or helpfull scripts here. DEFEAT means DEFEAT.
Absolutely must have for everyone who like challenging realistic wargames. Game is pretty old, but dont be fooled by that, it looks perfect and dont have even close analogues anyway.
PROS
Strong concept, mix of Close Combat indepth detalisation and Total War beauty.
Photo realistic scenery, dynamic weather and day\\night cycle.
Realistic physics (terraforming, ballistics, weight, traction and torque for vehicles, etc..)
REAL night battles (this will impress you)
High replay ability
AI capable to surprise (you will see)
Realistic and hard wargame not for everyone, no balance and cybersport ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t (you are warned)
CONS
Limited choice of locations and units (compared to mainstream games)
Not the best unit animations
Voiceover is trash (who needs it anyway)
No fancy tutorials (not a big problem for a dedicated wargamer but a nightmare for a casual)
Some questionable things here and there (just couple of them)
Heavy impact on system. Forget about recommended system specs. You will need a TOP 2016 hardware to turn everything on.
No multiplayer (biggest dissapointment)
Highly recommended!

I grew up playing games like Close Combat and Combat Mission, but I always felt like those two games could be improved upon. Close Combat, particularly the 2nd and 3rd games in the series, were a great mix of highly tactical combat with campaign systems that allowed your units to fight battles which affected future battles and operations. While the later games went on to have bigger battles and maps, they lost a bit of the magic of the early games where the battles felt much more like struggles and where your past mistakes could lead you to be stuck in situations in Arnhem, or wherever, where you had 4 squads and needed to hold on for a half hour to get a decent cease fire. On the other hand, the Combat Mission series took the war to 3D but kept the extremely complex morale system and tank combat. Yet I never found the series quite as engaging due to a lack of any meaningful campaign system and clunky, abstracted interface and graphics. What I always wanted more was a strategic system like that of the later Close Combat series mixed with 3D graphics, and I think I've found that in the Graviteam Tactics series.
I've now played a handful of different operations on some of the expansions as well as the original map and I've enjoyed it immensely. There was much talk about the terrible interface and whatnot in the reviews, but I think if you've played Close Combat or CM the controls are more or less normal, especially when using the right click interface to use the most common movement commands. That being said, the learning curve here will still be large for anyone new to the series and you probably won't do well your first battle. Incredibly, the game starts you out with a night mission where you will probably wonder at first if the game is even working. Once the first firefights kick off and you see tracers flying you'll probably be entertained enough just watching, but most people will probably be baffled as to how to do anything. The graphics and sounds as a whole do a great job of making you feel like you're really in a frozen battlefield, though the sounds aren't the highest quality.
I somehow won my first operation, despite having no idea how it really worked. I still don't really understand resupply or what half the indicators mean, even after reading the manual. But it's still a ton of fun and gives some really unique gameplay. The strategic layer adds a ton to the game, leaving you to make the decision to press for an attack with weakened troops or hold back and regroup. Sometimes you'll find yourself forced to defend for the 6th battle in a row with a couple of platoons reduced to a few squads with no ammo in a town reduced to rubble. When it comes to the battles themselves, they're an hour or less in length and vary wildly in how they go. At times you'll have battles where you and the enemy immediately cease fire because you're so weak. Other times you'll have a 45 minute long running gun battle with tanks exploding left and right and hundreds of casualties.
Generally your men do what you tell them to do, though you don't need to micromanage too much in this game. Even just using the right click command modes, there's a great variety of commands to give you flexibility. Morale and command are modeled well and I haven't seen many times where my men reacted in unexpected ways. Most battles I have played I enjoy, even when getting destroyed by the enemy, which happens more in this game than I'm used to from other games! Enemy AI tends to be smart and will maneuver around you if they find a way. Cover is well utilized in the game, with buildings, forests, hedgerows, etc giving your men cover in what feels like a realistic way. Using certain commands you can tell your men to find cover when they get to a place which is a great feature.
That all being said, this game isn't perfect. Tank pathfinding can be terrible and inexplicably dumb. Tanks will sometimes crash into a tree and not realize that they can back up and go around it. Sometimes things happen when it comes to the results of a battle which make no sense, and there's no real explanation of why you just knocked out 10 tanks and lost none but got a total defeat. Sometimes your men decide to lay in a field rather than the fence with bushes 5 feet away from them. But my biggest complaint thus far is with the friendly AI units.
In operations where you have allied units they will be AI controlled on the strategic map as well as in any battles where you have your own troops involved. I have found that on the strategic level they're worse than useless, with Tiger tank units moving to a far off, peaceful corner to defend nothing while Russian tanks destroy my lines just to the side of them, or my lone KV units deciding they just don't feel like fighting battles and moving behind my lines to hang out. If by some unfortunate event end up in a battle where you have all infantry and the AI controls your tanks or AT guns, forget it and just run away. The tanks will probably go get stuck in a ditch (or in one case, my AI tank decided to crash into a destroyed tank hull and get stuck there) or drive off away from your defenses. The AT guns will probably be in the middle of a forest and will ignore that road 20 feet away where the enemy tanks have to drive. Luckily, I've read that you can turn the AI control off and use the units as your own, with some penalties, which is still much better than letting the AI ruin your game.
Overall, however, the pros far outweigh the cons. This is a highly realistic, beautiful wargame which is a great successor to the Close Combat series. If you always wanted a 3D version of that and found other games lacking, this game is worth checking out. The AI isn't perfect, but the enemy AI at least is generally good and can beat me much of the time. The DLC that I have played are all very cool and well worth picking up, especially during a sale when it's 2 or 3 bucks for an operation which should give you 10-20 hours of new gameplay. I plan on buying the next game in the series once I've finished this one and all the DLC I bought, and I expect it to be great as well!

The story is fantastic. Absolutely a 10/10. It's just so well thought out. The pacing is just so perfect. The characters are extremely, extremely believable, and everyone's motives make sense. The story is somewhat dynamic, and is affected by your choices. It's emotional. Like, really, really emotional. You're gonna get really frikin' close to a certain little girl, and you're gonna feel sad when other characters die. But, a genuine sadness. Like, as in, you're gonna not like it when they die (ok, well, not EVERY character, some you're gonna wanna punch in the face), and you're gonna think "that's not fair. How come they have to die?". In terms of story, this game is an absolutely master piece.
The replay value is really, really awesome as well. Because the story is affected by your actions, every time I made some sort of decision the first thing I thought would always be "man, can't wait to see how the other decisions would have turned out".
The gameplay gets the job done. It's really just there to make it not a TV Show.
Two features that I really really like are how after each episode, you get to see the all the major choices you made, as well as what percentage of the player base made the same choice, or the opposite one. It's really cool to see how similarely or differentely other people think to you.  The second feature that I really enjoy is the lack of quick saving. The game has check points, meaning you don't have to do any thinking in terms of saving the game. Honestly, although I am extremely guilty of using quick saves, I really appreciate games that don't have them. Take a game like Dishonored. Part of the fun is figuring out how to get yourself out of sticky situations, but because of the quick saving feature, if I messed up in even the slightest way I would just go back, reload and be back in business. I accidentally got Ghost for some of the levels because of it.
But keep in mind, because this game saves at certain points for you, this absolutely is not something you'll hop into for 5 minutes then hop out. Only play it when you have a decent chunk of free time (I recommend a minimum of 20 or so minutes).
Does this game have bugs? Yes. Does it have the occassional frustrating gameplay bit? Yes. Does that mean you shouldn't buy this game? Absolutely not. Despite there being some apparant flaws, I would still give this game a 10/10. It's not perfect, but it's a a damn master piece, and honestly a work of art. "But Doctor, video games can't be art". Ha, try saying that after playing this.
Thanks for reading, and if you see any typos please tell me.
In short, if you're not fans of classic games, don't buy/play this games. The bad AI and many bugs makes this games bad.

A lot of people seem to hate this game becuase it is too different from its predecessors and to some extent I can see what the complaints are about, however I don't think the game is as bad as people claim. Before I wrote this review I went back to Jagged alliance and Jagged alliance 2, loved both those games and played them a lot (btw the ui in those two games haven't aged well, specially the first game).
Jagged Alliance Back in action is more of a spiritual succesor rather than a "Jagged Alliance 3" and for that I think they did a decent job. The ui is much better than previous installments and the real time combat (which you can pause to give orders) is a refreshing additon that makes the game feel more fluent than previous installments. That being said I am a big fan of the Xcom remake by Firaxis and I can see the potential of turnbased combat done well. A future installment of Jagged Alliance could possibly add a optional feature where you could play "old school" with turnbased or real time. I don't find this to be a big issue.
What I do think is a big issue with this game is lack of "finishing touches", kind of poor item configuration and lack of modifications such as in previous installments (i.e. combining different materials to make new items or improve current items). By finishing touches I am referring to items that seem to have the wrong stats (there are mods that reconfigure items to the proper stats and ammo type), there's a ton of useless items in game that have no use at all (During my first playthrough it took me quite some time to figure out the clock and broken controller couldn't be applied to C4 to make a bomb). The game lacks many features that would have been handy, such as improved tooltip, an option to carefully open doors (since every enemy on the map seem to hear you when you open a door for some reason), an actual sneak system (you know as in previous installments). The tool tip in the game doesn't really give much info, i.e. the different traits that the mercs have don't actually mention what bonuses they get for i.e. "Expert Melee" (Another thing that mods sorted). One of the features I really miss is the ability to train your mercs, which is really needed for most of the mercs you recruit from Arulco (or you'll end up with a lot of "mules"). You could obviously train them by having them fight, repair or act as medic, but most of them have so poor stats that they can't do any of that decently.
Controls are good, I like the tactical system where you can give your mercs several commands and even sync their movements, however their pathfinding is horrible. More than once I've setup my mercs for an ambush while the last guy tries to run over people rather than around them and mess up my setup (since after a while the one being run up against moves to let the idiot pass). The fact that you never have to sleep is handy but unrealistic and makes the game faster paced than it should be. Rather than sleeping you can simply give your mercs something to eat to regain stamina. My "elite" squad didn't sleep for 7 days straight while they went from sector to sector and cleared it all out (and since there are plenty of medical supplies and food this was never an issue). The resting system from previous installments forced you to be more tactical about your choices, so you wouldn't be vulnerable during your main squads downtime.
The music in the game is ok, works well with the combat and at least I didn't get bothered by it in the long run.
I think the reason I like this game so much is more about the potential it has/had rather than the actual outcome. It had so much potential, but it seems almost as if the developers didn't have time to finish the game, it certainly lacks polish.
If you enjoyed this game I recommend trying out Jagged Alliance Crossfire, pretty much the same game but with a new mission. There are also some dlcs with just a tactical map mission (I tried one of them which was with Igor, Shadow and Fox), was quite fun but lasts you for about 30-60min depending on your playstyle).
If you do play this game my suggestion is play on hard since normal is simply too easy (keep in mind this is a tactical game your mercs are not rambo) and when you have finished the game try one of the good mods i.e. Realistic mod by Killatomate
, which sorts out many of the issues I've mentioned.

I know I'm about a year late on playing this game, but I have just finished it and need somewhere to let out the extra emotions that overwhelmed me over the course of this game. I'd like to start off by making it clear that this is my first "Tales of" game and am definitely going to be playing more in the future.
First, I would like to say straight away, that this game is not for everyone, and I would say that a majority of the negative reviews on here are from either people who are long time fans of the series who have very reasonable critique for the game or people who fall into the category of "not for everyone". So with that out of the way, here we go:
I bought this game on impulse without any prior thought, these are the exact kind of games I love, the sort of Hack-and-Slash RPG story rich game was right up my alley, however what first drew me in was the artstyle, as you can probably see, it is definitely unique, and not in a bad way. I must say I'm a sucked for the more anime artstyle games. So the art combined with the very fluid animations that blend together really well, especially during combat are something not just any developer could handle, and I understand that this is something strong in the series.
The story was intriguing from the very beginning and hits you with the flashbacks early on, I probably put the first 10 or so hours into the very first time launching the game because I was sucked in and couldn't look away. The characters are arguably the best part about the game, and with such a diverse cast, the writers did a phenomenal job bringing every character to life and having them develope as the game went on. This game balances seriousness with comedy perfectly as well.
Now the start of the game was very strong, but you will emotionally attached to some of the characters, and that will help fuel you for the mid to end game where the story really takes off. The soundtrack in this game really helps ignite the strong moments and set the game into motion, and you'll be asking for more. This is a game you will not forget and I'm basically writing this because I don't want to.
Unfortunately, there is no such thing as a perfect game and there was one con that could make or break the game for people and that is how a lot of the areas in the game are large and for the most part empty. Don't get me wrong, the environments are great, the colorful lands really pop out. The problem lies with the vast emptiness of space filled with nothing but enemies. There is not a lot of interactivity in the environment and so you feel like walking through a void most of the time.
Another problem with the game was the grindy feel it had to it. The combat was really enjoyable for me and I didn't mind the grindy part, but sometimes it was really time consuming and I felt guilty passing by an enemy so I would always go back for it.
On the topic of combat, the way combos work in the game is really satisfying, even if you set up your bindings to tap one button an entire fight (which is one thing some people might not like, but you can always spice things up if you really wanted). I feel like there are no two artes you couldn't string together without making a fluid combo. There are 6 different characters to play as, each with varying combat styles so theres something for everyone.
If I could say just a couple words to describe this game it would be: "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;
Forgive me for the crappy formatting, but I'm literally writing this off the top of my head, just minutes after reaching the ending.
I will give a warning, this is a long game so be prepared for that but I encourage you to not give up on it because it is truely a masterpiece. Do yourself a favor and PLAY THIS MAGNIFICENT GAME. Apparently there's also a demo, so there is no downside to playing it and I promise that at the very least anyone would get some entertainment out of the story.

This is a very tenuous thumbs up.  The pause/realtime system was indeed a break & a daring experiement for the franchise, but I think it works.  I'm not one of those "turn based purists" who think anything else is blasphemy.  I'm fine with it, actually.
The characters are familiar, and most of returning player expectations are met in that it delivers what it says on the book - a reboot of JA2 into a new game engine.  The same systems are all in play, and that's a good thing.  It's got your sector-by-sector conquer and consolidate, your cheesy dialogs and plenty of gun-fetish to go around.
But it also falls flat in some areas.  Any real firearms enthusiast can find a hundred different flaws, errors and downright screw-ups in that equipment list.  The AI, both friendly and enemy, is questionable at best.  A lot of the light humor from JA2 has either turned dark or disappeared.  With the helicopter removed, supply logisitics are simply nightmarish, now.  Most offensive of all, Elliot is gone.
, all that being said... when I look at this game and compare it to all the increasingly horrible crap out there that tries to leech JAs name whilst simulataneously grinding that name into the mud... I find myself compelled to defend the easily superior quality of this product on general principle.
The combat is still solid (usually), the tactics still interesting, the new problems that each town presents still challenging, and overall... yes, it's still fun.  Far from perfect, but fun.
In short, it is not the best JA game out there, but at least I can say is really
a proper JA game and not some crappy knock-off and/or wannabe junk.  It may just be JA2's ugly brother, but it's still family.  That's more than I can say for the rest of the garbage out there.

Welcome to Black Mesa where we take the role of Dr. Gordon Freeman, a physicist recently employed at this research facility located in the New Mexico desert.
Another normal day for Freeman, until a new crystal is up for testing, and all hell broke loose by opening portals between our world and the extraterrestrial one!
presents a top-tier sci-fi storyline about a simple person who has to fight for survival in a complex facility infrastructure, fighting not only aliens, but also military and mercenaries who try to destroy the entire complex.
The game treats the player with a mist of doubt and mystery, as we travel from section to section in hope to find answers, but only to find most devastating effects of the invasion. Fellow scientists and security guards are as oblivious as us, but this doesn't stop the player from teaming up with them for survival.
As the plot goes, the game delivers hints in small amounts by leaving trails of information with each new objective, as we explore the facility compound.
The storyline isn't practical, but leaves a huge deal of assumption to the player, and The G-Man proves exactly that. This is deliberate, and I for one love Half-Life direction, as mystery suits extremely well within Black Mesa.
When I first started
, I knew it was going to be good, but not that good!!! We shouldn't forget this game was released in the late 90's, and back then, this game had much higher standards of gameplay from every other FPS. Even almost 20 years later, Half-Life is still an enjoyable first person shooter to new gamers, and this just proves to how advanced
was back in the day.
Although this game is a classic, to me, was a refreshing adventure, as I no longer find games as these on the market. A game with no RPG elements, and yet delivers different type of approaches thanks to impressive AI and other mechanics that even some games released in today's age, can only dream of accomplishing.
Throughout the adventure, Freeman must survive the alien attacks, which teleport to our world with nothing in their instinct but killing us. Each enemy is susceptible to noise, so it's possible to stealth kill each enemy as long as a one-hit kills the target. Some aliens, however, are also manipulated by the smell of other small dead creatures, such as the bullsquid. Others, such as the vortigaunt show a cowardly behave, and become easy preys at close range scenarios. Those are just some examples one can use to survive the Black Mesa invasion, but thru out the years, players have found numerous ways to survive!
From time to time we actually have to escort scientists to open doors, or extra locations for more gear. These escort missions are actually fun to do, and far from boring and tedious as games usually portray them. I always enjoy having a scientist with me, I find their remarks quite funny considering the situation at hand!
Although the crowbar is Freeman's trademark, the rest of the arsenal available is satisfying, from the standard pistol, assault rifle, shotgun, grenades, crossbow, and even some pretty cool prototype machine devices! If you think this is cool, you can even use some alien weaponry too.
uses smart gun positioning, that when used correctly, can deliver the player some pure amusing moments of satisfaction. It's also satisfying when we finally figure out what weapon to choose on each enemy, and thanks to quick-save, there's no excuse not to explore all possibilities.
The design shows its age, but an HD patch is available within the game, that significantly increases the game quality, and with pretty much any resolution at your disposal, plus external mods out there,
can really become next-gen. Personally, I never felt the need to, but it's a choice.
Overall visuals are good, old but remarkable and atmospheric capable of leaving a trial to everyone who plays, and this is exactly why I'm not surprised why so many players feel nostalgic when comes this title!
The game delivers a fantastic journey from a simple day at work, to finishing off an Alien boss in a otherwold location, through the radioactive swears, to desert canyons, and even several science labs. An epic science fiction adventure, from a time where simply playing the game was a conquest. With linear levels yet quite disperse, and some simple and small puzzles between, you'll never feel you're in the same area twice. Even labs have a very distinct feeling and visuals, and the deeper you go, the darker are the secrets and it becomes obvious, Black Mesa is not just another facility!
Although NPC's are just groups of scientists and guards, there is one special NPC that changed everything for me... The G-Man! This is probably the most iconic character (other than Freeman himself), and I can't stop having a massive vibe from
(
), and overall influence of one of my favorite TV Series. This is obviously a personal comparison, as Half-Life is extremely distinct and offers a tremendous identity on its own.
Other NPC's deliver small amounts of dialogues, keeping it short and simple, but doesn't really affect the game at all. The soundtrack is based on ambient, and key moments during the game!
Replayability is present, not only by mods, but also by difficulty, with the hard-mode proving to be a nice challenge!
Overall
is a fantastic title, worth it of all the praise from the fans throughout the years. I enjoyed every single moment I had with this game, and some of the mods I tried. My journey won't end here, as I'm sure I'll return to the original. After all; "
".
9/10

Disclaimer/Disclosure: I have been a long time RTS lover, and that most definately includes the predecessor games of this, being Total Annihilation & Supreme commander. So much so that I decided to back this in the KS stage.
+£30 for new players to buy into a unique RTS, at a large discount as an upgrade for EA buyers and free for KS backers.
+Functioning game from a group of people with a penchant for silly sci-fi RTS, who constantly plan to tweak and add to it.
+large scale, solar system spanning successor of the wonderful Supreme Commander & Total Annihilation classics.
+Throw whole PLANETS at your friends.
-Map/vision control can be... disorienting, compared to traditional 'flat-map' RTS's.
-£10 as an upgrade for EA backers can seem... steep, if one isn't an avid player, and can seem a slight slap in face for them when new players get it effectively £10 cheaper.
To me, PA is a fantastic game for a muck about with friends as well as a slightly more serious, if comic, RTS experience. From building and swarming hordes of little throw away tanks to simply catapulting a planet at someone when you've had enough of them, it provides what is currently a unique experience.
PA has, admittedly, had a 'rocky' Alpha/Beta/Early access. On top od this, the way this 'release' has been handled is... shaky. Not clear to those that don't take a clear mind to it and read it through, understand it.
The game works. Everything promised upon the kickstarter stage has been delivered, and then some. And now they are releasing what they consider to be 'The game', plus additional, unplanned content, whilst dropping the old, 'original' from sale. And I can see why; the original was an EA, and had a LOT of reviews from it's time during EA, many complaining of features or issues that have since been added or dealt with over development. As such, they were in effect, out of date. So, The 'release' version is given it's own release, it's own page, and it's own chance to be judged not for what it was, but what it _IS_.
Yes, this is a bit of a niche game. Yes, the handling of the PR side on this release/upgrade is... not ideal. No, there is no scam or grand cash grab scheme here.
What is here is a wonderful and unique RTS experience, stemming from an even better branch of RTS's and acompany trying to go i alone away from the pressure of publishers.
And you know what? As something different to play every now and again, I quite like it.

While the game can be entertaining at times, there are major flaws with the design...
- Mercenaries are traditionally retired Special Forces down to those with minimal Armed Forces training.. Regardless, anyone working in a team would know not to shoot their own team-mate; the biggest game-play flaw to-date is that your own men will shoot the other. I've tried in many different configurations from 2 to 3 men per team. When I try to have the front man crouch and the rear man stand ( as is one important form ) the rear-man ends up in front because of issues with pathing and the front man, now rear, shoots the rear man, now front... Same with 3 man team, I try to have 1 crouch and 2 stand ( so 2 standing fire on either side of the crouched shoulder ) but the issue still arises. No matter the positions whether all crouched, proned, standing or in various different settings ( so they can move together ) they end up shooting each other.
- Pathing is terrible, team-mates get stuck in corners and run for ages before the system corrects the issue.
- Tutorial is heavily scripted and if you complete an action prior to it asking ( such as repairing the weapon ) then the tutorial breaks and you can no longer continue.
- Group pathing is also terrible, as mentioned in - number 1; the group does not move as one when you want it to if you want the game to be played as a RTS without setting up the space-bar system ( but players still don't move together even when you try ). Another issue is with rotation, ie you have finally got the crouched man in front and the standing man in rear, now when you want to move 90 to 180 degrees in another direction, it is reversed ( and lets hope the ai is in the correct position so your team-mates don't shoot each other ).
- When you order an item from the "online store", there is no estimated time to arrival regardless of whether you select "Standard shipping" or "Expedited shipping".
- Online Store Receipt doesn't list what you ordered.
- Online Store E-Mail when your items arive doesn't state which order arrived with which items.
- No common sense among mercenaries in this game. This game is more frustrating that enjoyable.
- If you give a weapon to a recruit and leave to the world map while the recruit is pulling the weapon out ( read as: They received the weapon, the dialog closed, the animation is playing ) the money, the weapon and the recruit is lost. You have to find or buy a new weapon in order to recruit the person for a second time.
- On level load, players randomly shoot their own team-player.
- Kill cam resets YOUR camera settings ( and game-play continues without being able to stop it when active meaning it needs to be disabled in the gameplay options [ game-play is the right spot for it because it interferes with it ] )
The game is riddled with bugs.

Fillmonov had never wanted to be a soldier but when the motherland called he took up arms, assigned as the leader of a small squad of artillery spotters in Makeev Halit's regiment. He didn't know much about the operation they were being sent on, only that the Germans had holed up on a hill and needed to be dislodged so the army could advance. It was his first taste of battle. Makeev led the regiment through a forest quietly and everyone thought that the germans must have gone home as they had received no fire. That notion was ended as they reached the end of the woods and ran right into the german's dug in fighting positions. They had been waiting and opened fire. The lucky men managed to get into cover behind trees and soon Fillmonov was one of the senior leaders still standing. He tried to call in artillery but the chaos of the battle made it impossible. Makeev went down to a burst of machine gun fire and the regiment was scattered to a few pockets of men desperately taking cover. Unaware of their prediciment the commisar ordered them forwards again. Fillmonov refused the order and instead stayed in cover behind the trees with the few remaining memebers of his regiment. He could tell by the gunfire in the distance that the other regiments were also getting hammered by German fire and he just kept his head down and prayed that they would break through to rescue him and his men. This didn't happen. Fillmonov took a fatal rifle round to the chest just one minute before relief arrived to sweep over the German positions. His regiment ended that battle with only three men left standing. All were killed in the battle to take the next german position farther along.

The story is fantastic. Absolutely a 10/10. It's just so well thought out. The pacing is just so perfect. The characters are extremely, extremely believable, and everyone's motives make sense. The story is somewhat dynamic, and is affected by your choices. It's emotional. Like, really, really emotional. You're gonna get really frikin' close to a certain little girl, and you're gonna feel sad when other characters die. But, a genuine sadness. Like, as in, you're gonna not like it when they die (ok, well, not EVERY character, some you're gonna wanna punch in the face), and you're gonna think "that's not fair. How come they have to die?". In terms of story, this game is an absolutely master piece.
The replay value is really, really awesome as well. Because the story is affected by your actions, every time I made some sort of decision the first thing I thought would always be "man, can't wait to see how the other decisions would have turned out".
The gameplay gets the job done. It's really just there to make it not a TV Show.
Two features that I really really like are how after each episode, you get to see the all the major choices you made, as well as what percentage of the player base made the same choice, or the opposite one. It's really cool to see how similarely or differentely other people think to you.  The second feature that I really enjoy is the lack of quick saving. The game has check points, meaning you don't have to do any thinking in terms of saving the game. Honestly, although I am extremely guilty of using quick saves, I really appreciate games that don't have them. Take a game like Dishonored. Part of the fun is figuring out how to get yourself out of sticky situations, but because of the quick saving feature, if I messed up in even the slightest way I would just go back, reload and be back in business. I accidentally got Ghost for some of the levels because of it.
But keep in mind, because this game saves at certain points for you, this absolutely is not something you'll hop into for 5 minutes then hop out. Only play it when you have a decent chunk of free time (I recommend a minimum of 20 or so minutes).
Does this game have bugs? Yes. Does it have the occassional frustrating gameplay bit? Yes. Does that mean you shouldn't buy this game? Absolutely not. Despite there being some apparant flaws, I would still give this game a 10/10. It's not perfect, but it's a a damn master piece, and honestly a work of art. "But Doctor, video games can't be art". Ha, try saying that after playing this.
