This game is, in a bizarre way, a kind of guilty "pleasure". HOWEVER, unlike other guilty pleasures of mine, where I geniunely enjoy them despite other people's opinions, I fully know this is game is awful. The reason I enjoy Daikatana the way I do is that I find it to be the textbook example of how good or interesting concepts don't always result in a good product.
On paper, the game seems like it SHOULD have been one the best shooters of the late 90's/early 2000's. Old school FPS gameplay, four periods in history to fight in that each have a unique set of weapons and enemies to keep things fresh, RPG-style leveling up mechanics, AI-controlled sidekicks that fight along side you, an in-depth storyline(Well, more in-depth than Doom and Quake at least) AND it was being spearheaded by the John FREAKIN Romero of iD Software fame! What could go wrong?
EXECUTION. That, and lots of mismanagement during the development, but mostly the execution. Remember all the concepts I metioned above? All of them turned to crap in some way.
-The AI sidekicks? They're horribly programmed, which means most the time they'll get themselves stuck on random level geometery all the time they're not running right into enemy fire and getting themselves killed.
-The RPG mechanics? They're... extremely simplistic, but okay. The only upgrades that really matter are the damage and HP increases.
-The storyline? It serves it's purpose of giving an excuse why you're traveling through time, but none of the characters are interesting in the slightest. Pretty bad considering Ion Storm (the developers of this title) released DEUS EX only a month later the year this came out. (Before you say anything, I know it was a different studio that made Deus Ex than Daikatana)
However, it's not ENTIRELY a write-off. Like I said in the beginning, the concepts behind this game seem like they would make a great game if they were put into the hands of a better team. I also think the soundtrack is pretty decent, too. Each time period has a different style of music to fit the mood. My personal favorite tracks are from the first and final episodes.
If you're interested in how NOT to make a first person shooter, or you're interested in so-bad-it's-good games, Daikatana is a must play! Otherwise, I would just buy Deus Ex, a much superior game from Ion Storm.

Wizorb is a Breakout style game that combines the familiar gameplay of Breakout with RPG elements. How does this interesting combination work together? Quite well, actually. While there are apparent flaws in the game at some moments, as a whole, Wizorb is worth playing.
While RPG elements are present, there is no real "story" to speak of. Simply put, you're a Wizard who uses paddleball magic to defeat monsters. Neat! By earning a high score and defeating enemies, you are awarded with gold (GP). This gold can be used to purchase extra lives, help the people of Tarot Village, and charms - such as triple balls, a magnet, double damage, and more - that are lost upon death. Gold is very plentiful in the game, making affording these things practically a non-issue. While this is not a flaw, it removes some thinking from the game.
Why is this game called Wizorb? There are also magic elements. You can cast fireballs to help kill monsters and destroy blocks, summon gusts of wind to direct your ball, and set your ball on fire to add penetration. Unfortunately, I largely ignored these mechanics as I did not really need them - there are no stages or puzzles that require clever use of magic, they merely make the game easier. You are limited in your magic use by a "mana" pool, preventing the game from getting too easy. There are missed opportunities to fully flesh out the use of magic in this game, however is is still a fun and innovative system.
There are four worlds in the game each containing 12 stages and a boss fight - there are additional bonus levels besides this. Each of these worlds carries its own theme and introduces new blocks and enemies.
The stages are - for the most part - well designed. I felt as though the later stages became too long and had too many invulnerable blocks, though it was still enjoyable. There are a few "cheap" things in the game such as instant-death, however they are sparse enough to not ruin the enjoyment too much.
The game's art style is very pleasing to the eye. It takes inspiration from the games of old, giving a pixelated look. This means the game has / will age very well. The enemies are pleasing to look at and fit the theme of the game; the bosses especially are very well designed artistically.
As soon as you click a button on the main menu, you'll be met with a satisfying sound that gets you ready for the game. A classic RPG-esque sound plays whenever you damage an enemy, and the Breakout "dink" sound plays when our ball hits a block. While none of these sounds are amazingly designed, it all fits the theme of the game spectacularly.
My playthrough on Normal took about 4 hours. However, earning a high score on a level awards you with a star ranking for that world, giving something to work towards. There is also a Hard difficulty, achievements, and an in-game leaderboard.
I have very few annoyances with the game. However, you can only have one save file at a time. If you complete the game on Normal, your save file will be completely deleted if you want to play the game again on Hard difficulty. The game may also be difficult to get used to initially, especially if begun on Hard, however I do not consider this a real issue.
While it has its flaws, Wizorb gives a very interesting take on the standard Breakout gameplay. Each world was fun to play with each level being a joy to get through.

Yes, there are issues (as you'll see by the plethora of reviewers here who claim Titans is a cash-grab). Let's not forget that TA in its day would've cost the same, or more, as Planetary Annihilation - it just so happens that PA needed the Kickstarter campaign, with the milestone promises and subsequent issues that come with it, whereas TA was created in a simplier time whereby the financial investment required to create such a game was far more forgiving. The base mechanics of this game are great - it's accurately reminiscent of Total Annihilation (TA) and expands on it well by extending its reach to interplanetary proportions (as the name implies). Since Early Access it's become very efficient in maximising system resources. I achieved High graphics settings on my $600 PC tonight, at a solid framerate, which is more than I can say for many games. There's something very humbling about watching a sunrise over my modest little planet as a new day dawns and casts rays over my fabrication bots, which reminds me that I ought to finish building the engines that'll thrust my modest little planet into my opponent's modest little planet and destroy practically everything in its way.. humbling indeed. As far as scale is concerned, that sentence should've summarised it for you - this game represents a war that begins on the ground, with a single unit, and can (and will) escalate to proportions that you may or may not be able to control.
I played a match of PA tonight and I enjoyed it. I'm an RTS enthusiast - I can't get enough of Supreme Commander, and often I'll load up TA in a virtual machine and try to re-live some of that excitement I had as a teenager with too much time on his hands. I'm extremely critical of RTS games for this reason - I've been playing them since I could identify the keys on a keyboard - so for me to return to this game speaks volumes for its adherence to the core fundamentals of a good RTS.
I feel a need to defend this game, because the most popular reviews seem to condemn the "cash-grab" nature of the release. I ask those reviewers one simple question; if you promised PA in its full entirety, and it fell short because the sheer expectation from the fan base was so broad that you were obligated to deliver, wouldn't you do whatever was required to get those expectations met? Titans is a huge step toward exactly that, and despite its issues (which I'm sure will be resolved - Uber isn't EA, after all) this game will become everything the TA/Supreme Commander/RTS enthusiast fan base was hoping it would be.
TL;DR? Rome wasn't built in a day. Respect the numerous changes this massive game has gone through since Early Access, which is the stage in which I started playing this game. If you're new to this game, take the negative reviews with a grain of salt and give it a go; the worst that can happen is that you think it's crap and you can request a refund!

Just one tiny thing about me is that I'm the type of person where good gameplay can carry bad story or no story, but a good story cannot carry bad gameplay for me.
I started off on hard and only two fights gave me any challenge but they were fun because of that. One was the boss fight vs the exorcist woman and the other was a dire beast fight. Those two fights were so far a part from each other though and there is so much filler trash fights along the way that it's not worth it. Now you could say well just dont do all those trash fights, but the game compels you to do them not only just for exp but to master skills from your gear. Then there's the dungeons you fight everything in. So far the dungeons have been pretty boring and uninspired. Nothing different from the usual JRPG corridors of old with all the chests and secrets in plain sight.
The game's not all bad though, from what I've experienced of the story so far it actually seems pretty cool. You pretty much play as the bad guys, but not. It's definitely not the first time this type of story has been told but compared to a lot of other games it's still unique enough to enjoy. It's definitely a story I'd like to know more about but not enough to slog through hours of boring button mashing.
Now I'm still recommending it though, why? Because the gameplay isn't terrible and it isnt unplayable. Like I said during the challenging fights I definitely had fun. And the story and characters seem good and fun. So if you're not like me and dont mind an easy game for the story please go right on ahead.
I'm mainly writing this for the people who are like me and wanted to get back into JRPGS. This game is a JRPG through and through from the boring linear corridors to the countless lame trash fights. I was hoping for the gameplay to be so fun that I would want to clear every mob on the field but the gameplay couldnt support that and it all just became a boring chore.
If you're into JRPGs already go for it, otherwise I don't think this game transcends the genre enough to recommend to just anyone.

I've played a few Tales games and I think Tales of Berseria is a decent addition to the franchise. It does come with it's ups and downs though.
The combat system is very fast paced, fluid, and easy to pick up on since you can just mash one button repeatedly to get a great combo. The English voice acting is okay for the most part. Anyone over 18 has a fairly decent voice, however anyone below that sounds almost cringeworthy. I couldn't stand Kamoana's nail's-on-chalkboard voice and had to skip nearly every cut scene/skit she was in. Good thing there are subtitles.
As for the plot, it's a slow build up. Back stories and explainations are vague at most and won't be revealed until much later in the game usually in side quests. ToB is regarded as a stand alone game even though it's a prequel to ToZ. I never knew that until later when some friends told me, and I think if I had played ToZ, let alone own it, before or after ToB some of the plot points would have made a bigger impact.
All in all, I'd give Berseria 7/10. It is a good game with plenty of content and replayability. Afterall, I have 80+ hours and that's just on my first playthrough.

They've remembered how to make a Tales game.
Pros:
* The story is really good. It's infinitely better than Zestiria's cliche story.
* The characters are refreshing and unique
* You know that really cliche RPG protagonist? The guy that's brave, probably has a sword, a few friends, and wants to save the world just because they're a good guy? Well, fear not. This game's characters are not cliche like Zestiria's protagonist.
* The battle system is great, just like Zestiria's. The most unique thing about it is that every attack is now an art and you assign them to any button you want. You can actually do different and unique combos, unlike previous games where your basic "A" button combo never changes.
* 60 fps. (You can also play at 30 fps, if your computer is slower.)
* There's a good equipment enhancement system that allows you to make your weapons stronger using materials you found around the world, obtained from defeating enemies, or obtained from disassembling weapons you aren't using.
* Extra bosses. Just like in Zestiria, every map has a boss you can seek out and fight. Berseria takes this one step further. If you're doing well against enemies in an area, a dire foe has a chance to spawn. This is another boss you can fight. However, dire foes usually have the ability to spawn in a few different areas, so there isn't one dire foe per area, unlike the bosses you can find by walking around.
* An incentive was added to actually fight these bosses. You get these item things that give you new abilities in battle. Very cool.
* Traveling around the world is easy, unlike in Zestiria. There are items you can use to warp to towns and dungeons. The items you need to do that aren't THAT rare, so travel between cities isn't a big problem. Also, when you're well into the game, you get a hoverboard that lets you walk around faster.
* The soundtrack is amazing.
* There are tons of minigames to do. Playing them ears you Tales Coins. IIRC, everything you can buy with them isn't that good, so you don't need to feel pressured to play the minigames if you don't want to.
* The game keeps track of your active sidequests, like Zestiria.
Cons:
* Dungeons are very, very bland. I'm surprised nobody else has said anything in their reviews. Similar to Tales of Zestiria, the dungeons just feel like big empty rooms just jam packed with tons of enemies to make sure it takes you forever to get to the end. There's very little you can interact with in the dungeons. RPGs struggle with this often, and Berseria didn't do much IMO to make the dungeons fun to go through. It also doesn't help that they're so big. When I think of dungeons in this game that have stuff to interact with, or a puzzle, only one dungeon comes to mind.
* Costumes that should already be in the base game exist as overpriced DLC. The swimsuit you can get without DLC is bland and everybody has the same one. The $12 Summer Holiday Costume pack has the unique ones that should've been included in the base game.
* I feel I need to mention this again Look at the price at this stupid costume DLC. I did some quick math. If you bought all the costume DLC, you would spend $60.93. That's more than the base game costs.
* There's an okay number of side quests. I think they could've done better.
* 60 or 30 fps cap only. You can't have 144 fps. Not that big of a deal.
Verdict:
I would recommend this game to any JRPG fan. It has the good story you want, a fun battle system, and good music. The only big problem is the long and tedious dungeons. They're bland and you spend so much time fighting enemies. If you can get over that, play this game. If you can't go play the Mario & Luigi RPG series.
So, what can I say? Realy, I am commenting on the first game of one of the best game series for PC ever created, there are no words to explain how great these games are.
Extremly casual and about nothing feels good about it. I haven't ever experienced a worse melee combat than in this game, which sets the base opinion about all the other combat systems as well.

So, I finished my first run on WotC (link WotC-review:
and with also 200+ hours on my former 2nd account I think that I can now make a review about this game.
To say sth at the very beginning, this game is great. It keeps me playing it and is a magnificent turn-based strategy title.
Story: Following a new aspect the game starts with the scenario of the aliens having conquered whole earth. XCOM is now not more than a resistance group which tries to rescue humanity that now mainly has trust in the Elders and in ADVENT, a alien-human-like hybrid organisation that keeps free will supressed and that has official control over the earth.
The story is mainly told through specific story missions and researching several corpses or devices. It is not that amazing, but it has that much a turn-based strategy game like this needs.
Gameplay: Is split in general into two "modes": Guerilla-Missions and Base management. The base management let us do several things on our base AVENGER: Building specific facilities with several functions such as training soldiers etc., researching corpses and devices so we can create equipment and have other advantages, building equipment, managing soldiers and exploring the geoscape. On a map you can scan for ressources, accept missions and make contact to the resistance networks. Missions will mainly appear randomly while scanning, I'll continue talking about them below. The aliens also have specific "Dark Event Cards" which are projects giving you disatvantages. You can mainly clean one of them via specific mission.
The Guerilla missions are turn-based missions. You take the control over a troop of 4 soldiers (at the beginning) which can be expanded to 6 via upgrades. The main soldier classes are Sharpshooters, sniper rifle users and also skilled in using pistols, Specialists, medic troops also having the ability to hack specific things, Grenadiers, explosion troops, and Rangers,
equipped with a sword for close range. Later on you can also unlock Psi-Operatives, psionic gifted soldiers, as well as other units depending on how many expansions you have installed.
In such missions you have to take out enemies, save civilians, save VIP etc. depending on mission type. The enemies of this game are well designed and vertasile.
I just want to warn from one "issue": The shots are always depending on an percentage. To make it short, it could mean to have a 95%, a 97%, a 99% and even a 100% miss. And a 1% hit. I encountered all of that for myself. It's sometimes ridiculous.
DLC: Here is a short summary of the CONTENT expansions which have released released yet:
- Alien Hunter: Adds a new mission, some items and three bada$$ boss aliens which are REALLY tough. If you wanna suffer, go and get it :). Definetely NOT recommended for beginner.
- Shens Last Gift: Adds a mission and a new robot unit.
- War of the Chosen: See link above, heavy expansion.
Mods: The mod support via steam workshop and Nexus is amazing! Contains cosmetic mods, new enemy mods, tweak mods, high-difficulty mods, making-game-easier mods etc. There are so many magnificent mods by the community available that I cant now live without!!! There is also a complete total convention named Long War 2 by Pavonis Interactive which is great! The mod support is basically one of the best Ive ever seen. And if you have a few program skills you can create mods by your own via development tool.
To just make a conclusion: This. Game. Is. Great. It's really addictive!!!! Definetely recommended for fans of turn-based strategy games.

- The character moves so slowly. Too slow for a game which requires so much running around like this one. After a while you receive Wanderer's Ventite, an item which says that it increases your map movement speed by 10%, though i can hardly see the difference (AND SERIOUSLY WHY DO YOU HAVE TO ADD SUCH AN ITEM IN THE GAME INSTEAD OF MAKING THE CHARACTER RUN AT ACCEPTABLE SPEED???). Everything that can be said about this game has been said, but the most important question would be, does the game still hold its own to this day? To this my response would be, “more than you’d expect”.
Initially, I was lured back to the series after “Epistle 3 Leaks”. While I anticipated a mediocre trip aided by my nostalgia goggles, I was pleasantly surprised by how well the title aged, like fine wine that tasted better over time. There are several reasons to why I derived to this conclusion, allow me to convey each in description below.
Firstly, the GoldSrc engine might be a bit dated graphically, but it is good enough to represent whatever model it needs within the game play, delivering good performances with smooth animation. You will come to appreciate how detailed the models for each entity are, despite their low polygon count. Comparing to the games today, you will noticed just how much work was put into optimisation, along with full on compatibility with a range of operating systems. Something I wish I could say the same for the developers today.
Secondly, the plot of Half Life was well written by Marc Laidlaw, it is just as good today as it was back in the yesteryear. You will be drawn in by the dubious stance of Black Mesa in its teleportation research, its lack of care in human resources as well as ethics. As well as the mysterious Xen forces and Nihilanth’s motive in invading Earth. The enigma that is G-Man still puzzles us to this day in who exactly he works for.
Thirdly, the AI technology in this game is just phenomenal. Marines would work in concert with one another, putting down suppressing fire while encircling you from behind. Houndeyes would hunt in packs with a leader, changing their behaviour and attack pattern based on the pack’s strength. Vortigaunts would retreat in fear but regroup in numbers, rallying in the safety of cover. Hardly any of these advances are even visible in games today, which are just upsetting to say the least.
Fourthly, the arsenal which Gordon can play with is very well designed, each gun has its own specific use and none of them are ever obsolete, just because you found a new shiny gun. Each section of the stages can be tackled with different weapons in different play styles. Sure they might not be perfectly balanced in multiplayer, but a community still exists to this day for its death matches, that should speak for the quality in itself.
If you have the fortune to play Half Life before, then I believe no amount of convincing is required. However, if you came from a newer generation of video game enthusiasts, you should give this title at least a single try in your lifetime. No regrets, Mr Freeman.

The decision to recommend this game or not is probably the most difficult I ever had on Steam.
I'm old enough to have seen the dawn of videogaming, I like very much science fiction and I do not dislike FPS if they have a good story to tell. For some strange coincidence I never tried HalfLife so far, I knew it was considered a master piece and I thought I would have played it sooner or later, untill almost 20 years later ...
The story is pretty simple. You start moving all the way in a secret base down to you laboratory, this trip makes you realize the huge size of the base. Something went wrong during an experiment, and aliens arrives on this side of the universe. Then it's time to  flee for your own sake, meeting and cooperating with other survivors on the road. Aliens are bad enough, then you are going to survive to the army, which isn't sent in to to help survivors, but to clean the mess.
The graphic is outdated, few skins for scientists and guards becoming soon repetitive. Acting voice and sounds are outdated too. During all the playtime I've been very engaged, I felt being a survivor running for my life, trying to help people along the road and find solutions fo move forward.
Control isn't good, there's always a feeling of slipping on ice and jumps are difficults.
I meant to finish it, but motion sickness moved in. I'm not able to play for more than 60 minutes before experiencing it and after several sessions I eventually quit.
It's clear to me that this game was a masterpiece, it made history, but 20 years later it's not enjoyable anymore.
All in all I think you should try it, there's often the opportunity to get a good valve games bundle. This game has overwhelming positive reviews, and mostly all the negative are biased against valve for having quit the development of the line (which is a pity)
I'm looking forward to play BlackMesa and HalfLife2.

The game is a solid 8. It exceeds in Character building and story telling.
The combat is decent, nothing spectacular.
The one downfall is exploration.
Let me explain.
The areas are massive, sprawling maps filled with absolutely nothing but monsters and a few chests here or there. They're basically waste lands.
You have to wait until HALFWAY through the game to get arguably the best item- the geo board.
This lets you move at about 1.3x speed than normal. Great for fields.
that's fine and dandy, right?
No.
To use the board you have to grab the geo panel in the area, first. That wouldn't be a problem other than the fact the geo panel is usually a screen before the end of the area.
This is especially tedious because in dungeons and field alike, sometimes there are "puzzles"- More or less switch gimmicks that are linear and take no thought to figure out, but they force you to walk alllll the way to the other side of the map and back to get. In one area, it's maddening.
Then there's fast travel. It's great when it works, but often times you can fast travel because you haven't activated a skit. Sometimes, skits appear when you get to a certain point on a map. Sometimes they're beneficial to the story, othertimes not. Regardless, they hinder you from freely going town to town dozens of time in your adventure. It makes no sense that they don't let you warp, and then show you the skit you missed.
This game would be a solid nine if the exploration were fixed, and a solid ten if the combat were more involved. Don't get me wrong, it's still a great game. I've put 75+ hours into it- but you must have patience, because honestly? I'd say the pacing is worse than Tales of Zestiria.

Having played this game on and off for over the course of 4 years, I suppose I can safely not recommend this game.
The point of the game was to level up a character, max out its stats, and use the character to run dangerous and challenging dungeons and events in hopes of getting rare loot and collecting more fame (leaderboard points instead of Exp. after hitting max level). Eventually your character would die, as is inevitable in a permadeath game, at which point you'd be rewarded for a life well spent which hopefully involved acquiring a bunch of expensive and rare loot to sell off or use to fund a new character's stat progression and repeat the process anew.
This was not always the case though. A couple years ago there was a 1-time use item called the Amulet of Resurrection that acted as a life condom and safely teleported your character to the Nexus if you were "killed". As a result, players could safeguard themselves from death and the wealthiest players were able to afford multiple amulets in order to continue cheating death. This has since been removed shortly after Kabam bought the game.
While the "topping the leaderboards" aspect is still there and the game is back to being permadeath, PAY2WIN has been implanted so much into the game that it's effectively made melee classes overpowered to near invincibility and made the Priest class (traditionally underpowered party healer) obsolete. What does that mean? Well, players can buy pets with varying skills such as Heal, Magic Heal, etc etc, which they feed through use of experience or gold with items in order to level them up. The higher the level, the faster and better the heals. These pets act as pocket healers and the whole thing is pretty expensive but it pays off when you have a little buddy that heals you so much and so quickly that you can stab a Sphinx in the face without worrying about HP loss.
Inb4 git gud. Players shouldn't have to spend a bunch of money for pocket healers that essentially let them ignore shotguns to the face.
Weapons and armors from mid to high tiers (excluding the ones unique to realm and dungeon bosses) can easily be purchased in the marketplace in the Nexus. This only requires some gold which can be purchased from the in game store for a couple bucks.
Bots. Tons of spam bots everywhere but that's easily ignorable if you change chat visibility on your settings. However this may be changing since the game changed hands a couple months earlier and the new owners have introduced bans in the once lawless land of Kabam-owned ROTMG.
If you ignore all the P2W and everything mentioned above, then yeah, I guess it's kinda alright. The new owners are keeping the P2W aspect but also getting involved with the players. It's certainly fun enough at first but if you're like me, you'll feel it's a waste of time when everyone and their grandma can pay their way to curbstomp everything.

Bastion is a game that every Gamer HAS to play.
Let me explain something: I don't normally play or like games similar to Bastion. I'm not a fan of action games like this, even if they have a lot of depth in combat like Bastion does. What makes me like this game so much, then?
Its the unique method of storytelling. There is narrator who narrates everything that happens as you play, commenting on plot events or things the player does. Sometimes, he just fills in the lore during downtime. This narrator also has an "epic movie" kind of voice that makes it fun to listen to. Essentially, Bastion puts a new spin on storytelling, and it is really clever.
Some other great aspects are the beatuiful art styles of the game and the way the world builds around as you walk through it. Also, it has a wonderful award winning soundtrack (it definately deserves it!)
The gist of the game is that the world of Caeldonia, some sort of flying city, suffered "the calamity" as was wrecked. You play as "the kid", one of the few survivors. What caused the Calamity? What was it? How do you fix it? Did anyone survive? Play to find out. There are even a few points where you have to make a tough decision that influences what happens next.
As far as combat, it can be repetive. But take that with a grain of salt, since action games are supposed to be like that and I'm not an expert on it anyway. It seems fluid and responsive enough, and while it isn't clever or groundbreaking, it isn't bad either.

Graviteam is a Ukranian based game developer, the same one responsible for acclaimed Tank Sims like Steel Armor. In Operation Star, they have very much brought their extreme attention to detail to bear on one of the most well-rounded WW2 RTS games on the market. Highly detailed renders, an expansive selection of units, massively scaled engagements, and a well developed campaign mechanic make Operation Star one of the most tactically realistic games out there, with countless opportunities to make the Ostfront yours.
The downsides: To play the game well, you face  a sizeable learning curve, as Operation Star will walk you through multiple interfaces that can control units from the company sized level, all the way down to the individual soldier. The interfaces themselves can be somewhat esoteric and time-consuming, and there are many ways to make mistakes. Communication lines, supply, morale. All of these things can work against you when first learning the interface.
Operation Star is also very graphics intensive, with its massive scale and sometimes overwhelming number of units. The optimzation is not ideal, and the issues will be taxing for older or less powerful platforms.
All in all, Operation Star is intensive and not without its issues, both in gameplay and system requirements, but you are very much getting into a game that will provide an immensely accurate and realistic depiction of what it takes to command an army.

There is a quick battle setup, but I really wish it could generate random battles based on your mission and the strength of the units you pick.  It does take a lot away to know exactly what units the enemy has and where they will start.
The unit selection is sort of limited.  I'm not sure if this is due to what was in use in the exact areas at the exact times simulated, but there are a fair number of 1942-3 appropriate vehicles from both sides that could be added.  This is especially true of air support, which is represented by only two aircraft on each side, and air defense, which neither side has any of.  The Il-2 would be a lot less scary with even a 20mm on a halftrack.
All in all, this is a good buy for anyone into 'serious' wargaming.  Steep learning curve, but quite immersive, and a lot of replayability.  If you want to see if the new Graviteam release, Mius, is for you, this is a budget priced way to find out.

Completely revising my review on SFV, as the games been out for awhile now and my feelings on the game have heavily changed.
THINGS I WON'T BE MENTIONING IN THIS REVIEW. THE♥♥♥♥♥♥RELEASE THIS GAME HAD. I don't feel like that's relevant in todays market when talking about this game. Yes, it released way too early at a 60 dollar price tag. The content has changed since then, so let's not beat a dead horse.
PROS
- Character roster is pretty diverse
- Cross play, so the community is never really dead
- The story mode is a thing
- Voice acting and music is solid. Not amazing, but decent enough.
- The fighting is fun if you're not playing in a competitive aspect.
- Netcode isn't... awful. This will be elaborated in the cons though.
- FGC will keep this  game alive until SF6 or some other odd circumstance
- Great modding scene. Some of these mods are top quality. Be warned for some NSFW mods though.
- DLC characters technically free if you earn the Fight money to buy them. I've bought 3-4 characters with fight money, so it's definitely possible to get the characters by doing character trials, the story mode/individual character stories, Fight money weeklies, and survival.
CONS
- STICK SUPPORT IS STILL NOT HERE! What the ♥♥♥♥ Capcom?
- Competitively, this game is incredibly unbalanced. Season 1 was chun/nash/ryu/mika city. Now it's Guile/Urien/Rog/Laura city. It's a powercreep for weaker characters getting hella buffed, and stronger characters getting hella nerfed. It's a♥♥♥♥♥♥way of balancing the game. There's apparently going to be another balance update to address this, but hopefully it'll make things a bit more centered as opposed to just basically crapping on anything great and making♥♥♥♥♥♥into super gold.
- Despite the story mode existing, it's not amazing. it's generic and nothing special. It's not unfun, just not fantastic.
- As stated, the netcode for this game isn't awful. But it's not great either. Some matches may feel like they're basically local, while others are jittery and awful due to the rollback. This isn't GGPO, but it's GGPO lite. It's incredibly frustrating to play SFV knowing netcode can be so unreliable.
- Rage quitting is still an issue. There was a patch released to try to punish rage quitters by basically putting them in purgatory, but was rolled back due to some issues.
- Game feels casual friendly. Obviously you won't be amazing if you're just a casual player, but if you're looking for an incredibly heavy combo based fighter, go towards another fighting game.
- IMO the character models are pretty odd. I'm not a fan of the asthetic.
- Censored character intros/SA's in this game. You can mod them back in, but it's just stupid.
- Servers can be shotty at times. Good lord this games servers  go down randomly or for maitanence frequently, and it can be pretty frustrating if you're looking to play online.
- Cash shop costumes and stages are a bit overpriced imo.
- Survival mode is awful and is the only way to get colors for the default costumes unless you buy them. ♥♥♥♥ that.
Overall, idk how to feel about SFV. I actually liked it more when SFV released, and now I just kinda only care about modding it. Everything about it screams "meh" in comparison to other fighting games I've played. If you are interested in it, I would recommend it for you if you enjoy mods and a competitive fighting game, but this game is almost a year old and is still suffering from issues that should be fixed by capcom. Hopefully this will happen soon, but I'm gonna stay skeptical until they actually make these changes.

While the graphics are gorgeous and the idea kind of cute, this Breakout/Arkenoid clone doesn't do enough to deviate from its roots, leading to gameplay almost always slowing to a sudden, grinding halt. While the magic system might have been able to help alleviate this a bit, your overall magic carries over between levels, leaving you wondering if you want to use a fireball on that last block now or save it for the next, even "harder" level. Magic can be refilled, but only if you find a potion or the ball doesn't hit anything for eight bounces; potions are much too difficult to come by, and by the time the latter happens you'll have probably already saved & quit. And don't ask me how townspeople in a 2D game managed to be so one-dimensional, but like the spell system they do nothing to dull the pain of so much repetitive gameplay.
Overall there's just too little spellcasting and too much ball-bouncing for this game to be worth anything to anyone but the most diehard of Breakout/Arkenoid enthusiasts. If you're really desperate for block-breaking with a twist, try Shatter, which is everything this game could have been sans retro coating.

Oh my god... So let me tell you. I just finished my first complete game of XCOM 2. I bought it when it came out and I enjoyed it. But I lost track of the game and did not get back to it, even though I was essentially on the last mission. Then I got the DLC and played it again. I lost track of it again and didn't complete my playthrough. I relate this history to you so you can understand how the DLC has changed the game. It is a game that was good in its release version. It was better with the DLC. But what I want to tell you is that the War of the Chosen is something else entirely.
Adding War of the Chosen to XCOM 2 is like buying a whole new game, a very good whole new game. But that's not all, it's like you bought that new game and then by some black alchemy blended it into a game you already had, and already really liked. The result is amazing.
Let me tell you why... War of the Chosen jailbreaks your options. Character (soldier) development in XCOM 2 was good, but still somewhat limited. Also, there wasn't much you could do with them once they hit Colonel. This is no longer true. There are two principle ways you can now advance soldiers in an incredibly flexible way. The first is the addition of an ability to use ability points to purchase abilities you choose not to take when they get promoted. Each soldier also gets a random assortment of abilities from other classes they can add on. The combinations are fascinating and sometimes you level up new soldiers just to see what they'll figure out. You can also give small boosts to individual stats by sending soldiers on covert missions. They have other objectives, but for me the real advancement was small permanent stat boosts for my favorite soldiers. The result? Tons of customization before you even start handing out equipment.
Once you get your soldiers decked out with custom skills you also have the opportunity to train them in 2-man teams. These teams deployed together provide additional actions, free shots, and a bonus to resist the mental strain of combat.
Also, pulling from popular mods, War of the Chosen adds a 'tired' function so that even after a flawless mission some soldiers will need rest before fighting again. It encourages developing a deep bench of talent which spices up the game by keeping you from falling in a rut of killing aliens in only one way with your one squad of super soldiers.
And the equipment is still incredibly varied. You can now research advancements to slot additional modifications into your weapons and to reuse ones as you change the weapons around. Welcome to the weapon modification bonanza.
Then there are factions. Factions are an excellent addition to the game both in terms of story and gameplay. With a global alien government you may have been wondering how it was that only a couple dozen humans in a highjacked alien ship managed to do *anything* about the alien invasion. No longer the case. There are now three advanced and fascinating factions, even if each is a little homogenous. They also each give you a completely unique new class of soldier. There are covert marksmen (reapers), defected alien-human hybrid advent (skirmishers) and a new class of psionic soldiers (Templar). Their additions are a welcome spice and the idea that other humans are out there fighting the good fight helps the story feel 'beefier.'
The Chosen themselves (alien hunters stalking you) do effectively add mid-game stress, though if you love tweaking a squad out with abilities the aliens will quickly become punching bags. The game is not easy. But it rewards a deft and flexible hand. Your super soldiers can still be injured or die very quickly, but a carefully managed turn will mow aliens down at a rate that will make you wonder who is whose worst nightmare. On the other hand, bungle it and watch your soldiers go down to precise focused fire. Success still rests on a knife's edge. Even with my final squad of carefully developed super soldiers, it took careful thinking to sequence abilities in their most deadly combinations. Were the combinations deadly? Oh my, yes. Did the aliens stand a chance? As long as I physically avoided giving myself brain damage and kept my five year old from jumping on my mouse arm and sending soldiers out into the middle of a firefight with no cover (it's happened), no they did not. But managing the whole process so that XCOM was that capable, that was glorious.

As most Tales of Games, this game will only start to get good after you already invested a good amount of time in it. This time it were 20 hours into the game when I finally started to enjoy it. In fact, I didn't really like it at all in the beginning. The lack of Artes makes the Artes-tree look like a joke and the tutorial area, while serving as a background as to why Velvet is the way she is, felt too long and tedious. With that said, it's a pretty good game and probably in my top 5 Tales of games list. I'd like to cover some points though:
-story: The game starts out really strong and you are basically playing as the bad guys, slaughtering your way through villages and cities on your way to avenge Laphicet's death. That was pretty great. However, the devs do a 180° turn at the end of the game and now you are basically playing as the good guys. I really wished they would stick with the evil theme till the end. Since I'm pretty sure that we won't see another evil themed cast for a while, I think it was a wasted opportunity
-characters: The cast in this game is really strong with Eizen and Magilou being among the best characters in the series. The only character I didn't really like was Eleanor since she felt out of place. Always looking down the rest of the party and acting like she was above everyone else. I guess her only purpose was to give fans the "good girl". I personally could have done without her
-difficulty: the difficulty is all over the place. I picked the highest difficulty as soon as it was available that is hard -> intense -> chaos. The game is super easy. 99% of the battles you'll crush the enemy before he can even move. And then there are those 1% battles later in the game aganst dire foes that will wipe you out without any chance of fighting back. I would have wanted a better balance there.
-skill system: It sucks. Skills are tied to your equipment and you are basically just swapping out gear to get the skills. I want a real skill sytem like in Xillia back. Upgrading gear is beyond pointless because you will constantly swap out your gear for better stats and/or skills by the time you are able to upgrade your gear, especially on the higher difficulties since you get so much grade for battling. By the time I reached the highest possible gear I was already finished with the game so I couldn't even upgrade that one. It's just a mess.
-dungeons and puzzles: Dungeons and areas in general are really bland. They mostly consist of hallways and large areas with a ton of enemies slapped on to them. Puzzles, or "puzzles", are basically nonexistent since all you have to do for the majority of the game is pressing X on a switch right next to the door you want to open. I wish they go back the more advanced puzzles of games like Symphonia or Abyss.
-voice over: The english voices are really top notch. Minor 2 complaints would be 1) Velvet's voice actor often talks through her teeth to sound angry which not only sounds stupid, it also is used in situtations were it doesn't really make sense. 2) Kamoana (see point: Kamoana)
-Kamoana: Oh boy. If this was a 10 out of 10 game then Kamoana single handedly would put it down to 9 out of 10. This is by far the most disgusting and annoying character I've ever encountered in any medium be it videogame, movie or books. Her voice will make your ears bleed and her dialouge will result in losing brain cells. I started skipping through every scene she was in. I don't understand what the devs were thinking when they created this character.  I guess they wanted us to feel pitty for her, but that didn't work, at least for me. Absolutely disgusting character
I realize this was more of a rant than a review. Anyway, it's a good game with a lot flaws.

Tales of Berseria is the sixteenth (wow who knew?) entry in the popular Tales series of JRPGs by Bandai Namco Entertainment released Jan. 24th 2017.
Berseria shares the same world as the previous game in the series, Tales of Zestiria however it takes place in the distant past. The plot of the game is your standard fare for anime/JRPGs. You play as Velvet Crowe, a small town girl who loses her family through a mixture of betrayal and a disease known as daemonblight. Velvet becomes infected with daemonblight and transforms into a special daemon who feeds off of eating other daemons. After spending three years in prison Velvet escapes and vows to hunt down her betrayers. All in all not a terrible story but nothing groundbreaking.
Characters are much the same, with the familiar archetypes that have been seen over and over again. You get new party members for battle at a nice pace and the VA work is acceptable. While there are some good characters here, they fit into the same tropes you would see in any JRPG or Anime and none leave a lasting impression.
Gameplay in Berseria is also fairly cliche. You spend time split between traveling between towns collecting information/quests and in dungeons. The dungeon layouts are fairly linear with some branching paths that will circle back around to the main path after a room or two. Enemies will wander around the areas and if contacted will begin a battle sequence which is my biggest gripe with the game.
Combat in Berseria is a lot like a real time version of the combat in the Hyperdimension series. You are given a variety of different attacks that before a battle (or in the pause menu during a battle) can be chained together and assigned to a button. Each attack usually has a type of enemy that it deals bonus damage to and these bonuses can also be chained together for even more damage. Additionally you have to manage your “souls” which is basically the number of attacks you can perform in a chain before having to stop and recharge. You start a battle with 3 and can gain or lose them based on defeating enemies in each encounter or you can lose them by using some of your special attacks. In tougher battles you have the option of expending souls in an attack called a “break soul” These are large powerful attacks that cost you a soul but also heal you for a percentage of damage dealt.
While all this sounds good in theory, most battles come down to examining the enemies when a battle starts and creating a attack chain that will give the optimal bonus damage followed by smashing that button over and over again until the battle is over. The combat ended up being really simplistic and much like FF XIII I was often just smashing the X button every encounter and coming out just fine.
I’ve always been a big fan of JRPGs with the Chrono series and Persona being some of my favorites but don’t feel the genre has aged particularly well. Gameplay and combat never seems to evolve enough to feel like a truly new experience and while that may be fine for some, in a year where great game after great game is being released Berseria doesn’t set itself apart.
Tales of Berseria is a fine game and if you are a fan of the series I think the advancements to the combat system in this entry will delight you but I still came out of the experience feeling like I have played this game before. There just isn’t enough variety in the gameplay or a story that is captivating enough for me to enjoy playing a game this long (~50 hours) the whole way through. While there are some good parts here, overall the game doesn’t do enough to distinguish itself in a very crowded genre and I can only recommend it to true fans of the series.

Review Tales of Berseria
Tales of Berseria is an hack and slash japanese role playing game, and it's probably prequel of Tales of Zestiria but i'm 100% sure about it. Tales of Berseria's world is so vast that it seems like an open world just like Tales of Zestiria but actually both is not an open world game. It's an exploration game to be precise, The game isn't all that bad though but it's kinda boring especially the battle system, why ? Read further and you'll get the answer. As for the story, it's very anime just like usual.
To be honest, i've already bored of this game after over than 20 hours, don't get the wrong idea, it's not like that i'm suck or what but it wasn't all that good especially the combat. IMO, the combat feels so off, it feels like a mash button game even though it's supposed to be a hack and slash but you can barely dodge at all/ I mean like, the time that were given to dodge is extremely short and it's some kinda hard to read the animation.
Let's talk about it from the beginning
So, what you can do in this game ? Alot of things such as fighting, crafting, combining, exploring, etc but i'm not sure if you can call all that doing something. There's a lot of things to do, but it literally will start to get bored so fast, why ? 1st, the world is so big and you're moving so damn slow, you'll need to defeat certain powerful monster to get the key items that'll make you walk faster, 2nd the combat is so repetitive even though you can set up your own combos. 3rd The combat is awfully bad, and so easy even though i'm playing in the hardest difficulty that i can possibly do at that moment.
Let me explain the gameplay a bit, it's hack and slash, the ammount of combos you do will be limited by some kinda gauge that you can earn in battle when you kill the enemy or stun them or something like that. you will be  movied into the battle when you're encoutering an enemy, you can stack up the enemy so that you can earn more rewards including more money and item drop but remember if you're stacking the enemy, they will surely grow stronger than how it should be. You can customize your own combos as you leveled up since you can only obtain another artes through level up. There's also, cooking effect to give you some kinda booster in battle such as restore health, restore your gauge, etc, it'll also restore your health immediately outside battle
+ Smooth camera moves, it's even more smooth than in Tales of Zestiria even though the price is lower than Tales of Zestiria.
+ Good PC port, so far i have only seen few odds thing inside the game, and it has 60 fps on both cutscene and gameplay, and i don't experience such a thing as crashes or something.
+ Story is goods but very like anime, but i guess that's normal for JRPG.
+ Have both japanese dub eng sub and eng dub eng sub. Both of the dub are surprisingly good, i like the eng dub more than the japanese dub though, since i think japanese dub is not suited for game..
+ Graphic and arts are also good, some or maybe many people maybe said that it's bad or something, but i think that it's pretty good for JRPG, more like it's normal for JRPG.
+ Game inside the game, there are several mini games to obtain some custom for the character which is actually pretty fun to play.
+ Lots of accessories to be put to your character to make them cute or weird or maybe something hilarous.
- Surround audio system is not supported, the game won't make any noise if you turn the audio from stereo to surround, but it's not a major problem.
- Repetitive gameplay, the gameplay and combat were just the same as far as i can remember, except the mini games which is good for change paces.
- The game is too easy even in hardest mode available in my current state, but i think it can be upgraded to be even more harder but you'll need to kill certain monster before you can do it.
- Character's move speed in world map is way too slow for the vast world out there, need to defeat alot of strong monster to get your movement speed up.
I can't say i recommend this game to all RPG lovers there, but probably i'll recommend it to weab out there or maybe RPG lover who doesn't mind a repetitive gameplay. There aren't alot of bug that have a huge impact to the game. I think it's nont overpriced even at full priced but it's to those who doesn't mind the repetitive gameplay.

This game has the potential to be far greater than SimCity ever could be, considering EA's corporate greed holds it back so much these days. It features enormous cities and very easy-to-use interface systems to create a city EXACTLY the way you want it to look even with road-following decorations and multiple ways to plop out zones, then zooming in and "walking" around if you so desire - the level of detail is astounding, and I've personally been playing this series since it's predecessor, City Life, came out back years ago. The game has a major downside though - it's outdated 2005 graphics engine is a 32 bit engine not optimized for multi-core. No matter how good your PC is, the game is limited to only using 1 core and up to 4 gigs of ram - 2 gigs by default, editing the config file is needed to crank 4. This means large cities on even the toughest PCs will lag like all hell, while your PC shows virtually no sign of wear, often running far below 20% of max capacity. Community guides even state you have to quit and reload the game every hour and possibly even change your graphics settings far below what your computer should be able to support just to keep it running in larger cities.
Specs arent the issue for those of you claiming I have a bad computer - I run a hex core 3.5 ghz intel i7, have 64 gigs of ram, and 2 nvidia titans, and yet I clock as little as - well, 0 FPS at times. I have also tried it on a laptop running a quad core 2.7 ghz i7 with 32 gigs of ram and a GTX 680M with the same issues.

The presentation of Wizorb is superb, every time I boot it up it feels like I've just stuck a cartridge into the SNES - both the visuals and the sound hit their mark (unlike the orb which is still bouncing around aimlessly). You play as a mighty Wizard who's immense magic power seems to transform him into a...stick. Well, a paddle. Seeing that his next feat of insurmountable power is conjuring a little floating orb, this isn't as useless as it sounds.
The game at it's heart is a breakout style brick breaking game where you rebound a ball using a small paddle you control into the targets until none remain. Although there are a couple of spells such as engulfing your ball in flames to pass through multiple blocks or subtly altering its direction with a breath of wind, they really don't do all that much to change up the game and crucially, don't always stop you from the dreaded 'last brick standing' challenge of rebounding around the level for a few minutes until you get lucky enough to hit that last, stubborn brick.
You're tasked with helping a small village rebuild as you venture out and defeat monsters and destroy targets of varying shapes and sizes (I'm not quite sure what great threat a bush is to the already destroyed village, but its your task to crush them into leafy pulps!). The highlight to the gameplay is the boss battles, which is a neat little twist that see's you fighting a much tougher enemy that has a few skills of their own - it's just a shame this sort of thing wasn't the norm, as other enemies simply act as mobile targets.
I played the game with a mouse (the clicky kind, not the squeaky kind) and found the controls to be smooth and responsive, although I did get a slight stutter now and then - nothing that impacted the gameplay, but it did come close.
It's hard to recommend Wizorb to all but the biggest Breakout fans as it just doesn't offer that much compared to other brick breaking games, despite the wonderful presentation. If you're a fan though, its a fair price for what's on offer.

It gives you a notification when you're supposed to make a turn; however, if you're like me you end up missing some of those turns taking a completely different route to the finish never seeing the other cars again.
It does still have road rage and boost, but in normal races I end up taking people down at the starting line then never seeing them again.  It lacks the arcadeyness that made the series awesome.
It does have a lot of events though since every intersection has another event.  It also has a lot of collectibles (crashing into billboards, through gates, jumps) which will give you something to do but in the previous versions all your collectibles were just achievements, like getting a takedown off a mountain road ('gone fishin'').
So, in conclusion if need for speed (minus cops) mixed with burnout sounds good for you then you should buy it, otherwise don't waste your money.

I was really trying to decide between purchasing the Enemy Within expansion of XCOM: Enemy Unknown or XCOM 2. If you do your research, you'll find the main (perceived) negatives around XCOM 2 are things like the mission timers.
I have to say, this has not been a big deal to me. It gives you a really good number of turns to complete the objective, not the entire mission. Sure, at times, I'll have to complete the objective like hacking the terminal or shooting the relay antenna when I'd prefer to shoot at an enemy. It's not a great feeling being engaged in combat and exposing a solider to potential death for the sake of completing a mission. However, most of the time I complete the timed missions with 1-3 turns to spare so it's really not a big deal. The addition of Stealth adds a unique element to the game. If you're waffling between these two choices like I did, easily just get XCOM 2. It's a really well designed game.
I was able to defeat the game in about 30 hours of playtime. This was "save scumming" as I want to see all of the content. (For those who don't know, save scumming is when you reload a mission if it goes poorly).
My main critique of the game is that on my second playthrough, I decided to go to "Ironman" mode where the game doesn't save along the way unless you exit the client (so it saves your progress only, not your history). I didn't realize how many bugs were in the game until I couldn't reload! For instance, one mission one of my soldiers just died for no reason. The Alien turn didn't show anyone shooting at her. Strangely, looking at her corpse, there was still a full life bar hovering above her, but I couldn't click on her, she had no status, just couldn't interact with her as if she was part of the environment. She was my main medic, so you can imagine I lost the mission and it wrecked my entire Ironman campaign. As fun as Ironman was to play, I can't possibly play Ironman again knowing that there are game-breaking bugs (which if they haven't fixed by now, they never will).
As with other XCOM titles, replayability for me is low. Not sure why I'd spend 30 hours beating the game then play what is essentially the exact same content, perhaps slightly different sequence. War of the Chosen has some good reviews, but it's clearly not worth $39.99 USD even if it adds a lot of content, that's the price of a few new games during Steam's sales. I will probably pick it up when it reaches 50% off.
I don't play many single player games, but 30 hours seems low to get through the content. Maybe it's not. I would definitely recommend this game, however, especially now that you can get it for < $20 on sale it's easily worth that price tag.

Review Tales of Berseria
Tales of Berseria is an hack and slash japanese role playing game, and it's probably prequel of Tales of Zestiria but i'm 100% sure about it. Tales of Berseria's world is so vast that it seems like an open world just like Tales of Zestiria but actually both is not an open world game. It's an exploration game to be precise, The game isn't all that bad though but it's kinda boring especially the battle system, why ? Read further and you'll get the answer. As for the story, it's very anime just like usual.
To be honest, i've already bored of this game after over than 20 hours, don't get the wrong idea, it's not like that i'm suck or what but it wasn't all that good especially the combat. IMO, the combat feels so off, it feels like a mash button game even though it's supposed to be a hack and slash but you can barely dodge at all/ I mean like, the time that were given to dodge is extremely short and it's some kinda hard to read the animation.
Let's talk about it from the beginning
So, what you can do in this game ? Alot of things such as fighting, crafting, combining, exploring, etc but i'm not sure if you can call all that doing something. There's a lot of things to do, but it literally will start to get bored so fast, why ? 1st, the world is so big and you're moving so damn slow, you'll need to defeat certain powerful monster to get the key items that'll make you walk faster, 2nd the combat is so repetitive even though you can set up your own combos. 3rd The combat is awfully bad, and so easy even though i'm playing in the hardest difficulty that i can possibly do at that moment.
Let me explain the gameplay a bit, it's hack and slash, the ammount of combos you do will be limited by some kinda gauge that you can earn in battle when you kill the enemy or stun them or something like that. you will be  movied into the battle when you're encoutering an enemy, you can stack up the enemy so that you can earn more rewards including more money and item drop but remember if you're stacking the enemy, they will surely grow stronger than how it should be. You can customize your own combos as you leveled up since you can only obtain another artes through level up. There's also, cooking effect to give you some kinda booster in battle such as restore health, restore your gauge, etc, it'll also restore your health immediately outside battle
+ Smooth camera moves, it's even more smooth than in Tales of Zestiria even though the price is lower than Tales of Zestiria.
+ Good PC port, so far i have only seen few odds thing inside the game, and it has 60 fps on both cutscene and gameplay, and i don't experience such a thing as crashes or something.
+ Story is goods but very like anime, but i guess that's normal for JRPG.
+ Have both japanese dub eng sub and eng dub eng sub. Both of the dub are surprisingly good, i like the eng dub more than the japanese dub though, since i think japanese dub is not suited for game..
+ Graphic and arts are also good, some or maybe many people maybe said that it's bad or something, but i think that it's pretty good for JRPG, more like it's normal for JRPG.
+ Game inside the game, there are several mini games to obtain some custom for the character which is actually pretty fun to play.
+ Lots of accessories to be put to your character to make them cute or weird or maybe something hilarous.
- Surround audio system is not supported, the game won't make any noise if you turn the audio from stereo to surround, but it's not a major problem.
- Repetitive gameplay, the gameplay and combat were just the same as far as i can remember, except the mini games which is good for change paces.
- The game is too easy even in hardest mode available in my current state, but i think it can be upgraded to be even more harder but you'll need to kill certain monster before you can do it.
- Character's move speed in world map is way too slow for the vast world out there, need to defeat alot of strong monster to get your movement speed up.
I can't say i recommend this game to all RPG lovers there, but probably i'll recommend it to weab out there or maybe RPG lover who doesn't mind a repetitive gameplay. There aren't alot of bug that have a huge impact to the game. I think it's nont overpriced even at full priced but it's to those who doesn't mind the repetitive gameplay.

TLDR: Best Tales game I've played -- If you're a Tales fan, this is a must have. Engaging and intriguing plot. Interesting characters. Fun combat system. Voice acting and dialogue are really good for an anime RPG.
Honestly, the trailer doesn't do this game much justice; I initally just got the game because I'm a sucker for the Tales series, and this just looked like a dumb edgy anime game to me on first impression.
It feels like you're playing as the antagonist of the story, setting an interesting plot, and it came with many unexpected plot twists. What I particularly enjoyed was the diversity in each character's motives and values and how they all just fell perfectly into place to create this beautiful work of art. The developers did a fantastic job of gradually revealing the backstories of each character over the course of the game and tying everything together, allowing the player to make connections in the plot (before the characters do).
there are a lot of sidequests and fun extra things like costume pieces that I am continuing to thoroughly enjoy. I've put about 80 hours in this so far, and I'm still working on sides.
They really developed the combat system with this one. It's easier than in previous Tales games to quickly switch characters and "micromanage" everyone in the party. Also, the playable characters are very diverse in their skills and specialities (unlike in Zestiria).
: Despite not being turn-based, you have good control over your other party members in that you can set specific strategies for each character to affect how they fight, such as how they should conserve their mana, who they should focus attacks on, etc.
: Good.
There's a good bit of foreshadowing in the plot, and I would really like to play it again to see if I catch a lot of things I missed the first time.
: There's a "Grade" system that basically gives you points on how well you beat battles. (Using several factors: Did you forego items on a boss fight? How many KO's were there? Etc.) You collect grade throughout your playthrough, and after you beat the game, you can choose to start a new file using the grade you collected to get certain perks, like twice the EXP, carrying over certain things, and so on. This can make your next playthrough faster and maybe easier to complete certain achievements.

Trove... Where to start with Trove...
I was a long time player of Trove, disregard the time I've played, as I started sometime way back in 2014, near the end of closed beta, I believe, and the game was great. The combat was simple enough that anyone could pick it up and, after a few battles, know how to play their class. The worlds were flooded with people looking to find new recipes and improve their cornerstones in any way, while also looking for gear and xp. The worlds were beautiful and it felt like you were actually getting somewhere when you went from one world to another, as new biomes were added and new enemies alongside it. Everything could be done for free, at the time there were only 3 classes (I think...), gunslinger, knight, and fae trickster. You started the game with the knight and the gunslinger, and every other class could be bought with the ingame currency, Cubits. New classes were added left and right (I took a liking to the Dracolyte), and it felt like the devs truly cared about the game, as they fixed every bug someone came acrossed.
As I continued to play, they introduced more things, such as the dragons. The dragons started out pretty simple, you had little "missions" that would pop up every once in a while, tasking you with completing dungeons, and if you used a certain class, you'd get 2 points rather than one, and you'd need 5 points to get your first dragon cache (sorry if any of these things aren't the correct terms, haven't played in a while), and another if you got somewhere in the 20s. These caches had a chance to give you things such as dragon essence and souls, which were used to ascend and get companions and mounts. The concept was great, I had fun with it, and many others did too.
After a while it started to go downhill REALLY quickly. The first sign was, well, the devs removed the ability to buy classes with cubits. At first it seemed harmless, they still gave out class coins every once in a while, and the classes themselves weren't too expensive. Then they added gems, which I'm not too familiar on, but supposedly just make you straight up better than others, and the things to obtain them were either really rare (rare, RNG, same thing, just RNG is less reliable), or could be bought with real cash. At this time, I quit, the community was destroyed, the game was broken, and nothing was rewarding.
Game used to be good, then Trion did what Trion does best.
Edit: Take what I say with a grain of salt, haven't played in a while.

This game is bad.  You already knew that.  Everyone knows that.  It\'s notoriously bad.  Career sinking bad.  Company ending bad.
It\'s NOT the worst game ever made.  Not even close, not by a long shot.  I wouldn\'t even say it\'s the worst AAA title.  But it\'s bad to the point of being nearly unplayable at portions.  The weapons are terribly designed.  The graphics are at least decent for the time, but that\'s the best you can say about them.  The story is nonsensical.  There as no thought put into balance.  And the AI is simply atrocious.  Worst part are the design choices that have you with AI teammates that are suicidal, force you to share ammo and health pickups with them, give you a game over if they die, and are required to be with you to make stage transitions.  The only saving grace with them is that you can usually tell them to wait at the beginning of the map and then play without them.  In fact, it may be the ONLY way to get past some areas.
There were ways to have fixed the teammates.  But even that doesn\'t leave you with a game worth playing.  It just, ultimately, feels like the people who made this game were in over their head - amazing when you consider that this was what John Romero banked his legacy, and company, on.  It shows that he didn\'t really take the right messages from when he worked on Doom etc. at Id.  Maybe he learned some from this, Romero\'s Lament.
Unless you absolutely want to see just how bad the game\'s design really can be, don\'t bother with this game.  It just isn\'t worth the headache.

Bastion is a wonderful game.  The art is beautiful and the storyline is just enough for an indie game to bring you back.  For the game itself, I give it a 9/10 - I fell in love with it and, although it's short, it is an experience not often found in games these days.
As far as gameplay, major events do not seem to require sound.  Almost everything happens on screen and has a screen shaking effect for important events, whether on or off screen.
For gameplay accessibility, I give it 10/10 - the game can be played to completion without or with limited sound.
Bastion is fully captioned, but can be confusing about who is talking at first.  There is a narrator that speaks during the gameplay.  It's not essential information for the game, but it does add to the story.
For subtitles, I give it 8/10.  It was hard to figure out who was talking at first until I saw the character/narrator much later.
Bastion is single player only.  No rating.
The game's visual signals for events and full captions make it fully accessible for deaf/hoh gamers.  Hearing players frequently comment on the amazing soundtrack associated with the game that plays during gameplay and ties in with the story.  If you're hoh, you may still be able to enjoy some of the tracks.  Otherwise, no vital information is solely passed through sound.
Overall, 9/10 for this amazing indie action/RPG game.

I completed this game a long time ago and I don't find myself having fond memories of it.
It's a Breakout / Arkanoid style game that tries to mix in RPG mechanics, except they don't really play all that big of a role. Gold collection isn’t balanced well and you’ll just be too rich before you know it, unless you want to grind enough to purchase the joke ending.
There’s no world map except for a tiny town with maybe two points of interest.
High-score mechanics weren’t well thought-out either: the worlds all have a maximum score you can attain by a flawless playthrough where you catch all falling objects, never die, and clear all bonus rooms. That is, except for the worlds with a fairy that drops a random number of gems in one of the levels, meaning that you need to repeat your flawless run of the whole world over and over until the fairy drops enough gems to get you higher on the scoreboard.
The magic system was especially disappointing: there’s really not enough mana to abuse your magical powers at any point, so you might as well be playing without it.
Also, you need to finish all levels in a world at once, or you have to start from the beginning. Better learn to hold onto those powerups, or you’ll just be losing them constantly. It can get frustrating.
The graphics are very well-animated pixel art, I’ll give it that. And it does kind of get fun if you can collect the cool powerups and learn to play without dying all the time. But the music is awful, the RPG mechanics might as well not be there, and playing through entire worlds at a time just gets tedious. You might like it, but I wouldn’t pay more than $1.50 for it if I were you. For an awesome brick-breaker, go play Shatter instead!

But Graviteam is a small team of enthuasiasts from eastern Ukraine, Kharkiv. Despite your political views devs need your help with money. Don't let the great idea die, support and enjoy it.

First of all this will be a review of the actual game, not a rage review of the day 1 release ( which didn't go too well as expected).  As most people are aware of on day 1 the servers couldn't handle the massive load from both the PC and PS4 players so I was barely able to play properly due to constant disconnects. Now on day 2 I can say most of these issues have been solved, sadly the damage had been done with most of the steam reviews being driven by anger when written, well not this one.
So what does SF V have to offer for 60$ ? As you've propably read from other reviews it doesn't have the content to match the 60$ price, the game being rushed to Esports purposes. More free content has been promised from March and more in the months to follow. What is bothersome though is the attitude players have towards the lack of content considering Capcom announced everything the game will have and will not have at launch and now they ask for refunds due to their lack of knowledge of what they're buying but guess what if you look over all of that the game itself is outstanding.
The graphics are eye candy for human eye, all possible with the Unreal Engine 4. The characters feel alive, beautiful. The combos are flashy, the battle stages are more interactive ( even though there are still some small image errors sometimes).If you do want to play this game properly you will need a very strong video card to handle it because this game uses mostly video card resources.
The gameplay feels fresh, the combos are easier to execute, I feel in control of my character. The game is well in balance at the moment with all characters. There are new battle mechanics like the V-trigger which make your combos even flashier and more dangerous to opponents. Also there's the V-reversal that lets you counter an enemy attack using the V-trigger.
Compared to the SF IV series this game barely has issues when playing online against other players which is admirable considering the PC and PS4 play together for the first time in a fighting game ( which is one of the reasons why the servers couldn't take it on day 1).
The soundtrack is addicting. I loved it way before the game released, they remixed all the themes from the previos SF IV characters and it sounds just lovely. I could listen to it all day.
What the game does lack right now is single player content like arcade mode, character trials and other single player content you'd expect from a fighting game.It also is not compatible with some PS4 controllers and also some fightsticks that use dinput.There's also no way to change the key bindings if you're not happy with the current ones. Changes have been promised to us on the next update to solve most of these problems.
If this was TL;DR for some people I'll summarise everything with pros and cons.
PROS:
-fresh gameplay with awesome new battle mechanics that focuses on online gameplay  ( do not buy it right now if you want it for the single player)
-redesigned character combos
-amazing graphics, too amazing for a fighting game
-soundtrack that gets stuck in your head
-online fights are mostly very stable compared to SF IV ( with some ocassional lags from people with very slow internet)
-most of the charged combos have been removed in favor in non charged attacks
-the menu is simple to navigate through
-you can unlock everything in the game from characters to costumes/colors for free with in game currency that you earn by playing
CONS:
-lacks support for PS4 and fight sticks that use dinput unless you use 3rd party software
-key bindings can not be remapped unless you use external methods
-barely any single player content to enjoy at this moment with more promised later
-quite demanding when it comes to a video card
-the game feels unfinished currently until more content is added ( should have had an early access label on it)
This is what you're getting for 60$. Do I regret paying for this game despite its cons? I definitely do not, because if you look over what it lacks and look at what it has it's a very good game, it's just more waiting needed that I know a majority are not willing to do. I have faith that the game will get better and better and people will forget about their bad experiences.
If you're a SF V fan I welcome you to this game.
