This could have been a great game. It had the potential to be a worthy successor to the excellent JA1 and JA2 games of our youth. Nice graphics, a decent combat system. Unfortunately, it seems they never really got round to finishing the game. It's like they cut a load of corners, spent too much time designing junk items (like a wide variety of t-shirts and food items), didn't properly test it, rushed it to market and then started on the DLC cashgrab as soon as they could.
A few gripes and missing features :
There's several really annoying bugs (for example, items in sector inventory will disappear randomly and only reappear if you save and reload). Gameplay is unbalanced - expect to face off against skilled, well-armed enemies with your two or three pistol-wielding mercs pretty early on. If you move into an occupied sector, expect to be dumped right next to the enemy forces - you need to move next to the danger area and manually enter the zone if you want to try any kind of stealthy approach.
There are cars and lorries all over the landscape but none of them are usable. Forget about quick transport between locations.
Explosives can only be used at specific weak points in walls so forget about making your own entrance to a building. You'll often find locks that can't be picked or forced. You can't shoot locks or blow up doors.
Mercs and militia will happily jump on landmines, even when they've been detected. There's no autopause when a mine is detected, either, so if you're sending a merc through a potentially mined area, do so carefully.
The militia system has been horribly simplified. Rather than go through the tedium of vetting recruits and teaching them to use guns, why not just hand that random person on the street, potentially violent prisoner in a locked cell or hospital patient found in a locked ward an assault rifle? What could possibly go wrong?
Only one weapon attachment is allowed at a time and is removed if you change weapons. Want a silencer, laser sight and fancy optics on that gun? Forget it. Want to switch to another gun when your inventory is full? Drop something first.
Shooting an enemy will interrupt and stun them (fine, that's a good idea) yet hitting them with a baseball bat or machete doesn't, allowing the enemy a chance to beat the snot out of your merc.
IMP no longer exists. Forget about making your own merc.
Enjoyed those witty interactions between mercs or those cutscenes of Deidranna abusing her staff in JA2? Interesting, well-written dialogue with NPCs? You won't find them here. By the time you're storming the palace you'll just want the game to be over and done with.
Conclusion : Meh. Don't bother. Unless it's really, really cheap in a sale.

It pretty much goes without saying that Daikatana is not a very good game, and you don't need a Steam recommendation to tell you that. What I will say instead is that I don't believe this game deserves as much hate as it gets.
When most people call Daikatana the "worst game ever" or something similar, what likely comes to mind is the first of the four episodes, featuring a long expanse of swamp featuring every shade of "vomit green" you can imagine, terrible weapons that damage yourself more often than they damage anything else, tiny frogs and dragonflies that are overly difficult to actually hit with the early weapons of the episode, and braindead AI companions that are more hindrances than helpers. And these are all completely fair complaints, and it's understandable that most people probably gave up after a few hours of it. But after you complete episode 1 and move on to the rest of the game, the game almost immediately jumps up 2 or 3 points in quality and becomes a somewhat fun shooter. The AI is still terrible, and it's pretty much mandatory to either play it in co-op (which replaces the AI partners with two friends at the expense of lacking all story cutscenes) or install the 1.3 fan patch (which you should do anyways, really) and disable the AI partners altogether, but the weapons, enemies, level design, and environments are all vastly better than in the first episode and actually come pretty close to being a good game. It's still ultimately not a great FPS, and I don't consider it a "must-buy" game by any means, but if you have a few friends and want to see what the deal was with Daikatana then you might as well go for it, considering it goes down to like $1 every so often. Games like Daikatana are the reason I wish Steam had a "Maybe" option for reviewing, because I can't necessarily recommend or anti-recommend this game.

I played it when it launched for the 360, and couldn't get into it.  However, I just bought it on sale, and beat it right away.  That just tells you games are funner in full HD with a smooth framerate.  Its unique, its got kind of an OK story, but its mostly about whacking enemies on the head in a variety of ways.  Controller only though from what I can tell.  What I really liked about it is the game has a kind of customizable difficulty.  You can make the game easier with flasks that give you a variety of attributes.  Each level you gain gives you an extra slot for flasks.  Or, you can make the game harder by calling on the gods at a shrine.  Each different god you call on makes the game harder in different ways (think skulls in the Halo series).  And then there are the weapons and loadouts.  Weapons are upgradable, and have two different upgrade paths (which can be mixed to your liking).  Loadouts consist of 2 weapons (one long range and one melee is usually preferable) and a special.  The game is worth the praise from the media IMO, and is worth a try. It has a newgame+ mode, which it does right by giving you cool **** all the way until the very end of the game, kind of tempting you to start in newgame+ immediately.

I would not call Planetary Annihilations : Titan a new game or a "stand-alone expansion".
What it really seems to be is the original intention of Planetary Annihilation, with new window dressing and a few new units to go with the tag. For those who weren't here or endured it, it's safe to say that the "original" planetary annihilation had loads of issues upon release (I'm referring to the proper release here, not the early access or any of the other test periods). I recall how my friends had trouble just adding each other to the buddy list(which was separate from Steam) and how it took us about twenty minutes just to get everyone into the same custom game. Once things got rolling, someone inevitably dropped out or crashed for seemingly random reasons. One of us could not alt-tabb from the game without killing it, destroying a planet didn't even register at times and many features seemed to be unpolished or even flat-out missing.
In short, it just wasn't ready. It looked and worked like a game during a mid-Beta stage, at best, and it would take another year before things got to a good point.
The developers however, to their credit, kept slowly grinding away on the fixes and improvements. I recall reading through some of the patchnotes thinking these changes would be the sort of thing you'd expect halway through Development, not half a year after release. Unit stats were flung across the board, some were removed entirely, some were added and others had their behaviour changed drastically.
So, now that we're here at long last, what is Planetary Annihilations: Titans?
In short, it's the sheer spectacle of commanding thousands (yes, thousands) of tiny units and sending them across several planets to obliterate your enemies. It's command & conquer on drugs. It's Defcon with visible cannon fodder. It's a multi-tasking hell where you're required to command air, sea and land units while simultaneously sending nukes, spaceships and all manner of misery in your opponent's direction. In a word, it's EPIC.
But all of this comes with the bitter after taste and the constant reminder that this is what I paid for and was expecting to have about a year ago. I funded this project when it entered BETA (wasn't able to pay for kickstarter) and people are rightfully annoyed by this business maneuver to "re-sell" the old idea for a higher price.
Final word:
The game itself is awesome and I cannot give it a thumbs down without being unfair. Play it, especially with friends and enjoy the havoc.
However, it must be mentioned that the project seems to have been estimated and/or managed poorly. The business of releasing unfished products and then "rebranding" them for profit really needs to stop. My trust in Kickstarter projects is dwindling by the day and it seems more and more like this sort of mess is the norm rather than an exception.

Well this is quite a hard choice... up or down... I had fun, but I think the downsides are a bit to many to recomend that game at a cost over 15 Euro...
Let me explain (as if you have a choice ;) )
I really liked the story, the characters AND the talking. Man there was a lot of talking! It would have been a great anime to watch.
But as a game... It had two major downsides for me:
The leveldesign is beyond boring... huge areas filled with a vast amound of nothingness and to make it really tedious, you have to walk through several levels again and again. there is a beaming system, but it is not as nice as it could be. Often it is locked, because the walking will trigger a conversation between the charakters... which, as I said, I really enjoyed, but why does the game make me walk for several minutes through empty levels for that?
Especially at one point of the story. There you have to walk down in a cellar of a big building... and out again... again... and again. the building itself is  constructed out of the same 10 assets in every corner and the layout makes no practical sense at all (this is the fact for every building!). For example: who builds a sewer with 6m high walls and hallways about 10m wide? makes no sense! ok this is common for jrpgs and hack n slays... but still.
Second downside: the fighting!
And you do it A LOT... the system is rather fun, but  I still prefer the one from Symphonia, at least it is not as horrible as in Zestaria. But it is so easy! "Why don't you raise the difficulty?" you may ask... because higher difficulties than "normal" only means LESS xp... and thats a poor way of making it harder. You'll just end up grinding for hours, which for me is not fun at all. So I began skipping the fights after about 25 hours in the game. I just fought when a new type of enemy showed up and killed them once. Besides that I only fought bosses and some of the special "hard" monsters which I encountered on my way (I did not search all of them). But I had never any trouble defeating them. This caused the last boss to be 12 levels above my group. This fight was a bit challenging, but I still beat him on my frst go. All the other fights, whith only very few exceptions were a cake walk... I'm not a fan of hard or unfair games, never the less a bit of challange makes the gameplay interesting.
other little downsides:
- I liked the story, but it is quite forseeable... Symphonia did a much better job on that part.
- the "crafting system" is anoying... ok, You don't have to buy anything ever, because you can easiely desmantle the warehouse of stuff you always carry arround (defeating a strong enemy spawns about 5 swords, 3 pairs of boots, 2 sets of armor and several rings) and upgrade the equipment you gave the group... but that kinda takes the fun out of looting or finding something special... because the upgraded stuff is in most cases better than any special weapon.
- Bienfu has a really nasty voice (english) and he talks a lot.... BIEEEEEEN!
- there is no exploring because there is nothing to explore.
little upsides:
- playing the bad people who want to stop the chosen one is refreshing for a change
- battles contain a serious amount of wooosh-the-screen-is-full-of-pink-explosions-while-all-characters-screem-something... yes I like that... sometimes
- an antique, magic, stone-hoverboard, which lets you move faster an overrun weak enemies, nice!
- the feeling of releave, when the point in the story is reached, where the little girl with the smokey-bar-voice finally stops whining all the time, sadly she never starts to sing classic jazz ...
To come to an end:
- I recomend this game only in a sale for about 15 Euro tops.
- my playtime is the pure story playthrough without getting much into the 3 sidequests and without grinding (because it`s really not neccassary)... and listening to ALL conversations I could find of cause.
- Why are there mods to make the game even easier? Do you want to play it with one hand, because you seriously paid the ridicules amount of money for the beachclothing DLC? :D
- English is not my native laguage, so if you've found any errors in my text, you are free to keep them... yes really! Take them as token of my graditude for reading this long review. ;)

This is not a game for Street Fighter fans.
Firstly let me say that I grew up with Street Fighter. I played in arcades, I played at home, I love Street Fighter. Between PC and Xbox 360 I have thousands of hours (607 hours on Steam alone) for USF4.
There are two aspects of this game that we have to talk about. The game play, and the technical issues. We might as well start with the technical issues. This was talked about a LOT in beta, and it's still an issue in the "finished" product. The lack of support out of the box for arcade sticks is horrible. I can't even begin to imagine why they made that decision. Their loyal fans spent hundreds of dollars on arcade sticks for SF4, and now they're not even supported for SFV. In order to use an arcade stick, you have to use third party software to map keys to the arcade stick. Weak, Capcom, weak.
I suppose in a way it's almost forgivable because the game is so basic that you don't need an arcade stick, but we'll get to that later. The UI is clunky and unintuitive. The matchmaking is awful, but that's pretty standard for Capcom. Countless network errors and issues. In order to play with friends you have to create a "lounge" - but that feature doesn't work. Searching for friends with Steam names or with Battle IDs (the game's username system) - Sometimes you can find your friends, sometimes you can't. We have yet to be able to successfully create and join a lounge though.
The AI is horrible but better AI is "coming soon." - So at the moment I've been able to do, all my friends have been able to do, is play against random people.
The game is very obviously unfinished. Parts of the in-game menu are greyed out with a promise that features are coming in March. It's sad that Capcom felt the need to rush this game out.
Lets talk briefly about the game play. Assuming you actually get to play, don't expect a high skill ceiling, don't expect to learn medium to long combos. This game has removed almost all of the finer points of Street Fighter. What's left is a very basic 6-button fighting game with very small combos. That's it, that's the game play. Sad isn't it? Street Fighter fans: If you've ever introduced a friend to fighting games and they complained and whined and said it was unfair that you knew advance tactics, this is the game for them.
Bland, uninteresting, unfinished, broken. But hey, they got the season pass up there so you can preorder some DLC! Game's not done, but lets buy the DLC eh?! Save your money, easily the worst Street Fighter game ever made.

This review is for the Windows version. The MAC/Linux version is unplayable at this point.
I am a fan of JA2 and i was quite disappointed when JABIA was released. It was unfinished and overpriced on release. But things have changed. Most of the game's problems can be fixed by using mods and the price of the game has decreased considerably. I played the modded Windows version for 220 hours and really enjoyed it. I can only recommend this game.
The story/scheme of the game is very similar to JA2: You are hired to liberate a small 3rd world country and can only afford to send in a few wannabe mercenaries. You start to liberate/loot remote locations in order to get your hands on more money and better weapons while you recruit NPCs and improve their skills.
In contrast to JA2 this game is in 3D and in real time. Which is awesome in my opinion. You dont have to watch 40 AI moves until it is your turn. You can pause and intervene at any time. The game offers a lot of freedom. You can run away from tough battles and come back later with better equipment. You can even leave the first battle of the game and explore instead.
There are a few flaws, however:
-Mercs have less character compared to JA2 and there is no option to create your own mercenary.
-AI is just as stupid as in JA2 and attack squads are very predictable
-Animations in this game feel like placeholders (all weapons have same reload animation and sound)
-Annoying melee combat. Guns cannot be fired at melee range and melee hits damage all of your gear.
-Explosives (C4) can only be placed on brittle walls. you cannot set traps for enemies.
-You will spend a lot of time managing your inventory
-Militia is not very useful and recruiting is tedious.
-You cannot train/repair/heal on the strategical map (which was a nice feature in JA2)
-Enemies cheat / have superhuman skill (fixed by mod)
-Weapons are imbalanced and have wierd stats (fixed by mod)
-Broken Stealth: enemies hear you walk/climb from up to 150m (fixed by mod)
-Broken Camouflage: camouflage not working properly, especially at night (fixed by mod)
People also complain about horrible aimtime in CQC, but this can be solved by using the Run stance (F3) at close range. This will result in rapid-fire instead of aimed-fire.
Some reviewers claim that combat gameplay is "micromanagy" and "tedious". In my opinion combat is very simple and entertaining as long as you avoid common mistakes and use hotkeys. It is even possible to play the game completely in real time without any pausing as long as you know what you are doing.
Watch the following gameplay videos and decide for yourself:
MODS
Mods are very important to make this game more enjoyable. They are free and very easy to install. Mods fix most of the bugs, improve gameplay, improve balance, weapon progression, tweak AI, improve textures/sounds and add new weapons and ammo types. If you are interested in bugfixes, improved gameplay and new content, check out this mod:
It took 530 hours to create this mod and the amount of fixes and improvements is considerable.
More mods can be found here:
However, a few problems cannot be fixed by mods and remain:
-performance issues in some locations
-equipping militia is a tedious task
-animations glitch from time to time (ladder/repair/heal)
-sometimes enemies are able to shoot through their own cover
Conclusion:
If you can live with the problems mentioned above you should consider buying this game. $10 is not much for potentially 100 hours of entertainment, is it? ;)

Despite its flaws, I loved this game. I played it to completion and enjoyed it immensely. It may not do tactical combat as well as the original Jagged Alliance series, but for me the visceral feel of the pausable-real-time gameplay makes up for it. I bought the bundle for $13.59 a while back and I was thoroughly satisfied with my purchase; it's currently on sale for even less than that.
Probably the most satisfying moments were the close quarters blasts, whether charging into a room with a shotgun or waiting for an enemy just around the corner with a readied assault rifle or machinegun. The AI is too predictable for a conservative strategy to be very enjoyable in most cases. It was often possible, but not very rewarding, to grind the enemy down from long range, with the exception of a few spots in the game where a daring assault is necessary due to the layout. But sending Wolf running into a room to empty his shotgun into an enemy's guts never got old for me.
The chief feature of combat in this game, and to my knowledge what sets it apart from all other games, is the timer that begins counting when you order your merc to fire a shot. The time to take a shot is a simple mechanic, but it has critical consequences for how you plan your tactics. Timing interacts with posture, so that postures where you take less accurate shots also allow you to get your shots off faster. It also depends on your choice of firearm, as well as the range. In a close quarters encounter, who gets off the first shot is the difference between life and death. You need to understand and take advantage of this mechanic to play the game effectively. In my opinion, more than anything else this one thing is what makes the game interesting.
I liked the artwork, especially in the cities. I've been to Latin America a number of times, and the look of the buildings gave the place an authentic Caribbean feel. The look of the game gives you the feeling that you're fighting over real places in the real world. The characters' accents are silly (as is the minimal plot), but that's in keeping with the original Jagged Alliance games and it's entertaining if you're not touchy about such things.
I wasn't too crazy about the defensive part of this game. The militia is useless, so you have to park a squad in one place to stop enemy attacks. (Since enemy squads always follow nearly the same path, they always come up the road into the same city, and always from exactly the same angle.) While I got some entertainment out of devising different ways to defend the chokepoint, it wasn't much of a serious challenge one I realized that I could clog the enemy's entry path with mines and take out half of the assault party before they got close enough to shoot at me. Since I kept defending the same terrain over and over, it would have been nice to be able to erect some kind of fortifications.
I've also played "Jagged Alliance: Crossfire", which is a sort of companion to this game. That game's campaign seems like a better fit for this particular game system, and I probably would have enjoyed it more than JABIA if it weren't for a show-stopping bug that might (no guarantee) force you to abandon your game halfway through and start over from scratch. That bug in "Crossfire" makes "Back in Action" by far the better purchase, though if you get "Crossfire" as part of the bundle then it's still worth playing.
I found that the difficulty progression worked pretty well. If it's too tough for you early on, there's a DLC that gives you a few assault rifles to start with; you won't get much ammo for them early on, but they can come in handy in an early fight or two to get you over the hump. The latter half of the game was maybe on the easy side because it's possible to pick off a few enemies, rest up, and then come back; the dead enemies are replaced eventually, but if you keep hammering a location you'll wear it down long before that replacement happens. The final battle was a rush, as the close-range, exposed approach practically forces you to make a running assault. If you ever feel unchallenged, you can always get more aggressive to increase the excitement level; charging into engagements recklessly will get you killed quickly, so a violent assault has to be executed very carefully.
The variety of weaponry seems interesting at first (though other games have far more), but it's somewhat of a waste of time. In the end you realize there are only a few best weapons and there's no point using any others. Early on you have to shoot whatever guns you can get ammo for, but once you reach the financial tipping point where you're buying ammo daily instead of relying on what you can scrounge up, you will prefer only a few guns of choice. I think this "best gun" phenomenon is a problem for nearly every modern warfare game out there, though.
There's plenty more to be said about this game, but others have already said it. If it sounds interesting, I'd go ahead and get it if I were you. It's not flawless, but if you're like me you'll enjoy it anyway.

Obligatory comment re: having played all the JA series, XCOM, Shadowrun Returns, Antisquad, et cetera. The JA reboot's problem is that after six hours' play, you can see the exact moment that the developers shrugged, said "meh, it's good enough" (or ran out of budget) and handed it over to the modding community to fix its many glaring problems.
It looks nice, but lacks the soul of the original. You'll find your local militia getting overwhelmed regardless of equipment. Many maps are simply too large for a small squad to beat, and the enemy forces are both vicious and highly mobile. There are any number of glaring line of sight and cover issues, and equipment degrades so fast you'd think you were swimming through acid. Overwatch fire is ineffective. The metagame of protecting your territory and hiring more teams or getting new equipment is just tacked-on rather than integrated into the overall experience.
All in all, and being a huge fan of small-unit tactics games, I'd say give this one a miss. If you never played JA2 you'll find this game frustrating because it's bad. If you did play JA2, you'll find yourself uninstalling this and going back to it because this is just so unfulfilling.

Where do I get started? I'm not going to be comparing this game to other sandbox titles like a lot of the other reviewers were doing and I am also extremely biased so don't expect any negative comments. That being said, here's my review.
Starbound is an extremely enjoyable game to those who like 2-D sandbox adventure games with somewhat of a degree of platforming elements. it's charming, colorful, creative, and allows YOU as a player to be creative in your builds. There's a variety of races to choose from, ranging from the standard Humans, the bird people Avians, the intelligent primate Apex, the traditional and Japan-inspired fish people Hylotl, the medieval robot Glitch, the predator and cannibalistic plant people Florans, and finally the wild west style Novakid gas bags.
The beginning plays out pretty slow but tends to accelerate as you gain traction and find more and more expensive materials to craft better gear. The main quest is actually optional except for the first few missions, at least until you get your ship working. The only thing that really bothers me is the lack of player build creativity early on. You're forced to play a specific way until you get to the 5th and 6th armor tiers, which then allow you to integrate some real variety into your playstyle.
If I was a professional critic I would probably do a better job at criticizing this game and actually have more constructive, un-biased things to say. Though I am not a professional critic, I still feel inclined to give a final rating. Therefore, I rate this game 8/10. It's a solid game, definitely worth the money, it just has room for improvement.

"Takes some guts to wear that!" Said an innocent bystand critiquing my knockoff sweatpants, converse shoes and tank top as I left a clothes shop before I battered him to death in the rain with his own umbrella.
Sleeping Dogs is hands down the best sandbox game of recent years. GTA IV is good and so is Saints Row 2+3, but Sleeping Dogs is on another level. You're an undercover cop who goes by the name of Wei Shen tasked with taking down the largest group of Triads in Hong Kong. Let me start off by saying the work gone into Hong Kong is unreal. The city itself matches the dirty dark tone of the story with run down alley ways, gritty feeling buildings and slovenly streets. The roads are peppered with grimy neon signs and street gangs stand on nearly every corner. There are not many likeable characters in the story, everyone has left their morals and kills without remorse or respect but this adds to the atmosphere, it involves you. You're told who you should be rooting for, but in this dog eat dog world, it's hard for the player to really pick a side when everyone is as bad as each other. The gameplay is satisfying, from drivings cars to scaling construction sites to fighting gangsters who were unlucky enough to run into Wei Shen. The radio stations are superb, and driving a scooter whilst weaving in and out of traffic to The Ride Of The Valkryies is an exceptional experience. There's lots to do in the city of Hong Kong as you do missions for both the Triads and the Cops, collectables to find such as statues which help you unlock new combat moves giving you incentive to dive down every nook and cranny. Every moment you spent in Sleeping Dogs, you're living and breathing a double life in Hong Kong and it feels marvelous and it plays excellently too. It's a perfect companion to such movies as Infernal Affairs and Hard Boiled (both Hong Kong crime movies). Sleeping Dogs is the sleeper hit you're missing out on.

Serena is a short 3D point and click adventure, although it is wrongly classified as "horror". There's nothing particularly "gut wrenching" about the atmosphere of the game, as stated in the description on the store page, but other than a few mischaracterizations, the title is solid for a freebie.
You are an unnamed man who is trying desperately to figure out where your wife Serena disappeared to. You start out sitting at the kitchen table in your small, cozy cabin in the woods, with a picture of you and your beloved in front of you; her face is blurred, and you struggle to recollect your memories of her. The remainder of the game is spent piecing together memories in an attempt to remember what events have transpired; the ending has a brilliant and unexpected surprise twist that is sure to give you at least a small tingle down your spine.
The monotone color scheme of the graphics really help to set the depressive mood of Serena. There are a few objects to interact with, and clicking on them multiple times will grant an array of randomized lines regarding said object. The entire game is one long puzzle, lasting about half an hour at best, that can be quite cryptic. You must click certain objects in a specific order to advance the game, and there are no indications as to where to go or what to examine. The voice acting is decent, though not astonishing, and the same can be said for the gentle soundtrack.
With "over 40 contributors", one would expect more from Serena. The premise of the game is doable by one or two people alone, and you spend the entire game inside the cabin with no cutscenes or extra effects. Due to the tags on the store page, I was personally expecting a more horror inspired game, but taking the game for what it is... it's alright. Since it's free, there's no harm in checking in out for yourself, just go in with appropriate expectations and you will enjoy the title far more.

This is not an easy game, so if you are a casual gamer or impatient, pass on this one. Remember that you are a part of a STRUGGLING rebel group trying to overthrow a goverment, so expect it to be difficult to kill hundreds of soldiers with a couple squads of 6 or less mercs(though you can have multiple squads in the same location, you'll just have to tab between them). As a fan of strategy games, I can say that this game does have an unusually steep difficulty curve, but not an impossible one. You can expect to lose and replace squad members(unless you're a fan of copious saving and reloading), and you may have to retreat a few times, but with the right prep work a single mid-level merc can take out a squad of 15 without taking a hit. You MUST have a strategy in mind before moving in, and you must learn to be flexible. As the in-game time progresses, locations receive more and more reinforcements, so you must act quickly to secure a few early and get your daily income up to otherwise the entire game will be an uphill battle. Arming the locals is crucial, unless you leave some mercs behind to defend against the ai squads which is a good idea in a few locations. For those who say this game is too hard, I would be happy to write a strategy guide(not a walkthrough), but only if someone comments that they would like one, not going to spend the time if no-one is going to read it.

A night operation. I'm not a military man but without night vision equipment it would be difficult to see the enemy. However this works both ways and I had the advantage of greater manpower and greater weapons.
So the operation started at 4am, my halftracks rumbled in towards the town from the left and my infantry from the right. A platoon of halftrack engineers I sent to the river crossing next to the town so I could move straight over after the battle. Barely five minutes later, one of my infanry platoons saw the enemy pretty much right on top of them. With my firepower and supporting troops the firefight was over quickly with the entire enemy platoon being eliminated. I was pleased and ordered my troops to converge on the village.
However at the river my engineers began taking fire from a single machine gun from the forest, perfect positioning to engage my forces as they crossed. However the engineers were no rookies and followed my orders to attack the forest and clear it out, the battle was still in my favour. To the right hand side of this engagement the enemy was spotted, I assumed it was another machine gun, set up to give a crossfire killzone and so I quickly ordered my reserve squad within the platoon to sweep in and at least supress it with support from my heavy halftrack. This gun was eliminated with a lucky shot and was immediately destroyed as the dismounted engineers closed. As a looked at the destroyed weapon my eyes widened with fear. It was an Anti-Tank gun, well people, they never travel alone. I ordered a platoon in the villlage to come to the aid of my engineers as there were now more men in the forest than I had thought.
Suddenly as I looked for heavy halftrack to move to engage, it burst into flames. The unlucky crewmembers running out ablaze, in between them I saw a lone Russian solider crawling by the vehicle, he had slipped by and had molotoved my heavy support. Following this my men in the village came across entrenched Russian infantry, bogging them down in a firefight so they were now unable to support my isolated platoon, a retreat could not be ordered as they were already in too deep into the forest and to bring them out was suicide. Two minutes later the village was in my control and the enemy was offering a ceasefire. I had won at the expense of a platoon, a hollow victory.
However I now knew exactly what the enemy had and I knew exactly what to use aginst them. After all that was just the first battle.

I do not recomment this if you liked any of the previous games.
What's good:
-The music is catchy but not annoying.
-The camoflage mechanic makes sense but is barely working in hiding a merc that is in the enemies vision cone.
Instead of using one type of camoflage like in the old games you wear different clothes with different camoflage colours that add up to a cumulative percentage.
-The online shop is available right away and has unlimited stock for each item a day which makes equiping a squad.
What's bad:
-No SELF MADE MERC.
Unless you use an editor to change a pre existing Merc you won't be able to make your own out of "Balancing Issues".
-No proper tutorial.
-Blatant crippling streamlining.
*Weapons can't be pre build anymore. No different Ammo types, only 1 type of attachment and no preloading weapons unless they were once equipped and reloaded. Attachments also take up a slot in your inventory once you change weapons and have to be reattached.
*The Map and Menues are so simplyfied that they turned useless.
*Squad management is not explained and barely there.
*Training, Sleeping and support roles like Medica Care and Item Fixing are gone. Only weapons can be repaired once by one.
*Severely reduced controls.No wire clippers for fences, No shooting of easy Locks, no grabing of guns out of enemies hands, no shooting of civilians or NPCs,
NO USE OF C4 ON ANYTHING OTHER THEN WALLS THAT ARE CRACKED AND HAVE A GREEN SPOT ON THEM.
NO DESTRUCTABLE TERAIN, FENCES or NORMAL WALLS.
Appart from that NPCs seem to always have the better Aim and perception even with inferior Weapons.
On Normal Difficulty
As a sample: Scope with 100 Marksman and Sniper Rifle expert perk armed with an ANTI MATTER RIFLE and 12xScope wasn't able to kill a person wearing a Helmet with a headshot.
A weapon that should DESTROY anyone that gets hit.
On a different note the same merc couldn't hit a Target that was WELL in range eventhough it sayd "Certain to Hit" while the target was able to shoot and nearly kill her with a Sub Machine Gun.
This shows bad balancing.
For a tip:
Get grenades and Launchers. Using grenades on enemies around corners to flush them out is the only propper way to get rid of them since even expert mercs with 100 Marksman Skill won't be able to hit a targed 5 Meters away from them.
Even if they hit they won't do any noticable damage unless you use pistols or shotguns up close.

- RNG seeding. Sometimes. Game bug and need to reload? Well rest assured that if you attempt to do things the same way you did the first time when they worked, none of it will this time, nor will it if you try a further 50 times consecutively, because this game likes to be a shifty special snowflake when it comes to RNG seeding and you'll never be able to tell if it's on or off.
- Average mission time greater than 1 hour, and if you think you're getting out of this game playing less than that without a crash, think again. You will have the opportunity to spend about 2 and a half minutes building your base and other important things before the game says; Here's three identical new missions, they all have time limits to start and you will lose the game if you don't do them all!
- Soldier classes will randomize, even if your soldier already has a class you are happy with from the character pool. This has been somehow physically made worse since the first game, since it is no longer even possible to edit a save file and fix the soldier class. You are completely stuck with this game's decision forever.
Enough said. First game was better, though they are both terrible regardless.

A great take on the action/adventure sandbox/gang genre a la GTA. Sleeping Dogs is set in Hong Kong and revolves around the various Triad gangs residing there. It makes for a brilliant change of pace from the typical American Gang norm. Sleeping Dogs does tend toward the more serious end of the genre as opposed to something like Saints Row, but if you like Drama, you're in for a treat!
+ Great setting - Hong Kong at night in the rain looks incredible, and the hawkers everywhere add to the atmosphere
+ Solid story
+ Interesting and diverse characters and motivations
+ Great melee combat system
- Bad PC port has bugs and general oddities
- Core graphics are pretty dated although the lighting is top notch (looks amazing with the neon lights illuminating the city in the rain)
- Poor performance, even on relatively high end system
- Controls aren't the most responsive, and while you do get used to them, they aren't in common usage or particularly intuitive (right-click as the action button?!?!!?)
Overall a very worthwhile game with a compelling storyline, characters and environment. Just be prepared to fight with the controls and general fluidity of gameplay a bit.

Now, it is really hard to talk about this game without spoiling it, so i'll just start off now, i will spoil this game because it is just so goddamn good. Everything about it is PERFECT. (Aside from a few things of course.) To start off, we have the gameplay. It's a classic point-and-click adventure with telltalle's usual twist. Unlike most other games, this game's choices do have an affect on things. There are some things that will provide hard decisions that will end up being usless. Like the one part where you have to ration out food to your group. Most of this game is just depressing. I used to say minecraft story mode was an emotional joyride. Then i realised that i was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in saying that, because that was the biggest waste of money ever. This game on the other hand, is a real emotional joyride. You will go from loving a character to hating them in seconds Next, The story. The story is pretty simple, your character is being arrested for having killed a senator for the state of georgia after you caught him sleeping with your wife. You're on the highway when you run into one of the walkers, and fly off the street into a nearby forest. The rest is history. And third, the characters. the characters are very likeable, like clementine, and doug. Others you will feel sympathy for like Ben. And some are just GOD reincarnated, like kenny. I love kenny. I miss kenny. Rest in peace kenny. Anyway, the final point that i'll make is the ending. the ending is phenomenal, it ends when you die. Literally, the ending is clementine shooting you after you've been bitten. It's REALLY emotional. Now, season 2 isn't better, but it is good. If you can get the two in a bundle, get it. But don't start with season 3. Season 3 is mediocre. Season 1 is the best. Get season 1 if you can.

Half-life is an outstanding video game series that broke ground in the industry and claimed numerous awards. Normally i'd write individual reviews for all the installments in the series, i've instead decided to take a much more interesting route for such an interesting line of games. I am going to review every single game in chronological order as one giant review. If this has already been done then take it as pure adulation for the original.
Now without further ado...
HALF-LIFE<
Half-life, the first in the series, is an FPS unlike any other. Its combination of story and level design brought interest and awe ever since its release in 1998. If you are looking for what half-life gave inspiration to in the world of today, just take a short look around the FPS genre and you'll find ample examples.
PROS:
-The story is very well paced and put together very nicely. You play as Gordon Freeman, an MIT graduate working at the science and research facility of Black Mesa for years, going through a normal day at work when an experiment goes incomprehensibly wrong. Not spoiling the rest in case you haven't picked up a copy in the 20 years its existed.
-The environment is very immersive as it is a long seamless road to the end of the game with, as the definition of seamless implies, zero cutscenes or immersion breaking interruptions. Give or take two particular instances.
-The gunplay is as much as anyone would expect from a first person shooter. The wide arsenal available is pleasently loud, very powerful feeling, and quite fun to use when eliminating the enemy.
-The ending, the cherry on top of every game, is absolutely perfect. Sets up a sequel in what i would consider the least forced way possible ever.
-Has an HD reskin to give a fresh coat of paint to this forefather of gaming.
-Comes implemented with a multiplayer arena.
-Moddb is your best friend when your bored of the campaign.
CONS: (Not even half-life is safe from sin, sorry) Please note that i am extremely aware that this game is an oldy.
-Controls feel floaty and thats not very great to say when this game is a puzzle platformer.
-While the guns feel and sound powerful, one or two show otherwise. In my numerous playthroughs of this game i've always had to unload nearly an entire clip of assault rifle into a soldier before he eventually died. Found every other gun to be fine though but it should be all of them working together with zero outliers.
I am glad this game came around when it did and i am glad i got to enjoy it back in 2002 when i first played it. Sure i didn't really understand what it was at the time but i enjoyed it as much as everyone that came before and after me. I might speak the brutal truth when i say that if this game came out today it wouldn't have been as influential as it is. It would be praised heavily for its story and gameplay but eventually it would become one with the ever growing pile of first person shooters we're stuck with today. This isn't a shot at the game by any stretch, just a little two sence is all.
As for the game though, this is a must must must have to me. I picked the entire series up in a frantic buy a summer sale or two ago and it honestly kinda lives to its retail price. I don't expect you'll have any trouble deciding what to choose when the time comes again.

As a backer of Planetary Annihilation, I paid close attention to the evolution of the project, all the hiccups, all the cuts that had to be done, and all the new ideas that kept being implemented by the devs, and by suggestion of the community. There were dark times, there were great times. Bad builds and good builds. In the end, Planetary Annihilation ended up being an average RTS. Perhaps my expectations - based on the kickstarter campaign - were too high for what was realistically feasible. I haven't played it actively for a few months.
And then Titans landed. This new chapter in PA's history is everything I wanted from the original.
Performance wise, the game runs superbly even with hundreds of units on screen, and every detail looks crisp and very well designed. The art direction is perfect for the fast paced action and the dozens of different units available. Makes everything easily recognizable even in the heat of battle. The sound and music design are incredible, making the action even more over the top.
The available maps are great and varied, but that is not that important considering the system editor works really well too. It allows the player to create brand new systems at will, with all sorts of planets and asteroid fields. From gas giants to small dwarf planets, everything can be created and edited. Symmetry can be added to planets to created perfectly balanced competitive arenas as well. New structures are available to add even more variety to map design.
Balance wise, I can't say much yet, considering I haven't played the hell out of it to form an opinion on any sort of imbalance. In all honesty, I'm not worried. Considering the years of tweaking Planetary Annihilation already had and the great community that is always deeply involved in helping the devs tweak the game balance, there shouldn't be much to worry about.
In the end, Titans is a very solid RTS that will hopefully last many years to come.

Planetary Annihilation: TITANS is a standalone expansion for Planetary Annihilation, an RTS in the sub-genre occupied by Total Annihilation and Supreme Commander, both games it is clearly heavily influenced by. The expansion was provided for free to all Kickstarter backers of the original game (a pretty classy move) and is at the time of writing available to purchasers of the original for a 66% discount.
So should you buy it? Well, if you loved Planetary Annihilation, or thought it could have been great with more unit variety, deeper orbital play, more map terrain, and some experimental units, then the answer is a resounding YES. If you're looking for a deep story campaign then this still isn't the RTS for you.
Personally, I love it. It's everything an expansion pack should be. It introduces new units, terrain, mechanics, maps, a new game mode,.. It's still PA, but it's different in all the right ways. All these elements come together to provide a deeper, richer experience than the base game alone. Titans bring the experimental units people wanted, and do so while feeling accessible rather than wonder units you will never see in a normal game.
Almost all the new units slot into new roles which provide new opportunities for play, and in some instances change how existing maps will be tackled. Suddenly that lava at your back on Forge is no longer safe because Drifter hover tanks can traverse it. The river behind your base can now be crossed by an Atlas. The fortress planet you built could be visited by a Helios titan dropping a Manhattan mobile nuke on you followed by an invasion force through the Helios's on-board teleporter.
It's also backwards compatible, so TITANS owners can revert to classic PA at any point and play with people who don't have the expansion.
The expansion also adds a much needed interactive tutorial to solve the issue of the brutal learning curve that existed in the base game. The normal difficulty for Galactic War has also been made easier so new players aren't tricked into what was previously a pretty tricky mode. Still, I'd recommend you go from the tutorial to skirmish first so you get all the toys to practice with.
I've had great fun playing it so far, and I look forward to hundreds more hours with the game. Especially as Uber have continued to update the game with further technical improvements following release.
EDIT: and now with the Legion Expansion community mod adding an entire second faction to the game the value of this has improved even further.

I love the game but at times it can seem grindy and repetitive. Plenty of characters to play as, once you unlock or buy them, you can swap between them at any time. You get two free classes without much effort, more if you decide to refer a friend and use their class coin, but you must reach a high level to finally get it. The characters that are more advanced cost actual money but can be crafted if you're willing to put the time into it. Trove is essentially a grind game where you raid dungeons endlessly in open worlds and collect loot. When you reach a certain power level that increases with better loot, you can move onto a new world where you repeat the looting process, an endless loop of looting. If you like a game that feels rewarding, I can recommend this to you. Personally, this is my type of game. Despite the repetition, I enjoy putting time into it because it feels rewarding and your appearance changes with different loot so you don't always look the same. If you love what anything looks like, you can save its appearance and apply it to something different and keep its stats, I really enjoy that option. Plenty of interaction, each world has its own chat and there is a main hub where you can talk to people or find your friends and play together. You can also build your own home but within a limited square, the great part about this is you can transport your house anywhere you go for free. You can only spawn the home within squares that are randomly placed around every world. Only you can edit or destroy them. All interactable furniture placed inside of your home is usable by everyone, but it's personalized for them. Only you can access anything you have stored. There are trading stations but you have to be a very high level to use them, as for the player market.

I started playing the Tales series with Zestiria, which I liked a lot but the game had a lot of problems. Plotholes, skimmed over details in the story, confusing equipment enhancing system and overal annoying gameplay mechanics both in the overworld and battle segments.
Tales of Berseria overwhelmingly improves on Zestiria in almost every single way.
The game's story is far more interesting, with genuinely hilarious and dark moments although like any anime, some parts fall under the usual storyline tropes. The game's story, skits and cutscenes make the entire gameplay experience just like watching an anime and the combat realy makes you feel powerful and meaningful. The characters in Berseria are also all entirely interesting, each with their own set of unique movesets and playstyles while maintaining quality in their own sub-plot lines. Beseria clears up the problems in several of the unfinished plot lines in Zestiria while keeping its own story much more interesting in comparison.
The combat is outstanding, Zestiria's felt like a mess which ended up being generally unenjoyable. I had an absolutely blast in Beseria, the characters movesets, blast combos, mystic arts and how they interact with each other made every combat session a challenge to become even more efficient and even more deadly.
Even the overworld experience is great, with features I wont get into to save the spoilers but any player of Zestiria will nod in approval when the slowly unlocked features become available.
Tales of Beseria really is the game that Zestiria should have been and any fan of JRPGs or animes would love to have played through this game for its story alone. This is easily one of the best JRPGs I have ever played and I cant wait for the next one to be released.

I played JG2 in the past. It was very hard game, with strong team management and fruitfull (and very frustratic) battles over all places in Arulco. Sinde then, any many many mods we all waits for an other step into the genre.
Instead of next step we have simply remake. It has very nice graphic, and new deep of battles density thanks to plan'n'action game style. You need to use covers, silence killing, melee skills, land mines and everything you can got from you squads (automated rocket rifle rocks!). On this part I haven't found many bugs (most likely game is well patched now), only one frustratic bug:
When your mercs are in small space, AI have very big issues to avoid collissions. I don'd need to explain that such situation during firefight usually ends with save loading or with farewell to your wonderfull killers.
Of course in compare to the previous JA game (especially JA2), this product have some not implemented features, and that  makes game too easy on management level (especially if you don't want to speed up too much like me):
- Merc contract NEVER ends - so if you play a long game, it's quite easy to have almost all mercs (obviously some of them don't want to work with each other)
- Mines resources (so also your income) never ends.
I hope, I don't need to explain that without such limitations, you end up with stack of useless money (I've ended with 900k), for which you're buing repair kits, special ammo or Guardian vests at best. Most of the weapon or ammo, or even bunch of granades are easy to gather from army of dead enemies.
Also If you gather good team with 2 paramedics and 1 Sniper (I've used my Amazon team for this with Raven, Spider, Fox, Vicki and 2 others) then you can simply go through the whole map, in the gaps between enemy zones and simply take over southern Sam site (next to Meduna). So in general: I liked game VERY much, I enjoyed the time I spent on it and for sure I'll back to it with some mods that are available over internet, but for some veterans it might be a little bit too easy, especially when you setup your ground.

Graviteam Tactics: Operation Star is not for you if you are simply a gamer.  This is a game for tacticians;  The armchair generals who have the patience to get past the immense learning curve.  Do not expect to just jump right in and take command.
Your troops won't always just go and do what you tell them.  If they are being torn apart, they may run away terrified on their own.  Your soldiers may take the initiative and, with a lack of orders, charge headlong towards the enemy to destroy his positions.  If your unit commander dies, multiple assets and communication break down.  If your communications aren't effective, your units can't recieve orders.
The interface, though at first confusing, begins to make sense after paying attention during tutorials.  If the player is willing to accept some devestating losses in the first few attempts, it isn't so bad.  The layout is effective enough to apply all the necessary options for troop formations, movement and types of fire.  It just takes some orientation to understand how to apply these options.
I am somewhat well versed in combined arms tactics and skills covered in Marine Corps warfighting doctrine (MCPD-1) and easily understand how  and why this title is actually utilized in European militaries to train infantry officers and platoon leaders.  The enemy UI is challenging and responds realistically and effectively to offense, but tends to do poorly when advancing or attacking.  He tends to stop dead in his tracks during attacks when fired upon and consistently maintains a defensive posture.  Hopefully in the future this can be tweaked a bit to give the UI a more impactful attack pattern.
You will find that application of standard military tactics per doctrine is played out extremely effectively.  I.e. Deploying maching guns with long and unobstructive lines of sight, overlapping with infantry and armour.  Or, combined arms suppressive fire.
Graphics are of the era this game was originally produced.  Don't expect a melt-your-face mindblowing world here.  But the graphics are good enough to get the job done and can still really impress at night.  Smoke, tracers and explosion lighting give the game a real atmosphere.  Speaking of atmosphere however; the ambient audio makes me want to throw my speakers across the room.  Noises like a rooster♥♥♥♥♥♥a-doodle-doo'ing every 10 seconds become like nails on a chalkboard.
Fans of the Close Combat series, Combat Mission series, and even the Total War series will likely appreciate this game.  Be warned however, the learning curve is several hours.  Highly reccommended with enthusiasm.

Graviteam Tactics is a game that used to be called Achtung Panzer, but after some sort of nonsense involving the old publisher, they had to change the name when it went on Steam. Or something. I don't know the specifics.
But it's a good game. More people should know about it. It's not very accessible and the UI is confusing, but once you get the hang of it, it's a good time. Though I'll admit, after nearly 25 hours so far, I still don't totally know what I'm doing. That speaks partly to the game's depth, but also how to the lack of transperancy regarding mechanics.
At its most superficial level, it's kind of like a Total War game set in World War II. But it's a lot more of a sim than Total War is, and the design intent is very different. The Ukrainian fellows who made Graviteam Tactics are well known in sim nerd circles for their tank simulators, at least one of which used to be on Steam but doesn't seem to be any more and I don't know why. Their obsession with WWII and tank damage models served them well for making a game of a grander scale, where you command little germans or little soviets in squads and weapons teams, and whose lines of communication and chain of command you must manage as you order them to march onwards towards the slaughter. After a battle in this game, one can find the battlefield littered with meat. Manflesh, to be exact.
You have a bird's eye view of the happenings, starting with the turn-based operations map where you move companies of men and tanks around, check their supply and tell them where and whom to attack. Once a battle commenses you get dumped into the planning stages of the real-time mode, where you set up your little soldiers and give them their opening orders. Opening orders are important, because they have no command cost and allow you to set up your plan and watch it unfold. Your squads and teams for the most part work on their own, though you can of course order them, but they decide on their own behind which trees to take cover, when to shoot and when to hit the deck -- you have no control over such precise details. The best you can do is tell them a general location to move to and a general direction to concentrate their fire. There is little micromanagement in the game, and you are even disuaded from trying to micromanage, as giving orders costs you command and the more into the fire your men get, the harder it is to command them. It's a neat little system, but it isn't readily apparent when you start the game up. It took me more than a few games--and reading more than a few game guides, of which, I might add, there are scant few--to know what the hell the blue bar at the top of the screen meant and why it would change when I tried to order my half-dead, panicking engineer squad to suck it up and advance into machinegun fire (which is a terrible tactic, by the way).
Between battles you can manage your men, splitting up their squads and allocating ammo and fuel for vehicles. It's a fun a little management game, and is pretty simple. You cannot build units in the game, so what you start with is what you get, though there are usually reinforcements showing up on certain turns and whose arrival and availability you are well informed of.
Operations are dynamic and different each time you play, with the possibility of fighting over the same town or the same hill across multiple battles, each side taking and subsequently losing the objective over the course of one or two in-game days. It gives the game a fun, fluid and unpredictable narrative that enhances replayability.
In addition to the operational campaigns, you can also play individual battles with units from force pools on any part of the included maps. What's kind of lame, though, is that you can't set it to have the computer generate the enemy force, so you always know exactly what the enemy has right from the get go. Major bummer for me.
BUT IN CONCLUSION: it is a solid game that deserves more press and more people talking about it.

The Bad:
Too easy - The AI isn't challenging in the slightest and does not make any real use of tactics beyond "charge straight ahead".
Doesn't have multiplayer, so you can never get an actual challenging match.
Default version on Steam has a game-breaking CTD when you increase game speed - requires hunting down a patch outside of Steam to fix.
Expensive DLC in the $10-$15 range, each of which only add a couple scenarios. (Perhaps ~4-8 hours of content each, at best) Not worth the price and over half the DLC isn't even available on Steam anyways.
The Good:
The fundamental core mechanics are good, the gameplay is good, the UI is good, and the game runs pretty well.
But the above issues, especially the lack of multiplayer, really hurts the game overall.
This is a game that absolutely necessitates multiplayer to overcome its greatest shortcomings: Easy AI and lack of content.
In light of the fact that I /have/ put a good number of hours into the game (though most on my record are from idling with the program open), I've decided to change my review to a recommendation. But know that without multiplayer support, this game is seriously missing out on replayability and challenge.

As someone who is always looking for a new game to play, I was more than happy to give this little game a go, especially with the amount of positive reviews it had. Let me say, I'm glad I did. For a free game, this is really well done. You play the part of a man who is in his cabin in the woods, waiting for his wife to return. He has no idea where she is and so he starts to look for clues around his home as to her whereabouts, making sweet little comments about each item. Then it starts to get...creepy, and you realise that absence doesn't make the heart grow fonder, it makes it remember...
I really did enjoy this game. It was short, but as a free game, I see no reason to complain and it was long enough to keep you satisfied with the story. It is more psychological than scary as there is no jumpscares but some things said and seen may leave you raising an eyebrow or wide eyed.
For what it is, I really think this is worth playing as the story is good and the graphics are pretty solid! Besides, it's free. What have you got to lose?

Considering the fact that it is free, and that it is an effort to keep the always-struggling adventure genre alive, you should really give it a chance. Now...let's see...
The colorless graphics are perfect for telling this kind of story. They look almost sepia and I feel they really reinforce the atmosphere in the game. The sounds are just the bare necessities like creaking floorboards, ticking clocks and of course: the voice acting (which is well done). All of them serve their purpose well.
And then... the story itself... what can I say? It is short, dark and powerful. Part of it resonated with me, and at times I was shocked at how much the protagonist thought like I, and probably like we all, sometimes do.
This game isn't asking you to solve puzzles, it's not trying to blow you away with state-of-the art graphics or sounds, nor is it trying to entice you by offering endless online multiplayer, it is not even very long. "But, what is left then?" you may ask. Well, for me that's the feeling I'm left with after playing it. I will be taking a lesson away from this. I won't tell you which one. Play the game. Maybe you'll know. Maybe you'll find your own lesson. Whatever... I can only say there is something there. Something I don't see very often in video games.

I didn't play any of "Tales of ..." games before, so I can't compare Berseria to them. It's my first JRPG experience and I enjoyed it very much. I enjoyed it so much that I couldn't stop myself from playing it all the day. It has some charm and I just couldn't resist it. Let's first talk about the main advantages of this game:
--Great and interesting story. From the beginning till the end it hooks you up and you are being intrigued till the last moment. Besides the main story line, there are a lot of side missions, which extends the plot and helps you to learn the world much better.
--Original and charismatic characters. In my opinion, this is the main advantage of this game, this is what makes this game so interesting. You are playing with non-cliche-heroic characters, you are playing with demons,witches and pirates themselves! It's really interesting to observe how they interact with each other and how things are not so one-sided with them and their worldviews
--Side missions,mini-games, other side-stuff. I mentioned it above, but I also have to add that it helps you to relax from the missions and battles, just enjoy the world you are playing in.
--Combat system. It has some downsides as well, but I liked the variety of techniques you can use in order to defeat a certain enemy. You can fight as a supporter or as a main damager, whatever is suiting your style.
Now let's talk about some disadvantages:
--The duration of the game. It takes around 100 hours to complete the main story line, some important side missions and defeating all the bosses in this game. Not that it's boring, but it's just exhausting at some point. So, if you don't have much free time, be ready to spend lots of days in this game
--Combat system. Despite its variety of techniques, it has just a lot of delicate issues which you have to always keep in mind. You will be learning new things about the combat every time till almost the half-point of the story line, which is quite a lot. So it's just to overloading for a player to memorise every combination and trick he/she can use.
--Monotonous gameplay. In my opinion this is the main problem with the game. After playing about half of the game, everything will just come to one strategy of playing- kill tons of monsters, listen to the dialogues,watch cut-scenes. Again ,again and again you will be doing this till the end of game.
--Graphics quality. Well, I don't particularly find this as a big issue, but if you enjoy playing very cinematic and beautiful games, this one may not be what you'll appreciate. Although, I think graphics is not what makes this game great.
CONCLUSION:
Despite having more cons than pros, I think that the quality of the story and the characters overweights all the minuses the game has. I definitely recommend you this game, I am pretty sure you'll enjoy it as much as I did.

A short but sweet story that follows two girls recounting how they met. Overall, I wouldn't say it's anything special, but it certainly did a good job at what it was trying to be. There were very few issues I had with the game, but at the same time, I wasn't blown away by anything either. The novel is kinetic, which I don't like. But unlike other kinetic VN's (like eden*) I didn't feel like this subtracted a lot from the experience. Still, a good VN, and I'm happy I played it.
My breakdown:
PROS:
+Voice Acting. Nerine Akimoto (Miya), and Kuroi Neko (Risa) did absolutely superb work with their roles. Not one mistake as far as I could tell, and they nailed their characters flawlessly. Definitely the strongest element of this VN.
+Art style. Apart from a few issues with character design, the game is really solid with its art. Some great CGs.
+Heartfelt story. Story is quite beautiful. There isn't much to it, but what they do is quite wholesome and heartwarming.
CONS:
-Soundtrack. I thought the soundtrack was rather weak. It wasn't awful, but it wasn't good either. Some scenes would have really benefitted from a stronger OST.
-Short. For the price, the game is really short. I normally consider $1 an hour to be reasonable. You could get through the game in 3 hours without much effort, making it not worth the $8 tag it has. Definitely something you want to pick up on sale.
-Some odd design. Miya's name is orange for some reason. The opening scene was really difficult to follow because of this, as I couldn't tell who was Miya and who was Risa for a bit. Name colour should always be the same as hair colour, or a hair accessory imo. Unamed character names were odd too. They reused "girl A" (or girl 1. I forgot which one they used) for three different characters. Three WILDLY different characters I should add. They shouldn't have reused the same name like that. But I guess I'm nitpicking a bit here.
-Scores-
Story: 6
Characters: 6
Art: 6
Music: 4
Enjoyment: 6
Overall: 6/10
tl;dr short and sweet kinetic novel. Pick it up on sale if it interests you.

Lot of negativity going around in reviews and the forums that don't concern how good or bad the game is. Just a lot of venting it seems. So here are some facts about the price tag for all interested.
* 40$ Will buy you Titans, which will run on its own without the original game, plus with the new DLC
* It is 13$ or so if you already own PA, which given all the new units, maps and such is fair for new DLC these days.
* They no longer sell PA. No real point the game with its DLC is the same price as PA was a few days ago, maybe even cheaper.
Honestly I do not see where any of it equals a money grab but that is entirely up to each consumer to decide. As it is PA : Titans is a great entry level to play the game.
Now on to the actual game. Is Planetary Annihilation: TITANS any good? That isn't a very easy question to answer as even for fans of Supreme Commander and Total Annihilation, such as myself, there are some very discernable differences in the gameplay as well as many similarities. It will all come down to if the nuances of this game strike your fancy or not. So lets discuss some of the big things fans of those games I mentioned will probably need to know about over all. This is for new PA players as well as those looking at the DLC items.
* Galactic War - This feature pretty much forms the bulk of your singleplayer experience. In it you start with a couple systems and try to take over other systems battle by battle. You start off typically with a barebones of technology. That being the ability to make a basic unit fabricator such as vehicles as well as a few defenses and resource items. After each battle if victorious you can search the planet and chose a technology to boost you for future operations. You only have a limited number of slots so you have to chose wisely. Luckily you can forget some techs or unlock extra tech slots. You continue attacking system to system till you find each of the three enemy factions leader systems and defeat them.
* Planets - The big deal of the game, IE "Planetary" Annihilation, are the planets. That being sphereical spatial bodies circulating a sun or other planets. These planets form the maps for which you will wage war. Your view of the battlefield might be a bit jarring given its very stark difference from the mostly top down views of the genre. You'll rotate around these planets regularly and depending on your settings, north might appear south or East might seem north. There are setting in which the game will lock the planets so that north is always north and so on. You can zoom in and out as needed. In the end this feature will probably be the biggest game maker or breaker for most fans.
* Unit Roster - While fundamentally similar to TA or SupComm, the rosters of units and buildings are also different in a manner. Sure you still have the fighting quadrio, Land, Air, Water and Bots. Yes your buildings are still focused around Energy and Metal consumption and storage. That is where a lot of of the simularities end. The Roster this time around is more, 'Focused." That being smaller. The units, much like SupComm form tiers. You start off with tier one and work up to tier two. Unlike SupComm you only have two tiers. Though from my experience there seems to be less filler units and most of them have a very defined purpose. Planetary Annihilation's Units and particularly its buildings function a lot more for the planetary scale. You'll find lots of units meant for planet to planet travel, attack and defense, as well as utility.
* Titans (DLC) - The games namesake. These are at their very essense what you'd expect in SupComm as, 'Experimentals." That being very large, powerful units that can wreck untold havoc if not checked. The ones I've gotten to use thus far are extremely powerful and almost seem game breaking, but that has only been in AI play. I imagine just like in SupComm preventing enemies from building them is a major part in the balancing, as well as map intel and preparations. One of them can even blow up a planet as a bomb.
* New Units (DLC) - There are several new units in the game, most of them are combat units rather than buildings. You'll find that they fill in the gaps and offer a few new options. For instance the Bot Fabricators now offer Sub Commanders in the advanced version. They function similar to SupComm's SubComms in that they are functionally similar to the main commander, but won't lose you the game if they die. They are powerful and definitely worth persuing as they function as an advanced fabricator unit but also have strong combat ability. There are hover tanks that can cross water, transport planes and many other items. Though I couldn't tell you the exact count. What I will say is they all fit well into the theme and have their uses.
Those are the major items of interest in how this game differs from PA Vanilla with its DLC but similar past games such as the popular Supreme Commander. If you are a fan of SupComm or Total Annihilation chances are one of the first two items will decide your enjoyment of the game. As for PA players, the worth of this expansion for you really depends on if you want the big powerful titan units, extra regular units as well as new maps and other features. From my personal experience I did feel like they filled in some gaps that I felt the game was missing. I only see them as a worthy edition and I didn't mind the 13$ pricepoint at all.
Lets talk pros and cons
PROS;
* The Game has some spectacular weapons and features. Blowing up planets or ramming them into each other are some of the most spectacular RTS finishers I've seen.
* While a bit jarring the planet features can be fun and add a whole new dimension to the gameplay. Defending or attacking isn't just driving across a piece of land, you sometimes have to go into space and assault other planets.
* (DLC) The Titan units, particularly the Big Bot and the Tank, whatever their names are (Sorry), are easily the stars of the show. Though the planet bomb can be rather spectacular in its own way.
* (DLC) The new map items, such as terrains, are a welcome feature
* (DLC) The new units flesh out strategies and offer new options.
* The Galactic war can be fun and its nice to have a sense of progression from match to match.
* You can design your own planet systems if you feel like you want to have certain planets and options available to you in Skirmish or Multiplayer.
* There are different commanders to chose from. While all purely aesthetic, they are a nice option.
* The game is very easy to step into for veteran SupComm or Total Annihilation players, featuring many of the same sort of controls and gameplay styles.
CONS;
* The AI is not particularly good even at its max difficulty. I highly suggest you run an AI mod if you're willing and AI battles are what you prefer.
* The Galactic war, while a great concept, at its current state is really lackluster. None of the factions ever try to take back territory. (Or Even have the ability) Nor does it seem like taking planets has any effect on their tech options. At the base level theres little to no strategy involved other than selecting where to attack next.
* Some of the commander designs actually cost money to unlock
* (DLC) Doesn't seem the AI will ever build titan units to use against you. (I might be wrong but thats my experience)
* The game can be downright taxing on a computer even with well above recommended stats at times. But this could be based on computer factors.
* SupComm players will feel like theres something missing in the tech trees. That loss of a tier can make the game feel shallow at times.
* (DLC) The titans have pathfinding issues and most vs AI Matches will end before you can really utilize them.
Hope this Review helps. Overall I liked the content even if there is work needed. I'd recommend trying it.

V0.1.16 review
Blackwake is a pirate/privateer simulator currently in early access. Developed by Mastfire Studios, Blackwake has a huge amount of potential.
The core gameplay of Blackwake is dictated on whether the player is the captain of their selected ship or not. Captains control the ship and give orders while the rest of the crew loads cannon, fix holes, shoot guns, pump water out, put out fires and board ships. Blackwake is multiplayer only, which means the player must play with other real people, which of course, has its upsides and downsides. The players objectives can vary from keeping their tattered ship afloat, taking down an enemy ship, or boarding another ship. Players will go head to head, 3 boats vs 3 boats, one larger one and 2 smaller ones per team. The first team to reduce the Enemy's tickets to 0 wins.
The multiplayer only aspect of Blackwake seems to have mostly upsides to downsides. Of course players will be on bad teams with bad players once in a while but the vast majority of players seem to know what their doing and when to do it. I could not fathom playing Blackwake with AI. Players are generally nice and usually know which side starboard is.
Blackwake does a lot of things right:
Constantly updating
Great concept and ideas
Looks fairly decent for being such an early build
The multiplayer runs smooth
Great time killer and a great deal of fun
Blackwake does some things wrong:
The voice acting is horrendous
Can be very glitchy
Lacks features for now
Lacks tutorial
Relies heavily on the captain's skill
As a work in progress build, Blackwake has a lot of great ideas and concepts in it, and I will be very excited to see what comes out of it. For $21.99CND it is a tad expensive but if the price stays the same as features get added  it's worth it. Pick it up on sale or with some friends for a great time plundering.
Happy pirating.
