I'd first played the demo few months back and found the story interesting so that's why I bought "Blue Rose" in the first place. After I've finished the full game I can say it's more than just that. Yesterday I was up and reading until 3 am thinking "I should be able to complete this ending soon." As you probably figured it out already, it's not a short read. But for the price given that is to be expected. There a few plot twists and in my opinion it's always good to have at least one in any story.
I liked all of the characters, even the "bad guys". Sometimes one would say something funny that made me lol more than once. And there were times when other would do something unpredictable. Saying they are well-drawn would be an understatement. So I think the characters are one of the pros in "Blue Rose".
The music is good and not irritating. I've really enjoyed one track a lot. However there were times when I read with no music in the background and others with just some sounds repeating every few seconds. Therefore I can say it's so-so.
The art is something exceptional. It's probably the best of all of the visual novels that I'd read. When thinking about well-drawn characters and stunning art I will probably remember that I've seen such in a game called "Blue Rose".
Because of the art and the story I think that something like 10 euro would have been a reasonable price for this game but 20 is a bit over the top. Honestly, for this price one would expect a lot more. The game is not perfect hence the mixed reviews.
Personally I got "Blue Rose" for 1 TF2 key (2,20 euro) which is about 1/10 of the full price or 90% off. At this price I can recommend the game. On the other hand I wouldn't recommend paying 20 euro for ANY visual novel. So if there was a neutral review I would have given the game exactly that. But because I got it fairly cheap and I've found more pros than cons I am leaning towards a "Yes".

I really like this game. You're racing in a city built for racing, but there still is other traffic to avoid. This keeps the game interesting. There's a lot of variety: five types of racing, several dozen cars, collectibles, and more. As well as every street has a time to beat. There's a race where you have to destroy the other racer's cars, as well a trying to survive the trip with other cars trying to destory yours. And that's just single player. You can race online against others in a wide variety of modes. Using a webcam; you'll receive a picture of the people you beat (from the moment of impact) and they'll receive a picture of you when they make your car crash. One of the best things about the game I think is how they handle crashes. Because, you will crash. A lot. But it is not a death sentence as in a lot of other racing games. You're back on the road in about 5 seconds. And you can still win the race after your car has crashed. This also goes for your opponents, though.
As for the down sides: 1. There are really just 8 finishing points in the game, after a while that gets really repetitive.  2. The game takes a long time to load, with a lot of different screens and menus. 3. There's a 'showtime mode' where you crash your car on purpose and destroy other cars to get points. It doesn't seem to work properly and is largely based on luck. When I was looking online to see if I was doing something wrong: nope, it really doesn't work well.
Still, a great game, definitely worth the money (especially at a discount). FInally: play with a controller to enhance your experience.

Blue Rose is a Visual Novel set in a fantasy world, where two factions are fighting for domination in a war. Caught up in the middle are ordinary citizens who are trying to make a new life for themselves. Enter the protagonist, Lena, a Templar of the Blue Rose whose actions have implications on the lives of the villagers whether she likes it or not.
I found Blue Rose to be the best VN I have played to date. I am quite aware there are many other VNs out there and many are better than Blue Rose, but for me, this is the one that takes the cake. Admittedly I haven't played as many as other people who review VNs, but that's also because I typically don't like VNs very much. I'm just not a fan of the genre. But this one had me stuck to my computer for several hours reading through the various plot lines.
Sound: The background music was okay. I had no issues with it, nor was I impressed with it.
Graphics: For what seems like an independent group of developers putting this together, I was rather pleased with the attention to detail. Sure, it's not the greatest art in the VN world, but it's definitely above some strange titles like High School Romance or Last Days of Spring.
Controls: I never though I'd need to write about controls in a VN, till I played Last Days of Spring which gives you next to no ability to customize the experience. Blue Rose offers controller support, text skipping both new and previously read messages, auto play, and more. Definitely has what's necessary to make VN'ing a pleasurable experience.
Story: This is truly where Blue Rose shines. While there are the edgings of some standard tropes among the characters, there are also unique characters that are interesting to find out about. Some VNs have this annoying habit of allowing you to 'make' choices but really all you end up with that is different is perhaps 30 lines of story, and a different ending with a different person at the end. As you explore the universe that Blue Rose is set in, you'll discover more about the characters than you thought you would as you explore the different paths. Their motivations become clearer as you explore the different story arcs. As you progress down those different paths, you'll find a very different story plays out each time, though the first main two might be a little similar. But don't skip the bad endings, aside from being part of the achievements, they also fill in gaps and show very interesting aspects of characters when provoked.
Overall: 7.2/10 - I don't even like VNs but this happens to be a very good one. I'm sure people can recommend better, but for me, I was impressed with it. It very much reminded me of the old Choose your own Adventure books where the story actually changed instead of just changing a love interest. VNs tend to run higher in cost, so I can't evaluate price fairly, but I probably wouldn't spend $20 myself. But again, I'm not a fan of the genre. Take that for what it's worth.

Tales of Bersersia tells a wonderful story involving a cast of great characters, who go through their own character developments. None so tragic as the tale of the main protagonist, hers is a rollercoaster of highs and lows that will pluck at the players heart strings. A journey that involves love, loss, betrayel, hatred and redemption. You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll not soon forget.
The story is supported by good sound and music, as well as excellent voice acting. Parts of the story are told through high quality animated cutscenes.
As a whole this port is well done, runs very smooth and works well with a controller.
The combat itself is quite complex which can also be a bit of a turn off. I'm not a big fan of how the combat insists on locking you onto an enemy when the combat system supports hit detects just fine. Would've rather been allowed to run around a bit more freely on the battlefield. Switching targets can also be annoying as its either unreliable, or reliable but requires you to essentially pause the game for a moment.
On the plus side it allows you to mix and match your combo chains, and the combat system has a surprising amount of depth to the whole. It even has no trouble with some high-risk/high-reward kind of skills, that if used improperly can really hurt you... but if used well...
I mostly went for the main story myself. Expect this adventure to sweep you along for a good 40 hours or so. Introducing new mechanics all along the way. Can't say i ever got bored playing, even for a moment, as i found myself constantly interested in finding out where the story was going to take me next.
Tales of Bersersia is truely a work of art and well deserves the overwhelming praise that is is receiving. Don't miss out on this epic tale.

Daikatana is actually a GOG (Good Old Game).  I’ve given a lot of negative recommendations for old games gleaned off of Humble Bundle packs because I think most outdate themselves.  I put this game on par with Half Life - it’s good.
First of all, and as I have found with other old games, widescreen support and controls are goofy.  However, the gaming community has come up with an unofficial 1.3 patch that fixes bugs, reduces loading times, enables widescreen and anti aliasing support, and generally improves the game.  This is fantastic, download it here and use 7z to unzip it to the install directory (it doesn’t have an installer so make sure to unzip to directory). Note, the patch will corrupt all your save games so best to install first.
But this game is fun!  Part of that is because its a FPS with an interesting story based on the Quake engine.  Hard to go wrong really.  So while I rarely recommend these old games, this is one that is actually fun.
Edit 09/21/2014: I can't finish the game because of a game-breaking bug.  Mikiko gets stuck in an entry way and I cannot continue.  No way to execute her or make her move.  Reloading old saves isn't fixing the problem.

First, I need to say that I don't know why this Visual Novel is so underrated. It has a lot of defects - and I'll talk about some below - but it's still an average Visual Novel. There's a lot of crap Visual Novels out there made only for the sake of the fanservice and they have tons of positive reviews. That seems pretty unfair to me.
The game is kind of short, so it might be a good game to get in a bundle or a good sale. I've seen it in bundles pretty cheap a lot of times. It can be classified more as an Otome Game than as Fantasy Visual Novel, because only a few after the game starts, the main plot is a bit shoved aside to focus more and more in the romantic relation between the characters. Or I should say between Lena and the one you'll pursue as her love affair in game. Also, many people related that they couldn't get attached to any of the characters even with the lots of interaction between them. And yeah... some characters are pretty standart and cliché at all, in my opinion. So it's easy to feel nothing for them.
Another boring thing is that the "replayability" of the game sucks: most of the game parts will be pretty much the same if you decide to start a new route after completing your first one.
The art style is decent. It’s not amazing, but it has a certain charm. BG was ok, BGM was fine too. That being said, Blue Rose is a nice Visual Novel overall and you can have fun with it.

This otome visual novel feature a female protagonist Lena Ehrenfeldt who is a Templar of the Blue Rose, tasked with escorting a noblewoman Lady Adale to Caere to attempt a negotiation for help in the war between Tanves and Helen. Things didn't go as planned, with a dragon attacking the escort party and Lena ends up in an undiscovered remote village. Achievements involve reaching a good romance ending with Simon who is Lena's commanding officer, Gavin who is a former Helenian soldier and a recent settler in the village, Tobias who is the hunter and woodsman of the village, Erin who is the barmaid of the village and the sister of the local village herbalist or with Aran who is the local spirit and takes an interest in Lena's arrival. The game has plenty of save slots to enable quicker replays to reach a different romance ending or to see an alternative bad ending, character portraits next to each location to guide the player to choose which place to go during most parts of the game and the option to skip and fast-forward any section of the game.
Soundtracks and overall game presentation are decent. Recommended when at sale or in a bundle offer as all endings can be reached and the entire game's unlockable CG and extra content at gallery can be completed in less than 10 hours.

was, overall, a good experience and I enjoyed it very much. I played it through with a friend and this is an important distinction because it definitely colors different portions of the game positively and negatively. For example, the story benefited from the group experience, but aspects of the gameplay felt like
too much with an extra player.
As a JPRG, the core of the experience lies in the anime-style story instead of the gameplay. Personally, I really enjoyed Berseria's story and grew quite attached to the cast of characters. I especially liked that it reminded me of the early parts of
, following a self-confessed badgirl who is absoultely driven to accomplish her goal of vengeance. It's a nice departure from the more standard "group of friends set out to save the world" story. It also means you spend the story asking yourself if she's going to redeem herself or ultimately accept the monster that she is, which I find is a very intriquing dramatic question.
Fans of the Tales series, especially Symphonia, might remember the game often asking the player to make decisions which would have both long- and short-term effects on the story. Berseria does not have any of these, unless they are so well hidden that I completely missed them. You do not decide whether to tackle an objective this way or that and there are no hidden conversation options that later mean you do or do not have a character in your party. Personally, I prefer it this way with JPRGS, even if I'm generally of the opinion that other forms of media are better at telling a strictly linear story. The biggest positives with this, to mre, are not feeling the need to replay a 30+ hour game to see the other options, nor feeling like you messed something up by not getting the "Perfect, Golden, Super Great" ending.
Berseria follows the standard 'classic' JPRG formula of splitting most of its gameplay between a field/exploration section and a combat section. There is also a heavy emphasis on menus to handle what its always handled, mostly equipping, buying, and selling items and handling other things like skills and cooking. It is here I would be amiss not to pose my biggest issue with Berseria that taints almost every atom of its design:
As a fan of subtractive game design, I'm often taken aback by how JPRGs seem to emphasize making things as complicated as possible, Final Fantasy in particular seems to take pride in coming up with a brand new, overly complicated way to learn skills with each new iteration. Berseria is no stranger to this and seems to attempt to take it to 11 or even 12. Every aspect of the game is crowded with ideas that could perhaps be interesting on their own, but have no room to breathe or be expanded on, and are even actively harmed by other things they interact with.
For example: the equipment system, which is probably the biggest offender and ties into almost everything else.
Like most RPGS, the game is littered with different tiers of upgrades for every slot of each of your characters' loadouts. Like you'd expect, these have various numbers which make them better / weaker in combat, but they also have skills and not even just one
of skill (though all of them are passive +small% bonuses). Each weapon/armor/etc will have a skill on it that your character can permantly learn, a handful of skills that have a chance to activate when you upgrade it, and random skills in addition that are different for every weapon even of the same type. The sheer number of items and the fact you are constantly switching in order to learn the skills are entirely at odds with the idea that the game then wants you to dismantle items to upgrade other items at the shops. The amount of micromanaging required to get the most out of this system is astounding. Luckily, it seems you can just choose to not bother with it and merely go in order from the weakest to strongest items, mastering all the learned equipment skills as you go along.
The combat skill system is also a victim of this problem. Each character has 16 slots to fill with different skills, 4 for each facebutton in combo-chain order. Each of these skills has a cost and a damage associated, an element, types of enemies it's more effective against, status ailments it can apply, and roughly belongs in one of two categories that are then effected by how many of each of the two categories of skills you've in the same chain to reduce their cost or increase their casting speed. The game teaches you early that enemies are weak to certain elements, and that you should take advantage of this by chaining together skills of those elements in order to make an opening so that the rest of the attacks in the chain deal even more damage. Once again, the amount of micromanagement needed to get the most out of this system is simply incredible. Luckily, again, it seems you can choose to not bother with this, either, assigning a button (A by default) to "You Decide", where your character will use whatever ability automatically. Battles are then still interesting enough, in my opinion, just managing your chacaters special attacks and super special, watch me do an awesome attack cutscene, attacks.
This overcomplication and micromanagement thing is entirely subjective, though. It was a huge turn-off for me, especially because it was both myself and a friend playing, but I know others who get into JPRGs specifically for that kind of stuff. I'm happy to say that, at the very least, you can not bother with it and have a splendid time. We are playing on hard mode, didn't grind at all, are about 10-15 levels under the random monsters in the dungeons, and still each battle starts with an amusing line of how strong the enemies look because we're so underlevelled... before we wipe the floor with them in about 20 seconds.
The other big issue with the gameplay are the dungeons. They are absolutely dreadful. The overal design is a single theme of reused textures in a large dungeon designed by someone with a deadline at midnight and a pad of graph paper. Virtually nothing in them is any good, the rooms are pointless, and the "puzzles" are just a waste of time. Each puzzle is usually coming to a locked door, going down the hallway to the left and hitting a switch going down the hallway to the right and hitting a switch, and then returning to and going through the door.
There's not much to say here. I found Berseria to be an adaquete port and had no technical issues during the entire time I was playing.
It might be worth saying we played with the English VAs and they are, for the most part, quite good in my opinion. This might be colored by meeting them in person, though. Otherwise, non-important NPC acting is hit or miss - some of them are reaaaally bad - and the same voices get reused a lot.  You're going to hear a LOOOOOOT of Lucien Dodge.
Despite everything I may have said, I still recommend Tales of Berseria to anyone looking for a nice "JRPG Experience". The story's good, the gameplay's overly complicated but still fun (even/especially if you don't bother with the tedious micromanagement), and the dungeons are awful, but I still really enjoyed playing it through.

Pros: The game is a lot of fun with a simple concept; ship on ship duels where you are a simple crew member. Teamwork is the object of the game and only a true team can win. It is absolutely worth 20-25 bucks.
Cons: The graphics will eventually need to be upgraded. It has pretty basic textures and some of the sky boxes need to be reconsidered by the devs (the red one sucks). The matchmaking system should probably be redesigned at some point, the choose you own lobby system is as retro as the graphics.
About the Game: The game itself is fairly simple a team of between 1 and 3 ships is manned by the players.
Players vote on who gets to be the Captain. The captain sails the ship and talks to the crew. If the Captain does a bad job the crew can vote to "mutiny" and a new captain will be assigned.
Being a crew member is fairly simple. You can load and fire cannons. Resupply the guns as a powder monkey. Repair holes in the hull and fix damaged sails. Grab a bucket and put out fires. Board the enemy ship when it comes along side. Thats really it!
The game is fun and has promise to turn into an arcade style winner. It gets my stamp of approval for what its worth.

Telltale Game's The Walking Dead: Season One can be considered one of the best games in my book. This game gets you so interacted within the storyline & plot, with it's rich character development, & amazing ost. While taking place within the same universe as Robert Kirkman's The Walking Dead comic series, it does a perfect job with recreating the design & feel of those books themselves.
This is a story that you'll never forget, I played this game back in 2015 on my Xbox One, and I still remember to this day everything that happened, and while I saw the games were on sale, I decided to pick them up, to replay them all. I couldn't be happy enough with the ending, while I still remember to this day getting so emotionally upset about everything that happened.

You can really understand the bond that these characters go through, and what they're all feeling. I felt like these were family members, people I could relate to. I enjoyed playing through this game, and would have to give it a score of 9.5/10. If you ever get the chance to play this game for the first time, do it!

But really it does not describe it justice. The thrill and challenge of the game is a real buzz. There are nearly no limits to how far you can challenge yourself under the most strenuous situations.
Go watch some gameplay or try a demo or trial the full game if you can. It is like marmite: you will either love it or hate it.
If you like strategy what-so-ever though, you will absolutely fall in love.

Despite the short time I have put into this game right now Steam, due in most part to my work, I do wanna say that I am making this review/opinion from my experience of this game series while I was in college back in the early 2000s.
What I can say from this short time is that, this is very slick, this is probably even more slick than the game GG X / X2 Reloaded that I played for hundreds of hours and that impression came from just a couple of full playthroughs. (If this title interests you by the by, those older other tie in names to the series mentioned are definitely worth a recommendation too. They are just as good as this, only slightly older versions and a very tiny bit outdated in places)
To the pros of fighting games and this series, you might like this.. This is a definitely testing game for fast reflexes, combos and strategy on the fly, the only downside is unless you may have some biases with the art style in the game, which in contrast opinion, is possibly the strongest suit right next to the gameplay and controls.
I can't speak much more in depth than what I know from tournaments and the tricks of being very good skill-wise in this game, as I am not really a hardened veteran / pro of this game, so for a more detailed opinion, this might not be it.
For casuals, it might be a bit hard to recommend as the game is fairly difficult, but that I don't think should be a bar to set for casual players, as it is not impossible to learn as you go, That's after all how a lot of us learned the basic jist of the game and got better at it, we just played it and even if we lost, we all kept trying harder and better the next time. :)
The most important way to decide if you want the game in my opinion, that depends on whether you really are convinced that this is a game you want to play and if you're confused by what that means, I'll use myself as the example of how I got into this game. Back when I used to play the other games a lot, I wasn't into fighing games, it actually was more the style and entire presentation of the game, the characters and all the other sweet things found here, such as tricky moves to pull off, Overdrive moves, etc., all those things in combination made me hyped enough to pick it up and play the hell out of it, just having fun however stupidly or good I was playing. Even now I'm not That good at this game, but god damn if I do not enjoy playing it..
In short, it doesn't matter how good you are with fighting games, if you have the time to play it and you just want to play it based on what you've seen for yourself about the game, I dont think a skill ceiling will be enough to stop you from getting into this game.. This is possibly the most solid fighting game ever. I can't imagine how good Xrd is if it is better than this game. Heavy Metal Rock was something I didn't like when I first encountered Guilty Gear music and although it was pure rock and I hated it at first, this is really the best video game music I can think of. As for the characters, each has a lot of story behind them that you have to play or research multiple games to fully understand.
Every character in this game is really cool and over-the-top. The game was basically balanced by making characters extremely powerful, but be thankful you didn't get a version where Eddie was able to destroy anyone if in the hands of a master player. Even bottom tier characters can take tournaments as people are known to play Sol and Ky despite them being rated near the bottom of tier lists.
You will be dealing with a very complex game in Guilty Gear. Special moves aren't super easy to do and you will have a lot to be remembering. But you can basically optimize how you handle any situation through skill because of things like Faultless Defense (take no damage and space away any attack), Full Roman Cancel (stop attacking mid-move to perform another move) and Gold Burst (gives a huge boost in tension if it hits or is blocked).
Accent Core Plus R is not only the most balanced version of the game, but it also gives characters the most attacks they have ever had in the XX series.
The game is really fast paced and not really beginner/casual friendly, so I don't quite recommend you buy this game until you get adjusted to 2D fighters and how to learn them, but the game is very rewarding to play due to the fact that you can continuously improve your performance with the various mechanics and moves and large cast of characters.
This game is basically a must play, but I guess on the other hand, if you don't try this, at least try Xrd, which has much more advanced training for new players and a more flexible gameplay style.

Great game, especially for early access. The terraria-esque feel coupled with the massive variety of landscapes gives the game a very immersive atmosphere, and makes exploring fun (especially in the early hours). Each planet has at least one large dungeon, and you'll be finding new dungeons even after fifty hours of gameplay.
The community is great (check out
and the devs are friendly and interactive with the community, featuring community builds and talking with their players on Reddit. The devs also keep a day to day blog on the updates they make to the game, so you can always get a hint of what's coming in the next new update.
I do have a few qualms with this game, though. Once endgame has been reached, there is little to do, as you have already explored most planet types, and the only planets that are actually challenging are uninteresting wasteland and volcanic planets. In addition, microbiomes and their exclusive items are linked to planet types, which are linked to difficulty, so there are many cool items that you can't find at a high tier.
Also, updates are few and far between. While I do have hope that the game can become even better, we have to wait six months between each major update to try out new things. Fortunately, the game does have unstable and nightly modes, which are updated with new content right after the content is created. Note here that little bug testing is done on the nightly mode, so game-breaking bugs are to be expected.
Overall, this game is one of the most promising early access games I have played, and aside from getting a little boring after 200 hours, it's a great experience up until then. I reccomend.

The new units also have some neat mechanics like the air units that can fight anything and generate power. What I love are the new audio ques and enhanced UI. UI wasn't touched too much but it was tweaked enough that I noticed and appreciated it.The sounds though were vastly diversified adding a whole layer of variety to the mix.

The new units themselves as stated before are unique enough to get excited for. Like star destroyers or the Aircraft carrier that sends out fighters or the walking nuke which has no purpose other than to explode or even the giant walking earthquake machine (as depicted by the big logo) . My personal favorite are the nanomites which die really quickly but eat away at anything faster than you can imagine. I played one game and managed to get a sea of them. The assult on my enemies base was very rewarding.
In short if you are a PA fan already I give this a thumbs up so long as the big opening sale is going for 13$ (which it will cary on for some time)
If you are not a PA fan this is the whole game plus the new stuff for 13$ If you enjoy a good RTS at all this game is perfect for you.

This is probably one of my favorite visual novels. That being said I have a lot of complaints. Here we go:
+ Story - finally story that touches more mature/darker themes.
+ Setting of the game, secluded village is nice idea, and I like time period as well.
+ Romance - we don’t need so much dating simulators and I am really pleased that romance is finally secondary objective in one Visual Novel. It feels mature as well, there isn’t cringe worthy elements like in most VNs.
+ Writing - I liked that I could love or hate a character depending on which path I took.
+/- Choices - decent variety of endings or love interests but I sometimes wasn't satisfied with choices game made for me.
+/- Music - it felt like decent choice but nothing I will want to hear again.
- Visual aspects of the game – I didn’t like almost any of it, I don’t find any character appealing, and while some of the scenery is decent I would like it to complement description better, I want to see those changes on the mountain I’ve read so many times.
- Price - I bought it in a bundle and I am very satisfied with the game but I can't recommend it for this price. If it’s on sale for 70% off or more you should consider it.
- That I couldn't skip text that I’ve already read in the endgame. It's annoying and it artificially adds length to the game which is bad thing.

I think I picked up Daikatana from a humble bundle with some games that I legitimately wanted.  Even so, I can't help but feel that I've been slighted.  I have truly been made John Romero's ♥♥♥♥♥.  What follows is a recollection of my time with the game.
The game starts with Hiro Mishamuramoto (our hero) who is swinging swords in some warehouse.  Then a guy with a staff and probably tattoos knocks on the door.  It is in the ensuing conversation that the rich tapestry of Daikatana's plot is unraveled and we are introduced to the conflict between the Mitsubishis, the Inoharas, the Daikatanas, the regular Katanas, and time and space I think.  In a flourish of narrative excellence, the conversation is cut short (albeit not short enough) by ninjas punching everyone in the face.
Our Hiro then decides that the best course of action is to hide in the staff guy's coffin (who was punched so hard that he died).  We do.  Then what I can only assume are the second most important characters, the guys who pick up coffins on the road.  They are so terrible at their jobs that they routinely make bets on how many of the dead they will disrespect on any given day.  A bunch of coffins fall out of the back of their dump truck, a classic start to an adventure if I've ever seen one.
Then you get out of the coffin, which was a mistake, because that's really where the game was telling me I belonged.  You get a metal god hand and a gun of green stuff.  Then, mosquitos.  I really appreciate that they were able to put such a short sound byte for the mosquitos noise, so that I could really get the hang of it.  Anyway, they kind of fly at you and you kind of shoot them, and then they die explosively like everything dies in this game.  Except in cutscenes with ninjas.
After I mastered mosquito killing, I moved on to the turrets that kill you within 3/4 of a second, which I appreciated.  Too many games nowadays give you a chance, not portraying the world as the bleak and hopeless and unfair affair that it is, and they give you like three seconds to not die, which is weak.  Anyway, the turrets are invincible.  So I exploded.
After that, I ran past the turret and I exploded, much to my chagrin, due to a nearby frog.  I don't think he did anything, but it probably had to do with time and space.  I didn't have the trusty Daikatana yet, not having killed Ishiro Mugamaya yet, but I did have the ION CANNON which shoots ions.
After surmounting the combined obstacles of mosquito, turret and frog, I was repeatedly killed by the crocodile brothers.  That's fair.  I probably couldn't take them in real life even if I had lightning fists.
So I thought, this first level has been going pretty well.  But what if I just ran past everything?  Turns out, that wins the game.  At least until you get to the bridge.  Don't get me started on the bridge.
So on the bridge, there are these flying searchlight guys that get really irritated and write you sternly worded letters until you leave or until three seconds have passed.  I shot them.  Then I ran into a wall and disintegrated, at which point I was notified that "Hiro Mayazakiwakawoo fails at life", and such a thing I had never supposed, only having died 5-8 times.
If you hang out by the wall, TEN insects appear along with a big insect and they wreck you good.  Or at least they would have, if I hadn't backed into a corner SO hard that the corner destroyed me and my head flew across the level.  The camera solemnly panned to a dancing crocodile, which I can only assume was the best in eulogy technology that games had access to at the time.
tl;dr still a better love story than twilight 3/10

This is a Visual Novel: a kind of interactive story where the player takes some decisions for the main character in key points of the story, building the story through its end, which depends on the decisions taken. There are no other playable elements in the game. VNs often have romanceable characters (this game has a few male and a female) and adult/erotic content (this game has none of it). Sometimes VNs have some simulation elements or other minigames (this has none).
The player takes the role of a female young knight in a fantasy world. During a escort mission, travelling through an isolated frontier region with other knights, they are attacked by a dragon and she gets separated of the group. She awakes injured in a rogue settlement, while she tries to recover, found out about her missing companions and decide what to do in the end.
As for visual novels go, this is one of my favourite, and I've played many, AAA and indie, old and new.
Apart from the setting being different from the overused slice of life, or clumsy teen founding harem themes, the world they live in is consistent, the writing is solid (at least more than the average, let me clear that since this seems to be a common issue for other reviewers), there aren't mayor avoidable-through-proof-reading errors, and the character actions and decisions don't feel forced, hasty, idiotic or unnatural. Too very often I feel embarrased for the actions of the characters I play, or the reactions from the secondary characters. This game was not the case. Both the main and secondary characters were mostly deep, relatable and likable in different grades that depend on the player (and limited by the extension of the game). For me, playing this female character was enjoyable. I'd define her as a strong, courageos woman unused to act outside of the role of a champion of her faith, but not so much as to fall in tomboy or social failure archetypes.
For the art, you should judge yourself from the featured screenshots and video. Character art is anime style, and in spite of questionable anatomic features (a bit too over-stylized, some weird necks, but -thank god- plausible busts, too much ash hair but fortunately no other fancy animeish colors) and lack of detail (characters look unquestionably good, and that's the problem: they all look in their twenties), they are expressive, of enough quality, and finally fit the serious tone of the story.
I find the length of the game in my range of comfort, which means that other players may feel it a bit short. The game may lack a bit in content. Some endings may be a bit too similar, but others are pretty interesting. I'd add that this is one of the only games a played without skipping already read parts in a second playthrough.
I'm glad and proud to recommend this game.
The main reason for that is "I enjoyed the game": good setting and story, relatable and likable main character and appropiate length.

Characters/Story 8/10
Graphics 7/10
Music	7/10
Gameplay 4/10
TL;DR
Get this if:
1. It's on sale.
2. You don't need deep gameplay, a good story/characters is enough to satisfy you.
I'm not going into details for the story and characters due to spoilers, but I think they were good. The main character is a anti-hero set out on a revenge quest, which was a nice change of pace from the ordinary "save the world". She also never really delved into the edgy personality which so many dark heroes have. So the story and characters are definitely the highlight of the game and probably, most likely, why this game has overwhelmingly positive score.
But, while this would be sufficient for an anime or a book, this is a game, and a game has gameplay. Which is exactly where Berseria falters and why I cannot give a blanket recommendation. The battle mechanics are the main gameplay so lets start with that:
The game has a real-time combat system where you control one, and only one, character. Each button (XBone: A, B, X, Y) is tied to a certain attack and together you can make a combo. By default, the game itself will set which attack is tied to which button by its own, but you can change this to your preference and make your own combos. Once you start gaining some levels you will get new attacks you can utilize. You also have something called souls, this is how many attacks you can chain together without waiting. You typically start with 3 souls which means you can make 3 attacks before you have to wait a second. Now, you can increase or decrease this soul value, this is done by stunning, perfect dodging, killing or inflicting a status ailment on an enemy. If you do so you will gain 1 soul. You can have a maximum of 5 souls, more with certain abilites, which means you can make 5 attacks in a row. But, if you are stunned or hit with a status ailment, you lose 1 soul, which means you can make 1 less attack. Having only 1-2 souls is very bad and can be a quick death in dangerous encounters on harder difficulties.
To make it a bit more complex you can also make a "break soul" attack, each character has its own but I'll focus on Velvet since she is the main character and I have no inclination to play as anyone else. To make a break soul attack you have to have 3 souls and it will lower your soul value by 1. But it is a very strong attack, heals you and breaks guards and flips downed opponents, more importantly, it puts Velvet into a "theonized" state where she will do increased damage the lower HP she has, her HP will gradually drain but she cannot die, be stunned or get any status ailments. She can still take damage, but can only go down to 1 HP, at which point she will make a final attack and lose her theonized state. This also happens if you try to make an attack while you have used all the attacks already, for example a fourth attack if you only have 3 souls. The thing is, you can instantly use another break soul after the theonized state as long as you have 3 souls. This means you will be more or less invincible for the majority of the battles and is why many people regard her as OP. Because as long as you can get stuns and status ailments on enemies, you cannot die.
That said, on harder difficulties and on special encounters, typically "Dangerous encounters" where you aggro more than 1 enemy at the same time on the map, you can still die easily. Why? Because 1 stun is enough to kill you, even though you have full health at the time, especially if more than one enemy attack you at the same time. Even if you survive, you will lose 1 soul because you were stunned and if this puts you on 2 souls you cannot save yourself with a break soul and might be stunned again and die. On normal difficulties however and normal encounters, this is hardly a problem because you have a low chance to get stunned and the enemy doesn't hit nearly as hard. Expect to never die if you play on normal. So, you might think that hard difficulties are the way to go then? Well. Harder difficulties also makes the enemy into damage sponges will will slow down the game significantly which is a problem in and of itself.
So what's bad about this system? To start with, you only have control over 1 of your characters, which means the other characters will be completely under the control of the AI. Hell, you can make the AI take over your character as well, this way you don't have to do anything. Truly a great mechanic, let the game play itself for you. Regardless, it typically just turns into a chaotic mess and all you have to do is to spam attacks and break soul whenever you're not invincible. That's basically 95% of all battles, just try it out yourself in the demo. On some bosses and dire foes, especially on harder difficulties you probably want to check their weaknesses and use a combo that exploit it, to have a higher chance of stunning/status ailment them. But even then it is pretty simple as long as you can manage your souls, dodges and break soul attacks.
So the combat mechanics is a bit meh. I think other games, like Xenoblade and Kingdom Hearts handled real-time combat with RPG elements (levels, HP, weapons, skills e.t.c.) much better. For once they were not as big of a cluster ♥♥♥♥ like this one and you felt more in control.
That's the combat system. But the game has more gameplay than just combat, how about exploration. Well, the game is very linear, though it opens up at the end, it sadly reminded me of Final Fantasy XIII. No, it is not nearly as bad or linear, but the exploration is sorely lacking. You eventually get a ship, but you don't get to use it, no ship battles, no sea exploration, you just click on a map and you get instantly teleported there, there is no overworld, it's just small maps interconnected. Oh, that's right, there's a small mini-game involving the ship, basically, you send it to different corners of the world and you wait 30 min to get some loot, rinse and repeat. There's no thought behind it, just send it away and wait 30 seconds. If you have played Neptunia, it is like Stella's Dungeon except much simplier.
You also get a base, but it must be the most lack-luster base I've ever seen in a jRPG, nothing like Suikoden or Skies of Arcadia. You might think that it might change appereance and maybe you could upgrade it by spending money, but no, nothing happens with it. To even call it a base is a insult to other jRPGs that actually have one.
Something else that is completely bland and boring is the dungeons. I just cannot describe them better than just bland. There's just nothing there, no puzzles, no interesting environments, just bare corridors filled with monsters. I've seen these complaints even from those who like the game and recommend it. The dungeons suck.
Finally, how about some mini-games? The only mini-game that was worth playing was the card game, a very simplified game but fun nonetheless. There is also fishing, you know how that works? Just press A. That's it, the character will do everything for you, some animation with a fishing pole and you get your fish. I feel like that encompasses how little effort has put into the gameplay of the game. Yeah, we're going to have a fishing game. Oh how will it work? Just press A. That's it.
I just, it's so bad. Did they run out of money or something? There are also some other mini-games that are not worth mentioning.
The game is not terrible but it is sorely lacking in the gameplay department. Like I said in the beginning, buy it if it is on sale and you care more about story and characters rather than deep gameplay.

I was born in Bosnia. My parents were killed in the wars, and I was left an orphan. I was adopted by an old turnip farmer, and he raised me as his own. I thought that my life was going to be ruled by poverty, but one day, fortune struck. An old laptop fell off the back of a truck. and it was mostly unharmed. I knew what I was destined to do: make Let's Plays of Minecraft and Spooky Games. I started squatting in an abandoned house above a Starbucks, stealing internet from them and luckily, the old house still had power.
I had hit a brick wall, though. I didn't have any money, and I only had food and water from the farm, and from discarded pastries and half-caf diet iced caramel frothaccinos with cigarrette butts in them that people so carelessly left on the tables as they left the store, or went to the bathroom.
After months of despair, today, yes today ladies and gentlemen, was the day I finally found a game I could afford. For only nineteen cents, this game would launch my Let's Play career, and I would make millions of Youtube dollars.
I fished a quarter out of a wishing well and ran as fast as I could to the farm. I asked my adopted father if I could have the money from his Mastercard if I gave him the same amount in cold, hard cash, and when he said no, I just took his credit card and bought it anyway. Don't worry, I put both the card and the quarter back in his wallet soon after.
Ladies and gentlemen, today is the day I start my Let's Play career, and when the money I get from videos from this game starts rolling in, I'll finally be able to buy Minecraft and start making millions.
Ladies and gentlemen...you're looking at the next PewDiePie.

Daikatana does have flaws, I guess that's not the best to start a review, but Daikatana is such a complicated title to review because of all the stuff that surrounds it :) Even though the side-kicks and some parts of the level design are what I'd consider a flaw on a game, there are many levels on which the design is pretty awesome, very varied, very fun and amazing. The weapons are extremely varied also, and they play very well, they fit the environments and are fun as ♥♥♥♥ to shoot.
It's hard to talk about the side-kicks, I don't know if it's because I'm a programmer, or what, but the truth is, that the side-kicks do get stuck in some areas, and are not that helpful in general (sometimes I'd rather leave them behind, kill everything, and then go back to get them), but they actually amazed me a lot of other parts, like there are huge maps on the Greece and Norway episodes on which they run around with you flawlessly, they jump around, go inside tunnels, crouch, perform complicated jump sequences on top of platforms, and it's really amazing that they were able to do this back in the day, as I mentioned they do have flaws, but you have to keep in mind that some of the people who worked on this were modders, and Romero was probably used to working with Carmack, and the kind of programming to do this stuff is pretty hard, which he mentions on this interview:
Had they had more time (but pressure was probably too big already), it probably would have been better, but still it wouldn't have lived to the expectations people had, the very aggresive marketing campaing didn't help in this regard. And if you think "more time are you insane?", remember that half the team left Ion Storm in the middle of the development, which must have had a very big impact on the project, specially on the programming side.
I feel like most of the press went on the hate wagon, and didn't give this an objective chance. I feel that since the marketing was so aggresive, they decided to be aggresive reviewing it, and maybe that's not a good thing. I'll do say that the mosquitos and frogs on the first episode are annoying and made me quit the game when it came out years ago, but I thought I'd give it another shot later on, and got it on a sale, and after the swamp level, the game is a lot of fun, entertained, and varied like no other.
The multiplayer is insanely good. Deathmatch feels like an evolution or a true succesor to Quake 1. I do think Quake 3 is way more balanced competitively, but for friend splatter deathmatch free for all anything goes fun, it's ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.
Graphics are mixed, some stuff looks dated, and didn't seem to have aged well, but some areas look really cool, and level design shines sometimes. But having came out after games like Half-Life, Quake 3, and Unreal Tournament ('99), it's fair to say, it was behind in this area, I don't judge games by their graphics, but by their gameplay (which in Daikatana is awesome), but back in the late 90s, this was a big deal.
My final note on Daikatana is that it is pretty awesome. Definitely not even close to what the press made it out to be. It's very fun, and if you workaround its flaws, it's a cool, fun game.
To me the game feels like something in between a 6 or 7 out of 10. Closer to 6, and maybe without the flaws I mentioned it would have been a 7.
I recommend it if you have patience and work around the flaws, and want to have fun with the multiplayer. Otherwise if you want stuff like the side kicks to just work, you'll most likely not enjoy it and become frustrated.

Imagine a function that everyone's invited to. It's all over social media and touted as the biggest event of the year.  You plan on going because all your friends and colleagues intend to, but days pass and you forget to RSVP. Your calendar stops functioning and you lose sight of all your big appointments. It's with a pang of sadness that I write this review, that sort of feeling when you finish a long-running TV show and wish there was more.  Tales of Berseria is a beautiful storytelling experience that offers a level of emotional depth I wasn't aware was possible in a JRPG.  The game's biggest strength is easily its story, so if you're not prepared for cutscenes, this will be an immediate deal breaker.  However, if you wany that experience, you're in for a treat.
For context, I have never played a Tales game and the last JRPG I've bought was FF10 (unless you count the Fire Emblem series, which I don't).  For a newcomer to the series, Berseria was easy enough to follow.  The gameplay, like most JRPGs, falls into two main categories -- exploring the world and combat.  The level design is straightforward and linear, though tends to hide that fact with "hidden" paths, bonus bosses, and minor collectibles.  Combat is fast and frantic, played in real time.  Basic foes and bosses are simple until the last third or so of the game where enemy resistances suddenly become a much bigger factor, and bosses in particular can offer a sudden and significant challenge.  Despite this, combat itself is also pretty simple, with an emphasis put on positioning, blocking, and dodging.
The graphical style, while simple, is crisp and clean and offers lightning fast loading speeds.  The audio is generally excellent as well.  The soundtrack is, while not literally the best I've heard, still great and each piece is used appropriately to help set the right tone.  Voice acting is hit-or-miss for minor characters, but superb for the main cast.  Special shoutouts to go to the main character's husky and anguished voice after the prologue, and the nerdy, bookworm pirate voiced by Talesin Jaffe who somehow knows a little bit about everything.  Great casting choice there, by the way.
The game's biggest strength is easily its story.  There are few twists and turns here.  In true anime style, the characters tend to overthink and analyze everything, so something that could have been a twist has usually been suggested as a possible outcome.  That comes with the territory, along with the way that the game uses almost every stereotype that exists in a classic JRPG.  Listing examples would start to spoil things, but don't be surprised if you roll your eyes a few times for just how predictable some things turn out.  It's part of the charm.
The story's true strength lies not in the plot itself, which in itself is merely passable, but its character building.  As you recruit your party, each characters motivations, emotions, past, and ambitions are explored.  There is a TON of dialogue as characters explore the world and merely talk to each other.  Sometimes it's about a recent event, other times it's about where they are, or a follow-up on what someone said about something, or other times it's just a humorous observation one wishes to share with the others.  All of these skits, as the game calls them, are gems.  In almost any other game the constant interruptions would be annoying, but considering they're optional (with a button prompt), an important part of the world building, and written extremely well, I was never bothered by them.  Indeed, if you plan on skipping them, you're missing out on what I'd argue is the main focus here.
I have relatively few complaints.  The tutorial is awful; I didn't feel like I actually understood the basic mechanics behind combat, aside from attack like a madman, until about 5 hours in.  The game also trains you poorly with how late into the game it is until enemies start having meaninful resistances to certain attack types.  Battles tend to be either brain dead simple, or one stun and attack combo away from being killed -- sometimes in the same fight.  I'd have enjoyed a more varied breadth of difficulty that was somewhere in between.  Lastly, there's a fair amount of backtracking here -- most areas are visited at least twice.  Doesn't bother me, but I know that can annoy others.
Overall, there's a lot to like here and I strongly recommend it.  If I did number ratings, this would be in the 9-9.5/10 range.  It's tough to predict how long it will take to beat this one, as it depends on how many bonus bosses and sidequests you seek out, if you listen to all the cutscenes/skits, if you try to avoid the random battles, and if you like revisiting towns to see if there's new interactions.  I beat this in about 50 hours (I've around ~15 hours in offline if you're looking at my playtime at the time of writing, so bear that in mind) by playing through the main story, listening to all skits as they came up, putting in no real effort to avoid fights, and defeating most bonus bosses, but not really doing any sidequests.

I got hooked on XCOM when they gave it out as part of the PS Plus. I never thought it possible for a tactical game to be so fun and so deep on a console. I eventually got it on PC with the expansion pack, and finally I got around to getting XCOM 2.
Well, in the XCOM tradition, someone complained the first one was too easy. And they cranked it up to eleven. Just like Terror of the Deep.
Once again we were given smooth and deep tactical combat that gives no quarter. It manages to be deep and difficult without going bonkers and losing its focus. The geoscape is still a world map, but it's very different from the predecessor, with many twists and traps awaiting you. The game also has an outright baffling variety of missions, maps and incredible customization options for your soldiers. It also looks even better than the already good-looking Enemy Unknown. XCOM 2 really does take what its predecessor paved and builds an excellent game by expanding on it in many ways while changing things - and it's obviously well thought-out; it doesn't lose anything, it's nicely refreshing but it... well, doesn't become alien. After all, your guys shoot aliens.
While it can be frustrating as all hell, ultimately this makes it all the more rewarding. It's tough and unfair, but paradoxically in a fair way. Aside from the smooth gameplay and good visuals, we get a game that never coddles you and tries to bash your head in. At the same time, you can beat it. It actually builds immersion. You have to rely on your wits and smarts. You are commanding humanity's last hope on a desperate mission... and you can turn around a war that's already been lost. The difficulty isn't just because. It's because you are actually facing an impossible task.

I won't go too in depth with my review, because I didn't get that far in to it; on my own that is. Now the graphics in this game are nice, I can't bash them very hard, especially because it's a free game. During the first few minutes of the game, I could see what the atmosphere was going for. Simply a cabin in the woods, with some old antiques scattered around the house, along with some of the player's and Serena's personal items. The cabin is very simplistic, something I like art style was. There were also some nice background noises to help set the mood.
But here's where the problem sets in: This game wants you to look at EVERYTHING, and I am not skimping out saying that. Anything that the player, (we'll just call him Henry, since I don't think they actually said his name), can interact with has to be clicked multiple times to get taken to the next part of what "story" I actually got to. I seriously tried my hardest to beat this game, but it ended up frustrating me. There was a part of my play-through that Henry said "Why even torture myself trying to remember?" and I audibly agreed with him.
There were some parts of the game that started to creep me out, like when I looked at the picture on the table to see that Serena's face had changed from a blurred out face, to a happy/bored look, to an angry scowl, or when Henry started to talk violently. But they all got faded out by my frustration toward Henry, and how much I could see why Serena doesn't seem to like him in his head.
It became incredibly annoying when Henry just refused to interact with anything that I wanted to look at. There was the dresser, and the constant wanting to just go outside! And once I thought that I solved whatever puzzle was laid out for me, I rushed back to the table wanting to see if the picture changed; only to see that it hadn't.
Look, the fact that I didn't enjoy this game very well could be my fault entirely; maybe I got too mad too fast. I only played it for a little over an hour, but Henry's whining just turned me off from the play-through in the end. Now how far did I get? I'm not sure how to level it in stages, but it was just when Henry constantly is whining about how much he hates her, and how much he's too upset to even think. I've always enjoyed point-and-click games; something about them fascinates me. But this seemed like it was doing the exact opposite, like it was deliberately trying to turn me away, and just give up. If that’s the case, then Serena succeeded.
When I quit the game, I went to look at a guide on YouTube to see how to win it; not to my surprise, I missed a couple things in the background of the game that I didn’t think to look. But that began to frustrate me more! I looked at the window, the stove, the cast iron pan, every drawer I could find, the two paintings, even a thing that wasn’t graphically there; dust next to a nightstand. And yet I still failed.
So in closing; if you’re a casual gamer that has an interest in horror games, I wouldn’t recommend this. If you’re a gamer that enjoys getting mad for whatever reason, then by all means, go try this out. Let me state this one more time though, because I want to give the devs credit for making a game that I did enjoy for a little bit: It very well could be my fault that I didn’t like it, it could be that I was just too stupid to beat it on my own. And to be fair; the game was free, so I don’t know what I was expecting. Thanks for listening!

[Spoiler-Free Review]
Not since X-men's Juggernaut has there been anyone so determined to destroy the very building blocks of an industrially advanced civilization. Wizorb encourages you to join geriatric shape-shifter, Cyrus, as he rids the world of a million menacing bricks in a desperate effort to save the world. Stand in solidarity as Cyrus cuts grass, smashes crates, and burns to ash, baby animals and other nefarious forces who happen to be standing in his way.
The game is probably most renowned for incorporating RPG elements into paddle-and-ball gameplay (reminiscent of Breakout/Arkanoid/Devilish), but the RPG aspects are really quite an afterthought as the game's main play mechanic revolves around clearing separate, self-enclosed sections called "Worlds". Don't expect sweeping dialogue or character development.
Wizorb looks like a game made in the 80's, sounds like a game made in the 90's, and plays like a game made by true retro game fans. I'll be watching for more from Tribute Games. In the meantime, break down the walls with Wizorb!

I could not recommend more.
GGXX AC +R is a freaking amazing fighting game, and by far my favorite game in my favorite franchise in fighting games.
To be honest, I didn't play any Guilty Gear for years since I last played GGXX on GBA (or was it GGX?), but the presence of the franchise on Steam made me buy it to revive my love (and nostalgia) for this game, and what I discovered was like a brand new experience, even though I was familiar with it years ago. It's the same game, it looks and feels like it, but it also feels as it has grown, in a positive way, you know?
So, let's go to the review, starting with the story.
-Well, story wise, I'm still finishing story mode of most of the characters, but I'm kinda lost since I don't remember anything of previous games, so I've read about the story before this one, and it's pretty good and interesting. Kinda confusing at first glance, though, but still good.
-Great art and character design, sprites in this game (the whole franchise, in fact) are amazing, and the stages (background places and all) are equally great, each having their own "feeling".
-Characters are as great as design. They all really charismatic, each in their own ways, and if you like the game and play it for a couple of hours, you'll likely remember them all. They all have their own essence and personality, which is pretty well worked through story. Other good think I think about the characters is that you can kinda "feel" their personality only by fighting against or using them, which is something every fighting game should at least try to accomplish.
-I don't know if I really have to say this, but this game has the best soundtrack I've EVER had the pleasure to hear in any fighting game, and I'm not sure if that's really true but it really feels that this franchise got famous mostly because of it's soundtrack. The voices of all characters are great, and is also one of the best dub I've heard in fighting games (Except when Jam starts screaming, that's kinda annoying since I always play this with the volume at max... But still great dub for her too)
SOUNDTRACK IS PURE DIVINE COMPOSITION MADE BY THE GODS THEMSELVES. I just thought I should remember that part.
-There are plenty to do in the game, with various modes options and unlockable, plus the achievements makes it even better, with some being REALLY hard to accomplish, so it's all a great challenge for those looking for it.
-Which takes me to my next and final point, the gameplay. Now, Guilty Gear is not like other fighting games we know (except for those that followed his path), and it's kinda hard to explain but I can resume it in two words and one phrase: "Frenetic", "combos" and "love for the character". This last one my not make much sense if you're a stranger in the franchise, but you REALLY need to love the character you're playing. I mean, you don't have to worship them or love only them and don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about other characters in the game, but you NEED to love the character if you want to fully master him or them, For example, I love May, Jam, Ky, A.B.A and Chipp, those are my favorites and I my main/best characters, the ones I master (almost) completely, but that doesn't mean I can't play with Justice, Baiken or Millia (if that was the case I would never finish even story mode). And of course, there's some I simply can't make one combo right, like Potemkin, so I just stick to some tricks and finish his story, but would never pick him on versus mode.
Got what I'm trying to say? That complement the character's session I was talking about earlier, each having their own gameplay, so if you get this game and doesn't like one or two, try a few more of them before saying the game sucks, maybe you can find your character(s).
Also, if you play or played BlazBlue, Dead or Alive, Tekken, Street Fighter, The King of Fighters or whatsoever, be warned that your knowledge of those fighting games may not be too useful. I tried playing BlazBlue thinking the the opposite side and what happened was "ah, I play Guilty Gear and I'm pretty good at it, so this might be okooooooh♥♥♥♥♥♥this is different. Why are things so sloooooooow!!! WHERE IS MY COMBOS? WHY I CAN'T MAKE A COMBOOOO?! SOMEONE HELP ME PLS", so be careful.
And btw, the game is difficult as heaven (or hell), so if you like challenges, go for it. Sometimes it's so hard it gets you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I actually lost count of my rage quits in this game, but it's probably between 20~50. (Really, I feel like a no-life waste in society for playing this in maniac/very hard, and also kinda masochist)
-So after all...
Guilty Gear is a REALLY frenetic fighter where the most important things are combos, knowing your character and understanding the gameplay in general, so you probably won't get anywhere smashing random buttons all the time and hoping something good happens, you really need to practice and work your way to get better in this wondeful (and pretty much forgotten on the mainstream fighting game scene) franchise.
I'll give it a 10/10 without regret, but I know and understand that it might have some problems (not having a rage quit counter being one of them), though I don't really think things like "too difficult" can be considered a problem (right, IGN-san? c:), and I think that even with said problems, it doesn't impact on the score for me. And yes, I consider this to be the best fighting game ever made.

Sometimes the CGs looks decent, other times you can tell when the proportions are off. - Romance feels lacking and unbalanced between routes. There are kiss scenes in 2 routes while the others end platonically as far as I can tell. Not enough chemistry is shown for the relationships to progress naturally.
- The routes fall on the short side. The pacing of the story goes by quick. To me, it felt like a 12 episode anime that got crammed into a 2 hour movie. I would have liked more explanations about backstory or world lore. In fact, there are quite a few things that are left unexplained. Game time takes place over 15 or so days.
- I did not feel attached to any character. The extra stories added what I felt was lacking in the main game and wished there were more mini-scenes peppered between the days.
- Linear choices. Every choice is A or B. Each character has a good and bad ending. There are little to no variations. I found myself skipping most of the common parts in later routes.
Personally, the parts with the non-humans were the best. If this game is on sale or in a bundle and you generally like fantasy themed stories, then go for it.

Titans is a stand-alone expansion, and for what it is, it delivers. Of course, Uber's problem is that PA was vastly overhyped and rushed to release. Hence, there's a bunch of people complaining that Uber is pumping out another game for the $$$ (which, after their failed 2nd KS Human Resources which was a blatent moneygrab, is understandable.)
Lets step back from the churn and consider what Titans brings:
The titular feature is, of course, titans (think Supreme Commander experimentals). Uber sold PA as SupCom+, and lots of people were disappointed when there weren't big spiderbots in the game. I think this is another problem of Uber's hype-machine: the new titans are cool, but it's not like vanilla PA felt lacking without them (speaking as someone with 300 hours in vanilla). The new titans are just
. The new hovertanks make assaulting naval bases a lot less of a pain, and the tank titan is a great big hovertank with battleship guns! Overall, the new titans are a neat addition to endgame armies beyond bigger and bigger tank swarms.
Orbital had a pretty big overhaul, and is no longer just fighter swarms. Now, you've got great big hulking battleships, scouts, etc. This is another one of those areas that Uber overhyped, and the lack of big♥♥♥♥♥star destroyers was a big dissapointment when PA "launched". The new units are pretty cool, but at launch, the battleships seem a bit OP against ion cannons (which are supposed to counter orbital, but just sorta get creamed when you drop a few battleships on them).
My biggest disappointment with Titans was what it did not include: performance improvements (or if it did, wasn't noticably faster) PA always ran slow, given that Uber advertised thousands of units (and 64 players, remember that?) and delivered a game that could only handle hundreds. Titans is very much more of the same. Expect end-game to continue to lag.
That's a highlight of what was added in this
(hear that, haters? Not a new game, it's a $13.60 expansion). Now, what about for people who have never played vanilla PA?
Overall, Titans is PA but better. I paid $13.60 for it, and thought it was a fair deal considering the new content. For new players, it's about the same price as the original (whoch IMO was a bit overpriced) but with more content.
Uber is at fault for over-hyping everyone's expectations, but that by no means makes Titans a bad game.

So I look through all other reviews on the website, and I see that everyone has like 0.1, 0.2, etc hours on game. It was hard, my spirit almost broke, my eyes bled every time a shot was fired, or a hit was taken. At times I almost gave up. Times the game was buggy to the point of unplayability. At one time, because I turned on unlimited saving, I was unable to progress through a certain portion of the game. "Your wish is not my command"
"You could have asked me to move"
"Black racial sterotype"
I follow the motto every game a deserves a chance. This game made me question my beliefs.
Finally I got to the acropolis, and I stepped onto a switch. So yeah, do I recommend this game? No, but there is one thing this game has left with me. Appreciation for other games, a newfound knowledge of how spoiled we have been with our good games like Batman, Borderlands 2, Dragon Age and so forth.
The grass is greener, the sky is clearer then ever, and with one last look, I walk outside taking away the one line from the game that remains with me to this day

A solid action-jRPG, but not without its weak points. Story - average.

All in all, i consider the game worth the discounted price i payed for it during a sale, i have doubts about its value for a full price.

Where do I begin with Berseria?
Berseria is a fun game.  As a fan of the Tales of series, I picked up Berseria a while ago and though it was very confusing at first, I got really into it.  I don't know how the game works with KB/M since I used a PS4 controller which feels very fluid.  For the multiplayer folks, I haven't played this game with anyone yet to see if it works just as flawlessly as it does for singleplayer.
You assign abilities, called artes, to your four face buttons.  They vary from healing, to defending, to spells and to attacks.  Basic attacks from previous Tales of games are gone.  You can switch characters out from the side lines if you need to quickly heal someone.  Combat is extremely smooth and combos flow smoothly though they may not always land because the previous attack moved you or the enemy out of range.  It was rough when I first started because I thought I was wasting TP to attack and didn't know how to keep souls filled but the help menu explains it quite plainly.
Though I only played Velvet, each of the characters felt different in their playstyles in the brief period of time I played them when Velvet died.
Soundtracks are alright I guess.  I don't really pay attention to them (because the combat at higher difficulties demand your complete attention) though it could just be seen as the soundtracks are forgetful.
EDIT:  I just listened to Velvet Crowe's soundtrack, courtesy of another review on here by Saibot and it is absolutely fantastic.
Graphics are fantastic.  60 FPS with great visual design beats anything Zestiria all day every day.
I went from Berseria to Zestiria and that was a huge mistake.  I also literally just wrote my first Steam review there since that's how bad Zestiria is.
If you didn't like Zestiria for anything like poor optimization or 30 FPS, then play Berseria.  Berseria fixes pretty much everything wrong with Zestiria.  Camera is absolutely amazing.  Controls (with a controller) feels amazing and fluid AND intuitive (something many people don't consider).  The game runs like smooth butter and looks fantastic as a result of the 60 FPS.
I highly recommend the higher difficulties since they feel much more rewarding and drop better gear.  Gear makes much more of a difference than levels in Berseria.  The rewards in higher difficulties are amazing though you want to be careful since you can literally die in like 3 hits from just a random mob or your entire party can get wiped by a single spell.
They all have varied backgrounds and have good interaction with each other.
though I couldn't stand her at first, is by far my favorite character in the whole game now though I still don't like it when she says "Magikazam."  They have tons of lines in and outside of battle and the ending battle dialogue can be funny.  Skits are humorous too (and you don't need to be on a save point to view them - cough Zestiria).
The overworld's characters have life too.  Though yeah, they say the same lines, they're consistent in their character (like if someone is a whiny farmer's son, they'll stay a whiny farmer's son with even a small bit of development to be a bit less whiny).
Berseria though a slight bit grindy with the equipment system, is a top tier Tales of game.  The story is a bit different from your average Tales game and the combat is absolutely phenomenal.  Berseria is leagues above the unplayable trash known as Zestiria so if Zestiria is making you hesitant to try this game, just forget about Zestiria.  Berseria fixes everything wrong about it and more.

This actually is a very good game, There are very few Turn Based Stratergys these days that add the character bulding elements quite so well.  Its a very challenging game that can lead to frustration, sometimes losing hours of saves because one of the guys you spent hours on died!  Most of the time you can get them up with a medic but you can quickly take on catastrophic casualties.
The side missions can be difficult and not very well explained, there are a fair few good guides for the faint of heart and if your one of these hardcore types I am pretty sure they can keep you going for a good while.
Supplys can be hard to work out, and the flow of time is very odd at times :D  The story really is neither here nore there. If you looking for Depth and story telling this is not the game for you. If you want to spend hours and hours planning your perfect kills then this is the game for you.
Stealth is very hard to master on this game, You always feel like your guys could not hit a cows♥♥♥♥♥♥with a bango.  You learn to never expect your guys to take out a key target with one shot.. I find lining up a fire death squad works great but then you quickly find you have a ton of guys charging in at you.
The AI, is really nothing to write home about, They respond when they hear or see things, this can be quite a long distance too... But if you silently slaughter someone, and run away, they will quite happily step over their dead body.. Just assume they hated them so much they care little they died horrifically.
Overall, the game hits the spot when it comes to upgrading a team, and shooting things turn based style. Lots of options of weapons, Lots of options of entry into buildings, Lots of configurations in building your team.
What is really missing from this game, is your own customed avatar of death. Its by far the one thing i hate, you cant create your very own guy with your own specific set of skills to start you off and that my friends is a damn shame.
OVERALL RATING 80%

A fun game that on the surface seems a whole lot like Terraria. While the two games do have a lot in common, and share a similar look and playstyle, both stand out as great games for entirely different reasons. Terraria is a true sandbox take on the 'metroidvania' genre with a fun degree of RPG and roguelike elements. Starbound clearly wants to be more focused on story and character building, but it still has some way to go in that department. It has tons of potential, though. If it can manage to handle the details and long term polish with half the finesse of Terraria, I don't see how it could be seen as not worth the asking price. Especially at some of the sale prices it hits, this is a game you can easily get lost in for many many hours... If you enjoy sandboxey roguelikes/ -lights, especially space/sci-fi ones, you have probably already given this a try. If not, I suggest doing so. If you have, but its been a year or two, this (just like Terraria) is one game that with all the work put in over the years, definitely deserves a fresh install/savegame to see whats new... I would rate it at least a 7/10 at this point, with it having been more like a 5 or so during its (at times quite frustrating) early development.
