Ford Racing Off Road, like the other Ford Racing games, is pretty much fast food in game form: It's cheap, functional, provides a few hours of decent satisfaction (except Street Racing ugh), but it's not exceptional. You get a selection of 18 different Ford (and Land Rover) trucks and SUV's in this one, so that's cool I guess, even though Ford Racing 3 still has WAY more variety.
There are a couple different environments you end up racing in, like a desert and a snow-capped mountain. Most of the bonus race types from Ford Racing 3 return, along with some new ones, like one that involves collecting hidden artifacts and another where you try and pass as many gates as possible but sometimes turning around to get to them can be faster. The car handling is okay and damage actually means something in this one; basically you'll start to notice your car not hit the same top speed it used to. Cosmetic damage is much harder to notice though; it takes a lot of hits for a couple scratches to show up on your bumper.
Basically what I'm saying is this: Ford Racing Off Road is okay, like Ford Racing 3 before it. Nothing special or fantastic, but good enough if you're looking for a decent albeit generic arcade racer to kill some time. So why the thumbs down? It's simple really.
Unlike Ford Racing 3 (or Street Racing even), the PC version of this game has one critical flaw:
This was literally my first hour of setting this game up to run properly:
I don't care what the reasoning for this silly decision was. The two prior Ford Racing games work just fine with gamepads, let alone most every other racing game ever released post-PS1. The fact that just this one doesn't,
is reason enough for me not to recommend this version to the average user.
Ford Racing Off Road is an average but cheap and enjoyable (enough) budget racer to the point I can recommend the game, but I can't recommend this version to everybody. To anyone that doesn't own a Steam Controller and isn't a Windows PowerUser™, just buy Ford Racing 3 instead. If you already played that and want more, skip Ford Street Racing and buy this game, but NOT ON PC. Get the PS2 version or something. At least that version supports analog steering and won't occasionally reset your display settings so you have to go back into the config EXE and reset your display resolution.
Seriously, this much trial and error...for a Ford Racing game. If you still get this with all the above in mind, don't say I didn't warn you.

This game can be summed up in one word: Mediocre. If you like dating VNs and/or fantasy stories, get this game when it's on deep sale or included in a bundle. (I got it as a present from a friend.)
I am, admittedly, a harsh critic when it comes to VNs because I have high expectations and prefer games with good gameplay elements. In terms of gameplay, Blue Rose has potential but unfortunately the choices are uninteresting because most of them aren't meaningful and the map system is a bit too linear.
The story also falls short; I agree with other reviewers that the premise set up is interesting, and some of the tidbits about the world are interesting, but the worldbuilding was half-baked at best and would occasionally break my immersion (Simon assuming that the village chief was a man was one instance; in a world where women seem to have equal opportunities, why would he assume the leader must be male?). I did enjoy the branching story (each character had a unique good and bad ending), but the repeat text in a diverging branch (ie. when the same scene is reached from a different path) was unskippable, so I found myself clicking to get through it and hoping I wasn't missing any flavor text. Tighter prose could have helped alleviate the tedium, but I would have prefered that they had programmed the game properly so that it would skip repeat text (honestly, did they copy the same scene over and over because they couldn't figure out how to either use jumps and variables to control the differing text? I don't know.)
The art and animation are the most polished parts of the game by far. While some of the backgrounds were obviously 3D renders, they fit in surprisingly well with the rest of the game's backgrounds. I thought the character art was pretty, but I was bothered by the extremely narrow bodies. The white-ish hair of the three male characters also made it extremely hard to tell them apart on the map. It was so bad that my friend and I joked that someone on the dev team had a Sepiroth fetish. The game also utilized Ren'py's animation capabilities to its fullest; I was quite impressed with the art direction in many of the scenes.
The great art is why the horrible UI baffles me so much. They barely customized the dialog box; keeping the horrible Ren'py bold for the label and adding a background gradient without bothering to adjust the height of the text, so the first line overlaps with the gradient and makes it hard to read. The Gallery was also very basic, rows of CGs split into pages instead of the more typical character-based gallery pages. I feel like the devs underestimated how important a good UI is for player experience.
Overall, the game was entertaining enough for me to play through in its entirety. I didn't find it fun enough to justify the almost $20 price tag, but I'd say it is probably good enough for VN fans to pick up on a 50% or more sale.
As an aside, Steam's crappy forced "recommend"/"not recommend" system was almost enough to make me not write this review, since I don't feel comfortable recommending it but I feel less comfortable
recommending it (given that I played through all the content of the game). If they want to force a quantitative review that they can stick up on the page, why the heck won't they give us a more nuanced rating system?!?! Sigh.

Blue Rose is a visual novel about a knight, Lena, that ends up in a remote village. Depending on her choices, you will end up romantically with one of the characters - though it will also influence revelations about the story or not.
In itself, the plot is very interesting as Lena is confronted to stay true to her oath or to dismiss it when the enemy isn't really one. She's also hard on herself but she needs also to learn to appreciate her skills. Each character is also having a good background: Simon, her captain, seems to get on her nerves because of her crush if you want to follow Simon's path, Tobias is showing sympathy and coldness each time to her, as he's crushing on her but also very focused on protecting everything around, Gavin is quite the seductive and funny guy but with a secret that could kill him, Aran is very mysterious and very curious about human relationships as he's not used to that form and Erin is very cheerful and very happy to see Lena, but she also seems to be sad sometimes.
However, it doesn't mean that you have only one bad ending and the rest is romance. Indeed, each character has a bad and a good ending. It's also interesting to experience them fully as it's a matter of life or death. It also means to save often as the choices are also including who you're going to see when you're on the map.
The graphics are good, I loved the art style and the soundtrack was very fitting.
Everything was reunited for a good length of pleasure. However, Blue Rose fails. A single element killed the fun.
Too much dialogues and not enough choices to make a break. You click, you click, you click, you choose an option, you click, you click, you click, you click. In the end, you're loosing interest in the plot because there are too much information at once.
You'll ask why I'm descending it in flames as there is another visual novel which is more an interactive book than a game (Shan Gui). In Shan Gui, you don't have many routes to think and you can learn something from it thanks to the links to Wikipedia. It's the goal of the game in reality. In Blue Rose, you're here to really take Lena to her destiny and the only thing you really do is to read many dialogues before finally getting some action with the choice.
You can't skip dialogues the first time they're appearing, which is normal but you wish you can. I was bored and if I did complete the game, it's because I was interested to see each route and to have a 100% in achievements.
Blue Rose could have been a very good visual novel if the gameplay was more balanced. Every condition was reunited for a good moment and the length of the dialogues killed the fun for me. I would recommend to avoid it if you're easily bored. There are better visual novels out there, like Hatoful Boyfriend for example.

I've played PA for almost 3k hours on and off steam, and I'd all but given up on it.  There were few updates, the balance was static and simplistic, and the orbital layer (including the super weapons) felt like a gimmick.  I told the devs I wouldn't be coming back unless they fixed those problems.
Well, I'm back.  They haven't fixed everything - but they did a damn good job trying.  Orbital now has a basic layer of depth to it - three units in different roles instead of one swarm unit.  Super weapons now have additional members:  the Titans.  For those of you from SupCom, these are experimentals, through and through.  Naval and land now interact in amazing and interesting ways with the addition of hover destroyers, hover tanks, and a nanite swarm that eats everything.  They've finally added a unit that counters the Ultimate Weapon (boom bots):  the lightning bot.
Uber did it right this time.  This should have been the release, absolutely.  But you cannot get salty at Uber - they released early due to financial issues and a previous contract.  This expansion will be to PA what SupCom: FA is to SupCom.
I usually withold my judgement on such things, but this expansion has been in the works for months and months.
I'd also like to take a moment to talk about the price.  For those of you who do not know, the Titans expansion is free for KS backers (due to the risk they took backing Uber), 66% off for previous owners (Veteran players), and $40 for everyone else.  This is, in my book, a sound business decision and a great one for the community.  It's a massive content patch, and it is worth every penny.
Compare that to Elite Dangerous or Guild Wars 2 recent expansion announcements.  They're making their players pay almost full price for those expansions.  You can't tell me Uber is making a money grab when you've got devs like Frontier and ArenaNet running around.

In Sum: There is almost a cool game buried in here, but there are too many problems to make it worth bothering with.  It is like the Heaven's Gate of gaming.  1.5/5.
Daikatana, where do I begin?  Well, it's not entirely a bad game, in fact, parts of it are outstanding.  But it never completely gets away from the glaring issues.  Unfortunately, I think, the game's reputation as a bad game make it hard to look at what does work.  I don't want to say this is a bad game, it's kind of a good game.  It's a broken and unfinished game that should not have been released in the form it was.
I didn't play this on release, and only knew of the game by reputation.  It was infamous for a prolonged developement, and a certain ad campaign that people took offensively.
The game starts off in a future Japan, with a bit of a convoluted story involving a magic sword and three feuding families.  The beginning stages play like a classic FPS of the era, but the enemies are very unpopular.  You start off punshing mosquitos and frogs with your fist, and people find these enemies annoying.  Personally, I find them less irritating than the remotes in the Dark Forces/Jedi Knight series.  Once you get past this area, the game will change drastically.
The game becomes a time-travelling single player co-op FPS from there, exploring an exaggerated take on history and mythology.  Don't go to this game expecting accuracy, that isn't close to what they were going for.
And it's the imaginative parts that are what make the game good.  The game is effective at building atmosphere and anticipation as you go through the historic parts of the game.  Each episode changes the design so much it's almost like several different games.  The middle segments are enjoyable.  But there are parts of the game where less attention was paid, and they are seriously broken.  The difference between the good and bad parts is shocking.
The biggest issue in this game is the AI.  You have two teammates who come in and out of the game, and when they are around, they impede more than they help.  They simply break the game.  It also seems that one of the AI, Superfly Johnson, got the most polish, and is somewhat capable of working with the player, but Mikiko's AI is so badly broken that she is basically an enemy and hinders the player.
The game's story wants to be heavy and interesting, but it is so campy and not a lot of attention was paid to it.  It's not especially original or strong, but it has it's own feel.
There are a lot of mistakes in the voices and cutscenes that make it seem like story was an afterthought.  For example, actors seem to have trouble pronouncing things consistently, such as the name of King Gareth.  The voice performances also border on outright racism, with asian characters mixing l's and r's, and a black character crying hysterically over the death of the main character if you lose, only to rob his corpse for his shoes and wallet.  The game was designed with the deathmatch smack-talking attitude of the infamous ad, but the offensive parts get to be too much at times.
There are a lot of bugs in this game, despite patches.  In the end, that is what has killed this game for me.  The bad AI could be could excused by the age of the game, the awkward level designs could be creative issues, but the bugs causing weapons to malfunction or you to be unable to move, make parts of the game unbearable.
I will defend on controversial choice, though.  The Save Gem system is very unpopular, but I didn't have much trouble with it.  It discouraged me from exploiting saves too much, as a result I got better at the areas.  It is like a precursor to check points, but when combined with the bugs in the game, it does make things worse.
So, not nearly the worst game in the world, but it should never have been released like this.  A disappointment only so much that there was some potential for greatness, and sometimes it reached close to it.

Like many in the West, I was introduced to the Tales games through Symphonia. Since then, I've beaten a good number of the games we've gotten releases for (Symphonia as previously mentioned, Abyss, Legendia, Vesperia) and played partway through a couple more (Xillia, Graces). By and large, I love the Tales series.
And this is, hands-down, the best one I've played.
The story teeters right on the edge of being, well... too edgy. At times it goes there, but well-timed, well-written comic relief and sympathetic antiheroes who are arguably the villains of the piece pull it back from being a depressing experience. The combat is solid, the VA work in English and Japanese is stellar (except for a minor character who shall remain nameless, who I wished the story would get rid of or at least STOP HER CRYING), and the story is an interesting dip into darkness even for a series that's noted for having moral ambiguity in its characters. Not since Legendia have the Tales games had a main cast this enjoyable; even the token annoying kid character grows and improves by leaps and bounds until he's one of the best characters in the story.
The only major complaint I'd say I have about the game is that it does lean a little heavily on backtracking at times, and for a JRPG with no world map, this can start to feel like a slog. However, the game had just enough to do, just enough new juicy story, just enough lines from Magilou (objectively the best character, I will fight you), to pull me through the occasional weak moment. This is not a perfect game, but it's damn close. I had thought after playing through Persona 5 that I had my JRPG of the year, but this game unseated it handily.
So magikazam and Devouring Claw your way to bloody chaos. It's a fun time.
There are nanobots and carriers and orbital battleships and giant stompy robots. The soul that Planetary Annihilation has needed for so long has arrived, and it sounds like explosions.

My experience with Burnout Paradise has been a bit underwhelming. The graphics are really pretty, and the racing parts are good at getting the adrenaline pumping. It's an open world racing game where your objective is unlocking new vehicles and finding collectibles. If you like that, then this is your game.
What kills it for me the most are the moments that interrupt the flow of the game -- specifically, the slow-motion scenes every time you do a stunt or come close to wrecking and the unskippable voice-overs. Keep in mind, all of this is my opinion, but the way I see it is this: In a racing game, game flow is everything. When I'm driving a race car, I want the drive to flow smoothly because driving fast and passing opponents are what I find rewarding. I get into the zone, so to speak, so every time that flow is broken, it feels like a punishment.
In Burnout Paradise, there are game elements that are meant to be punishing (crashing, being taken down, failing a stunt, etc.) and there elements that are meant to be either helpful or rewarding (explanatory narration, slow motion cinematic for taking down an opponent or completing a stunt, etc.). However, since both the rewards and the punishments interrupt the game flow, all of them feel like punishments. To be specific, changing both the camera angle and the game speed is disorienting and takes me out of the zone. There have been a handful of times where I would takedown another racer only to crash into a wall myself because my concentration was broken while admiring the slow motion carnage.
What's more, it's pretty clear from the awkward interface design that this is a console port. At the time of writing this review, I haven't yet tried Burnout with a controller, so it's possible that using a controller will make the game feel much better.
The gameplay itself is pretty fun. That feeling of adrenaline you get when screaming down the road in a race car while taking down other racers is very thrilling. Unfortunately, I feel as though I spend just as much time, if not less time, racing as I do watching dramatic slow-mo shots, listening to some guy's voice, or fiddling around in menus.

In short: I got my money's worth and recommend this game for anyone who likes to take combat at his/hers own pace.

Jagged Alliance 2 still remains my favorite game of all times and is right up there with X-COM as prime examples of TBS gaming at it's best. Back in Action is the tragic reality of what happens when classic IP's go up for sale in a gaming industry were Call of Duty and Halo are the kind of titles that investors would rather commit to.
Back in Action does not deserve to carry the name. And BitComposer has done the franchise a great injustice by allowing such a game to be made, and not to mention alienating the old fans by asking us for our input (via their forum in the infancy of the games development) and then doing the exact opposite of what the majority asked for.
And when sales and reviews were terrible... they still insisted that Turn Based Games are dead... And then XCOM Enemy Unknown was released...
If you never played JA or you aren't to concerned with deep strategic gameplay mixed with a serious learning curb, then you might enjoy this. The environment is open, so you can stop anywhere on the map, although the scripted action takes place in dozens of marked locations on the map such as towns, hideouts, sam sites, mines etc. Lots of weapon types. Not perfect tho. Explosives are there but redundant. Fancy Shotguns come too late. I don't use body armour as it falls apart too fast, don't need it. Only one attachment per weapon, although I'm happy with a scope. 3D environment is nice but camera is a little restrictive. But hey there are some mods that resolve the balance issues. I'm a fan of the original JA games. This one started out ok, but turned into a disappointment way too quick.
What I simply don't like in this one is the difficulty curve, or should I say the steep changes in enemy arsenal and numbers. First you're up against like six enemies equipped with machetes and revolvers. Next sector you're up against 20 guys with assault rifles and grenades. I mean... WHAT?! In the old JA games, there were never such differences between neighboring areas, save for late-game ones.
Then there's the issue with very micromanage-y combat, hard to read environments (sometimes a branch of a tree blocks vision, other times a man-sized ventilation shaft offers zero protection) and clunky interface that by default assumes you want to keep queueing new actions to happen after old ones are complete, unless you manually clear old orders first. Every. Single. Time. Guns also can't be fired in melee range, apparently, and melee hits register still after the target is ten meters away.
Lots of potential, but poor execution and lack of steady progression killed the fun for me way too quick. Can't recommend. Shame.

Turn-based tactical strategy involving a combination of outfitting squads of soldiers, and then taking them into combat to resist an alien menace. You need to develop competence at both to win. Punishing AI and percentage-based chances to hit (made mostly reliable by smart positioning) make losing the people you've trained and built up all too easy, and death is permanent. You can reload and try again, or live with the consequences, but few other games come close to investing you in your team. As a 2nd itineration of XCom, I prefer XCom2 because it felt a little less formulaic in terms of the path to growing your economy, and the addition of hand-to-hand combat makes for even more harrowing encounters. If you haven't played any version of XCom, then you owe it to yourself to give it a try.

At first Starbound was a game I bought, in VERY early access because I loved Terraria and also enjoyed Minecraft a bit. Starbound promises nerly limitless exploration, thousands of worlds to venture and gut for ore and trees. Each world is of some type. An enermous volcanic planet can have  icy pools of poison or precios liquid fuel at its surface. A mile below the surface could lie an ancient Avian tomb or dungeon. Fallen travelers could have left their goods stowed away safely, or not, in small tombs deep beneath the surface, just begging to be rediscovered, only to find it contains a bandage and 5 red flares.
The soundtrack on this gem is.. unlike any game, EVER. It blows my mind. It's full of emotion, wonder, and sadness. I get chills from the music for this game.
Starbound was incredibly fun from the start. the story was all but existent, but the core gameplay was there. I spent many many hours offline playing with my brother on LAN. (I have at least two hundred more hours than steam reflects)
Eventually we stopped playing as much. We'd hit the "end" of the game, went through character and world wipes as the Chucklefish team expanded and improved the game experience.
I released a neat-ish mod in March 2014, and soon after stopped playing; everyone was waiting for the next big update.
I played a few times afterward, seeing the early removal of pickaxes as the main mining method. The ship's state of early disrepair. And again stopped.
Fast forward to last week. I'm sitting here at the computer and see ' "XXXXXXXXXX" is playing Starbound ' in the corner, and I think: "Okay, sure.."
I'd stopped following the dev updates months ago. Busy life and all. Launching the game presented a professional and information rich Game launcher (better than before) and after launching; the all new dev logo, a cuter load screen.
I'll do a TL;DR from here.
I started an avian character as I had always. I began the game, and repaired my ship. I expected to find nothing interesting in the world below.. But again I was mistaken and sunk many many hours into a newly polished, beautiful sounding, playing, looking game.
I cannot wait to see what they bring to the future.

Now I can reccomend this game, but it was released in a very confusing way that lead me to believe this was 40$ for everybody, even people who already owned the original PA.
On the one hand this is awesome, orbital battleships? awesome, aircraft carrier? awesome, doomsday device? YES ALL OF MY YES. In addition to that every tier of units for every factory got something new, and every advanced builder got a new titan to build. Some of the new units are crazy, one of them is just a dirt cheap swarm of nanites that cost practically nothing, have almost no health. and can be built faster than they can be shoved off the building platform.
In addition to all that complaints about planets feeling flat have been adressed with the addition of raised and lowered ground(from what I've seen its like in starcraft 1).
And all of that is fantastic and really makes the game pretty crazy.
However on the flipside, for some reason this is a standalone expansion for Planetary Annihilation for 40$ when it really, REALLY should have just been DLC or something. EDIT: I'm being told that if you already own PA then this is on sale for you, if you already own PA then your target price for this expansion should be around where you would place a DLC expansion pack.
EDIT 2: ok it turns out that I posted this review really really early and when it was up they hadn't actually put in the "66% off PA:Titans if you already own PA" deal. I will update this review once I've played more of titans and I can get a feel of how they've chagned the game.

Daikatana is a first person shooter, made with the Quake 2 engine. If you're into Quake 2 and speedy running, muddy textures and great gunplay, then chances are this is the game for you.
Since this is a Quake 2 engine game, you're able to sprint fast, including turning sprint so its always on. If you want to move slow, you'll crouch and move. You can jump and you'll need it for some of the precision first person platforming. You'll tackle run, gun, puzzles, avoid meat grinders and swim.
I feel the real barrier of entry was the first level or two, because it is a swampy mess of ideas and traps. There are hitscan turrets that will pop up and kill you pretty quickly unless you just run past them. In the second level you're forced to destroy one, but after running from them, it seemed strange to destroy it. There is a laser doorway that will kill you if you walk through them, forcing you to take an alternate route, but an enemy drops a mega shield that announces 'you are now protected.' Yep from everything but the laser door the mega shield is in front of. It just seems like a poor choice. Announce that you're protected, then have an unprotectable death trap. It just puts me off as a player to go through that level when nothing else is as bad as that. Nothing is as questionable as some of the design choices in the first level. Not to mention the excessively long introductory cut scene. Luckily you can skip it. Heck you can even go into the options to disable it entirely.
Once the game gets going beyond the bug hunt levels at the start of the game, Dai-Katana ends up feeling like crawling complex similar to Half Life 1. You'll go into air ducts, up ladders, ride conveyer belts, solve underwater puzzles, use wall mounted health machines cleverly named 'Hosportals' and hit switches for a lot of things. On the other hand Quake was constant action with no button pressing and minimal searching or story.
Since you'll be going through a complex, the enemies go from real frogs, gators and dragon flies to mechanical frogs, big mechs, hover drones, ceiling mounted sentries and typical soldiers. The soldiers will chatter before they start firing at you, and they're not much of a threat. They just stand there and take bullets, in fact everything just comes at you taking bullets. Not only does the AI seem flat, but Quake had frills like enemies being knocked down from gunfire. Those touches to detail feel missing from Dai-Katana.
Outside of enemies, there are plenty of friendly folks just trying to do their job that will either stand there, run away or cower in fear. Those are nice touches that I did enjoy. Not everything is out to get you. You can still shoot them if you'd like. Sadly with poor enemy design and AI come corridor like levels for the most part. Most maps are just hallways and rooms, with one way in and another way out. Sometimes the hallways will go up a ramp or down a staircase. It is all very simple map design.
With lame enemy design and simple rooms to shoot them in, at least the guns are a joy to shoot, but you can injure yourself with every gun. You get to have an ion blaster that will bounce shots off walls, so you can shoot yourself and electrocute you if you shoot it under water. You'll find rocket launcher, a sticky grenade launcher that explodes in proximity to enemies and yourself, some sort of flack gun that fires 3 times when you pull the trigger once and knocks you back. There is also a seismic bomb launcher that will fire a giant projectile that bounces around and causes massive splash damage that can most likely kill you or your partners, even through walls. The problem with every weapon hurting you is the poorly map design. Enemies are right there when you open a door or turn a corner. You'll have to shoot a room full of enemies through doorways with doors that open and close. Since every weapon can hurt you, its an issue when the door closes and you're forced in a bottleneck over and over again. It is not fun and it happens with almost every room.
One thing that makes the game stand out are the allies, including the legendary Superfly Johnson of course. These allies can sometimes be a help and you can command them. You will see them grab guns, shoot enemies and give you hints as to what to do next. They can crawl through vents and go up ladders to follow you. Unfortunately, they move slowly compared to you. When an AI partner dies, its game over. One AI partner is okay, two becomes a chore to manage. You can only command one at a time, so if they're both stuck trying to run into a wall, you need to command one to stop, then switch to the other and command that one to stop. Then they will turn toward you so you can command them to follow you again one at a time. Wow. Half Life 1 did it so much easier, just target one and 'use' button to toggle so they follow you or stand still. Their path finding is awful and you need to exit with them.
Another thing this game has going for it is armor that allows your character to level up. Once you level up, you can put an attribute point to power, attack, speed, acro(batics?) and vitality. Its a nice addition, but doesn't really feel needed or game changing. All enemies give experience points, even the ones cowering in fear not trying to kill you.
At the end of the first episode, you're thrown through time into the Greek era and then medieval times. The enemies change to their era themes and you get all sorts of weapons. It might sound cool, but it boils down to 99% of enemies are melee and you have virtually limitless long range ammunition, upgraded damage and health with full armor. So I feel needlessly over powered when nothing can hurt me but lava death traps for 2 full episodes and hours of gameplay. That just isn't fun, so to amp up the challenge, I use melee weapons and nothing can hurt me on normal difficulty.
Daikatana however has a load time based on V-Sync which seems odd, so if you have V-Sync enabled the game won't just instantly load on my modern PC like other games will. You need to wait for the audio ticking of the load bar. I can't seem to find any V-Sync control in the game or options. People have explained its in the 1.3 patch, but why wouldn't the Steam version include it with this 15 year old game?
Going through the game I've found a few bugs and issues, things like bullets hitting things that aren't there and the hall of mirror effect with untextured walls. Enemies dying a second time if you close and open a door before their death animation ends. Those are just visual, but issues of getting myself stuck in areas like traps are bigger issues that cause me to load the latest save game. I've found glitches that when opening doors it will freeze the game for a few seconds and when it opens I'll be somewhere else in the room. The hover drones cause some sort of error when I strafe, it halts me as if I'm running into an invisible object. The collision detection seems off with the sticky grenade launcher so my grenades will stick to the air and the grenades wait for something to come close to them.
You need save gems in order to save the game. You need to find them. I guess I'm okay with that, especially since it saves you with every loading screen / check point. Luckily the options has a setting to allow unlimited saves.
The game as a whole just feels like poor game design choices with a great game engine like if you have a fast exotic sports car and the mechanic tells you it will run better if we put frogs in the back seat, flatten the tires and put it under water. There are plenty of moments where you might scratch your head not only as to what you're supposed to do next. From youtube videos, I never understood why this game is bad, but after playing it, I know why its bad.

TL;DR
No need to suffer through Symphonia or Zestiria to enjoy this game.
Combat CAN be insanely simplistic. One Button Bayonetta for the main character.
Depth of story is actually pretty impressive. Great job of explaining morals/ethics as well as the consequences of choice.
Skits are entertaining, though not as humorous (overall) as Zestiria
Feels pretty damn linear.
I have never seen an RPG try so hard to force an emotional connection to the main "protagonist". While forced, it is done quite well.
Cohesive plot, which is rare for this type of game.
Some of the cut scenes are drawn out a bit much, but the ability to fast advance/skip means you won't be falling asleep.
Did I mention One Button Bayonetta? Yeah, ToB has gotten slack for simplifying combat over ToZ, but it's flashy and responsive, and no need for finger gymnastics that keyboard pros aren't necessarily known for on a controller.
Pretty decent job at pacing. Currently level 22 and, with the exception of a few areas where fast travel wasn't possible due to trigger points for plot, leveling hasn't felt like a chore. There has, so far, been no reason to stick around an area and grind enemies for experience or gear.
The characters are well-written and play off one another quite well, except for the annoying twit (because there's always an annoying twit with these things). While her dialogue is purposefully over the top, she has her moments.... stupid witch.
If you've only played Tales of Symphonia, I'd suggest playing Zestiria before this offering. If you've played Zestiria, definitely pick this one up. Although you need not have played the previous games available on Steam to enjoy this, if you've played at least 3/4 of ToZ, Berseria will have some surprises for you.
10 hours into Tales of SYmphonia and I want to snort arsenic. Zestiria held me til about the fifth hour of my second playthrough with 94 hours alone in my first time around. I have almost 17 hours into Berseria and am actually looking forward to beating the game still.
Out of the three games, Zestiria seems to have the most to do, regardless of how much of it is "busy work" and not essential to beating the game. Berseria, though, has been more fun just due to the cut scenes, overall plot, and character development.

The SonoHana Series, a bunch of visual novels that revolve around the relationship of two girls at St. Michael Girls’ School, the series is very well known and loved by yuri fans. This was the first official English release of a title from this series. Usually this series covers some 18+ scenes, however this is steam, so this was just a short and sweet love story suitable for all ages.
This novel is what you call in fanfiction terms a “pre-slash”. Which means it doesn’t show the start of the romantic relationship, but rather their friendship.
is the sincere, kind and dependable girl loved by everyone at her school.
is the new transfer student. The student that has perfect grades and fits into the "silent and cool" type of character, until she starts skipping most classes. Risa can’t stand for having someone doing that in her class, and so she makes it her mission to get Miya to stop playing truant.
The girls' personalities were very lovable and cute and very well developed throughout the short playtime of the novel. As much as how the main focus in the novel was about their school life, we got glimpses about their personal lifes. Namely, a slight idea about the relationship between the girls and their families. The interactions between the girls were really entertaining while the serious moments between them were quite touching. The dialogue in the novel didnt seem forced like most romance novels and it felt a lot more natural and it was backed up by the well done translation of the original.

The art was very nice, but there are only apperances of the two main characters despite some other girls and teaches being involved in some of the conversations. The novel could have used more background variety and most of the CGs were really similar to each other. The voice acting for the two lead characters was great, but the supporting characters had terrible voice acting sadly. They should have left out the voiceovers for the extra characters since they didn't bother creating sprites for them.

These issues aside, I'd highly recommend "A Kiss For The Petals - Remembering How We Met" for someone looking to put in a few hours in reading the background of a very cute and pure love story, it's a short read. But the playtime was just enough to tell the simply charming story of these two lovely girls.

Free to Play here:
For a cheesy looking game, this has to be one of the most enjoyable games I have played.
Town of Salem is a clicking game that requires you to team up with innocents, mafia or by yourself to win as your role. Every person in the game gets a role every match, and you must use the role to your advantage in order to win as a team or depending on your role, by your self. This game sometimes gets me in the front of my chair focusing and thinking heavily on what to do or plan something out. In Town of Salem, luck, the skill of socialization and manipulation plays a big part in this game. Being a mafia requires you to murder everyone and make yourself look innocent, while being a innocent requires you to team with fellow innocent member while using your role to discover who is the mafia and gather information based on your role so you can win with your team.
Truly, I love this game so much for how simple yet complex it can be, but for how advanced you have to think mentally and play. You murder someone with one click, but you have to think before killing certain people. Should I murder someone because they have been framing me or should I not because I will look suspicious and his death note may potentially reveal information about me?
If you play this game already and love it, support the developers by buying this title. If you don't, try the game on the website, and see if you actually enjoy the game or not.

Pros:
- It is an older game, yet the aesthetics are still quite lovely.
- The game runs smoothly with little to no fps dipping on a five-year-old PC.
- The crash physics are just so fun. :)
- A variety of game modes are linked seamlessly together via the free roam Paradise City.
- There is an ever-increasing difficulty curve with vehicle unlocks that make the challenge worthwhile.
The "OK":
- The AI is decent at what it does, but is also relatively predictable.  Still, it can offer a challenge.
-  Online races are enjoyable, but "Freeburn Online," the multiplayer open world environment, has a couple issues.  Most prominently, the games that can be started by the host often require close proximity between players for an enjoyable match to commence, yet a match can be started with players spread out all over the map.
Cons:
- The UI on the PC is a bit rubbish.  The menu is divided into four or five panels that have to be flipped through via the F1 and F2 keys.  There is also very little mouse support.  The "Easy Drive Menu" is helpful, but is only intuitive if one has a numpad.  Otherwise, it is a confusing muddle.
- The initial controls are ported over from the console version (e.g. 'Q' and 'A' used for accelleration instead of 'W' and 'S').  Those can be modified from one of the menu panels, though.
- No windowed mode support.  The only way to run this game in windowed mode (that I know of) is via a third party piece of software.
- The store servers are no longer online, making purchase of DLC impossible.
Overall, the game is quite enjoyable.  It has a strong single player experience with a decent quantity of online activities.  The dated UI and a few other bothersome features can make it difficult to first get into the game, but they are not annoying enough to dissuade me from recommending the game.

A fun game that on the surface seems a whole lot like Terraria. While the two games do have a lot in common, and share a similar look and playstyle, both stand out as great games for entirely different reasons. Terraria is a true sandbox take on the 'metroidvania' genre with a fun degree of RPG and roguelike elements. Starbound clearly wants to be more focused on story and character building, but it still has some way to go in that department. It has tons of potential, though. If it can manage to handle the details and long term polish with half the finesse of Terraria, I don't see how it could be seen as not worth the asking price. Especially at some of the sale prices it hits, this is a game you can easily get lost in for many many hours... If you enjoy sandboxey roguelikes/ -lights, especially space/sci-fi ones, you have probably already given this a try. If not, I suggest doing so. If you have, but its been a year or two, this (just like Terraria) is one game that with all the work put in over the years, definitely deserves a fresh install/savegame to see whats new... I would rate it at least a 7/10 at this point, with it having been more like a 5 or so during its (at times quite frustrating) early development.

At first, this plays exactly like XCOM EU. The base is basicly the same, the missions / playstyle is... But hey, it's XCOM, so what do you expect.
When focusing on the differences: those I like. Psionics is not an end-game thing, randomly assigned to your soldiers but you can actually train them. Also the way you can / have to select missions, possibilities to upgrade weapons, base and stuff feel good. The Doom-timer of EU (which I didn't like) has changed (Procect A****R progress) and I like the way it introduces pressure. Especially because you can set back the timer often enough to not having to rush the game.  Also, this game is now mod-friendly, and the mod community is active and of good quality (at least, the mods I have tried).
Many people complain about the mission timers. Yes it's a tactical shooter, and no some timers are not that logical. But it adds a sense of urgency to it, and makes choices for using cooldown-timer abilities a bit harder. I personally don't think the timers are a problem, the game might sometimes be too easy without them.
And last but not least: the story. It continues the EU story and adds some extra. I like it.
No Cons?
Oh, yes there are... Next to RNG (it's never a good moment for things to go wrong, but hey a 90% chance is still a 1 in 10 fail...), there is performance. About half the time I have to re-start the game (sometimes multiple times) because it gets in an unplayable 1fps mode. After switching to other applications (eg. to check on what research you want to do) or screen lock, this happens as well. Quite irritating, but usually when you play the game and don't do anything else, it keeps on going just fine. I'd like this fix... maybe they did it in the WotC DLC, but I havent got that one yet.

Out of the several other fighting games that I have in my Steam Library, this has to be at the very least in my top 3, if not the best I've played so far.  Even though I'm complete garbage at fighting games in general, I found myself playing this game and being driven to enhance my skill, despite it being an old game.  The roster is quite large, with varying playstyles across the board, save for two characters that are semi-clones of the two main characters, but even then, they play drastically different from their original counterparts.  There are a handful of characters that can be picked up easily and can help develop skills and fundamentals for the characters that are more difficult to learn.  However, the game's difficulty in some of it's modes can be troublesome for new players, so if you're a completionist, remember to set it to a lower level lmao.  As for local play, I personally enjoy the Team Vs. Mode, it definitely has that King Of Fighters feel to it, playing out like a crew battle, where the winning character moves on to fight the next with some of their health restored if they took any damage, and there's always the classic One-on-One Vs. Mode.  The mechanics can be quite a task to understand for newer players too, but compared to the three different Roman Cancels in Xrd to the two in ACR, for newer players, even the one less tech to know definitely means an easier learning experience.  The speed at which the game plays is intense, and it's probably the only GG title in my library that I can run, since the only other GG game I own is Xrd, and my laptop isn't the best.  However, netplay can be tempermental at times, sometimes when I try to invite someone, or even the other way around, the guest of the room will randomly be kicked, so this might be a game that you'll most definitely want to play local multiplayer with.  Even with the netplay issues, most of the time it's not an issue, since most people don't go online.  But if you have a less than stellar setup, can find yourself a friend with a Steam-supported controller, or even an arcade stick, this game will kill time for you like no one's business.

Before the Xrd series came out, Guilty Gear as a fighting game franchise has gone through a long period of time as a traditional 2D fighting game, and it has built quite a reputation among the FGC community. Most GG fans can agree that the franchise peaked when the XX version came out in 2003 with an extreme commercial success, being the version that has defined the franchise for the years to come. For a long time, when you mention the name "Guilty Gear", most people are identified with the XX games that were released in the 2000s.
ArcSys has spent almost 10 years perfecting the X2 games, releasing #Reload and Accent Core, each title includes a plethora amount of expansions and spin offs. Their X2 run ends with this version, Accent Core Plus R.
It is safe to say, being the concluding version, this game has the most balanced and improved gameplay out of all the X2 versions. It is hard to be able to locate any flaws in this version. For me, the only thing that bothers me is that the stages that are unlocked by beating the Story Mode paths are not playble in the online games. And I miss the voicelines that were incorporated in the pervious X2 versions, which are removed in AC+R.
If anyone wants to experience Guilty Gear's finest, most balanced and most completed gameplay of the franchise, this is definitely the version you are looking for.

And making it a standalone expansion? Pointless. Splits the userbase, leaves people who didn't upgrade in the dust. Some will upgrade to still be able to play, and others will just leave, especially at this price point.
Good (but small) expansion, dumb pricing, dumb as a standalone. Don't buy at full price.

TITANS is, essentially, just DLC for the original Planetary Annihilation, posing as a standalone expansion. For a more accurate view of PA's reception please refer to its store page:
TITANS introduces new planets, some minor updates and a whole load of new units. However, the game is still plagued with poor enemy AI and poor pathfinding. My units are unable to work out the shortest route and sometimes simply get stuck. This is an issue that has persisted ever since the alpha, and still has not been completely tackled. While Uber has worked on these issues, they are still there.
I've also had some problems with placing buildings near walls, where the building's outline suggests the building fits and can be constructed, but my units refusing to do my bidding. Just like kids.
The biggest issue, for me, has always been the camera. Representing maps on a sphere introduces its own set of challenges, and while I don't think Uber, neccessarily, missed the ball here. I would've loved a feature where I could 'flatten' my planet, in order to create a flat 2D representation of it.
For new users, TITANS should definitely be the way to go, it represents the product - more or less - that EA and KS backers were expecting but never recieved. Luckily, KS backers can expect to receive TITANS at no additional costs. While EA backers who paid the same price as KS backers are shafted. However, anyone who owns PA before the announcement of TITANS does get a 66% discount. Regardless when you purchased PA.
For those that bought themselves into PA through KS and EA - steer clear. For those looking for a new RTS, get TITANS, as it offers the same and more content as PA.

I haven't even played through half of the game yet, I'm on 13 hours of gameplay so far yet I've already fallen in love with this game.
As an avid tales fan, I expected this to be like any other tales game. It wasn't.
The combat in this game is something I disliked at first, but found myself slowly enjoying it. Unlike Zestiria it's combat system is based on combinations of different buttons pressed instead of using the joystick+ square button.
There is a very large variety of artes (skills) that can be chosen from, and the great thing about them is... none of them go obsolete. You can stick with the moveset you have at the start of the game and it would still be able to carry you through, though you'd want different moves with different elements to target enemy weakness'. Combat is not a focal point of this game though- which brings me to my next point, something I felt could've been done better.
The game's soundtrack is lackluster. Though individually the ost is still an amazing piece of work, but it was one-upped by Zestiria which came before it. The soundtrack didn't have any epics that would make you feel extremely compelled to by the soundtrack, it more serves are background ambience during fights to not bore you. It's there, it serves it's purpose but it's just not THAT good where it deserves Zestiria praise.
Last and certainly the most prominent, the story.
(due to spoilers I'll try to keep this as vague but most informative as possible)
The story in this game is amazing. It made me feel heart-aches during the tutorial with it's quick twists, honestly from other tales games you would expect there to be a buildup from before everything went to hell- not in this one. The character's are all very well fleshed out, they have goals and motivations (all lovely people) with some cheesy dialogue to chuck in every now and then (but it's not too cheesy where it's unnatural) The story is blatantly darker than a majority of other tales games, but it's still able to keep a good sense of humor every now and then to lighten the mood.

I've been on steam for something like 13 years and I have only written a single review. I didn't even really like that game that much but I was testing the (at the time new) review system.
Tales of Berseria is amazing, I am totally captivated by this game. The best JRPG i've played since Final Fantasy 6. Incredible story, voice acting and writing. Out of a cast of hundreds, maybe one side character annoyed me. Characters are written with deep personalities and flaws. The story is unique and well told, scenes leave you feeling an impact and having to take in what happened. Sometimes even an unanimated conversation can get intense. Emotion vs. Reason is a BIG recurring theme in the story, which relates very much to the real world today. It never gets political though, which is such a huge credit to its writers. Things never go as you expect and moments can turn dark quickly.
The action combat system can be as simple or complex as you make of it. Multiple difficulties that can be changed anytime and loads of essential modern day conveniences without losing the J in JRPG. (Lets be honest, FF15 was more western RPG than Japanese.) Tons of items, tons of skills, attacks, combos, enemies and upgrades. Huge mostly open maps with some linear sections throughout, never feels like you are on rails even though you are generally only moving the direction the story takes you.
Cons? If I had to think of any. Some combat moves aren't explained very well. (Hint: You can chain Mystical Artes (LT) by using the direction pad up and down to switch in other characters, resulting in huge damage.) A few of the side scenes can get a little anime-cringey, but 99% of them hit the mark. Theres a bit too much item management due to loot dropping like candy and often a trip to the store can take 15 minutes figuring out what to dismantle or sell. A lot of items are just used to learn their skils and then are quickly discarded.

Free to Play here:
For a cheesy looking game, this has to be one of the most enjoyable games I have played.
Town of Salem is a clicking game that requires you to team up with innocents, mafia or by yourself to win as your role. Every person in the game gets a role every match, and you must use the role to your advantage in order to win as a team or depending on your role, by your self. This game sometimes gets me in the front of my chair focusing and thinking heavily on what to do or plan something out. In Town of Salem, luck, the skill of socialization and manipulation plays a big part in this game. Being a mafia requires you to murder everyone and make yourself look innocent, while being a innocent requires you to team with fellow innocent member while using your role to discover who is the mafia and gather information based on your role so you can win with your team.
Truly, I love this game so much for how simple yet complex it can be, but for how advanced you have to think mentally and play. You murder someone with one click, but you have to think before killing certain people. Should I murder someone because they have been framing me or should I not because I will look suspicious and his death note may potentially reveal information about me?
If you play this game already and love it, support the developers by buying this title. If you don't, try the game on the website, and see if you actually enjoy the game or not.

I wanted to like Blue Rose, but there are too many issues with the novel that hold it back from what could have been a great story.  While there is plenty of potential here, the unpolished writing, underdeveloped characters and lifeless world prevent the story from leaving any emotional impact on the reader. These deficiencies are then hidden beneath a somewhat polished veneer.
Our story begins with Lena, a Templar of the Blue Rose, escorting a diplomatic envoy when her party is attacked by a raging dragon.  Knocked unconscious in battle, she wakes to find herself under the care of a young hunter in an area of the forest that by all knowledge should be uninhabited.  Discovery of a secret village nestled in the mountains leads her to question all that she has known as war threatens the peace of this idyllic refuge.
Despite an intriguing setup, the story never goes anywhere interesting.  Dragons, magic, war and politics, all ideas ripe with creative storytelling, yet they linger impotently as our protagonist wanders from place to place with no direction.  By the time the villain is revealed and the story finally grabs hold, I had long lost interest in the world and its inhabitants.  Insufficient world building only adds to the problem.  Those little details that hint at something more, small ideas that create history and give depth, are either conspicuously absent or quickly brushed over so as to never allow them a chance to fully realize.  The resulting image is a rough sketch rather than a colorful portrait.
Well written characters can absolutely prop up a weak story and carry interest to the end, even if it's only to witness how their personal plot lines resolve.  Sadly, not one of Blue Rose's characters are interesting enough to carry the narrative.  Each of the guys (and girl) play to his respective trope, but never grow beyond that.  The story does nothing to challenge who these people are nor give them a means to develop; what you see is what you get. What we learn of their histories and motivations changes little of how I view them in the end.
And there's our heroine, Lena, a blindly devoted Templar of the Blue Rose whose only character flaw is an unquestioning dedication to her kingdom's cause.  Why this is viewed as a bad thing we'll never know, the only justification given is "war is bad." Perhaps if we were privy to the corruption that she was too blind to see, it might be understandable.  Beyond that, I question what makes her so appealing that everyone falls for her. Is it the fact that she's one of the few female Templars, or that she carries a sword and can fight?  It's certainly not her limitless empathy, overwhelming kindness or keen intellect, as she's never given an opportunity to sufficiently exhibit these traits let alone prove herself more than the dutiful soldier that she is.  Every romance, save possibly Simon, makes little sense given her disposition.
Compounding the character and plot issues is the unpolished writing style.  Wordiness.  The developer needs to look up the term, because I don't think he understands how exhausting it is to read through wordy writing.  When your reader stumbles over sentences because the word flow is encumbered by needless description, you have an issue with wordiness.  When you can cut out 90% of the instances of "just," "still," "really," "even," and practically all tenses of "to be", and the action still makes sense, you have a problem with wordiness.  This is all despite hiring an editor to clean up the script prior to hitting Steam.  I tried my hardest to drudge through the writing, and while it reads slightly better than before, it's still too much of a chore.  I am constantly correcting not only wordiness, but awkward sentence structure, conflicting verb tense, and the many glaring typos spread throughout.  All I want is to experience the story, but the words keep getting in the way.
That said, the remainder of the presentation is fairly polished.  Although the artwork isn't incredible, it's pleasant enough with some nicely drawn CGs and character sprites.  I also quite enjoyed the background images, especially the forested areas with their lonely, tranquil feel.  The orchestral soundtrack is a highlight which features enchanting themes that give off an air of fantasy and adventure.  But as much as Blue Rose looks and sounds pretty, it's not enough to make up for major problems in the writing.
I want to support indie developers, especially visual novel writers, because this is a genre that is sorely underappreciated, but I cannot in good conscience promote a game that has so many problems simply because I want to see a developer succeed.  It boggles my mind how many reviewers champion Blue Rose as one of the better OELVN's when these issues greatly hinder the potential it has.  If you absolutely must own it, wait for a sale or bundle, $20 is way too expensive for the quality of storytelling we are given.
Bottom Line: Not recommended.

If you haven't tried a visual novel, you may want to do some research, they're not like other games.
I've fallen down the rabbit hole of Otome visual novels: Dandelion, Nameless, Hakuoki, Re:Alister...
Blue Rose reminds me of Alister, but longer, a little more in-depth story and it is the fantasy story instead of being an online gamer going in and out. It has sweet scenes, but is set over 14 days, so be aware that only so much can happen, as opposed to the years of Hakuoki or months of Dandelion. The protagonist isn't that "easy" and I think they do a good job making her a capable, kick-butt fighter while still having her oblivious edge that lets an Otome game spin out the romantic fluff a little more.
There's no stat building, just the "choose your own adventure" options that open different dialogue and opportunities down the road.
I also haven't run into any of the off-the-wall sexual inuendo that can pop up in some of these games. (There's no Yuri-type to cause the random occurance of a mini-pony.) So would recommend it for younger girls.
There are quite a few CGs and the art is nice. Some repetition, but if you do a story an evening with some breaks between, I wasn't too annoyed at some of the repetition.
I've only gone through Tobias, Simon and Gavin and am looking forward to Aran next.
I think its worth the money, I've been playing for awhile and enjoying it. Not to mention Otome games are rare compared to most game categories and I'd really like to see more of them, our early support counts!
Enjoy!

What to know about this VN? I really enjoyed it when I originally bought it, and since replying it now on Steam enjoyed it just as much. It's purely story based so no stat building, which I liked. It doesn't try to trick you so you can usually aim for an ending and get it without use of a walkthrough.
The story is well developed and thought out. It focuses more on decisions and their consequences than solely on romance, which is something I loved about it. I appreciate when the overall story is just as important as whichever character you are pursuing. The romance is certainly there, but if you're looking for a lot of pure romantic scenes you're not going to find them here. There are very few CGs of even kisses. Ultimately it feels more realistic. There's a lot the characters have to deal with, both plot-wise and personal, and Lena only interacts with the characters over the course of two weeks. The relationships are slowly built but solid and feel real because of it.
They're all very well developed with their own personalities and opinions that they stick to. It's stated in the VN itself that everyone has their own reasons for being in the town, and there's certainly more to all of them than the impression you get when you first meet them. They grow over the course of the two weeks, especially Lena herself. Lena makes an excellent main character because she's strong but isn't overpowered. At times she still must rely on other characters, but other times she's completely capable of relying on herself.
It made me laugh. It made me go back and reread scenes. I'd certainly recommend it.

You want more XCOM, the screenshots and videos look good, but you're on the fence. You saw the negative reviews: time limits, random difficulty spikes, being rushed around. Sadly it's all true. In the first few hours XCOM2 tries to force its weird pace on you and if you want to win, you must reject its advances. You'll have to put on your big boy pants and make it clear that YOU are the commander, and that YOU will decide what missions to take and when. You will hit those "Ignore" buttons. You must do so, for the good of all humanity.
Bradford, the Mary Sue avatar of the game designer, will do his best to make everything sound extremely urgent. My favorite moment was when I took a mission because he said "we cannot afford to lose this opportunity" - then when the first XCOM agent died he went "we cannot afford to take losses like this, the mission objective is not worth it".
Oh yeah?
That's what I yelled at the screen when he forced me to take the mission, but who didn't listen?
Who didn't listen to the Commander, Bradman?
After that the game became amazing. I can't say the game is perfect, because nothing is, but this game comes as close to it as I could imagine. I remember seeing it during it's Kickstarter days and thinking how amazing it would be, but was worried the devs would be of the variety most Early Access projects come from. Make an incomplete game, stack the player's cash, and then go sit on a beach somewhere instead of improving their game. Not these guys though. They took the time to put a hold on another game mode addition to improve upon the existing content. They will not be charging for DLC, it will come as free content updates for all players. There will be no pay-to-win items purchaseable in-game. On top of all of this, they've remained dedicated to this project and it's players from the start.
As far as the gameplay goes, it is solid, smooth, and satisfying. I never thought I would enjoy watching an animation of a musket reloading, but this game accomplished that. The chaos creates a visceral atmosphere that quenches your virtual bloodlust. Firing a cannon shot that takes out half the enemy ship's crew, ramming a dying ship to finish it off, or grappling the enemy to board and execute in a first-person close quarters battle aboard the enemy ship. All the while members of your ship's crew will be expected to repair any damage sustained, and pump out any water you've taken on. You may even have to occassionally throw a few buckets of water on a fire that breaks out. It's non-stop, hectic, team-driven chaos... and it's amazing. You will find yourself amazed at the skill of some of the captains you encounter.
The community isn't great, but it's good. Most people you will come across during a match are helpful, attempt to complete the objectives of the game, and are generally easy going(Pirate banter is frequently a part of crew or faction chat). Then there are some, just as in any game, that are disruptive, immature, or generally unskilled in any capacity. They in no way diminish the overall value of this game however, so I cannot even list this as a con. The only thing about the current system I would like to see a change in is the inability to join a server, faction, or ship with friends. You pretty much have to time a simultaneous mass joining, and then hope there's enough slots on the same faction, and at least one of the ships, for you all to join. I would hope the dead horse beating about Early Access Alpha's not being a complete version of the game will allow most to excuse things like this. Either way, the hardest part of public games is finding a server with open slots... they stay full almost around the clock.
To sum up this lengthy review(I'm so sorry for those of you who made it here), this game is worth whatever price they charge for it. It's fun, exciting, and even competitive. I genuinely have not had this much fun on a game in a long time. Please show your support for it and join in on the fun. See you on the High Seas(or at the bottom of them)!

FPS games were one of the things that allowed me and my father to bond when I was a young child. Watching him play half-life 1 is one of the most vivid memories I have. We would get stuck in places back when walkthroughs weren't that popular and there was no youtube, and we would work it out together. I remember us being stuck on Blast Pit and then on Power Up for hours, I remember how frustrated we were when we lost all of our weapons in Residue Processing. Neither me or him spoke english very well, so it was a difficult learning curve - we weren't sure what we had to do, sometimes, and the characters speaking didn't help that much. I remember our fascination when we teleported to Xen and how excited we were to finally beat the boss. It was absolutely amazing, it was like magic. What a breakthrough HL was to that time.
My father passed away two years after the release of Half-Life 2-2. I know it's silly, but I feel like I can't get full closure on his death until I beat the entire story he (and I) started. I can't begin to say how mad I am at Valve for letting that franchise go. Reading the leaked script had me in tears thinking how much I wish I could discuss the story with him. Hell, I interrupted a date with my GF so I could read it. She was mad at me for at least a day. I don't give a shet. No one understands how much the story means to us, people who played the entire franchise right after each game was released, when they looked so amazing, fresh and new. Even nowadays a very small amount of games has told a story so rich and unique. And for that, I hate Valve with all of my forces for letting Laidlaw and Faliszek leave; for letting gold digger games like Dota 2 and CS:GO rise and take control over their company; for selling their souls so deep that they can't even spend a small fraction of their fortune on a small game that could bring so much joy to their loyal and fanatic fanbase.
I swear to God, I'm angrier at Valve for killing HL3 than I am at Roose Bolton for killing Robb Stark. The North remembers, Valve. We all freaking remember.

Planetary Annihilation: TITANS is an "expansion" that changes the original PA for the better. New maps, units, experimentals and game options provide an all around better experience. There have been alot of performance improvements which are a nice addition as well. While there are a ton of little features added, I will highlight the major improvements.
UNIT ROSTER: The variety of units has increased significantly. Having been familiar with all the different unit icons from PA, I can no longer recognize the unit composition that people construct. The variation of units have their own particular play style. Many of the strategies that were in PA are now easily countered by these new units too. This is good because it encourages new strategies from the previous  BOLO, DOX, GREN showdown.
ORBITAL: The Orbital gameplay has been improved greatly. The variety of orbital units and change in how the jigs work has allowed for the orbital to be a legitimate threat in games now. Prior to Titans, the decision to invest in the gas planet was dependent on who could claim it the quickest. This rapidly gave one player the advantage economically over another in a short period of time. Gas giants now, with the additions and alterations, can now be more easily defended. As  a result, gas giants can now be a secure form of economy for individuals that wish to invest into it.
INVASION: Invading planets has gotten easier. One of the titans is an orbital platform. The best way to describe it is If an anchor and a teleporter had a child and it could move. Very effective. Planets can still be defended, but players better be prepared for this ridiculous specimen.
SCALE: Tier 2 units and the titans will require the player to consider advancing into stronger tech. Players will be rewarded for investing in the new tech unlike before. If PA was heavily favoring quantity> quality, PA:Titans restores it back to the middle.
MAPS: The maps have more elevation to them now. Some may complain that the terrain is more "platform based" and it takes away from the actual planet view. While I do agree on this observation, I think its nice to have the option. With all these platforms, suddenly their is a higher ground that provides a greater strategic advantage.
Having only played 2 hours of this, I can say that this summary is pretty valid. Again, PA:Titans is essentially an "expansion" to PA and many of the quirks and style is transferred over to this game. The difference now is that PA: Titans doesnt feels half baked compared to its predecessor.
If you had PA and liked it, buy this.
If you had PA and thought it lacked variety, buy this.
If you had PA and didnt like the pace/ gameplay, be cautious on purchasing this.

Tales of Berseria is amazing, I am totally captivated by this game. The best JRPG i've played since Final Fantasy 6. Incredible story, voice acting and writing. Out of a cast of hundreds, maybe one side character annoyed me. Characters are written with deep personalities and flaws. The story is unique and well told, scenes leave you feeling an impact and having to take in what happened. Sometimes even an unanimated conversation can get intense. Emotion vs. Reason is a BIG recurring theme in the story, which relates very much to the real world today. It never gets political though, which is such a huge credit to its writers. Things never go as you expect and moments can turn dark quickly.
The action combat system can be as simple or complex as you make of it. Multiple difficulties that can be changed anytime and loads of essential modern day conveniences without losing the J in JRPG. (Lets be honest, FF15 was more western RPG than Japanese.) Tons of items, tons of skills, attacks, combos, enemies and upgrades. Huge mostly open maps with some linear sections throughout, never feels like you are on rails even though you are generally only moving the direction the story takes you.
Cons? If I had to think of any. Some combat moves aren't explained very well. (Hint: You can chain Mystical Artes (LT) by using the direction pad up and down to switch in other characters, resulting in huge damage.) A few of the side scenes can get a little anime-cringey, but 99% of them hit the mark. Theres a bit too much item management due to loot dropping like candy and often a trip to the store can take 15 minutes figuring out what to dismantle or sell. A lot of items are just used to learn their skils and then are quickly discarded.

Ever since I received a beta invite, I sort of disliked how different Street Fighter V was to the other games before it, but I never thought it was a terribly bad decision overall.
Now that the full game has been released, I've found all the worries I had were addressed over the beta periods.
Soon after realising the game was a blast to play compared to the previous Ultra Street Fighter IV, I quickly fell for Street Fighter V's renewed focus on fundamental skills and measured play.
I'd go as far as to say that this may turn out to be the best Street Fighter for both casuals and veterans alike.
There are no universal safety nets like Street Fighter IV's focus attack. Instead, each character has unique methods for dealing with threats, resulting in varied and tense fights. In the hands of a casual player Street Fighter V's new mechanics are satisfying with low execution demands.
At tournament levels, however, they're technical and strategic tools that demand a great degree of understanding and mastery. I can already tell that Street Fighter V is making me think about the fights and type matchups, while being less reliant on easy counters.
Crucially, I don't feel like I've had enough experience playing online. With a small player base and both the beta and launch servers in flux, it's too early to properly judge the net code and, as a result, deliver a solid verdict.
When I have been able to fight online, my connection has been very sporadic with the majority of my matches ending in a disconnect half way through the match, but not all of my online battles had this problem occur.
Street Fighter V has so little single-player content at launch that the efficacy of its online components is paramount.
The lack of extra-curricular activities is a huge problem, especially for casual Street Fighter players.
The "Challenge Mode" activities intended to help you build skill and earn in-game cash was not ready for launch.
There is a short story campaign for each character, and by "short," I mean that they last anywhere from two to five minutes, spanning two to four fights from beginning to end.
In the case of Fang, one of the four newcomers on the roster, he has only two fights against one opponent (M. Bison), and that's it.
Every battle in story mode is also incredibly easy; you can win by simply spamming projectiles.
You may have heard that Bengus, the artist responsible for some of Capcom's most iconic artwork, has created visuals for the character stories, but don't get too excited: the quality of work here is a far cry from the beautifully rendered art he produced in the '90s and early '2000's...
The storyboard-like images here are inconsistent in quality, with noticeable disparities in detail from one to the next.
While it's disappointing, the cut scene audio that accompanies the badly drawn artwork is phenomenal. Each actor gives a great performance for each character.
The upside to finishing the character story mode is that it nets you 100,000 Fight Money, but only once. Based on Capcom's plans for the near future, that sum is just the right amount to purchase a new character.
You also unlock a new costume in story mode, but you unlock it for purchase from the in-game shop, not for immediate use. I expect this sort of thing from free to play titles like Tekken Revolution for PS3, but not from a full release fighting game.
The fact that the game ties every significant unlockable to one form of currency or another is frustrating, but you can't put your earnings to use yet because the in-game store isn't ready.
Furthermore, the valuation of Fight Money, relative to what it takes to acquire it, is weird.
A hard fought victory online nets 50 Fight Money, which seems like peanuts when compared to the 100,000 fight money received from the crudely drawn story sequences.
Otherwise, you're left with Survival mode; and that's it. It's serviceable, offering four tiers of consecutive fights where you can unlock new colours for each character's default costume, but by allowing you to trade in points earned during rounds for health and power boosts, survival turns into an easy snooze fest...
Street Fighter V is a clean slate, for better and for worse. It's got new and returning mechanics, characters, move sets, and peculiarities that change the flow of combat in exciting ways, but it doesn't have much to entertain anyone who isn't a competitor.
Despite its mainstream appeal, Street Fighter is known for having esoteric systems beneath the surface that most people miss. That is as true as ever with Street Fighter V.
It means there is depth to explore for those who want it. With the right tutorials and activities at their disposal, new players should be able to understand these over time, but I'm not certain when these tools will arrive or what they will offer.
When I'm playing Street Fighter V with friends, I'm completely lost in the heat of the moment. Win or lose, I'm attracted to the thrill of its action-oriented combat system, which discourages overcautious behaviour and keeps fights moving along. There's an excellent foundation here, and for now, I am going to keep playing until I've got a more structured opinion on this game.
For now, this review is only based on my beta participation and the 3 or so hours I've spent in the full release.
When the time comes, I'll update the review with a more fleshed out review.
