So, obviously with the release of 1.0 I'm going to be re-writing my review along with everyone else. Enjoy! Or don't. You have free will.
With the release of 1.0, as you can read with almost every other review, there's lots of ups and down with the update, and I'm not gonna lie, it's suffered a bit. I still, however, find it an incredibly fun game with less and more than was in the early access game.
Pros
- More, better looking cosmetic items
- No longer needing to follow the main storyline to progress to different planets.
- A coherent storyline as opposed to the various odd jobs you'd do around the outpost
- More blocks that were previously unobtainable/obtainable through destroying them are now craftable
- Crew members
- Steam Worshop
- Achievements! (If you're into that)
- Survival mode (As a roleplayer, I love this!)
- Fleshed out objects, art, items, etc.
- Bugs are fixed pretty fast
- Exploration is still really fun
Cons
- Story is rather cliche, not very imaginative
- Novakids are pretty much just "there". No villages, no missions, no furniture, only some rare colonists if you build your own colony
- Ocean worlds are still a ♥♥♥♥♥ to explore
- Vehicles are pretty much useless, save for the hoverbike when it comes to underwater exploration, though the strobe light it has is annoying
- Progression to the next main storyline mission is incredibly annoying and arduous
- Racial weapons are no longer a thing, for some reason
- Getting furniture is a pain, as most racial furniture can only be found in villages and not bought
- FPS issues
- Shared universes (meaning progress you make on one character is shared with another)
- Bosses are either no challange at all or ridiculously hard (Looking at you, Big Ape)
tl;dr Great game if you're looking for a game to just wander around in, not so much if you're looking for a story heavy game.

Town of Salem is a game based on "Werewolves". "Werewolves" is a party game, however this works a bit different.
The Werewolves team is replaced by the Mafia (although a Werewolf role still exists in game). The Mafia's goal is to eliminate the Town, while he Town tries to get rid of the Mafia. Typically, some people in Werewolves do not get a role at all, or get a role that ties them with another player but has no special significance to the non-werewolves. Town of Salem takes this a step futher by giving everyone a role, and everyone plays a part in the survival of the town, not just a select few. There are even some Townies (that's what we call people sided with the town) that are able to KILL at night, making them a more crucial role because they can eliminate key Mafia members.
The game mainly revolves around the gallows in the center of town. During the day, the players have a short period of time with which to discuss evidence and things they may have found out. Then, they put someone up on the stand and they have to testify. Occassionally, they are able to prove themselves innocent and get off, but more often then not, they are killed. This is one of the only ways Townspeople can get someone evil out, so be careful.
Even if you do die, don't leave! You are an integral part of the Medium's role, and can also speak with other dead players. This means you can speculate on the town's performance through the rest of the game, and cheer them on too.
Some people do not like to be Mafia or Town, and this is where the game is spiced up a bit, with the introduction of neutral roles. Some can kill (a Serial Killer or the before-mentioned Werewolf), some can try to decive the town (the Jester or Executioner), or some can choose their side (Amnesiac or Survivor).
Even if you don't want to chuck in the 5$, make sure to check out
, because the game can still be played for free there. However, I suggest you do pitch in the 5$ for the Steam client, because it's faster and without ads. Also, not only do you get 5$ worth of Town Points (1300 of the in-game currency), you also support the awesome developers that made this game. The game can get so intense that almost no two games are ever the same, providing a fresh experience everytime you join.
TL;DR version
-Modified game of the party game Werewolves
-Everyone gets a role
-Everyone is an integral part of it
-Get rid of the evil roles
-Get sides
-PITCH IN YOUR MONEY because it helps!
-A fresh experience each time
Get the game!

While I
recommend this game, I cannot recommend it to anyone who
A) does not already play fighting games
or
B) is not prepared to spend a bunch of hours learning why GGXX (and beyond) is one of the best fighters ever!
Why?
Because it offers more freedom of choice than other fighters.
How?
For instance, in most fighting games, you're (rightfully) quite screwed if you do a bad jump. In Guilty Gear you don't stop thinking at the jump. Will the jumping character attack, air-block (or air-instant block, a sort of semi-parry) any ground normals, spend meter for blocking anti-air specials, double-jump, air-dash forward/backwards? (Not counting character specific stuff as triple jumping etc.)
The character (mechanics) design is quite extreme too, since almost every character has one or more exception from the standard game mechanics, like: triple jump, double air dash, parry, delayed wakeup on sweep, not being able to dash, being able to level up specials and supers, having a heat gauge that allows for more damaging normals but also running the risk of over-heating unless venting steam (yeah, really) and more...
Of course, my recommendation is quite biased:
I was a casual arcade game scrub since the start of the 1990s and took a liking for 2D fighting games. When I came across the console version of Guilty Gear XX #R and more importantly, people who played it seriously, GG almost became more than a game to me.
I played the game with my friends for hours on a daily basis. I went to tournaments, domestic as well as abroad. This was before there were any real prize money to speak of, meaning that VERY few (if anyone) would actually have their expenses covered. Still, I have zero regret for the time and money I have spent playing this game!

Tales of Berseria is a great game.
It is not a perfect game, but it is a great game.
It's strongest aspect is the story.
You play as Velvet Crowe, a woman on a mission of revenge after a betrayal most foul.  (Which already is a plus considering this is the first Tales game in roughly 25 years to feature a solo female protagonist. And an anti-hero no less.)
Though, I say that with a bit of an asterisk, as usually, it's not the story itself that's the good part; it's the characters who inhabit that story that makes it worthwhile. Our primary cast of six work well together and their interactions are a joy to watch, between our anti-hero Velvet, Cursed Tough Guy Pirate Eizen, Deteremined and Empathetic Rokurou Rangetsu, Stiff and Earnest Eleanor Hume, Cinnamon Roll Laphicet, and Goof Off Witch *Deep breath* Mazhigigika Miludin do Din Nolurun Dou(Or Magilou for short), there is both gravity and humor in all their interactions, which is my personal favorite.
The combat system, while it has a bit of a learning curve, becomes very satisfying when the concepts behind it finally solidify. And this is someone who has just played Velvet most of the time.  The other characters have their own combat system that works fine in the game as a whole.
The music is appropriate for what it seeks to accomplish.
The voice acting, especially the english voice cast, led by Cristina V (more well known as Riven from League of Legends) as Velvet Crowe, is spectacular. In fact, I would rate the english cast's performance higher than the Japanese cast's due to the very noticable variety of how distinct each individual sounds.
And as a personal note, Erica Lindbeck deserves extra special props for voicing the hilarious and multilayered Magilou. She goes full ham and doesn't hold back with how silly, and poingiant, she can be and it works.
But like I said, it's not a perfect game and I will hide what really hurt my opinion of this game in a spoiler tag.
Tales of Berseria would have been my 2017 Game of the Year were it not for one thing.

So, despite all this, it's still a solid game with the positive outnumbering the negative.  I recommend it with reservations.

So after about 70 hours i finished the story of Tales of Berseria. I did not download any item packs and played on normal difficulty. I´ll just jump right into the review.
It fullfills its purpose. It is not espeacially good or bad. The characters are well designed and the animated scenes are beautiful. But tbh, i don´t really care about the graphic quality in this game.
First of all the soundtrack is amazing. No other than Motoi Sakuraba composed the soundtrack. It really has a big role in the atmosphere of the game. This is what i call art. Every scene is accompanied by a track, that fits perfectly. Joy, happiness or sadness, even the funny parts feel authentic.
Now the dub. Everything in this game is dubbed. The dubbing actors did an amazingly good job. I have no reason to play the Newgame+ with japanese dub. The english dub is by far better than expected and i´ll stick to that.
BUT this game has a bug. Many people cannot hear certain sounds when using 5.1 surround sound. In this case you also cannot hear the dub. Using the stereo mode fixes this problem, but can cause other sound issues. I recommend using a fix for that (just google it and you will find it).
The battle system is in realtime and pretty good, but not well explained. You have to figure out some stuff on your own. Tbh, i liked figuring stuff out, but i can see people being annoyed, because certain actions/skills don´t work they way they expected it. The items and ability system is easy to understand and the game is beatable without focussing too much on optimization. If you want to master every equipment or make very effective combos in battles it becomes a little bit more complex.
Outside from fights in dungeons you have to walk a bit until you unlock certain teleportation points. Outside from dungeons there is a quick travel system that is bound to a consumeable item. Since you should have absolutely no money problems, it is no problem to buy nearly endless of this stuff.
At a certain point ingame i nearly stopped caring about anything that has to do with gameplay, because the story gets such a strong peak, you could have given me 2d jump´n´run gameplay and i would have enjoyed this game.
Now some of the more important parts. The atmosphere in this game is convincing. I felt like i was part of the world ingame. This is achieved by the amazing soundtrack and also by many other little things. For example small conversations between characters (which are also dubbed) or even some background noises.
The characters all have their motivations to do whatever they do and no one feels out of place. There are many scenes where i thought: "Oh god no, why did you say that?" The first time was the point where my mindset changed. These characters HAVE a personality. Each of them. And the game is not afraid of showing this.
The characters develop while progressing in game. Everything happens for a reason. To fully understand what happened with some characters i had to rewatch scenes or let whatever happened rewind in my head. I paused the game many times, just being stunned, waiting for my brain to comprehend the situation.

"Get in my way and I'll eat you!" Not a whole lot of main characters that can say that and still be seen as the good guy. This is one of the best stories I've seen in a long time for RPGs in general.
I was hesitant at first to buy this, but resolved to do so at full price simply out of love of design of the main character. Everything else has been a bonus on top of that and to no small extent. Tales of... games have been lacking after the high bar set by Tales of Symphonia and the world of RPGs in general has been in little better shape. Berseria brings to the table, perhaps, the most intricate revenge plot I've ever seen which in turn ends up making the game one of the most unique I've ever played. I dare say this may be my favorite story so far, even above Symphonia, it's a hard decision.
I would note that I see one major issue with the game thus far and that is the start of all stories beside the primary plot. All characters beside the Velvet seem rather rushed into the party for reasons of little more consequence than everyone happening to be at a bar at the start of a DnD campaign. That said, the quality of the characters in both unique attributes and the standard of voice acting is just about enough to forgive this flaw. All lines as minor as a phrase in battle to the interactions they have together feels right and having nobody out of place. Even as the minor tales and plot points progress they largely seem to come to life instead of staying dead and falling flat.
Combat hails back to Zesteria, which has its ups and downs for certain, but has improved on many of the issues. The combat has also sped up considerably with the introduction of break souls. The entire thing feels rather quick paced overall and actually far more fluid than any iteration Tales has had so far. Enemies generally seem to respond appropriately to when your defenses are down and (aside from running into AOE abilities) even the character AI that helps you seems mostly competent. With the pace and attention paid to attack and defence it has actually had more of a flow reflecting real life combat.
This itself may be seen as a flaw because, much like real fights, many matchups are decidedly one sided and are really over before they've ever started. This does have an effect, on the other hand, of making potential level grind more tolorable.
I love fast combat, especially in a fictional scenario, so this has been right up my alley, but I can certainly see where it could be a turn off. It's not quite hack and slash, but it's close. Probably more comparable to the .hack//GU series of games.
Graphics are pretty low on my list of priority and, honestly, Berseria's not quite my taste, but something about it feels right for what it is. While past games have been rather...fluffy...for lack of a better term, Berseria uses a fairly crisp stylization; Characters and things pop instead of blend into the background. On the whole the world seems more alive for it, though it has also brought to my attention just how many textures are obviously copied and pasted everywhere. If I actually think on it, Tales games have been doing this for a long time and it's actually not surprising, but the clean cut of Berseria's style highlights it to me.
I have since finished the game and hold to my original thought that this is still the only linear story RPG that I look forward to playing through again in its entirety. I had actually put off finishing for a while because frankly I didn't want it to end (some part of me is yelling at the other part for finishing because now I know it's over). This has been my favorite gaming experience in years and, much like a good story in a book, it hurts to have actually finished it.

I'm generally a "Tales Of" fan, although not as much as I am for many other series.  In the past, I mostly enjoyed the games for their unique style of combat, a fluid action-based combat with more traditional RPG elements for exploration.  I also enjoyed the particular mythology used, the emotional turmoil common to many of the games and the efforts to get you invested in, if not all the characters, then at least the main ones.
This has not changed.
What I didn't like about the series was the lack of escalation, where outside of a few moments the game felt meandering and lacking tension.  In addition, the dialogue (or, in the very least, the localization) was always mediocre, always stilted and strange, with inter-party interactions coming across unnatural or forced.  But most of all, I disliked the lack of fallibility in the main characters; despite the efforts to get you invested in the characters, they felt impossible to understand.  They wrote in flaws but not fallibility; they questioned what happened but never what they were doing or why they were doing it.  This went for both the good guys and the bad guys; no one made any hard decisions.
This has changed.  Dramatically.
Vesperia made strides in making the characters more fallible, but only in the secondary characters; still, even that was a big deal, and a huge departure.  Berseria makes not just the characters themselves question why they are doing what they're doing, but they make you question it too.  The characters as they're introduced all have, at best, questionable motives.  The story takes a dark path at multiple points, and you're left wondering if you're rooting for the right person the entire time.
In addition, the dialogue feels a lot more flowing.  The characters seem to have much more natural conversations, with tough judgments and a more natural resistance to certain things, like personal questions (and a more natural progress of overcoming it).  The characters don't simply flock to and accept you like you're some magical shepherd (yes, that's a poke at Vesperia but also at Mass Effect), but instead bond to you for their own reasons, whether it's a twisted sense of honor or simply sharing a common goal for a while.
Finally, there's the pacing.  In a lot of these games (as in JRPGs but also specifically in the Tales Of series), especially in the first few hours, I feel the need to meander and explore in order to get a feel for the game (and front load XP, of course).  In many games, in order to mitigate this, they instead railroad you, limiting the space for exploration or making things like backtracking overly complicated.  Instead, this one just heaped on the drama.  I wanted to pursue the plot instead of exploring too much because I really wanted to know what happened next.  Battles and exploration actually *felt* tertiary to pursuing the main point of the game and learning more about the characters.  I wanted to know how that character managed to keep his desire for honor when betrayed by his family, or why this character can no longer taste but still eats food (even more entertaining when you realize there's a cooking mechanic!).  And if moving forward is the way to do that, then maybe that zone off to the left of the objective can wait until after.
The major weakness of this game is how many things go unexplained.  Without context, some of the major plot points, like the Malak or daemonification, can just feel off-putting and weird instead of curious.  If you're familiar with previous games in the series, especially Vesperia, it makes a lot of sense and generally doesn't need to be explained.  However, as the game is a standalone one and not really lauded even as a spiritual sequel, it can be hard to keep up with some of the lore as you go through the story.
It's been a long while since a game has actively made me crave for more, especially after the first two hours, regardless of genre.  It's an internal fight for me to not cancel all my plans and just play this game. From my review for the first two games:
(1st Game) - When I first saw this series, I didn't expect much, if anything from it to be perfectly honest. It looked like an iPad app targeting children, but as the levels advance and different map layouts are employed, there is a suprising amount of depth for such a casual game. I think it'd be impossible to "lose" while playing this, but getting a gold time on all levels took some thinking. If you're looking for a different type of game, give this one a shot. For the price, it was well worth it, plus easy achievements and trading cards!
(Second Game's review) - To add to this, the second game is more of the same, though there are some additional mechanics and the gameplay feels a bit tighter. Still not challenging, but you can hit some lulls if you aren't efficient and that in turn makes your play better since it's easy to see where you made a mistake.
If you liked the first one and can get it cheap, it's a good time waster and drives you to want to play one more level...and another...and another...
-----
Now as for #3, I'm going to have to give this one a negative.  It seems like more of the same, but just crammed with even more stuff.  Instead of novel mechanics or varying powerups, this one is a slog with many objectives just requiring grinding of a material to dig through.  Even the extra objective of clicking the birds that fly over a map add to the feeling of congestion to help kill time instead of making a satisfying objective.
It's a great Yuri VN, wish there are more of this series.
